## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Durgāprasāda and Kāśīnātha Pāṇḍuraṅga Paraba (eds.), Darpadalana of Kṣemendra, in Kāvyamālā, Part VI (Gucchaka 6), Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgara Press, 1890, pp. 66–118.

**E-text:** Members of the Rasāla team for GRETIL

**Evidence:**
- Explicitly stated in the GRETIL text header: 'Based on the ed. by Durgaparasad and Kashinath Pandurang Parab, Bombay 1890, Kâvyamâlâ : a Collection of Old and Rare Sanskrit Kâvyas ... [= 'collective' Kavyamala series], Part VI, pp. 66-118. Input by members of the Rasala team.'
- Confirmed in the GRETIL TEI header (sa_kSemendra-darpadalana.xml).

**Other editions:**
- B. A. Hirszbant (ed.), Über Kṣemendra's Darpadalana, St. Petersburg: Buchdruckerei der Kaiserlichen Akademie der Wissenschaften, 1892. — Early critical study and partial edition with German translation.
- E. V. V. Raghavacharya and D. G. Padhye (eds.), Minor Works of Kṣemendra, Hyderabad: The Sanskrit Academy, Osmania University (Sanskrit Academy Series No. 7), 1961, pp. 145–206. — Critical edition based on printed editions and manuscript collations included in the collected minor works.
- Brahma Mitra Awasthi and Sushama Arora (eds.), Hindī Darpadalana: Kṣemendra-kṛta Darpadalana kā adhyayana evaṃ Hindī anuvāda, Delhi: Indu Prakāśana, 1972. — Edition with critical study and Hindi translation.

**Translations:**
- Richard Schmidt, 'Kṣemendra's Darpadalana (Dunkelsprengung)', Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft (ZDMG) 69 (1915), pp. 1–51. (German)
- Brahma Mitra Awasthi and Sushama Arora, Hindī Darpadalana: Kṣemendra-kṛta Darpadalana kā adhyayana evaṃ Hindī anuvāda, Delhi: Indu Prakāśana, 1972. (Hindi)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in seven sections (vicāras), running from KDarp_1.1 to KDarp_7.73 (587 verses in total).

**Attribution:** Authored by the Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra (active mid-11th century CE). Kṣemendra explicitly names himself in the opening stanza (1.3).

The Darpadalana ('Crushing of Pride') is a seven-chapter satirical and didactic poem (upadeśakāvya) composed in 11th-century Kashmir by Kṣemendra. Each chapter (vicāra) targets one of seven traditional causes of conceit (madahetavaḥ)—noble birth (kula), wealth (vitta), erudition (śruta), physical beauty (rūpa), valor (śaurya), munificence (dāna), and asceticism (tapas)—demonstrating through general moral reflections and illustrative narratives (dṛṣṭānta) how excessive vanity leads to downfall and ridicule. The text exemplifies Kṣemendra's characteristic witty satire, psychological insight, and sharp critique of contemporary Kashmiri manners.

## GRETIL header

**Edition:** Durgaparasad and Kashinath Pandurang Parab, Bombay 1890, Kâvyamâlâ : a Collection of Old and Rare Sanskrit Kâvyas ... [= 'collective' Kavyamala series], Part VI, pp. 66-118.

**Entered by:** members of the Rasala team

**95% credible interval:** 875 CE – 1104 CE

**Posterior median:** 991 CE

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: 22 sargas, ending with Bhaṭṭi's closing verses 22.33–35 (composed at Valabhī under Śrīdharasena). Root text only.

**Also known as:** Bhaṭṭikāvya, Rāmacarita, Rāmakāvya

**Attribution:** Universally attributed to the poet and grammarian Bhaṭṭi. The poem's concluding verse (22.35) records that it was composed in Valabhī during the reign of King Śrīdharasena (Maitraka dynasty, late 6th to mid-7th c. CE). Later traditions sometimes conflated Bhaṭṭi with Bhartṛhari or Vatsabhaṭṭi, but modern scholarship considers Bhaṭṭi a distinct author.

The Rāvaṇavadha ('Slaying of Rāvaṇa', widely known as Bhaṭṭikāvya) is a 22-canto classical mahākāvya composed by Bhaṭṭi at Valabhī during the late 6th or 7th century CE. It narrates the story of the Rāmāyaṇa from Rāma's birth to his defeat of Rāvaṇa and coronation, serving simultaneously as the foundational masterpiece of the śāstrakāvya (grammatical court-epic) genre by illustrating Pāṇinian morphology, syntax (kārakas), verbal conjugation, and poetic figures (alaṃkāras). Explicitly composed for learned readers and students of grammar, the poem attained great pedagogical renown in India and exerted a decisive influence across Southeast Asia, serving as the primary textual prototype for the Old Javanese Kakawin Rāmāyaṇa.

**Coverage:** unclear — Empty placeholder stub; the catalog entry contains 0 segments and 0 characters. The complete work consists of six chapters (paricchedas): jaḍadravya (or triguṇadravya), jīva, īśvara, nityavibhūti, buddhi, and adravya.

**Also known as:** Tarkasiddhāñjana

**Attribution:** Universally and undisputed attribution to the Śrīvaiṣṇava polymath and Viśiṣṭādvaita teacher Vedānta Deśika (Veṅkaṭanātha, c. 1269–1370 CE).

The Nyāyasiddhāñjana ('Collyrium of Nyāya Logic / Conclusions') is a foundational ontological prakaraṇa of the Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta tradition composed by Vedānta Deśika (c. 1269–1370). Functioning as the ontological counterpart to his epistemological treatise Nyāyapariśuddhi, the work classifies and analyzes knowable reality (prameya) across six chapters (paricchedas): material substance (triguṇadravya/jaḍadravya), individual souls (jīva), God (īśvara), transcendental eternal realm (nityavibhūti), consciousness/cognition (buddhi/dharmabhūtajñāna), and non-substance/attributes (adravya). It adapts and reforms Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika dialectic within Rāmānuja's metaphysics and is historically indispensable for citing and preserving substantial fragments of lost early Viśiṣṭādvaita texts, particularly Nāthamuni's Nyāyatattva.

**Coverage:** unclear — Empty record (0 segment files, 0 segments, 0 characters); placeholder for the work. The Bhagavadgītā text with four commentaries is catalogued chapter by chapter as SA_GE07_bhg4c01u–SA_GE07_bhg4c18u (GRETIL bhg4c01u–bhg4c18u.htm).

**Also known as:** Gītā, Śrīmadbhagavadgītā, Bhagavadgītopaniṣad, Mahābhārata: Bhīṣmaparvan adhyāyas 23–40

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as part of the Mahābhārata (Bhīṣmaparvan). Modern scholarship treats it as an epic didactic interpolation composed between c. 2nd century BCE and 2nd century CE.

The Bhagavadgītā ('Song of the Lord') is an eighteen-chapter philosophical dialogue embedded within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata (adhyāyas 23–40 in the critical edition). Set on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra on the brink of fratricidal war, the warrior Arjuna is overcome by moral despondency and is instructed by his charioteer Kṛṣṇa, revealed as the supreme deity. The text articulates a seminal synthesis of disciplined action without attachment to fruits (karma-yoga), metaphysical discernment (jñāna-yoga), and devotion (bhakti-yoga), culminating in the cosmic revelation of Kṛṣṇa's Viśvarūpa. As one of the three foundational authorities (prasthānatrayī) of Vedānta, it has generated continuous commentary across Indian philosophical schools and remains central to Hindu religious thought.

**Also known as:** Harivaṃśapurāṇa, Harivaṃśaparvan, Mahābhārata-khilabhāga

**Attribution:** Traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as the khila ('supplement') to the Mahābhārata. Author field left empty in accordance with cataloguing conventions for epic and puranic literature.

Appendix I of the Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute (BORI) Critical Edition of the Harivaṃśa, the supplementary epic (khila) to the Mahābhārata detailing the genealogy, incarnations, and deeds of Kṛṣṇa. During critical editing by P. L. Vaidya, 45 extended narrative and liturgical passages found only in specific regional recensions—including substantial episodes like the Pārijātaharaṇa, battle sequences, and devotional stotras—were excluded from the critically reconstructed archetype and collected in Appendix I. These materials are essential witnesses to the regional expansion and sectarian development of Kṛṣṇa-centered literature across the first and early second millennia CE.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as the khila (nineteenth book or supplement) to the Mahābhārata.

The Harivaṃśa ('Genealogy of Hari') is the canonical supplement (khila) to the Mahābhārata, bridging late epic narrative with the early Purāṇas. Divided into three sections—Harivaṃśaparvan (cosmology and ancestral genealogies of the Solar and Lunar dynasties), Viṣṇuparvan (the earliest continuous biography of Kṛṣṇa, covering his pastoral youth in Vraja/Gokula and subsequent heroic feats), and Bhaviṣyaparvan (eschatology of the Kaliyuga, cosmogony, and devotional hymns)—it serves as the foundational narrative source for Kṛṣṇa's pastoral childhood (bālalīlā) across classical Vaiṣṇavism.

The Rāmāyaṇa, attributed to the sage Vālmīki and revered as the ādikāvya ('first ornate poem') of classical Sanskrit literature, is one of the two foundational epics (itihāsa) of ancient India. Composed across seven books (kāṇḍas) largely in anuṣṭubh verse, it recounts the virtuous life, forest exile, and struggles of Rāma, prince of Ayodhyā, whose quest to recover his abducted wife Sītā culminates in the defeat of the rākṣasa king Rāvaṇa. Linguistic and text-historical analysis indicates that the core narrative (books 2–6) took shape between roughly the 5th and 2nd centuries BCE, whereas books 1 (Bālakāṇḍa) and 7 (Uttarakāṇḍa), which incorporate an overarching theological framework depicting Rāma as an avatāra of Viṣṇu, were added by the 2nd to 3rd centuries CE.

Following Daśaratha's plan to crown Rāma as yuvarāja, Queen Kaikeyī, goaded by Mantharā, demands two boons: the exile of Rāma to the forest for fourteen years and the installation of Bharata as king. Rāma unhesitatingly departs with Sītā and Lakṣmaṇa, which precipitates Daśaratha's demise from grief; Bharata adamantly refuses the throne, follows Rāma to Citrakūṭa to plead for his return, and ultimately agrees to govern from Nandigrāma as regent for Rāma's wooden sandals (pādukā).

The Kāvyādarśa ('Mirror of Poetry') by Daṇḍin (c. late 7th–8th century CE) is among the foundational classical treatises on Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra). Comprising three chapters (paricchedas), it establishes a typology of poetic composition and outlines the ten poetic excellences (guṇas) distinguishing the refined Vaidarbha and ornate Gauḍa styles (chapter 1), classifies thirty-five figures of sense (arthālaṅkāra, chapter 2), and treats figures of sound (śabdālaṅkāra), verbal puzzles (prahelikā), pictorial verses (citrakāvya), and poetic flaws (doṣa, chapter 3). **Also known as:** Kāvyaprakāśa (kārikās only), Kāvyaprakāśakārikā, Kāvyaprakāśa (Kārikāvalī)

**Attribution:** The Kāvyaprakāśa was composed primarily by Mammaṭa Bhaṭṭa in 11th-century Kashmir. The Kāvyaprakāśa ('Light on Poetry') is the standard classical compendium of Sanskrit poetics (Alaṅkāraśāstra), composed in the late 11th century CE by Mammaṭa Bhaṭṭa in Kashmir and completed in the tenth chapter by Allaṭa. Arranged in ten chapters (ullāsas), it synthesizes the dhvani and rasa theories of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta with earlier formalist poetics, treating the definition and purposes of poetry, semantic functions of words, poetic blemishes, qualities, and figures of speech. This e-text preserves the Kārikāvalī, the complete metrical core of 142 mnemonic stanzas formulating the work's doctrinal framework.

The Āgamaḍambara ('The Pomp of the Scriptures' or 'Much Ado About Religion'), also titled Sanmatanāṭaka, is a four-act satirical and philosophical Sanskrit drama composed by the Kashmiri Naiyāyika Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. Set during the reign of King Śaṅkaravarman of Kashmir (r. c. 883–902 CE), the drama depicts ideological debates and socio-religious friction among Vedic Mīmāṃsakas, Buddhists, Jains, Cārvākas, Kāpālikas, and antinomian Nīlāmbaras. The plot follows the zealous Vedic graduate Saṅkarṣaṇa as he campaigns to suppress heterodox movements, concluding with a state-mediated resolution that legitimizes multiple religious traditions conforming to common social morality.

**Coverage:** partial — Cantos 1.1 through 14.31 (14 cantos out of an original 28). The text ceases at verse 14.31 where Johnston's edition ends.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Also known as:** Buddha-carita, Acts of the Buddha, Life of the Buddha, Sangs rgyas kyi spyod pa, Fo suo xing zan, 佛所行讚

**Attribution:** Ascribed to the Buddhist monk and master poet Aśvaghoṣa (c. 1st–2nd century CE), associated with the Kuṣāṇa court of Kaniṣka I. In early Nepalese manuscripts, the Sanskrit text survives only from 1.8 to 14.31. Cantos 1.1–1.7 and 14.32–17.61 were composed in 1830 by the Nepalese paṇḍita Amṛtānanda to repair the lost portions; in this e-text, Amṛtānanda's opening verses are included in parentheses with siglum C from Cowell's edition, while cantos 14.32–17 are excluded.

The Buddhacarita ('Acts of the Buddha') is a celebrated Buddhist court epic (mahākāvya) composed by the monk-poet Aśvaghoṣa in the early 2nd century CE. It narrates the life of Gautama Buddha from his birth in Lumbinī, sheltered youth, and Great Departure, through his ascetic strivings and defeat of Māra, culminating in his awakening under the Bodhi tree. Although the complete poem originally comprised 28 cantos (preserved in full only in Tibetan and Chinese translations), the Sanskrit text survives in ancient manuscript transmission only up to canto 14.

The Saundarananda is an early Buddhist Sanskrit mahākāvya in 18 cantos by Aśvaghoṣa relating the conversion of Nanda, the Buddha's handsome half-brother. Deeply attached to his beautiful wife Sundarī, Nanda is drawn into the monastic saṅgha against his inclination; the Buddha then uses a pedagogical device (upāya), first showing him celestial nymphs in Indra's heaven before having him guided toward the realization that even heavenly realms are ephemeral and fraught with suffering. The second half of the epic serves as an exposition of Buddhist mental training, psychological analysis, and meditative praxis (śamatha and vipaśyanā), culminating in Nanda's attainment of arhatship. In the final verses (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa explicitly declares his poetic purpose: he employed the sweet ornamentation of kāvya to make the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa) palatable to worldly audiences.

The Harṣacarita ('The Deeds of Harṣa') is a 7th-century CE ornate Sanskrit prose biography (ākhyāyikā) by court poet Bāṇabhaṭṭa celebrating his patron King Harṣavardhana of Sthāṇvīśvara and Kanyākubja (reigned ca. 606–647 CE). The work opens with an autobiographical account of Bāṇa's Vātsyāyana lineage and his summons to court before turning to Harṣa's royal line, the demise of King Prabhākaravardhana, the murder of Harṣa's elder brother Rājyavardhana, Harṣa's accession to the throne, and the recovery of his widowed sister Rājyaśrī from the Vindhya forest. As the earliest surviving historical ākhyāyikā in Sanskrit literature, it is both an exemplar of high gadyakāvya style (noted for elaborate śleṣa and long compounds) and a primary witness to early medieval northern Indian political and religious life.

The Bhallaṭaśataka is a late 9th-century collection of allegorical epigrams (muktaka) in the anyokti (anyāpadeśa) mode composed by the Kashmiri court poet Bhallaṭa. Composed in a context of declining royal patronage under King Śaṅkaravarman of Kashmir (r. 883–902 CE), the collection uses descriptions of natural phenomena, animals, and plants to satirize corrupt rulers, uncultured patrons, and the humiliation of virtuous scholars. The Daśakumāracarita ('Adventures of the Ten Princes') is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (gadyakāvya) by Daṇḍin (c. late 7th–early 8th century CE), recounting the interwoven picaresque adventures of Prince Rājavāhana and his nine companions across India as they seek romantic conquests, wealth, and political power. Distinctive for its vivid portrayal of secular, sub-courtly, and underworld life—featuring thieves, gamblers, courtesans, corrupt ministers, ascetics, and charlatans—the work is also famous for rhetorical tours de force, notably the seventh chapter composed entirely without labial phonemes (aniroṣṭhya). The surviving authentic composition covers eight central chapters, framed by later anonymous supplements (the Pūrvapīṭhikā and Uttarapīṭhikā) that supply the background and denouement of the cycle.

- V. M. Kulkarni (ed.), Jayadeva's Gītagovinda with the Commentary of King Mānāṅka, Ahmedabad: L.D. Institute of Indology, 1965. — Critical edition of an early Western Indian commentary.

**Translations:**
- Barbara Stoler Miller, Love Song of the Dark Lord: Jayadeva's Gītagovinda, New York: Columbia University Press, 1977. (English)
- Sir William Jones, 'The Gītagōvinda, or The Songs of Jayadéva', Asiatick Researches, vol. 3, 1792, pp. 185–207. (English)
- Friedrich Rückert, Gita-Govinda oder die Liebe des Krischna und der Radha, Erlangen, 1837. (German)
- Sir Edwin Arnold, The Indian Song of Songs, London: Trübner & Co., 1875. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete root text in 12 sargas and 24 prabandhas/aṣṭapadīs, spanning from GG 1.1 ('meghaiḥ meduram...') to GG 12.22 ('śrībhojadeva-prabhavasya...'). The e-text is formatted in sandhi-analyzed, word-divided form (in pausa) without commentary.

**Also known as:** Gītagovindakāvya, Aṣṭapadī

**Attribution:** The poem explicitly identifies Jayadeva, son of Bhojadeva and Rāmādevī (GG 12.22). He flourished at the court of King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal in the late 12th century CE, as corroborated by his praise of contemporary court poets (Umāpatidhara, Govardhana, Śaraṇa, and Dhoyī) in GG 1.3.

The Gītagovinda by Jayadeva (late 12th century CE) is a renowned lyric poem (gīti-kāvya or prabandha) celebrating the love, painful estrangement, mutual longing in separation (viraha), and erotic-mystical reconciliation of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā in Vṛndāvana, assisted by a confidante (sakhī). Divided into twelve cantos comprising twenty-four rhymed songs (aṣṭapadīs) assigned specific rāgas and tālas, framed by classical Sanskrit metrical stanzas, the work seamlessly blends classical court aesthetics with vernacular lyrical forms. It had an enduring impact on Vaiṣṇava devotional theology (especially Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism) and became foundational to Indian dance (notably Odissi), painting traditions, and temple ritual music.

The Kumārasambhava ('The Birth of Kumāra') is one of the celebrated mahākāvyas (court epics) composed by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). These eight cantos form the universally acknowledged genuine work of the poet, recounting the divine romance and union of Śiva and Pārvatī: from the magnificent description of the Himalayas and Pārvatī's birth, the destruction of Kāma by Śiva's third eye, Pārvatī's arduous penance and Śiva's testing of her devotion, through their celestial wedding and intimate divine honeymoon on Mount Gandhamādana in canto 8. The remaining cantos 9–17 found in extended vulgate manuscripts depict the actual birth of Kumāra (Kārttikeya) and the defeat of Tāraka, but are universally recognized as the composition of a later poet.

Kalāvilāsa ('The Play of the Arts' or 'The Grace of Guile') is an eleventh-century satirical poem in ten cantos composed by the Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra. Framed as instruction delivered by Mūladeva, the legendary prince of rogues, to Candragupta, the naive son of a wealthy merchant, the work catalogues and satirizes widespread forms of deceit, greed, and hypocrisy in medieval society—exposing corrupt bureaucrats and scribes (kāyasthas), merchants, quack physicians, astrologers, courtesans, and false ascetics—before concluding with an exposition of genuine, auspicious arts. The Līlāvatīsāra ('The Epitome of Līlāvatī') is a late thirteenth-century Sanskrit narrative kāvya in twenty-one cantos (utsāhas) composed in 1285 CE by the Śvetāmbara Jain monk Jinaratna. It condenses the extensive 1036 CE Prakrit romance Nivvāṇalīlāvaīkahā by Jineśvarasūri into classical Sanskrit verse. Framed as a spiritual discourse delivered by the monk Samarasena to King Siṃha and Queen Līlāvatī of Rājagṛha, the narrative traces the transmigrations and karmic trajectories of a linked circle of souls through multiple rebirths, illustrating the destructive consequences of the passions (kaṣāya) and promoting core Jain ethics of nonviolence (ahiṃsā) and monastic renunciation.

**Also known as:** Meghadūtam, Pūrvamegha and Uttaramegha

**Attribution:** Universally attributed to the classical Sanskrit poet Kālidāsa. Although the catalog record mentions Mallinātha's Sañjīvanī commentary (derived from the title of M. R. Kale's printed volume), this digital text contains only the poetic stanzas.

The Meghadūta ('The Cloud Messenger') is a classical lyric poem (khaṇḍakāvya / sandeśakāvya) composed in the seventeen-syllable mandākrāntā metre by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). Banished for a year to the remote hermitage of Rāmagiri by his master Kubera for neglect of duty, a grief-stricken yakṣa beseeches a passing monsoon cloud to convey a message of longing to his wife in the celestial Himalayan city of Alakā. The first part (Pūrvamegha) charts an evocative journey northward across central and northern India, depicting sacred shrines, rivers, and cities; the second part (Uttaramegha) describes Alakā, the melancholic condition of the yakṣa's beloved, and his intimate message of fidelity and prospective reunion. As the earliest surviving exemplar of its kind, the work established the widespread messenger-poem genre across South Asian and Inner Asian literatures.

**Also known as:** Kaliviḍambanam, Kaliviḍambanaśataka

**Attribution:** Explicitly attributed to Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita in the final verse (verse 102: kavinā nīlakaṇṭhena kaler etad viḍambanam / racitaṃ ...) and the terminal colophon (iti Nīlakaṇṭhaviracitaṃ Kaliviḍambanaṃ saṃpūrṇam).

The Kaliviḍambana ('Mockery of the Kali Age') is an influential satirical poem of 102 anuṣṭubh verses composed by the 17th-century South Indian poet, polymath, and minister Nīlakaṇṭha Dīkṣita. It offers sharp, epigrammatic lampoons of the corruption, hypocrisy, and professional charlatanism emblematic of the degenerate age. Its targets include quack physicians, greedy astrologers, fraudulent exorcists and tantric practitioners, unprincipled debaters, sycophantic courtiers, and venal relatives. Written in lucid, aphoristic Sanskrit, it is considered one of the masterpieces of post-classical Sanskrit satire.

The Haṃsadūta ('The Swan Messenger') is an early 16th-century Sanskrit messenger poem (dūtakāvya) in 142 śikhariṇī verses composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī. Modeled after Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, the poem describes Lalitā, a confidante of Rādhā, dispatching a swan from the banks of the Yamunā to Kṛṣṇa in Mathurā following his departure from Vraja. The Uttararāmacarita ('The Later Deeds of Rāma') by Bhavabhūti is a classical Sanskrit drama in seven acts (nāṭaka) dramatizing the tragic events of the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Rāmāyaṇa. The plot centers on Rāma's agonizing abandonment of the pregnant Sītā in deference to public slander, his acute remorse and grief twelve years later upon revisiting the Daṇḍaka forest, and their psychological reconciliation culminating in a play-within-a-play (garbhāṅka). The work is celebrated across the Sanskrit dramaturgical tradition as the supreme artistic exemplar of karuṇarasa (the aesthetic sentiment of pathos and compassionate sorrow).

The Anargharāghava ('The Priceless Rāghava') is a classical seven-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) by Murāri dramatizing the Rāmāyaṇa narrative from the arrival of the sage Viśvāmitra at Daśaratha's court through the victory over Rāvaṇa and Rāma's consecration at Ayodhyā. The play reframes the epic conflict through political intrigues engineered by Rāvaṇa's minister Mālyavat and de-emphasizes stage action in favor of elaborate lyrical description, elevated kāvya diction, and metrical artistry. Murāri, commonly placed between the late 8th and early 10th centuries CE (most likely ca. 900 CE), was widely admired and cited by Sanskrit poeticians as a master of ornate dramatic poetry.

The Abhijñānaśākuntala ('The Recognition of Śakuntalā') is a seven-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) by Kālidāsa, elaborating an episode found in the Mahābhārata. **Also known as:** Mṛcchakaṭika, Mṛcchakaṭikam

**Attribution:** The drama is attributed in its prologue (prastāvanā, act 1) to a king named Śūdraka, described as an erudite kṣatriya king, poet, devotee of Śiva, and master of the Vedas. His historical identity and date remain disputed; some scholars suggest royal authorship (e.g., an Ābhīra monarch), while many regard 'Śūdraka' as a legendary pseudonym or patron for an author who reworked and expanded the four-act play Cārudatta ascribed to Bhāsa.

The Mṛcchakaṭikā ('The Little Clay Cart') is a ten-act Sanskrit drama of the prakaraṇa genre, traditionally attributed to King Śūdraka and commonly placed around the 3rd to 5th century CE. Sharing its first four acts with the Cārudatta ascribed to Bhāsa, the play dramatizes the romance between the impoverished merchant Cārudatta and the wealthy courtesan Vasantasenā against the backdrop of political upheaval in Ujjayinī. The drama is celebrated for its realistic portrayal of urban life, colorful secondary characters (thieves, gamblers, shampooers, corrupt officials), court trial scenes, and its extensive use of varied Prakrit dialects.

The Bṛhatkathāślokasaṃgraha ('Verse Epitome of the Great Story') by Budhasvāmin is an episodic Sanskrit narrative kāvya recounting the adventures, romances, and courtships of Prince Naravāhanadatta, son of King Udayana, destined to become sovereign (cakravartin) of the Vidyādharas. The Hitopadeśa is a celebrated Sanskrit collection of animal fables and gnomic maxims composed in prosimetric campū form by Nārāyaṇa under the patronage of Prince Dhavalacandra [3882, 3887]. Drawing largely on the Pañcatantra as well as the Kāmandakīyanītisāra and the epics [19], the work is framed as practical instruction in statecraft and ethics given by the sage Viṣṇuśarman to the errant sons of King Sudarśana of Pāṭaliputra [21, 28]. It is divided into four thematic books: Mitralābha (Gaining Friends), Suhṛdbheda (Alienating Friends), Vigraha (War), and Sandhi (Peace) [18, 2076, 3889]. Renowned for its direct syntax and pragmatic political wisdom (nīti), it has served for centuries as an essential introductory reader for students of Sanskrit.

The Kathāsaritsāgara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story') is an encyclopedic Sanskrit narrative kāvya in 18 books (lambakas) and 124 chapters (taraṅgas), comprising roughly 21,388 stanzas, composed in Kashmir by the Brahmin poet Somadeva between c. 1063 and 1081 CE. Structured around the epic framing quest of Prince Naravāhanadatta to attain the sovereignty of the Vidyādharas, it preserves the most complete surviving northern adaptation of Guṇāḍhya's lost Paiśācī Bṛhatkathā. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 70 tales within the framing narrative (textus simplicior). Contains the root Sanskrit prose and verse, including Prakrit verses with Sanskrit chāyā, concluding at tale 70 with 'iti śukasaptatau saptatitamī kathā / iti śukasaptatiḥ samāptā'. The modern Sanskrit and Hindi 'Vinodinī' commentary advertised in the opening line is omitted.

**Also known as:** Çukasaptati, Shuka Saptati, Seventy Tales of the Parrot

**Attribution:** The core Śukasaptati collection is anonymous. While the ornate recension (textus ornatior) is attributed in some manuscript traditions to Cintāmaṇi Bhaṭṭa, the present e-text contains the anonymous simpler recension (textus simplicior).

The Śukasaptati ('Seventy Tales of the Parrot') is a popular Sanskrit frame-tale narrative (kathā). When the young merchant Madanavinoda embarks on a lengthy commercial journey abroad, his wife Prabhāvatī is tempted by dissolute companions to pursue illicit liaisons; her wise parrot keeps her at home each night by narrating an ingenious story of wit, trickery, or adulterous escape, cunningly breaking off the tale until dawn. Over the course of seventy consecutive nights, the parrot deters her from infidelity until the merchant returns. Renowned for its realistic depiction of rogue life and practical cleverness, the collection enjoyed immense popularity throughout Asia and formed the direct basis for the Persian Ṭūṭī-nāma.

The Padmapurāṇa is one of the eighteen classical Mahāpurāṇas, traditionally ranking second in size with approximately 55,000 ślokas. Extant in distinct northern (five khaṇḍas) and western/southern (six or seven khaṇḍas) recensions, it comprises encyclopedic accounts of cosmogony, dynastic genealogies, pilgrimage guides (tīrthamāhātmya, notably for Puṣkara and the Gaṅgā), and substantial Vaiṣṇava narrative material including independent versions of the Rāma and Kṛṣṇa legends. Renowned for its encyclopedic scope, it combines traditional Puranic cosmogony, genealogies, and avatāra narratives with extensive epitomes of classical and medieval technical disciplines. Organized into seven saṃhitās (Vidyeśvara, Rudra, Śatarudra, Koṭirudra, Umā, Kailāsa, and Vāyavīya), it harmonizes Vedic-Brahmanical theology with Pāśupata asceticism and temple worship. It contains central mythological cycles including the liṅgodbhava, the marriage of Śiva and Pārvatī, the birth of Kumāra and Gaṇeśa, and the twelve jyotirliṅgas, alongside detailed liturgies for liṅga worship, mantra recitation, and initiation.

The Viṣṇupurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas and is widely regarded by Indologists as the most unified exemplar of the classical pañcalakṣaṇa ('five characteristics') genre. Structured as a six-book dialogue between the sage Parāśara and his disciple Maitreya, the text articulates a Vaiṣṇava cosmology and theology identifying Viṣṇu as the supreme, all-encompassing Brahman. **Attribution:** The Vedāntasyamantaka was historically attributed by several earlier scholars and editions (e.g., Nalinīkānta Gosvāmī 1930 and Haridās Dās) to Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa. The Vedāntasyamantaka ('The Syamantaka Jewel of Vedānta') is an early 18th-century introductory compendium (prakaraṇa) of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Vedānta by Rādhādāmodara Gosvāmin. Divided into six chapters termed kiraṇas ('rays'), the work systematically expounds epistemology (pramāṇa-nirṇaya) and five core ontological categories: īśvara (the Supreme Divinity, identifying Kṛṣṇa as the ultimate prameya), jīva (individual souls), prakṛti (material nature), kāla (time), and karma (action). By integrating the Dvaita concept of viśeṣa to articulate the Caitanya school's acintya-bhedābheda (inconceivable identity-in-difference) theology, it directly influenced the major philosophical works of Rādhādāmodara's disciple Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa, notably the Govindabhāṣya and Siddhāntaratna.

The Vṛndāvanamahimāmṛta ('Nectar of the Glories of Vṛndāvana') is a devotional poem in śatakas (centuries of verses) ascribed to Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī (16th c.). It glorifies Vṛndāvana/Vraja as the eternal abode of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa and expresses longing to dwell there in devotion. Tradition speaks of 100 śatakas, of which 17 are printed. The DharmaNexus e-text for this entry is empty.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** R. P. Kangle (ed.), The Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra, Part I: A Critical Edition with a Glossary, 2nd ed., University of Bombay Studies: Sanskrit, Prakrit and Pali, No. 1, Bombay: University of Bombay, 1969.

**Other editions:**
- R. Shamasastry (ed.), Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, Bibliotheca Sanskrita No. 37, Mysore: Government Branch Press, 1909. — Editio princeps, based on palm-leaf manuscripts found in Tanjore and Mysore.

- Patrick Olivelle (ed. & tr.), King, Governance, and Law in Ancient India: Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, New York: Oxford University Press, 2013. — Critical edition and annotated English translation with re-evaluated textual stemma.

**Translations:**

- R. P. Kangle, The Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra, Part II: An English Translation with Critical and Explanatory Notes, University of Bombay Studies: Sanskrit, Prakrit and Pali, No. 2, Bombay: University of Bombay, 1965 (2nd ed. 1972). (English)
- L. N. Rangarajan, The Arthashastra, New Delhi: Penguin Books India, 1992. (English)
- Patrick Olivelle, King, Governance, and Law in Ancient India: Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, New York: Oxford University Press, 2013. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text containing all 15 adhikaraṇas (books), 150 adhyāyas (chapters), and 180 prakaraṇas (topics), terminating with the final verse and colophon at 15.1.73.

**Also known as:** Kauṭilīya Arthaśāstra, Kauṭilīyārthaśāstra

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Kauṭilya (also known as Viṣṇugupta or Cāṇakya), chief minister to Candragupta Maurya (late 4th century BCE). Modern historical and statistical analysis (Trautmann 1971, McClish 2012, Olivelle 2013) demonstrates that the text is composite, composed in distinct strata and redacted into its surviving form between the 1st and 3rd centuries CE.

The Arthaśāstra is ancient India's foundational treatise on statecraft, political economy, judicial administration, and diplomatic strategy. Divided into fifteen books (adhikaraṇas), it systematically covers the education and discipline of the king, ministerial appointments, internal civil and revenue administration, civil and criminal law (dharmasthīya and kaṇṭakaśodhana), espionage, interstate relations (the mandala theory and the sixfold foreign policy, ṣāḍguṇya), military logistics and warfare, and the methodological hermeneutics of treatises (tantrayukti). Treating artha (material welfare and power) as the foundation of royal and societal flourishing, it provides an exceptionally detailed blueprint for state institutions in classical India.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the 7 adhikaraṇas (1.1.1 to the concluding verses 7.1.52v–59v, Fezas's numbering) with section headings in French ('livre', 'leçon', 'section'); followed by Jean Fezas's 193 French notes ((1))–((193)), which form part of the e-text (segments ~2600–3044).

**Also known as:** Vātsyāyanakāmasūtra

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Vātsyāyana (often styled Mallanāga Vātsyāyana in later commentarial tradition), who explicitly identifies himself in concluding verse 7.1.56 as having synthesized and condensed the earlier Kāmaśāstra tradition of Bābhravya Pāñcāla and other predecessors.

The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana (c. 3rd–4th century CE) is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāmaśāstra, systematically treating the pursuit of pleasure, courtship, love, and aesthetic refinement within the classical trivarga framework. Formally modeled on the scholastic prose structure of Kauṭilya's Arthaśāstra, its seven books (adhikaraṇas) cover general principles of life, sexual technique, marriage, the duties of a wife, extramarital relations, the life and profession of courtesans, and esoteric erotic recipes. It provides an indispensable documentary view of urban culture (nāgaraka-vṛtta), gender relations, and material life in ancient and classical India.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** The Charakasaṃhitā of Agniveśa, Revised by Charaka and Dṛḍhabala, with the Āyurveda-Dīpikā Commentary of Chakrapāṇidatta, edited by Vaidya Jādavaji Trikamji Āchārya, Varanasi: Chaukhambha Sanskrit Sansthan, 1994 (The Kashi Sanskrit Series, no. 228; reprint of the 3rd Nirnaya Sagar Press edition, Bombay, 1941).

**E-text:** Oliver Hellwig for GRETIL (caraka_u.htm; TEI sa_agniveza-carakasaMhitA-parts-comm.xml)

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL legacy header (1_sanskr/6_sastra/7_ayur/caraka_u.htm): 'Agnivesa: Carakasamhita (selected parts; see below) with the Ayurvedadipika / Based on the ed. by J. Trikamji / Varanasi: Chaukhambha Sanskrit Sansthan, 1994 / (Kashi Sanskrit Series, 228) / Input by Oliver Hellwig'
- TEI header gretil_sa/sa_agniveza-carakasaMhitA-parts-comm.xml confirming Oliver Hellwig's data entry and the exact excerpt breakdown matching the Chaukhambha reprint of Trikamji's edition
- Opening commentary contains Cakrapāṇidatta's mangalaśloka ('guṇatrayavibhedena mūrtitrayam upaiyuṣe...')

**Other editions:**
- Vaidya Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya (ed.), The Carakasaṃhitā of Agniveśa, Revised by Charaka and Dṛḍhabala, with the Āyurvedadīpikā Commentary of Cakrapāṇidatta, Bombay: Nirnaya Sagar Press, 1922; 2nd ed. 1935; 3rd ed. 1941. — Standard critical vulgate edition upon which most modern reprints and studies are based.
- Gaṅgādhara Kaviratna (ed.), Carakasaṃhitā: with the Jalpakalpataru Commentary, 3 vols., Calcutta: Pramadā Press / Samvāda Jñānaratnākara Press, 1868–1877. — First complete printed edition of the text, containing Gaṅgādhara's extensive sub-commentary.
- Shree Gulabkunverba Ayurvedic Society (ed.), The Caraka Saṃhitā: Expounded by the Worshipful Ātreya Punarvasu, Compiled by the Great Sage Agniveśa and Redacted by Caraka and Dṛḍhabala, 6 vols., Jamnagar: Shree Gulabkunverba Ayurvedic Society, 1949. — Major multi-volume edition with multilingual apparatus and translations.
- Priya Vrat Sharma (ed., tr.), Caraka-Saṃhitā: Agniveśa's Treatise Refined and Annotated by Caraka and Redacted by Dṛḍhabala, 4 vols., Varanasi: Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1981–1994 (Ja Krishnadas Ayurveda Series, 36). — Standard academic edition and English translation with critical notes.

**Translations:**
- Avinash Chandra Kaviratna and Pareshnath Kaviratna (tr.), The Charaka-Samhita: Translated into English, Calcutta: Published by the translators, 1890–1914. (English)
- Ram Karan Sharma and Bhagwan Dash (tr.), Agniveśa's Caraka Saṃhitā: Text with English Translation & Critical Exposition Based on Cakrapāṇidatta's Āyurvedadīpikā, 7 vols., Varanasi: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series Office, 1976–2002 (Chowkhamba Sanskrit Studies, 94). (English)
- Priya Vrat Sharma (tr.), Caraka-Saṃhitā, 4 vols., Varanasi: Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1981–1994. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** excerpt — Contains only selected passages and chapters: Sūtrasthāna 1.1–43, 12.1–17, 26–28; Nidānasthāna 7.1–14; Vimānasthāna 1; Śārīrasthāna 1.1–30; Cikitsāsthāna 1, 1.3–2.4, 22. In the local database repository, the record under key SA_GS40_caraka is currently unpopulated (0 segments), while the segmented file corresponding to this GRETIL e-text is stored under SA_GS40_caraka_u.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Carakasaṃhitā (Agniveśa, root text)
- Āyurvedadīpikā (Cakrapāṇidatta, commentary)

**Also known as:** Agniveśatantra, Caraka, Carakasaṃhitā with Cakrapāṇidatta's commentary, Carakatātparyadīpikā

**Attribution:** The root teachings of the medical treatise are traditionally ascribed to Ātreya Punarvasu and set down by his pupil Agniveśa as the Agniveśatantra; the treatise was subsequently redacted and expanded by Caraka (c. 1st c. BCE–2nd c. CE), and missing portions (about one-third of the text, primarily in the Cikitsā-, Kalpa-, and Siddhisthānas) were supplied by Dṛḍhabala (c. 4th–5th c. CE). The included commentary, Āyurvedadīpikā, was authored by the 11th-century physician-scholar Cakrapāṇidatta.

The Carakasaṃhitā is the foremost canonical compendium of Āyurveda (classical Indian medicine) and the premier authority of the Bṛhattrayī ('Great Triad'), devoted primarily to internal medicine (kāyacikitsā). Divided into eight sections (sthānas) across 120 chapters, the work details pathophysiology, etiology, diagnosis, pharmacology, and dietetics based on the tridoṣa humoral model, alongside extensive treatments of ethics, embryology, and dialectical debate (vāda). This digital text preserves selected chapters of the compendium accompanied by the authoritative eleventh-century commentary Āyurvedadīpikā by Cakrapāṇidatta.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Ultimately the Nirṇaya Sāgar vulgate: Suśrutasaṃhitā, ed. Vaidya Jādavji Trikamji Ācārya (and Nārāyaṇ Rām Ācārya), Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgar Press (1915; 2nd ed. 1931; 3rd ed. 1938; many Chaukhambha reprints), mūla text only, taken over via an intermediate digital file whose exact source and printed exemplar are not stated.

Hariprapanna's readings).

**Translations:**

- Singhal, G. D. et al. Ancient Indian Surgery Series. 10 vols. Varanasi: Singhal Publications / Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1972–1982. (English)

- Hessler, Franz. Suśrutas: Ayurvedas. Id est Medicinae Systema a venerabili D’hanvantare demonstratum a Susruta discipulo compositum. 3 vols. Erlangen: F. Enke, 1844–1850. (Latin)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete mūla text in 186 adhyāyas across all six sections: the five sthānas of the Pūrvatantra (Sūtra- [46 ch.], Nidāna- [16 ch.], Śārīra- [10 ch.], Cikitsā- [40 ch.], and Kalpasthāna [8 ch.], totalling 120 chapters) and the Uttaratantra (66 ch.), concluding with Uttaratantra 66.18 ('iti sauśrute āyurvedaśāstre uttarasthānaṃ samāptam').

**Also known as:** Sushruta Samhita, Sauśruta, Sauśrutasaṃhitā

**Attribution:** Traditionally framed as teachings imparted by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to Suśruta and other pupils. The text represents a multi-layered compilation that underwent redactions in the early centuries CE (traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna as pratisaṃskartā), with the Uttaratantra appended later to supplement the surgical core with the remaining branches of classical Āyurveda.

The Suśrutasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Āyurveda (the Bṛhat-trayī) and ancient India's premier authority on surgery (śalyatantra). Framed as instructions delivered by Divodāsa Dhanvantari, king of Kāśī, to his student Suśruta, it describes surgical instruments, practical anatomy through human cadaveric dissection, and operative procedures such as rhinoplasty, couching of cataracts, lithotomy, and abdominal suture. The treatise comprises 186 chapters divided across the five sthānas of the Pūrvatantra (Sūtra-, Nidāna-, Śārīra-, Cikitsā-, and Kalpasthāna) and the supplementary Uttaratantra, which treats ophthalmology and ENT (śālākya), pediatrics (kaumārabhṛtya), toxicology/psychiatry (bhūtavidyā), and general medicine (kāyacikitsā).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text containing all 12 adhyāyas of the Manusmṛti along with Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Manusmṛti (Manu, root text)
- Manubhāṣya (Medhātithi, commentary)

**Also known as:** Mānavadharmaśāstra with Manubhāṣya, Manusmṛti Medhātithibhāṣyasahitā, Mānavadharmaśāstram Medhātithibhāṣyopetam

**Attribution:** The root treatise Manusmṛti (Mānavadharmaśāstra) is traditionally attributed to the primordial sage Manu (revealed through Bhṛgu), though modern scholarship treats it as a composite metrical Dharmaśāstra of anonymous authorship composed between c. 2nd century BCE and 3rd century CE. The commentary Manubhāṣya was authored by Bhaṭṭa Medhātithi, son of Vīrasvāmin (c. 9th–10th century CE, probably from Kashmir). As attested in the concluding colophon (12.126), parts of the commentary that had fallen into lacunae were restored under the patronage of King Madanapāla (14th century).

The Manusmṛti (or Mānava-Dharmaśāstra) is ancient India's foundational and most influential metrical code of socio-religious duty (dharma), statecraft, jurisprudence, and penance. Medhātithi's Manubhāṣya (c. 9th–10th century CE) represents the earliest surviving and most comprehensive commentary on the text, celebrated for its rigorous application of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to reconcile textual tensions and develop sophisticated legal reasoning. Surviving incompletely in manuscript witnesses, the commentary was partially restored in the 14th century under King Madanapāla and remained a primary benchmark for subsequent Dharmaśāstra commentarial traditions and digests.

The Viṣṇusmṛti (or Vaiṣṇava-Dharmaśāstra) is a major Sanskrit legal treatise combining prose dharmasūtra style with framing verse passages. Framed as a dialogue in which Viṣṇu as the cosmic boar (Varāha) instructs the rescued Earth goddess (Vasundharā), the work treats varṇāśramadharma, royal administration (rājadharma), civil and penal law (vyavahāra), inheritance, bodily purity, ancestor rites (śrāddha), penances (prāyaścitta), and devotional worship. Originating in an ancient Dharmasūtra of the Kāṭhaka tradition of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (c. 300 BCE–100 CE), its extant redaction took shape around the 8th–10th century CE in Kashmir, uniquely combining classical jurisprudence with early Vaiṣṇava theology.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Vedic teacher/sage Baudhāyana (Bodhāyana), the eponymous founder of the Baudhāyana carana of the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Philological scholarship demonstrates that the work is multi-layered and composite.

Divided into four praśnas (books), the treatise covers the sources of dharma, initiation and student life, duties of the householder and king, judicial procedure, civil and criminal law, inheritance, penances, and the āśramas. It is composite in composition: Praśnas 1 and 2 constitute the archaic core (c. 3rd–2nd century BCE), whereas Praśnas 3 and 4 represent later accretions. The text is celebrated for its explicit recognition of regional customary law (ācāra), highlighting contrasting customs between northern and southern Brahmins.

The Gautamadharmasūtra is one of the earliest extant aphoristic legal treatises of ancient India, traditionally affiliated with the Rāṇāyanīya and Kauthuma schools of the Sāmaveda. Composed in concise prose sūtras, it systematically expounds the sources of sacred law (dharma), rules for life stages (āśrama), student initiation (upanayana), householder duties, dietary and purification rules (śauca), occupations of the four social classes (varṇa), the duties and judicial functions of the king (rājadharma, vyavahāra), rules of inheritance and partition (dāyabhāga), and expiations for ritual and moral transgressions (prāyaścitta). The Yogavāsiṣṭha (also known as the Vāsiṣṭhamahārāmāyaṇa) is a monumental philosophical and narrative epic of nearly 27,000 verses framed as a dialogue between the sage Vasiṣṭha and the young prince Rāma in the royal court of Ayodhyā. Divided into six books (prakaraṇas)—Vairāgya, Mumukṣuvyavahāra, Utpatti, Sthiti, Upaśama, and Nirvāṇa—the work expounds an idealist, non-dual philosophical vision through philosophical exposition interspersed with elaborate frame stories and allegories. It teaches that the phenomenal universe is a projection of the mind (manomaya) and advocates self-inquiry (vicāra) leading to liberation while living (jīvanmukti). Modern scholarship has demonstrated that this vulgate text represents a later Vedanticized recension of the 10th-century Kashmiri Mokṣopāya.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete; the Tantravārttika as an independent work covers Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 through Adhyāya 3, Pāda 8 of Śabarasvāmin's Bhāṣya on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra. (The preceding Pāda 1.1 Tarkapāda is commented upon in Kumārila's verse Ślokavārttika, while Adhyāyas 4 through 12 are treated in his Ṭupṭīkā).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Mīmāṃsāsūtra (Jaimini, root text (lemmata / adhikaraṇa sūtras for adhyāyas 1.2–3.8))
- Tantravārttika (Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, commentary)

**Also known as:** Tantravārtika, Mīmāṃsāvārttika, Tantraṭīkā

**Attribution:** The Tantravārttika is universally recognized as the work of the 7th-century Mīmāṃsā philosopher Kumārila Bhaṭṭa, forming the central and most extensive component of his tripartite sub-commentary on Śabarasvāmin's Śābarabhāṣya.

The Tantravārttika is the primary prose sub-commentary composed by the 7th-century philosopher Kumārila Bhaṭṭa on Śabarasvāmin's Śābarabhāṣya on Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra, covering Adhyāya 1, Pāda 2 through Adhyāya 3, Pāda 8. Serving as the central work in Kumārila's tripartite commentary on the Bhāṣya (flanked by the verse Ślokavārttika on 1.1 and the concise notes of the Ṭupṭīkā on Adhyāyas 4–12), it develops a comprehensive defense of Vedic ritualism, textual exegesis, and Brahmanical orthopraxy. The work is renowned for its seminal analyses of the semantic force of Vedic injunctions (vidhi), the epistemological and evidentiary authority of explanatory passages (arthavāda) and mantras, the validity of Smṛti and regional customs (ācāra), and the formal criteria governing ritual subordination (śeṣatva).

The Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa (commonly called the Āpadevī) is a standard 17th-century introductory primer (prakaraṇa) of the Bhāṭṭa school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā composed by Āpadeva. Written in lucid prose, it provides an organized exposition of Vedic hermeneutics, defining dharma, explaining the two modes of productive efficiency (śābdī and ārthī bhāvanā), and classifying Vedic statements into injunctions (vidhi), mantras, appellations (nāmadheya), prohibitions (niṣedha), and explanatory eulogies (arthavāda). The Kumārikākhaṇḍa is the largest and most important surviving section of the Manthānabhairavatantra, representing the canonical apex of the Paścimāmnāya (Western Transmission) or Kubjikā school of Kaula Tantrism. Preserved almost exclusively in medieval Nepalese manuscripts, the work serves as an indispensable bridge connecting early Trika and Krama tantrism with the later Śrīvidyā and Nātha traditions.

Raffaele Torella, Rome: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (IsMEO), 1994 (Serie Orientale Roma, 71); 2nd revised ed., Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 2002 (repr. 2013, 2021). — First complete critical edition of both kārikās and the vṛtti, recovering the lost concluding portion of the text based on a Malayalam palm-leaf manuscript.

**Coverage:** unclear — The digital file in this repository is currently empty (0 segments, 0 characters), having been withheld or left unpopulated due to copyright flagging ('source': 'under copyright'). **Works in this e-text:**
- Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā (Utpaladeva, root text)
- Īśvarapratyabhijñāvṛtti (Utpaladeva, autocommentary)

**Also known as:** Īśvarapratyabhijñā, Pratyabhijñākārikā, Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikāvṛtti, Pratyabhijñāsūtra

**Attribution:** Utpaladeva (fl. c. 900–950 CE in Kashmir), disciple of Somānanda, composed the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā and simultaneously authored his concise autocommentary (vṛtti) on it, as confirmed by Abhinavagupta.

The Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā along with its autocommentary, the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvṛtti, constitutes the foundational doctrinal treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') school within non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed by Utpaladeva in the first half of the 10th century CE. Through rigorous epistemological and metaphysical argumentation engaging Buddhist logicians (such as Dignāga and Dharmakīrti), Grammarians (Bhartṛhari), and Nyāya thinkers, Utpaladeva demonstrates that individual consciousness is essentially identical to the supreme Lord (Maheśvara / Śiva), possessed of intrinsic powers of knowledge (jñāna) and action (kriyā). Spiritual liberation consists in the intuitive recognition (pratyabhijñā) of this already-present divine sovereignty.

- N. Aiyaswami Sastri, Suvarṇasaptati Śāstra: The Sāṃkhya-kārikā-saptati of Īśvarakṛṣṇa with a commentary reconstructed into Sanskrit from the Chinese translation of Paramārtha, Tirupati: Sri Venkateswara Oriental Institute, 1944. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete e-text of all 73 kārikās along with the complete Māṭharavṛtti commentary, including the introductory narrative upodghāta and the concluding colophon (ity ācāryeśvarakṛṣṇaproktāyāḥ sāṅkhyasaptatyā vṛttir ācāryamāṭharakṛtiḥ samāptā).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Sāṃkhyakārikā (Īśvarakṛṣṇa, root text)
- Māṭharavṛtti (Māṭhara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Sāṃkhyasaptati, Sāṅkhyakārikā, Sāṃkhyakārikāmāṭharavṛtti

**Attribution:** The root verses are composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 350–450 CE). The prose commentary Māṭharavṛtti is traditionally attributed to Māṭharācārya. While earlier 20th-century scholars (e.g. Belvalkar) considered it to be the direct 5th-century Sanskrit original translated into Chinese by Paramārtha (as the Suvarṇasaptati), later scholarship (Solomon, Larson, Bhattacharya) regards the extant Sanskrit Māṭharavṛtti as a somewhat later redaction (c. 8th c.) sharing a close common ancestral textual core with the Gauḍapādabhāṣya and Sāṃkhyavṛtti.

The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the classical foundational text of the Sāṅkhya philosophical tradition, formulating its dualist metaphysics of conscious self (puruṣa) and primordial nature (prakṛti), the evolution of the twenty-five cosmic principles (tattvas), the three guṇas, and liberation through discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti). The Māṭharavṛtti is an essential early-to-medieval Sanskrit prose commentary that preserves traditional mythological background—such as the transmission lineage of Kapila and Āsuri—as well as detailed illustrative parables. Because it shares extensive verbatim and doctrinal parallels with the Gauḍapādabhāṣya and Paramārtha's 6th-century Chinese Suvarṇasaptati, it is an indispensable witness for tracing the evolution of classical Sāṅkhya exegesis.

**Coverage:** complete — Contains all 72 kārikās of the Sāṃkhyakārikā alongside the full Jayamaṅgalā commentary, beginning with its initial maṅgala verse ('adhigatatattvālokaṃ...') and concluding with the terminal colophon following kārikā 72.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Sāṃkhyakārikā (Īśvarakṛṣṇa, root text)
- Jayamaṅgalā (Śaṅkarārya, commentary)

**Also known as:** Sāṃkhyasaptati, Sāṃkhyasaptatiṭīkā Jayamaṅgalā, Jayamaṅgalā

The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa is the classical foundational treatise of Sāṃkhya philosophy, articulating its dualist ontology of insentient nature (prakṛti) and pure consciousness (puruṣa), the evolution of the twenty-five tattvas, three epistemic pramāṇas, and liberation through discriminative insight. The Jayamaṅgalā is an important early medieval running commentary (ṭīkā) that provides lucid grammatical and philosophical expositions for all 72 verses. It constitutes an essential witness for the early textual and doctrinal transmission of classical Sāṃkhya alongside the Gauḍapādabhāṣya, the Māṭharavṛtti, and the Yuktidīpikā.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Brahmasūtra (Bādarāyaṇa, root text)
- Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (Śaṅkara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya, Śārīrakabhāṣya, Vedāntasūtra (Śāṅkarabhāṣya), Brahmasūtraśāṅkarabhāṣya

**Attribution:** The root Brahmasūtras (Vedāntasūtras) are traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa (traditionally identified with Vyāsa). The commentary is Śaṅkara's (Śaṅkarācārya, c. 8th century CE) celebrated Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya, universally acknowledged in modern scholarship as his primary authentic philosophical work.

The Brahmasūtrabhāṣya (or Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya) is Śaṅkara's magnum opus and the foundational commentary of Advaita Vedānta on the Brahmasūtra of Bādarāyaṇa. Preceded by the renowned Adhyāsabhāṣya on beginningless transcendental superimposition, the commentary demonstrates that empirical multiplicity is rooted in avidyā and establishes the absolute non-duality of Brahman and the identity of the individual self (ātman) with Brahman. Across four chapters (samanvaya, avirodha, sādhana, and phala), Śaṅkara harmonizes Upaniṣadic statements, refutes competing traditions (including Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, and Buddhism), and expounds knowledge of non-duality as the sole direct means to liberation.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete Sanskrit text in five chapters (prakaraṇas), interspersed with an English translation and introductory/concluding editorial matter by Swami Mokshadananda.

**Also known as:** Jīvan-mukti-viveka

**Attribution:** According to tradition, Vidyāraṇya was the monastic name assumed by Mādhava (Mādhavācārya, brother of Sāyaṇa) upon entering sannyāsa at the Śṛṅgeri pīṭha in the 14th century. While his early Mīmāṃsā, smṛti, and doxographical works bear the pre-monastic name Mādhava, his major late Advaita treatises (Jīvanmuktiviveka, Pañcadaśī) are authored under the monastic name Vidyāraṇya.

The Jīvanmuktiviveka ('Discrimination of Liberation while Living') is an influential 14th-century Advaita Vedānta treatise by Vidyāraṇya. Across five prakaraṇas, the text examines the nature of and scriptural authority for living liberation, the eradication of latent mental impressions (vāsanākṣaya), the dissolution of the mind (manonāśa), the five purposes served by liberation-in-life, and the renunciation of the enlightened knower (vidvatsaṃnyāsa). The work is celebrated for its synthesis of classical Advaita epistemology with the practical yogic disciplines of Patañjali's Yogasūtra and the Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha, maintaining that enduring experiential tranquility in life requires the coordinated practice of tattvajñāna, vāsanākṣaya, and manonāśa.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Bhāmatī covering all four adhyāyas (1.1.1 through 4.4.22), beginning with the seven maṅgala verses and closing with the author's six signature verses and the final colophon.

**Also known as:** Brahmasūtraśāṅkarabhāṣyavibhāga Bhāmatī, Śāṅkarabhāṣyavibhāga Bhāmatī

**Attribution:** Composed by Vācaspatimiśra (Vācaspati Miśra I, fl. 9th–10th century CE; his floruit is dated to either c. 841 CE or c. 976 CE depending on the era assigned to the year 898 mentioned in his Nyāyasūcīnibandhana). In the six concluding signature verses at the end of Adhyāya 4 (4.4.22), Vācaspati praises his patron King Nṛga and mentions his earlier works across the darśanas: the Nyāyakaṇikā (Mīmāṃsā), Tattvasamīkṣā (Vedānta), Tattvabindu (Mīmāṃsā/śabdabodha), and his treatises on Nyāya, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, and Vedānta.

The Bhāmatī by Vācaspatimiśra (fl. 9th–10th century CE) is an authoritative Advaita Vedānta sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and the foundational text of the Bhāmatī school (contrasted with Prakāśātman's Vivaraṇa school). Synthesizing Śaṅkara's hermeneutics with insights from Maṇḍana Miśra's Brahmasiddhi, Vācaspati articulates classic doctrinal positions, notably that the individual self (jīva) is the locus (āśraya) of beginningless nescience (avidyā) while Brahman is its object (viṣaya), and that meditative contemplation (dhyāna/upāsanā) mediated by a purified internal organ (manas) serves as the proximate cause of liberating intuition. The text spans the entirety of the Brahmasūtras and generated an influential sub-commentarial lineage, prominent among which are Amalānanda's Kalpataru and Appayya Dīkṣita's Parimala.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** Not determined. The text was taken from wisdomlib, and the printed source behind wisdomlib's Sanskrit text was not found. It is not Abhyaṅkar's BORI edition with Darśanāṅkura, and the checks below do not match it to the Umāśaṅkar Śarmā 'Ṛṣi' edition either.

The archive.org OCR of Umāśaṅkar Śarmā 'Ṛṣi''s Chowkhamba edition (item sarva-darshana-sangraha-prof.-uma-shankar-sharma-rishi) cites the same passage as '( बृह० उप० २।४।१२ )' (line 3577). The citation format therefore does not match, and the Gemini draft's 'probable' attribution to that edition is not supported.
- In the archive.org OCRs of Abhyankar (BORI), the Chowkhamba print and the Venkatesvara 1925 Hindi edition, no match was found for the slash-style references or the 'tatsadbrahmaṇe' invocation. The OCR quality is poor, so this is a weak negative.

**Other editions:**

G. Mainkar, 1978). — Standard modern scholarly reference edition with commentary.

**Translations:**
- E. B. Cowell and A. E. Gough, The Sarva-darśana-saṃgraha: or, Review of the Different Systems of Hindu Philosophy by Mádhava Áchárya, Trübner's Oriental Series, London: Trübner & Co., 1882 (translates chapters 1–15; 2nd ed. 1894, repr. Varanasi: Chowkhamba, 1961). (English)
- Johannes Bronkhorst, Compendium of All Philosophies: The Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha Translated, Leiden: Brill, 2025. (English)
- Madan Mohan Agrawal, The Sarva-Darśana-Saṃgraha of Mādhavācārya, with English Translation, Transliteration and Indices, Delhi: Chaukhamba Sanskrit Pratishthan, 2002. (English)
- Paul Deussen, Allgemeine Geschichte der Philosophie, vol. 1, part 3, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1908, pp. 190–344 (translates chapters 1–9). (German)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text containing all 16 chapters (darśanas): Cārvāka, Bauddha, Ārhata (Jaina), Rāmānuja, Pūrṇaprajña (Madhva), Nakulīśapāśupata, Śaiva, Pratyabhijñā, Raseśvara, Vaiśeṣika (Aulūkya), Akṣapāda (Nyāya), Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā), Pāṇinīya, Sāṅkhya, Pātañjala (Yoga), and Śāṅkara (Advaita Vedānta).

**Also known as:** Sarvadarśanasaṅgraha, Sāyaṇamādhavīya

**Attribution:** The introductory verses and colophons identify the author as Mādhava (Mādhavārya), son of Sāyaṇa (Sāyaṇamādhava), whose preceptor was Sarvajñaviṣṇu. He was traditionally conflated with his famous uncle Mādhavācārya (later Vidyāraṇya, brother of Sāyaṇa). Anantalal Thakur suggested authorship by Cannibhaṭṭa, son of Sarvajñaviṣṇu. Chapter 16 (Śāṅkaradarśana) is omitted in most northern manuscripts and was transmitted separately in some traditions, leading scholars (such as Johannes Bronkhorst) to debate whether the 16th chapter was originally composed together with chapters 1–15.

The Sarvadarśanasaṃgraha is an encyclopedic 14th-century Sanskrit doxographical survey of Indian philosophical systems composed in the Vijayanagara Empire by Mādhava (Sāyaṇa-Mādhava). It presents sixteen distinct schools in an ascending hierarchy of doctrinal adequacy, progressing from the materialist Cārvāka through Buddhism, Jainism, various Vaiṣṇava and Śaiva traditions, the classical orthodox systems (Vaiśeṣika, Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Pāṇinian linguistics, Sāṅkhya, Yoga), and culminating in Advaita Vedānta (Śāṅkaradarśana) as the pinnacle of philosophical knowledge. Each tradition is articulated from an insider perspective before its presuppositions are critiqued and superseded by the subsequent system, making the work one of premodern India's most important compendia of philosophical thought.

The Atharvavedasaṃhitā (Śaunaka recension) is the canonical fourth Veda of ancient India, comprising 730 hymns arranged across 20 kāṇḍas. It encompasses healing charms, exorcisms, apotropaic formulas, domestic and royal rites, alongside sublime metaphysical and cosmogonic hymns such as the Pṛthivīsūkta (Hymn to the Earth, 12.1) and the Vrātya book (Book 15). **Also known as:** Atharvaveda-Saṃhitā, Atharva-Veda Saṃhitā, Atharvaveda

**Attribution:** Traditionally viewed as apauruṣeya (authorless revelation) and attributed to the ancestral seer lineages of the Atharvans and Aṅgirases (hence also called Ātharvaṇāṅgirasa).

The Atharvavedasaṃhitā is the fourth collection of the Vedic scriptural canon, preserved principally in the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions. Unlike the sacrificial focus of the Ṛgveda, Sāmaveda, and Yajurveda, it encompasses a wide range of domestic, magical, and medical hymns, including incantations for healing, apotropaic charms against hostile powers, blessings for prosperity and harmony, and royal coronation rites. It also preserves notable speculative, cosmogonic, and philosophical hymns—such as the Bhūmisūkta (hymn to the Earth) and hymns to Skambha and Prāṇa—that mark an important conceptual transitional phase toward early Upaniṣadic thought.

**E-text:** Anshuman Pandey (University of Washington), first released April 1998 in CS/CSX encoding with ITRANS/LaTeX markup; archived in GRETIL as samavedu.htm (1_sanskr/1_veda/1_sam) and converted to TEI (sa_sAmavedasaMhitA.xml). The Sanskrit Library catalogue lists a 1999 Pandey version as one source of its XML Kauthuma text.

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL header and ilx_skt TEI header: 'Input by Anshuman Pandey ... Updated on: 08 Marc 1998; complete ed.' No printed edition is named.

This numbering is common to several prints, so it does not identify the edition. The Gemini draft's claim that the text conforms to Sātavalekar is unverified.

**Other editions:**

- Satyavrata Sāmaśramī (ed.), Sāmavedasaṃhitā with the Commentary of Sāyaṇācārya, 5 vols., Bibliotheca Indica 71, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1871–1878. — Major Indian scholarly edition with Sāyaṇa's bhāṣya.
- Śrīpāda Dāmodara Sātavalekar (ed.), Sāmaveda-Saṃhitā (Kauthuma-śākhā), Pardi: Svādhyāya Maṇḍala, 1956. — Widely cited standard Devanāgarī edition with svara accents and sequential numbering 1–1875.
- B. R. Sharma (ed.), Sāmavedasaṃhitā with Padapāṭha and the commentaries of Mādhava, Bharatasvāmin and Sāyaṇa, Tirupati: Kendriya Sanskrit Vidyapeetha, 1967. — Scholarly multi-commentary edition.
- Willem Caland (ed.), Die Jaiminīya-Saṃhitā mit Auszügen aus den Kommentaren, Breslau: M. & H. Marcus, 1907. — Critical edition of the rival Jaiminīya recension.

**Translations:**
- John Stevenson, Translation of the Sanhitá of the Sáma Veda, London: Oriental Translation Fund, 1842. (English)
- Theodor Benfey, Die Hymnen des Sâma-Veda, herausgegeben, übersetzt und mit Glossar versehen, Leipzig: F. A. Brockhaus, 1848. (German)
- Ralph T. H. Griffith, The Hymns of the Sāmaveda, Benares: E. J. Lazarus and Co., 1893. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete Kauthuma ārcika text, verses numbered continuously 1–1875: Pūrvārcika (Āgneya, Aindra and Pāvamāna kāṇḍas, vv. 1–585), Āraṇyaka kāṇḍa and Mahānāmnyārcika (vv. 586–650, ending with the five purīṣapadas), and Uttarārcika (vv. 651–1875). Ends with the colophon 'iti sāmavedasaṃhitā samāptā'. Unaccented; no gāna (song-book) texts.

**Also known as:** Sāmaveda, Sāmaveda-Saṃhitā, Sāmavedasaṃhitā (Kauthumaśākhā)

**Attribution:** Traditional Vedic Śruti text of the Kauthuma recension, considered apauruṣeya ('unauthored revelation') in orthodox Hindu tradition and revealed to ancient ṛṣis; compilation is traditionally attributed in epic and Purāṇic traditions to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa and transmission to his disciple Jaimini.

The Sāmavedasaṃhitā is the liturgical verse collection (ārcika) providing the textual base (yoni) for the melodies (sāman) intoned by the Udgātṛ priest during Śrauta sacrificial rituals, particularly the Soma sacrifices. Preserved here in the standard Kauthuma recension, the collection comprises 1,875 mantras divided into the Pūrvārcika (single stanzas arranged by deity—principally Agni, Indra, and Soma Pavamāna—followed by the Āraṇyaka/Mahānāmnī section) and the Uttarārcika (strophes and triplets arranged according to ritual execution). With the exception of approximately 75 stanzas, all verses are drawn from the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā (predominantly Mandalas VIII and IX), frequently showing distinct dialectal and phonetic variations adapted to musical chant.

While Vedic texts are traditionally categorized as unauthored revelation (śruti/apauruṣeya), the text attributes specific thematic cycles to ancient authorities: Books 1–5 and 14 are closely associated with Yājñavalkya Vājasaneya, whereas Books 6–10 (the Agnicayana) preserve the traditions and lineage of Śāṇḍilya.

The Śatapathabrāhmaṇa ('Brāhmaṇa of a Hundred Paths') is the monumental prose ritual commentary attached to the White (Śukla) Yajurveda and the most extensive surviving Brāhmaṇa text. It provides detailed liturgical instructions, theological rationales, cosmological speculations, and mythological narratives (including the flood legend of Manu and the story of Purūravas and Urvaśī) for the principal Vedic śrauta rituals, including the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnihotra, Cāturmāsya, Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Agnicayana (the construction of the bird-shaped brick fire-altar), Aśvamedha, and Pravargya. In the Mādhyandina recension, it is arranged in fourteen kāṇḍas reflecting two major liturgical traditions: Books 1–5 and 14 represent the tradition of Yājñavalkya, while Books 6–10 preserve the altar-building doctrine of Śāṇḍilya. Originating in northern India around 800–600 BCE, the work constitutes a crucial transitional monument between early Vedic ritualism and the nascent philosophical thought of the early Upaniṣads.

The Kaṭhopaniṣad is a classical mukhya Upaniṣad of the Kaṭha school of the Black (Kṛṣṇa) Yajurveda, framed as an initiatory dialogue between the boy Naciketas and Yama, the lord of death. The Āpastambagṛhyasūtra is the domestic ritual manual belonging to the Āpastamba branch of the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda, forming part of the larger Āpastamba Kalpasūtra corpus. The accompanying ritual mantras are drawn largely from the separate Āpastamba Mantrapāṭha (Ekāgnikāṇḍa). This e-text presents the complete sūtras accompanied in full by two classic commentaries: Haradatta's concise Anākulā (c. 12th century CE) and Sudarśanācārya's exhaustive Gṛhyatātparyadarśana (c. 14th–15th century CE).

Divided into four prapāṭhakas containing forty kāṇḍikās, the treatise lays down rules for domestic fire offerings (pākayajñas), new- and full-moon rites, domestic seasonal sacrifices, ancestral rites (śrāddha), and the full cycle of life-cycle saṃskāras (including upanayana, marriage, and tonsure). Some readings are corrected from the manuscript, and the gap at fols. 181–198 is partly filled from Divyāvadāna (ed. Cowell & Neil, 1886), pp. 453–461.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Begins with the piṇḍoddāna (fol. 91v3) and ends with 'bhaiṣajyavastu samāptam' (fol. 239). The e-text marks these lacunae: fols. 95–140 missing (seg. 427), a gap of 46 folios; fols. 181–198 missing, partly filled from Divyāvadāna 453–461 (Sudhanakumārāvadāna, segs. 4078–4302); fols. 200–210 and 212–217 not present except as re-edited Anavataptagāthā portions (MSV,Wi); fols. 220–221 missing; jumps at 222→225 and 225→228; plus smaller akṣara losses. The Tibetan translation of the vastu is complete by comparison.

**Also known as:** Mūlasarvāstivāda-vinayavastu: Bhaiṣajyavastu, Vinayavastu, Vastu 6: Bhaiṣajyavastu, 'Dul ba gzhi, Sman gyi gzhi (Toh 1, chapter 6), Genben shuo yiqieyou bu pinaye yaoshi (根本說一切有部毘奈耶藥事, Taishō 1448)

**Attribution:** Canonical Vinaya literature of the Mūlasarvāstivāda school, traditionally received as buddhavacana and transmitted anonymously within the monastic saṅgha.

The Bhaiṣajyavastu ('Chapter on Medicines') is the sixth section of the Vinayavastu in the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya. While opening with monastic regulations concerning permissible medicines, dietary schedules, and the care of ill monks, the vast majority of the chapter is narrative, incorporating numerous avadānas, jātakas, legendary travels of the Buddha to northwest India, apotropaic formulas (including an early version of the Mahāmāyūrī spell), and prophecy accounts. The text survives in Sanskrit birch-bark manuscripts from Gilgit and the Schøyen Collection, alongside canonical translations into Tibetan and Chinese.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the short recension (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā) in 32 segments, including the opening salutation, the dialogue between Avalokiteśvara and Śāriputra, the mantra, and the closing colophon (corresponding precisely to p. 97 of P. L. Vaidya's edition).

**Also known as:** Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtram (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), Prajñāhṛdayasūtra, Bhagavatīprajñāpāramitāhṛdaya, Heart Sūtra (short recension), Bore boluomiduo xin jing, 般若波羅蜜多心經, Shes rab snying po

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Traditionally delivered by the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara to Śāriputra under the inspired sanction of the Buddha. Modern scholarship (notably Jan Nattier 1992) has argued that the shorter Sanskrit text was redacted or back-translated from Kumārajīva's Chinese translation of the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, a hypothesis that remains a subject of ongoing critical debate.

The Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayasūtra ('Heart Sūtra') is one of the most widely recited and influential texts of Mahāyāna Buddhism, condensing the vast Prajñāpāramitā literature into an essential doctrinal summary. This e-text presents the short recension (saṃkṣiptamātṛkā), which omits the traditional introductory frame (nidāna) and concludes directly with the mantra. Avalokiteśvara explains to Śāriputra that the five aggregates and all constituent phenomena of Buddhist abhidharma are empty of inherent existence ('form is emptiness, emptiness is form'), culminating in the celebrated mantra 'gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā'.

The Āyuḥparyantasūtra ('Discourse on the Limits of Lifespan') is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It provides a comprehensive scholastic catalogue of the life expectancies of beings across the cosmological realms, progressing from the hells (naraka) and hungry ghosts (preta), through the four human continents (Jambudvīpa, Pūrvavideha, Avaragodānīya, and Uttarakuru), to the heavens of the desire, form, and formless realms up to the summit of cyclic existence (Naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana). The Lalitavistara ('The Extensive Account of the [Buddha's] Play') is an elaborate Mahāyāna sūtra in 27 chapters composed in mixed Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit prose and verse. It narrates the sacred biography of Śākyamuni Buddha from his decision to descend from Tuṣita heaven, his miraculous conception and birth in Lumbinī, his luxurious princely youth, four encounters, and great renunciation, to his austerities, defeat of Māra, awakening beneath the Bodhi tree, and first turning of the wheel of Dharma in Ṛṣipatana. The Śālistambasūtra ('Rice Seedling Sūtra') is a foundational Mahāyāna sūtra on the doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda). **Coverage:** complete — Complete text across all 40 chapters (parivartas), beginning with the Nidānaparivarta (Vaidya p. 1) and concluding with the colophon of the 40th chapter (Vaidya p. 304).

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as buddhavacana delivered by Gautama Buddha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha, addressed principally to the bodhisattva youth Candraprabha (Candraprabha Kumārabhūta).

The Samādhirājasūtra ('King of Samādhis Sūtra', often cited by Indian Madhyamaka commentators as Candrapradīpasūtra) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture in 40 chapters expounding the meditative absorption (samādhi) that reveals the fundamental equality and emptiness of all phenomena (sarvadharmasvabhāvasamatā). Delivered by the Buddha on Vulture Peak to the youth Candraprabha, the text combines exposition of non-arising and ultimate reality with teachings on ethical discipline, ascetic practices (dhūtaguṇa), dhāraṇī formulas, and past-life narratives (jātakas). It was widely quoted as a scriptural authority on emptiness by Candrakīrti, Śāntideva, and Prajñākaramati, and served as a foundational sūtra source for contemplative traditions in Tibet, particularly Sūtra Mahāmudrā.

The Saddharmapuṇḍarīkasūtra ('The White Lotus of the True Dharma') is one of the most celebrated and influential Mahāyāna scriptures. It propounds the doctrine of the One Vehicle (ekayāna), declaring that the apparent three vehicles (śrāvakayāna, pratyekabuddhayāna, and bodhisattvayāna) are provisional pedagogical devices (upāyakauśalya) and that all beings are destined for unexcelled awakening. The Arthaviniścayasūtra ('Discourse on the Ascertainment of Meaning') is an early Buddhist doctrinal compendium that systematically presents twenty-seven core categories of Buddhist doctrine and meditation practice. It opens with a thematic list (uddeśa) followed by analytical definitions (vibhaṅga) of the five aggregates, eighteen elements, twelve sense fields, twelvefold dependent origination, four noble truths, twenty-two faculties, thirty-seven aids to awakening (bodhipakṣadharmāḥ), the absorptions (dhyānas), formless attainments, and the marks of a Buddha. Closely aligned with mainstream Abhidharma and Sautrāntika taxonomies, it served as the base text for Vīryaśrīdatta's 8th-century *Nibandhana*.

The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti ('Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī') is one of the most revered and influential liturgical and doctrinal scriptures of late Indian Buddhism. The Mahāsāhasrapramardanī ('Destroyer of the Great Trichiliocosm') is an influential apotropaic Buddhist sūtra and the first text of the fivefold Pañcarakṣā collection. Set at Gṛdhrakūṭa in Rājagṛha following earthquakes, storms, and demonic incursions in Vaiśālī, the Buddha instructs Brahmā, Indra, and the Four Great Heavenly Kings (caturmahārājas) in powerful dhāraṇī incantations and ritual procedures to avert epidemic diseases, evil spirits, and cosmic calamities. Flourishing in Sanskrit manuscript traditions across Northern India and Nepal from the medieval era onward, the scripture was translated into Tibetan (c. 800 CE) and Chinese (by Dānapāla in 983 CE, T 999), and its central protective force became personified as one of the Five Protective Goddesses.

- Walter Liebenthal, The Sutra of the Lord of Healing (Bhaishajyaguru Vaiduryaprabha Tathagata), Peking: The Society of Chinese Buddhists, 1936. (English)
- Raoul Birnbaum, The Healing Buddha, Boulder: Shambhala Publications, 1979. (English)
- Dharmachakra Translation Committee, The Detailed Account of the Previous Aspirations of the Blessed Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabha (Toh 504), 84000: Translating the Words of the Buddha, 2021. (English)
- Keiyō Arai (新井慧譽), Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra (Yakushi-kyō Kenkyū), Tokyo, 1974. (Japanese)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the sūtra from the opening nidāna (evaṃ mayā śrutam) through the twelve vows, pure land description, ritual prescriptions, and yakṣa generals' pledges, to the final title colophon (āryabhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājaṃ nāma mahāyānasūtram).

**Also known as:** Bhaiṣajyagurusūtra, Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhasūtra, Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājaprabhāva, Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabhasya Tathāgatasya Pūrvapraṇidhānaviśeṣavistara, 'Phags pa bcom ldan 'das sman gyi bla bai ḍū rya'i 'od kyi sngon gyi smon lam gyi khyad par rgyas pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo

**Attribution:** A canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist scripture presented as the teaching of Śākyamuni Buddha delivered in Vaiśālī in dialogue with the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī.

The Bhaiṣajyaguruvaidūryaprabharājasūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set in Vaiśālī, in which Śākyamuni Buddha expounds to the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī the twelve past aspirations made by the Tathāgata Bhaiṣajyaguruvaiḍūryaprabha (the Medicine Buddha) during his bodhisattva career. The text describes his eastern pure realm, Vaiḍūryanirbhāsa, and prescribes ritual veneration—such as reciting his name and sūtra, erecting images, and offering banners and lamps—to heal diseases, prevent untimely death, and protect states from turmoil. The work concludes with protective pledges uttered by twelve yakṣa generals.

**95% credible interval:** 386 CE – 590 CE

**Posterior median:** 518 CE

The Śrīguhyasamājatantra (also known as the Tathāgataguhyaka) is the foundational scripture of esoteric Mahāyāna Buddhism belonging to the Anuttarayoga / Mahāyoga class of tantras. In eighteen chapters (paṭalas 1–17 forming the root tantra and paṭala 18 serving as the Uttaratantra or explanatory continuation), it expounds the maṇḍala of the five Tathāgata families, deity yoga, consecration rituals, and subtle-body inner yogic practices.
