**Attribution:** Canonical Vinaya scripture preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit belonging to the Lokottaravāda branch of the Mahāsāṃghika school, as explicitly declared in the opening statement: 'āryamahāsāṃghikānāṃ lokottaravādināṃ madhyadeśikānāṃ pāṭhena vinayapiṭakasya mahāvastuye ādi' (vol. 1, p. 2).

The Mahāvastu ('The Great Story') is an extensive Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit canonical text preserved by the Lokottaravāda sub-sect of the Mahāsāṃghika school, nominally forming the opening section of their Vinayapiṭaka. It presents an expansive biography of the Buddha Gautama, tracing his past lives, his bodhisattva path across the ten spiritual stages (daśabhūmi), his vow under previous Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara, and his final awakening and initial teaching career. Rich in jātakas, avadānas, and early doctrinal discourses, the work was compiled and expanded over several centuries (c. 2nd century BCE to 4th century CE) and stands as a key witness for early Lokottaravāda supramundane buddhology and proto-Mahāyāna concepts.

**Attribution:** The Sekoddeśa is traditionally regarded as an excerpt from the fifth chapter of the lost Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddha or Mūlakālacakratantra), delivered by the Buddha to Sucandra, the king of Śambhala. Raniero Gnoli reconstructed and edited the Sanskrit text of the 174 verses from the single surviving Sanskrit manuscript folio, citations in Raviśrījñāna's Amṛtakaṇikāṭippaṇī, and the Sanskrit commentary of Nāropa (Sekoddeśaṭīkā); this reliance on Nāropa's commentary caused GRETIL to erroneously file the e-text under Nāropa.

The Sekoddeśa ('Summary of Initiation') consists of 174 verses traditionally considered an excerpt from the fifth chapter of the lost Kālacakra root tantra (Paramādibuddha). Presented as a dialogue between the Buddha and King Sucandra of Śambhala, it provides the fundamental exposition of the Kālacakra initiation system, including the seven worldly initiations of entering disciples and the higher supramundane empowerments. The text details subtle-body physiology, the visionary signs appearing in empty space (dhūmādi-nimitta), and the realization of imperishable bliss (akṣarasukha).

**Works in this e-text:**

- Bhāvanākrama III (Kamalaśīla, root text)

**Also known as:** bsGom pa'i rim pa, Stages of Meditation

**Attribution:** Composed in Tibet by the Indian Madhyamaka master Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) at the behest of King Trisong Detsen (Khri srong lde btsan) following the arrival of Chinese Chan masters. The Bhāvanākrama ('Stages of Meditation') by Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) is an influential triad of treatises formulating the graduated Mahāyāna path according to the Yogācāra-Madhyamaka synthesis. Composed in Tibet in connection with the Samyé (bSam yas) debate, it defends the classical Indian gradualist method of spiritual development against the sudden, non-conceptualizing quietism attributed to the Chinese Chan master Heshang Moheyan. Across the three works, Kamalaśīla systematizes the cultivation of compassion (karuṇā), the awakening mind (bodhicitta), and the balanced union (yuganaddha) of calm abiding (śamatha) and analytical discernment (vipaśyanā) leading to the non-conceptual realization of emptiness.

The Tattvasaṃgraha ('Compendium of Reality') by the 8th-century Madhyamaka-Yogācāra master Śāntarakṣita is a monumental verse treatise in 26 chapters (ca. 3,646 kārikās) providing an exhaustive critique of classical Indian philosophical systems. Grounded in the Buddhist epistemological framework (pramāṇa) of Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, it systematically refutes rival theories regarding primordial nature (prakṛti), God (īśvara), the eternal Self (ātman), the categories of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, the eternity of sound and Vedic authority, and various non-Buddhist epistemologies, while establishing Buddhist tenets such as universal momentariness, nominal exclusion (apoha), dependent origination, and the omniscience of the Buddha. It serves as one of the most important doxographical sources for 8th-century Indian philosophy, preserving extensive fragments and doctrines of otherwise lost Brahmanical, Jaina, and materialist thinkers.

The Tattvasaṃgraha by Śāntarakṣita and its Pañjikā by Kamalaśīla constitute an encyclopedic late 8th-century monument of Indian Buddhist philosophy. **Coverage:** complete — All 21 adhikāras (Mahāyānasiddhi ... Caryāpratiṣṭhā), verses + bhāṣya, ending '... caryāpratiṣṭhādhikāro nāmaikaviṃśatitamo 'dhikāraḥ // samāptaś ca mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra iti'. ca. 800 verse markers (Msa_1.1–Msa_20.61, Bagchi numbering, in which the final chapter is numbered 20); Bagchi page markers 2–180, i.e. the whole Bagchi text. Some lacunae of the unique manuscript are marked with dots/brackets as in the edition.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārakārikā (Maitreya, root text)
- Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkārabhāṣya (Vasubandhu, commentary)

**Also known as:** Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra, Mahāyānasūtrālaṅkāra, Sūtrālaṃkāra, MSA/MSABh, Theg pa chen po mdo sde'i rgyan, 大乘莊嚴經論 (Dasheng zhuangyan jing lun)

**Attribution:** The verses are attributed in the Tibetan tradition to Maitreya(nātha) (one of the 'five treatises of Maitreya', Tib. D 4020), in the Chinese tradition (T 1604) the whole work to Asaṅga; Bagchi's and the GRETIL edition title ascribe it to Asaṅga. The bhāṣya is generally attributed to Vasubandhu (Tibetan D 4026 names the author 'Vyavadātasamaya-mahābodhisattva', an epithet also found in the Sanskrit chapter colophons: 'mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāre vyavadātasamayamahābodhisattvabhāṣite'). Some modern scholars hold that kārikās and bhāṣya stem from the same author/circle.

The Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra ('Ornament of the Mahāyāna Sūtras') is a foundational Yogācāra treatise of ca. 800 verses in 21 chapters, here transmitted together with its prose bhāṣya. It defends the authenticity of the Mahāyāna as Buddha's word and systematically treats refuge, spiritual lineage (gotra), the arising of bodhicitta, practice, reality (tattva), the perfections, the factors of awakening and the bodhisattva's qualities and stages, culminating in buddhahood. The bhāṣya explains each verse and supplies the structure of the argument; the work was translated into Chinese (T 1604) and Tibetan (D 4020, 4026) and commented upon by Asvabhāva and Sthiramati.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: title line, ascription, all 30 kārikās (numbered Tvk_1–Tvk_30) and the closing colophon 'triṃśikāvijñaptikārikāḥ samāptāḥ / kṛtir iyam ācāryavasubandhoḥ'.

**Also known as:** Triṃśikā, Triṃśikākārikā, Triṃśikāvijñapti, Triṃśikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi

**Attribution:** Ascribed in the opening title line and concluding colophon to Ācārya Vasubandhu (kṛtir iyam ācāryavasubandhoḥ); the attribution to Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE) is universally accepted in Indian, Tibetan, and East Asian traditions.

The Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā (Thirty Verses on Representation-Only) by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE) is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra Buddhism. In thirty concise kārikās, it expounds the threefold transformation of consciousness (vijñānapariṇāma)—the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the afflicted mentation (manas), and the six object-cognizing consciousnesses (pravṛttivijñāna)—alongside the doctrine of the three natures (trisvabhāva). The work outlines the path to realizing mere representation (vijñaptimātratā), culminating in the transformation of the psycho-physical base (āśrayaparāvṛtti) and liberation.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Bodhisattvabhūmi comprising all four yogasthānas (Ādhāra-, Ādhārānudharma-, Ādhārapratiniṣṭhā-, and Niṣṭhāgata-yogasthāna), running from the opening gotrapaṭala to the concluding pratiṣṭhāpaṭala and final colophon.

**Also known as:** Yogācārabhūmi (Stage 15: Bodhisattvabhūmi), Bodhisattvabhūmiśāstra, Byang chub sems dpa'i sa

The Bodhisattvabhūmi constitutes the fifteenth and most influential section of the encyclopedic Yogācārabhūmi, composed in approximately the 4th century CE. It serves as an exhaustive manual of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path, systematically treating spiritual lineage (gotra), the generation of the aspiration for awakening (bodhicitta), the perfections (pāramitās), ethics (śīla), and the stages of spiritual maturation (vihāras and bhūmis). Its fourth chapter, the Tattvārthapaṭala, forms a cornerstone of early Yogācāra philosophy, presenting a foundational analysis of the inexpressible nature of reality (nirabhilāpyasvabhāva) underlying linguistic and conceptual designations (prajñapti).

(Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region, 16/1–2; Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2013). — Critical edition of Sthiramati's sub-commentary in Sanskrit, which embeds and discusses the root lemmas.

- Artemus B. Engle, The Inner Science of Buddhist Practice: Vasubandhu's Summary of the Five Heaps with Commentary by Sthiramati (Ithaca, NY: Snow Lion Publications, 2009). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete Sanskrit retro-translation from Tibetan in three adhikāras (rūpaskandha; vedanā-, saṃjñā-, and saṃskāraskandha; vijñānaskandha, āyatanas, and dhātus), arranged into 167 numbered prose sections, concluding with Shastri's two-verse Sanskrit reconstruction colophon.

**Also known as:** Pañcaskandhaka, Phung po lnga'i rab tu byed pa, Ta ch'eng wu yün lun, 大乘五蘊論

**Attribution:** Root text authored by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th c. CE). Note that this specific electronic text is not derived from an original Sanskrit manuscript, but represents a modern Sanskrit retro-translation/reconstruction from the Tibetan bstan 'gyur translation (D 4059 / P 5560) made by Shanti Bhikshu Shastri in 1955/1956. An authentic original Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript of the treatise was subsequently identified in the Potala Palace collection and critically edited by Li Xuezhu and Ernst Steinkellner in 2008.

The Pañcaskandhaprakaraṇa (or Pañcaskandhaka) is an introductory Abhidharma manual composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE) that presents a systematic categorization of mental and physical phenomena according to the Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda framework. It defines the components of existence categorized under the five aggregates (skandhas), twelve sense fields (āyatanas), and eighteen elements (dhātus), famously incorporating the specifically Yogācāra doctrines of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) and afflicted mentality (kliṣṭamanas) alongside the standard catalogue of fifty-one mental factors (caittas). This specific electronic text represents the 1955/1956 Sanskrit retro-translation from Tibetan executed by Shanti Bhikshu Shastri, which historically served as the primary Sanskrit surrogate for the work prior to the rediscovery and 2008 publication of the original Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript from the Potala Palace.

The Pañcaskandhakavibhāṣā is a major 6th-century CE Yogācāra Abhidharma commentary by Sthiramati on Vasubandhu's Pañcaskandhaka. It offers an exhaustive scholastic analysis of the five aggregates (skandha: form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness), mental factors (caitta), the eight consciousnesses—including the functions and proofs of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna)—and the sensory bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu). - Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya (Sthiramati, commentary)

**Attribution:** Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE) composed the 30 root verses (Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā). Sthiramati (c. 6th century CE, c. 510–570 CE) composed the prose commentary (bhāṣya), as confirmed by the closing colophon ('triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣyaṃ samāptam // kṛtir ācāryastiramateḥ //').

Vasubandhu's Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā ('Thirty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational work of Yogācāra/Vijñānavāda Buddhist philosophy outlining the three transformations of consciousness (ālayavijñāna, kliṣṭamanas, and pravṛttivijñāna), the three intrinsic natures (trisvabhāva), and the realization of cognition-only (vijñaptimātratā). Sthiramati's Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya (c. 6th century CE) is the sole surviving Sanskrit commentary on the text preserved in the original language. It systematically expounds Yogācāra psychology, the nature of mental factors (caitta), the role of metaphorical designation (upacāra) in establishing consciousness-only without external objects, and the soteriological progression toward fundamental transformation (āśrayaparāvṛtti).

The Viṃśatikāvijñaptimātratāsiddhi ('Proof of Mere Representation in Twenty Verses') is a foundational treatise of Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda philosophy composed by Vasubandhu in the 4th to 5th century CE. **Coverage:** complete — Contains the complete work: introductory prose, all 22 stanzas, full autocommentary (vṛtti), and closing colophon.

The bhāṣya is ascribed to Vasubandhu in the colophon: 'madhyāntavibhāgakārikābhāṣyaṃ samāptam // kṛtir ācāryabhadantavasubandhoḥ'.

The Madhyāntavibhāga ('Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a short Yogācāra verse treatise in five chapters, here transmitted with Vasubandhu's prose bhāṣya. It treats the characteristics of unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa) and emptiness, the three natures, the obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), the cultivation of the antidotes with its stages and results, and the supremacy of the Great Vehicle, presented as a middle way between reification and denial. The Sanskrit text survives in a single manuscript discovered in Tibet; Sthiramati's ṭīkā comments on both kārikās and bhāṣya.

Aiyaswami Sastri's edition.

**Also known as:** Tattvasiddhiśāstra, Tattvasiddhi, Chengshi lun, Ch'eng-shih lun, Jōjitsuron

**Attribution:** Authored in Sanskrit by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE). The original Sanskrit text was lost in India, surviving intact only in Kumārajīva's Chinese translation (T 1646, 成實論 Chengshi lun, 411–412 CE). This Sanskrit e-text represents the modern retroversion/reconstruction from Chinese into Sanskrit by N. Aiyaswami Sastri.

The Satyasiddhiśāstra (also reconstructed as Tattvasiddhiśāstra; Chinese: Chengshi lun) is an extensive Buddhist scholastic treatise in 202 chapters by Harivarman (c. 3rd–4th century CE), reflecting Bahuśrutīya and Dārṣṭāntika/Sautrāntika doctrines. Organized around an introductory section and the Four Noble Truths, it defends a two-truth framework affirming the emptiness (śūnyatā) of both persons and dharmas, and expounds the progressive dismantling of provisional, phenomenal, and ultimate conceptual constructs. While lost in India, Kumārajīva's Chinese translation formed the foundational text of the Chinese Chengshi (Japanese Jōjitsu) school.

The Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā (subtitled Āgamānusāriṇī) is Sthiramati's (c. 6th century CE) exhaustive Sanskrit sub-commentary on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya and the root verses attributed to Maitreya. ## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the opening portion of chapter 4 (traditionally Pratipakṣabhāvanāpariccheda, titled 'Phalanirdeśa' in the manuscript colophon), running from the introductory exposition of the thirty-seven bodhipakṣyadharmas through the commentary on kārikā IV.6 (on the five spiritual faculties, pañcendriya). It breaks off before the commentary on the five powers (pañca balāni, kārikā IV.7ff.), seven limbs of awakening (bodhyaṅga), eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), and the subsequent exposition of the stages (avasthā) and fruits (phala), which complete the chapter in Yamaguchi's edition (pp. 165–198).

**Also known as:** Āgamānusāriṇī, Āgamānusāriṇī Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā, Madhyāntavibhāgasūtrabhāṣyaṭīkā, Pratipakṣabhāvanāpariccheda, Phalanirdeśa

**Attribution:** The sub-commentary is authored by the 6th-century Yogācāra master Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE) on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya (which itself glosses the root kārikās attributed to Maitreya/Asaṅga). In the surviving Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscript from Nepal, the chapter colophons and final colophon entitle the work 'Āgamānusāriṇī Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā' and explicitly attribute it to Sthiramati (ācāryasthiramati / ācāryabhadantasthiramati).

This text contains the opening portion of chapter 4 of Sthiramati's Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā (subtitled Āgamānusāriṇī in the manuscript colophons), an exegesis on Vasubandhu's Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya. The chapter analyzes the cultivation of meditative antidotes (pratipakṣabhāvanā) formulated as the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣyadharma). The present e-text covers the exegesis through the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), and four bases of psychic power (ṛddhipāda) to the five spiritual faculties (pañcendriya), explaining their functions in entering the four noble truths and progressing through the stages of preparation and penetration.

**Posterior median:** 542 CE

## Overview

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Mahayana, Yogacara)

**Genre:** tika (sub-commentary)

**Estimated date:** c. 6th c. CE

The fourth chapter (Pratipakṣabhāvanāpariccheda, 'Cultivation of the Antidotes') of Sthiramati's Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā, in the new critical edition prepared by Sebastian Nehrdich. The chapter treats the cultivation (bhāvanā) of the thirty-seven factors conducive to awakening (bodhipakṣya-dharma) as antidotes (pratipakṣa) to the obstacles set out earlier in the text: the four applications of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna), the four right efforts (samyakprahāṇa), the four bases of supernatural power (ṛddhipāda), the five faculties (indriya) and powers (bala), the seven factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga), and the eightfold noble path (āryāṣṭāṅgamārga), glossing Vasubandhu's bhāṣya word by word.

**History:** Composed by Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE), the most prolific commentator of the early Yogācāra tradition. This record designates a fresh critical edition of the Sanskrit text of chapter 4, established directly from the Nepalese manuscript and collated against the standard editions and the Tibetan witnesses.

**Related works:** Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā (Maitreya/Asaṅga), Madhyāntavibhāgabhāṣya (Vasubandhu), Madhyāntavibhāgaṭīkā (full work; cf. `SA_T06_sthmavt`, `SA_T06_sthmavtyg`, `SA_T06_sthmavt1`)

The ninth chapter of the Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, titled Ātmavādapratiṣedha ('Refutation of the Assertion of a Self') or Pudgalaviniścaya ('Investigation of the Person'), is an unversified prose treatise appended to Vasubandhu's masterwork. In this text, Vasubandhu defends the canonical Buddhist teaching of selflessness (anātman) against the personalist doctrines of the Buddhist Vātsīputrīya / Pudgalavādin tradition as well as non-Buddhist substantialist soul theories of the Nyāya and Vaiśeṣika schools. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: all kārikās of chapters 1–8 (VAkK_1.1–8.43; chapter 9 has no kārikās), with chapter colophons. Numbering slip: kārikā 2.32 is labelled 'VAkK_2.33' (so 2.33 occurs twice and 2.32 seems missing), but the text is present.

**Also known as:** Abhidharmakośa, Abhidharmakośamūlakārikā, Chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi tshig le'ur byas pa, Apidamo jushe lun ben song (阿毘達磨俱舍論本頌)

**Attribution:** Universally accepted as the work of the Buddhist master Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE), who also authored the auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya).

The Abhidharmakośakārikā consists of approximately six hundred verses in eight chapters composed by Vasubandhu (c. 4th–5th century CE), synthesizing the doctrinal system of the Sarvāstivāda-Vaibhāṣika school of Abhidharma. The text classifies all conditioned and unconditioned phenomena across eight subjects: ultimate constituents (dhātu), sensory and psychological faculties (indriya), cosmological realms (loka), intentional action (karma), underlying afflictions (anuśaya), noble spiritual paths and attainers (mārgapudgala), transcendent cognitions (jñāna), and meditative absorptions (samāpatti). Designed for memorization, it served as the baseline verse manual upon which Vasubandhu constructed his famous auto-commentary (Abhidharmakośabhāṣya) offering critical Sautrāntika critiques of Vaibhāṣika tenets, and it remains the fundamental Abhidharma textbook throughout East Asian and Tibetan Buddhism.

Haribhaṭṭa's Jātakamālā is an ornate collection of Buddhist birth stories composed in campū form (alternating classical Sanskrit prose and verse) around the 5th century CE. Written in deliberate emulation of Āryaśūra's famed Jātakamālā, Haribhaṭṭa's work illustrates the bodhisattva's cultivation of the perfections (pāramitā) while relying extensively on narrative traditions closer to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda avadāna literature rather than the Pāli Jātakas. **Coverage:** complete — Contains the complete text: the opening benedictory stanza, all 140 numbered sections of numerical categories, and the concluding colophon.

**Also known as:** Dharmasangraha, Dharmasārasamuccaya

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna in the closing colophon ('iti nāgārjunapādaviracito 'yaṃ dharmasaṃgrahaḥ samāptaḥ'). Modern scholarship regards this attribution as pseudepigraphic and considers the work a scholastic compendium of numerical lists assembled later in the first millennium CE.

The Dharmasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit Buddhist glossary consisting of 140 numbered entries categorizing doctrinal concepts and numerical dharmas (mātṛkā). It enumerates foundational Buddhist frameworks common to early Buddhism and Mahāyāna, including the three jewels, three vehicles, five Buddhas, four immeasurables (brahmavihāra), perfections (pāramitā), aggregates (skandha), sense fields (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and conditioned mental factors (caitasika). The text served as an essential pedagogical and reference manual for monastic education, especially within the Nepalese Buddhist manuscript tradition.

The Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra (also known as the Ekallavīratantra) is an Anuttarayoga / Yoginī-class Buddhist tantra focused on the wrathful deity Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa (Acala) and his consort Dveṣavajrī (Vajradhātvīśvarī). Chapter 2 of the Bhagavadgītā (designated Sāṅkhyayoga, 72 verses) forms part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata and serves as a foundational synthesis of the poem's philosophical teaching. In it, Kṛṣṇa addresses Arjuna's despondency by distinguishing the eternal, indestructible self (ātman) from the perishable physical body, propounding action without attachment to results (karmayoga), and detailing the characteristics of the sage of steady wisdom (sthitaprajña). This e-text provides the Sanskrit root verses interwoven with four classic commentaries: the influential Subodhinī of Śrīdhara Svāmin, the dialectical Advaitic Gūḍhārthadīpikā of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava expositions Sārārthavarṣiṇī of Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Gītābhūṣaṇa of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

**Attribution:** The Bhagavadgītā is traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. Śrīdhara Svāmin's Subodhinī dates to c. 14th–15th century. Chapter 3 (Karma-yoga) of the Bhagavadgītā contains 43 verses wherein Kṛṣṇa resolves Arjuna's perplexity regarding the relative merits of renunciation/knowledge (jñāna) versus engagement in action (karma). Kṛṣṇa establishes that physical inaction is impossible and prescribes selfless performance of duty without desire for fruit (niṣkāma karma) as a sacred sacrifice (yajña), warning against desire (kāma) and anger (krodha) as the primary obstacles. This electronic file presents the chapter alongside four major Sanskrit commentaries: Śrīdhara Svāmin's concise Subodhinī, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Advaita-Bhakti Gūḍhārthadīpikā, and the two major Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava expositions, Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthadarśinī and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Also known as:** Bhagavadgītā adhyāya 4, Jñānakarmasannyāsayoga, Brahmārpaṇayoga

**Attribution:** The root text of the Bhagavadgītā is an episode of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa. The four commentaries are by Śrīdharasvāmin (14th–15th c.), the Advaita scholar-devotee Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th c.), and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ācāryas Viśvanātha Cakravartin (c. 1626–1708) and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (18th c.).

Chapter 4 of the Bhagavadgītā (designated Jñānakarmasannyāsayoga or Brahmārpaṇayoga) spans 42 verses in which Kṛṣṇa outlines the ancient line of transmission (paramparā) of sacred wisdom, reveals the theological rationale for his divine descent (avatāra) in every age to preserve dharma, and expounds the nature of action (karma), improper action (vikarma), and inaction (akarma). He explains how work undertaken in the spirit of sacrifice and detached dedication to Brahman incurs no bondage, and exalts spiritual wisdom (jñāna) as the supreme sanctifier and fire that consumes all accumulated karma. In this e-text, each verse is presented with four distinct commentaries: the Subodhinī of Śrīdharasvāmin, the Gūḍhārthadīpikā of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, the Sārārthadarśinī of Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and the Gītābhūṣaṇa of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

**Attribution:** The Bhagavadgītā is an embedded episode within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa. This digital edition presents the root text alongside four commentaries spanning Advaita Vedānta and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism: the Subodhinī of Śrīdhara Svāmin (c. 14th–15th century), the Gūḍhārthadīpikā of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (c. 16th–17th century), the Sārārthavarṣiṇī of Viśvanātha Cakravartin (c. late 17th century), and the Gītābhūṣaṇa of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (c. 18th century).

Chapter 6 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Dhyānayoga or Ātmasaṃyamayoga (47 verses), expounds the discipline of contemplative yoga, detailing proper posture, sensory restraint, and moderate conduct as prerequisites for stilling mental fluctuations. It introduces the celebrated simile of the disciplined mind resting steady like a lamp in a windless place, reassures Arjuna that an unsuccessful aspirant is preserved from destruction and reborn into propitious surroundings to resume spiritual pursuit, and concludes by designating the devotee absorbed in loving devotion to God as the foremost yogi. In this composite digital text, every verse is followed by four commentaries representing the Advaita tradition (Śrīdhara Svāmin's Subodhinī and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā) and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition (Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa).

Śrīdharasvāmin's commentary is the Subodhinī (14th c.); Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's is the Advaitic Gūḍhārthadīpikā (late 16th c.); Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī (ca. late 17th / early 18th c.) and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa (18th c.) represent the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava commentary tradition.

Chapter 7 of the Bhagavadgītā (traditionally titled Jñānavijñānayoga, comprising 30 verses) opens the middle six chapters of the poem by distinguishing between the divine lower nature (aparā prakṛti: earth, water, fire, air, space, mind, intellect, and ego) and higher nature (parā prakṛti: the living entities that sustain the world). Kṛṣṇa explains the bewildering power of divine māyā constituted of the three guṇas, classifies devotees who seek him into four types (the afflicted, the inquisitive, the seeker of wealth, and the person of knowledge), and declares devotion (bhakti) to be the supreme means of transcendence. The accompanying four classical commentaries illuminate the verses from differing theological viewpoints: Śrīdharasvāmin balances Advaita with deep devotion, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī provides rigorous Advaitic exegesis accommodating intense Kṛṣṇa-bhakti, while Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa provide Acintyabhedābheda interpretations reflecting Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theology.

It features the famous declarations that the Supreme accepts even the humblest offering of a leaf, flower, fruit, or water given with devotion (9.26), and that single-minded devotional refuge delivers even the most fallen from sin (9.30–31). This e-text pairs the root verses with four detailed commentaries: the Subodhinī of Śrīdhara Svāmin, the Gūḍhārthadīpikā of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, the Sārārthavarṣiṇī of Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and the Gītābhūṣaṇa of Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

**Coverage:** partial — Contains chapter 10 (Vibhūtiyoga) complete in 42 verses (10.1–10.42), each accompanied by four commentaries. Line 1342 contains an editorial citation of Mahābhārata 12.201.4–5.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Attribution:** The root Bhagavadgītā is traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. The four commentaries represent distinct theological horizons: Śrīdhara Svāmin (c. 14th–15th c.) and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th c.) integrate Advaita Vedānta with personal Kṛṣṇa-bhakti, whereas Viśvanātha Cakravartin (late 17th c.) and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (18th c.) expound the Acintyabhedābheda philosophy of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.

Chapter 10 of the Bhagavadgītā, known as the Vibhūtiyoga ('Yoga of Divine Glories'), details Kṛṣṇa's cosmic manifestations and transcendent immanence at Arjuna's request. Declaring himself the origin of gods, great sages, and all cosmic faculties, Kṛṣṇa enumerates the foremost exemplars across diverse categories of existence as aspects of his supreme splendor, concluding that the entire universe is pervaded and sustained by a mere fraction of his power. In this digital text, each verse of chapter 10 is followed by four complete commentaries: the Advaitic yet bhakti-oriented expositions of Śrīdhara Svāmin (Subodhinī) and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (Gūḍhārthadīpikā), followed by the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics of Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī) and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (Gītābhūṣaṇa).

**Attribution:** The mūla text forms chapter 11 of the Bhagavadgītā (Mahābhārata, Bhīṣmaparvan 33 in the Critical Edition), traditionally attributed to Vyāsa. The four commentaries represent prominent classical Advaita-Bhakti and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava traditions: Śrīdharasvāmin (Subodhinī, c. 14th–15th century), Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (Gūḍhārthadīpikā, c. late 16th century), Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī, c. 1704), and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (Gītābhūṣaṇa, c. mid-18th century).

Chapter 11 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Viśvarūpadarśanayoga ('The Yoga of the Vision of the Universal Form'), forms the dramatic and theophanic climax of the dialogue between Krishna and Arjuna. Arjuna asks to see the divine cosmic form of the Lord, whereupon Krishna grants him divine vision (divya-cakṣus) and reveals his all-encompassing body blazing with innumerable mouths, eyes, and weapons, into which all creatures and warring heroes are drawn to their demise as Kāla ('Time/Death'). Awestruck and terrified, Arjuna offers extensive stotras and begs Krishna to return to his gentle four-armed and two-armed human form. In this e-text, all 55 verses are accompanied verse-by-verse by four influential Sanskrit commentaries: Śrīdharasvāmin's Subodhinī, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā, Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa.

**Coverage:** partial — Complete text of Chapter 12 (Bhaktiyoga, verses 12.1–12.20) together with all four commentaries for each verse, representing one chapter of the 18 chapters of the Bhagavadgītā.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Bhagavadgītā (Vyāsa, root text)
- Subodhinī (Śrīdharasvāmin, commentary)
- Gūḍhārthadīpikā (Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, commentary)

**Also known as:** Śrīmadbhagavadgītā adhyāya 12 saṭīka, Bhagavadgītā 12 with 4 commentaries

**Attribution:** The root text of the Bhagavadgītā is embedded within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata, traditionally ascribed to Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana). Śrīdharasvāmin (c. 14th–15th century) composed the Subodhinī; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (c. 16th century) composed the Advaita-bhakti commentary Gūḍhārthadīpikā; Viśvanātha Cakravartin (c. late 17th – early 18th century) authored the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava commentary Sārārthavarṣiṇī; and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (18th century) authored the Gauḍīya commentary Gītābhūṣaṇa (titled in the colophon as Śrīmad-Bhagavad-Gītopaniṣad-bhāṣya).

Bhagavadgītā chapter 12 (Bhaktiyoga, 20 verses) evaluates the comparative spiritual efficacy of meditating upon the unmanifest, imperishable Absolute (nirguṇa / avyakta akṣara) versus worship of the personal Divine (saguṇa / vyakta). Kṛṣṇa explains that while both orientations lead to liberation, the contemplative path of the unmanifest is arduous for embodied beings, whereas single-minded devotion directed to the personal Lord brings swift liberation through divine grace. The chapter concludes with a delineation of the tranquil virtues—such as non-malice, friendliness, forbearance, detachment, and equanimity in pleasure and pain—that characterize the devotee dear to the Lord. The accompanying commentaries synthesize and contrast the Advaita-bhakti readings of Śrīdharasvāmin and Madhusūdana Sarasvatī with the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theological interpretations of Viśvanātha Cakravartin and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa.

**Also known as:** Kṣetrakṣetrajñavibhāgayoga, Prakṛtipuruṣavivekayoga, Bhagavadgītā chapter 13 with 4 commentaries

**Attribution:** The root work Bhagavadgītā is traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa as part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. Śrīdhara Svāmin's Subodhinī dates to c. the 14th–15th century CE; Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā to the late 16th century CE; Viśvanātha Cakravartin's Sārārthavarṣiṇī to c. 1704 CE; and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa's Gītābhūṣaṇa to the mid-18th century CE.

Chapter 13 of the Bhagavadgītā (traditionally titled Kṣetrakṣetrajñavibhāgayoga or Prakṛtipuruṣavivekayoga, verses 1–34) delineates the fundamental metaphysical distinction between the 'field' (kṣetra, comprising the physical body, the senses, and psychological dispositions) and the 'knower of the field' (kṣetrajña, the conscious self and the indwelling Supreme Lord). Krishna expounds the twenty-four ontological categories of material nature, enumerates the moral and spiritual virtues constitutive of wisdom (jñāna), and characterizes the transcendent Brahman to be known (jñeya). In this digital edition, each verse is accompanied by four major commentaries spanning late-medieval and early-modern Vedānta: Śrīdhara Svāmin's Subodhinī (Advaita with devotional synthesis), Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Gūḍhārthadīpikā (scholastic Advaita Vedānta and bhakti), and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava Acintyabhedābheda commentaries of Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī) and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (Gītābhūṣaṇa).

**Attribution:** The Bhagavadgītā is traditionally attributed to Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana) as an integral part of the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. The four commentaries compiled alongside the root text represent two major Vedāntic streams: the Advaita/bhakti commentary Subodhinī by Śrīdhara Svāmin (14th/15th c.), the classical Advaita Vedānta commentary Gūḍhārthadīpikā by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th c.), and two canonical Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava commentaries: the Sārārthavarṣiṇī by Viśvanātha Cakravartin (late 17th/early 18th c.) and the Gītābhūṣaṇa by Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (18th c.).

Chapter 14 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Guṇatrayavibhāgayoga ('The Yoga of the Division of the Three Gunas'), analyzes the threefold constituents of material nature (prakṛti): sattva (purity, illumination), rajas (passion, desire), and tamas (inertia, ignorance). Kṛṣṇa explains how each guṇa binds the embodied self, shapes human psychology, and conditions post-mortem transmigration. The dialogue defines the marks and conduct of one who has transcended the guṇas (guṇātīta), concluding that unswerving devotional service (bhakti-yoga) is the direct means to overcome nature's constraints and attain realization of the divine foundation of Brahman. In this e-text, the twenty-seven verses of chapter 14 are presented alongside four influential commentaries representing classical Advaita/bhakti and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics.

**Attribution:** The Bhagavadgītā root text is traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. The four accompanying commentaries represent classical Advaita and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava traditions: (1) Subodhinī by Śrīdhara Svāmin (c. 14th–15th century, Advaita/Bhakti synthesis), (2) Gūḍhārthadīpikā by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (16th century, Advaita Vedānta), (3) Sārārthavarṣiṇī by Viśvanātha Cakravartin (late 17th–early 18th century, Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava), and (4) Gītābhūṣaṇa by Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (18th century, Gauḍīya Vedānta).

Chapter 16 of the Bhagavadgītā, titled Daivāsurasampadvibhāgayoga ('The Yoga of the Division between Divine and Demonic Endowments'), contrasts the twenty-six divine virtues (such as fearlessness, purity of mind, charity, non-violence, truthfulness, and humility) leading to spiritual liberation with demonic vices (including hypocrisy, arrogance, cruelty, lust, and greed) that bind souls to saṃsāra. Kṛṣṇa warns that materialistic and egoistic persons who reject transcendent moral orders descend into degraded births, concluding that scriptural ordinance (śāstra-pramāṇa) must serve as the authoritative standard for discerning duty from forbidden acts. In this e-text, the verses are accompanied by four influential commentaries by Śrīdhara Svāmin, Madhusūdana Sarasvatī, Viśvanātha Cakravartin, and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa, each offering verse-by-verse philosophical analyses integrating Advaita Vedānta and Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics.

Chapter 18 of the Bhagavadgītā, Mokṣasaṃnyāsayoga ('The Yoga of Liberation through Renunciation'), provides a comprehensive summation of the epic dialogue. Kṛṣṇa clarifies the distinction between total renunciation (saṃnyāsa) and the relinquishment of the fruits of action (tyāga), classifies knowledge, action, actor, intellect, resolve, and pleasure according to the three guṇas, and affirms the necessity of svadharma. The philosophical discourse culminates in verse 18.66 (the caramaśloka), urging total surrender (śaraṇāgati/prapatti) to Kṛṣṇa alone. In this e-text, the root verses are paired with the commentaries of Śrīdhara Svāmin (Subodhinī), Viśvanātha Cakravartin (Sārārthavarṣiṇī), and Baladeva Vidyābhūṣaṇa (Gītābhūṣaṇa).

The Bhagavadgītā ('Song of the Lord') is an 18-chapter philosophical dialogue of 700 verses, set on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra within the Bhīṣmaparvan of the Mahābhārata. Addressing the existential and moral crisis of the warrior Arjuna before the fratricidal battle, Kṛṣṇa expounds the nature of the imperishable self (ātman) and synthesizes the disciplines of detached action (karmayoga), knowledge (jñānayoga), and devotional surrender (bhaktiyoga). Culminating in the theophany of Kṛṣṇa's cosmic form (viśvarūpa), the work became a foundational text of classical Vedānta as the smṛtiprasthāna of the prasthānatrayī and one of the most widely commented-upon works in Indian religious literature.

The Ādiparvan ('Book of the Beginning') is the first of the eighteen books of the Mahābhārata. It frames the entire epic through King Janamejaya's snake sacrifice (sarpasatra) and the narration by the bard Ugraśravas Sauti to the gathered sages in the Naimiṣa forest. Following the catastrophe of the Kurukṣetra war, a despondent King Yudhiṣṭhira approaches the dying grandsire Bhīṣma, who lies on a bed of arrows, seeking counsel on how to rule and attain peace of mind. The Nārāyaṇīya (Mahābhārata 12.321–339) is a major theological tract of 19 chapters located near the end of the Mokṣadharmaparvan in the Śāntiparvan. It provides the earliest comprehensive textual witness to early Pāñcarātra and Bhāgavata doctrine within the epic literature, extolling Nārāyaṇa as the supreme transcendent deity and cosmic source of all manifestations. The Uttarakāṇḍa is the seventh and concluding book of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa, serving as an extensive narrative and mythological epilogue to the core epic. It begins with the sage Agastya narrating the origins, genealogy, and early exploits of Rāvaṇa and other rākṣasas, as well as the childhood deeds of Hanumān. **Works in this e-text:**

- Locana (Abhinavagupta, commentary)
- Bālapriyā (Rāmaśāraka, sub-commentary)

**Also known as:** Sahṛdayāloka, Kāvyāloka, Dhvanyālokalocana, Prauḍhalocanaṭippanī

**Attribution:** A long-standing debate in Sanskrit poetics concerns whether the metrical kārikās and the prose vṛtti of the Dhvanyāloka are by distinct authors (an older 'Dhvanikāra' vs. Ānandavardhana) or whether Ānandavardhana (fl. c. 850–880 CE in Kashmir) authored both. Although Abhinavagupta occasionally refers to them distinctly in his Locana, dominant tradition and modern scholarship widely attribute the formulation of the system to Ānandavardhana. Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE, Kashmir) composed the Locana. Rāmaśāraka (the Sanskritized name of K. Rāma Pishāroti, a traditional scholar from Kerala) composed the sub-commentary Bālapriyā (also styled Prauḍhalocanaṭippanī).

The first chapter (uddyota) of the Dhvanyāloka ('Light on Suggestion') by the 9th-century Kashmiri theorist Ānandavardhana, accompanied by Abhinavagupta's foundational 10th/11th-century commentary (Locana) and the modern sub-commentary Bālapriyā by the Kerala scholar K. Rāma Pishāroti (Rāmaśāraka). In this opening chapter, Ānandavardhana establishes the central thesis of the dhvani school: that suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha / dhvani) constitutes the essential soul (ātman) of poetry, distinct from literal (abhidhā) and metaphorical (lakṣaṇā) semantics. The text methodically refutes the three primary anti-dhvani positions: those denying the existence of suggestion outright (abhāvavāda), those identifying it with figurative indication (bhāktavāda), and those deeming it undefinable or ineffable (anirvacanīyatāvāda).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in six paricchedas (chapters 1–6) comprising approximately 398–400 kārikās, concluding with verse 6.66 which summarizes the distribution of topics across the six chapters.

**Also known as:** Bhāmahālaṅkāra

**Attribution:** The work is unanimously ascribed to the 7th-century rhetorician Bhāmaha (identified in chapter 6 as the son of Rakrilagomin / Ragrila).

The Kāvyālaṃkāra of Bhāmaha (c. 7th century CE) is one of the earliest extant systematic treatises on classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra), establishing poetics as an autonomous discipline distinct from dramaturgy. In six chapters (paricchedas) comprising approximately 400 verses, the work treats poetic genres, thirty-nine figures of speech (alaṃkāra), poetic defects (doṣa), logical and epistemological argumentation (nyāya, including a famous refutation of the Buddhist apoha doctrine), and grammatical correctness (śabdaśuddhi). Bhāmaha famously defines kāvya as the unified harmony of word and meaning (śabdārthau sahitau kāvyam) and identifies vakrokti ('oblique/striking expression') as the indispensable hallmark of genuine poetic language.

The Candrāloka is an elementary verse treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by Jayadeva Pīyūṣavarṣa in ten chapters (mayūkhas) in straightforward anuṣṭubh meter. The Rasagaṅgādhara ('Bearer of the River of Aesthetic Emotion') by Jagannātha (mid-17th century) is widely regarded as the culminating philosophical masterpiece of classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). Applying the analytical rigor and definitional apparatus of Navya-Nyāya logic, Jagannātha critically evaluates earlier poetic theorists, famously critiquing Mammaṭa, Viśvanātha, and Appayya Dīkṣita. The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtravṛtti of Vāmana (fl. c. 800 CE) is a foundational treatise of classical Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra), celebrated for propounding the doctrine that poetic diction or style (rīti) constitutes the essence or 'soul' of poetry (rītir ātmā kāvyasya). **Attribution:** Rājānaka Kuntaka is the author of both the root kārikā verses (tagged Vjiv_) and the accompanying prose exposition with supplementary verses (svavṛtti and antaraślokas, tagged VjivC_).

The Vakroktijīvita by Rājānaka Kuntaka (fl. late 10th to early 11th century CE in Kashmir) is a landmark treatise in Sanskrit poetics that presents vakrokti ('oblique' or 'striking expression') as the essential life-principle (jīvita) of all literature. Composed in kārikā verses alongside Kuntaka's own prose commentary (svavṛtti) and hundreds of illustrative literary citations, the work systematizes creative poetic deviation (vakratā) across six hierarchical levels of linguistic organization: phoneme/letter arrangements (varṇavinyāsa), lexical stems (pada-pūrvārdha), inflectional morphology (pratyayāśraya), sentential composition (vākya), thematic episodes (prakaraṇa), and overall plot structure (prabandha). Responding to the dominant dhvani theory of Ānandavardhana, Kuntaka seeks to integrate alaṅkāra, guṇa, mārga, and rasa into an all-encompassing aesthetic framework centered on the imaginative faculty and creative activity of the poet (kavi-vyāpāra).

The Kāvyaprakāśa is an 11th-century masterpiece of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) authored by the Kashmiri scholar Mammaṭa and completed in its tenth chapter by Allaṭa. The Kāvyaprakāśa is a foundational eleventh-century Sanskrit treatise on poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) composed by the Kashmiri scholar Mammaṭa and completed by Allaṭa. Arranged into ten chapters (ullāsas) combining kārikā verses and an authoritative prose exposition (vṛtti), the work synthesizes the dhvani (suggestion) and rasa aesthetics of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta with earlier taxonomic models of poetic figures and faults. It covers the definition and objectives of poetry, the three primary semantic functions of words (abhidhā, lakṣaṇā, and vyañjanā), stylistic blemishes (doṣas), excellences (guṇas), and phonological as well as semantic figures (śabdālaṃkāra and arthālaṃkāra), functioning as the preeminent textbook of classical Sanskrit literary theory.

The Śabdavyāpāravicāra ('Inquiry into the Operations of Words') is a short semantic-rhetorical treatise by the Kashmiri aesthetician Mammaṭa (c. late 11th–early 12th century CE). Sharing key formulations with the second and fifth ullāsas of his Kāvyaprakāśa, the text analyses the three major linguistic functions: denotation (abhidhā), indication (lakṣaṇā), and suggestion (vyañjanā / dhvanana). **Also known as:** Kavirahasya

**Attribution:** Authored by Rājaśekhara (son of Durduka and Śīlavatī, belonging to the Yāyāvara family), court poet of the Gurjara-Pratihāra rulers Mahendrapāla I and Mahīpāla I at Mahodaya/Kanyākubja (Kannauj).

The Kāvyamīmāṃsā ('Inquiry into Poetry') by Rājaśekhara (fl. c. 880–920 CE) is a major classic of Sanskrit literary theory focused on the practical training and culture of a poet (kaviśikṣā). Although planned on an encyclopedic scale of eighteen books, only the first book, the Kavirahasya ('The Poet's Secret') in eighteen chapters, is extant. The work offers valuable documentation of early medieval Indian literary life, describing the allegorical personification of poetry (Kāvyapuruṣa), the nature of innate poetic talent (pratibhā), royal assemblies and salons (kavisabhā), the classification of borrowing and plagiarism (haraṇa), poetic conventions (kavisamaya), and Pan-Indian cultural geography (deśavibhāga).

**Attribution:** Authored by Rūpa Gosvāmī (c. 1489–1564 CE), one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana, as confirmed by opening verses and the colophon ('iti dhvani-prasthāpana-paramācārya-śrīmad-rūpa-gosvāmi-prabhupāda-praṇītā śrī-nāṭaka-candrikā samāptā').

The Nāṭakacandrikā ('Moonlight of Drama') is a 16th-century dramaturgical treatise by Rūpa Gosvāmī, one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana. Synthesizing Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and especially Siṅgabhūpāla's Rasārṇavasudhākara—while consciously rejecting the formulation of the Sāhitya-darpaṇa—the work systematizes plot structure (sandhi, sandhyaṅga), hero types, and emotional states for dramatic poetry. It serves as both the dramaturgical theory behind Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava aesthetics and the technical companion to Rūpa's own devotional plays, Vidagdhamādhava and Lalitamādhava, establishing Kṛṣṇa as the ideal dramatic hero.

The Vyaktivivekavyākhyā (also called Vyaktivivekavicāra) is a 12th-century commentary by the Kashmiri rhetorician Ruyyaka on Mahimabhaṭṭa's Vyaktiviveka. This text contains the second chapter (dvitīya vimarśa), which analyzes poetic defects (doṣas) and syntactic improprieties (śabdānaucitya), examining five major faults: vidheyāvimarśa (faulty predication/emphasis), prakramabheda (lack of syntactic parallelism), kramabheda (misplaced word order), paunaruktya (redundancy), and vācyāvacana / avācyavacana (omission or unwarranted inclusion of expressions). Although Mahimabhaṭṭa composed the root work as a polemic against Ānandavardhana's dhvani doctrine by seeking to subsume suggestion into logical inference (anumāna), Ruyyaka's commentary provides indispensable grammatical and rhetorical elucidations while critically scrutinizing Mahimabhaṭṭa's positions.

**Coverage:** partial — Vidyācakravartin's Sañjīvanī commentary is preserved in full through the Arthālaṅkāraprakaraṇa (ending segment 4844). However, for Ruyyaka's root work, only the sūtras (prefixed in GRETIL markup with RuAss_) are provided, while Ruyyaka's prose vṛtti is not keyed continuously.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Alaṅkārasarvasva (Ruyyaka, root text)
- Sañjīvanī (Vidyācakravartin, commentary)

**Also known as:** Alaṃkārasarvasva, Alaṅkārasūtra, Sañjīvanī, Alaṅkārasarvasvasañjīvanī

**Attribution:** Ruyyaka (also called Rucaka, son of Tilaka; 12th c., Kashmir) authored the Alaṅkārasarvasva (sūtra and vṛtti), as corroborated in verse 2 ('rucakācāryopajñe... alaṅkārasarvasve') and by commentators like Jayaratha. Vidyācakravartin (Sakala-Vidyācakravartin III, fl. first half of 14th c., court poet under the Hoysala monarch Vīra Ballāla III) authored the Sañjīvanī commentary, as confirmed in the introductory verses (1–3) and the concluding colophon (segment 4843).

The Alaṅkārasarvasva ('The Essence of Poetic Figures') by the 12th-century Kashmiri theorist Ruyyaka is a standard manual of Sanskrit poetics that systematizes and analyzes more than eighty poetic figures (śabdālaṅkāras and arthālaṅkāras) within the dhvani-orientated framework of Ānandavardhana and Abhinavagupta. Vidyācakravartin's Sañjīvanī, composed at the 14th-century Hoysala court, is a detailed sub-commentary that clarifies Ruyyaka's technical distinctions, engages with earlier Kashmiri commentaries, and supplies original verses where previous illustrative examples were incomplete. In this digital text, Ruyyaka's sūtras are provided alongside Vidyācakravartin's complete Sañjīvanī commentary.

The Alaṅkārasarvasva is an influential 12th-century Kashmiri treatise on Sanskrit poetics by Ruyyaka (c. 1135–1150 CE). Composed in concise sūtras accompanied by a prose vṛtti, the work provides an analytical and exhaustive classification of over eighty figures of sense and sound (alaṅkāra), integrating traditional rhetorical taxonomies with the dhvani framework established by Ānandavardhana and Mammaṭa. Its celebrated introductory Bhūmikā offers a critical historical review of earlier poetic theories (Bhāmaha, Udbhaṭa, Vāmana, Kuntaka, and Bhaṭṭa Nāyaka), demonstrating that ornamental figures are functionally subservient to suggested aesthetic emotion (rasa/vyaṅgyārtha).

Venkatacharya) affirm royal authorship.

The Rasārṇavasudhākara ('Nectar-Moon to the Ocean of Rasa') is an encyclopedic 14th-century Sanskrit treatise on dramaturgy and aesthetics composed by King Siṃhabhūpāla II of the Recherla dynasty. Arranged into three comprehensive 'rays' (vilāsas)—Rañjakollāsa (dealing with dramatic personae, the typology of hero and heroine, and their aesthetic embellishments), Rasollāsa (treating the primary sentiments, transient emotions, excitant/ensuant factors, and the nature of aesthetic delight), and Nāṭakollāsa (treating plot structure, junctures/sandhis, and dramatic genres)—it synthesizes the traditions of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra, Dhanañjaya's Daśarūpaka, and Bhoja's Śṛṅgāraprakāśa. The work is especially prized by later commentators (notably Mallinātha and the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava theorists such as Rūpa Gosvāmin) for its rigorous definitions and rich repertoire of illustrative quotations drawn from classical poetry and drama.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all six vargas (chapters 1–6) containing the kārikās, illustrative verses (many drawn from Udbhaṭa's lost Kumārasambhava), and Pratīhārendurāja's commentary; also includes the 1915 Sanskrit prastāvanā by the editor Maṅgeśaśarmā.

The Kāvyālaṃkārasārasaṃgraha ('Compendium of the Essence of Poetic Ornaments') by the Kashmiri rhetorician Udbhaṭa (fl. c. late 8th – early 9th century CE) is a major foundational treatise of Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra). In six chapters (vargas), it defines, illustrates, and classifies forty-one poetic figures of sound and sense, modifying Bhāmaha's schema and introducing new categories such as punaruktavadābhāsa, kāvyahetu, and kāvyadṛṣṭānta. The accompanying Laghuvṛtti by Pratīhārendurāja (fl. mid-10th century CE) is the earliest surviving commentary on the work, providing valuable syntactic analysis, philosophical contextualization (integrating Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya tenets), and critical discussion of the emerging dhvani doctrine.

The Ujjvalanīlamaṇi ('The Blazing Sapphire') is an influential 16th-century treatise on devotional aesthetics and theology by Rūpa Gosvāmin, one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana. Written as a specialized sequel to his Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, the work presents an exhaustive analysis of madhura-rasa (the erotic-devotional sentiment), which Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism regards as the supreme aesthetic manifestation of devotion to Kṛṣṇa. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the aphorisms (sūtrapāṭha), comprising all 319 sūtras across 5 adhikaraṇas (12 adhyāyas): Śārīra (1.1–1.3), Doṣadarśana (2.1–2.2), Guṇavivecana (3.1–3.2), Ālaṅkārika (4.1–4.3), and Prāyogika (5.1–5.2). **Also known as:** Kāvyālaṅkārasūtrāṇi, Kāvyālaṅkārasūtrapāṭha, Kāvyālaṅkāra

**Attribution:** Attributed to the Kashmiri aesthetician Vāmana (c. late 8th to early 9th century CE), active at the court of King Jayāpīḍa of Kashmir (r. c. 779–813 CE). Vāmana composed both the root aphorisms (sūtra) and the auto-commentary (vṛtti / Kavipriyā).

The Kāvyālaṅkārasūtra is a foundational treatise of Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) composed by the Kashmiri aesthetician Vāmana (fl. c. 800 CE). It is celebrated as the quintessential exposition of the Rīti school, formulating the influential doctrine that style/diction is the soul of poetry ('rītir ātmā kāvyasya'). Divided into five adhikaraṇas (Śārīra, Doṣadarśana, Guṇavivecana, Ālaṅkārika, and Prāyogika), it systematically details the definition and purpose of poetry, poetic defects (doṣas), the ten verbal and cognitive excellences (guṇas), rhetorical tropes (alaṅkāras), and rules for literary grammatical correctness. In this e-text, only the sūtrapāṭha (the aphoristic sūtras without the prose auto-commentary) is preserved.

The Camatkāracandrikā is an eight-chapter (vilāsa) manual of Sanskrit poetics composed in the late 14th century CE by Viśveśvara Kavicandra at the court of King Siṅgabhūpāla II of Rācakoṇḍa. Modeling itself after earlier panegyrical alaṅkāra treatises such as Vidyānātha's Pratāparudrīya and Vidyādhara's Ekāvalī, the author crafts original illustrative verses that praise his royal patron. Conceptually, the work posits camatkāra (aesthetic wonder or delight) as the unifying essence of poetic beauty, systematizing its realization through seven distinct literary components: guṇa, rīti, rasa, vṛtti, pāka, śayyā, and alaṅkāra.

The Pratāparudrīya (or Pratāparudrayaśobhūṣaṇa) by Vidyānātha is a comprehensive early 14th-century manual of Sanskrit poetics and dramaturgy, composed at the court of the Kākatīya king Pratāparudra II of Warangal (r. c. 1295–1323 CE). Across nine chapters (prakaraṇas), it covers the hero (nāyaka), the nature of kāvya, dramaturgy (nāṭaka), rasa, poetic flaws (doṣa), poetic excellences (guṇa), and verbal and semantic ornaments (śabdālaṅkāra, arthālaṅkāra, miśrālaṅkāra). The treatise established a prominent South Indian tradition in which all illustrative examples exclusively praise the patron king, and its third chapter incorporates a complete five-act panegyrical play, the Pratāparudrakalyāṇa, designed as a model drama.

The second chapter (pariccheda) of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's 14th-century Sāhityadarpaṇa investigates the grammatical and semantic foundations of poetic discourse, focusing on the definitions of the sentence (vākya) and the word (pada). It elaborates the three classical conditions for syntactic and semantic coherence: semantic compatibility (yogyatā), mutual expectancy (ākāṅkṣā), and contiguity (āsatti). It systematically analyzes the primary linguistic powers (śabdavṛtti)—denotation (abhidhā), metaphorical indication (lakṣaṇā), and poetic suggestion (vyañjanā)—as well as the sentence-purport function (tātparyavṛtti) of the Abhihitānvayavādins. This digital file presents Viśvanātha's kārikās and autocommentary interwoven with two important traditional commentaries: the Locanā of the author's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā of Maheśvara Tarkālaṃkāra.

Pariccheda 3 (Rasādinirūpaṇa) is the theoretical core of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's 14th-century alaṃkāraśāstra compendium, the Sāhityadarpaṇa, substantiating the definition of literature formulated in chapter 1 ('vākyaṃ rasātmakaṃ kāvyam'). The chapter provides an in-depth exposition of rasa (aesthetic relish) as a transcendental (alaukika), blissful, self-manifesting state of consciousness, analyzing how the sthāyibhāva (durable psychological state) is brought to relish via vibhāvas (determinants), anubhāvas (consequents), and vyabhicāribhāvas (transitory emotions). It also details the classification of the rasas (śṛṅgāra, hāsya, karuṇa, raudra, vīra, bhayānaka, bībhatsa, adbhuta, and śānta), dramatic character types, and the comprehensive taxonomy of heroes (nāyakas) and heroines (nāyikās). This digital edition integrates the root kārikās and autocommentary with two important traditional commentaries: the Locanā by Viśvanātha's son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā by the Bengali logician Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra.

Chapter 5 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's 14th-century treatise on poetics, the Sāhityadarpaṇa, presented alongside the Vijñapriyā commentary of Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra and the Locana commentary of the author's son Anantadāsa. This chapter is devoted to vindicating the dhvani school's doctrine of suggestion (vyañjanāvyāpāra) as an autonomous semantic function (vṛtti) indispensable for conveying aesthetic relish (rasa), vastudhvani, and alaṅkāradhvani. Viśvanātha and his commentators systematically refute competing theories advanced by Mīmāṃsā, Nyāya, and other schools that attempt to reduce suggestion to literal denotation (abhidhā), sentence purport (tātparya), or syllogistic inference (anumāna).

**Coverage:** partial — Pariccheda 6 only (out of 10 paricchedas). Pariccheda 6 covers dramaturgy (dṛśyakāvya), containing 337 kārikās with prose vṛtti and both commentaries down to their concluding colophons.

**Also known as:** Sāhityadarpaṇa (ṣaṣṭhaḥ paricchedaḥ), Mirror of Composition

**Attribution:** Viśvanātha Kavirāja Mahāpātra, a high official (sāndhivigrahika) in fourteenth-century Orissa, authored the root treatise and prose vṛtti. The Locanā is by his son Anantadāsa. The Vijñapriyā is by Bhaṭṭācārya Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra (also called Maheśvara Nyāyālaṅkāra or Maheśvarabhaṭṭa).

Pariccheda 6 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's Sāhityadarpaṇa (14th century) provides an extensive synthetic treatment of Sanskrit dramaturgy (dṛśyakāvya). Viśvanātha systematically distinguishes dramatic art from audible literature (śravyakāvya) and classifies dramatic forms into ten major types (daśarūpaka) and eighteen minor types (uparūpaka). The chapter covers the components of dramatic action, the five stages and junctures (sandhi) with their sixty-four limbs (sandhyaṅga), hero and heroine typologies, dramatic styles (vṛtti), and theatrical conventions, drawing heavily from Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and Dhanañjaya's Daśarūpaka. In this digital text, the root text and autocommentary are accompanied by Anantadāsa's Locanā and Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra's Vijñapriyā.

Pariccheda 7 of Viśvanātha Kavirāja's 14th-century alamkāra treatise, the Sāhityadarpaṇa, provides a systematic treatment of poetic defects (doṣas). It classifies defects according to whether they pertain to the individual word (padadoṣa), a part of a word (padāṃśadoṣa), the sentence (vākyadoṣa), the meaning (arthadoṣa), or the aesthetic sentiment (rasadoṣa), while also outlining contexts where nominal faults cease to be defective or become poetic merits (guṇatva). In this e-text, the root kārikās and svopajñavṛtti are presented alongside two traditional commentaries: the Vijñapriyā of Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra and the Locana of Viśvanātha's son Anantadāsa.

**Coverage:** partial — Contains chapter 8 (Guṇavivecana, kārikās 8.1–8.16) complete, including Viśvanātha's prose vṛtti, Anantadāsa's Locanā, and Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra's Vijñapriyā; the complete Sāhityadarpaṇa comprises ten paricchedas.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Also known as:** Sāhityadarpaṇa: Guṇavivecana, Sāhityadarpaṇa: Guṇanirūpaṇa, Sahityadarpana Pariccheda 8

**Attribution:** Viśvanātha Kavirāja Mahāpātra (fl. 14th century CE, minister of peace and war under the Eastern Gaṅga kings of Kaliṅga) authored the kārikās and the vṛtti. The Locanā was composed by his son Anantadāsa. The Vijñapriyā was authored by the Bengali Naiyāyika Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya (c. 16th–17th c. CE).

Pariccheda 8 (Guṇavivecana) of Viśvanātha's fourteenth-century alaṅkāraśāstra treatise Sāhityadarpaṇa treats the poetic qualities (guṇa). Adopting the Kashmiri dhvani position elaborated by Mammaṭa, Viśvanātha argues that guṇas inhere essentially in the principal aesthetic emotion (rasa) rather than in mere sound or word configurations, reducing the traditional tenfold guṇa system of Daṇḍin and Vāmana to three primary qualities: mādhurya (sweetness/melting), ojas (vigor/expansion), and prasāda (perspicuity/clarity). This digital edition merges Viśvanātha's root kārikās (8.1–8.16) and svopajña vṛtti with two early commentaries: the Locanā by his son Anantadāsa and the Vijñapriyā by Maheśvara Tarkālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya.

The Sāhityadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Composition') is an encyclopedic 14th-century treatise on Sanskrit literary theory and dramaturgy composed in ten chapters (paricchedas) in sūtra/kārikā and prose vṛtti by Viśvanātha Kavirāja of Odisha. - Ruixuan Chen, 'Beobachtungen zur Turfan-Chandoviciti', Indo-Iranian Journal 56.1 (2013), pp. 41–60. — Re-examination and critical improvements to Schlingloff's edition based on new readings of SHT 654.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — The e-text has 365 segments. It reproduces Schlingloff's arrangement of the surviving fragments of SHT 654: I. Regeln zur Metrik (Versgruppe A: A.1–15; B: B.1–31), II. Chandoviciti, III. Metrik-Lehrtext. It ends at ChV_III_2_5. Large gaps are marked explicitly, e.g. 'ChV_I_A_5 nicht erhalten', 'ChV_I_B_11-21 nicht erhalten', 'ChV_II_2_34-41 nicht erhalten' and 'ChV_III_1_1-25 nicht erhalten'. Most surviving verses are only partly preserved, and lost syllables are shown with metrical symbols (^ _ X). The original extent of the work is unknown.

**Also known as:** Turfan-Chandoviciti, Texte zur Sanskritmetrik

**Attribution:** Verse ChV_II_1_1 (fragmentary) reads '... yāskapiṅgalasūtrebhyaḥ / mitradhareṇa ... kṛtiḥ cchandovicitiḥ'. The work is therefore presented as a composition by Mitradhara based on the sūtras of Yāska and Piṅgala. The name appears in a damaged verse, so the attribution rests on this single passage. The Patañjali attribution in the old catalog has no support in the text.

The Chandoviciti is a Sanskrit treatise on metrics. It is preserved only in fragments of a birch-bark manuscript from the Turfan finds (SHT 654), edited by Dieter Schlingloff in 1958. The surviving verses define metres in metrical form and name their basis as the sūtras of Yāska and Piṅgala, and verse II.1 names Mitradhara as the author. The fragments are early manuscript evidence for Sanskrit metrical theory outside the Piṅgala tradition proper. Ruixuan Chen (2013) improved their readings.

**Attribution:** The concluding colophon identifies the author as Mahāpaṇḍitasthavira Jñānaśrīmitra (fl. c. 975–1040 CE), the famed dvārapaṇḍita at Vikramaśīla. The attribution is corroborated by Tibetan tradition (Tōhoku 4305 / D4305) and modern scholarship.

The Vṛttamālāstuti ('Garland of Metres Praise') is an 11th-century Buddhist devotional hymn and versified manual of Sanskrit metrics (chandaśśāstra) by the Vikramaśīla scholar-monk Jñānaśrīmitra. Comprising 154 stanzas praising the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Mañjughoṣa), the work illustrates approximately 150 classical metres by weaving the metrical name directly into each stanza while exemplifying its metrical structure. Along with Ratnākaraśānti's Chandoratnākara, it was a fundamental textbook of prosody in late northern Buddhist monastic colleges and was translated into Tibetan by Pang Lotsāwa Lodrö Tenpa.

The Vṛttaratnākara of Kedārabhaṭṭa (c. 10th–11th century CE) is the most widely disseminated and taught manual of classical Sanskrit prosody (chandaśśāstra) in South Asia. Structured in six concise chapters of 136 verses, it covers metrical definitions and the trika/gaṇa syllabic foot notation, mātrāvṛtta (moraic) metres, samavṛtta, ardhasamavṛtta, viṣamavṛtta, and the six metrical pratyayas (combinatorial algorithms such as prastāra, naṣṭa, and uddiṣṭa). **Coverage:** unclear — The catalog entry contains no e-text data (0 segments, 0 characters). It represents an unpopulated placeholder in the DharmaNexus database.

**Also known as:** Abhinayadarpaṇam, The Mirror of Gesture

**Attribution:** Attributed to the mythical sage Nandikeśvara (frequently identified in tradition with Taṇḍu, the attendant of Śiva). Modern scholarship considers the surviving treatise to be a medieval South Indian compilation, broadly dated between the 10th and 13th centuries CE.

The Abhinayadarpaṇa ('Mirror of Gesture'), attributed to the legendary sage Nandikeśvara, is an indispensable Sanskrit manual on classical Indian performing arts, particularly central to the tradition of Bharatanatyam. It is primarily devoted to āṅgikābhinaya (bodily and gestural expression), systematically enumerating and defining gestures of the single and combined hands (asaṃyuta- and saṃyuta-hastas), movements of the head (śirobheda), eyes (dṛṣṭibheda), neck (grīvābheda), and eyebrows, as well as postures (sthāna), movements (cārī), and gaits (gati). The work functions as a practical handbook connecting theoretical dramaturgy with dance choreography.

The Nāṭyaśāstra is the encyclopedic foundational treatise of classical Indian dramaturgy, performance, dance, and music, traditionally attributed to Bharata Muni. It provides detailed prescriptions on theatre architecture, preliminary rites (pūrvaraṅga), acting styles and bodily gestures (abhinaya), classifications of dramatic compositions (daśarūpaka), costuming, makeup, prosody, and musical scales and instruments. The Daśarūpaka ('Ten Forms of Dramatic Art') by Dhanañjaya is an influential late 10th-century treatise in four chapters (prakāśas or paricchedas) condensing and systematizing the dramaturgical teachings of the Nāṭyaśāstra. **Attribution:** Abhinanda explicitly identifies himself as the son of Jayanta Bhaṭṭa (the celebrated Kashmiri Nyāya philosopher, author of the Nyāyamañjarī) in the introductory verses (1.2, 1.10–1.12) and in the canto colophons. He is distinct from his contemporary Gauḍa Abhinanda (son of Śatānanda), the author of the epic Rāmacarita.

The Kādambarīkathāsāra is an eight-canto metrical epitome of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's celebrated 7th-century prose romance Kādambarī, composed in Kashmir in the late 9th century CE by Abhinanda, son of the Nyāya logician Jayanta Bhaṭṭa. **Translations:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains 112 stanzas matching the recension in Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara's Kāvyasaṅgraha (with concordance numbers to the 102 stanzas of Arjunavarmadeva's recension). The e-text file contains the full collection twice: lines 0–579 present a plain text version, and lines 580–1158 present the same text with LaTeX footnote markup.

**Also known as:** Amarukaśataka

**Attribution:** The anthology is traditionally attributed to the poet Amaru (or Amaruka). A well-known Vedāntic legend found in Mādhavācārya's Śaṅkaradigvijaya claims that Ādi Śaṅkara entered the corpse of the deceased King Amaru in order to master kāmaśāstra. Modern scholarship treats the collection as having crystallized around an authentic core of stanzas by Amaru, which then expanded across four principal recensions (Western, Southern, Eastern, and that of Arjunavarmadeva).

The Amaruśataka is an anthology of approximately one hundred independent single-stanza verses (muktaka) in classical meters devoted to erotic love (śṛṅgāra). Each stanza presents a self-contained vignette illustrating psychological and emotional dynamics between lovers—including youthful modesty, lovers' quarrels and wounded pride (māna), separation (vipralambha), and reconciliation. Extensively cited by rhetoricians such as Ānandavardhana, Abhinavagupta, and Mammaṭa, the collection is regarded as an archetype of suggestive poetry (dhvani) and aesthetic flavor (rasa).

**Attribution:** Composed by Ānandabhaṭṭa, who identifies himself as a descendant of Anantabhaṭṭa (a Drāviḍa Brahmin family settled in Bengal), at the request of King Buddhimanta Khān of Navadvīpa in Śaka 1432 (1510 CE). The author incorporates materials from earlier sources, specifically a lost contemporary biography of King Vallālasena by Śaraṇa Datta and the Vyāsapurāṇa attributed to Bhaṭṭa Siṃhagiri. An alternative two-part recension was published in 1889 by Hariścandra Kaviratna, where the Pūrvakhaṇḍa is attributed to Gopālabhaṭṭa (c. 1300 CE) and the Uttarakhaṇḍa to Ānandabhaṭṭa.

The Vallālacarita is a 16th-century Sanskrit biographical chronicle recounting the life, lineage, and reign of King Vallālasena (Ballāl Sen, r. c. 1158–1179 CE) of the Sena dynasty of Bengal. Completed around Śaka 1432 (1510 CE) at the behest of Buddhimanta Khān of Navadvīpa, the text blends historical memory with social legends. It is a central source for the study of medieval Bengali social history, particularly regarding the traditional origin of Kulīnism (kaulīnya-prathā) among Brahmins and Kāyasthas, the migration and gotras of Gauḍa Brahmins, and the royal reclassification and demotion of merchant (Suvarṇavaṇik) and yogic (Nāth) communities.

Following the classical gnomic tradition exemplified by Bhartṛhari, it reflects upon the vanity of worldly pursuits, the transient nature of wealth, youth, and bodily existence, and the pitfalls of sensual attachment. **Also known as:** Buddha-carita, Buddhacaritamahākāvya

**Attribution:** Attributed to the Buddhist poet-philosopher Aśvaghoṣa (c. 1st–2nd c. CE). The authentic Sanskrit text breaks off at 14.31; verses 1.1–1.7 and other lacunae reflect modern Sanskrit reconstructions from Tibetan.

The Buddhacarita ('Acts of the Buddha') is an early Sanskrit court poem (mahākāvya) composed by the Buddhist author Aśvaghoṣa in the 1st–2nd century CE. Although the complete narrative comprised twenty-eight cantos narrating the life of Siddhārtha Gautama from his birth to his parinirvāṇa and the distribution of relics (fully preserved in Tibetan and Chinese translations), only the first fourteen cantos (concluding with the enlightenment) survive in the authentic Sanskrit manuscript tradition. Masterfully synthesizing sophisticated kāvya aesthetics with Buddhist philosophy, it is the earliest surviving complete court epic in Sanskrit literature.

The Saundarananda ('Handsome Nanda') by Aśvaghoṣa (c. 1st–2nd century CE) is one of the earliest extant Sanskrit mahākāvya court epics, preserved complete in eighteen cantos [1460, 1461]. It dramatizes the conversion of the Buddha's handsome half-brother Nanda, who is deeply attached to his sensual love for his consort Sundarī. Through skilful pedagogy, meditation instruction, and visions of heavenly nymphs juxtaposed with the perils of cyclic existence, the Buddha leads Nanda step by step to spiritual maturity and arhatship. In the closing stanzas (18.63–64), Aśvaghoṣa articulates a seminal defense of Buddhist kāvya, explaining that ornate poetry serves merely as a sweet coating to administer the bitter medicine of liberation (mokṣa).

The Kādambarī is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (kathā) composed in the 7th century CE by Bāṇabhaṭṭa and finished by his son Bhūṣaṇabhaṭṭa. Renowned for its intricate sentence structure, ornate imagery, and complex nested frame stories spanning successive rebirths, it tells the intertwined tales of Prince Candrāpīḍa and Princess Kādambarī alongside Puṇḍarīka and Mahāśvetā. This e-text preserves the final section of Bāṇabhaṭṭa's Pūrvabhāga (varṇanas 84–122), describing Candrāpīḍa's journey to Mount Hemakūṭa with Mahāśvetā, his first meeting and deepening love with Kādambarī, and his eventual journey back to Ujjayinī.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 18 cantos (BhKir_1.1–18.48; 2080 segments representing the full 1030+ verses of the poem).

**Also known as:** Kirātārjunīyam

**Attribution:** Universally attributed to Bhāravi (fl. c. 6th century CE), whose terminus ante quem of 634 CE is established by Ravikīrti's Aihole inscription (coupling Bhāravi's fame with that of Kālidāsa). He is also linked with the Pallava court of Siṃhaviṣṇu and King Durvinīta in the introductory biographical material of Daṇḍin's Avantisundarī.

The Kirātārjunīya is an 18-canto mahākāvya composed by the 6th-century poet Bhāravi, elaborating an episode from the Vanaparvan of the Mahābhārata. The epic narrates Arjuna's journey to Mount Indrakīla in the Himalayas to perform penance and procure divine weapons for the Pāṇḍavas, his duel and wrestling combat with Śiva disguised as a mountain hunter (kirāta) over a slain boar, and Śiva's revelation and bestowal of the Pāśupata weapon. Celebrated in classical Sanskrit literary theory for gravity of meaning (arthagaurava), political discourse (nīti), and virtuoso poetic ornamentation (especially the citrakāvya constraints of canto 15), it constitutes one of the traditional 'five great court epics' (pañcamahākāvya).

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the 11th-century Kashmiri court poet Bilhaṇa (author of the Vikramāṅkadevacarita). The poem circulated widely across India in distinct regional recensions (notably Kashmiri/Western and Southern/Eastern) embedded in varied frame narratives (such as the Vidyāsundara story), which has led modern scholars to debate whether the core collection was expanded by later poets.

The Caurapañcāśikā is a famous classical Sanskrit lyrical sequence of fifty stanzas in the Vasantatilakā meter, each verse opening with the evocative anaphora 'adyāpi' ('even now'). Framed by tradition as the death-row lament of a clandestine lover awaiting execution after an illicit affair with a princess, each stanza presents a self-contained, vividly sensory recollection of the beloved's physical charms and their shared intimacy. Traditionally attributed to the 11th-century Kashmiri poet Bilhaṇa, the poem became one of the most celebrated works of classical Indian secular erotics (śṛṅgārakāvya), inspiring miniature painting cycles and vernacular adaptations throughout South Asia.

The Kuṭṭanīmata ('The Bawd's Counsel', also known as Śambhalīmata) is a satirical and didactic verse novel comprising 1,059 stanzas mostly in the āryā metre, composed by Dāmodaragupta, prime minister to the Kārkoṭa king Jayāpīḍa of Kashmir (r. c. 779–813 CE). The Daśakumāracarita ('The Tale of the Ten Princes') is a celebrated Sanskrit prose romance (gadyakāvya) composed by Daṇḍin (c. late 7th–8th century CE). Within a framing story of ten companion princes separated during an expedition and later reunited, each prince recounts his worldly adventures through the royal courts, forests, gambling dens, and underworlds of classical India. This e-text comprises three ucchvāsas from the core work: Ucchvāsa 3 (Upahāravarman's exploits regaining his ancestral realm of Mithilā through disguise, burglary, and court intrigue), Ucchvāsa 5 (Pramati's stratagems and winning of the princess Navamālikā in Ujjayinī), and Ucchvāsa 6 (Mitragupta's maritime adventures, capture by Yavanas, and four nested tales illustrating proper conduct).

The Pavanadūta ('Wind Messenger') by Dhoyī is a 12th-century dūtakāvya composed in 104 mandākrāntā verses at the court of King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal. Modeled closely on Kālidāsa's Meghadūta, the poem describes Kuvalayavatī, a Gandharva maiden on Mount Malaya in South India, who falls in love with Lakṣmaṇasena during his southern conquest (digvijaya) and sends the southern wind (pavana) to carry her message northward to his court at Gauḍa.
