- TEI header: 'data entry: Walter Slaje; contribution to GRETIL: Walter Slaje'
- End of e-text contains the heading '2.1. Noten zum Text', reflecting the section division of Slaje's 1993 monograph.

**Other editions:**
- Georg Martin Dursch (ed. & tr.), Ghatakarparam, oder das zerbrochene Gefäss: ein sanskritisches Gedicht, nebst den Kommentaren, Berlin: F. Dümmler, 1828. — Editio princeps of the Ghaṭakharparakāvya with an anonymous Sanskrit commentary and French translation by A.-L. Chézy.
- Madhusudan Kaul Shastri (ed.), The Ghaṭakarpara-kāvyam with the commentary of Abhinavagupta, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies 67, Srinagar: Research Department, Jammu & Kashmir State, 1945. — Critical edition of the Ghaṭakarparavivṛti by Abhinavagupta.
- Jatindra Bimal Chaudhuri (ed.), The Ghaṭakarpara-yamaka-kāvya: with the commentary Vimalā of the editor, Calcutta: Prācyavāṇī Mandira, 1953. — Edition of the poem with modern Sanskrit commentary.
- Francesco Sferra, 'Critical Edition of the Ghaṭakharparaṭīkā Attributed to Tārācandra', in: Alice Consonni et al. (eds.), Anantaratnaprabhava: Studi in onore di Giuliano Boccali, Milano: Ledizioni, 2018, pp. 347–383. — Critical edition of another commentary on the Ghaṭakharparakāvya.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary, comprising the preliminary prose and verse exegesis on maṅgala and mahākāvya status, detailed glosses on all 23 stanzas of the Ghaṭakharparakāvya, concluding verses 1–5 by Kuśalamiśra, and the scribal colophon of Rājānaka Ānandarāma dated Saṃvat 72.

**Also known as:** Gūḍhadīpikā, Ghaṭakharparagūḍhadīpikā, Ghaṭakharpara-Gūḍhadīpikā, Ghaṭakharparagūḍhārthadīpikā

**Attribution:** In the opening verse (v. 2), the final verse (v. 5), and the concluding colophon, the commentary is designated as Gūḍhadīpikā. Kuśala identifies himself as the son of Bālakṛṣṇa, grandson of the astronomer Śrīpati, and great-grandson of Kṣemaṅkara. Concluding verse 5 contains a chronogram dating the work's completion to Bhādrapada śuklāṣṭamī, Vikrama Saṃvat 1748 (1691 CE): 'nāgavedācalābje [1748] tu cābde 'bhūd Gūḍhadīpikā'.

The Gūḍhārthadīpikā (entitled Gūḍhadīpikā by its author) is a late 17th-century Sanskrit commentary by the Kashmiri scholar Kuśalamiśra on the Ghaṭakharparakāvya, a 23-stanza yamaka poem traditionally attributed to Kālidāsa. Composed in Vikrama Saṃvat 1748 (1691 CE), the commentary opens with an extensive theoretical defense of the work's classification as a mahākāvya and an inquiry into its opening verses regarding the requirement of an auspicious invocation (maṅgalācaraṇa). It then provides detailed grammatical, lexical, and semantic analyses of all 23 verses. This e-text is Walter Slaje's critical edition based on the Śāradā codex Cod. Sanskrit 23 of the Austrian National Library in Vienna.

Narrated through the reciprocal discourses of two court poets, Snigdhakaṇṭha and Madhukaṇṭha, before Kṛṣṇa, the Pūrvacampū recounts Kṛṣṇa's manifest pastimes (prakaṭa-līlā) in Vraja/Vrindavan. The Gopālacampū of Jīva Gosvāmin is the principal campū (mixed prose-and-verse kāvya) of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition, narrating the complete life and pastimes of Kṛṣṇa within a devotional and theological framework rooted in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa. This file contains pūraṇas 5 and 6 of the Uttaracampū, recounting the slaying of the elephant Kuvalayāpīḍa, the wrestlers, and Kaṃsa himself, followed by Kṛṣṇa bidding a sorrowful farewell to Nanda Mahārāja and the Vraja cowherds as they return to Gokula.

Chapter 29 of the Uttaracampū (entitled 'Bhāvikathāpramāṇaprathana') constitutes a theological narrative interlude within Jīva Gosvāmin's 16th-century masterpiece Gopālacampū. Active in the first half of the 12th century CE during the reign of King Uccala and King Somapāla of Rājapurī (for whom he composed the historical kāvya Somapālavilāsa), he is lauded by Maṅkhaka in Śrīkaṇṭhacarita 25.75. The Mugdhopadeśa ('Instruction of the Naive') is a 12th-century didactic and satirical Sanskrit poem in 66 verses composed by the Kashmiri poet Jalhaṇa. Belonging to the Kashmiri satirical-cautionary tradition exemplified by Dāmodaragupta's Kuṭṭanīmata and Kṣemendra's Samayamātṛkā and Kalāvilāsa, it warns inexperienced young men against infatuation and the deceitful, mercenary arts of courtesans (veśyās). The poem concludes with autobiographical reflections on the stages of human life, travels to various courts, and the poet's resolve to spend his old age worshipping Śiva on the banks of the Ganges.

Jānakīpariṇaya ('The Marriage of Sītā') is a classical seven-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) composed in the late seventeenth century by Rāmabhadra Dīkṣita of the Thanjavur court circle, dramatizing the Rāmāyaṇa narrative of Rāma winning and marrying Sītā. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 12 sargas comprising all 24 prabandhas (aṣṭapadīs) and connecting narrative verses in classical metres, concluding at verse 12.32 with the colophon 'iti śrī-jayadeva kṛtau śrī-śrī-gīta-govinda-mahā-kāvye suprīta-pītāmbaro nāma dvādaśa sargaḥ' followed by 'samāptam idaṃ kāvyam'.

**Also known as:** Gītagovindakāvya, Gītagovindamahākāvya, Aṣṭapadī

**Attribution:** Composed by Jayadeva, active in Bengal during the reign of the Sena king Lakṣmaṇasena (late 12th century CE). Verse 1.4 explicitly names Jayadeva alongside contemporary Sena court poets (Umāpatidhara, Govardhana, Śaraṇa, and Dhoyī).

The Gītagovinda of Jayadeva (composed in late 12th-century Bengal) is a celebrated lyrical kāvya celebrating the passionate love, separation (viraha), and joyful reconciliation of Kṛṣṇa and Rādhā. Comprising 12 cantos structured around 24 rhymed aṣṭapadīs (eight-couplet songs set to specific rāgas and tālas) framed by narrative and descriptive stanzas in classical metres, the work innovatively bridges classical Sanskrit kāvya traditions with vernacular song performance. Its synthesis of theological bhakti and refined erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) deeply influenced Gauḍīya and pan-Indian Vaiṣṇavism, inspiring enduring traditions of music, classical dance, and temple ritual across South Asia.

**Also known as:** Saṅkalpakalpadrumakāvya, Saṅkalpa-kalpa-druma, Saṅkalpakalpavṛkṣa

**Attribution:** Firmly attributed to Jīva Gosvāmin of Vṛndāvana (c. 1513/1517–1598/1608 CE); he names himself in the opening section (v. 4: 'vṛndāraṇye jaran jīvaḥ kaścit prāha manaḥ prati') and cross-references verses from his own Gopālacampū.

The Saṅkalpakalpadruma is a late Sanskrit devotional-poetic work by Jīva Gosvāmin consisting of over 700 verses, composed in his old age as an address to his own mind (manaḥ-śikṣā). The work employs the allegory of a wish-fulfilling tree (kalpadruma) divided into four parts: root (janmādi-līlā, the manifest narrative pastimes of Kṛṣṇa), trunk (nitya-līlā, the eternal eightfold daily pastimes or aṣṭakālīya-līlā), branches (sarvartu-līlā, seasonal pastimes across the six seasons), and fruit (phala-niṣpatti, the ultimate attainment of loving service). It serves a contemplative function as a devotional distillation of the theology formulated in his magnum opus, the Gopālacampū, synthesizing manifest and unmanifest līlā for internal meditation.

Modern scholars have frequently debated the authenticity of this attribution due to its stylistic simplicity and the absence of citations by early commentators such as Mallinātha, but Indian tradition and standard anthologies continue to ascribe it to Kālidāsa.

The Ṛtusaṃhāra ('Gathering of the Seasons') is a descriptive lyric poem (khaṇḍakāvya) in six cantos, traditionally ascribed to Kālidāsa and widely regarded as his earliest surviving work. In rich sensory imagery, the poem depicts the six classical Indian seasons—summer, rains, autumn, early winter, winter, and spring—intertwining panoramic nature scenes with the erotic moods and romantic longings of lovers. Historically, it holds a seminal position in Indological history as the editio princeps of printed Sanskrit literature, published in Calcutta by Sir William Jones in 1792.

The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') is a lyric poem composed in 111 mandākrāntā stanzas by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). An exiled yakṣa, separated from his beloved wife and pining on Mount Rāmagiri, enlists a passing monsoon cloud to carry a message of reassurance to his home in the mythical Himalayan city of Alakā. The poem is divided into two sections: the Pūrvamegha, charting the cloud's journey across the landscape of north-central India, and the Uttaramegha, describing the splendour of Alakā and the sorrow of the faithful wife. Other recensions vary in length: the Kerala recension commented on by Rāghavānanda has 31 verses, while the common Southern/Śrīvaiṣṇava vulgate contains 40 verses.

**Also known as:** Mukundamālāstotra

**Attribution:** The poem identifies its composer as King Kulaśekhara in the final verse (v. 34: rājñā kṛtā stutiriyaṃ kulaśekhareṇa). In traditional Hindu accounts, he is identified with Kulaśekhara Āḻvār (c. 9th century CE), the Chera king and Śrīvaiṣṇava saint credited also with the Tamil Perumāl Tirumoḻi. While some modern scholars debate whether the author of the stotra is identical with the royal dramatist Kulaśekhara Varma (author of Subhadrādhanañjaya and Tapatīsaṃvaraṇa), traditional and scholarly consensus attributes the Mukundamālā to Kulaśekhara.

The Mukundamālā ('Garland of Mukunda') is a celebrated Sanskrit devotional lyric (stotra) composed by King Kulaśekhara in praise of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa. Using a variety of classical meters and intricate phonetic ornamentation (anuprāsa), the author expresses total surrender (prapatti), renunciation of mundane ambition and heavenly rebirth, and the singular plea to remember Kṛṣṇa's lotus feet at the moment of death. The work exists across distinct regional recensions (a 31-verse Kerala recension, a 34-verse Northern recension, and a 40-verse Southern recension); this e-text contains the complete 34-verse Northern recension printed in the Kāvyamālā.

Written in classical metres including Śikhariṇī, Mālinī, and Pṛthvī, the verses extol Śiva's ascetic iconography—the crescent moon, poison-darkened neck, skull ornament, and Gaṅgā flowing in his matted locks—while expressing detachment from worldly distraction and total surrender to the deity. The Śiśupālavadha ('The Slaying of Śiśupāla') is a canonical 20-canto court epic (mahākāvya) composed by the poet Māgha in the late 7th or early 8th century CE. Expanding an episode from the Sabhāparvan of the Mahābhārata, the narrative recounts the slaying of the insolent king Śiśupāla of Chedi by Kṛṣṇa during Yudhiṣṭhira's Rājasūya sacrifice. The Mālatīmādhava is a ten-act drama of the prakaraṇa genre composed by the 8th-century poet Bhavabhūti. Set principally in the city of Padmāvatī, it depicts the fraught romance between Mādhava and Mālatī (alongside the subplot of Makaranda and Madayantikā), which faces obstacle from an imperial court betrothal and terror from Kāpālika sorcerers in cremation grounds before reaching resolution through the interventions of the Buddhist nun Kāmandakī and her disciple Saudāminī. This e-text contains the complete Sanskrit text of the play accompanied throughout by the detailed Sanskrit commentary (ṭīkā) of the 14th/15th-century Maithila scholiast Jagaddhara.

Expanding the Nalopākhyāna from the Mahābhārata, it recounts the romance and svayaṃvara of King Nala of Niṣadha and Princess Damayantī of Vidarbha through their marriage and courtly union. Ranked alongside the Kirātārjunīya and Śiśupālavadha in the Bṛhattrayī ('Great Trio') of classical mahākāvyas, the poem is famed for its extreme stylistic intricacy, mastery of śleṣa (puns), and wide-ranging philosophical erudition.

Weaving dynastic history and panegyric with mythological and romantic motifs, the poem chronicles the king's quest and courtship of the Nāga princess Śaśiprabhā, culminating in his expedition to the underworld, the slaying of the demon king Vajrāṅkuśa, and their wedding.

The Setubandha ('The Building of the Causey' or 'The Causeway'), also titled Rāvaṇavaha ('The Slaying of Rāvaṇa'), is a celebrated mahākāvya in 15 cantos (āśvāsas) composed in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit by the Vākāṭaka ruler Pravarasena II (c. 5th century CE). Highly extolled by Daṇḍin, Bāṇabhaṭṭa, and Ānandavardhana, it is the foremost extant epic in Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit and a major touchstone of classical Indian poetics.

- Sheldon Pollock, ed., The Śṛṅgāratilaka of Rudra Bhaṭṭa with the Rasataraṅgiṇī Commentary of Gopāla Bhaṭṭa, draft critical edition, 2018. — Modern critical edition incorporating the commentary of Gopāla Bhaṭṭa.

**Translations:**
- Sheldon Pollock, A Rasa Reader: Classical Indian Aesthetics, New York: Columbia University Press, 2017. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in three chapters (paricchedas 1–3), ending at verse 3.57 and the closing colophon (segment 990).

**Also known as:** Kāvyarasālaṅkāra

**Attribution:** Rudrabhaṭṭa was conflated with the Kashmiri poetician Rudraṭa (author of the Kāvyālaṅkāra, fl. c. 850 CE) by Richard Pischel in the editio princeps (1886). However, subsequent scholarship (Jacobi, S. K. De, P. V. Kane) established that Rudrabhaṭṭa is a distinct, later author composed roughly between the late 10th and 11th centuries CE (terminus ante quem provided by citations in Hemacandra's Kāvyānuśāsana).

The Śṛṅgāratilaka ('Ornament of the Erotic') of Rudrabhaṭṭa is an influential treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṃkāraśāstra) in three chapters (paricchedas). Composed around the 10th or 11th century CE, it represents an early milestone in transposing the aesthetic theory of rasa and emotional states (bhāvas) from dramaturgy (nāṭya) directly to poetic literature (kāvya). Focusing preeminently on the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) and the systematic typology of lovers and heroines (nāyaka- and nāyikā-bheda), Rudrabhaṭṭa illustrates theoretical definitions with original and anthologized kāvya stanzas.

The Vāsavadattā of Subandhu (composed c. late 6th to early 7th century CE) is an ornate classical Sanskrit prose romance (kathā). The narrative recounts how Prince Kandarpaketu and Princess Vāsavadattā experience dreams of each other, seek each other out, elope, undergo separation after Vāsavadattā is petrified into stone by an ascetic's curse, and are reunited once the touch of Kandarpaketu restores her to life. **Coverage:** complete — Complete drama in six acts (Acts 1–6), including opening stage directions, Prakrit dialogues accompanied inline by Sanskrit chāyā in square brackets, and concluding with the Bharatavākya (6.19) and colophon (iti svapnanāṭakam avasitam).

**Also known as:** Svapnavāsavadattam, Svapnanāṭaka

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the ancient playwright Bhāsa. Recovered from Malayalam palm-leaf manuscripts in Kerala by T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī in 1910–1912 among the 13 'Trivandrum plays'. While Bhāsa's authorship of a Svapnavāsavadatta is famously recorded by Rājaśekhara (Sūktimuktāvalī 4.48) and celebrated by Kālidāsa (Mālavikāgnimitra 1.1), the degree to which the surviving Kerala manuscripts represent Bhāsa's pristine original or a stage adaptation shaped within the Kūṭiyāṭṭam theatrical tradition remains actively debated in Sanskrit scholarship.

The Svapnavāsavadatta ('The Dream of Vāsavadattā') is a six-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) dramatizing episodes from the Udayana legend cycle of the Bṛhatkathā. To facilitate King Udayana's political alliance with King Darśaka of Magadha and recapture his kingdom from the usurper Āruṇī, Minister Yaugandharāyaṇa arranges the staged death of Queen Vāsavadattā in a fire at Lāvāṇaka and conceals her under the identity of Lady Āvantikā in the care of Princess Padmāvatī. The dramatic and psychological climax occurs in Act 5 (the dream act / svapnāṅka), where the sleeping Udayana addresses Vāsavadattā in what he believes to be a dream while she secretly comforts him, leading to their eventual reunion and royal restoration in Act 6.

**Also known as:** Veṇīsaṃhāranāṭaka, Veṇīsaṃvaraṇa

**Attribution:** The work is unanimously attributed to Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa (who bore the epithet or title Mṛgarājalakṣman, as attested in the prologue to Act 1, line 55). He is traditionally placed in the late 7th to early 8th century CE (c. 675–750 CE), an upper limit confirmed by quotations of verses from the play in early treatises on alaṃkāraśāstra such as Vāmana's Kāvyālaṃkārasūtravṛtti (c. 800 CE) and Ānandavardhana's Dhvanyāloka (9th century CE).

The Veṇīsaṃhāra ('The Binding of the Braid') is a six-act classical Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) by Bhaṭṭanārāyaṇa (fl. c. 700 CE) based on the Mahābhārata war. The plot centres on the vow taken by Bhīmasena to avenge the public humiliation of Draupadī by slaying Duḥśāsana and Duryodhana, refusing to let her braid her hair until it has been washed and bound with their blood. Celebrated across classical Indian dramaturgy (notably in the Daśarūpaka and Sāhityadarpaṇa), the play is renowned as an archetype of the heroic (vīra) and furious (raudra) aesthetic sentiments and a model of classical plot construction (sandhis).

**Coverage:** fragment — Extremely fragmentary remains of three early plays preserved on palm-leaf fragments from the Berlin Turfan collection (SHT 16 and SHT 57). For the Śāriputraprakaraṇa, only scattered portions of acts 8 and 9 (including the final colophon) are preserved; the allegorical drama and courtesan drama survive only as isolated speech and verse fragments.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Śāriputraprakaraṇa (Aśvaghoṣa, root text)
- Allegorical Buddhist Drama (root text)
- Prakaraṇa with a Courtesan (root text)

**Also known as:** Bruchstücke buddhistischer Dramen, Śāriputraprakaraṇa, Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa, Buddhist Dramatic Fragments

**Attribution:** The Śāriputraprakaraṇa (or Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa) is explicitly attributed to Aśvaghoṣa (son of Suvarṇākṣī) in the surviving colophon of Act 9 (SHT 57). The two other plays preserved in the same manuscript find (SHT 16)—an allegorical play featuring personified qualities (Buddhi, Dhṛti, Kīrti) and a comedy featuring a courtesan (gaṇikā), a vidūṣaka (Komudagandha), and a rogue (duṣṭa)—are anonymous, though Lüders and subsequent scholarship suggest they stem from the same Kuṣāṇa-era Buddhist dramatic circle.

This e-text contains the oldest surviving specimens of Indian dramatic literature, discovered on palm-leaf fragments from Kizil near Turfan (Central Asia) and datable to the Kuṣāṇa period (c. 1st–2nd century CE). The principal identifiable play is Aśvaghoṣa's Śāriputraprakaraṇa (or Śāradvatīputraprakaraṇa), a nine-act play dramatizing the conversion of the Buddha's foremost disciples, Śāriputra and Maudgalyāyana. Preserved alongside it are fragments of two anonymous Buddhist plays: an allegorical drama featuring personifications (Buddhi, Dhṛti, Kīrti) and a prakaraṇa or social comedy involving a courtesan (gaṇikā), a rogue (duṣṭa), and a jester (vidūṣaka). These fragments are of foundational importance for the history of classical Sanskrit theatre and the early history of Middle Indo-Aryan dialects (archaic forms of Māgadhī, Ardhamāgadhī, and Śaurasenī).

**Coverage:** partial — Contains only the metrical verses across all five acts (Nā_1.1 to Nā_5.41, including the concluding bharatavākya), omitting all intervening Sanskrit and Prakrit prose dialogue and stage directions.

**Also known as:** Nāgānanda, Nāgānandanāṭaka

**Attribution:** Attributed to the 7th-century North Indian emperor Harṣa (Harṣavardhana / Harṣadeva, r. c. 606–647 CE), to whom the dramas Ratnāvalī and Priyadarśikā are also ascribed. Later literary critics (notably Mammaṭa, Kāvyaprakāśa 1.2) recorded the tradition that court poets (such as Dhāvaka or Bāṇabhaṭṭa) composed works in Harṣa's name in exchange for royal patronage; however, modern Indological scholarship recognizes Harṣa's royal authorship or direct courtly sponsorship.

The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Serpents') is a five-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) attributed to King Harṣa of Kanauj (7th century CE), dramatizing the Buddhist legend of the Vidyādhara prince Jīmūtavāhana. The opening acts combine standard courtly kāvya romance with Jīmūtavāhana's courtship and marriage to Princess Malayavatī, while the fourth and fifth acts center on his Bodhisattva-like self-sacrifice: offering his own flesh on the slaughter stone to Garuḍa to rescue the young Nāga Śaṅkhacūḍa. Moved by Jīmūtavāhana's radical compassion and non-violence, Garuḍa renounces the slaughter of serpents and revives those previously consumed. Famous for invoking both the Buddha (munīndra / jina) and the Hindu goddess Gaurī, the work is an exceptional surviving exemplar of classical Buddhist dramatic literature.

The Ratnāvalī is a four-act romantic court drama (nāṭikā) attributed to King Harṣa of Kanauj (Harṣavardhana, r. c. 606–647 CE). Based on the Udayana legendary cycle derived from Guṇāḍhya's Bṛhatkathā, it depicts King Udayana of Vatsa falling in love with Sāgarikā, an attendant to Chief Queen Vāsavadattā who is eventually revealed to be Princess Ratnāvalī of Siṃhala (Sri Lanka). Featuring motifs of mistaken identity, a pet starling (śārikā) repeating romantic secrets, and a faux palace fire staged by a court magician (aindrajālika), the play is treated by classical dramaturgs (such as Dhanañjaya in the Daśarūpaka) as the standard exemplar of the four-act nāṭikā genre.

The Mattavilāsaprahasana ('The Farce of Drunken Sport') is a 7th-century one-act Sanskrit satire (prahasana) by the Pallava monarch Mahendravarman I, set in Kāñcīpuram. The plot follows a drunken Kāpālika ascetic, Satyasoma, and his consort Devasomā, who misplace their skull begging bowl (kapāla) and wrongly accuse a Buddhist monk, Nāgasena, of having stolen it. A Pāśupata ascetic is called in to arbitrate the dispute until a madman arrives with the bowl, which he had recovered from a stray dog, clearing the monk of blame. The play satirizes contemporary sectarian friction and religious hypocrisy among Kāpālikas, Pāśupatas, Buddhists, and Jains, and survives as a staple piece in Kerala's classical Kūṭiyāṭṭam theater.

His date is debated, generally placed between the 5th and early 7th century CE (often connected with Maukhari king Avantivarman mentioned in the final bharatavākya variant).

The Mudrārākṣasa is a celebrated seven-act political drama (nāṭaka) attributed to Viśākhadatta, dramatizing the statecraft of Cāṇakya (Kauṭilya) following the overthrow of the Nanda dynasty. Uniquely devoid of romantic subplots or supernatural elements, the drama hinges entirely on espionage, political psychology, and the exploitation of a dropped signet ring (mudrā) to compel Rākṣasa—the loyal minister of the fallen Nandas—into accepting office under the newly established Mauryan emperor Candragupta. The work is renowned as an intricate literary manifestation of classical Indian political philosophy (arthaśāstra and nītiśāstra).

Cantos 1–3 of a 9th-century Sanskrit court epic (mahākāvya) retelling the Rāmāyaṇa story. Unlike traditional epic narratives that start with Rāma's youth, the poem commences in medias res at Mount Mālyavat, where Rāma laments his separation from Sītā as the monsoon ends. Cantos 1–3 describe the onset of autumn, Lakṣmaṇa's words of consolation and resolve, nightfall and moonrise on the mountain, and morning rites followed by strategic deliberation before departing for Lake Pampā.

Transferring analytical categories from poetics (guṇa, alaṅkāra, jīvita, and parikara) to female physical charm, Ruyyaka provides a taxonomy of ten innate qualities of feminine beauty (such as lāvaṇya, chāyā, and saubhāgya), personal ornamentation (gems, gold, garments, cosmetics), vital expressions of youth, and accompanying settings and retinues from the perspective of an urban aesthete (nāgaraka / sahṛdaya).

The Pādatāḍitaka ('The Kick') by the late Gupta-era poet Śyāmilaka is the longest and most celebrated of the four satirical monologue plays preserved in the Caturbhāṇī. Spoken entirely by a viṭa (cosmopolitan man-about-town), the play recounts his journey through the streets of Sārvabhaumanagara (Ujjayinī) to convene a council of rogues to prescribe a comedic expiation (prāyaścitta) for a high-caste gentleman kicked on the head by a courtesan during a lovers' quarrel. - The master Kathāsaritsāgara TEI header on GRETIL (sa_somadeva-kathAsaritsAgara.xml) credits Elena Artesani as contributor and specifies: 'Based on the edition by Durgaprasad and Parab, Bombay : Nirnaya-Sagar Press 1915'
- The verse extent and numbering (SoKss 12.8.21 to 12.32.41) correspond exactly to the text printed on pp. 406–466 of the 1915 Nirṇaya Sāgar Press revised edition

**Other editions:**

- Paṇḍit Durgāprasād and Kāśīnāth Pāṇḍuraṅg Parab (eds.), The Kathâsaritsâgara of Somadevabhaṭṭa, Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgar Press, 1889 (1st ed.); 4th ed. revised by W. L. S. Paṇśīkar, 1930. — Standard Nirṇaya Sāgar Press vulgate.
- Jagadīśalāla Śāstrī (ed.), Kathāsaritsāgaraḥ, with Hindi translation, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1970. — Widely cited Nagari reprint edition with Hindi translation.

**Translations:**
- C. H. Tawney (tr.), The Ocean of Story: Being C.H. Tawney's Translation of Somadeva's Kathā Sarit Sāgara, edited with introduction, notes, and terminal essay by N. M. Penzer, 10 vols., London: Chas. J. Sawyer Ltd., 1924–1928 (reprinted Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1968). (English)
- Katsuhiko Kamimura (tr.), 『屍鬼二十五話 ― インド伝奇集』 (Tōyō Bunko 323), Tokyo: Heibonsha, 1978. (Japanese)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains only the Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā cycle embedded in Book 12 (Śaśāṅkavatīlambaka), from taraṅga 8, verse 21 to taraṅga 32, verse 41 (verses SoKss_12,8.21–32.41 / Vet_0.1–25.41; 4,410 half-verse segments / 2,205 verses). The complete Kathāsaritsāgara comprises 18 lambakas, 124 taraṅgas, and roughly 21,388 verses.

**Also known as:** Kathāsaritsāgara: Vetālapañcaviṃśati, Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā (Somadeva recension)

**Attribution:** Composed in Kashmir c. 1063–1081 CE by the Śaiva Brahmin court poet Somadeva Bhaṭṭa (son of Rāma Bhaṭṭa) for Queen Sūryavatī, wife of King Ananta of Kashmir.

The Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā ('Twenty-Five Tales of the Vetāla') section of Somadeva's 11th-century Kashmirian epic Kathāsaritsāgara is embedded within Book 12 (Śaśāṅkavatīlambaka, taraṅgas 8.21–32.41). In this classic frame narrative, King Trivikramasena (the archetype of King Vikramāditya) undertakes to retrieve a corpse inhabited by a vetāla (ghoul) from a cremation ground for an ascetic named Kṣāntiśīla; during each transport, the vetāla tells an intricate riddle-tale that compels the king to break silence to render judgment, resetting the journey until the final tale exposes the mendicant's murderous deception. Somadeva's verse rendering is one of the two earliest surviving complete Sanskrit recensions of this world-famous cycle of wonder-tales.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the poet-philosopher Bhartṛhari, whom tradition frequently identifies with the 5th-century grammarian-philosopher of the Vākyapadīya. As shown in D. D. Kosambi's critical text-historical studies, the centuries circulated widely in fluid regional recensions and accrued extensive anthological additions around an authentic core.

A collection of three 'centuries' (śataka) of gnomic and lyric epigrams traditionally attributed to Bhartṛhari: the Nītiśataka on worldly prudence, ethics, and civic conduct; the Śṛṅgāraśataka on the pleasures, moods, and pitfalls of erotic desire; and the Vairāgyaśataka on renunciation, transience, and ascetic withdrawal. The triad moves across the classic aims of life (dharma, artha, kāma) toward ultimate spiritual dispassion (vairāgya). Widely anthologized, memorized, and translated, it remains among the most influential works in the Sanskrit subhāṣita tradition.

Modern scholarship distinguishes this Kashmirian anthologist (placed variously between the 12th and 15th centuries) from the 10th-century Kashmiri commentator Vallabhadeva (author of commentaries on Kālidāsa, Māgha, Mayūra, and Ratnākara).

The Subhāṣitāvalī ('A Garland of Eloquent Sayings') is a premier Sanskrit poetic anthology compiled in Kashmir by Vallabhadeva. The complete anthology comprises 3,527 verses distributed across 101 thematic sections (paddhatis), citing roughly 360 named poets alongside anonymous stanzas spanning over a millennium of classical Sanskrit literature. It represents an indispensable witness for many lost poets and works, especially from Kashmir. This digital file covers the opening 1,040 verses, comprising initial devatāstuti (invocations to deities), gnomic and moral epigrams (nīti, vidyā, dhana), and anyokti verses.

The Rājataraṅgiṇī (or Dvitīyā Rājataraṅgiṇī) of Jonarāja (d. 1459 CE) is a Sanskrit verse chronicle continuing Kalhaṇa's celebrated 12th-century history of Kashmir down to the reign of Sultan Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (r. 1420–1470 CE). This e-text also includes the approximately 350 stanzas interpolated in the late 16th century by an anonymous Kashmiri editor known as Pseudo-Jonarāja.

The first skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa establishes the narrative, theological, and devotional frame for the scripture. The eleventh book (skandha) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa narrates the events leading to the end of the Dvāpara Yuga, including the curse of the sages on the Yadu dynasty, their tragic fratricidal collapse at Prabhāsa, and Kṛṣṇa's ascension to his transcendent realm. The theological and philosophical core of the book (adhyāyas 6/7–29) is the Uddhavagītā, an extended exposition imparted by Kṛṣṇa to his companion Uddhava concerning jñāna, bhakti, renunciation, the nature of prakṛti and puruṣa, and the twenty-four spiritual teachers of the Avadhūta. It is among the most commented-upon parts of the Purāṇa in Vaiṣṇava traditions.

The twelfth and concluding skandha (book) of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa opens with a prophetic account of post-Mahābhārata royal dynasties up through the Kali Yuga (including the Nandas, Mauryas, and Śuṅgas), followed by a description of the moral, spiritual, and physical degeneration of humanity in the Kali age and the advent of the Kalki avatāra. **Attribution:** The root Purāṇa text is traditionally attributed to Vyāsa (Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana). Chapters 29–33 of the tenth skandha of the Bhāgavatapurāṇa, known as the Rāsa-pañcādhyāyī ('five chapters on the rāsa dance'), narrate Kṛṣṇa's autumn-night circle dance (rāsalīlā) with the cowherd maidens (gopīs) of Vraja, his temporary disappearance to dispel their pride, their anguished laments and song of longing (Gopīgīta), and his reunion with them in ecstatic devotional union. This section is universally regarded as the aesthetic and devotional climax of the Purāṇa. The included commentary, the Bhāvārthadīpikā by Śrīdharasvāmin (c. 14th century), interprets the erotic-devotional līlā within an Advaita-theistic framework as the triumph over desire (kāmavijaya) and served as the authoritative baseline for all subsequent Vaiṣṇava hermeneutics.

**Also known as:** Nīlamata, Kaśmīramāhātmya

**Attribution:** The Nīlamatapurāṇa is an anonymous regional Upapurāṇa and sthala-māhātmya of Kashmir, traditionally framed as an instruction given by the sage Bṛhadaśva to King Janamejaya narrating the teachings of Nīla, king of the Nāgas, to the sage Kaśyapa.

The Nīlamatapurāṇa (composed c. 6th–8th century CE) is an early regional Purāṇa and the foremost sacred topography (sthala-māhātmya) of ancient Kashmir. It narrates the mythic origins of the Kashmir Valley through the draining of the primordial lake Satisaras by Kaśyapa and the gods, establishing the subsequent coexistence of humans, Nāgas, and Piśācas under the guidance of Nīla Nāga. The text provides a comprehensive record of ancient Kashmiri festivals, domestic rituals, and tīrthas, and served as the principal early source consulted by Kalhaṇa for his 12th-century historical chronicle Rājataraṅgiṇī.

The second part (Uparivibhāga or Uttaravibhāga) of the Kūrmapurāṇa consists of 44 chapters. It opens with the Īśvaragītā (chapters 1–11), an influential philosophical text modeled after the Bhagavadgītā in which Śiva discourses on knowledge, yoga, and liberation, synthesizing Pāśupata-leaning Śaiva theology with Sāṃkhya-Yoga and Advaita Vedānta. ## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete Revākhaṇḍa belonging to the Skandapurāṇa recension in 116 adhyāyas (1.1–116.22), which constitutes a single section of the vast Skandapurāṇa corpus.

**Also known as:** Revākhaṇḍa, Bṛhat-Śrīnarmadāpurāṇam Revākhaṇḍam, Narmadāpurāṇa, Bṛhannarmadāpurāṇa

**Attribution:** Framed within an opening colloquy between Śiva and Skanda leading into the primary dialogue between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and King Yudhiṣṭhira; traditionally classified as a khaṇḍa of the Skandapurāṇa.

The Revākhaṇḍa is a sacred geographical and pilgrimage text (tīrthamāhātmya) celebrating the holy sites along the course of the Narmadā (Revā) River in Central India. Structured largely around dialogues between the sage Mārkaṇḍeya and Yudhiṣṭhira, the work delineates the ritual circumambulation (parikramā) of both the northern and southern banks, detailing origin legends, shrines, and devotional benefits (phala). As shown by Jürgen Neuss, this 116-chapter recension is the genuine Skandapurāṇa Revākhaṇḍa, distinct from the 232-chapter text of the Vāyupurāṇa tradition mistakenly printed as SkP 5.3 in the Veṅkaṭeśvara edition.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Vyāsa and framed as narrated by the Sūta Lomaharṣaṇa to the sages of Kurujāṅgala; in modern scholarship recognized as an anonymous composite tīrthamāhātmya incorporated into the Vāmanapurāṇa tradition.

The Saromāhātmya is a 27-chapter pilgrimage manual (tīrthamāhātmya) preserved as an insertion or appendix to the Vāmanapurāṇa (placed between chapters 23 and 24 in the All-India Kashiraj Trust critical edition). Framed as a discourse delivered by the bard Lomaharṣaṇa to the ṛṣis assembled in Kurujāṅgala, it provides an elaborate eulogy of Kurukṣetra and its sacred lakes, notably Brahmasaras (identified with Rāmahrada and Samantapañcaka) and Sannihita-saras, alongside sacred sites along the Sarasvatī and Dṛṣadvatī rivers. The text blends pilgrimage itineraries with local mythology, celebrating Sthāṇutīrtha and recounting both Vaiṣṇava legends (the Vāmana avatāra) and Śaiva myths.

**Attribution:** A secure composition of the Śvetāmbara philosopher-monk Haribhadrasūri (c. 8th century CE). Haribhadra identifies himself by name in verse 699 (ācāryaharibhadreṇa śāstravārtāsamuccayam) and incorporates his customary sobriquet bhavaviraha in verse 700.

The Śāstravārtāsamuccaya ('Compendium of Philosophical Discourses') is a major 8th-century doxographical and polemical treatise in 701 anuṣṭubh verses across 11 chapters (stabakas) by the Śvetāmbara master Haribhadrasūri. The work presents a systematic survey and critique of non-Jain philosophical traditions, including Cārvāka materialism, theism (Īśvaravāda), Sāṃkhya dualism, Buddhist theories of momentariness (kṣaṇikavāda) and idealism (vijñānavāda/śūnyavāda), Advaita monism, and Mīmāṃsā rejections of omniscience. Haribhadra examines each perspective critically while adhering to the Jain framework of non-one-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) and concludes with an exposition of the nature of omniscience and spiritual liberation.

Of the 12+ śāsanas listed in the introduction (incl. tattvopaplava and anekānta), the last ones are missing; the work is transmitted incomplete in only two manuscripts (Trikha 2012: 107, cited in Freschi & Maas 2017).

**Also known as:** Satya-śāsana-parīkṣā, Satyasasanapariksa

**Attribution:** Authored by the prominent Digambara Jaina philosopher and logician Vidyānanda (Vidyānandin, c. 9th–10th century CE). The opening maṅgala verse names him: 'vidyānandādhipaḥ svāmī vidvaddevo jineśvaraḥ' [0].

The Satyaśāsanaparīkṣā ('Investigation into the True Teaching') is a Digambara Jaina doxographical and polemical treatise in prose and verse composed by the philosopher Vidyānanda (Vidyānandin, c. 9th–10th century CE). The work systematically examines rival Indian philosophical schools—including Advaita Vedānta (Parabrahmādvaita), Śabdādvaita, Buddhist Vijñānādvaita and Sautrāntika, Citrādvaita, Cārvāka, theistic and non-theistic Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā—testing them against the epistemic criterion of non-contradiction with perceptual experience and reliable testimony (dṛṣṭeṣṭāviruddhatva). By demonstrating internal and experiential inconsistencies in each monistic or one-sided system (ekānta), Vidyānanda seeks to establish Jaina non-one-sided realism (anekāntavāda) as the sole valid teaching; the surviving text breaks off mid-sentence during the critique of Bhāṭṭa and Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā.

The Stavacintāmaṇi ('Wish-fulfilling Jewel of Praise') is a Kashmiri devotional hymn in 120 verses composed by Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa (c. late 9th to 10th century CE). Expressing the philosophy of non-dual Śaivism (Trika, Spanda, and Pratyabhijñā), it articulates intense devotion (bhakti) to Śiva as the experiential realization of identity between the individual consciousness and supreme reality. Because of its doctrinal and poetic depth, it became a standard hymn within Kashmir Śaivism and was famously commented upon in the 11th century by Abhinavagupta's pupil Kṣemarāja.

The Bījanighaṇṭu (also termed Mantrakośa) is a tantric glossary in 87 verses containing cryptic names and esoteric designations for Sanskrit phonemes and mantric seed-syllables (bījas). Presented as a revelation spoken by Śiva and claiming derivation from the Bhūtaḍāmara and Yakṣaḍāmaratantra traditions, it supplies deity epithets and elemental associations for individual letters as well as composite syllables (such as śrīṃ, hrīṃ, krīṃ, and klīṃ). The work serves as a practical decoding key for reconstructing esoteric mantras (mantroddhāra) embedded in tantric ritual texts.

**Also known as:** Devīkālottara, Devīkālottaratantra, Jñānācāraprakaraṇa, Jñānācāravicāra

**Attribution:** Revealed scriptural text of the Śaiva tradition, cast as an exposition given by Śiva (Īśvara) to the Goddess. In manuscript colophons it frequently presents itself as the 65th paṭala of the Jñānakāṇḍa of a 24,000-verse Devīkālottara, though no other paṭalas are attested.

The Devīkālottarāgama (or Devīkālottara) is a concise 84-verse Śaiva scriptural text presented as a dialogue in which Śiva reveals the essence of liberating knowledge (jñāna) and conduct (ācāra) to the Goddess. Although presented in manuscript colophons as the 65th chapter of a putative 24,000-verse redaction of the Kālottara, it has circulated independently as a complete treatise. In marked contrast to ritual-oriented Śaiva Siddhānta scriptures, the work sets aside external worship, mantras, maṇḍalas, and prāṇāyāma in favor of meditation on non-dual, supportless awareness (nirālamba / niṣkala jñāna). Because of this contemplative orientation, it was commented upon by Nirañjanasiddha (drawing on a Kannaḍa commentary, likely from a Vīraśaiva context) and gained lasting reception in later South Indian Advaita-oriented Śaivism, including within the circle of Ramaṇa Maharṣi.

Walter Slaje (2015) demonstrated that the 18-verse hymn is an anthological compilation (florilegium) centered on Ardhanārīśvara. Seven of the stanzas are opening maṅgala verses from Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī (1.2, 2.1, 3.1, 4.1, 5.1, 6.1, 8.1), while verse 17 is from Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa's 14th-century Stutikusumāñjali (15.37) and verse 18 is from Śrīvara's late 15th-century Rājataraṅgiṇī (1.1.2). An 18-verse Kashmirian stotra praising Śiva in his composite androgynous form as Ardhanārīśvara, highlighting the aesthetic and paradoxical harmony between the divine male and female halves (Śiva and Pārvatī). Long catalogued as an independent work by Kalhaṇa, it was shown by Walter Slaje to be a late composite florilegium bringing together invocatory stanzas from Kalhaṇa's Rājataraṅgiṇī alongside verses from Jagaddhara Bhaṭṭa's Stutikusumāñjali and Śrīvara's Rājataraṅgiṇī.

- Pandit Rajachandra Nyayapanchanan (ed. & trans.), Karatoyāmāhātmya, with Bengali translation, Bengal, 1298 B.S. [1891 CE]. — Editio princeps, based on local manuscripts; reprinted in Sen (1929).

**Translations:**
- Pandit Rajachandra Nyayapanchanan, Karatoyāmāhātmya, Bengal, 1298 B.S. [1891 CE]. (Bengali)
- Dipsikha Acharya, Sudip Khasnobish, and Chanchal Adhikary (eds.), Locating the 'Local' in South Asia: Critical Themes in the History of Northern Bengal, Routledge, 2025, Appendix: 'Karatoyāmāhātmya, the English Translation'. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 85 anuṣṭubh stanzas (KtoM_01–85), comprising two thematic sections: Pauṇḍrakṣetramāhātmya (vv. 1–60) and Karatoyāmāhātmya proper (vv. 61–85), ending with the final colophon.

**Also known as:** Pauṇḍrakṣetramāhātmya, Karatoyāmahātīrthamāhātmya

**Attribution:** A regional Purāṇic sthalamāhātmya purporting to belong to a larger lost work, the Uttara-Pauṇḍra-khaṇḍa. The closing colophon attributes composition to Paraśurāma (paraśurāmaviracitam), framed within a dialogue between Sūta and Śaunaka recounting an interlocution between Śiva and Pārvatī. The historical author is anonymous.

The Karatoyāmāhātmya is an early medieval regional sthalamāhātmya in 85 verses extolling the sacred Karatoyā river and the holy precinct of Pauṇḍravardhana (modern Mahasthangarh, Bogra District, Bangladesh). Set as a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī reported by Sūta to the sages, the text relates the mythic origin of the Karatoyā from the water poured onto Śiva's hands during his marriage to Pārvatī and surveys the holy bathing places, shrines, and lingas established by Paraśurāma in Pauṇḍrakṣetra. Verses from the text are cited in medieval dharmaśāstra and lexical commentaries as early as Sarvānanda's Ṭīkāsarvasva (1159 CE) and Devaṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā, confirming its currency in the twelfth century.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Lakulīśa (or Nakulīśa), an incarnation of Śiva regarded as the 2nd-century CE revealer and founder of the Pāśupata order.

The Pāśupatasūtra is the foundational aphoristic scripture of the Pāśupatas, the earliest documented sectarian Śaiva ascetic movement of the Atimārga. Arranged around the five doctrinal categories (pañcārtha: effect, cause, yoga, ritual observance, and cessation of suffering), the work outlines the discipline of the initiated ascetic. This regimen includes controversial practices such as acting crazed, trembling, limping, and courting social contempt to divest demerit onto onlookers, culminating in continuous contemplation of Rudra-Śiva to achieve the permanent end of suffering through divine grace (īśaprasāda).

The Ekākṣarakośa is a short monosyllabic dictionary (ekākṣarakośa) attributed to the 12th-century Buddhist grammarian and lexicographer Puruṣottamadeva. It catalogues individual vowels and consonant syllables together with their diverse divine, cosmological, and conventional lexical meanings. Originally composed to assist poets in metrical composition and verbal puzzles, it was later adopted by Tantric practitioners as a key manual for deciphering cryptic seed-syllables (bījamantras) and coded ritual formulae.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkara (Śaṅkarācārya). Modern critical scholarship (beginning with W. The Saundaryalaharī ('Wave of Beauty') is a celebrated Tantric devotional hymn of 100 (or 103) stanzas composed in the śikhariṇī metre in praise of Tripurasundarī (the Great Goddess of the Śrīvidyā tradition). The hymn falls into two distinct divisions: the first 41 verses (frequently transmitted independently as the Ānandalaharī, or 'Wave of Bliss') articulate the esoteric doctrines of Śrīcakra worship, mantra, kuṇḍalinī-yoga, and the non-dual union of Śiva and Śakti; the second portion (verses 42–100/103) presents an elaborate head-to-toe (keśādipāda) poetic description of the Goddess's transcendent physical form. Although universally ascribed by Indian tradition to Ādi Śaṅkara, modern critical scholarship dates the poem to between the 11th and 14th centuries CE on theological and internal grounds.

The Śivadṛṣṭi ('The Vision of Śiva') by Somānanda (c. 900–950 CE) is the foundational philosophical treatise of the Pratyabhijñā ('Recognition') tradition of Kashmir Śaivism. Composed across seven chapters (āhnikas), the work articulates a radical non-dual pantheism maintaining that all manifestations in the universe, conscious as well as insentient, are identical with Śiva's autonomous dynamic consciousness. Chapters 1–3 establish this theology of divine will (icchā) and power (śakti) while refuting opposing positions, notably the Śāktas, the linguistic monism (Śabdabrahmavāda) of Bhartṛhari, and dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta doctrines.

**Attribution:** Traditional Śaiva lore attributes the composition to the gandharva Puṣpadanta, who is said to have composed the hymn to seek Śiva's forgiveness after losing his invisibility. Norman Brown demonstrated that the original core comprised 31 verses (as preserved in the 11th/12th-century Amareśvara temple inscription at Māndhātā), and treated the stanzas naming Puṣpadanta as later accretion verses.

The Śivamahimnastava ('Hymn on the Greatness of Śiva'), traditionally ascribed to the gandharva Puṣpadanta, is one of the most celebrated and widely recited devotional hymns in Hinduism. Composed predominantly in classical Śikhariṇī metre, the poem meditates upon Śiva's paradoxes, cosmic acts, and absolute transcendence beyond the reach of language and sectarian division (notably verse 7, which reconciles the Vedas, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, and Vaiṣṇava traditions as diverse streams converging into one ocean). The earliest epigraphic witness is preserved at the Amareśvara temple at Māndhātā on the Narmadā (inscribed in 1063 or 1163 CE), confirming an original core of 31 stanzas prior to later accretions.

The Śivasūtra is the foundational revealed text of the non-dual Kashmiri Trika school, outlining the nature of supreme consciousness and the three successive means (upāyas)—śāmbhava, śākta, and āṇava—by which the bound soul realizes its inherent identity with Śiva. This e-text pairs the root sūtras with the Śivasūtravārttika of Varadarāja (alias Kṛṣṇadāsa), a verse exposition that versifies and condenses the classic prose interpretation provided in Kṣemarāja's 11th-century Śivasūtravimarśinī. Through accessible anuṣṭubh verses, Varadarāja systematically elucidates the metaphysical definitions of bondage, the dynamics of divine energy (spanda/mātṛkā), and yogic integration.

The Śivopaniṣad is an early medieval Śaiva treatise in seven chapters (adhyāyas) belonging to the eight-text Śivadharma corpus, preserved predominantly in Nepalese manuscripts. Framed as a dialogue between Mahākāla and the sage Ātreya, it outlines a path of liberation tailored for lay devotees, expounding the triadic ontology of paśu, pāśa, and pati/śiva, the recitation and power of the two-syllable name Śiva, external ritual and internal worship (mānasapūjā), yoga, and righteous conduct (śivācāra). The Ratnatrayaparīkṣā ('Examination of the Three Jewels') is an influential 10th–11th-century Sanskrit doctrinal treatise in 322 verses by the Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta scholar Śrīkaṇṭhasūri. Instead of examining the school's general ontological triad (pati, paśu, and pāśa), the work focuses specifically on the 'three jewels' defined as bindu (the material cause of pure sound, language, and the pure universe), śakti (the conscious power of the Lord), and śiva (the supreme agent and consciousness). Drawing heavily on earlier Kashmirian exegesis (especially Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha), it provides a detailed metaphysical exposition of the pure path (śuddhādhvan), phonematic cosmogony, and soteriological initiation.

**Translations:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains vilāsas 1–11 of the total 20 vilāsas. Missing verses listed in the source header: 3.52, 3.223–224, 5.268, 10.294, and 11.244. Sanātana Gosvāmin's Digdarśinī commentary is included only in vilāsa 5; the other vilāsas provide root text only.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Haribhaktivilāsa (chapters 1–11) (Gopālabhaṭṭa Gosvāmin, root text)
- Digdarśinī (Sanātana Gosvāmin, commentary)

**Also known as:** Bhagavadbhaktivilāsa, Śrī-Haribhaktivilāsa

**Attribution:** The Haribhaktivilāsa explicitly identifies Gopālabhaṭṭa Gosvāmin (disciple of Prabodhānanda Sarasvatī) as compiler in its introductory verses (1.2) and chapter colophons [12083]. However, early Gauḍīya sources, including Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja's Caitanyacaritāmṛta (Madhya 24.327–332) and Narahari Cakravartin's Bhaktiratnākara (1.197–198), affirm that Sanātana Gosvāmin played the principal role in composing or redacting the work in Gopālabhaṭṭa's name. Sanātana also authored the authoritative commentary Digdarśinī, portions of which are embedded in vilāsa 5 of this file.

The Haribhaktivilāsa is the foundational ritual handbook and behavioural digest (smṛti / nibandha) of early modern Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇavism, composed in Vṛndāvana during the 1530s. Across its twenty vilāsas, the work systematizes normative devotional orthopraxy, citing thousands of verses from Purāṇic, Tantric, Pāñcarātra, and Vedic sources to ground devotional practices in canonical authority. This portion (vilāsas 1–11) treats initiation (dīkṣā), guru-disciple duties, morning rites, purification, sacred marks, offerings, and the elaborate procedures of daily temple and domestic worship (arcana).

The Rādhākṛṣṇārcanadīpikā ('Lamp Illuminating the Worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa') is a theological and ritual treatise in mixed prose and verse composed by Jīva Gosvāmin in the 16th century. It establishes the doctrinal justification for the paired worship of Rādhā and Kṛṣṇa (specifically in the form of Rādhā-Dāmodara), drawing extensively on Purāṇic, Tantric, and Smṛti proof texts. Jīva argues that true worship of Bhagavān necessitates the worship of His devotees, establishes the gopīs as His foremost devotees, and demonstrates that Rādhā, as His supreme internal pleasure potency (hlādinī-śakti), must be worshipped alongside Him.

The Bhāvanāsārasaṃgraha is a major 19th-century Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava anthology compiled by Kṛṣṇadāsa Tātapāda of Govardhana as an aid to rāgānugā-bhakti meditation and interior mental service (mānasī-sevā). This electronic text preserves the first two divisions, covering the dawn awakening (Niśāntalīlā) and morning activities (Prātarlīlā).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains the full 40 verses of the standard South Indian Śrīvaiṣṇava recension plus the traditional introductory verse (taniyan, 'ghuṣyate yasya nagare...'). Recensions vary from 31 verses (Kerala/Rāghavānanda) and 34 verses (Kāvyamālā) to 40 or 53 verses (Gauḍīya/Northern recension).

**Also known as:** Mukundamālāstotra

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Cēra king Kulaśekhara, counted as one of the twelve Āḻvārs of the Tamil Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition and author of the Tamil Perumāḷ Tirumoḻi. Modern scholarship dates him between the 8th and early 9th century CE.

The Mukundamālā is a celebrated Sanskrit devotional hymn (stotra) attributed to the Cēra ruler and Śrīvaiṣṇava saint-poet Kulaśekhara Āḻvār (c. 8th–9th century CE). Consisting of 40 lyrical stanzas in the standard South Indian recension, the hymn addresses Kṛṣṇa/Viṣṇu under the epithet Mukunda ('bestower of liberation'). The verses give impassioned voice to absolute surrender (prapatti), renunciation of worldly aims and heavenly pleasures in favor of loving service, and the famous plea to remember the Lord at the hour of death before bodily infirmity supervenes.

The Laghubhāgavatāmṛta is a foundational theological treatise composed by Rūpa Gosvāmī (mid-16th c. CE) summarizing and systematizing the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava ontology outlined in Sanātana Gosvāmī's Bṛhadbhāgavatāmṛta. The Kṛṣṇāmṛtamahārṇava ('The Great Ocean of the Nectar of Kṛṣṇa') is a devotional manual and anthology compiled by Madhvācārya (c. 1238–1317 CE), the propounder of Dvaita Vedānta. In addition to theological praise, it details orthoprax Vaiṣṇava conduct (sadācāra), including the sanctity of the Ekādaśī fast, the veneration of Śālagrāma stones, and niṣkāma karma as the path to liberation.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete prosimetric campū text, concluding with all four traditional final verses (segments [2693]–[2704]).

**Also known as:** Muktācaritra, Muktācaritram, Śrī-Muktācarita

**Attribution:** Uncontested traditional and scholarly attribution to Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī (c. 1495–1571 CE), one of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana. The work concludes with verses dedicating the poem to Rūpa Gosvāmī, mentioning Jīva Gosvāmī, and expressing affection for Kṛṣṇadāsa Kavirāja ('kṛṣṇa-kavi-bhūpati').

The Muktācarita ('The Tale of the Pearl') is a campū-kāvya combining Sanskrit prose and verse, composed around the mid-16th century by Raghunāthadāsa Gosvāmī, one of the Six Gosvāmīs of Vṛndāvana. Framed as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and his queen Satyabhāmā in Dvārakā, Kṛṣṇa recounts an incident from his youth in Vraja during the Dīpāvalī festival: when the gopīs refuse to give him pearls to ornament his beloved cows, Kṛṣṇa plants pearls in the earth and harvests bountiful pearl creepers, whereas the envious gopīs sow pearls with milk and butter but reap only thorny bushes. The work focuses on the witty banter, mock disputes, and commercial bargaining over the jewels between Kṛṣṇa, Subala, Madhumaṅgala, Rādhā, and Lalitā, illustrating the intimate erotic-devotional theology (mādhura-līlā) of the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava tradition.

The Prakāśasaṃhitā (also referenced in manuscript catalogues as the Paramatattvanirṇayaprakāśasaṃhitā) is a Vaiṣṇava Āgamic text belonging to the Pāñcarātra canon, framed as a dialogue between Śrīhaṃsa (Viṣṇu) and Brahmā. Strikingly distinctive among Pāñcarātra saṃhitās, its doctrinal tenets closely mirror Dvaita Vedānta theology, including the innate threefold classification of individual souls (traividhya: muktiyogya, nityabaddha, and tamoyogya), the eightfold cosmic agency of Viṣṇu (sṛṣṭyādyaṣṭakartṛtva), cosmogony, and devotional ritual practices. Passages ascribed to a Prakāśasaṃhitā are cited as authoritative in the works of Madhvācārya and the later Dvaita tradition.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the root work (kārikās, prose introductions, and illustrative verses) across all four divisions (vibhāgas: pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara) and their component laharīs, concluding with the author's final stanzas and scribal/editorial colophon.

**Also known as:** Haribhaktirasāmṛtasindhu, Bhakti-rasāmṛta-sindhu

**Attribution:** Universally accepted as the work of Rūpa Gosvāmin, one of the Six Gosvāmins of Vṛndāvana. The concluding stanza (lines 7215–7216) dates the composition to Śaka 1463 (1541 CE) while Rūpa was residing in Gokula.

The Bhaktirasāmṛtasindhu ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotional Rasa'), composed in 1541 CE by Rūpa Gosvāmin, is the foundational work of Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava devotional theology and aesthetics. Adapting the classical rasa theory of Bharata's Nāṭyaśāstra and medieval alaṃkāraśāstra, Rūpa establishes devotion (bhakti) directed toward Kṛṣṇa not merely as a bhāva (transient emotional state), but as the supreme aesthetic and ontological sentiment (bhakti-rasa). Organised in four quadrants (pūrva, dakṣiṇa, paścima, and uttara vibhāgas), the text comprehensively systematises the categories of devotional practice (sādhana, bhāva, prema), the constituent components of aesthetic emotion (vibhāva, anubhāva, sāttvikabhāva, vyabhicāribhāva), the primary rasas (śānta, dāsya, sakhya, vātsalya, madhura), and the secondary devotional sentiments along with discordant mixtures (rasābhāsa).

**Attribution:** Presented within the narrative frame as revealed originally by Nārāyaṇa and communicated by Śiva to Nārada on Mount Kailāsa, related by the narrator Sūta. Although bearing the title 'tantra' and drawing upon Sātvata/Pāñcarātra terminology, it is an independent work distinct from the classical Pāñcarātra 'Sātvatasaṃhitā'.

The Sātvatatantra is a Vaiṣṇava scriptural text in nine paṭalas framed as a dialogue between Śiva and Nārada on Mount Kailāsa. Diverging from classical tantric ritual manuals, it centers on the philosophical cosmology of Viṣṇu-Kṛṣṇa, the emanation of the three cosmic puruṣa forms (Kāraṇodakaśāyī, Garbhodakaśāyī, and Kṣīrodakaśāyī Viṣṇu), and the supreme efficacy of bhakti and the divine name. It is entirely distinct from the ancient Pāñcarātra jewel-text Sātvatasaṃhitā and served as an important theological proof-text for Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava authors such as Rūpa, Sanātana, and Jīva Gosvāmin.

The Vaikhānasa tradition places Śrīnivāsamakhin in the 11th century CE, though some modern scholars consider a date between the 14th and 17th centuries possible.

The Daśavidhahetunirūpaṇa ('Demonstration of Ten Reasons') is a major polemical and theological treatise of the Vaikhānasa Vaiṣṇava tradition, composed by Śrīnivāsamakhin as the introductory treatise (upodghātabhāga) to his Vaikhānasasūtratātparyacintāmaṇi. The author sets out ten systematic arguments demonstrating the Vedic orthodoxy, ritual superiority, and primordial authority of the Vaikhānasa Kalpasūtra and temple image worship (arcāvatāra). Drawing heavily upon Vedic literature, Upaniṣads, Purāṇas, and Dharmasūtras, the treatise defends distinctive Vaikhānasa practices—such as prenatal branding (viṣṇubali) and exclusive hereditary priesthood—against rival traditions, particularly the Pāñcarātra and Smārta schools.

Both internal evidence and Gaudiya tradition confirm Jīva Gosvāmī as the ultimate author and architect of the philosophical system.

The Bhagavatsandarbha is the second treatise of Jīva Gosvāmī's foundational 16th-century theological work, the Ṣaṭsandarbha (or Bhāgavatasandarbha). Centering its inquiry around the tripartite definition of Absolute Reality in Bhāgavata Purāṇa 1.2.11 (brahmeti paramātmeti bhagavān iti śabdyate), the work establishes that Bhagavān—the supreme personal God possessed of all potencies—is the highest and most complete manifestation of Non-dual Consciousness (advaya-jñāna), whereas impersonal Brahman is an unmanifest, partial revelation. Across 118 anucchedas, Jīva details the intrinsic divine potency (svarūpa-śakti) with its threefold aspects of sandhinī (existence), saṃvit (knowledge), and hlādinī (bliss), expounds the trans-material nature of the divine realm (viśuddha-sattva), and defends the eternity of the Lord's transcendent anthropomorphic form (vigraha), abode (dhāman), and associates (parikara).

The Ajaḍapramātṛsiddhi ('Proof of a Conscious Knower') is one of three short treatises comprising Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī, written in the first half of the 10th century to establish the foundational tenets of non-dual Pratyabhijñā philosophy. In this edition, the lost original auto-commentary is replaced by a concise modern Sanskrit Vṛtti composed in 1919 CE by Kashmiri scholar Harabhaṭṭa Śāstrī.

The Viṣṇudharma is an early Vaiṣṇava devotional and ritual handbook of approximately 4,200 verses in 105 chapters, generally dated to the 3rd–5th century CE. Framed as an exposition given by the sage Śaunaka to King Śatānīka, it instructs householders and lay devotees on the worship, liturgy, mental contemplation, vrata observances, and festivals dedicated to Viṣṇu. **Works in this e-text:**

- Kāśikāvṛtti (Jayāditya, Vāmana, commentary)

**Also known as:** Kāśikā, Pāṇinīyavṛtti, Pāṇinīyāṣṭādhyāyīsūtravṛtti

**Attribution:** The Kāśikāvṛtti is traditionally attributed to two 7th-century CE grammarians: Jayāditya, credited with adhyāyas 1–5, and Vāmana, who composed adhyāyas 6–8. This division is attested by manuscript colophons and acknowledged by commentators including Jinendrabuddhi and Haradatta. The Chinese pilgrim Yijing (I-tsing), who studied in India in the late 7th century, confirms the work's status and places Jayāditya's death around 660 CE.

The Kāśikāvṛtti is the earliest surviving complete running commentary (vṛtti) on the nearly 4,000 grammatical aphorisms of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, jointly authored in the 7th century CE by Jayāditya (adhyāyas 1–5) and Vāmana (adhyāyas 6–8). It provides concise rule paraphrases, explicitly supplies ellipsed terms carried over by anuvṛtti, and presents an extensive corpus of illustrative examples and counterexamples drawn from classical usage and older treatises. By synthesizing Kātyāyana's vārttikas, Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, and Candragomin's Cāndravyākaraṇa, the work served as the core pedagogical textbook of classical Pāṇinian grammar and inspired major sub-commentaries such as Jinendrabuddhi's Nyāsa and Haradatta's Padamañjarī.

The Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini (c. 5th–4th century BCE) is the foundational text of Sanskrit grammar (vyākaraṇa) and one of the earliest comprehensive generative linguistic treatises. Organized into eight chapters (adhyāyas) of four quarters (pādas) each, its nearly 4,000 aphorisms (sūtras) systematically derive the phonological, morphological, derivational, and syntactico-semantic structures of Sanskrit using a sophisticated formal meta-language that includes technical codes (anubandhas), sound-class abbreviations (pratyāhāras), and strict rule-ordering principles. The Paribhāṣenduśekhara ('Crest-Jewel of Interpretive Maxims') by the 18th-century grammarian Nāgeśabhaṭṭa is the foundational and most authoritative treatise on the interpretive metarules (paribhāṣās) governing Pāṇinian grammar. It compiles, classifies, and critically analyzes the maxims drawn from Patañjali's Mahābhāṣya, Kātyāyana's Vārttikas, and traditional usage, elucidating their textual indicators (jñāpaka), scope, and hierarchical interactions across three thematic sections. Serving as an indispensable manual for advanced grammatical reasoning, the treatise superseded earlier paribhāṣā collections and generated more than two dozen Sanskrit commentaries.

The Samanvayadiś ('Compass of Syntactic Concord') by Kuḍaka (c. 11th–12th century CE) is the earliest known manual of a distinctive local Kashmiri grammatical tradition dedicated to Sanskrit syntax (samanvaya / anvaya). It condenses the comprehensive Siddhāntakaumudī of his teacher Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita into 1,279 select sūtras from Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, reorganized according to a topical, derivation-focused order (prakriyā) rather than the sequential order of the eight adhyāyas. **Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Buddhist lexicographer and poet Amarasiṃha, who is reckoned as one of the nine gems (navaratna) of Vikramāditya's court and generally assigned to the Gupta period (c. 4th–6th century CE).

The Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (universally known as the Amarakoṣa) is classical India's most celebrated Sanskrit synonym dictionary and thesaurus, composed in śloka metre by the Buddhist scholar Amarasiṃha (c. 4th–6th century CE). This file contains the complete first division, the Svargādikāṇḍa, which arranges nominal vocabulary conceptually into ten thematic sections (vargas): deities and heaven (svarga), sky and celestial bodies (vyoman), spatial directions (diś), time and seasons (kāla), intellect and mental states (dhī), speech and sound (śabda), theatre and musical performance (nāṭya), the subterranean realm and serpents (pātāla), hell (naraka), and water and aquatic flora (vāri). Alongside synonyms, the text systematically teaches grammatical gender (liṅgānuśāsana) through context, syntactic gender markers, and explicit exclusion rules.

The second book (kāṇḍa) of Amarasiṃha's classical 5th–6th century Sanskrit lexicon, the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (commonly known as the Amarakoṣa). Designated the Bhūmyādikāṇḍa ('earthly division'), it arranges synonyms across ten sections (vargas) covering the terrestrial realm: the physical earth, settlements and architecture, mountains, flora and medicinal herbs, fauna, humanity, and the social classes and vocations (Brahmins, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras). ## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete third book (Sāmānyakāṇḍa) of the Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana, comprising five sections: viśeṣyanighnavarga, saṃkīrṇavarga, nānārthavarga, avyayavarga, and liṅgādisaṃgrahavarga (480 root verses plus 25 interpolated verses, numbered through 3.5.1032 / 513 verses total). Kāṇḍas 1 and 2 are preserved in separate e-texts.

**Also known as:** Amarakoṣa, Amarakośa, Trikāṇḍa, Sāmānyakāṇḍa

**Attribution:** Universal tradition attributes the work to Amarasiṃha, traditionally placed around the 5th–6th century CE and numbered among the legendary 'Nine Gems' (navaratnas).

The Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana (commonly known as the Amarakoṣa) by Amarasiṃha is the preeminent classical Sanskrit metrical thesaurus, composed in anuṣṭubh verses to facilitate memorization. The third kāṇḍa, known as the Sāmānyakāṇḍa ('General Section'), departs from the cosmological and sociothematic arrangements of books 1 and 2 to classify words by formal and grammatical criteria: adjectives and relative qualifiers (viśeṣyanighna), general miscellaneous terms (saṃkīrṇa), homonyms arranged by final consonant (nānārtha), indeclinables (avyaya), and a systematic synthesis of morphological and syntactical rules for determining nominal gender (liṅgādisaṃgraha).

**Coverage:** partial — Covers pp. 1–83.7 of the 125 pages of Sanskrit text in the 1940 GOS editio princeps. **Also known as:** Tattvopaplavasiṁha, Tattvopaplavasimha of Shri Jayarasi Bhatta

Although traditionally affiliated with the Bārhaspatya/Cārvāka tradition, Jayarāśi propounds radical epistemological skepticism (tattvopaplavavāda), rejecting even the positive empirical/materialist assertions of classical Lokāyata.

The Tattvopaplavasiṃha ('The Lion that Devours all Principles/Categories') is a unique philosophical treatise of radical epistemological skepticism composed by Jayarāśi Bhaṭṭa in the late 8th or early 9th century CE. Loosely affiliated with the Cārvāka/Lokāyata school, Jayarāśi turns dialectical reasoning against all accepted instruments of valid cognition (pramāṇas)—including perception, inference, analogy, and verbal testimony—arguing that because no pramāṇa can be established without begging the question, no metaphysical or empirical entities (tattvas) can be affirmed. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text corresponding to all 43 pages of the Trivandrum Sanskrit Series edition (TSS 62).

**Attribution:** The palm-leaf manuscripts preserved in Malayalam script give no author name. In the Keralan manuscript tradition and in Karl Potter's Encyclopedia of Indian Philosophies (DU554), the work is conjecturally associated with Mahopādhyāya Rāghavānanda (c. 14th century CE), the Keralan Advaitin commentator on the Bhāgavatapurāṇa. However, the editor T. Ganapati Sastri and modern doxography specialists (Wilhelm Halbfass, Marek Mejor) treat it as anonymous. It is distinct from another Keralan compendium of the same title by Melputtūr Nārāyaṇa Bhaṭṭa (1560–1656 CE).

The Sarvamatasaṃgraha is a concise Sanskrit doxography composed in Kerala from an Advaita Vedānta perspective. It opens with an epistemological overview (pramāṇanirūpaṇa) detailing eight means of valid cognition, followed by an exposition of heterodox (Cārvāka/Lokāyata, Jaina, and four Buddhist schools) and orthodox schools (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā, and Uttara-Mīmāṃsā). The systems are presented in a hierarchical ascending order, concluding with non-dual Brahma-realization as the ultimate purport of philosophy.

**Also known as:** Devāgamastotra, Devāgama

**Attribution:** Attributed to the Digambara Jain philosopher-ācārya Samantabhadra (ca. 5th–6th century CE).

The Āptamīmāṃsā ('Critique of the Trustworthy Authority'), also known as the Devāgamastotra after its opening words, is a foundational 114-verse philosophical treatise by the Digambara master Ācārya Samantabhadra (ca. 5th–6th c. CE). Beginning as a theological inquiry into what qualifies an individual as a truly omniscient, authoritative teacher (āpta), it establishes that miracles and external divine manifestations cannot establish authority; rather, true authority belongs only to one who has eradicated internal passions and whose teachings cannot be invalidated by reason or experience. Samantabhadra applies the sevenfold conditional predication (syādvāda / saptabhaṅgī) and many-sided ontology (anekāntavāda) to refute one-sided (ekānta) philosophical positions across rival Indian traditions (Buddhist, Advaita Vedānta, Sāṅkhya, and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika), creating the dialectical framework that shaped the subsequent Jain logical tradition.

**Attribution:** Composed by the Maithila polymath and court poet Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara (also referred to as Jyotirīśa or Jyotirīśvara Ṭhakkura, author of the Maithili prose encyclopedia Varṇaratnākara and the farce Dhūrtasamāgama), who flourished under King Harisiṃhadeva of the Karṇāṭa dynasty of Mithilā/Tirhut (r. c. 1285–1324 CE).

The Pañcasāyaka ('The Five Arrows', named for the flower arrows of Kāmadeva) is an influential medieval Sanskrit handbook of erotology (kāmaśāstra) in five chapters. Composed in the early 14th century by the Maithil scholar-courtier Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara, it draws upon earlier authorities including Vātsyāyana, Bābhravya, Nandikeśvara, and Kokkoka's Ratirahasya. The Kāmasūtra of Vātsyāyana (composed c. 3rd–4th century CE) is the foundational Sanskrit treatise on kāma (erotic desire, pleasure, and aesthetic enjoyment), one of the four traditional goals of human life (puruṣārtha). Divided into seven adhikaraṇas, the text surveys general principles of life, sexual union, courtship and marriage, the domestic conduct of wives, extramarital affairs, courtesans, and erotic/aphrodisiac recipes. Beyond physical intimacy, the work presents a detailed manual on urban sociology and the cultured lifestyle of the sophisticated citizen (nāgaraka), serving as the canonical source for all subsequent Indian erotic literature.

The Kādambarasvīkaraṇasūtra with its accompanying prose commentary is a satirical, mock-śāstric text preserved in the Kāmaśāstra tradition. In 34 aphorisms and elaborate scholastic prose, it deploys the technical argumentation of Navya-Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā to argue that the consumption of liquor (kādambara / vāruṇī) before and during lovemaking is an indispensable causal prerequisite (paramakāraṇa) for sexual fulfillment. The author cites classical mahākāvyas (Raghuvaṃśa, Kirātārjunīya, Śiśupālavadha) as authorities and facetiously concludes that observant practitioners will attain pleasure, offspring, and the celestial abode of Urvaśī.

It systematically synthesizes dhātuvāda (metallurgical operations and transmutation into precious metals) with dehavāda (iatrochemical rasāyana therapy aimed at rejuvenation and bodily immortality). The work is especially significant in the history of medicine and yoga for its detailed exposition of Haṭhayoga principles (Ṣaḍaṅgayoga, cakras, and prāṇāyāma) in ullāsa 1.20, as well as for preserving one of the earliest and most detailed accounts of the medicinal and ritual preparation of cannabis (bhaṅgā) in Sanskrit literature.

**Attribution:** Universally attributed to Vāgbhaṭa (son of Siṃhagupta, pupil of Avalokita), usually dated to the 6th or 7th century CE. Scholarly debate continues on whether the author is identical to the Vāgbhaṭa of the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha (Vāgbhaṭa I vs. Vāgbhaṭa II), but the composition of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya itself is indisputably ascribed to Vāgbhaṭa.

The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya ('Heart of the Eight Branches of Medicine') is a classical Sanskrit treatise on Āyurveda composed by Vāgbhaṭa, datable to circa the 6th–7th century CE. It synthesizes and condenses the teachings of the earlier foundational traditions of Caraka and Suśruta into six divisions (sthānas): Sūtra-, Śārīra-, Nidāna-, Cikitsita-, Kalpasiddhi-, and Uttarasthāna. Renowned for its poetic elegance and pedagogical clarity, it is counted as one of the 'Great Triad' (Bṛhattrayī) of Indian medicine and has served as a central clinical authority in South Asia (particularly Kerala) and across Asia via Tibetan and Arabic transmissions.

Arranged into three divisions (Pūrvakhaṇḍa, Madhyakhaṇḍa, and Uttarakhaṇḍa), the work is renowned for its detailed Vargaprakaraṇa (materia medica / nighaṇṭu section), which integrates indigenous and imported substances, as well as for its early documentation of syphilis (phiraṅgaroga) and its treatment with China root (copacīnī). This e-text is an incomplete transcription containing only the first two drug groups (Harītakyādivarga and Karpūrādivarga) and an unfinished excerpt (vv. 1–54) of the third group (Guḍūcyādivarga).

The author strongly emphasizes firsthand laboratory experimentation and verification over uncritical textual transmission, and the work served as a primary source for subsequent treatises such as the Rasendrasārasaṃgraha.

The Rasahṛdayatantra ('Heart of Mercury'), composed in 19 avabodhas (chapters) in āryā metre by Bhikṣu Govinda (Govindabhagavatpāda, c. 10th century CE), is the earliest surviving systematic treatise of the Sanskrit alchemical tradition (rasaśāstra). The Rasaratnākara of Nityanātha (Nātha siddha, c. 13th–14th c.) is a major compendium of medieval Indian alchemy and iatrochemistry, divided into five khaṇḍas. The Rājanighaṇṭu (also known as Nighaṇṭurāja or Abhidhānacūḍāmaṇi) by Narahari is a comprehensive Āyurvedic materia medica and medical lexicon composed around the 14th century CE. The Rasādhyāya is an authoritative medieval manual of Indian alchemy and iatrochemistry (Rasaśāstra), structured into 21 thematic sections (adhikāras) and 481 verses. - Acharya Balkrishna (ed.), Āyurveda Mahodadhi (Suṣeṇa-Nighaṇṭuḥ), Haridwar: Divya Prakashan, Patanjali Yogpeeth, 2013. — Devanagari text with Hindi translation and commentary.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Extant text as edited from surviving manuscripts: the beginning is mutilated, starting mid-verse at verse 5 (verses 1–4 are lost), running through the beverage, food, and dining sections to the concluding Vastravarga (v. 3) and the final treatise colophon (samāpto 'yaṃ suṣeṇakṛtagranthaḥ).

**Also known as:** Āyurvedamahodadhi, Annapānavidhi, Suṣeṇanighaṇṭu, Suṣeṇavaidyaka

**Attribution:** The work is attributed in its colophons to Suṣeṇa (samāpto 'yaṃ suṣeṇakṛtagranthaḥ; suṣeṇakṛte vastravargaḥ). He is cited as an authority on dietetics and materia medica by later medieval authors, notably in Hamsarāja's Nidāna, Dīpacanda Vācaka's Laṅghanapathyanirṇaya, and Raghunātha's Bhojanakutūhala. The presence of 'siṅghaṇacūrṇa' in manuscripts points to a date no earlier than the 13th century (reign of the Seuna/Yādava king Siṅghaṇa, r. c. 1210–1247 CE).

The Āyurvedamahodadhi (Annapānavidhi section), attributed to the physician Suṣeṇa, is a specialized Ayurvedic treatise on dietetics and personal regimen (svasthavṛtta). It categorizes and explains the properties, digestibilities, and therapeutic effects of waters (pānīyavarga), milks and dairy preparations, fermented beverages, grains, pulses, fruits, vegetables, oils, and meats, ending with table manners and a brief section on garments (vastravarga). Likely composed in the 13th–14th century, it was frequently drawn upon by subsequent dietary compilations such as the Bhojanakutūhala.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 25 chapters (paricchedas), comprising the Mūlatantra / Cikitsādhikāra (chapters 1–20) and the Uttaratantra (chapters 21–25), followed by the concluding supplementary section on death prognostication (Ariṣṭanirūpaṇa) and the author's final colophon verses.

**Also known as:** Kalyāṇakārakam

**Attribution:** Composed by the Digambara Jain monk Ugrāditya (a pupil of Śrīnandi of the Desiya Gaṇa / Pustaka Gaccha), who resided at Mount Rāmagiri in Veṅgī (Trikaliṅga). He is dated to the first half of the 9th century CE (c. 790–850 CE) based on internal references associating him with the Eastern Cālukya ruler Kali Viṣṇuvardhana V and the court of the Rāṣṭrakūṭa emperor Nṛpatuṅga Amoghavarṣa I.

The Kalyāṇakāraka is a comprehensive 9th-century Sanskrit Ayurvedic treatise composed by the Digambara Jain monk Ugrāditya. Divided into 25 chapters across two main divisions—the Mūlatantra (chapters 1–20) and Uttaratantra (chapters 21–25)—along with a concluding section on the prognostication of fatal signs (Ariṣṭanirūpaṇa), it is among the earliest surviving Indian medical compendia to detail the chemical purification (śodhana) and incineration (māraṇa) of mercury and other minerals for therapeutic formulations. Consistently framed within Jain ethics of non-harm (ahiṃsā), the work prohibits meat, alcohol, and honey in pharmacological treatments, replacing them with herbal and mineral substitutes while harmonising classical Ayurvedic eight-fold medicine with Jain doctrinal philosophy.

The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdayasaṃhitā is one of the three foundational classics of classical Ayurveda (the bṛhattrayī), composed in metrical verse by Vāgbhaṭa (ca. 7th century CE). It synthesizes and condenses the medical traditions of the Carakasaṃhitā and Suśrutasaṃhitā across six divisions (sthānas) comprising 120 chapters: internal medicine, pathology, anatomy, surgical techniques, pharmacology, and toxicology. Renowned for its poetic lucidity and practical therapeutic orientation, it became the preeminent medical handbook across South Asia, Central Asia, and Tibet.

Jan Meulenbeld observes that the text lacks an explicit internal authorial statement within its verses and is technically anonymous, though verse 1 explicitly frames the lexicon as an exposition of the difficult drug names found in the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha.

The Aṣṭāṅganighaṇṭu is an Ayurvedic medical lexicon (nighaṇṭu) in 408 verses attributed to Vāhaṭa. The first part glosses synonyms and therapeutic actions of the drug groups (gaṇas) taught in Vāgbhaṭa's classical treatises (primarily the Aṣṭāṅgasaṃgraha), while the second part (viprakīrṇa) inventories medicinal plants, foodstuffs, poisons, minerals, and general clinical terminology. It is historically notable as the earliest extant medical text to mention kumārī (Aloe vera), and it served as a recognized authority cited by medieval commentators including Indu, Aruṇadatta, and Hemādri.

The Rasaratnasamuccaya is an authoritative Sanskrit compendium of Indian alchemy and iatrochemistry (rasaśāstra) attributed to an alchemical author named Vāgbhaṭa (c. 13th–14th century CE). It synthesizes theoretical, metallurgical, and pharmacological knowledge from earlier treatises such as the Rasārṇava and Rasahṛdayatantra, covering mercury, minerals, crucibles, apparatus (yantra), and laboratory layout. This partial electronic text contains chapters 1 through 12, encompassing the alchemical definitions, purification and processing of rasas and metals, laboratory instruments, and the initial chapter on the clinical management of fevers (jvara).

The Rasaratnasamuccaya is a seminal compendium of Indian alchemy (rasaśāstra) and iatrochemistry composed around the late 13th to early 14th century CE by Rasa-Vāgbhaṭa. Drawing extensively on earlier tantric and metallurgical authorities, it systematizes the purification (śodhana), incineration (māraṇa), and therapeutic compounding of mercury (pārada), mineral categories (mahārasa, uparasa, sādhāraṇarasa), gems, and metals, as well as describing laboratory design, apparatuses (yantra), crucibles (mūṣā), and fire pits (puṭa). This e-text contains chapters 1 through 18.29ab accompanied by the late modern Sanskrit commentary Rasaratnasamuccayabodhinī and accompanying glosses.
