The Hāyanaratna ('Jewel of the Year') is an encyclopedic Sanskrit treatise (nibandha) on Tājika astrology—the Sanskritized tradition of Perso-Arabic horoscopy—composed in 1649 CE by Balabhadra Daivajña under the patronage of the Mughal prince Shāh Shujāʿ. The work deals systematically with annual horoscopy (varṣaphala, solar revolutions), the sixteen distinctive Tājika planetary configurations (yogas), planetary dignities, and lots (sahamas). It is a vital source for the history of astrology and intercultural transmission in South Asia, preserving extensive citations from earlier Tājika authorities spanning five centuries.

The Āryabhaṭīya is a foundational, highly compact Sanskrit treatise on mathematics and astronomy composed by Āryabhaṭa in Kusumapura (Pāṭaliputra) in 499 CE at the age of 23. Comprising 121 verses across four sections (Gītikāpāda, Gaṇitapāda, Kālakriyāpāda, and Golapāda), it expounds an alphabetic numeral notation system, geometric and algebraic operations, a sine table, an accurate approximation of π (3.1416), and the kuṭṭaka algorithm for indeterminate linear equations. In astronomy, it details cosmological time cycles, planetary models, eclipses, and famously asserts the diurnal axial rotation of the Earth.

- Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya (Bhāskara I, commentary (Gītikāpāda, Gaṇitapāda, Kālakriyāpāda, Golapāda 1–6))
- Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya (Someśvara, commentary (supplementing lacuna in Golapāda 7–50))

**Also known as:** Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya, Āryabhaṭatantrabhāṣya, Daśagītikāsūtra and Āryāṣṭaśata with commentary

**Attribution:** The root work Āryabhaṭīya was composed by Āryabhaṭa (born 476 CE, work composed c. 499 CE). The commentary was written in 629 CE at Valabhī by Bhāskara I. Because surviving manuscripts of Bhāskara I's commentary break off after Golapāda verse 6, editor K. S. Shukla supplied the remaining section of the commentary (Golapāda 7–50) from the work of Someśvara (11th–12th century), who had prepared a concise bhāṣya abridging Bhāskara's exposition.

The Āryabhaṭīya of Āryabhaṭa (composed 499 CE) is an early classic of Indian astronomy and mathematics divided into four chapters: Gītikāpāda (astronomical constants and alphabetical numeral notation), Gaṇitapāda (arithmetical, geometrical, and algebraic methods including the sine table and the kuṭṭaka algorithm for indeterminate linear equations), Kālakriyāpāda (reckoning of time, planetary velocities, and eccentric-epicyclic models), and Golapāda (celestial sphere and spherical astronomy). This volume features the 7th-century Āryabhaṭīyabhāṣya of Bhāskara I (written 629 CE at Valabhī), the oldest extant commentary on the text, noted for its extensive worked practical problems and defense of Āryabhaṭa's system. Because the manuscript tradition of Bhāskara's commentary breaks off after Golapāda 6, the missing final portion (Golapāda 7–50) is supplemented from the concise commentary of Someśvara (11th–12th century), which was composed directly as an abridgment of Bhāskara's bhāṣya.

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text is incomplete. It contains verses and short prose remarks numbered BG_1 to BG_149, breaking off mid-verse at BG_150c ('vistāritā') in the section on quadratic equations in multiple unknowns (anekavarṇamadhyamāharaṇa). It lacks the remainder of verse 150, the eleventh section on products of unknowns (bhāvita), and the concluding verses/colophon (full recensions contain 212–231 verses).

**Also known as:** Avyaktagaṇita, Bhāskarīyabījagaṇita, Siddhāntaśiromaṇi: Bījagaṇita

**Attribution:** Authored by Bhāskara II (Bhāskarācārya, 1114–c. 1185 CE) as the algebraic section of his mathematical and astronomical opus Siddhāntaśiromaṇi (composed c. 1150 CE). The text consists of metrical rules (kārikā) and illustrative examples (udāharaṇa), accompanied in places by Bhāskara's own brief prose explanations (vāsanā).

The Bījagaṇita ('Seed Computation' or 'Algebra') of Bhāskara II (b. 1114 CE), composed around 1150 CE, is the foremost classical Sanskrit treatise devoted exclusively to algebra, forming the second mathematical branch of his Siddhāntaśiromaṇi alongside the arithmetic Līlāvatī. The Bṛhajjātaka (or Horāśāstra), composed in the 6th century CE by Varāhamihira of Avantī, is the foundational and most authoritative classical Sanskrit manual of natal and horoscopic astrology (jātaka / horā). The Bṛhatsaṃhitā ('Great Compendium') of Varāhamihira (ca. 6th century CE) is the fundamental classic of the saṃhitā (natural omen, divination, and mundane astrology) branch of Indian jyotiṣa. Formed around a post-Varāhamihira core (ca. 7th–8th century CE) and progressively expanded, it constitutes the foundational textual authority for modern predictive Vedic astrology.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: 28 adhyāyas with chapter headings prathamo'dhyāyaḥ through aṣṭāviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ (the chapter 5 heading is missing or differently spelled in the file), ending with the upasaṃhāra verses 28.1–6, which name Mantreśvara of Śālivāṭi and Sukuntalāmbā (kṛtā yā phaladīpikā || 6||).

**Also known as:** Jātaka-Phaladīpikā, Phaladeepika

**Attribution:** In the concluding verses of Chapter 28 (vv. 5–6), the author names himself as Mantreśvara (śrīśālivāṭijātena mayā mantreśvareṇa vai), a Brahmin astrologer born in Śālivāṭi (identified with Tirunelveli in Tamil Nadu), who composed the text by the grace of goddess Sukuntalāmbā. South Indian oral tradition sometimes connects or identifies him with Mārkaṇḍeya Bhaṭṭatiri of Kerala. His date is debated in scholarship, ranging from the 13th to the 16th century CE; V. Subrahmanya Sastri argued for c. 16th century based on internal parallels with Vaidyanātha's Jātakapārijāta.

The Phaladīpikā is an authoritative medieval handbook of genethliacal astrology (jātaka / horā) composed in 28 chapters (865 verses) by Mantreśvara. It synthesizes classical astrological teachings into a practical and concise guide, covering planetary strengths (ṣaḍbala), the significations of the twelve houses (bhāvas), planetary combinations (yogas), daśā predictive systems (notably Viṃśottarī and Kālacakra), transits (gocara), and the calculation of Aṣṭakavarga and Upagrahas (such as Māndi/Gulika). It is widely studied across South Asia alongside Varāhamihira's Bṛhajjātaka and Vaidyanātha's Jātakapārijāta.

The Ṛgvedavedāṅgajyotiṣa (also known as Ārcajyotiṣa) is the Ṛgvedic recension of the Vedāṅgajyotiṣa, the earliest surviving Indian text on mathematical astronomy and calendrical calculation, traditionally attributed to Lagadha. In 35 concise anuṣṭubh verses, it lays out a lunisolar calendar designed to determine the precise times for Vedic sacrifices, based on a five-year yuga consisting of 62 synodic months (including two intercalary months) and 1,830 civil days. The text details the coordinate system of 27 nakṣatras with their presiding deities, the positions of the solstices and equinoxes, rules for calculating tithis and nakṣatra portions, and seasonal variations in daytime length measurable by a water-clock (clepsydra).

The Līlāvatī is the foundational arithmetic and geometry treatise composed around 1150 CE by Bhāskara II (Bhāskarācārya) as the opening part (pāṭīgaṇita) of his comprehensive astronomical work Siddhāntaśiromaṇi. The Sūryasiddhānta is the most prominent and authoritative classic of traditional Indian mathematical astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra). Composed in fourteen adhyāyas of Anuṣṭubh verses, it is framed as celestial instruction imparted by a solar deity to the asura Maya. The treatise expounds planetary mean and true motions, spherical astronomy, solar and lunar eclipses, planetary conjunctions, heliacal risings and settings, cosmography, astronomical instruments, and time measurement. The extant version reflects a medieval redaction that served as the primary foundation for calendar computation (pañcāṅga) across premodern India.

**Also known as:** Tikanikāyātrā, Tikanika-yātrā

**Attribution:** Traditionally and in modern scholarship attributed to Varāhamihira (6th century CE). Al-Bīrūnī explicitly mentions the Tikanikayātrā in the 11th century among Varāhamihira's works. Ajay Mitra Shastri observes that verse 1.2 (an invocation mentioning Gaṇeśa) is likely a later interpolation since it is found in only one manuscript.

The Tikanikayātrā is the shortest and most concise of the three treatises on expedition and military astrology (yātrā) composed by the 6th-century astronomer-astrologer Varāhamihira (alongside the Bṛhadyātrā and Yogayātrā). Across nine short chapters totaling 103 verses, it sets forth rules for determining auspicious moments for military departures, astrological aspects of the planets and asterisms (nakṣatras), and auspicious and inauspicious omens. The text was already known to al-Bīrūnī in the 11th century and was edited from manuscript witnesses by Vasantkumar R. Pandit in 1951.

The Bṛhadyātrā (also known as Bṛhadyogayātrā, Mahāyātrā, or Yakṣāśvamedhīya) is Varāhamihira's most extensive treatise devoted to military and journey astrology (yātrā). This represents Part 1 (pp. 1–233) of Rangaswami Aiyangar's 1941 reconstructed edition; the remaining six kāṇḍas (Saṃskāra, Ācāra, Śrāddha, Āśauca, Āpaddharma, and Prāyaścitta, pp. 234–386) are not present in this file.

**Also known as:** Bārhaspatyasmṛti, Bārhaspatyamanusaṃhitā, Bṛhaspatisaṃhitā, Bṛhaspatismṛti Vyavahārakāṇḍa

**Attribution:** Ascribed traditionally to the Vedic and purāṇic sage and preceptor of the gods, Bṛhaspati (and in tradition considered a direct amplification/re-exposition of Manu's code, hence known also as Bārhaspatyā Manusaṃhitā). As the original smṛti text is lost, this text was reconstructed from citations in medieval commentaries and nibandhas (especially Lakṣmīdhara's Kṛtyakalpataru, Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā, and Varadarāja's Vyavahāranirṇaya) by K. V. Rangaswami Aiyangar.

The Vyavahārakāṇḍa of the Bṛhaspatismṛti is an ancient legal treatise reconstructed from citations preserved in medieval Hindu commentaries and law digests (nibandhas). Composed around the 4th to 6th century CE, it belongs to the classical Dharmaśāstra tradition alongside Manu and Nārada, focusing intensively on jurisprudence and judicial administration. It covers the constitution and grades of law courts, the duties of judges, judicial procedure across four stages (pādas), evidence (documents, witnesses, and divine ordeals), and substantive civil and criminal law arranged across the eighteen classical titles of dispute (vyavahārapadas).

**Attribution:** Composed by Mitramiśra, son of Paraśurāma Miśra and grandson of Haṃsa Paṇḍita, under the royal patronage of the Bundela ruler King Vīrasiṃhadeva (Bir Singh Deo) of Orchhā (r. 1605–1627 CE), whose genealogy is detailed in the introductory verses.

The Samayaprakāśa ('Illumination of Ritual Times') is an extensive section of Mitramiśra's encyclopedic Dharmaśāstra digest, the Vīramitrodaya, composed in the early seventeenth century under King Vīrasiṃhadeva of Orchhā. It systematically analyzes the calendrical and temporal rules (kāla/samaya) governing Hindu ritual obligations, discussing lunar days (tithi), intercalary months (malamāsa), solar ingresses (saṅkrānti), festivals, and vows (vrata). Drawing heavily upon smṛti and purāṇic sources as well as medieval authorities, it became a standard authority for ritual timing within the Banaras school of Dharmaśāstra.

The Nāradasmṛti is a classical Dharmaśāstra treatise uniquely devoted almost entirely to legal procedure and substantive law (vyavahāra), omitting the standard sections on customary conduct (ācāra) and expiation (prāyaścitta). It opens with an introductory section (mātṛkā) on the administration of justice, courts, plaint procedure, and evidence, followed by twenty chapters treating the eighteen traditional titles of law (vyavahārapadas) as well as theft and divine ordeals (divya). ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete root text (mūla) in 12 adhyāyas comprising 592 verses (numbered up to 12.82 due to fractional/variant numbering). Adhyāyas 1–11 constitute the Ācārakāṇḍa and adhyāya 12 forms the Prāyaścittakāṇḍa. The Vyavahārakāṇḍa found in Mādhavācārya's commentary contains no mūla verses of Parāśara.

**Also known as:** Parāśarasmṛti, Pārāśaradharmasaṃhitā, Pārāśarasmṛti, Parāśaraśāstra

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Vedic and purāṇic sage Parāśara, father of Vyāsa. Modern critical scholarship dates the extant versified text to approximately the mid-to-late first millennium CE (between c. 6th and 8th century CE, though some scholars argue for an earlier core c. 100–500 CE); it was established as a standard authority by the time of Medhātithi and the 11th–14th-century nibandhas.

The Parāśaradharmasaṃhitā (or Parāśarasmṛti) is an influential classical Dharmaśāstra text canonical for its claim to define the yugadharma specifically designated for the Kali age (Kalau Pārāśarāḥ smṛtāḥ, 1.24). Comprising 592 anuṣṭubh verses organized into 12 chapters, it expounds rules of customary conduct and purity (ācāra, chs. 1–11) and rites of expiation (prāyaścitta, ch. 12). The treatise is notable for introducing pragmatic modifications to classical law tailored to the diminished moral capacity of the Kali age, such as permitting agriculture to twice-born householders and outlining conditions for the remarriage of women. It does not contain an internal section on jurisprudence (vyavahāra), a lacuna that was famously supplemented in the 14th century by Mādhavācārya in his comprehensive commentary, the Parāśaramādhavīya.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Vaikhānasadharmasūtra in 3 praśnas comprising 34 kāṇḍikās (Praśna 1: 11 kāṇḍikās; Praśna 2: 8 kāṇḍikās; Praśna 3: 15 kāṇḍikās). In the 10-praśna Vaikhānasasmārtasūtra, this corresponds to Praśnas 8–10 (Caland's edition, pp. 112–145, preserved as inline page/line markers in the e-text).

**Also known as:** Vaikhānasadharmapraśna, Vaikhānasa Dharmasūtra, Vaikhānasasmārtasūtra (praśnas 8–10)

**Attribution:** Traditionally ascribed to the seer Vikhanas (as reflected in the text's concluding words 'iti vikhanāḥ'), revered in later tradition as a manifestation of Brahmā or Viṣṇu. The work represents the dharmasūtra portion of the Vaikhānasa school affiliated with the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

The Vaikhānasadharmasūtra constitutes the dharmasūtra portion (Praśnas 8–10) of the Vaikhānasasmārtasūtra, belonging to the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda. Across three praśnas, the work details the duties and occupations of the four social classes (varṇas) and life-stages (āśramas), providing classical Sanskrit literature's most elaborate typology of hermits (vānaprasthas/vaikhānasas) and ascetics (bhikṣus). Combining late Vedic smārta jurisprudence with pronounced early Vaiṣṇava devotional features (such as the worship of Nārāyaṇa), the work is generally assigned to the 3rd or 4th century CE.

The remainder of Prakaraṇa 6 (chapters 6.120–6.374) and subsequent khilas are omitted.

**Also known as:** Mokṣopāyaśāstra, Mokṣopāyasaṃhitā, Yogavāsiṣṭha (original Kashmirian recension)

**Attribution:** Composed by an anonymous author in 10th-century Kashmir (c. 950 CE, associated with the Pradyumna hill / Hari Parbat in Śrīnagar), referred to by editors as 'Anonymus Casmiriensis'. In the frame story, the sage Vālmīki relates the dialogue between Vasiṣṭha and Prince Rāma to Bharadvāja. Between the 11th and 14th centuries, the Mokṣopāya was expanded and recast into the orthodox Advaita-Vedāntic text known as the Yogavāsiṣṭha (or Vasiṣṭha-Mahārāmāyaṇa).

The Mokṣopāya ('Means to Liberation') is a 10th-century Kashmiri philosophical narrative poem composed near Śrīnagar. It expounds a radical non-dual idealism maintaining that the empirical cosmos is a mental projection created by cognitive construction (saṅkalpa / manas), and teaches liberation-in-life (jīvanmukti) achieved through rational inquiry, self-reliance, and detachment from mental constructs while actively engaging in worldly life. Framed as instructions delivered by the sage Vasiṣṭha to the young prince Rāma, its doctrine is communicated through intricate philosophical allegories and narrative cycles. Philological research has demonstrated that the Mokṣopāya constitutes the original recension underlying the later, heavily altered and expanded Yogavāsiṣṭha.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — The e-text contains the complete text of Durvekamiśra's sub-commentary as preserved in the single known palm-leaf manuscript and printed in the 1949 Baroda edition (pp. 233–411).

**Also known as:** Arcaṭāloka, Hetubinduṭīkāyāḥ Ālokaḥ, Hetubindvanuṭīkā

**Attribution:** Durvekamiśra explicitly names himself as author in the opening title ('paṇḍitadurvekamiśrakṛto hetubinduṭīkālokaḥ', line [1]), in the concluding stanzas ('kṛto 'yam arcaṭāloko nibandho bālabāndhavaḥ', line [6123]), and in the final colophon ('kṛtir iyaṃ paṇḍitadurvekamiśrasyeti', line [6128]). In the concluding stanzas (line [6120]), he acknowledges his teacher Jitāri ('guror jitāreḥ sa khalu prasādaḥ').

The Hetubinduṭīkāloka (also known as Arcaṭāloka) is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (anuṭīkā) by the late Buddhist master Durvekamiśra (fl. c. late 10th to early 11th century CE) on Bhaṭṭa Arcaṭa's Hetubinduṭīkā, which comments on Dharmakīrti's logical manual Hetubindu. Durvekamiśra, a disciple of Jitāri active in Eastern India, offers a detailed defense and critique of Arcaṭa's positions on the threefold character of logical evidence (trairūpya), the refutation of non-Buddhist theories (notably Naiyāyika and Mīmāṃsaka tenets), and disagreements with earlier commentators like Dharmottara. Preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript from the Jaina bhaṇḍāras at Patan, it serves as an indispensable witness to late Indian Buddhist logico-epistemological philosophy (pramāṇavāda).

The Dharmottarapradīpa ('Lamp on Dharmottara'), composed around the late 10th or early 11th century CE by Durveka Miśra, is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (anuṭīkā) on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā, which comments on Dharmakīrti's foundational logical manual, the Nyāyabindu. The Mīmāṃsāsūtra (or Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtra), traditionally attributed to Jaimini, is the foundational text of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā darśana. Arranged into twelve books (adhyāyas), hence known as the Dvādaśalakṣaṇī, the aphorisms formulate the rules of interpretation (nyāya) for the ritual injunctions (vidhi) of the Vedic corpus. The work provides systematic epistemological arguments for the intrinsicality of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya) and the eternality of language and the Veda, establishing hermeneutic canons that deeply influenced Dharmaśāstra, Vedānta, and Indian legal interpretation.

Both authors are prominent exponents of the 17th-to-18th-century Navya-Mīmāṃsā school of Varanasi, which infused classical Bhāṭṭa exegesis with the rigorous dialectical tools of Navya-Nyāya.

The Jaiminīyanyāyamālāvistara is an influential 14th-century Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā treatise composed by the Vijayanagara scholar-statesman Mādhava. Modeling itself on Jaimini's twelve-chapter Mīmāṃsāsūtra, the work distills every topic (adhikaraṇa) into metrical mnemonics (the nyāyamālā) and expands each in a concise prose auto-commentary (the vistara) covering the topic's subject matter (viṣaya), doubt (saṃśaya), opponent's argument (pūrvapakṣa), and resolved orthodox conclusion (siddhānta). This first chapter (Adhyāya 1) examines the foundational epistemology and authority of the Veda, establishing the authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) and eternal nature of Vedic words and sentences, the authority of Smṛti and custom, and the hermeneutical distinctions among injunctions (vidhi), explanatory eulogies (arthavāda), mantras, and ritual nomenclature (nāmadheya).

**Coverage:** partial — Contains adhyāyas 1 through 7 (ending with Śabara's commentary on the concluding adhikarana of adhyāya 7, pāda 4) out of the 12 adhyāyas of the complete Mīmāṃsāsūtra and Śābarabhāṣya.

**Attribution:** The root sūtras are traditionally attributed to Jaimini (c. 4th–2nd century BCE). In the commentary on MS 1.1.5, Śabarasvāmin cites at length an older commentary by the Vṛttikāra (often associated with Bhavadāsa or an unnamed early predecessor).

The foundational aphorisms of the Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā school attributed to Jaimini, accompanied by its earliest surviving commentary, the Śābarabhāṣya of Śabarasvāmin. Together they establish the epistemological foundations of Vedic exegesis, arguing for the intrinsic validity of cognition (svataḥprāmāṇya), the eternal authorlessness of the Veda (apauruṣeyatva), the inherent relation between word and referent, and the concept of unseen ritual efficacy (apūrva). This partial e-text encompasses adhyāyas 1 through 7, treating the sources of dharma, ritual classifications, subsidiary relations (śeṣatva), and the opening rules governing the transfer of ritual details (atideśa).

Nayavīthī ('The Path of Reasoning') is the third prakaraṇa of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, a foundational 9th-century treatise of the Prābhākara school of Pūrva-Mīmāṃsā. Composed entirely in 77 kārikās, this chapter articulates and defends the distinctive Prābhākara thesis that all cognitions are intrinsically veridical (sarvavijñānayathārthatva). Śālikanātha expounds the Prābhākara non-apprehension theory of error (akhyāti), arguing that experiential illusions (such as mistaking mother-of-pearl for silver) do not constitute a single mistaken cognition (anyathākhyāti), but rather two distinct mental episodes—an incomplete perceptual apprehension and a memory stripped of its temporal reference (smṛtipramoṣa)—whose difference goes unnoticed due to non-discrimination (vivekāgraha).

Amṛtakalā ('The Digit of Nectar') is the fifth chapter of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, composed in 76 kārikās. It offers a concise metrical compendium of Prābhākara Mīmāṃsā epistemology, defining valid knowledge (pramāṇa) as apprehension distinct from memory (anubhūti) and defining the five pramāṇas admitted in the Prābhākara system: perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), scripture/verbal testimony (śāstra), comparison (upamāna), and presumption/postulation (arthāpatti). The chapter concludes with a systematic refutation of non-apprehension (anupalabdhi/abhāva) as an independent sixth pramāṇa, defending the Prābhākara doctrine that absence is identical with the bare locus.

Prakaraṇa 13 of Śālikanāthamiśra's Prakaraṇapañcikā, titled Aṅgapārāyaṇa ('Investigation of Auxiliary Elements'), presents the Prābhākara school's comprehensive doctrine on the nature, function, and taxonomy of ritual accessories (aṅga). The chapter is divided into two paricchedas: the first investigates proximate or directly operating accessories (sannipattyopakāraka, such as thrashing or sprinkling), while the second examines unmediated or distantly operating auxiliaries (ārādupakāraka, such as the prayāja offerings). Śālikanātha refutes rival Bhāṭṭa views on accessory injunctions (aṅgavidhi) and establishes how both classes of subsidiaries contribute to the principal unseen efficacy (apūrva/niyoga).

**Coverage:** partial — Contains only adhyāya 1, pāda 1, sūtras 1–5 (the core epistemological section of the Tarkapāda, including the Vṛttikāra passage), ending at line 830 with 'tasmād avirodhaḥ'. The full Mīmāṃsāsūtra and bhāṣya encompass twelve adhyāyas.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Mīmāṃsāsūtra (Jaimini, root text)
- Mīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya (Śabarasvāmin, commentary)

**Also known as:** Śābarabhāṣya, Śabarabhāṣya, Mīmāṃsābhāṣya, Pūrvamīmāṃsāsūtrabhāṣya, Tarkapāda, Vṛttikāragrantha

**Attribution:** The root sūtras are attributed to the sage Jaimini. The commentary is by Śabarasvāmin (Śabara). Under sūtra 1.1.5, Śabara cites and comments upon an extended passage by an older commentator ('vṛttikāras tv āha'), traditionally identified with Upavarṣa or Bhavadāsa.

This text comprises the opening epistemological section (Tarkapāda, sūtras 1.1.1–5) of Jaimini's Mīmāṃsāsūtra with the commentary of Śabarasvāmin (Śābarabhāṣya, c. 4th–5th century CE). It lays out the foundational epistemology of the Pūrva Mīmāṃsā school: the investigation of dharma (dharmajijñāsā), Vedic injunction (codanā) as the sole epistemic means for suprasensory dharma, the definition of perception (pratyakṣa), and the innate, beginningless relationship between linguistic expressions and their meanings (autpattikaḥ śabdārthasaṃbandhaḥ). Under sūtra 1.1.5, Śabarasvāmin incorporates the famous Vṛttikāragrantha, which systematically defines the pramāṇas (including inference, analogy, presumption, and absence) and defends the permanent self (ātman) against Buddhist epistemological and idealist critiques.

The Tarkasaṃgraha of Annambhaṭṭa (17th c.) is the definitive introductory primer of the syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system, systematically outlining the seven ontological categories (padārtha) and four means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa). Rāmānuja Tātācārya's (1928–2017) modern sub-commentary (Bālapriyā). Together, these layered texts elucidate the terse mūla definitions and defend foundational Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika theses using the technical vocabulary and methodology of Navya-Nyāya dialectics.

The Tattvacintāmaṇi ('Thought-Jewel of Reality') by Gaṅgeśa Upādhyāya (c. 14th century) is the foundational text of the Navya-Nyāya ('New Logic') school of Indian philosophy. Structured across four books corresponding to the four classical Nyāya pramāṇas (pratyakṣa, anumāna, upamāna, and śabda), the treatise introduced a formal technical language of relations, delimiters (avacchedaka), and qualifiers that transformed classical Sanskrit philosophical methodology. This e-text contains the first half of the fourth book (Śabdakhaṇḍa), which defends verbal testimony as an independent, irreducible source of valid knowledge against Vaiśeṣika and Buddhist reductionism, examines semantic preconditions for sentential comprehension (ākāṅkṣā, yogyatā, āsatti, tātparya), and investigates lexical signification up to the Jātiśaktivāda.

The Nyāyakumudacandra is an exhaustive Sanskrit philosophical commentary composed by the Digambara master Prabhācandra (c. 980–1065 CE) on Akalaṅka's Laghīyastraya. Written during the reign of the Paramāra ruler Jayasiṃhadeva, the text systematically expounds Jain epistemology (pramāṇa), logic, and ontology (anekāntavāda, syādvāda, naya). It engages in extensive dialectical critique of Buddhist (particularly Dharmakīrti and his commentators), Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā systems, and represents, alongside Prabhācandra's Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa, one of the foremost monuments of medieval Jain philosophy.

The Nyāyasūtra, attributed to Akṣapāda Gautama, is the foundational treatise of the Nyāya school of classical Indian epistemology and logic, redacted between approximately the 2nd century BCE and the 2nd century CE. In five books (adhyāyas) divided into ten daily reading units (āhnikas), it expounds sixteen dialectical and epistemological categories (padārthas), beginning with the four means of knowledge (pramāṇa: perception, inference, analogy, and testimony) and the twelve objects of knowledge (prameya). The Muktivāda is an analytical Navya-Nyāya monograph composed by Gadādhara Bhaṭṭācārya (c. 17th century) investigating the soteriological concept of liberation (mukti / apavarga). Applying the school's precise formal definitions, Gadādhara demonstrates that liberation is fundamentally the absolute, permanent cessation of suffering (ātyantikaduḥkhanivṛtti) rather than experiential positive bliss. **Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete text of Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 2 (from the kathālakṣaṇaprakaraṇa opening to the puruṣāśaktiliṅgadoṣasāmānyalakṣaṇaprakaraṇa colophon and verse 20). The full text of the Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi covers Adhyāyas 1–4 of the Nyāyasūtra, while Adhyāya 5 is commented upon separately in Udayana's Bodhasiddhi (Nyāyapariśiṣṭa).

**Also known as:** Nyāyanibandha, Tātparyapariśuddhi, Pariśuddhi

**Attribution:** Udayana (also known as Udayanācārya, fl. late 10th to early 11th century CE; traditionally dated c. 984 CE on the basis of his Lakṣaṇāvalī) composed the Pariśuddhi as an exhaustive sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā.

The Nyāyavārttikatātparyapariśuddhi (commonly known as the Nyāyanibandha) by Udayana (c. 10th–11th century CE) is an authoritative sub-commentary on Vācaspati Miśra's Nyāyavārttikatātparyaṭīkā, forming the culminating work in the classical Nyāyacaturgranthikā commentarial chain on Gautama's Nyāyasūtra. This section covers Nyāyasūtra Adhyāya 1, Āhnika 2, examining dialectical topics including the three types of debate (vāda, jalpa, vitaṇḍā), fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), quibbling (chala), futile rejoinders (jāti), and grounds of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Udayana defends classical Nyāya realism and epistemic criteria against Buddhist critiques, refining the formal rules and categories of philosophical debate.

The Nyāyabhūṣaṇa ('Ornament of Nyāya') is Bhāsarvajña's extensive 10th-century auto-commentary (saṅgrahavārttika) on his concise epistemological treatise, the Nyāyasāra. Structured across three chapters according to the three pramāṇas accepted by the author (perception, inference, and verbal testimony), the work introduces several heterodox positions within Nyāya, including the rejection of comparison (upamāna) as a distinct means of knowledge and the assertion that final liberation involves the positive experience of eternal bliss (nityasukhasaṃvedana). The treatise is a primary source for 10th-century philosophical controversies, featuring extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists (notably Dharmakīrti and Prajñākaragupta) as well as Cārvāka skeptics and rival Brahmanical systems.

The Padārthadharmasaṃgraha by Praśastapāda (c. 6th century CE) is the classical prose reformulation of the Vaiśeṣika system, systematically classifying reality into six padārthas (substance, quality, action, universal, particularity, and inherence) and articulating classical Vaiśeṣika theories of perception, inference, atomic physics, and liberation. The Nyāyasūtra of Akṣapāda Gautama (c. 2nd–3rd century CE) is the foundational text of the Nyāya school of classical Indian philosophy, organizing epistemology, logic, dialectics, and soteriology around sixteen cognitive and debate topics (ṣoḍaśapadārtha). This section covers the first daily lesson (āhnika) of Book 5 of the Nyāyasūtra together with Vātsyāyana's Nyāyabhāṣya, focusing entirely on futile rejoinders (jāti). The Nyāyāvatāra is a concise 32-verse Jain treatise on epistemology and logic (pramāṇaśāstra) treating perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), verbal testimony, internal pervasion (antarvyāpti), and the doctrine of perspectives (naya) in the context of anekāntavāda. Historically ascribed to Siddhasena Divākara, the text is now dated to c. the 8th century CE and attributed to Siddhasena Mahāmati, who engaged systematically with the Buddhist logic of Dharmakīrti. Siddharṣigaṇin's 10th-century commentary, the Nyāyāvatāravivṛti, provides a comprehensive exposition of each verse, vigorously defending Jain epistemological positions against rival Buddhist, Nyāya, and Mīmāṃsā objections.

The Nyāyakusumāñjali ('Offering of a Handful of Flowers of Reasoning') by Udayana (fl. c. 975–1050 CE) is the foundational treatise of classical Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika rational theology, presenting a sustained philosophical defense of theism (īśvaravāda) against non-theistic and materialist opponents. The work is composed in metrical verses (kārikās) accompanied by Udayana's extensive prose auto-commentary. In this first stavaka, Udayana refutes Mīmāṃsā, Cārvāka, and naturalistic objections by establishing the reality of unseen moral factors (adṛṣṭa) and arguing that non-intelligent cosmic causes necessitate an omniscient intelligent creator and supervisor.

The fourth chapter (Stavaka 4) of Udayana's Nyāyakusumāñjali refutes the Mīmāṃsaka challenge against divine omniscience. **Translations:**
- V. N. Jha, The Philosophy of Injunctions, Delhi: Pratibha Prakashan, 1987. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** unclear — No segment file exists for SA_GSP29_vidhi (0 segments, 0 characters), so the extent cannot be checked. By title the entry is meant to be the Vidhivāda section of the Śabdakhaṇḍa of the Tattvacintāmaṇi; that section is already contained in SA_GSP29_gangtciu (Tattvacintāmaṇi, Śabdakhaṇḍa, Sansknet/GRETIL; 'vidhivādapūrvapakṣaḥ' at segment 1147, 'vidhivādasiddhāntaḥ' at segment 1420).

**Also known as:** Vidhivāda, Tattvacintāmaṇi: Vidhivāda

**Attribution:** Authored by Gaṅgeśopādhyāya (Gaṅgeśa, 14th century CE), the Mithilā philosopher who founded the Navya-Nyāya school.

The Vidhivāda ('Discourse on Injunctions') is a key chapter within the Śabdakhaṇḍa (the fourth book, dealing with verbal testimony) of Gaṅgeśa's monumental Tattvacintāmaṇi (fl. c. 1320–1350 CE). It investigates the semantic and cognitive mechanisms behind injunctive verb forms (such as the optative/liṅ suffix), analyzing how linguistic utterances motivate human action. Gaṅgeśa rigorously refutes rival Mīmāṃsā views—including the Prābhākara doctrine of command/duty (kārya/niyoga) and Kumārila's theory of linguistic and objective impulsion (śābdī and ārthī bhāvanā)—establishing instead the classic Nyāya thesis that an injunction conveys that an action produces a desired result (iṣṭasādhanatā), is feasible through human effort (kṛtisādhyatā), and generates no overriding detriment (balavadaniṣṭānanubandhitva).

The Nyāyapariśuddhi ('Purification of Logic') is an epistemological and logical treatise by the 14th-century Viśiṣṭādvaita master Veṅkaṭanātha, designed to reformulate Nyāya epistemology to conform with Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. The Nyāyapariśuddhi ('Purification of Nyāya') by the 14th-century Viśiṣṭādvaita polymath Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedāntadeśika) is a major epistemological treatise intended to adapt and refine classical Nyāya methodology in accordance with Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. This section represents the second āhnika of Adhyāya 4 (Smṛtyadhyāya), which concludes the treatment of the means of valid knowledge (pramāṇa-pariccheda). This section contains the first lesson (prathamam āhnikam) of the fifth chapter (Prameyādhyāya), turning from the analysis of pramāṇas (epistemic instruments) to ontology and knowable entities (prameya). **DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GSP30_abhmal1u`

**Author:** Abhinavagupta

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Verses 1.1–399: Jürgen Hanneder (ed.), Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998; verses 1.400–1135: Madhusūdan Kaul Shāstrī (ed.), The Mālinīvijaya Vārttika of Abhinava Gupta, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS) No. 31, Srinagar: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State, 1921.

**E-text:** Jürgen Hanneder (entered and contributed to GRETIL)

Madhusudan Kaul Shastri, Srinagar 1921, KSTS XXXI) ... Jürgen Hanneder'.

**Other editions:**
- Madhusūdan Kaul Shāstrī (ed.), The Mālinīvijaya Vārttika of Abhinava Gupta, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS) No. 31, Srinagar: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State, 1921. — Editio princeps based on Śāradā and Devanāgarī manuscripts.
- Acharya Krishnananda Sagar (ed.), Śrīmālinīvijayavārtikam, Kheda: Madhavanand Ashram / Varanasi: Krishnānand Sāgar, 1985. — Reprint/re-edition based on the KSTS edition.

**Translations:**
- Jürgen Hanneder, Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete first kāṇḍa (prathamaḥ kāṇḍaḥ, verses 1.1–1.1135). The work consists of two kāṇḍas; kāṇḍa 2 is catalogued separately under SA_GSP30_abhmal2u.

**Also known as:** Mālinīvijayavārttika, Mālinīvārttika, Mālinīślokavārtika, Śrīmālinīvijayavārtika

**Attribution:** Authentic work of the Kashmirian nondual Śaiva polymath Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). The opening verses invoke his teachers (Śambhunātha, Bhūtirāja, Lakṣmaṇagupta) and include an explicit punning signature naming himself (verse 1.13).

The Mālinīślokavārttika (or Mālinīvijayavārttika) is Abhinavagupta's extensive verse commentary on the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the central scriptural authority of the nondual Trika Śaiva lineage. In Kāṇḍa 1, Abhinavagupta develops an expansive theological and philosophical exegesis primarily from the tantra's opening maṅgala, elaborating nondual metaphysics, epistemology, the ontology of Śakti, the theology of divine revelation (āgama), and the descent of divine grace (śaktipāta) while engaging rival Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya perspectives.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Madhusudan Kaul Shastri (ed.), The Mālinīvijaya Vārttikam of Abhinava Gupta, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS), No. 31, Srinagar: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State, 1921.

**E-text:** Jürgen Hanneder for GRETIL (Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages), file abhmal2u.htm

**Evidence:**

Madhusudan Kaul Shastri, Srinagar 1921, KSTS XXXI)'. Since this file contains Kāṇḍa 2 in its entirety, the source edition is exclusively Kaul Shastri's 1921 KSTS 31 edition.
- The verse count and text agree with KSTS 31 (verses 2.1–2.335).

**Other editions:**
- Jürgen Hanneder (ed.), Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998. — Critical edition covering only Kāṇḍa 1, vv. 1–399.
- Acharya Krishnanand Sagar (ed.), Śrīmālinīvijayavārttikam, Varanasi: Krishnanand Sagar, 1985. — Re-edition based on KSTS 31.

**Translations:**
- Jürgen Hanneder, Abhinavagupta's Philosophy of Revelation: An Edition and Annotated Translation of Mālinīślokavārttika I, 1–399, Groningen Oriental Studies 14, Groningen: Egbert Forsten, 1998. (English (Kāṇḍa 1, verses 1–399 only; Kāṇḍa 2 remains untranslated into English))

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete second kāṇḍa (verses 2.1–2.335) of the two kāṇḍas that comprise the full Mālinīślokavārttika (1,470 verses total; Kāṇḍa 1 contains 1,135 verses and is catalogued under SA_GSP30_abhmal1u).

**Also known as:** Mālinīvijayavārttika, Śrīmālinīvijayavārttika, MVTv, MVV

**Attribution:** Uncontested work of the Kashmirian non-dual Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE), who explicitly identifies himself in the final stanza (verse 2.335: kāśmīriko 'bhinavaguptaḥ / mālinyādimavākye vārttikam etad racayati sma).

The Mālinīślokavārttika (also known as Mālinīvijayavārttika) is Abhinavagupta's verse commentary on the opening verse of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the paramount scriptural authority of the Kashmirian non-dual Trika tradition. The work unfolds an extensive metaphysical, epistemological, and soteriological system across two books (kāṇḍas). This second kāṇḍa (verses 2.1–2.335) expounds the role of purified reasoning (tarka) as an indispensable aid to realization, the dynamic heart-vibration (hṛdayaspanda) of Śiva-Śakti, the ontology of bondage (mala, māyā), and non-dual initiation (dīkṣā).

**E-text:** Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages (GRETIL); data entry by Oliver Hellwig.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text comprising all 22 āhnikas, beginning with the opening maṅgala verses (AbhTs_1.1–1.3) and ending with chapter 22 verse 54 on the Kulayāga rite (AbhTs_22.54).

**Attribution:** An authentic and universally accepted work composed by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE) in Kashmir as a concise prose summary of his verse magnum opus, the Tantrāloka.

The Tantrasāra ('Essence of Tantra') is Abhinavagupta's prose compendium summarizing the doctrinal and ritual core of his encyclopedic verse work, the Tantrāloka. Divided into twenty-two daily lessons (āhnikas), it expounds the non-dual metaphysics and soteriology of Trika Śaivism and Kaula ritual traditions, systematically covering the four means of liberation (anupāya, śāmbhava-, śākta-, and āṇavopāya) alongside detailed instructions for initiation (dīkṣā), mantras, and esoteric ritual practices.

# Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GSP30_adyapppu`

**Author:** Ādyanātha

**Collection / category:** Treatises / GSP30 (GSP30 Philosophy Śaiva (Śāstra 3))

**Source:** GRETIL (Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages)

**Link:** [https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil/1_sanskr/6_sastra/3_phil/saiva/adyapppu.htm](https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil/1_sanskr/6_sastra/3_phil/saiva/adyapppu.htm)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Mukundarāma Śāstrī, ed., The Bhāvopahāra of Cakrapāṇinātha with the Vivaraṇa of Ramyadeva, followed by Bodhapañcadaśikā and Anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā. Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS), No. 14, text iii, pp. 1–8. Bombay: Printed at the Tatva-Vivechaka Press, 1918.

**E-text:** Somadeva Vasudeva for GRETIL

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL header explicitly credits the edition by Mukundarama Shastri, Bombay: Tatva Vivechaka Press, 1918 (giving 'Kashmir Series of Sanskrit Texts and Studies, 13' [recte 14, as KSTS 13 is the Ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasaṃdoha]) and data input by Somadeva Vasudeva.
- Ending verse Aprp_*1 reproduces Mukundarāma Śāstrī's editorial colophon verse: 'seyāṃ kāśmīrabhūpāla-saṃśritena prakāśitā / satā mukundarāmeṇa sanmude 'stu śive 'rpitā //'.

**Other editions:**
- Digital transcription by the Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog nos. M00004 and M00517), entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (2012), reproducing the KSTS 1918 text. — Digital version

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 50 verses (Aprp_1–50) plus an editorial concluding śloka (Aprp_*1) by the editor Mukundarāma Śāstrī.

**Also known as:** Parāpañcāśikā

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to Ādyanātha (iti śrīmadādyanāthaviracitā anuttaraprakāśapañcāśikā samāptā; also referred to as Ādinātha). As noted by Alexis Sanderson, verses from this work were transmitted and utilized liturgically among South Indian Śākta Śaiva lineages connected to the Parātriṃśikālaghuvṛtti tradition.

A 50-verse nondual Śaiva philosophical poem expounding supreme consciousness (Śiva/anuttara) as pure awareness (prakāśa) intrinsically united with reflective dynamism (vimarśa). It explains the manifestation and withdrawal of cosmic manifestation across the thirty-six principles (tattvas), establishing that objective reality is non-different from the supreme light, and describes spiritual liberation as the reabsorption of differentiated perception into universal spanda. Preserved primarily in Kashmirian manuscripts, it also enjoyed significant reception in South Indian Śākta Śaiva ritual traditions.

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** Not determined. Encoded by Marino Faliero (July 1998) for the Gandharva-nagaram / DSO Sanskrit Archive (Rome); the printed source is not named.

**Other editions:**

**Translations:**
- Lilian Silburn, Hymnes de Abhinavagupta, Paris 1970. (French)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: 8 verses (Śārdūlavikrīḍita) and the closing colophon 'iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptapādair viracitānuttarāṣṭikā samāptā'; one variant noted in the file (v. 2 'vilasa' for 'vihara').

**Also known as:** Anuttarāṣṭaka

**Attribution:** Universally accepted as an authentic short philosophical hymn of Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE), corroborated by the closing colophon: iti śrīmadācāryābhinavaguptapādair viracitānuttarāṣṭikā samāptā.

The Anuttarāṣṭikā ('Eight Verses on the Supreme/Absolute') is a concise philosophical stotra in Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre composed by the Kashmir Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). It articulates the Trika doctrine of anupāya ('no-means'), demonstrating that because non-dual consciousness (cidadvaya) is already the intrinsic nature of all reality, outward spiritual transmission (saṃkrāma), formal meditation, and ascetic striving are superfluous. Rejection and acquisition are discarded in favor of resting peacefully in reality as it is (svastho yathāvasthitaḥ), recognizing the world as an effortless manifestation of one's own conscious nature.

- Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti (Yogarāja, commentary)

**Also known as:** Paramārthasāra, Paramārthasārasaṃkṣepa, Paramārthasāravivṛti, Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti, Paramārthasāra with Yogarāja's Vivṛti

**Attribution:** The root work consists of 105 verses (predominantly in āryā metre, with verse 1 in upajāti) composed by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE), who adapted and recast the older Vaiṣṇava/Vedānta-Sāṃkhya Paramārthasāra attributed to Ādiśeṣa / Patañjali into an exposition of nondual Trika Śaivism. The commentary (vivṛti), explicitly titled Paramārthasārasaṃgrahavivṛti in the closing colophon, was composed by Rājānaka Yogarāja (fl. mid-to-late 11th c. CE), who identifies himself in the concluding verses as a direct disciple of Kṣemarāja.

The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Reality') is an introductory compendium of 105 āryā stanzas by the Kashmiri master Abhinavagupta (c. late 10th – early 11th c. CE), articulating the metaphysical and soteriological core of nondual Trika Śaivism. Adapted from an earlier Vaiṣṇava work attributed to Ādiśeṣa, the treatise outlines the emanation of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) through the playful self-expression (krīḍā) and sovereign freedom (svātantrya) of Śiva-consciousness, the contracted state of worldly bondage (saṃsāra), and liberation through self-recognition (pratyabhijñā). Yogarāja's vivṛti commentary (late 11th c. CE) expands Abhinavagupta's compressed verses into a systematic philosophical treatise, refuting Advaita Vedānta and Buddhist positions while clarifying the nondual Śaiva doctrine of divine grace (śaktipāta / anugrahaśakti).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text comprising all 52 anuṣṭubh verses, opening maṅgala, and closing colophons.

**Also known as:** Paryantapañcāśī

**Attribution:** Attributed directly to Abhinavagupta in the text's closing colophon (śrīmad-ābhinavaguptanāthasya) and attested as his work by Madhurāja of Madurai in the Gurunāthaparāmarśa (v. 8). Verses from the text are also quoted anonymously by Maheśvarānanda in the Mahārthamañjarīparimala (on v. 30) and in an anonymous South Indian Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinīvyākhyā. As noted by Alexis Sanderson, no Kashmirian manuscripts or citations are currently known; the text survives through a South Indian transmission represented by a codex unicus in the University Manuscripts Library, Trivandrum.

The Paryantapañcāśikā ('Fifty Verses on the Ultimate Limit') is a short philosophical treatise in 52 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to the non-dual Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). Synthesizing core teachings of the Trika and Krama traditions, the text delineates the non-dual reality of Bhairava, the manifestation and dissolution of the six cosmic paths (ṣaḍadhvan), and the four currents of energy (khecarī, gocarī, dikcarī, and bhūcarī) issuing from Vyomeśvarī into unitary consciousness. Known only from a single South Indian palm-leaf manuscript, the work was received and cited by later South Indian Śākta-Śaiva authors such as Maheśvarānanda and Madhurāja.

The Pratyabhijñāhṛdaya ('Heart of Recognition') is an influential introductory manual of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism composed in the first half of the 11th century CE by Kṣemarāja, the principal pupil of Abhinavagupta. Composed specifically for practitioners and novices lacking training in formal logic (tarka), the treatise distills the core metaphysics and soteriology of Utpaladeva's Īśvarapratyabhijñā into twenty concise aphorisms accompanied by Kṣemarāja's own explanatory commentary. - Sthaneshwar Timalsina, 'Contemplating upon the Image of Bhairava: A Study of Kṣemarāja's Bhairavānukaraṇastava', Journal of Indian Research, vol. 1, no. 1 (2013), pp. 142–152 (reprinted in Language of Images: Visualization and Meaning in Tantras, New York: Peter Lang, 2015, Appendix I, pp. 145–150). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of 48 verses in āryā metre, preceded by an invocation (oṃ namaś cidbhairavāya) and concluding with the authorial colophon.

**Also known as:** Bhairavānukaraṇastava

**Attribution:** Firmly attributed to Rājānaka Kṣemarāja (fl. c. 1000–1050 CE), confirmed by the closing colophon and by Kṣemarāja's own self-citations of the hymn in his Svacchandatantroddyota and Sāmbapañcāśikāvivaraṇa (on v. 15).

The Bhairavānukaraṇastotra ('Hymn on the Assimilation to Bhairava') is a 48-verse non-dual Śaiva hymn composed by Kṣemarāja in āryā metre. Rather than offering purely devotional praises, the hymn systematically decodes the terrifying Agamic iconography of Svacchandabhairava—his many weapons, ornaments of skulls and elephant skin, charnel-ground setting, and retinue—interpreting them as symbolic expressions of the dynamic powers of supreme, unconditioned consciousness (cidbhairava). The stotra illustrates the Trika and Krama synthesis of ritual visualization, aesthetic sentiment, and non-dual recognition (pratyabhijñā).

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Not stated in the e-text. The verses-only text (prathamo/dvitīyo/caturtho niḥṣyandaḥ headings; 25 + 7 + 19 + 2 verses, numbering restarting per section) follows the niḥṣyanda division of the kārikās as printed with Kṣemarāja's Spandanirṇaya: probably Madhusūdan Kaul Shāstrī (ed.), The Spandakārikās of Vasugupta with the Nirṇaya by Kṣemarāja, KSTS 42, Srinagar 1925 (or a derivative such as Jaideva Singh, Spanda-Kārikās, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1980).

**E-text:** Marino Faliero (Gandharva-nagaram / DSO Sanskrit Archive, Dipartimento di Studi Orientali, Università degli Studi di Roma 'La Sapienza', July 1998; incorporated into GRETIL)

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL file spandkau.htm has no source statement; only the footer "Gandharva-nagaram / DSO Sanskrit Archive" (Marino Faliero, Rome, 1998), a collection that generally does not cite its printed sources.
- The e-text is divided into niḥṣyandas with per-section verse numbering ending in a fourth niḥṣyanda of two verses (agādhasaṃśayāmbhodhi..., labdhvāpy alabhyam...), matching the sectioning used in Kṣemarāja's Spandanirṇaya; the heading for the third niḥṣyanda is missing in the e-text.
- The identification of a specific printed edition could not be confirmed (no page markers, no header); the earlier catalog note naming Kallaṭa's Vṛtti (KSTS 5) is likewise unsupported by the e-text.

**Other editions:**
- Jagadish Chandra Chatterji (ed.), The Spanda Kārikās with the Vṛtti by Kallaṭa, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS) 5, Srinagar / Poona: Aryabhushan Press, 1916. — Editio princeps of the 52-verse recension with Kallaṭa's Vṛtti.
- J. C. Chatterji (ed.), The Spanda Kārikās with the Vivṛti of Rāmakaṇṭha, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies 6, Srinagar, 1913. — Recension with Rāmakaṇṭha's Vivṛti.

- Madhusūdan Kaul Shāstrī (ed.), The Spandakārikas of Vasugupta with the Nirṇaya by Kṣemarāja, Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies (KSTS) 42, Srinagar: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State, 1925. — Contains the 53-verse recension followed by this e-text.
- Gopīnātha Kavirāja (ed.), Tantrasaṅgraha, pt. 1 (includes the Spandapradīpikā of Utpala Vaiṣṇava), Yogatantra-Granthamālā 3, Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit Vishvavidyalaya, 1970. — Recension with Utpalavaiṣṇava's 10th-century commentary.
- Gopīnātha Kavirāja (ed.), Tantrasaṅgraha, pt. 1 (includes the Spandapradīpikā of Utpala Vaiṣṇava), Yogatantra-Granthamālā 3, Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit Vishvavidyalaya, 1970. — Compendium of multiple classical commentaries.
- Lilian Silburn (ed.), Spandakārikā: Stances sur la vibration de Vasugupta, Publications de l'Institut de Civilisation Indienne (PICI) 58, Paris: Éditions E. de Boccard, 1990. — Critical edition, study, and French translation.

**Translations:**
- Jaideva Singh, Spanda-Kārikās: The Divine Creative Pulsation, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1980. (English)
- Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, The Stanzas on Vibration: The Spandakārikā with Four Commentaries, Albany: State University of New York Press, 1992. (English)
- Lilian Silburn, Spandakārikā: Stances sur la vibration de Vasugupta, Paris: Éditions E. de Boccard, 1990. (French)
- Raniero Gnoli, Testi dello Śivaismo medioevale: Spandakārikā, Torino: Boringhieri, 1999. (Italian)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — All verses of the four-niḥṣyanda arrangement (25 + 7 + 19 + 2 = 53 numbered verses); the heading of the third niḥṣyanda is missing between 2.7 and 3.1. Verse counts of the work vary between recensions/commentators (51–53).

**Also known as:** Spandasūtra, Spandaśāstra

**Attribution:** Authorship has been disputed since the early medieval period. Kṣemarāja (in his Spandanirṇaya and Spandasaṃdoha) and Utpalavaiṣṇava (in his Spandapradīpikā) attribute the verses to Vasugupta, characterizing them as a concise versified exposition of the Śivasūtras revealed to him. In contrast, Utpaladeva (in his Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī), Abhinavagupta (in the Tantrāloka), and Rāmakaṇṭha (in his Spandavivṛti) explicitly attribute the Kārikās to Vasugupta's pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. Modern scholars (e.g. Alexis Sanderson, Mark Dyczkowski) generally conclude that Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa was the author or formal systematizer of the verses based on Vasugupta's oral instruction.

The Spandakārikā is the primary doctrinal and meditative manual of the Spanda branch of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, composed in the 9th century CE and attributed either to the sage Vasugupta or his disciple Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. Across approximately 53 verses, the text expounds the principle of spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulse and creative vibration of absolute Consciousness (Śiva-Śakti) that constitutes the true nature of both macrocosmic manifestation and microcosmic cognitive awareness. Rather than prescribing the complete suppression of mental and sensory operations, the text teaches that by sustained introspective mindfulness of the subtle throb underlying emotions, sense-perceptions, and transitions between mental states, the practitioner attains direct recognition of their essential divine autonomy (svātantrya) and mastery over the psychic energies (cakreśvaratva).

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition: Somadeva Vasudeva's unpublished draft transcription (with emendations and notes) of the unique palm-leaf manuscript, National Archives Kathmandu, NGMPP reel A 35/3 (late Licchavi or early Kuṭila script), from a photocopy supplied by Diwakar Acharya; GRETIL timudghu.htm.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcription of the unique palm-leaf MS NAK (NGMPP A 35/3), starting at fol. 26r2. Timirodghāṭana paṭalas 1–12 (segments 0–575; colophon "iti timirodghāṭane dvādaśaḥ paṭalaḥ samāptaḥ"), with lacunae: fol. 27 missing in ch. 1–2 (the verse pīṭheśvaryo mahāghorā… quoted in PTV p. 201 and Śivasūtravimarśinī was evidently on a missing folio, per the GRETIL header), a further folio missing after ch. 3, and many illegible/abbreviated passages ("...", "*"). Then fragmentary material from about fol. 42v onward (Jñānaśūla passage; text ending "ete yogasadbhāvaḥ samāptaḥ", seg. 576–750), a Bhairava-uvāca passage with a list of Mothers (seg. 751–816), and the beginning-damaged Nirvāṇakārikā (seg. 817–831, about 13 lines). Whether the material after ch. 12 belongs to the Timirodghāṭana is not stated in the source.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Timirodghāṭana (root text (paṭalas 1–12, with lacunae))
- Untitled Kaula yoga material ending "ete yogasadbhāvaḥ samāptaḥ" (incl. a Jñānaśūla passage; ascribed in the text to Mīnanātha) (appended text(s) from the same manuscript (fragmentary))
- Nirvāṇakārikā (appended short text (fragment))

**Also known as:** Timirodghāṭa, Timirodghāṭanatantra

**Attribution:** Both works are scriptural/anonymous Śaiva esoteric compositions. The Timirodghāṭana is an archaic Kaula tantra framed as divine revelation of Bhairava, cited as authoritative by Abhinavagupta in the Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa and by Kṣemarāja in the Śivasūtravimarśinī (under the title Timirodghāṭa). The Nirvāṇakārikā is an anonymous short yogic treatise found at the end of the codex.

The Timirodghāṭana ('Dispelling of Darkness') is an early Kaula Śaiva tantra surviving in a single early medieval Nepalese palm-leaf codex. Significantly adapting older Vidyāpīṭha material such as the Siddhayogeśvarīmata, it interiorizes external cultic ritual, foregrounds possession by divine energy (rudraśaktisamāveśa) and the descent of power (śaktipāta), and teaches an antinomian path centered on the senses and the body. It served as a fundamental scriptural authority for nondual Trika masters including Abhinavagupta and Kṣemarāja, and is accompanied in this manuscript by the short yogic text Nirvāṇakārikā.

The Janmamaraṇavicāra ('Investigation into Life and Death') is a short Kashmiri non-dual Śaiva philosophical treatise in mixed prose and verse by Bhaṭṭa Vāmadeva (fl. c. late 11th–early 12th century CE). Rooted in the Trika and Pratyabhijñā traditions, the work examines the cycle of transmigration, embryological development, and bodily death, interpreting empirical birth and dissolution as the contraction and expansion of autonomous supreme consciousness (Maheśvara). The treatise is notable for combining Kashmiri Śaiva metaphysics with Āyurvedic medical doctrine (such as the Suśrutasaṃhitā) and citations of lost Śaiva āgamas.

**Attribution:** The final verse (v. 45) attributes the composition to Vāmanadatta, son of Harṣadatta (described as 'a lion in the forest of Mīmāṃsā', mīmāṃsāvanasiṃha). The author also composed the Dvayasaṃpattivārttika (or Bodhavilāsa). Modern scholars (including R. Gnoli, R. Torella, and M. Dyczkowski) distinguish this Śaiva/Krama yogic author from the Vaiṣṇava non-dualist Vāmanadatta who authored the Saṃvitprakāśa.

The Svabodhodayamañjarī ('Inflorescence of the Arising of Innate Awareness') is a short Kashmiri Śaiva contemplative tract of 45 verses composed by Vāmanadatta, son of Harṣadatta, around the mid-10th century. Closely resonant with the practical, anti-ritualist spirit of the Vijñānabhairavatantra, it presents methods for the effortless dissolution of conceptual thought (nirodha, vilaya) through ordinary perceptual and bodily experiences—such as eating, running, falling asleep, or attending to fading sounds and pleasant smells. Verses from the treatise are cited by Bhagavadutpala in the Spandapradīpikā and later Kashmiri commentators.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all four niḥṣyandas of the Spandakārikā (52/53 kārikās) together with Kṣemarāja's complete Spandanirṇaya commentary, including its introductory verses and closing colophon stanzas.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Spandakārikā (Vasugupta, root text)
- Spandanirṇaya (Kṣemarāja, commentary)

**Also known as:** Spandasūtra, Spandaśāstra, Spandakārikāsaṃgraha

**Attribution:** Authorship of the root verses (Spandakārikā) is traditionally debated: Kṣemarāja, Utpala Vaiṣṇava, and later Trika authors attribute them to Vasugupta (the receiver of the Śivasūtra), whereas earlier commentators such as Rāmakaṇṭha and Bhaṭṭa Bhāskara, as well as Abhinavagupta in certain contexts, attribute them to Vasugupta's pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. The commentary Spandanirṇaya is securely attributed to Kṣemarāja (c. first half of the 11th century CE), pupil of Abhinavagupta.

The Spandakārikā is a seminal verse treatise of the Spanda school of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, expounding spanda—the dynamic, unceasing pulsation of supreme consciousness (Śiva/Śakti) that underlies all cosmic manifestation, maintenance, and dissolution. Composed across four sections (niḥṣyandas), the verses present a contemplative methodology for yogic practitioners to recognize this vibrating consciousness within all sensory, cognitive, and affective states, leading to liberation in this life (jīvanmukti). This e-text provides the complete text of the kārikās together with the Spandanirṇaya, the influential eleventh-century commentary by Abhinavagupta's disciple Kṣemarāja, which systematically interprets the work through the synthetic theological framework of Trika and Pratyabhijñā.

Bhāsarvajña's 10th-century commentary, the Ratnaṭīkā, provides an authoritative exposition of these terms, elucidating the duties of the religious preceptor (ācārya) and practitioner (sādhaka), yogic disciplines, and the ultimate attainment of duḥkhānta (the cessation of suffering). Alongside the Pāśupatasūtra and Kauṇḍinya's Pañcārthabhāṣya, it is one of the few surviving foundational primary texts of classical Pāśupata Śaivism.

The Sāṃkhyakārikā (also known as Sāṃkhyasaptati), composed by Īśvarakṛṣṇa, is the foundational and earliest extant systematic treatise of the classical Sāṃkhya school of Indian philosophy. The Sāṃkhyakārikā of Īśvarakṛṣṇa (c. 4th–5th century CE) is the foundational and most authoritative classical treatise of the Sāṃkhya darśana. In approximately 72–73 āryā stanzas, it systematically expounds the dualistic metaphysics of unmanifest and manifest primordial nature (avyakta- and vyakta-prakṛti) alongside the multiplicity of pure conscious subjects (puruṣa). The text establishes the satkāryavāda theory of causation, analyzes the triad of guṇas (sattva, rajas, tamas), charts the 25 evolutionary principles (tattvas) and psychological schema (buddhi, ahaṃkāra, manas, indriyas, tanmātras, mahābhūtas), and teaches that discriminative insight (vivekakhyāti) dissolves the misidentification of consciousness with nature to achieve final isolation and liberation (kaivalya).

The Sāṃkhyasūtra (or Sāṃkhyapravacanasūtra) is an aphoristic treatise in six adhyāyas (527 sūtras) articulating Sāṃkhya metaphysics, traditionally attributed to Kapila but compiled in the late medieval period (c. 14th–15th century CE). The first three books expound core ontological doctrines (puruṣa, prakṛti, the evolutes, and the mechanics of bondage and liberation), the fourth provides illustrative parables and allegories, and the final two refute rival philosophical schools and recapitulate the system. Appended to the root text in this file is the Tattvasamāsa, a concise mnemonic compendium detailing the twenty-five tattvas and auxiliary categories of Sāṃkhya, arranged here in two sections: Tattvapāda and Prakīrṇapāda.

The Sāṃkhyaparibhāṣā is a late, syncretistic definitional manual composed in mixed prose and verse. Although titled as a Sāṃkhya work, it integrates Sāṃkhya cosmological categories (the twenty-five tattvas) with Advaita Vedānta concepts—explicitly citing the classical Advaita guru lineage from Gauḍapāda to Śaṅkara and the fourfold spiritual prerequisites (sādhanacatuṣṭaya)—as well as elements of Yoga and Haṭhayoga praxis. The work survives in a single fragmentary manuscript witness edited by Vindhyeśvarīprasāda Dvivedin.

The Sāṃkhyatattvakaumudī by the polymath Vācaspatimiśra (fl. c. 9th–10th century CE) is the most influential and authoritative commentary on Īśvarakṛṣṇa's foundational Sāṃkhyakārikā (c. 4th–5th century CE). Because of its clarity and systematic acumen, Vācaspati's commentary eclipsed earlier expositions and became the standard interpretive framework for classical Sāṃkhya in later Indian philosophy.

The Tattvasamāsa ('Compendium of Principles') is a very brief mnemonic outline consisting of between 23 and 27 aphorisms (sūtras) that summarize the central ontological, cosmological, and psychological categories of classical Sāṃkhya philosophy. It lists the fundamental categories including the eight material causes (prakṛti), the sixteen evolutes (vikāra), the conscious subject (puruṣa), the three constituents (guṇa), cosmic evolution and dissolution, and the faculties and conditions governing bondage and release. Traditionally attributed to the mythic sage Kapila, the surviving text represents a medieval scholastic syllabus that served as the basis for several commentaries, such as those by Kṣemānanda, Bhāvāgaṇeśa, and the author of the Kramadīpikā.

The Yuktidīpikā is the most comprehensive and philosophically intricate surviving classical commentary on Īśvarakṛṣṇa's Sāṃkhyakārikā, composed anonymously around the 7th–8th century CE. The Padārthadharmasaṃgraha (commonly known as the Praśastapādabhāṣya) is the definitive classical treatise of the Vaiśeṣika philosophical school, composed by Praśastapāda (c. 6th century CE). The Vaiśeṣikasūtra is the foundational treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school of classical Indian philosophy, traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. Organised into ten adhyāyas of two āhnikas each, it elaborates an atomistic and pluralistic realist ontology structured around fundamental categories (padārtha): substance (dravya), quality (guṇa), motion/action (karman), generality (sāmānya), particularity (viśeṣa), and inherence (samavāya). The work investigates physical causation, the elementary constituents of matter, and perception and inference, maintaining that spiritual liberation (niḥśreyasa) arises from discriminative knowledge of reality induced by dharma.

The Vaiśeṣikasūtra is the foundational text of the Vaiśeṣika school of classical Indian philosophy, establishing a categorical realism structured around substances, qualities, motions, universals, particularities, and inherence. Candrānanda's running commentary (Vaiśeṣikasūtravṛtti) is the earliest surviving direct commentary on the sūtras, having been rediscovered in the mid-twentieth century and critically edited by Muni Jambūvijaya in 1961. Candrānanda preserves an archaic recension of the sūtrapāṭha that markedly diverges from the later vulgate represented by Śaṅkara Miśra's Upaskāra, making it fundamental for understanding pre-classical and early classical Vaiśeṣika thought.

The Mānamanohara of Vādivāgīśvara (ca. 11th–12th century CE) is an independent, dialectically sophisticated treatise of the Vaiśeṣika school. Setting out to vanquish rival disputants, the work systematically presents and defends Vaiśeṣika ontology and epistemology, featuring rigorous proofs for the existence of God (īśvarasiddhi), the composite whole (avayavisiddhi), indivisible atoms (paramāṇusiddhi), and the self (ātman), while defending the classic category doctrine against Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Advaita Vedānta objections. The treatise was an influential reference point in late medieval philosophical debates and is cited by authors such as Citsukha, Śaśadhara, and Vedāntadeśika.

**Coverage:** partial — The DharmaNexus segment file is empty (0 segments). The source data for this textname, /home/sebastian/data/mitra-data-collection/skt-en/aligned/GSP33vedanta-desika.tsv, has 123 Sanskrit–English rows. Rows 1–95 are Ratnāvalī verses (numbers between 3 and 130 appear, with gaps; the full work has 130 verses). Rows 96–123 are Dramiḍopaniṣatsāra verses (up to 26, with 24–25 repeated). The Sanskrit is OCR text with heavy corruption.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Dramiḍopaniṣattātparyaratnāvalī (Vedānta Deśika, root text)
- Dramiḍopaniṣatsāra (Vedānta Deśika, appendix (companion work))

**Also known as:** Drāmiḍopaniṣattātparyaratnāvalī, Drāviḍopaniṣattātparyaratnāvalī, Dramidopanishad Tatparya Ratnavali, Dramidopanishad Tatparyaya Ratnavali (old catalogue title)

**Attribution:** Uncontested traditional and scholarly attribution to Vedānta Deśika (Veṅkaṭanātha).

The Dramiḍopaniṣattātparyaratnāvalī is a Sanskrit poem of 130 verses by the Śrīvaiṣṇava teacher Vedānta Deśika (Veṅkaṭanātha, 13th–14th c.). It sets out the purport of Nammāḻvār's Tamil Tiruvāymoḻi (the 'Dravidian Upaniṣad'), one verse for each decad, and names the divine qualities each decad celebrates. The companion Dramiḍopaniṣatsāra (26 verses), included here in part, condenses the same teaching. Together they express the Ubhayavedānta view that the Tamil hymns carry the same authority as the Sanskrit Upaniṣads.

**Attribution:** The root aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Bādarāyaṇa (identified in the Dvaita tradition with Veda-Vyāsa). The foundational Dvaita commentary (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya) is by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, c. 1199–1276 or 1238–1317 CE). The subcommentary (Bhāṣyadīpikā or Ṭippaṇī) is by Jagannāthatīrtha (Jagannātha Yati, c. 18th century CE), disciple of Raghunāthatīrtha of the Vyāsarāya Maṭha.

This text comprises the third section (pāda) of the first chapter of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra alongside Madhva's foundational Brahmasūtrabhāṣya and Jagannāthatīrtha's subcommentary (Brahmasūtrabhāṣyadīpikā). Within Dvaita Vedānta exegesis (samanvayādhyāya), this pāda demonstrates that scriptural designations that might prima facie suggest individual souls or other deities—such as the abode of heaven and earth (dyubhvādyāyatana), the akṣara, the dahara (subtle heart space), and vaiśvānara—exclusively and primarily denote Brahman/Viṣṇu. The section also contains the Devatādhikaraṇa and Apaśūdrādhikaraṇa concerning qualifications (adhikāra) for Vedic study and knowledge.

The Brahmasūtra (also known as the Vedāntasūtra or Śārīrakasūtra), traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, is the foundational systematizing text of the Vedānta school of Indian philosophy. Consisting of 555 terse aphorisms across four chapters (adhyāyas), it harmonizes Upaniṣadic statements regarding Brahman as the ultimate reality (samanvaya), defends Vedāntic doctrine against rival philosophical traditions such as Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhism, and Jainism (avirodha), outlines spiritual discipline and contemplative methods (sādhana), and delineates the nature and fruits of liberation (phala). This e-text preserves the full root text as isolated from Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya.

The total of 545 matches the sūtrapāṭha of Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya, but that identification rests only on the count and has not been collated. Sūtra text only.

**Also known as:** Vedāntasūtra, Śārīrakamīmāṃsāsūtra, Uttaramīmāṃsāsūtra, Bhikṣusūtra, Brahmasūtrapāṭha

**Attribution:** Ascribed traditionally to the sage Bādarāyaṇa (and in Hindu tradition frequently equated with Veda Vyāsa / Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana). Modern historical scholarship generally dates the core redaction between the 2nd century BCE and the 4th/5th century CE.

The Brahmasūtra (also known as Vedāntasūtra or Śārīrakasūtra), traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa, is the foundational aphoristic treatise of Vedānta philosophy and one of the three canonical pillars of the prasthānatrayī alongside the principal Upaniṣads and the Bhagavadgītā. In four chapters (adhyāyas)—devoted respectively to the concordance of scriptural texts (samanvaya), non-contradiction and refutation of rival systems (avirodha), spiritual practice and discipline (sādhana), and the fruit of liberation (phala)—it systematizes Upaniṣadic theology. This digital edition presents the complete root text according to the 545-sūtra recension followed by Rāmānuja in his Śrībhāṣya and preserved in the Viśiṣṭādvaita tradition, which differs in division and sūtra count from the 555-sūtra Advaita recension of Śaṅkara.

Hiriyanna) has demonstrated that they were two distinct thinkers maintaining substantially different epistemological and metaphysical stances.

The Brahmasiddhi ('Establishment of Brahman') is a foundational treatise of early Advaita Vedānta composed by Maṇḍanamiśra in four chapters: Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa. Written in kārikā form accompanied by an autocommentary in prose, it defends the non-dual reality of Brahman against the realistic epistemology of Mīmāṃsā, Buddhist nominalism and momentariness, and rivals in linguistics. Maṇḍana formulates key tenets that distinguish his philosophy from Śaṅkara's, such as locating ignorance (avidyā) in individual selves (jīva) rather than in Brahman, and arguing for repeated meditation (prasaṅkhyāna) to transform propositional śabda-cognition into immediate realization. The work served as a primary point of departure for Vācaspati Miśra's commentary (Tattvasamīkṣā) and the subsequent Bhāmatī tradition.

The Brahmasūtras of Bādarāyaṇa constitute the foundational systematic treatise of the Vedānta school of Indian philosophy. Nimbārka's Vedāntapārijātasaurabha is a concise, aphoristic commentary interpreting the text through the lens of Svābhāvika-bhedābheda (natural difference and non-difference / Dvaitādvaita), wherein the individual self and material world are considered distinct from yet essentially dependent on and inseparable from Brahman (personified as Kṛṣṇa-Gopāla). Śrīnivāsa's sub-commentary, the Vedāntakaustubha, systematically explicates Nimbārka's terse glosses, clarifying doctrinal points and defending them against rival Vedāntic interpretations.

Adhyāya 2 (Avirodhādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra establishes the internal coherence and rational defensibility of Advaita Vedānta by systematically resolving objections. In the first pāda, attacks on Brahman as the sole material and efficient cause based on rival Smṛti doctrines (such as Sāṃkhya) and rational dialectic are rebutted. The third and fourth pādas reconcile conflicting Upaniṣadic statements regarding the genesis of the physical elements, the unoriginated and eternal nature of the individual soul (jīva), and the vital faculties (prāṇas). Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā provides a lucid, influential gloss on Śaṅkara's Bhāṣya in accordance with the Vivaraṇa interpretive tradition.

**Attribution:** The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa (identified in tradition with Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa). The sub-commentary Ratnaprabhā (or Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā) on Śaṅkara's Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya was authored by Govindānanda (Govindānanda Sarasvatī, c. 16th–17th century), a disciple of Gopālasarasvatī. This text comprises the third adhyāya (Sādhanādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra accompanied by the Advaita sub-commentary Ratnaprabhā (Bhāṣyaratnaprabhā) of Govindānanda (c. 16th–17th century). The chapter investigates the spiritual means (sādhana) leading to Brahmavidyā and liberation: pāda 1 examines the transmigration and embodiment of the individual soul to foster renunciation (vairāgya); pāda 2 analyzes the nature of the self across waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and swoon alongside the nature of nirguṇa Brahman (clarifying the terms tat and tvam); pāda 3 harmonizes and synthesizes the various Upaniṣadic meditations (upāsanās and guṇopasaṃhāra); and pāda 4 establishes that direct knowledge of Brahman is an independent, sovereign means to mokṣa (puruṣārtha) distinct from and superior to ritual duties.

**Attribution:** The Brahmasūtra (Vedāntasūtra) is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa (often identified with Vyāsa). The commentary Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya (also cited as Brahmasūtrabhāṣya or Śārīrakabhāṣya) is the seminal text of the Advaita Vedānta tradition by Śaṅkara (c. 8th century CE).

The fourth adhyāya of the Brahmasūtra, traditionally termed the Phalādhyāya, systematically examines the fruit (phala) of Brahman-realization across four pādas with Śaṅkara's commentary. Pāda 1 establishes the necessity of repeated contemplation (āvṛtti) of the Vedāntic mahāvākyas, the destruction and non-clinging of past sañcita and future āgāmi karma upon awakening, and the continued operation of prārabdha karma until bodily demise, establishing the validity of living liberation (jīvanmukti). Pādas 2 and 3 detail the process of dying, the non-departure of the vital faculties (prāṇas) in the case of the knower of the unqualified Brahman, and the ascent via the path of the gods (devayāna / arcirādimārga) for worshippers of saguṇa Brahman. Pāda 4 articulates the nature of liberation (mokṣa) as the manifestation (āvirbhāva) of the individual self's non-dual nature identical with Brahman, and the souls' eternal non-return to the cycle of rebirth.

In this chapter, the Vedāntic proposition that Brahman is the sole material and efficient cause of the universe is defended against competing philosophies and apparent contradictions in sacred tradition. Pāda 1 refutes objections founded on Sāṃkhya-Yoga smṛtis and rationalist arguments; Pāda 2 dismantles rival ontological systems, including classical Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika atomism, Buddhist Sarvāstivāda, Vijñānavāda, Madhyamaka, Jainism, Pāśupata theism, and Pāñcarātra theology; and Pādas 3 and 4 resolve conflicting śruti passages concerning the cosmic elements (ākāśa, vāyu, etc.), the nature and agency of the individual soul (jīva), and the vital faculties (prāṇas).

Adhyāya 3 (Sādhanādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra systematically examines the spiritual means leading to liberation (mokṣa). Pāda 1 examines the soul's transmigration via the five fires (pañcāgnividyā) to cultivate detachment (vairāgya); Pāda 2 analyzes the states of waking, dreaming, deep sleep, and swoon to show that the true Self is transcendent and that Brahman is pure non-dual consciousness; Pāda 3 evaluates the Upaniṣadic meditations (vidyās) and establishes criteria for combining or separating divine attributes (guṇopasaṃhāra); and Pāda 4 establishes that knowledge of Brahman (brahmajñāna) directly accomplishes the ultimate puruṣārtha independent of ritual action, while specifying the role of ethical and contemplative disciplines. This e-text presents the sūtras with Śaṅkara's foundational bhāṣya and Govindānanda's Ratnaprabhā subcommentary.

**Coverage:** partial — Complete text of Adhyāya 2 (Avirodhādhyāya: pādas 2.1 through 2.4, comprising sūtras 2.1.1 to 2.4.22) along with the Bhāmatī commentary. Forms part of a four-file set in GRETIL (brsvbh1u to brsvbh4u) covering the four adhyāyas.

- Brahmasūtra (Bādarāyaṇa, root text)

**Attribution:** The Brahmasūtra is traditionally attributed to Bādarāyaṇa. The Bhāmatī is the seminal sub-commentary (ṭīkā / bhāṣyavibhāga) on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya composed by Vācaspati Miśra (10th century CE). In this e-text, Bādarāyaṇa's sūtras are embedded alongside Vācaspati's commentary, whereas Śaṅkara's bhāṣya appears only in pratīka citations.

Adhyāya 2 of the Brahmasūtra, known as the Avirodhādhyāya ('chapter on non-contradiction'), reconciles Advaita Vedānta against external criticisms and internal scriptural inconsistencies across four pādas. Pāda 1 answers objections based on smṛti and reasoning; Pāda 2 (Tarkapāda) critiques rival philosophical schools including Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Sarvāstivāda, Vijñānavāda, Jainism, and theistic traditions; while Pādas 3 and 4 resolve apparent scriptural contradictions concerning the creation of the elements, the nature of the jīva, and the sense faculties (prāṇas). Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī (10th century CE) provides lucid dialectical, logical, and grammatical analysis of Śaṅkara's bhāṣya, forming the foundational text of the Bhāmatī school of Advaita Vedānta.
