This text comprises the third adhyāya (Sādhanādhyāya) of Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtra alongside Vācaspati Miśra's 10th-century Advaita sub-commentary, the Bhāmatī. The chapter systematically examines the spiritual means (sādhana) to liberation across four pādas: the post-mortem transmigration of the soul and the cultivation of detachment (vairāgya; 3.1); the states of consciousness and the non-dual, relationless nature of Brahman (3.2); the collation and harmonization of Upaniṣadic meditations (upāsanā/vidyā; 3.3); and the primacy of direct metaphysical knowledge over ritual acts together with the necessary auxiliary virtues (3.4). Vācaspati Miśra clarifies and defends Śaṅkara's bhāṣya, providing influential formulations of the Bhāmatī school on ignorance (avidyā) and spiritual pedagogy.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Complete adhyāya 4 (Phalādhyāya, pādas 1–4, sūtras 4.1.1–4.4.22) with Vācaspati Miśra's Bhāmatī, opening with the Bhāmatī's two introductory verses ('nābhyarthyā iha santaḥ…', 'śaṅke saṃprati…') and ending with the concluding verses of the work; adhyāyas 1–3 are SA_GSP33_brsvbh1u–3u.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Brahmasūtra (Bādarāyaṇa, root text)
- Bhāmatī (Vācaspati Miśra, sub-commentary)

**Also known as:** Śārīrakamīmāṃsāsūtra with Bhāmatī (chapter 4), Vedāntasūtra with Bhāmatī (chapter 4), Śārīrakabhāṣyavibhāga Bhāmatī (adhyāya 4), Bhāmatī (adhyāya 4)

**Attribution:** Bādarāyaṇa is the traditional author of the Brahmasūtra. Vācaspati Miśra (fl. c. 9th–10th century CE) composed the sub-commentary Bhāmatī on Śaṅkara's Brahmasūtrabhāṣya. Śaṅkara is the author of the underlying commentary, but his full running text is absent here.

Adhyāya 4 (Phalādhyāya) of the Brahmasūtra forms the concluding chapter of Bādarāyaṇa's foundational Vedānta work, accompanied here by Vācaspati Miśra's (fl. c. 9th–10th century CE) celebrated Advaita sub-commentary Bhāmatī. This chapter analyzes the fruit (phala) of Brahman-knowledge, examining the necessity of repeated meditation (āvṛtti), the immediate annulment and non-attachment of past karmas upon realization, the post-mortem ascent along the path of light (devayāna / arcirādimārga), and the nature of liberation (mokṣa) as non-difference (avibhāga) from the Supreme Brahman. Vācaspati's Bhāmatī provides meticulous philosophical exposition of Śaṅkara's text and establishes key tenets of the Bhāmatī tradition, including the role of the mind (manas) in generating direct liberating insight.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of Gauḍapāda's kārikās across all four chapters (Āgama-, Vaitathya-, Advaita-, and Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa; 215 verses total).

**Also known as:** Gauḍapādakārikā, Gauḍapādīyakārikā, Māṇḍūkyakārikā, Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Gauḍapāda (c. 6th century CE), revered in the Advaita tradition as the teacher of Govindapāda and paramaguru of Śaṅkara. While traditional Vedānta treats the four prakaraṇas as a single continuous work by Gauḍapāda, some modern scholars have debated whether the four chapters originated as separate treatises.

The Āgamaśāstra (commonly known as the Gauḍapādakārikā or Māṇḍūkyakārikā) is the earliest extant systematic treatise of Advaita Vedānta, consisting of 215 verses divided into four chapters (Āgamaprakaraṇa, Vaitathyaprakaraṇa, Advaitaprakaraṇa, and Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa). Elaborating on the states of consciousness outlined in the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad, Gauḍapāda establishes the doctrine of absolute non-origination (ajātivāda), asserting that the unborn Self (ātman/brahman) alone is real while phenomenal multiplicity is an illusion akin to a dream or the circle traced by a whirling firebrand (alāta). The work is celebrated for its sophisticated dialectic, particularly in the fourth chapter, which draws heavily on Mahāyāna Buddhist concepts and terminology to articulate an orthodox Upaniṣadic non-dualism.

CE), who also uses his monastic name Ānandatīrtha in chapter colophons ('iti śrīmad-ānandatīrtha-bhagavatpādācārya-viracite...') and explicitly names himself as Madhva in the final signature verse (4.4.13: 'madhvo yattu tṛtīyam etadanumā granthaḥ kṛtaḥ keśave').

The Anuvyākhyāna is Madhva's versified dialectical supplement to his own prose Brahmasūtrabhāṣya, expounding Dvaita (Tattvavāda) Vedānta in 1,919 verses across four adhyāyas. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of Madhusūdana Sarasvatī's Siddhāntabindu commenting on all ten stanzas of the Daśaślokī, including the introductory upodghāta, the four final verses by Madhusūdana, and the closing colophon.

**Also known as:** Siddhāntatattvabindu, Daśaślokīvyākhyā

**Attribution:** The Siddhāntabindu is an influential 16th-century Advaita Vedānta commentary on the Daśaślokī attributed to Śaṅkarācārya, composed by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī (pupil of Viśveśvara Sarasvatī). In the fourth concluding stanza, Madhusūdana explicitly mentions that he composed this digest at the request of his disciple Balabhadra (bahuyācanayā mayāyam alpo balabhadrasya kṛte kṛto nibandhaḥ).

The Siddhāntabindu is a prominent 16th-century Advaita Vedānta treatise composed by Madhusūdana Sarasvatī as an elaborate commentary on the Daśaślokī attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Written at the behest of his pupil Balabhadra, the text transcends a simple gloss to provide a systematic digest of classical and post-Śaṅkara Advaita metaphysics, epistemology, and soteriology. Madhusūdana examines the meaning and lakṣaṇā analysis of the Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas ('tat tvam asi'), refutes non-Advaita positions (Cārvāka, Bauddha, Jaina, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Sāṅkhya), and clarifies key debates within the Advaita tradition, including dṛṣṭisṛṣṭivāda, pratibimbavāda, and avacchedavāda.

The Brahmasiddhi is the monumental philosophical treatise of Advaita Vedānta by Maṇḍanamiśra (8th century CE), written in a mixture of kārikās and prose auto-commentary. Structured into four chapters—Brahmakāṇḍa, Tarkakāṇḍa, Niyogakāṇḍa, and Siddhikāṇḍa—the work establishes nondual Brahman as the sole ultimate reality, offers a famous epistemological critique of the perception of difference (bheda), and rejects the Mīmāṃsā theory that Vedic authority is tethered to action-oriented injunction (niyoga). Maṇḍana's unique formulation of Advaita, particularly his view that avidyā resides in individual souls (jīva) rather than Brahman and his integration of meditation (dhyāna/upāsanā) into the path to knowledge, exerted a deep influence on Vācaspati Miśra and the later Bhāmatī tradition.

The Vibhramaviveka ('Discrimination of Error') is a verse treatise in 164 kārikās by Maṇḍana Miśra (fl. c. 8th century CE) examining the epistemology of perceptual error (khyātivāda). It critically evaluates rival classical theories—specifically Yogācāra ātmakhyāti, Mādhyamika asatkhyāti, and Prābhākara akhyāti—before analyzing anyathākhyāti / viparītakhyāti and demonstrating how the ultimate nature of error points toward indeterminability (anirvacanīyatva). The treatise is a fundamental document for the synthesis between late Mīmāṃsā epistemology and early Advaita Vedānta.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Vidyāraṇya (14th c., associated with Mādhava, brother of Sāyaṇa and Vidyāguru at Śṛṅgerī). The commentarial tradition (notably Rāmakṛṣṇa's Tattvadīpikā) and modern scholars (such as T. M. P. Mahadevan) observe that parts of the work were co-authored with or composed by his senior contemporary and preceptor Bhāratītīrtha (often dividing chapters 1–6 or 1–10 to Bhāratītīrtha and 7/11–15 to Vidyāraṇya).

The Pañcadaśī is a 14th-century verse prakaraṇa of Advaita Vedānta composed of fifteen chapters arranged into three pentads corresponding to the saccidānanda nature of Brahman: Viveka-pañcaka (discrimination of truth/reality, chs. 1–5), Dīpa-pañcaka (illumination of consciousness, chs. 6–10), and Ānanda-pañcaka (bliss of the Self, chs. 11–15). It serves as a comprehensive textbook explaining key Advaita concepts such as the mahāvākyas, cidābhāsa (reflected consciousness), māyā, and jīvanmukti.

In this section, Rāmānuja presents a sustained critique of the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika inferential proof for the existence of God (īśvarānumāna), demonstrating that Neither sensory perception nor cosmological inference can establish a transcendent creator. Consequently, he establishes that Brahman can be known only through Vedic scripture (śāstraikapramāṇakatva), which reveals the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) possessing infinite auspicious qualities and free from all cosmic blemishes.

The Upadeśasāhasrī ('Thousand Teachings') is the principal non-commentarial treatise (prakaraṇagrantha) universally acknowledged as an authentic work of Ādi Śaṅkara (fl. c. 8th century CE). Consisting of a metrical section (Padyabandha, 19 chapters) and a prose section (Gadyabandha, 3 chapters), it presents a concise exposition of Advaita Vedānta focusing on the identity of the individual self (ātman) with absolute reality (Brahman). The Vidhiviveka ('Discrimination of Injunction') is a seminal 8th-century treatise by Maṇḍanamiśra on Vedic hermeneutics and the philosophy of language. Composed in verse with an extensive prose autocommentary (svavṛtti), the work investigates the semantics of Vedic injunctions (vidhi) and the motive force that impels a person to act. Maṇḍanamiśra critically refutes rival theories—notably Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's concept of verbal efficient force (śabdabhāvanā) and the Prābhākara thesis of autonomous duty/obligation (niyoga/kārya)—establishing that prescriptive verbal forms convey that the enjoined act is an effective means to a desired end (iṣṭasādhanatā).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text comprising all 580 verses (vv. 1–580) of the standard vulgate recension, concluding with verse 580 (saṃsārādhvani tāpabhānu...) and the colophon '//iti śaṃkarācāryaviracitaṃ vivekacuḍāmaṇi//'.

**Also known as:** Vivekacūḍāmaṇiḥ

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Ādi Śaṅkara (the final colophon reads 'iti śaṃkarācāryaviracitaṃ'). Most modern scholars, following Paul Hacker and Sengaku Mayeda, regard it as a later Advaita work on grounds of doctrine and style. The GRETIL file itself labels the attribution 'attrib.'.

The Vivekacūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-Jewel of Discrimination') is one of the most widely read verse manuals (prakaraṇa-grantha) of Advaita Vedānta, composed in 580 verses. Set as a pedagogical dialogue between a spiritual teacher and a qualified disciple, it outlines the fourfold qualifications of an aspirant (sādhana-catuṣṭaya), analyzes the three bodies and five sheaths (pañca-kośa), elucidates the nature of māyā and ignorance, and demonstrates the fundamental discrimination (viveka) between the eternal Self (ātman) and the non-Self (anātman). The work culminates in the direct realization of non-duality and the characteristics of the liberated sage (jīvanmukta).

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text covers only the Ātmasiddhi, the first part of Yāmuna's three-part Siddhitraya (the subsequent treatises, Īśvarasiddhi and Saṃvitsiddhi, are contained in separate digital files). **Also known as:** Ātmasiddhi with Siddhāñjana, Ātmasiddhi, Siddhitrayam, Siddhitraya (Ātmasiddhi)

**Attribution:** The root work Ātmasiddhi is the first treatise of the Siddhitraya by the early Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya Yāmuna (c. late 10th to early 11th century CE). The commentary Siddhāñjana was composed by the 20th-century Śrīvaiṣṇava scholar-editor Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya (P. B. Annangaracharya, 1891–1982) while based at the Swaminarayan Sanskrit Pathashala in Vadtal, Gujarat.

The Ātmasiddhi is the first section of the Siddhitraya by the foundational Śrīvaiṣṇava philosopher Yāmunācārya (c. 10th–11th century CE). It defends the Viśiṣṭādvaita view of the individual self (ātman) as an eternal, distinct, self-luminous knowing agent (jñātṛ) against Cārvāka materialism, Buddhist soullessness and momentariness, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika conceptions of consciousness as an adventitious quality, and Advaita impersonal non-dualism. In this e-text, the surviving fragment of the root work is accompanied by the Siddhāñjana, a mid-20th-century Sanskrit commentary by Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.

He closes with 'granthabhāgo 'grimaḥ kvāpi netaḥ samupalabhyate / yāvallabdhasya vihitā vyākhyeyaṃ' (lines 996–997). The e-text is complete for what survives, but the work itself is a fragment.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Īśvarasiddhi (Yāmuna, root text)
- Siddhāñjana (Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇaṅgarācārya, commentary)

The Īśvarasiddhi is the second treatise of Yāmuna's Siddhitraya and survives only in part. It sets out a Mīmāṃsaka objection that no omniscient Lord can be proved by perception or inference, then begins Yāmuna's reply. The commentator suggests the reply leads to the Viśiṣṭādvaita view that the Lord is known from scripture. This e-text gives the surviving mūla with the 20th-century Sanskrit commentary Siddhāñjana by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.

The Gītārthasaṅgraha is a concise 32-verse treatise by the early Viśiṣṭādvaita master Yāmunācārya (c. 10th–11th century CE) synthesizing the philosophical and spiritual teachings of the Bhagavadgītā. **Coverage:** fragment — 18 kārikās (YIs_1–18) with Yāmuna's prose, from 'tatra kasyacid ekasya vaśe viśvaṃ pravartate' to 'ekapradhānapuruṣaṃ vivādādhyāsitaṃ jagat / cetanācetanātmatvād ekarājakadeśavat // 18 //'. **Also known as:** Siddhitraya (Īśvarasiddhi section)

**Attribution:** Attributed to Yāmunācārya (Āḻavandār, c. 10th–11th century CE), key early systematizer of the Śrīvaiṣṇava / Viśiṣṭādvaita tradition and grand-teacher of Rāmānuja.

The Īśvarasiddhi ('Proof of the Lord') is the second treatise of Yāmuna's Siddhitraya, a forerunner of Rāmānuja's Viśiṣṭādvaita. Yāmuna first gives a long Mīmāṃsaka pūrvapakṣa arguing that no means of knowledge can establish an omniscient creator. He then answers it with a series of inferences that the world is directed by a single conscious agent, using the analogy of a realm under one king. The surviving text breaks off after the eighteenth kārikā.

**Evidence:**

Its list of abbreviations and texts used (J-STAGE PDF, checked) reads: 'SS, AS samvitsiddhi, atmasiddhi in sri yamunacharya's Siddhitraya, Madras 1972'. He cites SS by page and line of that edition.

Mit einem Rekonstruktionsversuch der verlorenen Abschnitte, Wien: Verlag der ÖAW, 1988 (SbÖAW 504; Veröffentlichungen der Kommission für Sprachen und Kulturen Südasiens 21). — Critical edition. This is the basis of the parallel GRETIL e-text SA_GSP33_yamsvspu.
- Siddhitraya of Yāmunamuni, ed. Rāma Miśra Śāstrī, Benares: Chowkhamba Sanskrit Series, c. 1900. — Editio princeps. Series number and year not verified in this pass.
- Śrībhagavadyāmunamunipraṇītaṃ Siddhitrayam, Bombay, 1954. — Cited by Ishitobi, IBK 31.2 (1983), n. 18. Publisher not verified.

**Translations:**
- Roque Mesquita, Yāmunācāryas Saṃvitsiddhi, Wien: ÖAW, 1988. (German)

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — 207 numbered verses with a few prose connectives (YSsi_1–207). They run from 'ekam evādvitīyaṃ tad brahmety upaniṣadvacaḥ' to 'ghaṭād ṛte 'pi nirbhātaḥ paṭād iva ghaṭaḥ svayam' (YSsi_207), in the middle of the refutation of the sahopalambhaniyama argument. The Mesquita-based GRETIL text (SA_GSP33_yamsvspu) begins and ends at the same points. The e-text therefore has all that survives, but the work is a fragment.

**Also known as:** Siddhitraya, part 3: Saṃvitsiddhi

**Attribution:** A secure work of Yāmuna (also called Yāmunācārya or Āḷavantār, c. 10th–early 11th c. CE), one of the seminal ācāryas of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta.

The Saṃvitsiddhi, the third treatise of Yāmuna's Siddhitraya, is a verse polemic against Advaita Vedānta. It takes the Upaniṣadic 'ekam evādvitīyam' to deny any equal or superior to Brahman, not the reality of the world. It then criticises the doctrines of avidyā, of contentless consciousness, and of the non-difference of cognition and object. The surviving text breaks off during the refutation of the sahopalambhaniyama argument. Rāmānuja drew on it in the Śrībhāṣya's Mahāsiddhānta.

**Coverage:** fragment — The extant text of the Saṃvitsiddhi, numbered YSvs_1–439 following Mesquita's lines (GRETIL: 'Line numbering follows ed.'). Each number is a half-verse line, not a kārikā. The text runs from 'ekam evādvitīyaṃ tad brahmety upaniṣadvacaḥ' to 'ghaṭād ṛte 'pi nirbhātaḥ paṭād iva ghaṭaḥ svayam'. The editor's short connective notes, lacuna markers and emendation notes (e.g. '(em.; ... Ed / unmetrical)', '(?)') are kept. The Siddhitraya transmits the work incomplete, with lacunae, and Mesquita's attempted reconstruction of the lost portions is not part of the e-text.

The Saṃvitsiddhi ('Proof of Consciousness') is the epistemological treatise of Yāmunācārya's Siddhitraya, presenting a systematic defense of Viśiṣṭādvaita realism against Advaita Vedānta and Buddhist Idealism. Yāmuna critiques Advaita interpretations of major Upaniṣadic statements (such as 'ekam evādvitīyam') and refutes the concept of anirvacanīyakhyāti, arguing that consciousness inherently reveals distinct, qualified objects. Surviving only as a fragment (439 half-verse lines in Mesquita's edition), it served as a direct conceptual and textual model for Rāmānuja's Mahāpūrvapakṣa and Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the surviving text of Saṃvitsiddhi (151 verses plus prose passages) accompanied by the complete Siddhāñjana commentary. The file contains only the third section of the Siddhitraya (the Ātmasiddhi and Īśvarasiddhi are in separate files). As noted by the commentator at line 14 ('atra copakramamadhyāvasāneṣu bhūyān granthabhāgo luptaḥ'), the root text itself is historically incomplete and preserved with major lacunae.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Saṃvitsiddhi (Yāmuna, root text)
- Siddhāñjana (P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya, commentary)

**Also known as:** Saṃvitsiddhi with Siddhāñjana, Saṃvitsiddhi, Siddhitraya: Saṃvitsiddhi, Siddhitrayam (Saṃvitsiddhi)

**Attribution:** The root treatise Saṃvitsiddhi constitutes the third section of the Siddhitraya by the Śrīvaiṣṇava ācārya Yāmuna (c. 10th–11th century CE). The commentary Siddhāñjana was composed by the 20th-century Śrīvaiṣṇava scholar-pandit Prativādibhayaṅkara (P. B.) Aṇṇaṅgarācārya (1891–1983 CE) of Kanchipuram.

The Saṃvitsiddhi is the third treatise of Yāmunācārya's (c. 10th–11th century CE) celebrated Siddhitraya ('Triad of Demonstrations'), a foundational work of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. Written primarily in verse with argumentative prose transitions, the work offers an extensive critique of Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology, refuting the concept of contentless, undifferentiated consciousness (nirviśeṣa-cinmātra), the unreality of difference, and the doctrine of anirvacanīyatva. Instead, Yāmuna demonstrates that consciousness (saṃvit) is inherently qualified, intentional, and the attribute of an enduring knowing self (jñātṛ). This text directly influenced Rāmānuja's Mahāsiddhānta in the Śrībhāṣya. The digital file presents the surviving portions of the Saṃvitsiddhi accompanied by the 20th-century Siddhāñjana commentary by P. B. Aṇṇaṅgarācārya.

**Attribution:** The work is framed as an instruction delivered by the sage Gheraṇḍa to his student Caṇḍakāpāli. While traditionally associated with Gheraṇḍa, the text is an anonymous treatise composed in northeastern India (likely Bengal), dating to c. the late 17th or early 18th century.

The Gheraṇḍasaṃhitā is a classical manual of Haṭha Yoga composed in northeastern India around the late 17th or early 18th century, structured as a dialogue between the sage Gheraṇḍa and his disciple Caṇḍakāpāli. Departing from the fourfold or eightfold structures of other yoga treatises, it teaches a sevenfold discipline (saptāṅga) termed ghaṭastha yoga ('yoga centered on the body-vessel'), consisting of purification (ṣaṭkarma), posture (āsana), mudrā, sensory withdrawal (pratyāhāra), breath regulation (prāṇāyāma), meditation (dhyāna), and samādhi. Alongside the Haṭhapradīpikā and the Śivasaṃhitā, it stands as one of the three principal texts of premodern Haṭha Yoga.

The Haṭhayogapradīpikā by Svātmārāma (c. 15th century) is the best-known premodern manual of haṭhayoga. It draws heavily on earlier Nātha and tantric yoga texts. The Yogasūtra with the Yogasūtrabhāṣya (together known as the Pātañjalayogaśāstra) constitutes the foundational text of the classical Yoga darśana, traditionally dated to around 350–450 CE. Divided into four chapters—Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda—it establishes the philosophical definition of yoga as the cessation of mental fluctuations (cittavṛttinirodha) and elaborates the eightfold path (aṣṭāṅgayoga). The work provides a systematic exposition of meditation, epistemic validity, karmic latent impressions (saṃskāra), contemplative attainments (siddhi), and the ultimate liberation (kaivalya) of conscious spirit (puruṣa) from primordial matter (prakṛti).

**Attribution:** Traditional Vedic saṃhitā belonging to the Paippalāda school (śākhā) of the Atharvaveda, traditionally connected with the sage Pippalāda.

The Paippalādasaṃhitā is one of the two surviving recensions of the Atharvaveda (alongside the Śaunakasaṃhitā). ## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Complete text of Maṇḍala 1 of the Ṛgveda, containing all 191 sūktas (RV 1.1.1 to RV 1.191.16; 2,006 verses) divided into 64 vargas. Accents are omitted in this e-text format.

**Also known as:** Ṛgvedasaṃhitā (maṇḍala 1), Rigveda (Book 1)

**Attribution:** Traditionally viewed as apauruṣeya (authorless revelation) seen by Vedic ṛṣis. Maṇḍala 1 is a composite collection of mini-cycles traditionally attributed to diverse seer lineages, notably Madhucchandas Vaiśvāmitra (1.1–10), Medhātithi Kāṇva (1.12–23), Śunaḥśepa Ājīgarti (1.24–30), Gotama Rāhūgaṇa (1.74–93), Kutsa Āṅgirasa (1.94–115), Kakṣīvat Dairghatamasa (1.116–126), Parāśara Śāktya (1.65–73), and Agastya Maitrāvaruṇi (1.165–191).

Maṇḍala 1 is the opening book of the Ṛgvedasaṃhitā, consisting of 191 hymns addressed primarily to Agni, Indra, the Aśvins, the Maruts, Varuṇa, and Uṣas. It is composed of multiple smaller cycles attributed to distinct ṛṣi lineages (such as the Gotamas, Kutsas, and Agastyas), functioning alongside Maṇḍala 10 as an outer book framing the central 'family books' (Maṇḍalas 2–7). Among its most famous compositions are the riddle hymn of Dīrghatamas (1.164) and the early dialogue and riddle hymns.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains only the opening portion of the Pūrvabhāga: Prapāṭhaka 1, kaṇḍikās 1–39; Prapāṭhaka 2, kaṇḍikās 1–24; and Prapāṭhaka 3, kaṇḍikās 1–6 (ending at GpBr_1,3.6 //). The full text consists of two major divisions: Pūrvabhāga (5 prapāṭhakas, 135 kaṇḍikās) and Uttarabhāga (6 prapāṭhakas, 123 kaṇḍikās).

**Also known as:** Gopatha-Brāhmaṇa, Gopatha Brāhmaṇa

**Attribution:** An anonymous Vedic prose text affiliated with the Atharvaveda tradition (recognized in both the Śaunaka and Paippalāda recensions). The text is traditionally attributed to the seer Gopatha or takes its title from the office of the Brahman priest who guards (gup-) the sacrifice.

The Gopathabrāhmaṇa is the only surviving Brāhmaṇa text attached to the Atharvaveda tradition. Divided into two main sections, the Pūrvabhāga (five prapāṭhakas) presents cosmogonic narratives, mystical reflections on the syllable Om and the Gāyatrī, and an exaltation of the Atharvaveda and the supervising Brahman priest; the Uttarabhāga (six prapāṭhakas) treats Śrauta rituals in close structural alignment with the Vaitānasūtra. Recognized as one of the youngest extant Brāhmaṇas, it freely borrows and refashions passages from earlier Vedic texts, notably the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa and Kauṣītakibrāhmaṇa.

The work is celebrated for its extensive mythological narratives, ritual etiologies, and unique cultural-historical material, including the Vrātyastomas and sacred topography along the Sarasvatī River.

**Attribution:** The kārikās of the Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa are traditionally attributed to Gauḍapāda (c. 6th century CE), revered in Advaita Vedānta as Govinda Bhagavatpāda's teacher and Adi Śaṅkara's paramaguru. The accompanying commentary is traditionally attributed to Adi Śaṅkara (c. 8th century CE), though modern critical scholarship (notably Paul Hacker, Sengaku Mayeda, and Tilmann Vetter) has questioned whether it is by the author of the Brahmasūtrabhāṣya or stems from another early Advaitin.

The Alātaśāntiprakaraṇa ('Quenching of the Firebrand') is the fourth and final chapter (100 kārikās) of the Māṇḍūkyopaniṣatkārikā, accompanied here by the prose bhāṣya traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. Using the metaphor of a whirled firebrand (alāta) that creates illusory luminous forms without producing real multiplicity, the chapter expounds absolute non-origination (ajātivāda) and non-relational meditation (asparśayoga). It is famous in Indian philosophical history for framing Advaitic non-dualism through the dialectical terminology of Madhyamaka and Yogācāra Buddhism.

**Attribution:** A principal (mukhya) Upaniṣad belonging to the Ṛgveda, embedded in the second book of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka (AitĀ 2.4–6). Traditionally associated with the Ṛgvedic sage Mahidāsa Aitareya.

The Aitareyopaniṣad is one of the earliest classical prose Upaniṣads belonging to the Ṛgvedic school, embedded as chapters 4 through 6 in the second book of the Aitareya Āraṇyaka. It opens with a cosmogonic account in which the solitary ātman creates the cosmic realms, their divine guardians, and the cosmic person (puruṣa), into whom the cosmic deities subsequently enter as perceptual and physiological faculties. After reflecting on the threefold birth of the individual soul and liberation through the legendary Ṛgvedic seer Vāmadeva, the Upaniṣad concludes with an inquiry into the fundamental nature of the Self, identifying all phenomena and faculties with consciousness in the famous mahāvākya 'consciousness is brahman' (prajñānaṃ brahma).

**Also known as:** Bṛhadāraṇyaka-Upaniṣad, Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Kāṇva recension), Vājasaneyibrāhmaṇopaniṣad, Śatapathabrāhmaṇa (kāṇḍa 14, adhyāyas 4–9, Kāṇva recension)

The Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad ('Great Forest Upaniṣad') is the longest and one of the oldest of the principal Upaniṣads, belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda and forming the concluding section (adhyāyas 4–9 of kāṇḍa 14) of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. Preserved in two recensions (Kāṇva and Mādhyandina), the Kāṇva text is structured into three divisions: the Madhukāṇḍa (adhyāyas 1–2), the Yājñavalkyakāṇḍa or Muni-kāṇḍa (adhyāyas 3–4), and the Khilakāṇḍa (adhyāyas 5–6). Through celebrated philosophical debates involving the sage Yājñavalkya, King Janaka of Videha, Gārgī Vācaknavī, and Maitreyī, it presents seminal teachings on the non-dual identity of ātman and brahman, the negative theology of 'neti neti' ('not this, not this'), the pavamāna invocation ('asato mā sad gamaya'), and early formulations of karma and transmigration.

**Attribution:** The mūla is the Kāṇva recension of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Śukla Yajurveda; anonymous Vedic text). GRETIL describes the commentary as 'ascribed to Śaṃkara'; the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣadbhāṣya is generally accepted in modern scholarship as an authentic work of Śaṅkara (c. 8th century CE).

Adhyāya 5 of the Bṛhadāraṇyakopaniṣad (Kāṇva recension) constitutes the opening division of the Khilakāṇḍa ('supplementary section'). It comprises fifteen brāhmaṇas setting forth a sequence of meditative disciplines and symbolic upāsanās, including the famous contemplation on the fullness of Brahman ('pūrṇam adaḥ pūrṇam idam'), meditations on the syllable Om and the heart (hṛdaya), the solar and psychic persons, and the celebrated three-syllable instruction of Prajāpati ('da-da-da' interpreted as damyata, datta, dayadhvam). Śaṅkara's bhāṣya elucidates these auxiliary meditations as mental disciplines intended to steady and purify the mind in aid of brahmavidyā.

The Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya is Madhva's commentary on the Chāndogya Upaniṣad of the Sāmaveda. In it, Madhva interprets the Upaniṣadic narrative and teachings from an uncompromising Dvaita (dualist) theistic perspective, equating the supreme Brahman exclusively with Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa). He famously offers an alternative reading and explanation of the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' as 'atat tvam asi' ('thou art not that'), emphasizing the eternal and essential ontological distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the supreme Godhead.

**Attribution:** A minor Upaniṣad traditionally classed among the Sāmānya Vedānta Upaniṣads (no. 17 in the Muktikā canon, where it is assigned to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda). The Garbhopaniṣad is a minor Upaniṣad centered on embryology, human anatomy, and physiological contemplation integrated with Vedāntic and Sāṃkhya-Yoga soteriology. It details the month-by-month gestation of the embryo from conception to birth, the bodily components, humors, and tissues, and the fetus's awakening in the womb to memories of past lives and suffering, leading to a resolve to seek liberation through Maheśvara, Nārāyaṇa, or Yoga. The treatise concludes by homologizing the internal organs to the three Vedic fires and ritual instruments of the sacrificial arena and provides an enumeration of anatomical parts, identifying itself as a Paippalāda text on liberation.

The Īśopaniṣad (or Īśāvāsyopaniṣad) is one of the earliest and most influential mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads, consisting of 18 verses that constitute the 40th chapter of the Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda (here in the Kāṇva recension). Unlike most other classical Upaniṣads that belong to Brāhmaṇas or Āraṇyakas, it is uniquely positioned directly within the Saṃhitā proper. It reconciles active engagement in the world with radical spiritual renunciation under the overarching premise that everything is enveloped by the Lord (īśā vāsyam idaṃ sarvam), harmonizing ritual performance (avidyā) with higher meditative knowledge (vidyā), and concluding with invocations of the divine solar puruṣa and Agni.

The Atharvaśiropaniṣad ('Head of the Atharvaveda') is an early Śaiva and Pāśupata Upaniṣad traditionally attached to the Atharvaveda. It begins with the gods questioning Rudra about his identity, to which Rudra responds with a grandiose self-proclamation asserting that he is the sole eternal reality, transcendent and immanent in all deities, natural phenomena, and meters. The Śvetāśvataropaniṣad is a verse Upaniṣad belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, traditionally ranked among the late principal Upaniṣads and composed around the final centuries BCE. It occupies a pivotal transitional place in early Indian thought by synthesizing Vedic ritualism, Upaniṣadic monism, proto-Sāṃkhya ontological dualism (puruṣa, prakṛti, guṇas), and early Yoga meditative practices. The Śvetāśvataropaniṣad is a classical metrical Upaniṣad belonging to the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda tradition, dating approximately to the late centuries BCE. Comprising six chapters, it synthesizes older Upaniṣadic non-dualism with an explicitly theistic framework, identifying the supreme transcendent Brahman with the personal deity Rudra-Śiva (also addressed as Hara, Īśa, and Maheśvara). The text incorporates concepts that later became central to classical Sāṃkhya and Yoga—such as pradhāna/prakṛti, puruṣa, the guṇas, and physical postures and breath control for meditation—and concludes with an influential early articulation of personal devotion (bhakti) toward God and the guru.

The Pāraskaragṛhyasūtra is the principal manual of domestic ritual (gṛhyasūtra) of the Śukla (White) Yajurveda tradition, closely affiliated with the ritual literature of Kātyāyana. Structured in three kāṇḍas, it sets out aphoristic rules for domestic sacrifices (gṛhyakarmāṇi) and life-cycle sacraments (saṃskāras), including marriage, conception, childhood rites, Vedic initiation (upanayana), daily domestic fire offerings, and post-initiatory vows. It serves as the primary domestic ritual authority for the Mādhyandina and Kāṇva recensions in northern and western India.

In 21 brief khaṇḍas, it treats domestic ritual procedures, expiatory offerings (prāyaścitta), and specific rites such as the marriage to a Calotropis procera plant (arkakanyādāna) before a third marriage, while lacking standard household ceremonies like the regular vivāha. Because of its peculiar selection of rites and linguistic irregularities, scholars treat it as a late supplement or recast related to the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra tradition.

The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Ārya-Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the monastic disciplinary code and case-law collection for Buddhist nuns (bhikṣuṇīs). Transmitted in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit and preserved in a single medieval palm-leaf manuscript from Tibet, it comprises the full Bhikṣuṇīprātimokṣavibhaṅga (origin stories, precept formulations, word analyses, and non-offense clauses for the Prātimokṣa rules), followed by the Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka (miscellaneous legal and institutional rules) and uddāna summaries of the Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka. Contributed to GRETIL as bsu011_u.htm, https://gretil.sub.uni-goettingen.de/gretil/1_sanskr/4_rellit/buddh/bsu011_u.htm (TEI: gretil_sa/sa_bodhisattvaprAtimokSasUtra.xml).

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL header: 'Based on the edition by Nalinaksa Dutt: Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtram. Calcutta : Calcutta Oriental Press, 1931, p 11-19. Input by members of the Sanskrit Buddhist Input Project ... Sutra section, text no. 11'
- ilx_skt TEI header repeats the same source statement
- DSBC book page https://dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/89: editor Dutt, Nalinaksa; Calcutta Oriental Press, Calcutta, 1931
- Dutt's introduction, as reproduced at https://dlbs.liberal.ntu.edu.tw/FULLTEXT/JR-BH/bh117539.htm: Cambridge (Bendall) MS, 10 leaves, Rañjanā script, three parts, Part Two starting on fol. 5v
- Tatz 1986 bibliography (reference-literature/cleaned_Asanga's Chapter on Ethics ... TATZ 1986.txt:10513): 'Bodhisattvapratimoksa-sutra. Ed N. Dutt in Indian Historical Quar[terly]'
- E-text ending matches the end of the ritual section (self-ordination, 'vijñaptiḥ // 0 //'); none of the Upāliparipṛcchā material is present

**Other editions:**
- N. Dutt, Indian Historical Quarterly 7 (1931): 259–286 — Journal printing of the same edition, with Dutt's introduction (IHQ 7, 1931, pp. 259–286, confirmed by Edgerton BHSD s.v. Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa and the NTU Buddhism library catalogue). The Calcutta Oriental Press printing is presumably an offprint, so pp. 11–19 there probably correspond to about IHQ pp. 269–277 (an inference, not checked).
- Unrai Wogihara (ed.), Bodhisattvabhūmi, Tokyo 1930–36 (repr. Sankibo 1971); Nalinaksha Dutt (ed.), Bodhisattvabhūmiḥ, Tibetan Sanskrit Works Series 7, Patna: K.P. Jayaswal Research Institute, 1966 (repr. 1978) — Editions of the Bodhisattvabhūmi. Its Śīlapaṭala contains the vow ritual that Part 1 draws on. These are parallels, not editions of this text.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Dutt's manuscript (10 leaves) has three parts. (1) A ritual for conferring the bodhisattva vows, running to fol. 5v. (2) Extracts from the Upāliparipṛcchā/Vinayaviniścaya on a bodhisattva's offences and non-offences, ending 'iti bodhisattvaprātimokṣaḥ'. (3) A few lines on the last leaf. The e-text (77 segments) has only Part 1, the printed pp. 11–19 named in the GRETIL header. It runs from 'om namaḥ sarvabuddhabodhisattvebhyaḥ' to the self-ordination before a Tathāgata image, which ends with '... vijñaptiḥ // 0 //'.

**Also known as:** Bodhisattva-prātimokṣa-sūtram (Dutt 1931), Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa

**Attribution:** The work is an anonymous Nepalese compilation. The title comes from the scribal line 'iti bodhisattvaprātimokṣaḥ' on the last leaf of the single manuscript. Dutt (IHQ 7, 1931) holds that the contents have 'very little to do with' the Bodhisattvaprātimokṣa that Śāntideva quotes. He would rather call Part One a karmavākya, and he dates the composition to perhaps the 10th or 11th century. Part One draws on the vow ritual in the Śīlapaṭala of the Bodhisattvabhūmi, and Dutt marks those citations in his edition.

This is a short liturgical manual for conferring the threefold bodhisattva discipline: saṃvaraśīla, kuśaladharmasaṃgrāhakaśīla and sattvārthakriyāśīla. It covers the request to a qualified bodhisattva preceptor, confession, taking refuge, the threefold formal question and acceptance of the vows, and the sign that appears to the buddhas and bodhisattvas once the rite is complete. It ends with instructions for taking the vows by oneself before an image of the Tathāgata when no qualified preceptor is available. Much of the wording follows the vow ritual of the Śīlapaṭala of the Bodhisattvabhūmi.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the monastic rule code for bhikṣus according to the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin tradition, containing the introductory verses and upodghāta liturgy, all eight classes of rules (4 pārājika, 13 saṃghātiśeṣa, 2 aniyata, 30 niḥsargika-pācattika, 92 pācattika, 4 pratideśanīya, 67 śaikṣa, 7 adhikaraṇaśamatha), the verses of the seven past Buddhas, and the scribal colophon.

**Attribution:** Canonical Vinaya scripture of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school of early Indian Buddhism.

The Mahāsāṃghikaprātimokṣasūtra is the liturgical rule code of monastic discipline for monks (bhikṣus) belonging to the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin lineage, recited fortnightly at the poṣadha (confession) assembly. It sets forth 218 training rules systematically classified in descending order of severity: pārājika, saṃghātiśeṣa, aniyata, niḥsargika-pācattika, pācattika, pratideśanīya, śaikṣa, and adhikaraṇaśamatha. Composed in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit with substantial Middle Indo-Aryan morphological elements, this text represents the sole substantially preserved Indic Prātimokṣasūtra of the Mahāsāṃghika branch, preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript discovered in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains chapter 1 (Pravrajyāvastu) only, covering sūtras 1–647 along with their complete auto-commentary. The full Vinayasūtra contains over 4,000 sūtras covering seventeen vastus and the prātimokṣa rules.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vinayasūtra (Guṇaprabha, root text)
- Vinayasūtravṛtti (Guṇaprabha, commentary)

**Also known as:** Vinayasūtravṛttyabhidhānasvavyākhyāna, Vinayasūtrasvavyākhyāna, Pravrajyāvastu

**Attribution:** Both the root sūtras and the auto-commentary (svavyākhyāna / vṛtti) are composed by Guṇaprabha (c. 6th–7th century CE), as declared in the opening verses (sūtrāṇi vinayasyeyaṃ vṛttis teṣāṃ nigadyate) and the chapter colophon (vinayavṛttau svavyākhyānataḥ pravrajyāvastu samāptam).

Guṇaprabha's Vinayasūtra is the definitive scholastic digest of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya, condensing canonical narrative and disciplinary legal codes into concise aphorisms. This first chapter, the Pravrajyāvastu, sets forth monastic regulations and formal legal acts (karmavācanā) regarding novice reception (śrāmaṇeratvopanayana) and full ordination (upasaṃpad). Accompanied here by Guṇaprabha's auto-commentary (Vinayasūtravṛtti or Svavyākhyāna), it served as an authoritative reference work for Buddhist monastic jurisprudence in late Indian and Tibetan Buddhism.

**Evidence:**
- The DSBC bibliography for book 764 gives 'Pārājikā (Texts from Nepal)', Savitri Prakashan, Pune, 2013, with M. G. Dhadphale as editor/author (schema.org metadata) and pages 19–40.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete as printed in Dhadphale's edition, pp. 19–40. The page markers (19)…(40) follow the text of each page. It runs from the invocation of Vajrasattva through prāyaścitta for killing, govadha, sūtaka, śaucācāra and śrāddha, to the closing colophon 'iti prāyaścittavidhau śaucācāravidhe śrāddhaprakaraṇam iti samāptam'.

**Also known as:** Vajrasatvapārājikā, Prāyaścittavidhi

**Attribution:** Anonymous Newar Buddhist work. It opens with homage to Vajrasattva and announces 'prāyaścittavidhiṃ vakṣye śaucācāraṃ ca' (v. 1). It has nothing to do with Anupamavajra's Ādikarmapradīpa. It is one of the Nepalese 'pārājikā' texts published together by Dhadphale (Saddharma-, Vajrasattva-, Mañjuśrī-, Lokeśvarapārājikā).

The Vajrasattvapārājikā is an anonymous Newar Buddhist manual on expiation (prāyaścitta) and ritual purity, framed by homage to Vajrasattva and to the ācārya as Vajradhara. Despite the Vinaya term pārājikā in its title, it is addressed to Vajrācārya and lay communities, not to celibate monastics. It adapts Dharmaśāstra-style rules on liability and penance for homicide and cow-killing (govadha), birth and death impurity (sūtaka), purification (śaucācāra, including pañcagavya) and ancestral rites (śrāddha). The Sanskrit is irregular.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the work as edited by Gustav Roth (1970). It encompasses the foundational narrative of Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the eight gurudharmas (§§ 1–28), the full Bhikṣuṇīprātimokṣavibhaṅga (§§ 29–255; colophon at line 7849), the Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka (§§ 256–289; colophon at line 8584), and the concluding Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka uddāna summary (§§ 290–294; colophon at line 8759).

The Bhikṣuṇīvinaya of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school is the sole Vinaya text governing Buddhist nuns preserved substantially in Sanskrit. It recounts the origin narrative of the nuns' order with Mahāprajāpatī Gautamī and the formulation of the eight 'weighty rules' (gurudharma), followed by an extensive vibhaṅga (rule-by-rule casuistry and commentary) on the nuns' Prātimokṣa, miscellaneous disciplinary matters (Bhikṣuṇīprakīrṇaka), and a concluding uddāna summary of the monks' miscellaneous section (Bhikṣuprakīrṇaka). Preserved in an 11th–12th century palm-leaf manuscript found at Zha lu monastery in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, its Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit idioms make it a cornerstone witness for early Buddhist sectarian law and linguistics.

The Prātimokṣasūtra of the Sarvāstivādins is the fundamental monastic disciplinary code for Buddhist monks (bhikṣus) according to the Sarvāstivāda school, designed for communal recitation at the bi-monthly poṣadha observance. Reconstructed by Georg von Simson from Sanskrit manuscript fragments discovered in the Turfan oasis and other Central Asian sites, it constitutes the standard critical edition of the Sarvāstivāda monastic code.

The Varṣāvastu ('Chapter on the Rains Retreat') is the fourth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, regulating the mandatory three-month monastic retreat (varṣā or varṣāvāsa) observed during the monsoon. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Carmavastu, beginning with the opening uddāna and running through to the final colophon 'carmavastu samāptam' (lines 1–1296).

The Carmavastu is the fifth chapter of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, prescribing monastic rules governing the use of hides, leather mats, and footwear. It opens with the extensive narrative of the elder Śroṇa Koṭīkarṇa, his perilous voyage, visit to the realm of pretas, and his subsequent ordination under Mahākātyāyana. Koṭīkarṇa's journey to visit the Buddha in Śrāvastī prompts the allowance of regional dispensations for monks residing in remote border territories (pratyantajanapada), such as wearing multiple-soled footwear, frequent bathing, and using leather sitting mats. The remainder of the vastu details monastic regulations regarding permissible and prohibited types of shoes and skins, as well as the authorized possession of leatherworking implements like awls, knives, and thongs.

The Poṣadhasthāpanavastu is the fourteenth chapter (vastu) of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu, corresponding functionally to the Pātimokkhathapanakkhandhaka of the Pali Cullavagga. The Adhikaraṇavastu is the sixteenth chapter of the seventeen vastus comprising the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinayavastu. It systematically governs legal disputes within the monastic community, classifying conflicts into four types (vivādādhikaraṇa, anuvādādhikaraṇa, āpattādhikaraṇa, and kṛtyādhikaraṇa) and laying out the seven formal procedures (adhikaraṇa-śamatha) for resolving them. The Advayaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā is a condensed Mahāyāna scripture representing the Perfection of Wisdom in Fifty Lines (Ardhaśatikā or Pañcāśatikā Prajñāpāramitā). Set at Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, the Buddha instructs Subhūti that all spiritual paths and dharmas—including the six perfections, the eighteen kinds of emptiness, the bodhipakṣa dharmas, and the distinctive Buddha-qualities—are encompassed within the perfection of wisdom, which is ungraspable, intrinsically pure, and comparable to empty space. **Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna scripture presented as buddhavacana, framed as an interlocution between Śākyamuni Buddha and the elder Subhūti in the Jetavana hermitage at Śrāvastī.

The Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Diamond-Cutter Perfection of Wisdom Sūtra'), commonly known as the Diamond Sūtra or Triśatikā ('Three Hundred Lines'), is one of the most celebrated and influential scriptures in Mahāyāna Buddhism. Structured as a dialogue between the Buddha and the venerable Subhūti in the Jetavana grove at Śrāvastī, it systematically dismantles attachment to conceptual signs and ontological categories, teaching that bodhisattvas must practice generosity and cultivate supreme enlightenment without abiding in notions of self, living being, or dharma. The text is renowned for its characteristic dialectical formula asserting that a dharma is designated as such precisely because it is empty of intrinsic existence. First translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva in 401/402 CE, the sūtra became a cornerstone of East Asian Buddhist traditions—particularly Chan/Zen—and is celebrated for the 868 CE Dunhuang woodblock scroll, the world's earliest dated complete printed book.

The Saptaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 700 Lines', also designated Mañjuśrīparivartāparaparyāyā or Puṇyakṣetranirdeśa) is an influential Mahāyāna scripture belonging to the Prajñāpāramitā corpus. Set in Śrāvastī's Jeta Grove, it consists of profound dialogues between the Buddha, Śāriputra, and the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī emphasizing the unreality of dualistic categories, the unoriginated nature (anutpāda) of all dharmas, and the non-apprehending contemplation of the Tathāgata. The scripture is celebrated in East Asian Buddhist traditions for introducing the 'single-array absorption' (ekavyūhasamādhi, traditionally interpreted as the 'one-practice samādhi'), which links insight into the non-differentiated dharmadhātu to concentrated mindfulness of a Buddha.

The Pañcaśatikāprajñāpāramitā ('Perfection of Wisdom in 500 Lines') is a late Mahāyāna Prajñāpāramitā sūtra set on Vulture Peak in Rājagṛha, in which the Buddha instructs the Elder Subhūti on the nature of dharmas. The text is celebrated for integrating core Prajñāpāramitā emptiness ontology with Yogācāra terminology and concepts akin to the three natures (trisvabhāva), repeatedly analyzing dharmas in terms of non-existence (abhāva), actual/true existence (sadbhāva), and suchness (tathābhāva). Due to this synthesis, Tibetan Jonang master Dölpopa Sherab Gyaltsen and later gzhan stong thinkers considered it a sūtra of definitive meaning (nītārtha). Thought to be lost in the original Sanskrit, the sūtra was rediscovered in a unique palm-leaf manuscript preserved at the Norbulingka in Lhasa and first critically edited by Li Xuezhu and Fujita Yoshimichi in 2016.

Set on Vulture Peak (Gṛdhrakūṭa) in Rājagṛha, the Buddha Śākyamuni narrates to Ānanda how the monk Dharmākara, in the presence of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, generated the resolve for awakening and made forty-eight great vows to establish the western realm of Sukhāvatī and become the Buddha Amitābha (Amitāyus). The sūtra expounds the visual and spiritual splendors of this paradise, delineates the requirements for rebirth there through faith, recollection, and merits, and includes instructions addressed to the bodhisattva Ajita (Maitreya) on dispelling doubt.

This opening section includes the traditional nidāna on Vulture Peak, the catalogs of the arhat and bodhisattva assemblies, the Buddha's miraculous emanation of light illuminating countless world spheres, and initial dialogues with Śāriputra on practicing the perfection of wisdom through the radical non-apprehension (anupalabdhi) and emptiness of all dharmas. Framed as a dialogue between Jinaśrīrāja and Jayaśrī recounting the spiritual instructions given to King Aśoka by Upagupta, it glorifies the cosmic deeds and salvific emanations of Avalokiteśvara (Karuṇāmaya), promotes the six-syllable mantra (oṃ maṇi padme hūṃ), and details the merits of the poṣadha (aṣṭamīvrata) fasting ritual. The Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra is a major Mahāyāna scripture that circulated both independently and as the climactic final section of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra. It recounts the spiritual pilgrimage of the youth Sudhana, who is instructed by Mañjuśrī to seek out fifty-three spiritual mentors (kalyāṇamitra)—representing varied genders, occupations, and stations—to learn the practice of a bodhisattva. The Anityatāsūtra is a short discourse delivered by the Buddha at the Jetavana in Śrāvastī explaining that all conditioned phenomena (saṃskārāḥ) are impermanent, unstable, and subject to change. The Buddha illustrates universal mortality across all classes of society, heavenly beings across the three realms of desire, form, and formlessness, and even enlightened beings (arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas). The sūtra concludes with four gnomic verses on mortality and destruction parallel to stanzas found in the Anityavarga of the Udānavarga.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all one hundred stories arranged in ten vargas (AVŚ 1–100). The Kalpadrumāvadānamālā appended to Vaidya's 1958 printed volume is excluded here and maintained as a separate file in GRETIL.

**Also known as:** Śatakāvadānakathā, Pūrṇamukhāvadānaśataka, Pūrṇapramukhāvadānaśataka, Zhuanji baiyuan jing, 撰集百緣經

**Attribution:** Anonymous narrative anthology compiled within the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda tradition.

The Avadānaśataka ('A Century of Edifying Exploits') is one of the earliest and most structured Sanskrit anthologies of Buddhist narrative legends (avadāna), organized into ten thematic decades (vargas) containing ten stories each. Attributed to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda school and datable to roughly the 2nd–3rd century CE, the work illustrates the inevitable workings of karma and retribution across rebirths, focusing on predictions of future buddhahood and pratyekabuddhahood, arhatship, past-life deeds of the Buddha (jātakas), the torments of pretas, and noble acts of charity (dāna). It preserves early canonical clichés and formulas, and survives in Sanskrit as well as canonical Tibetan (Toh 343) and Chinese (T 200) translations.

**Attribution:** Canonical Buddhist sūtra (Buddhavacana) set at the Jetavana monastery in Śrāvastī.

The Āryānityatāsūtra is a short canonical discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī on the universal impermanence (anityatā) and inevitability of death for all conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra). The Buddha surveys all beings and classes—wealthy householders, brahmins, kṣatriyas, universal rulers, forest ascetics, and the devas across the desire, form, and formless realms—noting that none can escape death. Even arhats, pratyekabuddhas, and tathāgatas must eventually cast off their physical bodies (kāyanikṣepaṇa). The sūtra concludes with similes of fragile earthen pots and ripe fruits liable to fall, followed by famous verses on the cessation of conditioned existence.

The Ajitasenavyākaraṇa (or Ajitasenavyākaraṇanirdeśa) is a transitional Mahāyāna sūtra surviving in Sanskrit in the 6th–7th-century Gilgit cache and in Central Asian manuscript fragments, but absent from both the Tibetan and Chinese Buddhist canons. **Also known as:** Āryabuddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśanāmamahāyānasūtra, Āryabuddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśanāma Mahāyānasūtra, Buddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśa, Buddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇasūtra, Sangs rgyas kyi stobs skyed pa'i cho 'phrul rnam par 'phrul pa bstan pa zhes bya ba theg pa chen po'i mdo

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna sūtra regarded as buddhavacana.

The Buddhabalādhānaprātihāryavikurvāṇanirdeśasūtra is a Mahāyāna sūtra set on the banks of the Nairañjanā river and in the Āmrapālī grove at Vārāṇasī, centering on the miraculous transformations (vikurvaṇa) and superhuman displays (prātihārya) brought forth through the Buddha's samādhi. Prompted by the Buddha, the bodhisattvas Avalokiteśvara and Vajrapāṇi project radiant light across the ten directions to convert stubborn, immoral, and unfaithful beings, purifying their karmic defilements and gathering them before the Tathāgata. Through dialogues primarily involving Mañjuśrī, the sūtra sets forth a docetic Mahāyāna Buddhology, teaching that all conditioned phenomena, as well as the Buddha's earthly life and physical parinirvāṇa, are mere illusory displays (upāyakauśalya) like reflections in a clear mirror.

The discourse sets forth four factors, traditionally known as the four opponent powers (catuḥpratipakṣabala): remorse (vidūṣaṇāsamudācāra), antidotal virtuous deeds (pratipakṣasamudācāra), the resolve to refrain from repetition (pratyāpattibala), and reliance on refuge and bodhicitta (āśrayabala). Frequently cited by Indian masters, notably Śāntideva in the Śikṣāsamuccaya, it serves as the primary canonical foundation for Buddhist confession and purification rituals.

The Pratītyasamutpādamahāyānasūtra is a brief Mahāyāna scripture set in the Trāyastriṃśa heaven, where the bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara petitions the Buddha to deliver a teaching yielding boundless merit for the assembly. In response, the Buddha recites the famed dependent arising verse (ye dharmā hetuprabhavā...) and equates dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) directly with the Dharma body (dharmakāya) of all Tathāgatas, stating that whoever perceives dependent arising sees the Tathāgata. He teaches that fashioning even miniature caityas, bodhi trees, and umbrellas and reciting or depositing this verse inside them yields vast, Brahma-like merit (brāhmaṃ puṇyam) leading to rebirth in the Brahmaloka and the Śuddhāvāsa heavens. The sūtra serves as a crucial canonical justification for the widespread medieval Asian Buddhist practice of depositing the ye dharmā creed into stūpas, plaques, and images as a dharmakāya relic (dharmadhātu).

The Buddha enters a samādhi of great compassion that illuminates the cosmos, alleviating suffering and generating salvific transformations throughout the realms of existence. Expounding the protective power and spiritual empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) of all buddhas, the text incorporates extensive dhāraṇī and protective incantations, featuring solemn pledges to protect the teaching by Vajrapāṇi, the Four Great Kings, and eighty yakṣiṇīs. Preserved in Sanskrit in the Gilgit manuscript cache (ca. 6th–7th century CE), it was translated into Chinese by Yijing in 701 CE (Taishō 1375) and into Tibetan (Toh 98 / Toh 507).

A very brief Mahāyāna sūtra set in the underwater palace of the nāga king Sāgara. The Buddha explains that teaching and holding the four summaries or seals of the Dharma (caturdharmoddāna)—that all conditioned things are impermanent, all contaminated phenomena are suffering, all phenomena are without self, and nirvāṇa is peace—is equivalent to expounding all eighty-four thousand aggregates of the Dharma (dharmaskandha). This e-text is a modern Sanskrit reconstruction from the Tibetan translation (Toh 155), as no Indic manuscript of this short version has survived.

The Triskandhasūtra ('Sūtra of the Three Heaps', commonly referred to in Tibetan practice as the Bodhisattvāpattideśanā or the Confession to the Thirty-Five Buddhas) is a Mahāyāna liturgical text used for purifying infractions of the bodhisattva vows and moral downfalls. Its title refers to three key ritual actions: confession of moral faults (pāpadeśanā), rejoicing in merits (anumodanā), and the dedication of merit toward supreme awakening (pariṇāmanā). While it circulates independently as a ritual text across Nepal and Tibet, the liturgy also constitutes the central confession pericope embedded within the Mahāyāna Vinayaviniścaya-Upāliparipṛcchāsūtra.

A compilation of four canonical Āgama discourses reconstructed from Sanskrit manuscript fragments found in Central Asia (Turfan collection) expounding the ten powers (daśabala) of a Tathāgata. These powers—including perfect knowledge of what is possible and impossible (sthānāsthāna), the ripening of karma (karmavipāka), the states of meditative attainment (dhyānavimokṣasamādhisamāpatti), the spiritual faculties of sentient beings (indriyaparāparatā), and the eradication of contaminants (āsravakṣaya)—form the foundation of the Buddha's authority to proclaim the wheel of Dharma and utter his lion's roar (siṃhanāda). Belonging to the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda transmission, these discourses parallel texts in the Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99, no. 684) and Pāli Dasabala suttas in the Saṃyutta and Aṅguttara Nikāyas.

The Śārdūlakarṇāvadāna (Divyāvadāna Chapter 33) narrates how the low-caste Mātaṅga (Caṇḍāla) maiden Prakṛti falls in love with the Buddha's disciple Ānanda and attempts to entrap him with love sorcery, but is rescued by the Buddha, ordained as a bhikṣuṇī, and attains arhatship. **Attribution:** An anonymous anthology of Buddhist narrative literature written in Classical and Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit. The Divyāvadāna ('Divine Narratives') is an anthology of 38 Buddhist avadāna stories composed in Sanskrit, illustrating the workings of karma, past births, and moral causation through the lives of the Buddha, his disciples, householders, and monarchs. Compiled around the 2nd to 4th centuries CE, a major portion of the text draws directly from the Vinayavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda tradition. Set in the aquatic palace of the serpent kings Nanda and Upananda, the text relates the Buddha's instruction on loving-kindness (maitrī) as the supreme antidote to suffering, followed by protective dhāraṇīs and ritual manual procedures for bringing rain. While closely related to chapters 64–65 of the larger doctrinal Mahāmeghasūtra (T387 / Toh 232), this sūtra circulated independently throughout Asia as a specialized rain-ritual text (Tibetan Toh 235/657; Chinese T989, T991, T992, T993).

The Saṃghāṭasūtra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist sūtra set on Vulture Peak near Rājagṛha, consisting of dialogues between the Buddha and the bodhisattvas Sarvaśūra and Bhaiṣajyasena. It emphasizes the spiritual perils of cyclic existence, the visionary experiences of dying and intermediate states, karmic retribution and purification, and the boundless merit accrued from hearing, reciting, or copying the text. It was exceptionally widely copied in northwestern India and Central Asia, surviving in numerous Sanskrit manuscripts from Gilgit and Dunhuang, as well as Khotanese, Sogdian, Tibetan, and Chinese translations.

A Buddhist discourse extolling the karmic fruit and spiritual merit generated by fashioning, commissioning, and worshipping images of the Buddha (tathāgatabimba / buddhapratimā). The Buddha recounts the former life of Prince Suvarṇaprabha, who in the era of the past Buddha Vipaśyin was a destitute farmer who fashioned a Buddha image and as a consequence experienced countless rebirths as a universal emperor (cakravartin), Indra, and Brahmā before attaining arhatship. The sūtra systematically lists permissible image materials (clay, stone, ivory, wood, gold, bronze, brass/tin, silver, crystal, and gems) and provides rare early epigraphic/ritual textual evidence for enshrining either bodily relics (sadhātuka) or the Pratītyasamutpāda stanza (sapratītyasamutpāda) inside Buddha statues.

The Mañjuśrīmūlakalpa ('Root Ritual Manual of Mañjuśrī') is an encyclopedic Buddhist Mantrayāna ritual compendium in 55 chapters, framed as a Mahāyāna vaipulya sūtra and classified in Tibetan canons as a Kriyā-tantra. It details extensive ritual procedures centered on the bodhisattva Mañjuśrī and the Tathāgata family, including mantras, dhāraṇīs, maṇḍalas, cloth-painting painting rites (paṭavidhāna), mudrās, homa rites, and astrological divinations for both mundane and soteriological ends. Chapter 53 (Rājavyākaraṇaparivarta) preserves an important verse chronicle of northern Indian dynasties through the early Pāla era. Composed in layers, the core text dates to roughly the 5th–6th centuries CE, with successive accretions expanding the collection through the mid-to-late 8th century CE.

The Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti ('Chanting the Names of Mañjuśrī') is an influential Buddhist tantric scripture in 167 verses set within a prose frame, presented as a discourse delivered by Śākyamuni Buddha at the request of Vajrapāṇi. Dated to approximately the 8th century CE, the scripture generated extensive Indian commentaries (including works by Vilāsavajra and Mañjuśrīkīrti), played a central role in both Mahāyoga and Anuttarayoga tantric systems (most notably the Kālacakra), and remains one of the most widely recited liturgical texts in Nepalese and Tibetan Buddhism.

The Ekādaśamukha (also known as Ekādaśamukhahṛdaya) is an early esoteric Buddhist dhāraṇī-sūtra in which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara reveals his eleven-faced heart-spell (hṛdaya) before the Buddha in the Jetavana monastery at Śrāvastī. The Patna Dharmapada is an early Buddhist collection of gnomic and doctrinal stanzas composed in a distinctive Middle Indo-Aryan idiom (often designated Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit or Buddhist Prakrit) showing archaic phonological and morphological traits. Transmitted in a single 11th–12th-century palm-leaf manuscript discovered at Ngor monastery in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, the text comprises 414 verses across 22 chapters (vargas). It is an invaluable witness alongside the Pāli Dhammapada, the Gāndhārī Dharmapada, and the Sanskrit Udānavarga for comparative Buddhist textual criticism, and is widely assigned to the school of the Sāṃmatīyas.

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Luo Hong and Toru Tomabechi (eds.), Candrakīrti's Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (Vajrasattvasādhana): Sanskrit and Tibetan Texts. Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region (STTAR), vol. 6. Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2009 (distributed 2010), pp. 3–32.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), input and proofread by Miroj Shakya, Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods (NIEM), Kathmandu / University of the West, Rosemead, CA.

**Evidence:**
- Explicit page numbers in parentheses throughout the DSBC text—starting at '(3)' at segment 14 and proceeding sequentially through '(4)', '(5)', '(6)', '(20)', '(21)', '(26)', '(31)', and ending at '(32)' at segment 301—match the Sanskrit critical text pagination (pp. 3–32) of Luo & Tomabechi's editio princeps.

- DSBC TEI header for book_818 records input and proofreading by Miroj Shakya (NIEM/UWest).

**Other editions:**
- None. The 2009/2010 critical edition by Luo Hong and Toru Tomabechi (STTAR 6) constitutes the editio princeps of the Sanskrit text. — The edition was based on three Sanskrit manuscripts: two preserved in the Tibet Autonomous Region (MS A, palm-leaf, 12th c.; MS B, paper, dated 1301 CE) and one photographed by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana at Ṅor Monastery (MS G, palm-leaf, 12th–13th c.).

**Translations:**
- dPal gsang ba 'dus pa rnal 'byor chen po'i rgyud kyi srid pa skye ba'i rim pas rdo rje sems dpa'i sgrub thabs (Toh 1800 / D 1800, P 2673), translated at Vikramaśīla Mahāvihāra by Tathāgatarakṣita and Klog skya Gzhon nu 'bar; critically edited alongside the Sanskrit by Luo Hong and Toru Tomabechi (2009). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — The e-text preserves the entire work from opening namaskāra and introductory framing down through the concluding colophon, corresponding precisely to pages 3–32 of the critical edition by Luo Hong and Toru Tomabechi (2009/2010).

**Also known as:** Vajrasattvasādhana, Bhavotpattikrameṇa Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra, Guhyasamājamahātantre Bhavotpattikrameṇa Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra, Vajrasattvaniṣpattisūtra

**Attribution:** The colophon explicitly assigns authorship to Ācārya Candrakīrtipāda ('kṛtiriyamācāryacandrakīrtipādānām'). This is the tantric Candrakīrti, an influential commentator within the Ārya tradition of Guhyasamāja tantric exegesis (author of the Pradīpoddyotana), generally placed around the 9th–10th century CE and distinguished by modern scholarship from the 6th–7th-century Madhyamaka philosopher Candrakīrti.

The Vajrasattvaniṣpādanasūtra (also known as the Vajrasattvasādhana) is a foundational generation-stage (utpattikrama) meditation manual of the Ārya tradition of Guhyasamāja tantra exegesis, attributed to the tantric commentator Candrakīrti (c. 9th–10th century CE). It delineates the generation of the thirty-two deities of the Guhyasamāja maṇḍala centered on Vajrasattva in accordance with the process of human rebirth and embryonic development (bhavotpattikrama). Structured across three successive meditations—samādhirāja, maṇḍalarājāgrī, and karmarājāgrī—the practice systematically correlates ritual visualizations with canonical scriptural quotations cited across the seventeen chapters of the root Guhyasamājatantra.

The Pāṃśupradānāvadāna ('Legend of the Gift of Dust/Earth') constitutes chapter 26 of the Divyāvadāna and serves as the opening section of the Aśokāvadāna cycle. The Ratnamālāvadāna ('Garland of Jewels of Edifying Deeds') is a late Sanskrit Buddhist metrical collection of thirty-eight avadāna tales framed as instruction given by the arhat Upagupta to Emperor Aśoka. It versifies and expands narratives familiar from older collections such as the Avadānaśataka, illustrating the inexorable results of karma, devotion to the Three Jewels, and the cultivation of the Mahāyāna pāramitās. Preserved in Nepalese Sanskrit manuscripts, it was critically edited in full by Kanga Takahata in 1954.

**Translations:**
- Yutaka Iwamoto, translation/study in Sumāgadhāvadāna (Studien zur buddhistischen Erzählungsliteratur, 2), Kyoto: Hōzōkan, 1968. (German/English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the independent Sumāgadhāvadāna across 270 numbered paragraphs (SumAv_1 through SumAv_270), concluding with the standard colophon 'sumāgadhāvadānaṃ samāptam'.

**Also known as:** Sumāgadhāvadānasūtra

**Attribution:** Anonymous canonical/edifying Buddhist avadāna. Transmitted as an independent text in Nepalese manuscripts (as well as in Tibetan and Chinese translations), distinct from Kṣemendra's versified rendition in the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā (ch. 93).

The Sumāgadhāvadāna is an independent Buddhist narrative work (avadāna) in mixed prose and verse relating the story of Sumāgadhā, daughter of the prominent merchant and patron Anāthapiṇḍada of Śrāvastī. Married into the household of Vṛṣabhadatta in Puṇḍravardhana (Bengal), whose family reveres the Nirgranthas (Jains), she is repelled by the naked ascetics and miraculously summons the Buddha and his disciples from her roof. The aerial arrival and marvelous transformations of the Buddha and the arhats convert her husband's family and the entire city to Buddhism. The text concludes with karmic explanations by the Buddha, including Sumāgadhā's past lives and the ten prophetic dreams of King Kṛkin.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the 10-chapter intermediate recension (adhyāyas 1–10, concluding at segment 3518), followed by Newar scribal colophon verses dated Nepāla Saṃvat 934 (1814 CE).

**Also known as:** Svayambhūcaityasamutpattikathā, Dharmadhātusvayambhūtpattidharmamāhātmyasubhāṣitasūtra, Svayambhu Purāṇa, Madhyama-Svayambhūpurāṇa

**Attribution:** Anonymous Buddhist purāṇa and sthala-māhātmya from the Kathmandu Valley, Nepal. The internal dialogue is framed as an exposition delivered by the elder Jayaśrī to his disciple Jinaśrī (Jineśvara) at the Bodhimaṇḍavihāra.

The Svayambhūpurāṇa is the foundational mythic chronicle and pilgrimage guide (sthala-māhātmya) of Newar Buddhism in the Kathmandu Valley. It recounts the myth of the primordial lake (Nāgadaha) drained through the Chobhar gorge by the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, followed by the appearance of the primordial lotus and the self-existent flame (svayambhūjyotis) of the Dharmadhātu enshrined within the Svayambhū Mahācaitya (Swayambhunath). The work incorporates visits of the previous Buddhas of antiquity, legends of local tīrthas, deities, and nāgas, and the transformation of the valley into a Buddhist kingdom. ## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Composite digital collection based on four publications: (1) Jens-Uwe Hartmann, 'Neue Aśvaghoṣa- und Mātṛceṭa-Fragmente aus Ostturkistan', Nachrichten der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, Philologisch-Historische Klasse, 1988, Nr. 2, pp. 55–92 (Anaparāddhastotra, pp. 74ff., and an unidentified stotra fragment); (2) Jens-Uwe Hartmann, 'Der Praṇāmastava. Ein Buddhastotra aus den Gilgit-Funden', in: Petra Kieffer-Pülz and Jens-Uwe Hartmann (eds.), Bauddhavidyāsudhākaraḥ: Studies in Honour of Heinz Bechert on the Occasion of His 65th Birthday, Swisttal-Odendorf: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1997 (Indica et Tibetica, 30), pp. 285–296; (3) Sylvain Lévi, 'Autour d'Aśvaghoṣa', Journal Asiatique 215 (1929), pp. 255–285, specifically pp. 264–266 (Sattvārādhanastava); (4) Dieter Schlingloff, Buddhistische Stotras aus ostturkistanischen Sanskrittexten, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1955 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden, 1), pp. 82–116, 118 (Munayastava, Rāhulastava, Saṅghastotrastava, Brāhmaṇakṛtastava, Vasantatilakāstava, and didactic verses).

**E-text:** Jens-Uwe Hartmann (August 2002 for GRETIL)

**Evidence:**
- Explicitly stated in GRETIL file header (busto1_u.htm) and TEI header (sa_buddhist-stotras.xml).
- Inline section markers give exact bibliographical references to Hartmann 1988, Hartmann 1997, Lévi 1929, and Schlingloff 1955.

**Other editions:**
- Ernst Waldschmidt et al. (eds.), Sanskrithandschriften aus den Turfanfunden (SHT), Wiesbaden/Stuttgart: Franz Steiner Verlag, 1965– (vols. 1–12). — Catalogues and provides diplomatic readings of the Turfan manuscript fragments of these stotras.

**Translations:**
- Dieter Schlingloff, Buddhistische Stotras aus ostturkistanischen Sanskrittexten, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1955. (German)
- Jens-Uwe Hartmann, 'Neue Aśvaghoṣa- und Mātṛceṭa-Fragmente aus Ostturkistan', Nachrichten der Akademie der Wissenschaften in Göttingen, Philologisch-Historische Klasse, 1988, Nr. 2, pp. 55–92. (German)
- Jens-Uwe Hartmann, 'Der Praṇāmastava. Ein Buddhastotra aus den Gilgit-Funden', in: Bauddhavidyāsudhākaraḥ, Swisttal-Odendorf, 1997, pp. 285–296. (German)
- Sylvain Lévi, 'Autour d'Aśvaghoṣa', Journal Asiatique 215 (1929), pp. 264–266. (French)

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — A selection ('Selected:' in the GRETIL header) of fragmentary hymns from Central Asian (Turfan, Charkhlik) and Gilgit manuscripts, with lacunae marked 'x'. The Anaparāddhastotra begins at v. 10 and is incomplete (it incorporates the fragment Hoernle 149/250 = BL Or. 15009/149, not used in the 1988 edition); the Praṇāmastava is incomplete; many Schlingloff items are fragments. Only short excerpts of Schlingloff 1955 are included.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Anaparāddhastotra (Mātṛceṭa, hymn, incomplete (vv. 10–; Hartmann 1988: 74 ff.))
- Unidentified stotra (Charkhlik manuscript) (hymn fragment (Hartmann 1988: 90))
- Praṇāmastava (hymn, incomplete (Gilgit; Hartmann 1997))
- Sattvārādhanastava (hymn styled a Mahāyāna sūtrānta (Lévi 1929))
- "Beinamen Buddhas" (epithets of the Buddha) (verse fragment (Schlingloff 1955: 82 f.))
- Munayastava (hymn (Schlingloff 1955: 85–88))
- Rāhulastava (hymn (Schlingloff 1955: 89–92))
- Saṅghastotrastava (hymn (Schlingloff 1955: 92–94))
- "Udgatastotra" (with a reworking of vv. 32–39 from another manuscript) (hymn (Schlingloff 1955: 94–100))
- "Preis der Bekehrungen Buddhas" and further hymns in Vasantatilakā and Āryagīti (hymns (Schlingloff 1955: 100–113))
- Brāhmaṇakṛtastava and the following stotra fragment (hymn (Schlingloff 1955: 114–115))
- Unidentified stotras and a single verse (fragments (Schlingloff 1955: 115))
- Vasantatilakāstava (hymn fragment (Schlingloff 1955: 116))
- "Lehrgedichte aus Sammelhandschriften der Gruppe Buddhastotras" (didactic verses (Schlingloff 1955: 118))

**Also known as:** Buddhist stotras, Buddhistische Stotras aus ostturkistanischen Sanskrittexten (selection), Buddhastotrāṇi

**Attribution:** Mātṛceṭa is identified in the colophon to the opening work ('anaparāddhastotraṃ samāptaṃ kṛtir ācāryasthaviramātṛceṭasya'). The Sattvārādhanastava is styled in its Sanskrit colophon as a Mahāyāna sūtra ('samyaksambuddhabhāṣitaṃ sattvārādhanaṃ nāma mahāyānasūtrāntaṃ samāptam'), though the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 1126) traditionally attributes it to Nāgārjuna. The remaining texts are anonymous hymns and didactic stanzas preserved in Central Asian and Gilgit manuscripts.

A GRETIL selection of Buddhist Sanskrit hymns recovered from Central Asian and Gilgit manuscripts, entered by Jens-Uwe Hartmann from the editions of Hartmann (1988, 1997), Lévi (1929) and Schlingloff (1955). It contains the surviving stanzas of Mātṛceṭa's Anaparāddhastotra, an unidentified hymn, the Gilgit Praṇāmastava, the Sattvārādhanastava, and a series of mostly fragmentary hymns from the Turfan manuscripts (Munayastava, Rāhulastava, Saṅghastotrastava, Udgatastotra, Brāhmaṇakṛtastava, Vasantatilakāstava and others), ending with didactic verses.

# Dvādaśakāranayastotra

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T01_n2888u`

**Author:** Nāgārjuna

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T01 (Stotra)

**Source:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC)

**Link:** [https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/760](https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/760)

**Edition:** Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1994.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Geshe Lobsang Dorjee Rabling (ed. & restorer), 'Dvādaśākāranayastotram (Toh. 1135) by Ācārya Nāgārjuna', in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, Vol. 57, Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 2017.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), input and proofread by Miroj Shakya, Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West; released in the DSBC June 2018 update (book 760).

**Evidence:**
- The official DSBC announcement for the June 2018 update explicitly lists 'Dvādaśakāranayastotram edited by Losang Dorjee Rabling' among its new acquisitions.
- The CIHTS Restoration Department catalogue records the modern Sanskrit restoration and edition: 'Dvādaśākāranayastotram (Toh. 1135) by Ācārya Nāgārjuna, restored, critically edited Dr. Geshe Lobsang Dorjee Rabling, Dhīḥ Journal, Vol. 57, 2017'.
- The raw metadata's assignment to Janardan Shastri Pandey's Bauddhastotrasaṃgraha (1994) is demonstrably mistaken, as Pandey's compilation does not contain this stotra.

**Other editions:**
- Derge Tengyur, Toh 1135, rgyud 'grel, vol. ka, ff. 71b–72a (Tibetan translation: Mdzad pa bcu gnyis kyi tshul la bstod pa, translated by Tilakakalaśa and Blo ldan shes rab). — No ancient Sanskrit manuscript of the stotra has survived; all witnesses are Tibetan canonical texts.

**Translations:**
- Geshe Lobsang Dorjee Rabling, Hindi translation published with the Sanskrit restoration in Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, Vol. 57, CIHTS, Sarnath, 2017. (Hindi)
- Tyler Dewar, 'In Praise of the Twelve Deeds of the Buddha', Bodhi 8, no. 1 (2004): 33–34. (English)
- Nālandā Translation Committee, 'Praise to the Buddha', Boulder: Nālandā Translation Committee, 1983. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text comprising 1 initial unnumbered namaskāra stanza followed by 14 verses (verses 1–12 extolling the twelve deeds, verse 13 praising the distribution of bodily relics, and verse 14 dedicating merit).

**Also known as:** Dvādaśakāranayastotram, Dvādaśākāranayastotra, Dvādaśakāranāmanayastotra, Mdzad pa bcu gnyis kyi tshul la bstod pa, In Praise of the Twelve Deeds

**Attribution:** Traditionally ascribed to Ācārya Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan Tanjur colophons (Toh 1135 / P 2026: slob dpon chen po 'phags pa klu sgrub kyis mdzad pa). In modern Buddhological scholarship, this attribution is widely treated as apocryphal, as the hymn reflects a later standardized schematic enumeration of the Buddha's twelve deeds and was not included in early Indic lists of Nāgārjuna's genuine hymnic corpus (such as Atiśa's six praises).

The Dvādaśakāranayastotra is a Buddhist hymn of 14 verses praising the twelve exemplary acts (dvādaśa-kāra / mdzad pa bcu gnyis) in the career of Śākyamuni Buddha, followed by verses praising the distribution of relics into eight portions and dedication of merit. The stotra is canonical in Tibetan liturgy and traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna, but the original Sanskrit was lost. The e-text represents a modern Sanskrit restoration (punar-uddhāra) from the Tibetan canonical text (Toh 1135) prepared by Geshe Lobsang Dorjee Rabling at CIHTS, Sarnath.

**Posterior median:** 580 CE
