- Parenthetical markers (1) through (19) embedded throughout the transcription correspond to manuscript folio divisions noted in Liu's edition.

**Other editions:**
- Zhen Liu (ed.), The Dharmadhātustava: A Critical Edition of the Sanskrit Text with the Tibetan and Chinese Translations, a Diplomatic Transliteration of the Manuscript and Notes, STTAR 17, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2015, pp. 1–6. — Diplomatic transliteration of the unique palm-leaf manuscript from the Tibet Autonomous Region.

**Translations:**
- Karl Brunnhölzl, In Praise of Dharmadhātu: Nāgārjuna and the Third Karmapa, Rangjung Dorje, Nitartha Institute Series, Ithaca, NY: Snow Lion Publications, 2007. (English)
- David Seyfort Ruegg, 'Le Dharmadhātustava de Nāgārjuna', in Études tibétaines dédiées à la mémoire de Marcelle Lalou, Paris: Adrien Maisonneuve, 1971, pp. 448–471. (French)
- Osamu Hayashima, '『諸法界頌』考' [On the Dharmadhātustava], Nagasaki Daigaku Kyōikugakubu Shakaikagaku Ronsō 36, 1987, pp. 41–90. (Japanese)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Preserves the unnumbered opening verse followed by numbered stanzas (1)–(85) and the opening pādas of stanza 86, breaking off at 'jātya ......... (19)' across 19 manuscript folios. The full work preserved in Tibetan (Toh 1118) and Chinese translations contains 101 stanzas.

**Also known as:** Dharmadhātustotra, Chos kyi dbyings su bstod pa, Chos dbyings bstod pa, Zan fasheng song, 讚法界頌

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna (c. 2nd–3rd c. CE) as part of his Collection of Hymns (bstod tshogs / Stavakāya). Modern scholars (including Ruegg, Lindtner, and Liu) generally regard the work as dating from a later period (c. 5th–7th c. CE) due to its overt tathāgatagarbha and luminous mind doctrines.

The Dharmadhātustava ('In Praise of the Dharmadhātu') is a Mahāyāna devotional-philosophical hymn celebrating the dharmadhātu—the expanse of ultimate reality—as the inherently pure, radiant nature present in all sentient beings. Using classic similes such as butter concealed in milk, a lamp within a jar, and gold in ore, the poem illustrates how adventitious defilements veil this intrinsic purity, which is unveiled through spiritual cultivation and the realization of emptiness. The text serves as an influential bridge between Madhyamaka and buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha) traditions, particularly within Tibetan exegesis.

It forms the climactic conclusion of the Gaṇḍavyūhasūtra (the final chapter of the Buddhāvataṃsakasūtra) and circulated widely throughout Mahāyāna Asia as an independent liturgical text and devotional hymn. The Ākāśagarbhanāmāṣṭottaraśatastotra is a 16-verse Sanskrit Buddhist liturgical hymn composed in anuṣṭubh metre that enumerates the 108 epithets of the bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha ('Womb of Space'). It originates in chapter 19 (Sarvārthasiddhi-mahāmaṇḍala-vidhi-vistara) of the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha (STTS), where the Tathāgatas entreat (adhyeṣaṇā) Ākāśagarbha with this litany. The Avalokiteśvarastotra (also known as Lokanāthastotra) is a 25-stanza devotional hymn attributed to the Buddhist mahāsiddha Carpaṭipāda (Carpaṭi). Composed in the rhyming Mātrāsamaka metre, it represents one of the earliest prominent examples of systematic end-rhyme in Sanskrit Buddhist poetry. The poem concludes with praises of the bodhisattva's compassionate choice to remain in saṃsāra, his wonder-working powers, physical beauty, and manifestation through the three Buddha-bodies (kāyas).

A Buddhist devotional hymn (stotra) of 34 stanzas composed in elaborate classical kāvya style, primarily in the twenty-one-syllable sragdharā metre. It celebrates the sounding of the monastic wooden gong (gaṇḍī), framing its percussive rhythm as an acoustic manifestation of the Dharma that awakens living beings, summons the saṅgha, and dispels the hosts of Māra. Stanza 5 is noted for its acoustic mimicry of the gong strikes using onomatopoeic syllables ('ṛmpaṃ ṛmpaṃ... ṭama ṭama ṭaṭamaṃ...'). While canonical East Asian and Tibetan witnesses credit the work to Aśvaghoṣa, the surviving Nepalese Sanskrit recension attributes it to Āryadeva.

The Bhaktiśataka ('Century of Devotion', also known as Bauddhaśataka) is a 15th-century Sanskrit stotra composed in 107 verses across diverse classical metres by the Bengali Brahmin poet Rāmacandra Kavibhāratī, who immigrated to Sri Lanka and converted to Buddhism under King Parākramabāhu VI of Kotte (r. 1412–1467 CE). In verses 1–17, Yaśodharā speaks to her son Rāhula, recounting the Buddha's miraculous birth, royal marks, renunciation, austerities by the Nairañjanā river, and enlightenment under the Bodhi tree, instructing the child to revere his father. The final verse narrates Rāhula's joyful obedience upon seeing the Buddha. Functionally and thematically, it parallels the Theravāda Pali Narasīhagāthā.

Each verse recalls a distinct narrative episode or previous life (jātaka/avadāna) of the Buddha—including Maitrakanyaka, Supriya, Sudhana, Kuśa, and Saudāsa, and concluding with his journey from Kapilavastu to venerate the Svayambhū caitya in the Kathmandu Valley—invoking his protective power with the refrain 'sa no rakṣatu'. The Acintyastava ('Hymn to the Inconceivable [Buddha]') is a philosophical stotra of 59 anuṣṭubh verses attributed to Nāgārjuna, belonging to the Catuḥstava collection. Styled as praise of the Buddha, it articulates quintessential Madhyamaka philosophy by equating dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) with the non-substantiality (naiḥsvābhāvya) of all factors of existence. It examines the relativity of existence and non-existence, the four extremes of the tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi), the illusion-like character of conventional experience, the distinction between provisional (neyārtha) and definitive (nītārtha) teachings, and ultimate reality as transcending all discursive proliferation.

- Tibetan: Spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma, Degé Tengyur Tōh. 3960 (dbu ma) and Tōh. 4466 (Jo bo'i chos chung). — Canonical Tibetan translation by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna and Tshul khrims rgyal ba.

**Translations:**
- Richard Sherburne, The Complete Works of Atīśa Śrī Dīpaṃkara Jñāna, New Delhi: Aditya Prakashan, 2000 (Tibetan text and English translation). (English)
- James B. Apple, Atiśa Dīpaṃkara: Illuminator of the Awakened Mind, Boulder: Shambhala, 2019 ('Lamp for the Summary of Conduct'). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of 22 stanzas plus concluding half-verse (v. 23a) and colophon, corresponding to the entire work preserved in Tibetan.

**Also known as:** Caryāsaṃgrahapradīpa, Spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma

**Attribution:** By Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054), written in Nepal for an elder monk (sthavira) on the way to Tibet (v. 22 'nepālaviṣaye kṛtavān'; Apple 2019). The work is transmitted in the Tibetan Tengyur (Spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma, Tōh. 3960 and 4466). No Sanskrit manuscript is reported in the literature consulted, and this Sanskrit text is most likely a modern restoration from the Tibetan.

The Caryāsaṅgrahapradīpa ('Lamp Compendium of Conduct') is a concise manual of daily Mahāyāna practice composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE) during his journey through Nepal. Written for an elder monk who sought instruction focused on the Pāramitā path, the treatise lays out the daily routine of a bodhisattva: moral restraint, sensory control, division of the night for meditation and sleep, the sevenfold worship (saptāṅgapūjā), making stupas and images, and sharing food offerings with deities and beings. While acknowledging that Secret Mantra also attains awakening, it deliberately restricts its exposition to the exoteric Pāramitānaya.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of 134 anuṣṭubh verses (vv. 1–134) with closing colophon. Verses 1–5 and 7, which were missing in the unique palm-leaf manuscript, are printed in square brackets as reconstructed by P. B. Patel from the Tibetan translation (Sems kyi sgrib pa rnam par sbyong ba / Sems rnam par sbyong ba).

**Also known as:** Cittaviśuddhi, Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇanāma

**Attribution:** Attributed to Āryadeva, identified in modern scholarship as the tantric master Āryadeva (often designated Āryadeva II, fl. c. 8th–9th century CE), belonging to the Ārya school of Guhyasamāja exegesis and author of the Caryāmelāpakapradīpa, rather than the 3rd-century Madhyamaka philosopher Āryadeva (author of the Catuḥśataka) with whom Tibetan tradition conflates him.

The Cittaviśuddhiprakaraṇa ('Treatise on the Purification of the Mind') is a Vajrayāna verse treatise in 134 kārikās expounding the principle that spiritual liberation depends entirely on internal mental purity rather than external ritual ablutions or rigid asceticism. It argues that emotional afflictions and transgressive practices, when transformed through discernment of emptiness and skilful means (upāya), serve as the very antidote to bondage, just as poison can cure poison or water remove water from the ear. Doctrinally aligned with the Guhyasamāja exegesis of the tantric Āryadeva (Āryadeva II), the text supports its tantric hermeneutic by citing classical Vinaya rules and Mahāyāna precedents to demonstrate that moral value resides strictly in intentionality (āśaya).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete 50 verses and colophon. Verses 1–33 are drawn from the palm-leaf manuscript tradition (first edited by Lévi 1929), while verses 34–50 are modern Sanskrit retro-translations from the Tibetan version prepared by editor Janardan Pandey (1997).

**Also known as:** Gurusevādharmapañcāśadgāthā, Gurusevādharmapañcāśikā, Gurvārādhana, Bla ma lnga bcu pa, 事師法五十頌

**Attribution:** Ascribed in colophons and Indian/Tibetan/Chinese traditions to Aśvaghoṣa, or in some Tibetan lineages identified with Bhavya (Bha-bi-lha / Vāpilladatta). Modern scholarship considers the attribution to the classical poet Aśvaghoṣa pseudepigraphic; based on internal references to Anuttarayoga tantra rituals and early commentaries, the work dates to the late 1st millennium CE (ca. 9th–10th century CE).

The Gurupañcāśikā ('Fifty Verses on the Guru') is a classic Vajrayāna manual prescribing the obligations, ritual protocols, and devotional posture of a disciple toward the spiritual master (vajrācārya). Drawing on doctrines found in major Anuttarayoga tantras such as the Guhyasamāja, it details the criteria for examining a guru and disciple, behavioral etiquette, samaya vows, and the karmic consequences of guru disparagement. Although traditionally attributed to the 1st–2nd-century CE poet Aśvaghoṣa, the work is a medieval tantric compilation (ca. 9th–10th century CE) that became an indispensable prerequisite curriculum text in Tibetan Buddhism.

The prose exposition and the question-and-answer framework, which make up most of the work (cf. Wedemeyer 2007), are absent; e.g. chapter 1 consists of only three citations.

**Also known as:** Caryāmelāvaṇapradīpa, Caryāmelāpakapradīpam, Sūtaka, Sūtakamelāpaka, Spyod pa bsdus pa'i sgron ma

**Attribution:** Traditionally identified with the 3rd-century Madhyamaka philosopher Āryadeva, the text is actually the work of a distinct 9th-century tantric master of the same name ('tantric Āryadeva' or 'deutero-Āryadeva'), a central figure of the Guhyasamāja Ārya (Noble) tradition. In medieval Indian commentaries (e.g., Munidatta, Nāropā, Parahitarakṣita), the treatise is often cited by the abbreviated titles Sūtaka or Sūtakamelāpaka.

The Caryāmelāpakapradīpa ('Lamp that Integrates the Practices') by the tantric Āryadeva (c. 9th century) is a treatise of the Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja that sets out, in eleven chapters cast as answers to doubts (saṃśaya-pariccheda), the gradual path of the perfection stage: body, speech and mind isolation, illusory body, clear light and integration (yuganaddha). This e-text contains only the verses of the work, most of them citations from the Guhyasamāja and its explanatory tantras (Vajramālā, Saṃdhivyākaraṇa, etc.), together with the chapter colophons; the prose argument is not included.

**Attribution:** Anonymous Buddhist tantric manual belonging to the Mahāpratisarā / Pañcarakṣā ritual tradition. The scripture provides mantric formulas, invocations of world regents and Buddhist deities, and promises comprehensive physical and spiritual protection.

The Prajñopāyaviniścayasiddhi ('Attainment of the Certainty of Wisdom and Skilful Means') by the 8th-century tantric master Anaṅgavajra is one of the foundational texts in the Tibetan canonical cycle of the Seven Siddhi Texts (Saptasiddhi / Grub pa sde bdun). The Śrīsahajasiddhi ('Accomplishment of the Innate') by the Mahāsiddha Ḍombīheruka (c. 8th century CE) is an early Vajrayāna treatise on completion-stage (utpannakrama) yoga in the Hevajra Tantra cycle. The Tattvaratnāvalī ('Jeweled Garland of Reality') is an 11th-century doxographical treatise composed by the scholar-siddha Advayavajra (Maitrīpa). It classifies the Buddhist path into three vehicles (Śrāvakayāna, Pratyekabuddhayāna, and Mahāyāna) and four philosophical tenets (Vaibhāṣika, Sautrāntika, Yogācāra, and Madhyamaka), dividing the Mahāyāna into Pāramitānaya and Mantranaya. The Kālacakrāvatāra is a short technical manual (karaṇa) of Kālacakra calendrical astronomy by Abhayākaragupta. It gives procedures for computing the year, month and day constants, weekdays, lunar mansions, solar and lunar positions, eclipses and the variation of daylight in different regions, drawing on the Laghukālacakratantra and the Vimalaprabhā. Its epoch figure of 463 years is central to Newman's reconstruction of the Kālacakra epoch, and it survives in a unique palm-leaf manuscript copied in 1125 CE.

The Laghutantraṭīkā (also known as Lakṣābhidhānāduddhṛtalaghutantrapiṇḍārthavivaraṇa) is an important commentary by Vajrapāṇi on the introductory portion (verses 1–10 1/2) of the Cakrasaṃvaratantra (Laghusaṃvara). The work interprets the Heruka/Cakrasaṃvara system through an emergent Kālacakra framework, emphasizing internal subtle-body physiology, the retention of bodhicitta, and the integration of Yoginītantra practice within monastic discipline.

An anonymous Newar Buddhist compilation of pharmacological and magical recipes (siddhauṣadhi) said to be drawn from Buddhist tantras, beginning with material parallel to the Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇatantra. It covers bodily purification, remedies, aphrodisiac and fertility preparations (vājīkaraṇa), rejuvenation (rasāyana) and medicated oils and unguents, often with Caṇḍamahāroṣaṇa mantras. The date of compilation is unknown; DSBC lists it among modern (adhunātana) works.

The Laghusiddhāntakaumudī is a 17th-century pedagogical abridgement of Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammar composed by Varadarāja, a disciple of Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita. Reordering Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī topically after the pattern of Bhaṭṭoji's Siddhāntakaumudī, it selects approximately 1,272 essential sūtras along with concise vṛtti glosses and illustrative derivations across all core grammatical categories. Designed as an accessible entry point (bālapraveśa) into the Pāṇinian system, it has served as the paramount introductory Sanskrit grammar textbook across India for centuries.

**Attribution:** Traditionally ascribed to Nāgārjuna and preserved in the Tantra section of the Tibetan Tengyur (associated with the Guhyasamāja cycle / Ārya lineage). While Christian Lindtner maintained authorship by the foundational Madhyamaka philosopher Nāgārjuna, most modern scholars (including D. Seyfort Ruegg, Carmen Dragonetti, and Christian Wedemeyer) consider it the work of a later tantric master of the same name (c. 8th century CE) due to its synthesis of Yogācāra critique, Tantric terminology, and bodhicitta cultivation.

The Bodhicittavivaraṇa ('Exposition of the Awakening Mind') is a Buddhist verse treatise of approximately 112 kārikās expounding bodhicitta under two aspects: conventional bodhicitta (the compassionate resolve to attain awakening for the welfare of all beings) and ultimate bodhicitta (the direct insight into emptiness, śūnyatā). It presents an ascending doctrinal progression, refuting non-Buddhist doctrines and the Śrāvaka conception of skandhas, followed by a critique of Vijñānavāda mind-only idealism, culminating in the non-dual Madhyamaka realization. Although the complete Sanskrit text is lost and survives fully only in Tibetan translations (Tōh. 1800 / P. 2665), these 11 extant Sanskrit testimonia fragments preserve celebrated stanzas widely cited across classical Indian philosophical literature.

Both Indic commentaries (Candrakīrti, Nāropā) and the Tibetan canonical tradition (Bu ston, Tsongkhapa) uphold this composite authorship.

The Pañcakrama ('Five Stages') is the foundational manual of the completion stage (niṣpannakrama) according to the Ārya tradition of the Guhyasamāja Tantra. It outlines five sequential yogic stages of subtle-body meditation leading to awakening: speech isolation (vajrajāpa), mind purification (sarvaśuddhiviśuddhi / cittaviśuddhi), self-consecration / illusory body (svādhiṣṭhāna / māyādeha), clear light (abhisaṃbodhi / prabhāsvara), and nondual union (yuganaddha). Composed c. 8th–9th century CE, chapters 1 and 3–5 are attributed to the tantric Nāgārjuna, while chapter 2 is attributed to Śākyamitra.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 226 verses (numbered Pik_1 to Pik_226) with interspersed prose mantras and visualization instructions, concluding with the final dedication and author colophon (piṇḍīkramasādhanaṃ samāptam / kṛtirācāryaśrīnāgārjunapādānām).

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the tantric master Nāgārjuna of the Ārya tradition of Guhyasamāja exegesis (c. 8th–9th century CE), distinct from the earlier Madhyamaka philosopher of the same name.

The Piṇḍīkrama (also known as Piṇḍīkramasādhana or Piṇḍīkṛtasādhana) is the principal generation-stage (utpattikrama) liturgical manual of the Ārya exegesis of the Guhyasamāja Tantra, traditionally attributed to the tantric master Nāgārjuna (c. 8th–9th century CE). Consisting of 226 verses and interspersed ritual mantras, it details the purification of conceptual thought (vikalpa), the erection of the protective circle, the generation of the 32-deity Akṣobhyaguhyasamāja maṇḍala, and subsequent internal and external offerings. Although often transmitted alongside the completion-stage treatise Pañcakrama, it is an independent foundational manual for the Ārya school's practice.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete mūla text in 151 segments, comprising the initial mangala/praṇidhāna, the ritual and visualization instructions (mantroddhāra, maṇḍala, external/internal worship), closing verses, and the final colophon ('samāptoyaṃ tatvajñānasaṃsiddhirnāma svādhiṣṭhānaśceti'). It contains only the root text, not the Marmakalikāpañjikā commentary.

**Also known as:** Tatvajñānasaṃsiddhi, Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhināmasvādhiṣṭhāna, Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhināmasvādhiṣṭhānakrama, Vajravārāhīsādhana, dPal de kho na nyid ye shes grub pa

**Attribution:** Ascribed to the tantric master Śūnyasamādhipāda (also known as Śūnyasamādhivajra or Samādhivajra; Tib. sTong nyid ting nge 'dzin rdo rje). The spurious attribution to Ḍombīheruka and Dhyānacandra in the prior catalog metadata resulted from confusing the mūla text with separate commentary editions (specifically Dhyānacandra's Mahāsukhaprakāśikāṭīkā) and other Siddha siddhi-treatises.

The Tattvajñānasaṃsiddhi ('Attainment of the Gnosis of Reality') is an Anuttarayoga tantric sādhana and manual focusing on the goddess Vajravārāhī (a prominent form of Vajrayoginī), associated with the Cakrasaṃvara textual cycle. Composed circa the 10th to 11th century by Śūnyasamādhipāda (Śūnyasamādhivajra), the work outlines external and internal ritual sequences, mantroddhāra, maṇḍala layout, and svādhiṣṭhāna practices for realizing non-dual ultimate gnosis (mahāsukha / śūnyatā).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the sūtra as edited in Dhīḥ 44 (2007), pp. 129–147, extending from the initial nidāna in Kauśāmbī through the dialogue with Sucandra and Ānanda to the final colophon and the ye dharmā stanza.

**Also known as:** Vasudhārādhāraṇī, Āryavasudhārādhāraṇīsūtra, Āryavasudhārānāmadhāraṇī, Sucandragṛhapatiparipṛcchā

**Attribution:** Canonical Mahāyāna Buddhist dhāraṇī sūtra delivered by Gautama Buddha; preserved in Nepalese and Gilgit Sanskrit manuscripts, Tibetan Kangyur (Toh 662), and Chinese translations (T. 1162–1165).

The Vasudhārādhāraṇīsūtra is a canonical Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture set at Kauśāmbī, where the impoverished householder Sucandra asks Gautama Buddha how impoverished and ailing sentient beings may attain wealth, health, and relief from suffering. In response, the Buddha reveals the dhāraṇī, ritual procedures (kalpa), and recitation rules associated with the goddess of abundance, Vasudhārā, which he originally received in a previous aeon from the Buddha Vajradharasāgaranirghoṣa. Emphasizing that material prosperity must be accompanied by ethical discipline and charitable giving (dāna), the scripture attained widespread popularity across South and Central Asia and continues to play a prominent role in Newar Buddhist ritual culture.

The Vasudhārādhāraṇī is a Mahāyāna dhāraṇī scripture framed by a narrative setting in Kauśāmbī. The impoverished householder Sucandra approaches the Buddha to ask how one may obtain abundant wealth, grain, and prosperity in order to provide for a large family and sustain extensive charitable offerings. The Mṛtyuvañcanopadeśa ('Instruction on Cheating Death') by the late 10th- to early 11th-century Indian master Vāgīśvarakīrti is an influential Vajrayāna manual on diagnosing and averting untimely death. Across four chapters, the text details external and internal omens as well as physiological signs of impending death (ariṣṭa, maraṇalakṣaṇa) and outlines ritual, meditative, and yogic remedies (mṛtyuvañcana), centering prominently on White Tārā longevity practices. The text was translated into Tibetan (D 1748 / P 4807) in the mid-11th century by Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna (Atiśa) and Rin chen bzang po.

The only internal chapter colophon kept is that of chapter 8.

**Also known as:** Abhisamayālaṅkāra, Abhisamayālaṅkārakārikā, Abhisamayālaṃkāranāmaprajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstra

**Attribution:** In Indo-Tibetan tradition, the Abhisamayālaṅkāra is counted among the Five Treatises of Maitreya revealed to Asaṅga (c. 4th century CE). Modern Buddhist scholarship has debated whether Maitreyanātha was a historical human teacher of Asaṅga (as argued by Tucci, Frauwallner, and Ui) or whether the root verses were composed by Asaṅga himself and attributed to the celestial bodhisattva Maitreya.

The Abhisamayālaṅkāranāmaprajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstra is a central Mahāyāna verse treatise of 273 kārikās in eight chapters outlining the hidden path-structure implicit in the Prajñāpāramitā sūtras (specifically the Pañcaviṃśatisāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā). It classifies the spiritual path into eight clear realizations (aṣṭāv abhisamayāḥ) and seventy doctrinal topics (saptati padārthāḥ) leading from initial bodhicitta to complete omniscient buddhahood. Attributed to Maitreyanātha and transmitted to Asaṅga, it constitutes the foundational scholastic curriculum text for Prajñāpāramitā exegesis across Tibetan monastic institutions.

The Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha (also known as the Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārthasaṃgraha or Prajñāpāramitāsaṃgrahakārikā) is a 58-verse synopsis of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā composed by the Buddhist philosopher-epistemologist Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE). The Abhisamayālaṅkāra ('Ornament for Clear Realization') is a foundational Mahāyāna verse treatise composed of 273 kārikās arranged across eight chapters (adhikāras). Haribhadra's Sphuṭārthā (titled Abhisamayālaṅkārakārikāśāstravivṛti in the surviving Sanskrit manuscript tradition, composed c. late 8th century CE) is a concise running commentary (vṛtti) on the root kārikās of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra attributed to Maitreya. **Attribution:** A 20th-century Sanskrit manual authored by modern scholar Prof. Ram Shankar Tripathi (CIHTS, Sarnath). It is based upon the traditional Tibetan scholastic curriculum (don bdun cu / yig cha) for analyzing the 8 subjects and 70 topics of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra.

The Abhisamayālaṅkārāntaḥpātināṃ padārthānāṃ saṃkṣepato vivaraṇam is a modern Sanskrit scholastic manual written by Prof. Ram Shankar Tripathi as an appendix to his 1977 edition of Haribhadra's Abhisamayālaṅkāravṛtti Sphuṭārthā. Adopting the structure of traditional Tibetan monastic textbooks (don bdun cu), it delineates the eight general subjects (aṣṭau padārthāḥ) and seventy specific topics (saptatiḥ padārthāḥ) of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Each topic is systematically analyzed by its formal definition (lakṣaṇa), taxonomic divisions (bheda), and spiritual stage boundary (avadhi / sīmā).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary spanning all 32 parivartas of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, from the opening maṅgala verses to the concluding verses, ye dharmā formula, and scribal colophon. Lacunae marked by dots reflect physical damages in the palm-leaf manuscript.

**Also known as:** Āryāṣṭasāhasrikāyāḥ Prajñāpāramitāyāḥ Sāratamākhyā Pañjikā, Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitāsāratamānāmapañjikā, Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitāpañjikāsāratamā, Sāratamā Pañjikā, Sārottamā

**Attribution:** Authored by the Vikramaśīla mahāpaṇḍita Ratnākaraśānti (Śāntipa, ca. late 10th–11th c. CE). The author names himself in introductory verse 2 ('mando 'pi ratnākaraḥ') and the parivarta colophons consistently read '... sāratamānāmni pañjikāyāṃ ratnākaraśāntiviracitāyāṃ ...'.

The Sāratamā is an extensive Sanskrit commentary (pañjikā) by the Vikramaśīla master Ratnākaraśānti on the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā, mapped onto the eight abhisamayas of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra. Ratnākaraśānti interprets the sūtra from an Alīkākāravāda Yogācāra perspective, systematically critiquing Haribhadra's four-kāya interpretation of Abhisamayālaṅkāra chapter 8 and defending a three-kāya buddhology.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary as reconstructed into Sanskrit by Pema Tenzin, from the introductory maṅgalācaraṇa (lines 4–15) through the final closing verses and modern restoration colophon (lines 3081–3085).

**Also known as:** Vajracchedikāṭīkā, Āryavajracchedikāvistṛtaṭīkā, Vajracchedikābṛhaṭṭīkā, 'Phags pa shes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa rdo rje gcod pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa

**Attribution:** The work is an extensive commentary (vistṛtaṭīkā) by Ācārya Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE) on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā. The original Sanskrit text is lost; this Sanskrit version is a modern restoration/reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical translation by Ācārya Pema Tenzin (Pemā Tenjin).

The Prajñāpāramitāvajracchedikāṭīkā is an extensive commentary by the 8th-century Indian master Kamalaśīla on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra ('Diamond Sūtra'). Following classical Indian scholastic structure—setting out the purpose (prayojana), concise overview (piṇḍārtha), word analysis (padārtha), internal connection (anusandhi), and answers to objections—Kamalaśīla expounds the sūtra from a Yogācāra-Mādhyamika perspective. He details the path of the bodhisattva across the three grounds (adhimukticaryābhūmi, śuddhādhyāśayabhūmi, and buddhabhūmi) and refutes substantialist views while demonstrating two-fold selflessness. Because the ancient Sanskrit manuscript is lost, this e-text represents a modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan canonical version by Pema Tenzin.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains the complete verse treatise: 14 ślokas in total, consisting of 4 introductory stanzas, the 9 core stanzas (numbered 5[1] to 13[9]) illustrating the 9 similes of emptiness, and 1 concluding stanza (verse 14), with opening and closing colophons. It contains the kārikās only and does not include the prose autocommentary (ṭīkā).

**Also known as:** Āryāṣṭasāhasrikāyāḥ Prajñāpāramitāyāḥ Piṇḍārthaḥ, Āryāṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha, Bhagavatīprajñāpāramitānavaślokapiṇḍārtha, Prajñāpāramitānavaślokī, Navaśloka

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to Śrī-Kambalāmbarapāda (Kambalapāda / Kambala), the Mahāyāna master and tantric siddha (known in Tibetan as Lwa ba pa). While tradition considers him a single master, modern philologists debate whether the author of the Prajñāpāramitā/Madhyamaka treatises and the Vajrayāna siddha of the same name are identical.

The Navaślokī (also titled Āryāṣṭasāhasrikāyāḥ Prajñāpāramitāyāḥ Piṇḍārthaḥ) is a concise verse digest of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā attributed to Kambalapāda. The text consists of 14 ślokas: four introductory stanzas establishing that all perfections are unified in the Perfection of Wisdom, nine core stanzas that expound non-substantiality and emptiness using nine classical similes (including an optical reflection, a mirage, an echo, a dream, a mechanical puppet, and the moon in water), and a concluding dedication to supreme gnosis. The work represents an important synthesis of Prajñāpāramitā doctrine and Yogācāra-Madhyamaka philosophy and circulated widely in India, Tibet, and Song-dynasty China.

Opens with the five maṅgala stanzas ('yā sarvajñatayā nayatyupaśamaṃ...') followed by the sūtra commentary ('evamityādi'), and concludes with the royal praśasti of King Dharmapāla, concluding title verses ('yo'laṅkāro'bhisamaye tadālokaprakāśikā...'), author colophon ('kṛtiriyamācārya-haribhadrapādānām'), and ye dharmā pratītyasamutpāda verse.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Abhisamayālaṅkārāloka (Haribhadra, commentary)
- Abhisamayālaṅkāra (Maitreya, root text (embedded kārikās))

**Also known as:** Abhisamayālaṅkārālokā Prajñāpāramitāvyākhyā, Aṣṭasāhasrikāprajñāpāramitāvyākhyābhisamayālaṅkārāloka, Abhisamayālaṃkārāloka, Śes rab kyi pha rol tu phyin pa brgyad stong pa'i bshad pa mngon par rtogs pa'i rgyan gyi snang ba

**Attribution:** Haribhadra was an 8th-century Indian Buddhist scholar-monk of the Yogācāra-Svātantrika-Madhyamaka tradition who flourished during the reign of the Pāla king Dharmapāla (c. 775–812 CE), explicitly named in the concluding praśasti verse (lines 15362–15365). The commentary systematically interprets the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitā through the framework of Maitreya's Abhisamayālaṅkāra kārikās.

The Abhisamayālaṅkārāloka (full title: Abhisamayālaṅkārālokā Prajñāpāramitāvyākhyā) is Haribhadra's extensive commentary composed in the late 8th century CE under the patronage of the Pāla emperor Dharmapāla. From a Yogācāra-Svātantrika-Madhyamaka philosophical standpoint, it coordinates the 273 verses of the Abhisamayālaṅkāra with the corresponding prose passages of the Aṣṭasāhasrikā Prajñāpāramitāsūtra, demonstrating how the sūtra systematically articulates the eight realizations (abhisamaya) and seventy topics of the Mahāyāna path. As one of only two surviving Indian Sanskrit commentaries on the Aṣṭasāhasrikā (alongside Ratnākaraśānti's Sāratamā), it remains a primary foundation for Prajñāpāramitā exegesis across Indian and Tibetan Buddhist scholasticism.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Giuseppe Tucci, 'Catuḥstavasamāsārtha of Amṛtākara', in Minor Buddhist Texts, Part I, Serie Orientale Roma 9, Roma: Istituto Italiano per il Medio ed Estremo Oriente (IsMEO), 1956, pp. 235–246 (text on pp. 238–246).

**E-text:** GRETIL (Göttingen Register of Electronic Texts in Indian Languages); data entry by Klaus Wille (Göttingen).

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL header: 'Based on the edition by G. Tucci. Minor Buddhist Texts, part I. Roma 1956 (Serie Orientale Roma, 9), pp. 238-246. Input by Klaus Wille (Göttingen)'.
- Page break references embedded in the e-text correspond directly to Tucci's edition: '(Css 238)' through '(Css 246)'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Surviving fragment of the treatise preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript found by Giuseppe Tucci at Ngor Monastery in Tibet. The commentary on the first hymn (Lokātītastava) and the beginning of the commentary on the second (Niraupamyastava) are lost; the manuscript preserves the remaining portion of the Niraupamyastava commentary and complete commentaries on the Acintyastava and Paramārthastava (Tucci 1956, pp. 238–246; e-text segments 0–157).

**Also known as:** Catuḥstavasamārtha, Catuḥstavasamāsa

**Attribution:** Attributed in the final colophon to Paṇḍita Amṛtākara (catuḥstavasamāsārthaḥ paṇḍitāmṛtākarasyeti). Virtually nothing is known about the author; Giuseppe Tucci conjectured that he may have been an Indian paṇḍita who took shelter in Tibet in the late period of Indian Buddhism (c. 11th–12th century), but his exact dates remain undetermined.

The Catuḥstavasamāsārtha ('Summary of the Meaning of the Four Hymns') by Paṇḍita Amṛtākara is an Indian Madhyamaka commentary clarifying the doctrinal and contemplative import of the Catuḥstava attributed to Nāgārjuna. Preserved uniquely in an incomplete palm-leaf manuscript found at Ngor Monastery in Tibet, the extant text comments upon portions of the Niraupamyastava and the entirety of the Acintyastava and Paramārthastava. It elucidates the hymns' praise of the Buddha through the lens of non-conceptual wisdom, dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), emptiness (śūnyatā), and the advanced stages of the bodhisattva path.

The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Way of Awakening') is an influential Mahāyāna verse manual and classic of Buddhist devotional-philosophical literature composed in ten chapters by Śāntideva. It outlines the spiritual cultivation of the bodhisattva, tracing the generation and stabilization of the awakening mind (bodhicitta), ritual confession, vigilance (apramāda), guard over awareness (saṃprajanya), and the perfections of patience (kṣānti), vigor (vīrya), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and dedication of merit (pariṇāmanā). In 69 concise verses, it outlines the gradual course of spiritual development through the tripartite typology of spiritual capacities (adhama-, madhyama-, and uttamapuruṣa), harmonising sūtric bodhisattva practices with esoteric tantric initiations and monastic discipline. It sets forth the essential path of the Bodhisattva: recognizing suffering caused by dualistic grasping and afflictions, cultivating emptiness and compassion, generating bodhicitta, practicing the six perfections, progressing through the five paths, and removing the two obscurations to attain the three kāyas of awakening. No Indic manuscript survives; the text in this e-text is Ramesh Chandra Negi's 1992 modern Sanskrit retro-translation (punaruddhāra) made from the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 3949 / Toh 4469).

The Śūnyatāsaptati ('Seventy Verses on Emptiness') is one of the foundational works of the Yukti (reasoning) corpus attributed to Nāgārjuna. In 73 verses (predominantly in anuṣṭubh meter), the text argues that all conditioned and unconditioned dharmas—including the twelve links of dependent origination, time, the agent and object of action, and nirvāṇa itself—are empty of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) because they are dependently co-arisen (pratītyasamutpanna). The Vigrahavyāvartanī ('Dispeller of Disputes') is a core philosophical work by Nāgārjuna defending the Madhyamaka doctrine of universal emptiness (śūnyatā) against epistemological objections, particularly those framed by early Nyāya and realist Abhidharma thought. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 27 chapters (prakaraṇas) containing the root kārikās (two opening maṅgala verses followed by 447/448 verses, ending at 27.30), extracted from Vaidya's 1960 edition.

**Attribution:** Universal traditional and modern scholarly attribution to the Indian Buddhist philosopher Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE).

The Madhyamakaśāstra (widely known as Mūlamadhyamakakārikā) is Nāgārjuna's foundational philosophical treatise and the central text of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism. Comprising twenty-seven chapters and approximately 448 stanzas, it systematically deconstructs core metaphysical categories—such as causation, motion, sense faculties, the aggregates, selfhood, and nirvāṇa—through prasaṅga (reductio ad absurdum) argumentation. Nāgārjuna demonstrates that no entity possesses independent intrinsic nature (svabhāva), equating dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) directly with emptiness (śūnyatā) and the Middle Way.

The Cittotpādasaṃvaravidhikrama is an 11th-century liturgical manual composed by Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna setting forth the rite and sequence for arousing bodhicitta and formally receiving the bodhisattva discipline. Śāntideva's Bodhicaryāvatāra (c. 8th century CE) is a foundational Mahāyāna Buddhist poetic treatise detailing the development and practice of the mind of awakening (bodhicitta) through the perfections (pāramitā). Prajñākaramati's Bodhicaryāvatārapañjikā (c. late 10th to early 11th century CE) is the principal surviving Sanskrit commentary, offering running grammatical glosses, extensive canonical citations, and detailed Madhyamaka exegesis across chapters 1 through 9. Its extensive commentary on chapter 9 (Prajñāpariccheda) forms a crucial monument of late Indian Prāsaṅgika-Madhyamaka philosophy, critiquing both non-Mahāyāna Buddhist and non-Buddhist systems.

Chapter 1 (pratyayaparīkṣā, "examination of conditions") of Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā, his commentary on Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā. Here Candrakīrti defends Buddhapālita's prasaṅga method against Bhāviveka's demand for independent inferences (svatantrānumāna), and criticizes Dignāga's epistemology. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the modern Sanskrit reconstruction, ending with the treatise and translation colophons at segments [4932]–[4934].

**Attribution:** The Madhyamakāloka is an 8th-century independent treatise by Kamalaśīla (c. 740–795 CE). The original Sanskrit manuscript tradition is lost except for isolated fragments and citations in later Indian works (e.g. Abhayākaragupta, Prajñākaramati); the continuous Sanskrit text preserved in this e-text is the modern Sanskrit reconstruction (punaranuvāda) from the Tibetan canonical translation prepared by Penpa Dorjee.

The Madhyamakāloka ('Illumination of the Middle Way') is Kamalaśīla's (c. 740–795 CE) comprehensive independent treatise of Madhyamaka philosophy, traditionally counted among the 'Three Works of the Eastern Svātantrikas' (dbu ma shar ba gsum). Synthesizing Nāgārjunian emptiness with Dharmakīrtian epistemological logic (pramāṇa), the work systematically defends the lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena (sarvadharmaniḥsvabhāvatā), expounds the doctrine of the two truths and the single vehicle (ekayāna), and refutes non-Buddhist as well as rival Buddhist positions. **Coverage:** complete — Contains all 6 kārikās and the full prose vṛtti in modern Sanskrit retroversion from the Tibetan and Chinese versions.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Hastavālaprakaraṇa (Dignāga, root text)
- Hastavālaprakaraṇavṛtti (Dignāga, commentary)

**Also known as:** Hastavālanāmaprakaraṇa, Hastavālanāmaprakaraṇavṛtti, Hastavālaprakaraṇakārikā, Hastavālavṛtti, Muṣṭiprakaraṇa, Jie juan lun (解捲論), Zhang zhong lun (掌中論), Rab tu byed pa lag pa'i tshad kyi tshig le'ur byas pa, Rab tu byed pa lag pa'i tshad kyi 'grel pa

**Attribution:** Authorship is divided between the two Asian translation traditions. The Tibetan Tanjur (D 3844/3845, D 3848/3849; P 5244/5245, P 5248/5249) and Dunhuang Tibetan manuscripts ascribe the work to Āryadeva, which was initially accepted by F. W. Thomas and H. Ui (1918). However, the Chinese translations (T 1620, T 1621) explicitly ascribe it to Dignāga (Chenna). Since Frauwallner (1959) and Hattori (1968), modern scholarship widely agrees that the treatise belongs to Dignāga due to its close terminological and doctrinal parallels with his Upādāyaprajñaptiprakaraṇa and Ālambanaparīkṣā.

The Hastavālaprakaraṇa ('Treatise of the Handful' or 'Hand-Grasp') with its autocommentary (vṛtti) consists of six anuṣṭubh verses and prose commentary demonstrating the lack of inherent existence (svabhāva) in both composite macro-objects and partless indivisible atoms (paramāṇu). Employing the classic analogy of the rope mistaken for a snake and mereological part-whole analysis, the treatise shows that external entities are conventional conceptual designations (vyavahāramātra) without ultimate reality. The Indic original having been lost, the text survives in Tibetan and Chinese recensions and is known in Sanskrit through modern reconstructions.

It systematizes the bodhisattva path and Madhyamaka philosophy, pioneering the use of autonomous logical inference (svatantra-anumāna) to demonstrate emptiness. The Madhyamārthasaṃgraha is a concise Madhyamaka treatise in eleven stanzas setting forth the schema of the two truths (satyadvaya). It articulates a distinct hierarchical division of ultimate truth (paramārtha) into expressible/discursive (paryāyaparamārtha) and inexpressible/non-discursive (aparyāyaparamārtha), alongside conventional truth (saṃvṛti) classified into valid conventional reality (tathyasaṃvṛti) and false convention (mithyāsaṃvṛti). It is an influential pedagogical summary of Svātantrika epistemological taxonomy.

- The earlier catalogue edition statement (R. Bhattacharya, 'Verses Relating to Svabhāvavāda: A Collection') is not the source: that is an English-language collection of testimonia, whereas this e-text is a continuous Sanskrit argument.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Short tract (114 segments, c. 4,400 characters) as given by DSBC book 721; ends with the quoted Tattvasaṅgraha svabhāvavāda verses and has no colophon, so completeness relative to any printed source cannot be verified.

**Also known as:** Svabhāvavādaḥ

**Attribution:** Anonymous; no author is named in the e-text or in the DSBC catalogue. The work is a short Sanskrit prose tract (with quoted verses) arguing FOR svabhāvavāda/ahetuvāda against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika causality (prāgabhāva, Īśvara) and against Śaṅkara's līlā explanation of creation (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 2.1.33 is quoted as 'bhagavatpādāḥ'); the author speaks in the first person ('atra mayā ucyate'), cites Praśastapāda and the svabhāvavāda pūrvapakṣa verses that Śāntarakṣita reports in Tattvasaṅgraha ch. 4 (Svabhāvaparīkṣā, vv. 110ff.). Prose style (commas, polemics against Śaṅkara, compiled arguments) suggests a modern scholastic Sanskrit composition rather than a classical treatise, but this cannot be confirmed.

A short anonymous Sanskrit prose tract defending svabhāvavāda (things arise from their own nature without causes) against Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika causal theory (including prāgabhāva and Īśvara as creator) and against Śaṅkara's explanation of creation as līlā (Brahmasūtrabhāṣya 2.1.33). It closes by quoting the svabhāvavāda verses known from the pūrvapakṣa of Śāntarakṣita's Tattvasaṅgraha, ch. 4 (rājīvakesarādīnāṃ vaicitryaṃ kaḥ karoti..., kaṇṭakataikṣṇya). Despite its Madhyamaka classification in DSBC, it is not a Madhyamaka work.

Candrakīrti's Madhyamakāvatāra ('Introduction to the Middle Way'), composed in the 7th century CE, is a foundational Prāsaṅgika Madhyamaka treatise designed to introduce Nāgārjuna's Mūlamadhyamakakārikā along the structure of the Mahāyāna bodhisattva path. Structured around the ten bodhisattva stages (bhūmi), this sixth chapter corresponds to the abhimukhī-bhūmi ('Facing Ground') and the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). Chapter 6 comprises the philosophical core and roughly two-thirds of the entire work, expounding the refutation of intrinsic production (the catuṣkoṭi), an extensive critique of Yogācāra positions (such as the reality of consciousness, reflexive awareness, and the ālayavijñāna), the two truths, and the sixteen forms of emptiness.

Although transmitted independently in Nepalese and Tibetan collections as a stotra, these verses originally formed the concluding stanzas (nigamana) of Candrakīrti's Prasannapadā. The Niraupamyastava ('Hymn to the Incomparable One') is a devotional philosophical poem of 25 stanzas in anuṣṭubh metre composed by Nāgārjuna, forming part of his famous Catuḥstava ('Four Hymns'). The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way'), comprising 448 verses in 27 chapters, is the foundational philosophical treatise of the Madhyamaka school of Mahāyāna Buddhism composed by Nāgārjuna (c. 150–250 CE). **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Sanskrit manuscript edited by Giuseppe Tucci. The Mahāyānaviṃśikā ('Twenty Verses on the Great Vehicle') is a brief Buddhist treatise traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that synthesizes Madhyamaka and Yogācāra doctrines. The Vigrahavyāvartanī ('Averting of Disputes') is a foundational dialectical and epistemological treatise by Nāgārjuna, consisting of 70 verses accompanied by his prose autocommentary (vṛtti). In the first section (verses 1–20), an opponent representing Nyāya and other realist schools challenges the doctrine of emptiness (śūnyatā), arguing that if all entities lack intrinsic nature (svabhāva), Nāgārjuna's own statement must likewise be empty and ineffective. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the modern reconstruction, comprising an unnumbered opening homage, 60 kārikās (labeled Yukti_1 to Yukti_60), and a Sanskrit rendering of the Tibetan translation colophon mentioning Pa tshab Nyi ma grags (Sūryakīrti) and Muditaśrī.

**Also known as:** Yuktiṣaṣṭikā, Yuktiṣaṣṭikākārikā, Rigs pa drug cu pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa, Liushisong ruli lun (六十頌如理論)

**Attribution:** Universally attributed by Indian, Tibetan, and Chinese traditions to Nāgārjuna as part of his reasoning corpus (rigs tshogs / yuktikāya). Because the continuous Sanskrit original was long lost and only partially recoverable through citations in commentators like Candrakīrti, the continuous Sanskrit text in this file represents a 20th-century retroversion/reconstruction from the Tibetan translation prepared by Bimalendra Kumar.

The Yuktiṣaṣṭikārikā ('Sixty Stanzas on Reasoning') is an essential Madhyamaka treatise by Nāgārjuna, belonging to his collection of dialectical treatises (yuktikāya). In sixty verses following an opening homage to the Buddha, the work deconstructs substantialist assertions of existence (bhāva) and non-existence (abhāva), arguing that true understanding of dependent origination dissolves reified distinctions between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa. The continuous Sanskrit original having been lost in India, the e-text represents Bimalendra Kumar's 1993 modern Sanskrit retroversion based on the Tibetan canonical translation.

The Bodhicaryāvatāra ('Entering the Bodhisattva Path') is an 8th-century Sanskrit didactic and philosophical poem by the Madhyamaka master Śāntideva. Arranged in ten chapters, it serves as a practical manual for generating and sustaining the awakening mind (bodhicitta) and cultivating the six bodhisattva perfections (pāramitās). The Bodhicittotpādasūtraśāstra is a Mahāyāna treatise in twelve chapters expounding the generation of the resolve for awakening (bodhicitta), the bodhisattva vow, and the six perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). Preserved primarily in the Chinese Buddhist canon (T. 1659, translated by Kumārajīva) under an attribution to Vasubandhu, the work combines systematic scriptural citations with devotional and ethical exegesis. The Sanskrit text in this e-text is not an ancient manuscript transmission, but a modern Sanskrit retroversion prepared from the Chinese in 1949 by Bhadanta Shanti Bhikshu Shastri.

A 70-verse metrical treatise summarizing the teachings of the Śālistambasūtra ('Rice Seedling Sūtra'). Using the botanical metaphor of a sprouting rice seed, it explains the Mahāyāna doctrine of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) by contrasting external (plant growth) and internal (psychophysical twelvefold) causal sequences, underscoring the absence of an agent (kartṛ), enduring self (ātman), or divine creator (īśvara). **Also known as:** Pratītyasamutpādavibhaṅganirdeśasūtra, Pratītyasamutpādavibhaṅgasūtra, Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅgasūtra, Ādisūtra (Nidānasaṃyukta sūtra 16), rTen ciṅ 'brel bar 'byuṅ ba daṅ po daṅ rnam par dbye ba bstan pa'i mdo (Toh 211), Yuanqi jing / 緣起經 (Taishō 124)

The Pratītyasamutpādādivibhaṅganirdeśasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse delivered by the Buddha at Jetavana in Śrāvastī. It is divided into two parts: the 'fundamental exposition' (ādi), which articulates the standard twelvefold formula of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) from ignorance (avidyā) to aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), and the 'detailed analysis' (vibhaṅga), which provides concise definitions of each link. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the five samuccayas of the bhāṣya as published in Tatia's 1976 edition, concluding with the fifth chapter (Sāṃkathyaviniścaya, segment 4544) and the scribal colophon (segment 4545). Note that one palm-leaf omitted from Tatia's edition was later identified and edited by Robert Kritzer (2002).

**Also known as:** Abhidharmasamuccaya-bhāṣya, Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣyam, Chos mngon pa kun las btus pa'i bshad pa

**Attribution:** Authorship is historically disputed. The unique Sanskrit manuscript does not record an author in its colophon, recording only the patron/scribe (paṇḍita-vaidya-śrī-Amaracandra). The Tibetan Tanjur (D 4053) attributes the Bhāṣya to Jinaputra (rgyal ba'i sras). In Chinese tradition, Kuiji states that an early commentary was composed by Buddhasiṃha, while Sthiramati compiled the composite Abhidharmasamuccayavyākhyā (T 1606). Tatia's editio princeps ascribed the Bhāṣya to Sthiramati following Pralhad Pradhan, but modern scholars (such as Noriaki Hakamaya and Robert Kritzer) distinguish the Bhāṣya from the Vyākhyā and accept Jinaputra as the traditional author.

The Abhidharmasamuccayabhāṣya is an essential 6th-century Yogācāra prose commentary on Asaṅga's Abhidharmasamuccaya. It provides extensive analytical glosses on Asaṅga's concise definitions of mental factors, aggregates (skandha), sense bases (āyatana), elements (dhātu), and the path, harmonizing classical Abhidharma categories with foundational Yogācāra doctrines such as the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna). Preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript discovered by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Tibet and in Tibetan translation, it is traditionally ascribed to Jinaputra.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the root verses across all five chapters: 1. Lakṣaṇapariccheda (vv. 1.1–1.23), 2. Āvaraṇapariccheda (vv. 2.1–2.17), 3. Tattvapariccheda (vv. 3.1–3.22), 4. **Also known as:** Madhyāntavibhāga, Madhyāntavibhāgaśāstrakārikā, Dbus dang mtha' rnam par 'byed pa'i tshig le'ur byas pa, Bian zhong bian lun song (辯中邊論頌)

**Attribution:** In the Tibetan tradition, the root kārikās are attributed to the celestial bodhisattva Maitreya (or the historical teacher Maitreyanātha, c. 4th century CE) as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya' revealed to Asaṅga. In the Chinese canon (T 1601), the verses are generally attributed directly to Asaṅga.

The Madhyāntavibhāgakārikā ('Verses Distinguishing the Middle from the Extremes') is a foundational doctrinal treatise of the Yogācāra school, traditionally counted as one of the 'Five Treatises of Maitreya'. In 111 verses across five chapters—on characteristics (lakṣaṇa), obscurations (āvaraṇa), reality (tattva), spiritual cultivation and results (pratipakṣabhāvanā-avasthā-phala), and the supreme vehicle (yānānuttarya)—it formulates the middle way (madhyamā pratipad) as avoiding both the extreme of reification and that of nihilistic denial. The treatise provides classical expositions of unreal mental construct (abhūtaparikalpa), the three natures (trisvabhāva), and emptiness (śūnyatā) understood as the absence of subject-object duality within that construct.

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to the Vikramaśīla gatekeeper-scholar Vāgīśvarakīrti (fl. early 11th century). The work and its autocommentary are celebrated and quoted by contemporary and later authors such as Ratnavajra, Ratnakīrti, and Raviśrījñāna.

The Tattvaratnāvaloka is a concise 20-verse tantric philosophical treatise by the early eleventh-century Vikramaśīla master Vāgīśvarakīrti. The work surveys and critiques diverse definitions of the spiritual goal (sādhya) and ultimate reality (tattva)—contrasting non-Buddhist views and standard Pāramitāyāna models with multiple Mantrayāna interpretations—and culminates in an exposition of the fourth initiation (caturthābhiṣeka). Vāgīśvarakīrti also composed an extensive prose autocommentary (Tattvaratnāvalokavivaraṇa), which served as an important point of reference in eleventh-century scholastic debates.

The Triṃśikāṭīkā by Vinītadeva (fl. c. late 7th–early 8th century CE) is an Indian Yogācāra sub-commentary that provides a detailed word-by-word gloss on Sthiramati's Triṃśikāvijñaptibhāṣya, which comments upon Vasubandhu's Triṃśikāvijñaptikārikā. While preserved completely in Tibetan canonical translation, the Sanskrit text is attested only in a single fragmentary manuscript covering kārikās 4cd through 30. The text explicates key Yogācāra concepts including the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the afflicted mind (kliṣṭamanas), the active consciousnesses, the three natures (trisvabhāva), and the realization of representation-only (vijñaptimātratā).

The Trisvabhāvanirdeśa ('Exposition of the Three Natures') is a concise verse work of 38 kārikās by Vasubandhu presenting the classical Yogācāra doctrine of the three natures: the imagined (parikalpita), dependent (paratantra), and consummate (pariniṣpanna). **Coverage:** complete — Complete text across all five chapters (paricchedas 1–5), including both root verses and the running prose commentary (vyākhyā).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Ratnagotravibhāga (Maitreya, root text)
- Ratnagotravibhāgavyākhyā (Asaṅga, commentary)

**Also known as:** Ratnagotravibhāgamahāyānottaratantraśāstra, Ratnagotravibhāga Mahāyānottaratantraśāstra, Mahāyānottaratantraśāstra, Mahāyānottaratantraśāstravyākhyā, Uttaratantra, Uttaratantraśāstra, Theg pa chen po rgyud bla ma'i bstan bcos, Theg pa chen po rgyud bla ma'i bstan bcos rnam par bshad pa, Jiujing yisheng baoxing lun, Baoxing lun

**Attribution:** Authorship is historically disputed across Buddhist traditions. The Tibetan tradition attributes the root verses to the Bodhisattva Maitreya and the prose commentary (vyākhyā) to Asaṅga. The Chinese tradition (beginning in Fazang's commentaries and subsequent catalogs) attributes the entire treatise (Jiujing yisheng baoxing lun, T 1611, translated by Ratnamati in 511 CE) to *Sāramati (Jianyi / Suoluomodi). Extant Sanskrit palm-leaf manuscripts discovered in Tibet carry no author colophon. While Johnston initially considered Sthiramati (later retracted), modern critical scholarship (Takasaki, Schmithausen, Kano) distinguishes earlier and later textual strata, placing the final compilation and commentary in the 5th century CE and largely corroborating the link to Sāramati.

The Ratnagotravibhāga (also widely cited as the Mahāyānottaratantraśāstra or Uttaratantra) is the preeminent classical Indian treatise systematically articulating the doctrine of buddha-nature (tathāgatagarbha). Structured around seven 'vajra points' (vajrapada)—Buddha, Dharma, Saṅgha, the element/lineage of awakening (dhātu/gotra), awakening itself (bodhi), enlightened qualities (guṇa), and buddha-activity (karman)—the text demonstrates that the primordial, luminous nature of mind is present within all sentient beings, concealed only by adventitious defilements (āgantukakleśa). It synthesizes and comments extensively upon key tathāgatagarbha sūtras, notably the Tathāgatagarbhasūtra, the Śrīmālādevīsiṃhanādasūtra, and the Anūnatvāpūrṇatvanirdeśa.

The Bāhyārthasiddhikārikā ('Verses Establishing External Objects') is a major philosophical treatise in 188 kārikās by the 8th-century Buddhist realist thinker Śubhagupta. Defending an atomistic external realism against Yogācāra (Vijñānavāda) idealism, Śubhagupta mounts a systematic critique of idealist arguments advanced by Vasubandhu, Diṅnāga, and Dharmakīrti (particularly targeting the sahopalambhaniyama thesis and the denial of external causes for cognitions). While the continuous Sanskrit text is lost in India and survives as a whole only in classical Tibetan translation, this e-text presents N. Aiyaswami Sastri's modern Sanskrit retroversion.

The remaining twelve bhūmis (including the Śrāvakabhūmi and Bodhisattvabhūmi) and the four supplementary Saṃgrahaṇī divisions are not included.

**Also known as:** Yogācārabhūmiśāstra, Saptadaśabhūmiśāstra, Saptadaśabhūmika, Yogacaryābhūmi, Bahubhūmika, Maulī Bhūmi (bhūmis 1–5)

**Attribution:** Indo-Tibetan tradition attributes the text to Asaṅga (c. 4th century CE), while East Asian tradition regards it as revealed by the bodhisattva Maitreya to Asaṅga. Modern scholarship (e.g., Schmithausen, Aramaki, Deleanu, Kragh) analyzes the Yogācārabhūmi as an encyclopedic compilation composed in multiple chronological strata between c. 250 and 400 CE.

The Yogācārabhūmi is the fundamental encyclopedic compendium of the Yogācāra school of Indian Mahāyāna Buddhism. This digital text comprises the first five bhūmis of the seventeen stages in the basic section (Maulībhūmi): the stage connected with the five sensory consciousnesses (Pañcavijñānakāyasamprayuktā bhūmiḥ), the stage of mental consciousness (Manobhūmiḥ), and the three stages defined by the presence or absence of coarse discursive thinking and subtle investigation (Savitarkā savicārā, Avitarkā vicāramātrā, and Avitarkāvicārā bhūmayaḥ). These sections set out early Yogācāra psychology, sensory taxonomy, cognitive objects, caittas (mental concomitants), cosmology, the ālayavijñāna, karmic accumulation, and the degrees of spiritual realization (abhisamaya).

**95% credible interval:** 319 CE – 413 CE

**Posterior median:** 366 CE

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Prastāvanā §§1–5, chapter I §§1–49 and chapter II §§1–34 (to II.34B, the end of chapter II in Lamotte's paragraphing); chapters III–X missing. Bracketed numbers (8), (10) … (101), (102) running through the text appear to be the page numbers of the printed source.

**Attribution:** Traditionally and universally attributed to Asaṅga. The Sanskrit original is lost apart from citations in later works; this e-text is a modern restoration from the Tibetan and Chinese versions, very probably that of N. Aramaki (in Nagao 1982).

The Mahāyānasaṃgraha of Asaṅga is a foundational Yogācāra treatise organising Mahāyāna doctrine under ten headings, beginning with the ālayavijñāna as the 'support of the knowable' (ch. I) and the three natures (trisvabhāva) as its 'characteristic' (ch. II). It survives in Tibetan and several Chinese translations. This e-text is a modern Sanskrit reconstruction of the introduction and the first two chapters only.

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete Laukikamārga ('Mundane Path') section of the fourth Yogasthāna of the Śrāvakabhūmi (pp. 318–355 in Deleanu 2006, Vol. I; corresponding to pp. 439.3–470.6 in Shukla 1973), which is an excerpt of the larger Śrāvakabhūmi.

**Also known as:** Śrāvakabhūmi: Laukikamārga, Yogācārabhūmi (Śrāvakabhūmi: Laukikamārga), Laukikamārga

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Asaṅga in the Tibetan tradition and to Maitreya in the East Asian tradition. Modern historical-philological research (e.g., Schmithausen 1987, Deleanu 2006) demonstrates that the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, and the Śrāvakabhūmi in particular, is a composite text compiled in multiple chronological strata by early Yogācāra practitioners between c. 250 and 400 CE.

The Laukikamārga ('Mundane Path') section forms part of the fourth Yogasthāna of the Śrāvakabhūmi, the thirteenth section of the encyclopedic Yogācārabhūmi corpus. It provides an extensive canonical description of worldly meditation practice, detailing how a meditator cultivates seven progressive mental orientations (manaskāra) to achieve detachment from the sensual realm (kāmavairāgya) and enter the four meditative absorptions (dhyāna) and four formless realms (ārūpyasamāpatti). Unlike the supramundane path (lokottaramārga) that eradicates defilements through direct insight into reality, the mundane path suppresses worldly passions through progressive mental refinement.

- Taishō pagination markers ('C 328c5' through 'C 344b20') match Delhey's text-critical concordance to Xuanzang's Chinese translation in T1579.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Complete text of the Samāhitā Bhūmi (the 6th chapter of the Maulī Bhūmi / Bahubhūmivastu division of the Yogācārabhūmi), running from opening section (0) to the concluding colophon (Ω) at line 1476: 'yogācārabhūmau samāhitā bhūmiḥ samāptā' (MS folios H 63a6–82b6).

**Also known as:** Samāhitābhūmi, Samāhitā Bhūmi, Samāhitā Bhūmiḥ, Yogācārabhūmi: Samāhitā Bhūmi, 三摩呬多地, mnyam par bzhag pa'i sa

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Asaṅga in Tibetan and Indian tradition, and to Maitreyanātha / Maitreya Bodhisattva in the Chinese tradition (translated by Xuanzang). Modern textual scholarship (e.g., Lambert Schmithausen, Martin Delhey, Florin Deleanu) regards the Yogācārabhūmi corpus as an encyclopedic composite compilation assembled in multiple chronological strata during the 3rd to 4th centuries CE.

The Samāhitābhūmi ('Stage of Meditative Equipoise') constitutes the sixth chapter of the Maulī Bhūmi (Bahubhūmivastu) division of the Yogācārabhūmi. It offers an encyclopedic scholastic taxonomy of Buddhist concentration and meditation states, systematically treating the four dhyānas, eight liberations (vimokṣa), various samādhis, and meditative attainments (samāpatti), together with their accompanying mental factors (manaskāra) and meditative signs (nimitta). In modern Yogācāra scholarship, this section is widely recognized for preserving what Lambert Schmithausen identified as the earliest textual locus of the ālayavijñāna ('storehouse consciousness') concept, introduced to explain somatic survival and the continuity of mind during the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti).

This e-text contains Yogasthānas 1 and 2, which systematically treat the spiritual requisites of practice, the classification of disciples, qualified spiritual masters, ālambana (meditative objects), and initial tranquilization and insight. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Contains the complete text of all four yogasthānas as published in Shukla's 1973 edition (pp. 5–511), ending with the colophon '// śrāvakabhūmau caturthaṃ yogasthānam // samāptā śrāvakabhūmiḥ //'.

**Also known as:** Yogācārabhūmi: Śrāvakabhūmi

**Attribution:** Attributed to Asaṅga in the Tibetan tradition and printed by Shukla under his name; East Asian tradition attributes the overarching Yogācārabhūmi to Maitreya Bodhisattva. Modern historical-philological research (e.g. Lambert Schmithausen, Florin Deleanu) identifies the Śrāvakabhūmi as one of the earliest textual strata of the Yogācārabhūmi, likely circulating initially as an independent manual of Śrāvakayāna praxis before being incorporated into the encyclopedic treatise.

The Śrāvakabhūmi ('Stage of the Disciple') is the thirteenth section of the Maulī Bhūmi (basic section) of the Yogācārabhūmi corpus, constituting an extensive and systematic manual of Buddhist meditation and spiritual development. Structured into four yogasthānas (stages of spiritual practice), it treats the prerequisites for monastic life, spiritual disposition (gotra), initial entry into practice (avatāra), and the dual cultivation of calm abiding (śamatha) and insight (vipaśyanā) culminating in liberation. Although preserved as part of the Yogācāra canon, it systematically articulates classical Mainstream (Śrāvakayāna) praxis and doctrine.

**Evidence:**
- The GRETIL header explicitly credits the editions of Siglinde Dietz (1984) and Kazunobu Matsuda (1986), notes additional comparison with Sankarnarayan, Matsuda, and Yoritomi (2002), and names Klaus Wille as inputter.

Ramchandra Pandeya, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1975, pp. 137–208. — Editio princeps of the Ujjain Gilgit folios; contains numerous transcription errors and misplaced folios, subsequently corrected by Dietz (1984).
- Central Asian manuscript fragments from Turfan, catalogued in Sanskrithandschriften aus den Turfanfunden (SHT), ed. Ernst Waldschmidt et al., vol. 5 (1985), no. 1171, and vol. 6 (1989), no. 1458. — Small fragmentary Sanskrit manuscript witnesses of the Dharmaskandha discovered in Central Asia.

**Translations:**
- Xuanzang (玄奘), 阿毘達磨法蘊足論 (Apidamo fayunzu lun), Taishō Tripiṭaka no. 1537, vol. 26, pp. 453a–514b (12 fascicles, translated in 659 CE). (Chinese)
- Siglinde Dietz, Fragmente des Dharmaskandha: Ein Abhidharma-Text in Sanskrit aus Gilgit, Göttingen: Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht, 1984. (German)
- Watanabe Baiyū (渡辺楳雄), 『阿毘達磨法蘊足論』, in Kokuyaku Issaikyō (國譯一切經), Bidon-bu (毘曇部), vol. 3, Tokyo: Daitō Shuppansha, 1934. (Japanese)

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Preserves birch-bark folios from Gilgit: fols. 3–20 and 26 (from the collection at the Scindia Oriental Research Institute, Ujjain, ed. Dietz 1984) and fols. 21, 22, and 27 (National Archives of India / Gilgit Buddhist Manuscripts, ed. Matsuda 1986). These folios contain sections of three chapters of the 21-chapter treatise: the Pratītyasamutpādanirdeśa (ch. 21 in the Chinese version; ch. 14 in Dietz), the Śikṣāpadanirdeśa (ch. 1), and the Apramāṇanirdeśa (ch. 11).

**Also known as:** Abhidharmadharmaskandhapādaśāstra, Abhidharmadharmaskandha, Dharmaskandhapāda, Dharmaskandhaśāstra, Fayunzu lun, Apidamo fayunzu lun

**Attribution:** Conflicting traditional attributions exist in ancient sources: Sanskrit and Tibetan texts (such as Yaśomitra's Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā ad AKBh 1.11, Bu ston, and Tāranātha) attribute the treatise to Śāriputra, whereas the Chinese tradition (Xuanzang's translation colophon and Pu Guang's Jushe lun ji) attributes it to Mahāmaudgalyāyana. In modern historical-critical scholarship, it is understood to be an early, anonymously composed canonical treatise of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma Piṭaka (c. 2nd–1st century BCE).

The Dharmaskandha ('Aggregation of Dharmas') is one of the seven canonical treatises of the Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma Piṭaka (specifically counted among the 'six feet' or ṣaṭ-pādāḥ supporting the body of the Jñānaprasthāna) and is regarded alongside the Saṃgītiparyāya as representative of the earliest, sūtra-commentarial stratum of Abhidharma literature (c. 2nd–1st century BCE). The treatise compiles canonical doctrinal categories (mātṛkās)—such as the five precepts, stages of stream-entry, the limbs of awakening, dependent origination, and meditative absorptions—and glosses them with citations from early discourses. While preserved intact in Chinese translation (T 1537), the Indic text survives only in birch-bark manuscript leaves recovered from Gilgit and Central Asia.

The Abhidharmāmṛta (or Abhidharmāmṛtarasaśāstra) is an early, systematic manual of Sarvāstivāda Abhidharma attributed to Bhadanta Ghoṣaka, one of the four great venerable masters of the Vaibhāṣika lineage associated with the western/Gandhāran tradition. Organized into sixteen chapters (bindus), it provides a clear exposition of Buddhist scholastic categories, including charity and moral discipline, realms of rebirth, the skandhas, dhātus, and āyatanas, causal conditions, latent defilements, the path of meditation, and unconditioned dharmas. The Subodhālaṅkāra ('Lucid Ornamentation') is the foundational Theravāda manual of poetics and rhetoric in the Pāli language, composed in Sri Lanka in the late 12th or early 13th century by Saṅgharakkhita Mahāsāmi. **Edition used (determined):** Gyaltsen Namdrol [Rgyal mtshan rnam grol] (ed., restorer and tr.), Samdhong Rinpoche (gen. ed.), Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayam Āryadharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇaṃ ca [Pratityasamutpada hrdaya and Dharmadhatugarbhavivarana], Sarnath, Varanasi: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies (CIHTS), 1997 (Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica Series, 38).

**Other editions:**
- Marek Mejor, 'The Arya-dharma-dhatu-garbha-vivarana ascribed to Nagarjuna', in: Paul Harrison and Gregory Schopen (eds.), Sūryacandrāya: Essays in honour of Akira Yuyama on the occasion of his 65th birthday, Swisttal-Odendorf: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1998 (Indica et Tibetica, 35), pp. 125–134. — Critical study and edition of the Tibetan Tanjur text.
- Suniti Kumar Pathak, 'A Note on the Āryadharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa', The Indian Historical Quarterly 32.2–3 (1956), pp. 354–357. — Early study analyzing Tanjur dkar chag attributions and contents.

**Translations:**
- Gyaltsen Namdol, Pratītyasamutpādahṛdayam Āryadharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇaṃ ca, Sarnath: CIHTS, 1997. (Hindi)
- Adam Pearcey, 'Commentary on the Noble Essence of the Dharmadhātu', Lotsawa House, 2021 (online). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the short prose treatise corresponding to Toh 4101 / D 4101 (Derge Tengyur, mngon pa, vol. thu, fols. 222b1–223a4), including opening homage, full exposition of the 'ye dharmā hetuprabhavāḥ' stanza, and the retroverted Tibetan translation colophon (50 segments).

**Also known as:** Āryadharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa, 'phags pa chos kyi dbyings kyi snying po'i rnam par 'grel pa

**Attribution:** Attributed to Nāgārjuna in the Tibetan canonical colophon (Derge Tengyur Toh 4101 / D 4101, translated by Indian Upādhyāya Jñānagarbha and Ska ba Dpal brtsegs), although some Tanjur dkar chags connect it with Vinītavarman (Dul ba'i go cha). Modern scholars (e.g. Christian Lindtner, Karl Brunnhölzl) treat the attribution to the historical Madhyamaka master Nāgārjuna as apocryphal. Importantly, no Sanskrit manuscript of the work is known to survive; this e-text is a modern Sanskrit retroversion (reconstruction) from the Tibetan text prepared by Gyaltsen Namdol (Rgyal mtshan rnam grol) in 1997.

The Dharmadhātugarbhavivaraṇa is a brief canonical prose commentary traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna that analyzes the famous Pratītyasamutpāda stanza ('ye dharmā hetuprabhavā hetuṃ teṣāṃ tathāgato hy avadat...'). Contrary to what the title suggests, the text does not discuss tathāgatagarbha doctrine, but instead provides an Abhidharmic classification of the twelve links into five causes (hetu: avidyā, saṃskāra, tṛṣṇā, upādāna, bhava) and seven results (phala: vijñāna, nāmarūpa, ṣaḍāyatana, sparśa, vedanā, jāti, jarāmaraṇa), concluding with an etymological gloss on the epithets 'Tathāgata' and 'Mahāśramaṇa' in terms of forward (anuloma) and reverse (pratiloma) dependent origination. Preserved in the Abhidharma section of the Tibetan Tengyur (Toh 4101), the digital text here represents a modern Sanskrit restoration from Tibetan by Gyaltsen Namdol (1997).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of Yaśomitra's commentary across all eight metrical chapters (kośasthānas 1–8: Dhātu, Indriya, Loka, Karma, Anuśaya, Mārga-pudgala, Jñāna, and Samādhi). Yaśomitra's commentary concludes at the end of chapter 8 (colophon: ācāryayaśomitrakṛtāyāṃ sphuṭārthāyām abhidharmakośavyākhyāyām aṣṭamaṃ kośasthānaṃ samāptam) and does not cover the unversified prose appendix (the ninth chapter on the refutation of the pudgala).

**Also known as:** Abhidharmakośavyākhyā, Sphuṭārthā, Kośavyākhyā

**Attribution:** Authored by Ācārya Yaśomitra (c. 6th–8th century CE), a proponent of Sautrāntika tenets. In his introductory verses (vv. 5–6), Yaśomitra acknowledges his reliance on the earlier Abhidharmakośa commentaries of Guṇamati and Vasumitra, adopting what is sound in their expositions while correcting interpretations that diverge from orthodox doctrine (siddhānta).

The Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā is the only Sanskrit sub-commentary on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya that survives in its entirety. Authored by Yaśomitra from a Sautrāntika doctrinal stance, it supplies detailed word-for-word grammatical, semantic, and philosophical glosses on both the verses and autocommentary across all eight chapters. It is an indispensable source for the study of classical Abhidharma, preserving critical citations from lost Sarvāstivāda, Sautrāntika, and Mahāyāna treatises.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T07_sthtattva4`

**Author:** Sthiramati

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T07 (Abhidharma)

**Source:** Aggregated by Sebastian Nehrdich (Dharmamitra) from the published critical editions of Kazuo Kano and collaborators (2020–2022). Only Sthiramati's constituted Sanskrit is reproduced here.

**Editions used (one per Abhidharmakośa verse):**

- *AK 4.34* — Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, "The Fourth Chapter of the Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā: On Forbidding Intoxicating Liquor," in *Sanskrit Manuscripts from China III* (Proceedings of a panel at the 2016 Beijing International Seminar on Tibetan Studies), Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House, 2020 (critical edition and diplomatic transcription at pp. 122–128).
- *AK 4.35* — Kazuo Kano, Jowita Kramer, Takeshi Yokoyama, Hironori Tanaka, Sebastian Nehrdich, Keiki Nakayama and Kaworu Kominami, "律儀の獲得 ― 倶舎論安慧疏・業品第35偈の梵文和訳 ― [On the Attainment of Restraint: Sthiramati's Tattvārthā on Abhidharmakośa 4.35]," *Taihō zasshi* (対法雑誌 / Journal of Abhidharma Studies) 2 (March 2021): 63–98.
- *AK 4.36ab* — Kazuo Kano, Jowita Kramer, Takeshi Yokoyama, Hironori Tanaka, Sebastian Nehrdich, Keiki Nakayama and Kaworu Kominami, "律儀獲得の範囲と動機 ― 倶舎論安慧疏・業品第36偈ab句の梵文和訳 ― [The Field of Scope and Motivation of the Attainment of Restraint: Sthiramati's Tattvārthā on Abhidharmakośa 4.36ab]," *Taihō zasshi* (対法雑誌 / Journal of Abhidharma Studies) 3 (March 2022): 43–95.
- *AK 4.36cd and 4.37* — Kazuo Kano and Jowita Kramer, "The Fourth Chapter of the Tattvārthā Abhidharmakośaṭīkā: On Attaining Restraint, Non-Restraint and Neither-Restraint-nor-Non-Restraint," *China Tibetology* 36, no. 1 (March 2021): 81–99.

**Textual basis:** Constituted Sanskrit reading text of Sthiramati's Tattvārthā commentary on Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37 (within the fourth chapter, Karmanirdeśa), covering folios 1r1–2r6 of the Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet (Ms. "A," copies of which are kept at the China Tibetology Research Center, Beijing). The text was aggregated across the four editions above and ordered by Abhidharmakośa verse (4.34 → 4.35 → 4.36ab → 4.36cd → 4.37). Where a verse was edited in more than one paper (4.35 and 4.36ab), the later Japanese editions' corrected Sanskrit was preferred. This etext contains only Sthiramati's constituted Sanskrit: the Abhidharmakośa kārikā/bhāṣya, Saṃghabhadra's *Nyāyānusāra* parallels, the Tibetan translation, the critical apparatus (variant readings), and the Japanese/English translations given in the source papers are not included. Bold AKBh lemmata are not separately marked. Segments are split at the daṇḍa; the manuscript folio side (1r/1v/2r) is recorded in the folio field.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains Sthiramati's commentary on Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37 only (from chapter 4, Karmanirdeśa), corresponding to folios 1r1–2r6 of the Sanskrit manuscript preserved in Lhasa (TBRC/CTRC copy).

**Also known as:** Abhidharmakośabhāṣyaṭīkā Tattvārthā, Abhidharmakośaṭīkā Tattvārthā, Tattvārthā, Karakāśani, Chos mngon pa'i mdzod kyi bshad pa'i rgya cher 'grel pa don gyi de kho na nyid ces bya ba, Jushe lun shiyi shu (倶舍論實義疏, T 1561)

**Attribution:** Composed by the Yogācāra master Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE) as an extensive sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya.

This text preserves the surviving Sanskrit of Sthiramati's commentary (ṭīkā) entitled Tattvārthā on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya 4.34–4.37, located in the fourth chapter on action (Karmanirdeśa). It treats the debate over whether drinking alcohol constitutes an offense by nature (prakṛtisāvadya) or solely by prohibition (pratikṣepaṇasāvadya), the attainment of the three types of moral discipline (saṃvara: prātimokṣa-, dhyāna-, and anāsrava-saṃvara), their relationship to karmic path stages, and the definition of non-restraint (asaṃvara). The work is historically vital for showing Sthiramati's engagement with the competing views of the Sautrāntika and Sarvāstivāda traditions (especially Saṃghabhadra).

## Date estimate

**Estimated date:** c. 6th century CE (Sthiramati, c. 510–570 CE).

## Overview

**Tradition:** Buddhist (Abhidharma; a commentary on the Abhidharmakośa, by the Yogācāra master Sthiramati)

**Genre:** ṭīkā (sub-commentary)

**Estimated date:** c. 6th c. CE

The portion of Sthiramati's Tattvārthā (Abhidharmakośaṭīkā) commenting on Abhidharmakośa(bhāṣya) 4.34–4.37, within the fourth chapter (Karmanirdeśa, the exposition of action). The passages treat: the status of drinking intoxicating liquor as a transgression "by nature" (prakṛtisāvadya) versus "by prohibition" (pratikṣepaṇasāvadya) (4.34); the attainment of the three restraints — prātimokṣa-, dhyāna- and anāsrava-saṃvara — and the tetralemma (catuṣkoṭi) of their relation to past/present/future and to the preparatory, primary and consecutive parts of an act (4.35); the scope (aṅga), causes (kāraṇa) and objects of restraint, including whether it extends to beings out of reach (4.36ab); and the attainment of non-restraint (asaṃvara) and of neither-restraint-nor-non-restraint (4.36cd–4.37).

**History:** Composed by Sthiramati (c. 510–570 CE), among the most prolific commentators of the early Yogācāra tradition. His Tattvārthā commentary on Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya was long known only through Tibetan and Chinese witnesses until the recovery of a Sanskrit manuscript from Tibet; these passages were critically edited by Kazuo Kano and collaborators in 2020–2022 and are aggregated here into a single reading text.

**Related works:** Abhidharmakośakārikā and Abhidharmakośabhāṣya (Vasubandhu; cf. `SA_T07_vakobhk`, `SA_T07_vakobhau`), Sphuṭārthā Abhidharmakośavyākhyā (Yaśomitra; cf. `SA_T07_yabhkvyu`), *Nyāyānusāra* (Saṃghabhadra).

The Suvarṇavarṇāvadāna is an avadāna narrative recounting the story of Suvarṇavarṇa ('Golden-Hued'), born as the son of the merchant Divākara of Rājagṛha after Śakra instructs the merchant to take refuge in the Three Jewels. Gopadatta's Jātakamālā is an ornate Mahāyāna narrative work composed in campū style (alternating prose and verse), continuing the classical literary line of Āryaśūra and Haribhaṭṭa (c. 7th–8th century CE). Rather than surviving as a unified compilation in the Buddhist canon, 16 individual legends have been identified and edited by modern scholars from Nepalese story anthologies and Tibetan witnesses. This electronic text brings together 13 of these recovered legends, demonstrating Gopadatta's elaborate kāvya style and dramatic storytelling on Buddhist ethical themes.
