- Zhwa lu lo tsā ba Chos skyong bzang po (Dharmapālabhadra), Skyes pa rabs kyi bstod pa, Degé Tengyur, Toh. 1178 (vol. Ka, fols. 255v4–257v7). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete work in 20 Śārdūlavikrīḍita stanzas (Js_1–Js_20) plus closing author colophon line.

**Also known as:** Skyes pa rabs kyi bstod pa

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to Ācārya Jñānayaśas (ācāryajñānayaśasaḥ; Tib. slob dpon Ye shes grags pa). This early author (c. 6th–7th century) of Buddhist devotional stotras is distinguished in modern scholarship from the later Vajrayāna author of the same name.

The Jātakastava ('Praise of the Buddha\'s Former Births') by Jñānayaśas is a 20-stanza Mahāyāna devotional hymn (stotra) composed in the classical Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre. Framed by an opening confession of inadequate poetic capacity (verses 1–3) and a concluding dedication of merit for universal enlightenment (verses 19–20), stanzas 4–18 succinctly celebrate the Bodhisattva's extreme self-sacrificing deeds in previous lives—including feeding the tigress, giving away his wife and children, jumping into fire as the hare, giving up his tusks as Ṣaḍdanta, and slicing off his flesh as King Śibi. The Sanskrit text was preserved through Tibetan phonetic transliteration alongside a Tibetan translation in the Tengyur (Toh. 1178), representing the classical Sanskrit counterpart to the broader Asian tradition of jātaka encomia seen also in Khotanese.

**Posterior median:** 598 CE

**Coverage:** complete — Complete 16-verse text of N. Aiyaswami Sastri's reconstructed Sanskrit edition, including opening homage to Mañjuśrī Kumārabhūta and closing colophon.

**Also known as:** Bhavasaṃkrāntiparikathā, Bhavasaṅkrānti, Bhavasaṃkrānti, Bhavasaṅkrāntiśāstra, Bhavasaṃkrāntiśāstra, Bhavaparikathā, Srid pa las 'das pa'i gtam

**Attribution:** Ascribed in the Tibetan tradition (Dergé Tanjur Toh. 4162 and Toh. 3840) to Ācārya/Ārya Nāgārjuna and in the Chinese tradition (Taishō 1574, translated by Dānapāla / Shihu) to Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna. Furthermore, the original Sanskrit text of this work is lost; the text in this file is a modern retroversion/reconstruction from Tibetan and Chinese by N. Aiyaswami Sastri.

The Bhavasaṅkrāntiparikathā is a short Madhyamaka treatise of 16 stanzas traditionally attributed to Nāgārjuna, explaining how transmigration across existences (bhavasaṃkrānti) occurs without an enduring self or transmigrating entity (ātman/pudgala). It reconciles karmic continuity and rebirth with emptiness (śūnyatā) and dependent origination through analogies of dreams, reflections, and city-of-gandharvas illusions. As the original Sanskrit text is lost, this e-text preserves the 1938 modern Sanskrit retroversion prepared by N. Aiyaswami Sastri from Tibetan and Chinese sources.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Whole tale in 98 segments, from the opening 'kasmiṃścid deśe daṇḍītyabhihito brāhmaṇaḥ' to Daṇḍin's acquittal 'daṇḍī [ca] sarvāparādhebhyo mumuce iti ||'. The frame (Buddha's past-life identification) of the mDzangs blun chapter is not included.

**Also known as:** Story of Daṇḍin, dByig pa can (Tibetan, mDzangs blun), Tannijī pin 檀膩䩭品 (Xianyu jing, T 202)

**Attribution:** The tale of the poor brahmin Daṇḍin (Tib. dByig pa can, Chin. 檀膩䩭) belongs to the Damamūkanidānasūtra / 'Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish' (Tib. mDzangs blun; Chin. Xianyu jing 賢愚經, T 202), which survives only in Tibetan and Chinese. No original Sanskrit version is known; the bracketed supplements throughout the e-text ('[ sa ]', '[ babhūva ]', '[ daṇḍinā ]') and its close tracking of the Tibetan wording suggest a modern Sanskrit rendering of the Tibetan (the version used in Hahn's Tibetan textbook) rather than a manuscript text, presumably by the editor Biswanath Bhattacharya (a Visva-Bharati Tibetologist); this is an inference from the text, not stated by DSBC.

A short prose tale about the poor brahmin Daṇḍin, who, after losing a borrowed ox, is taken to the king's court and on the way causes a series of mishaps: he lames a runaway mare with a stone, falls from a wall and kills a weaver, and makes a carpenter drop the axe held in his mouth into a river. The king answers each plaintiff with a reciprocal penalty that makes the complaint absurd, so all withdraw and Daṇḍin is acquitted. The story is known from the Tibetan mDzangs blun and the Chinese Xianyu jing (T 202); this Sanskrit text appears to be a modern rendering, published by Biswanath Bhattacharya in 1970 according to DSBC.

Aiyaswami Sastri.

The Ālambanaparīkṣā ('Investigation of the Percept') is a concise foundational treatise in eight verses by the Buddhist epistemologist Dignāga (c. 480–540 CE). Dignāga defines a perceptual cognitive object (ālambana) through two joint criteria: it must act as the causal condition (kāraṇa/pratyaya) producing the cognition, and the cognition must bear its subjective appearance or form (tadābhāsa/ākāra). Arguing against externalist atomism (specifically the Sarvāstivāda and Sautrāntika models), he demonstrates that neither individual atoms nor aggregated atomic composites meet both criteria, ultimately concluding that the object cognized is actually an internal mental aspect appearing as if external, establishing the Yogācāra idealist doctrine.

The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhir anvayātmikā is a philosophical treatise by the eleventh-century Buddhist epistemologist Ratnakīrti (fl. c. 1000–1050 CE) of Vikramaśīla. It establishes the Buddhist doctrine of universal momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga) via positive pervasion (anvayavyāpti): whatever exists is causally efficient (arthakriyākārin), and causal efficiency can only occur instantaneously, not successively or simultaneously over time (kramākramābhyām). The Avayavinirākaraṇa ('Refutation of the Composite Whole') is a short polemical treatise by the late Buddhist logician Aśoka (c. late 10th to early 11th century CE). **Attribution:** Attributed in the opening rubric (Paṇḍitāśokaviracitā) and closing colophon (kṛtir iyaṃ paṇḍitāśokasya) to Paṇḍita Aśoka, a Buddhist epistemologist belonging to the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti school who flourished c. 970–1030 CE (late 10th to early 11th century), contemporaneous with Jñānaśrīmitra and Ratnakīrti. He is conventionally called Paṇḍita Aśoka in scholarship to distinguish him from the Mauryan emperor.

The Sāmānyadūṣaṇa ('Refutation of Universals') by Aśoka (c. late 10th to early 11th c. CE) is a short polemical treatise defending Buddhist nominalism against the realist ontology of Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika and Mīmāṃsā. Following Dignāga and Dharmakīrti, Aśoka argues that an eternal, unitary, and pervasive universal (sāmānya) cannot be established by either perception or inference, demonstrating that common verbal and mental designations are satisfactorily explained by causal capacities and differential exclusion (apoha). The text concludes with the celebrated five-fingers argument: one who claims to perceive a sixth common entity over and above the five distinct fingers might just as well perceive horns on their own head.

**Attribution:** Authentic work of the Buddhist master Dharmakīrti (fl. c. 6th–7th century CE), one of his foundational 'seven treatises' (saptaprakaraṇa) on epistemology and logic (pramāṇa).

The Nyāyabindu ('Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's concise foundational primer on Buddhist epistemology and logic, articulating the core doctrines of the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti school. Written in terse prose aphorisms (sūtras), the work is structured into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines perception as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta), formulates the threefold requirement of the logical reason (trairūpya), classifies valid reasons into essential nature (svabhāva), effect (kārya), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi), and provides a taxonomy of logical fallacies. Due to its clarity and pedagogical conciseness, it became the primary introductory manual of Buddhist logic in India and Tibet.

The Santānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mind-Streams') is a concise treatise by Dharmakīrti (c. 600–660 CE) traditionally numbered among his 'Seven Treatises' on logic and epistemology. Framed as a dialogue opening with a single verse and proceeding through 93 prose sections, it resolves the philosophical challenge of other minds from within the Vijñānavāda (Cittamātra) idealist system, directly rebutting the objection that idealism logically degenerates into solipsism. The Vādanyāya ('The Logic of Debate') is the last of Dharmakīrti's seven core treatises on epistemology and logic (pramāṇa), expounding his reform of dialectical and debate theory. Dharmakīrti mounts an extensive critique of the classical Nyāya system of twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna), arguing that genuine defeat in truthful philosophical inquiry (vāda) occurs under only two fundamental circumstances: the proponent's failure to state an essential component of a valid proof (asādhanāṅgavacana), and the respondent's failure to point out an actual fallacy (adoṣodbhāvana). **Attribution:** The commentary is composed by the Śvetāmbara Jain polymath Haribhadrasūri (c. 8th century CE), who refers to it in the closing colophon as the 'Śiṣyahitā nāma Nyāyapraveśakaṭīkā'. The base manual commented upon is the Nyāyapraveśa (or Nyāyapraveśakasūtra), traditionally attributed to Dignāga in Tibetan and early modern traditions, but established by modern scholarship based on early Chinese sources (such as Xuanzang and Kuiji) to be by Dignāga's disciple Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE).

The Nyāyapraveśapravṛtti (also titled Śiṣyahitā or Nyāyapraveśakavṛtti) is an 8th-century commentary by the Śvetāmbara Jain master Haribhadrasūri on the Nyāyapraveśa, an introductory manual of Buddhist pramāṇa logic authored by Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE). Haribhadrasūri provides a concise, student-oriented word-by-word explanation of the treatise's definitions of valid proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), their corresponding fallacies (ābhāsa), direct perception (pratyakṣa), and inference (anumāna). The commentary is a major historical milestone illustrating the cross-sectarian study and integration of Dignāgean Buddhist epistemology into early medieval Jain intellectual culture.

- Boris Vassilieff, ''Ju-shih Lun'—a logical treatise ascribed to Vasubandhu', Bulletin of the School of Oriental Studies 8(4), 1937, pp. 1013–1037 (study with extensive partial translation and commentary). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete reconstruction of the extant Chinese text in three prakaraṇas (chapter 1 on debate and refutation, chapter 2 on sixteen varieties of jāti, chapter 3 on twenty-two varieties of nigrahasthāna), corresponding to pp. 1–40 of Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 edition.

**Also known as:** *Tarkaśāstra, Rushi lun, Ru shi lun, 如實論, Ju-shih lun, Tattvasiddhi

**Attribution:** The treatise is traditionally attributed to Vasubandhu (Tianqin 天親) in the Chinese Buddhist canon (Taishō no. 1633, translated by Paramārtha in 550 CE) and early commentaries (such as those by Wengui and Kuiji). Modern scholars have debated this attribution: Giuseppe Tucci, Erich Frauwallner, and Hakuju Ui expressed skepticism, suggesting an earlier Buddhist author, whereas Boris Vassilieff and Motoi Ono (2017) have argued that it may represent an early logical treatise composed by Vasubandhu prior to his Vādavidhi. The Sanskrit original is lost; the present text is Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 Sanskrit retroversion from the Chinese.

The Tarkaśāstra (preserved in Chinese translation as the Rushi lun 如實論, Taishō 1633, translated by Paramārtha in 550 CE) is a major Buddhist treatise on debate and dialectics (vāda) representing the pre-Dignāga stage of Indian logic. It consists of three chapters: the first treats dialectical exchanges, valid proof, and the refutation of rival objections; the second provides a systematic classification and critique of sixteen futile rejoinders (jāti); and the third analyzes twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Because the Indic original is lost, the text survives in Sanskrit solely through Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 back-translation, which illustrates the historical evolution of the five-membered syllogism prior to Dignāga's reforms.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of Tucci's Sanskrit retroversion across all 4 prakaraṇas (1. vādalakṣaṇa/vādaprakāra, 2. nigrahasthāna, 3. vādanirṇaya, 4. jāti/vākyadoṣa), corresponding to pp. 1–32 of Tucci (1929).

**Also known as:** Fangbian xin lun, 方便心論, *Prayogasāra, Upāyakauśalyahṛdaya, *Upāyahṛdayaśāstra

**Attribution:** The original Sanskrit text is lost and survives only in a Chinese translation (Fangbian xin lun 方便心論, T 1632) completed in 472 CE by Kiṃkara (Jijiaye 吉迦夜) and Tanyao (曇曜). The earliest Chinese catalogue, Sengyou's Chu sanzang jiji, lists no author. A later attribution to Nāgārjuna (龍樹) appears in Fazang's commentary and Song editions of the canon. Giuseppe Tucci and Hakuju Ui rejected Nāgārjuna's authorship, viewing the work as an early Buddhist debate manual (possibly Bahuśrutīya); Yūichi Kajiyama and Michiko Ishitobi later defended the attribution to Nāgārjuna, though mainstream scholarship considers the authorship uncertain.

The Upāyahṛdaya (preserved only in the 472 CE Chinese translation Fangbian xin lun 方便心論, T 1632, and represented in Sanskrit by Giuseppe Tucci's 1929 retroversion) is an early Buddhist handbook of disputation and dialectics dating to approximately the 3rd to 4th century CE. Composed in four chapters, the manual treats the justification and eight fundamental constituents of debate (including the four pramāṇas, examples, and fallacies), occasions of dialectical defeat (nigrahasthāna), exemplary orthodox debate exchanges, and twenty classes of counter-objections (jāti). It provides a valuable pre-Dignāga witness to the development of early Indian debate theory and epistemology parallel to the Carakasaṃhitā and the Nyāyasūtra.

The Tarkabhāṣā ('Language of Logic') is a concise introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic composed by Mokṣākaragupta, a monk-scholar of the Jagaddala Mahāvihāra in northern Bengal dating to the late 11th or 12th century CE. The Ratnakīrtinibandhāvalī is a collection of ten philosophical monographs (nibandhas) composed in the 11th century CE by Ratnakīrti, a master at Vikramaśīla and pupil of Jñānaśrīmitra. The collection represents the final flourishing of classical Buddhist Pramāṇavāda and Sautrāntika-Yogācāra philosophy in northern India, formulating rigorous responses to Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā opponents. Major subjects addressed include the proof of the Buddha's omniscience (Sarvajñasiddhi), the refutation of God as creator (Īśvarasādhanadūṣaṇa), the apoha nominalist theory of word meaning (Apohasiddhi), positive and negative proofs of universal momentariness (Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi), the refutation of enduring entities (Sthirasiddhidūṣaṇa), the logic of invariable concomitance and reduction of valid cognitions (Vyāptinirṇaya, Pramāṇāntarbhāvaprakaraṇa), and an ultimate idealist critique of external objects and other minds (Citrādvaitaprakāśavāda, Santānāntaradūṣaṇa).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete reconstructed Sanskrit text (corresponding to pp. 1*–35* in Steinkellner 1967), ending with the explicit colophon: 'hetubindur ācārya-dharmakīrti-kṛtaḥ samāptaḥ'.

**Also known as:** Hetubindunāmaprakaraṇa, Hetubinduprakaraṇa

**Attribution:** Universally attributed to Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE) across Indian and Tibetan Buddhist traditions as one of his seven primary works on epistemological logic (pramāṇa, Tib. sde bdun). Major Sanskrit commentaries include Arcaṭa's Hetubinduṭīkā (with Durveka Miśra's Āloka).

The Hetubindu ('Drop of Reason') is a core philosophical treatise by Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE) expounding the theory of the logical reason or probans (hetu). Dharmakīrti defines the triple characteristic of valid evidence (trairūpya), classifies inferential evidence into effect (kārya), essential nature (svabhāva), and non-cognition (anupalabdhi), and refutes rival non-Buddhist views such as the sixfold characterization of the reason (ṣaḍlakṣaṇa). This digital text presents Ernst Steinkellner's 1967 scholarly Sanskrit reconstruction from the Tibetan canon and Arcaṭa's commentary, which served as the primary Sanskrit reference before the discovery and 2016 publication of the original palm-leaf manuscript.

Dharmakīrti composed an autocommentary only for this chapter, establishing core principles of Buddhist logic such as the threefold mark of the reason (trairūpya), the necessary ontological relation (svabhāvapratibandha) underlying vyāpti, and negative reasoning (anupalabdhi). It also contains his seminal exposition of the nominalist apoha ('exclusion') doctrine of semantics and conceptual differentiation, coupled with detailed refutations of rival Brahmanical theories of universals and Vedic scriptural infallibility.

The Sambandhaparīkṣā ('Investigation of Relations') is a concise treatise consisting of 25 verses in anuṣṭubh meter by the Buddhist epistemologist Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE), traditionally counted as one of his 'seven treatises on valid cognition' (pramāṇa-prakaraṇa). In this work, Dharmakīrti develops an uncompromising nominalist critique of the ontological reality of relations, refuting real entities such as inherence (samavāya), contact (saṃyoga), and external causal connections between distinct momentary particulars (svalakṣaṇa). Historically known in Sanskrit only through 22 verses cited by Jaina authors, the final three verses were recovered by Hideomi Yaita from the Tarkarahasya in 1989, and a complete Sanskrit manuscript of the text was subsequently identified at Drepung monastery.

- Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā (Śiṣyahitā) (Vinītadeva, commentary)
- Nyāyabinduṭīkā (Dharmottara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Nyāyabindu, Nyāyabindunāmaprakaraṇa, Rigs pa'i thigs pa zhes bya ba'i rab tu byed pa

**Attribution:** The root work Nyāyabindu is by Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th century CE). Stcherbatsky (1909).

The Nyāyabinduprakaraṇa ('A Drop of Logic') is Dharmakīrti's foundational introductory manual of Buddhist epistemology and logic, divided into three chapters: direct perception (pratyakṣa), inference for oneself (svārthānumāna), and inference for others (parārthānumāna). It defines valid cognition (pramāṇa), establishes the threefold mark of a sound logical reason (trairūpya), classifies inferential reasons into essential identity (svabhāva), causality (kārya), and non-perception (anupalabdhi), and details valid arguments and pseudo-reasons. This composite e-text presents Dharmakīrti's complete root treatise interleaved with the commentaries of Vinītadeva (Nyāyabinduvistaraṭīkā / Śiṣyahitā) and Dharmottara (Nyāyabinduṭīkā), together with an anonymous subcommentary (Nyāyabinduṭīkāṭippaṇī) for the first chapter.

Jitāri (c. 940–1000 CE), frequently referred to in Tibetan sources as Jetāri, was an influential late Buddhist scholar-logician affiliated with Vikramaśīla and an early teacher of Atiśa Dīpaṃkara Śrījñāna.

The Hetutattvopadeśa ('Instruction on the True Nature of the Logical Reason') is an introductory pedagogical primer on Buddhist logic (hetuvidyā) composed by the 10th-century scholar Jitāri. Closely following the model of the Nyāyapraveśa while incorporating Dharmakīrtian developments, the work outlines the three characteristics of a valid logical mark (trairūpya), the varieties of correct inferential reasons, and provides an exhaustive taxonomy of fallacies including defective theses (pakṣābhāsa), fallacious reasons (hetvābhāsa), and fallacious examples (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa).

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete reconstructed Sanskrit text in 111 numbered sections, including initial summary kārikās, detailed prose treatise on the conditions and fallacies of inference, author colophon (section 307), and retro-translated Tibetan translation colophon (section 308).

**Also known as:** Hetutattvopadeśaḥ, Gtan tshigs kyi de kho na nyid bstan pa

**Attribution:** Attributed to the 10th-century Buddhist epistemologist Jitāri (also written Jetāri, c. 940–1000 CE) of Vikramaśīla monastery, one of the teachers of Atiśa Dīpaṃkaraśrījñāna.

The Hetutattvopadeśa ('Instruction on the True Nature of the Logical Reason') is an introductory compendium of Buddhist logic (hetuvidyā/pramāṇa) composed by Jitāri in the late 10th century. Following Dignāga's Nyāyapraveśa and Dharmakīrtian pramāṇa terminology, it systematically expounds proof (sādhana), refutation (dūṣaṇa), the threefold mark of the reason (trairūpya), and the various fallacies of the thesis (pakṣābhāsa), reason (hetvābhāsa), and example (dṛṣṭāntābhāsa). This e-text preserves Durgacharan Chattopadhyaya's 1939 Sanskrit retro-translation made from the Tibetan translation prior to Tucci's recovery of the original palm-leaf manuscript.

The first item in the e-text is an introductory Sanskrit preface by the modern editor Anantalal Thakur.

The Nibandhāvalī is the modern title given to the corpus of twelve philosophical monographs by Jñānaśrīmitra (fl. c. 975–1025 CE), senior dvārapaṇḍita of Vikramaśīla and guru of Ratnakīrti. The treatises mount an advanced defense of Yogācāra-Sautrāntika and Pramāṇavāda epistemology against Brahmanical critics (notably Vācaspatimiśra) and Buddhist rivals, formulating foundational arguments on momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga), pervasion (vyāpti), non-cognition (anupalabdhi), nominalist exclusion (apoha), the refutation of God (īśvaravāda), and the reality of mental aspects (sākāravāda). This digital text corresponds to the 1959 editio princeps by Anantalal Thakur, but it is incomplete, breaking off mid-way through the Sākārasiddhiśāstra and omitting the Sākārasaṃgrahasūtra.

- Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā (Karṇakagomin, sub-commentary)

Karṇakagomin's Pramāṇavārttikasvavṛttiṭīkā is an extensive Sanskrit sub-commentary (ṭīkā) on Dharmakīrti's autocommentary (Svavṛtti) to the first chapter (Svārthānumāna, 'Inference for Oneself') of the Pramāṇavārttika. Composed around the 8th to 9th century CE, it draws heavily upon and expands the earlier commentary of Śākyabuddhi, offering thorough expositions of Buddhist epistemology, the exclusion theory of meaning (apoha), the nature of logical grounds (hetu), and extensive polemics against rival traditions including Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, and Sāṅkhya. Preserved in a single palm-leaf manuscript brought to light in Tibet by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana, the text is a vital witness both for establishing the text of Dharmakīrti's Svavṛtti and for tracing early post-Dharmakīrti epistemological debate.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vādanyāya (Dharmakīrti, root text)
- Vipañcitārthā (Śāntarakṣita, commentary)

**Also known as:** Vādanyāyaprakaraṇa with Vipañcitārthā, Vādanyāyaṭīkā Vipañcitārthā, Vipañcitārthā

**Attribution:** The root work is Dharmakīrti's Vādanyāya; the commentary is Śāntarakṣita's Vipañcitārthā, explicitly confirmed by the opening incipit ('ācāryaśāntarakṣitapraṇītayā vipañcitārthābhidhayā ṭīkayā saṃvalitaḥ') and concluding colophon ('vipañcitārthā nāma vādanyāyaṭīkā samāptā || || kṛtiriyaṃ śāntarakṣitapādānāmiti'). Vinītadeva composed a separate commentary on the Vādanyāya extant only in Tibetan (Toh 4240); assigning his name here was a metadata error.

The Vādanyāya ('Logic of Debate') is Dharmakīrti's final treatise on debate theory and the grounds of defeat (nigrahasthāna). Critiquing the classic Naiyāyika scheme of twenty-two defeat situations, Dharmakīrti reduces all points of defeat to two fundamental categories: failure to state an essential component of proof (asādhanāṅgavacana) by the proponent, and falsely alleging a defect where none exists (adoṣodbhāvana) by the opponent. Śāntarakṣita's 8th-century Vipañcitārthā is the sole surviving Sanskrit commentary on the text, providing extensive lexical explanations, contextual arguments, and refutations of rival non-Buddhist schools.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Whole tract from the Mañjuśrī benediction ('namo mañjuśriye', verse 'mugdhāṅgulīkisalaya…') to the author colophon, with small lacunae marked by dots and '( )' (segments 36, 39, 42, 98) where the manuscript is damaged. The same work, in a different textual form, opens SA_T11_vadasthananu (Iyengar's Vādasthāna).

**Also known as:** Jātivādanirāsa, Vādasthānāni (first section)

**Attribution:** The final colophon names Jitāri ('jātinirākṛtir iyaṃ jitāripādānām'); Tucci (Minor Buddhist Texts I, 1956) used this colophon for the spelling Jitāri rather than Jetāri. Jitāri (10th c., Vikramaśīla) is the accepted author.

The Jātinirākṛti ('Refutation of the Universal') is a short polemical treatise by the 10th-century Buddhist logician-philosopher Jitāri of Vikramaśīlā. Formulated as an opening tract among topics of debate (vādasthānāni), it refutes the realist doctrine of real and eternal universals (jāti / sāmānya) held by Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā thinkers. Grounded in Dharmakīrtian epistemological logic, Jitāri establishes that universals cannot be said to be either identical with or distinct from particular individuals, undermines the relation of inherence (samavāya), and refutes Kumārila Bhaṭṭa's reliance on recognition (pratyabhijñā).

The Anupalabdhirahasya ('The Secret of Non-Apprehension') is a treatise on Buddhist epistemology by Jñānaśrīmitra addressing the problem of negative cognition. Building on Dharmakīrti's framework, Jñānaśrīmitra defines non-perception (anupalabdhi) not as a mere absence of awareness (upalabdhivirahamātra), but as an implicative negation (paryudāsa) consisting in the apprehension of something incompatible or distinct. He defends the status of anupalabdhi as a valid inferential sign (liṅga) for proving absence (abhāva) against rival Buddhist formulations and non-Buddhist theories such as the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā doctrine of an independent means of knowledge (abhāvapramāṇa).

**Attribution:** Tibetan tradition (Degé Tengyur D4208 / Toh 4208) and some modern Indian editions (e.g., Muni Jambuvijaya, Sharma) attribute the work to Dignāga (Diṅnāga). However, Chinese tradition (starting from Xuanzang's 647 CE translation) and critical scholarship firmly attribute the manual to Dignāga's disciple Śaṅkarasvāmin.

The Nyāyapraveśakasūtra (commonly known as the Nyāyapraveśa), authored by Dignāga's pupil Śaṅkarasvāmin (c. 6th century CE), is an influential introductory manual of Buddhist logic and epistemology (hetuvidyā). It systematically defines the members of formal proof (sādhana) and refutation (dūṣaṇa), the three characteristics of a valid logical reason (trairūpya), the varieties of logical fallacies (pakṣābhāsa, hetvābhāsa, dṛṣṭāntābhāsa), and valid cognition through perception and inference. Translated into Chinese by Xuanzang in 647 CE, it became the standard foundational treatise for the East Asian Buddhist logical tradition (yinming / inmyō), and was widely preserved and commented upon in medieval India, notably by Jaina scholars.

**Also known as:** Pramāṇavārttikakārikā, Pramāṇavārtika, Tshad ma rnam 'grel, Tshad ma rnam 'grel gyi tshig le'ur byas pa

**Attribution:** Composed by Dharmakīrti (ca. 6th–7th century CE) as an expansive verse treatise elaborating and defending Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya. The e-text contains solely the root verses (kārikās) across all four chapters, without commentary.

The Pramāṇavārttika ('Commentary on Valid Cognition') is the foundational masterwork of Dharmakīrti (ca. 6th–7th century CE) and the definitive text of Buddhist epistemology, logic, and philosophy of language. Composed in verse as an extensive critical development of Dignāga's Pramāṇasamuccaya, it establishes perception (pratyakṣa) and inference (anumāna) as the only two means of valid cognition, formulates the Buddhist theory of conceptual exclusion (apoha), and provides rational defenses of the Buddha's authority, rebirth, and the Four Noble Truths. This e-text contains the complete set of metrical root verses (kārikās) across four chapters arranged according to the commentarial tradition of Manorathanandin.

The Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Vyatirekātmikā ('Proof of Universal Momentariness by Negative Concomitance') is a short philosophical monograph by Ratnakīrti, condensing and defending the epistemological arguments of his master Jñānaśrīmitra. Complementing his Kṣaṇabhaṅgasiddhi Anvayātmikā (which argues via positive pervasion), this treatise argues from negative contraposition: non-momentary (enduring) entities cannot exercise causal efficiency (arthakriyāsāmarthya) either in succession (krama) or simultaneously (akrama), and therefore cannot exist. Ratnakīrti pays particular attention to defusing the Nyāya objection that an inference with a non-existent subject (the unproduced or eternal entity) incurs the fallacy of lack of substratum (āśrayāsiddhi).

**Also known as:** Udayananirākaraṇa, Udayananirākaraṇam, Ācāryaratnakīrtiviracitam Udayananirākaraṇam

**Attribution:** First edited by Raghunath Pandey in 1984 under the title 'Ācāryaratnakīrtiviracitam Udayananirākaraṇam', who conjecturally attributed it to Ratnakīrti. This attribution was refuted by Gudrun Bühnemann (1983, 1984) and M. T. Much (1987), who established that the manuscript does not name Ratnakīrti and that the text is anonymous, composed by a late Buddhist logician post-dating Jñānaśrīmitra.

The Vādarahasya is a late Indian Buddhist epistemological treatise preserved in a single 42-folio manuscript in Proto-Bengali/Maithili script photographed by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Tibet (now preserved on film and glass negatives at the Bihar Research Society, Patna). The work defends core Buddhist philosophical doctrines—particularly momentariness (kṣaṇabhaṅga), the exclusion theory of meaning (apoha), and causal efficacy (arthakriyākāritva)—against the attacks of the 11th-century Nyāya master Udayana, especially those set forth in the Ātmatattvaviveka. Although published in 1984 under the title Udayananirākaraṇam and attributed to Ratnakīrti, philological research has shown the text to be anonymous and composed after Jñānaśrīmitra.

**Also known as:** Santānāntarasiddhi, Saṃtānāntarasiddhināmaprakaraṇa, rGyud gzhan grub pa zhes bya ba'i rab tu byed pa, Proof of Other Mindstreams

**Attribution:** The Saṃtānāntarasiddhi is traditionally listed as one of the seven primary epistemological treatises (sde bdun) of Dharmakīrti (c. 6th–7th c. CE), categorized as one of the four supplementary treatises ('limbs'). The full Sanskrit original is not preserved intact (though fragmentary Sanskrit folios from a commentary manuscript were identified by Junjie Chu in 2005/2011); the work survived completely in the Tibetan Tenjur (Toh 4219). This e-text is an modern Indic retro-translation/reconstruction into Sanskrit by J. S. Negi.

The Saṃtānāntarasiddhi ('Proof of Other Mindstreams') is Dharmakīrti's short philosophical treatise on the problem of other minds and the refutation of solipsism. Beginning with a single introductory verse followed by concise prose dialectic, Dharmakīrti shows that inferring the presence of an external continuum of consciousness by observing bodily and vocal activity operates with equal logical validity in an idealist (cittamātra/vijñaptimātra) ontology as in a realist one. The treatise concludes by examining the status and scope of telepathic cognition (paracittajñāna) possessed by yogins and awakened buddhas within an anti-realist epistemological framework.

The Vṛttamālāstuti is a specialized Buddhist devotional work and prosodical treatise composed by the Vikramaśīla philosopher Jñānaśrīmitra (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). Comprising 154 stanzas in praise of the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī, each verse defines and exemplifies a distinct Sanskrit metre while embedding its traditional metrical name. This e-text provides the complete root hymn accompanied by the learned prose commentary (vivṛti) of Śākyarakṣita (fl. late 11th–12th century CE), which discusses metrical caesurae, grammar, and literary nuances.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Chandoratnākara (Ratnākaraśānti, root text)
- Chandoratnākaravṛtti (Ratnākaraśānti, commentary)

**Also known as:** Chandoratnākarasvopajñavṛtti, Chandoratnākaraḥ svopajñavṛttyā samanvitaḥ, sDeb sbyor rin chen 'byung gnas

The Chandoratnākara ('Ocean of Metres') along with its autocommentary (Chandoratnākaravṛtti) by the 11th-century Vikramaśīla master Ratnākaraśānti is a foundational Buddhist manual of Indian metrics (chandaḥśāstra). Spanning six chapters, it systematically expounds syllabic metres (varṇavṛtta), moraic metres (mātravṛtta/jāti), and combinatorial algorithms (pratyaya) for calculating and generating metrical variations. A hallmark pedagogical feature of the treatise is that each definition is composed in the exact metre that it defines; the text played an influential role in the study of metrics in medieval Nepal and in Tibetan monastic universities.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Ten sargas, from the maṅgala to the defeat of Māra and the Awakening under the Bodhi tree (10.58), each with colophon; c. 640 verses. Some verse numbers in the e-text are mistyped (4.184–4.187 for 4.84–4.87) or missing (7.45, 10.29, 10.57), which are numbering slips, not omitted cantos.

**Also known as:** Siddhārthacarita, Siddhārthacaritakāvya, Siddhārthacaritra, Padyacūḍāmaṇimahākāvya

**Attribution:** Ascribed in the text to Buddhaghoṣa (ācārya), a namesake of the 5th-century Pāli commentator; nothing is known about him and the date is uncertain (Franceschini). The poem was probably composed in South India; it draws heavily on Kālidāsa's Raghuvaṃśa.

The Padyacūḍāmaṇi ('Crest-jewel of verses') is a Sanskrit mahākāvya in ten cantos on the life of the Buddha, from his stay in the Tuṣita heaven through his birth as prince Siddhārtha, youth, marriage, the encounters that lead to renunciation, and austerities, to the defeat of Māra and Awakening under the Bodhi tree. Its author, Buddhaghoṣa, is a namesake of the Pāli commentator and of uncertain date; the poem models itself closely on Kālidāsa, especially the Raghuvaṃśa.

The Kriyāsaṃgrahakārikā is a concise ten-verse mnemonic summary (uddāna) attributed to the tantric Nāgārjuna, outlining the essential sequence of Vajrayāna temple construction, consecration, and monastic ritual procedures. It enumerates the preliminary examination of guru and disciple, site selection and purification, propitiation of the earth deity and site serpent (vāstunāgaparīkṣā), brick-laying and architectural measurements, maṇḍala layout and thread-casting, fire rites (homa), image installation and consecration (pratiṣṭhā), monastic ordination (pravrajyā), and the repair of dilapidated shrines (jīrṇoddhāra). The thematic sequence mirrors the major chapters of Kuladatta's comprehensive manual, the Kriyāsaṃgrahapañjikā.

The Samyaksambuddhabhāṣitapratimālakṣaṇa (also known as the Pratimālakṣaṇa or Buddhapratimālakṣaṇa) is a primary manual of Buddhist iconometry (tālamāna). Framed as a discourse at Jetavana where the Buddha instructs Śāriputra on how devotees should fashion icons after the Teacher's parinirvāṇa, the text establishes canonical proportions (pramāṇa) for images of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas. Across 54 verses, it details precise measurements in bodily units (aṅgula, mātrā, vyāma) for the uṣṇīṣa, cranial contours, facial features, torso, and limbs, as well as distinct facial types (such as oval and round) for various classes of divine, human, and semi-divine beings. Widely preserved in Nepalese manuscripts and incorporated into both the Tibetan Tengyur and the Chinese canon, the work served as a fundamental textual authority for religious sculpture and painting in northern Buddhism.

In the opening verses (1–2), the text describes itself as compiling image-proportion rules taught by former sages in Buddhist treatises (ātreyatilake bauddhaśāstre'nyatra purātanaiḥ | uktaṃ yatpūrvamunibhiḥ pratimāmānalakṣaṇam).

The Ātreyatilaka (also titled Pratibimbalakṣaṇa) is a Sanskrit Buddhist manual of iconometry (śilpaśāstra) traditionally attributed to the sage Ātreya. Comprising 144 anuṣṭubh verses, it defines the tālamāna proportional canons and precise dimensional units (aṅgula, yava, kalā, etc.) for constructing sacred Buddhist images from crown to pedestal. The final section (vv. 141–144) details jīrṇoddhāra, prescribing religious rites for repairing, re-installing, or ritually decommissioning damaged, broken, or weathered earthen and metal icons.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in three parivartas corresponding to the entire extant Tibetan translation: Chapter 1 (verses 1.1–1.59, the origin narrative of painting involving King Bhayajit/Nagnajit, Yama, and Brahmā), Chapter 2, and Chapter 3 (verses 3.1–3.165, iconometric proportions [parimāṇa] ending at line 648 with 'iti citralakṣaṇe parimāṇo nāmstṛtīyaḥ parivartaḥ / yāvat brahmaṇaḥ parimāṇalekhayaḥ samāptaḥ').

**Also known as:** Citralakṣaṇam, Ri mo'i mtshan nyid, Nagnajiccitralakṣaṇa

**Attribution:** The original ancient Sanskrit text was lost in South Asia and survived solely in Tibetan translation in the Tanjur (Peking Q5806 / Toh 4317). Varāhamihira (6th c. CE) explicitly cites Nagnajit on image proportions in Bṛhatsaṃhitā 58.4. The Sanskrit text in this e-text is an artificial modern metrical retroversion from the Tibetan Tanjur composed by Asoke Chatterjee Sastri and published in 1987.

The Citralakṣaṇa is an ancient Indian śilpaśāstra treatise on painting and image proportions (iconometry), traditionally ascribed to King Nagnajit and cited by Varāhamihira (6th century CE) in the Bṛhatsaṃhitā [3915, 5657]. The first chapter relates the mythical genesis of painting: King Bhayajit, having vanquished naked pretas (hence named Nagnajit), disputes with Yama to retrieve a brāhmaṇa's dead son; Brahmā intervenes, instructing the king to paint the boy's likeness and breathing life into it [3970, Granoff]. The subsequent chapters detail iconometric standards (parimāṇa/tālamāna) for universal monarchs (cakravartins), gods, and other figures [8758]. Preserved solely in Tibetan in the Tanjur (Toh 4317 / Peking Q5806), this Sanskrit e-text represents Asoke Chatterjee Sastri's 1987 metrical reconstruction from the Tibetan.

The prose commentary (vivecana) is composed by an anonymous author who reveres Bhadravyūha.

The Stūpalakṣaṇakārikā is an architectural and ritual verse treatise composed by Bhadravyūha of the Mahāsāṃghika-Lokottaravādin school, setting forth the canonical dimensions, proportions, and structural units of Buddhist stūpas alongside a systematic doctrinal mapping of its components onto Buddhist dharmas (such as the 37 bodhipakṣikadharmas, the four noble truths, and the elements). It is accompanied by the anonymous Stūpalakṣaṇakārikāvivecana, a detailed prose commentary that interprets each stanza with reference to the Lokottaravādin Prakīrṇakavinaya and related monastic traditions. Preserved in a single early Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript, the work constitutes one of the rare surviving Sanskrit treatises on non-Tantric Buddhist stūpa architecture and architectural symbolism.

Following the Dignāga-Dharmakīrti tradition, it defines sensory perception (pratyakṣa) as non-conceptual (kalpanāpoḍha) and non-erroneous (abhrānta) cognition bearing a direct grasp of bare particulars (svalakṣaṇa). The chapter systematically critiques alternative theories and definitions of perception formulated by non-Buddhist traditions—including the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsakas, Śaivas, Vaiyākaraṇas, Naiyāyikas, Vaiśeṣikas, and Sāṃkhyas—as well as assessing earlier Buddhist definitions such as Vasubandhu's.

The Svastyayanagāthā is a 17-verse benedictory and apotropaic hymn preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit within the Chatravastu narrative of the Mahāvastu (Vol. I, pp. 290–295). It represents the northern Buddhist Sanskrit parallel to the well-known Theravāda Ratana Sutta (Sn 2.1 / Khp 6), chanted by the Buddha upon arriving in epidemic-stricken Vaiśālī as an act of truth (satyakriyā) to expel malicious non-human spirits and restore welfare. The Tarkarahasya ('Secret of Logic/Reasoning') is a late Indian Buddhist philosophical treatise and epistemological manual belonging to the Dignāga–Dharmakīrti school, preserved in a single Proto-Maithili/Proto-Bengali palm-leaf manuscript photographed by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Ngor monastery, Tibet. In five topical chapters, the text presents the definitions and number of valid means of cognition (pramāṇa), perception (pratyakṣa) and its subdivisions, epistemic objects, and inference and relations (examining Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā), while systematically refuting rival non-Buddhist views (Nyāya, Mīmāṃsā, Cārvāka). While its author remains unknown due to the lost manuscript conclusion and colophon, references to Dharmottara and Prajñākaragupta date the work to roughly the 10th or 11th century CE.

**Edition used (not determined):** not determined; DSBC (Sanskrit Buddhist Input Project) e-text, Śāstra no. 46, without named source. Candidate printed sources are V. Bhattacharya's edition in IHQ 4 (1928) and Frauwallner's text in WZKSO 3 (1959), but neither match was verified

**E-text:** Sanskrit Buddhist Input Project / Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (Nagarjuna Institute, Nepal and University of the West), Śāstra section no. 46; GRETIL bsa046_u.htm (TEI: sa_dignAga-yogAvatAra.xml)

**Evidence:**
- GRETIL and TEI headers credit only the DSBC input project (Śāstra no. 46) and name no printed edition.
- The e-text has a corrupt, apparently uncorrected text: the āryā verses are unmetrical in several places (e.g. 3ab 'jñeyaṃ vilokya sakalaṃ mā yogameva nirbhāsam'), there is a lacuna '............danaghavāyau' in v. 8, and only one bracketed conjecture '[yogī]' (v. 1). This looks like a reproduction of a manuscript-based text rather than a critically constituted one. The draft's claim of an exact match with Frauwallner 1959 could not be verified.
- Deleanu (2006) reports that the Yogāvatāra was critically edited by Frauwallner (1959) with use of the Nepalese manuscript of the Sanskrit original (one palm leaf; Sugawara 1990), and lists V. Bhattacharya, 'Yogāvatāropadeśa', IHQ (1928). Amar Singh (1984) states that the Sanskrit text names no author, whereas the e-text ends with 'kṛtir iyam āryadignāgapādānām'. The source of this colophon is therefore unclear and should be compared with the editions.

**Other editions:**
- Erich Frauwallner, 'Dignāga, sein Werk und seine Entwicklung', Wiener Zeitschrift für die Kunde Süd- und Ostasiens 3 (1959), pp. 83–164 (Yogāvatāra discussed and edited therein; exact pages not re-verified). — Critical edition using the Nepalese manuscript and the Tibetan translation (per Deleanu 2006).
- Vidhushekhara Bhattacharya (ed.), 'Yogāvatāropadeśa', Indian Historical Quarterly 4 (1928). — Listed by Deleanu 2006; pages not re-verified.
- Durgacharan Chatterji (1927): Tibetan text, Sanskrit restoration and English translation of Dharmendra's Yogāvatāropadeśa, which quotes the verses of the Yogāvatāra (per Deleanu 2006 and Amar Singh 1984). — Restoration of the commentary, not an edition of the Sanskrit original.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete 9-verse work including opening mangala (namas tārāyai) and closing colophon. Verse 8a contains the lacuna preserved in the manuscript tradition (............danaghavāyau...).

**Also known as:** rNal 'byor la 'jug pa, Ru yuqie lun (入瑜伽論)

**Attribution:** The Tibetan translation (D 4074) attributes the Yogāvatāra to Dignāga, and Frauwallner (1959) accepted it as an early Yogācāra work of Dignāga. Amar Singh (1984) and others doubt the attribution: Dharmendra's Yogāvatāropadeśa (D 4075) incorporates all the verses without naming Dignāga, and the Sanskrit manuscript is reported to have no author's name. The 'kṛtir iyam āryadignāgapādānām' colophon in this e-text therefore needs checking. Studies: N. Yoshida, IBK 15.2 [no. 30] (1967), pp. 148–149, and Bukkyōgaku kenkyū 24 (1967), pp. 61–65; Y. Sugawara, IBK 35.2 [no. 70] (1987), pp. 126–129.

A very short Yogācāra meditation manual in nine āryā stanzas, opening with homage to Tārā. After study and conviction, the yogin seated on a soft seat sees through the net of conceptualization, including the duality of grasped and grasper. He realizes the mind as without appearance and unarisen (anupalambha, tathatājñāna), and so reaches the path of the noble ones and works for the benefit of beings. The verses are also quoted in full in Dharmendra's Yogāvatāropadeśa.

The Buddhist Yoga Manual (conventionally known as Yogalehrbuch) is an untitled Sanskrit meditation handbook surviving in fragmentary manuscript leaves in North Turkestan Brāhmī from the Kucha region along the northern Silk Road (dated palaeographically to c. 7th century CE). The Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā (or Dṛṣṭāntapaṅkti) of Kumāralāta is an early Buddhist narrative collection composed in mixed ornate prose and verse (campū style). It presents illustrative moral tales (dṛṣṭānta/avadāna) teaching karma, devotion to the Buddha and Saṅgha, and early Dārṣṭāntika doctrinal stances. **Attribution:** Attributed to the early Buddhist poet Mātṛceṭa (fl. c. 2nd century CE). The work was famously described and praised by the Chinese pilgrim Yijing (I-tsing) in the late 7th century CE as widely recited across Indian monasteries, and it was preserved in Sanskrit manuscripts as well as Tibetan, Chinese, and Central Asian translations.

The Śatapañcāśatka ('Hymn of 150 Verses', also known as Prasādapratibhodbhava, numbering 153 verses in total) is a foundational Buddhist hymn of praise (stotra) composed in classical Sanskrit by the 2nd-century poet Mātṛceṭa. Structured across thirteen thematic sections, the work extols the Buddha's peerless compassion, bodily marks, intellectual qualities, moral perfection, and liberating teachings in an elegant kāvya idiom. As testified by the 7th-century Chinese pilgrim Yijing, the work was committed to memory and chanted daily in Buddhist monastic communities throughout India and rapidly spread to Central Asia, Tibet, and China.

**Edition used (not determined):** not determined; mūla text only, printed source not identified

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), book 807 (input Bibek Shakya, proofread Miroj Shakya per the draft/TEI header)

**Evidence:**
- DSBC book page 807 has no editor, publisher, place or year (the 'Editor' field repeats the title).
- The existing catalog raw_metadata says 'with the commentary (ṭīkā) of Jñānavimalagaṇi, ed. (Yashovijaya Jain Granthamala / Bhavnagar), 1940'. The Gemini draft instead names an edition by Auguste Kümmel (Leipzig 1940, Sammlung orientalischer Arbeiten 4). Neither could be verified in the reference literature or by web search, and they contradict each other.
- The e-text contains only Maheśvara's verses (four nirdeśas with restarting verse numbers, closing verses 45–49) and the colophon '... śrīmanmaheśvarakṛtau viśvaprakāśe śabdabhedaprakāśaḥ parisamāptaḥ', i.e. the text as the appendix of the Viśvaprakāśa. There is no trace of Jñānavimala's commentary, so an edition with the commentary is not demonstrated as the source.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete root text (mūla) consisting of 4 sections (nirdeśas): general orthographic variants (133 verses), ba/va variants (34 verses), sibilant variants (59 verses), and gender variants (44 verses, followed by 5 closing verses and final colophon), total 604 segments.

**Also known as:** Śabdabhedanāmamālā

**Attribution:** By Maheśvara (Maheśvara Kavīndra), author of the Viśvaprakāśa (dated 1111 CE), to which this work is appended, as the colophon shows ('viśvaprakāśe śabdabhedaprakāśaḥ'). The closing verses praise Maheśvara as a physician and poet. Aufrecht's Catalogus Catalogorum records a commentary by Jñānavimalagaṇi (1598 CE), which is not in this e-text. Both 1940 editions cited in earlier metadata are unverified.

The Śabdabhedaprakāśa ('Illumination of Distinctions among Words') is a 12th-century Sanskrit orthographic lexicon composed by Maheśvara as a supplement to his homonym dictionary Viśvaprakāśa (1111 CE). In four sections (nirdeśas), it catalogues allowable variations in Sanskrit phonology and spelling: general vocalic/consonantal variants, the interchange of ba and va, alternations among the three sibilants (śa, ṣa, sa), and differences of gender (liṅgabheda). It served as a practical reference for poets and scholars to verify legitimate variants and support verbal figures of speech like anuprāsa, yamaka, and śleṣa.

**Attribution:** The codex comprises 51 birch-bark folios written by at least four different scribes active in the Kucha oasis along the Northern Silk Road in approximately the 5th to early 6th century CE. The medical treatises draw upon ancient Āyurvedic authorities (Ātreya, Suśruta, Parāśara, Bheḍa, etc.), while the divinatory manuals belong to the cubomantic tradition associated with Garga.

The Bower Manuscript (Oxford, Bodleian Library MS. Ind. ch. c. 1) is a 5th- or early 6th-century birch-bark manuscript in early North-Western Gupta/Brāhmī script discovered in 1890 inside a Buddhist stupa near Kucha on the northern Silk Road. The codex contains seven distinct works: three Āyurvedic medical treatises (Part I including the Laśunakalpa on garlic, Part II the Nāvanītaka formulary, and Part III an untitled medical treatise), two manuals of cubomancy or dice divination (Parts IV and V, Pāśakakevalī), and two Buddhist protective spells against snakebite and poison (Parts VI and VII, belonging to the Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī tradition). It represents the earliest surviving direct manuscript witness of classical Indian medical literature and an invaluable monument of Central Asian palaeography and Buddhist monastic medicine.

The Nāgānanda ('Joy of the Serpents') is a five-act Sanskrit drama (nāṭaka) attributed to King Harṣavardhana (Harṣadeva, r. c. 606–647 CE). Uniting classical courtly romance with Buddhist Bodhisattva ideals, it dramatizes the legend of Prince Jīmūtavāhana, who foregoes his royal inheritance, falls in love with and weds the Siddha princess Malayavatī, and subsequently offers his own body on the slaughter rock to the eagle Garuḍa to rescue the Nāga youth Śaṅkhacūḍa. The drama opens with an invocation to the Buddha subduing Māra and concludes with Jīmūtavāhana's miraculous resurrection by the goddess Gaurī and Garuḍa's conversion to ahiṃsā.

The Svapnādhyāya (extant in the Tibetan Tanjur under the title Svapnohana / rMi lam brtag pa, Tōh. 1749) is a concise Buddhist treatise on oneiromancy attributed to the eastern Indian scholar Vibhūticandra (fl. late 12th–early 13th century). Philological research shows that the work is an abridged Buddhist adaptation of Jagaddeva's 12th-century oneiromantic manual, the Svapnacintāmaṇi.

Originating in the same esoteric milieu as the Cakrasaṃvara and Hevajra tantras, it features antinomian yogic discipline, cremation-ground rituals, and a prominent focus on Gāruḍa practices used for curing snakebite and counteracting poison. Chapters 9 through 14 cover post-initiatory caryā conduct, herbal and rasāyana lore, Gāruḍa-vidyādhara rites, sexual yoga, meditation on the subtle channels, and the ritual procedure of initiation (abhiṣeka).

The Ḍākārṇava (fully Śrīḍākārṇavamahāyoginītantrarāja, 'King of Tantras of the Great Yoginī, the Ocean of Ḍākas') is an encyclopedic Buddhist Anuttarayoga / Yoginītantra belonging to the Cakrasaṃvara corpus, structured into 51 chapters (prakaraṇas). Originating in eastern India between the late 10th and early 12th centuries, it synthesizes earlier Saṃvara traditions into an elaborate system featuring a massive 986-deity Heruka maṇḍala (chapter 15), tantric hand gestures and secret codes (chomā/mudrā, chapters 26–37), internal body yoga, and sacred geography. In South Asian linguistic history, it constitutes an essential monument for late Middle Indo-Aryan, preserving extensive dohās and songs composed in Eastern Apabhraṃśa.

Celebrated as one of the 'Seven Siddhi Texts' (Tib. grub pa sde bdun) transmitted in early Indo-Tibetan Mahāmudrā lineages, it rejects ascetic mortification, conventional caste purity, fasting, and external deity worship. The Saundaryalaharī ('Wave of Beauty') is a celebrated Sanskrit devotional and tantric hymn of 100 verses composed in the śikhariṇī metre in honor of the Goddess Tripurasundarī. The first section (verses 1–41, often known as Ānandalaharī) expounds Śākta philosophy, Śrīcakra diagrammatics, mantra theory, and Kuṇḍalinī yoga, while the second section consists of an ornate head-to-foot (keśādipāda) stotra describing the Devi's form. This digital volume presents the edition published by the Oriental Research Institute, Mysore, featuring Lakṣmīdhara's authoritative 16th-century commentary aligning Śrīvidyā with orthodox Samayācāra, accompanied by the Bhāvanopaniṣad with Bhāskararāya's commentary and the Devīpañcastavī.

- Revision log in header: 'Revision 0: Feb. 16, 2013 Part 1; Revision 1: Dec. 16, 2013 Part II added (now complete)'.
- Sequential manuscript folio markers present throughout the transcription up to folio 288a/b ('1b)', 'p. 2a)', '287b)', '288a)').

**Other editions:**
- No complete critical edition of the entire Bṛhatkālottara exists. Selected sections have been critically edited in academic monographs and theses: Libbie Mills (2011, DPhil thesis, Oxford) edited and translated architecture/iconography chapters (prāsādalakṣaṇa); Peter C. Bisschop and Nirajan Kafle (2025, Śaiva Rites of Fasting and the Gift of Cattle, Napoli: UniorPress) edited parallel ritual sections; Nina Mirnig, Dominic Goodall, and H. Venkataraman have edited individual chapters (e.g., damanotsava, śānti rites). — Other manuscript witnesses preserved in Kathmandu include NAK MS 5-778 (NGMPP Reel A 42/8), NAK MS 4-131 (NGMPP Reel A 43/1), NAK MS pam. 779 (NGMPP Reel B 25/2), and NAK MS 5-4632 (NGMPP Reel B 118/7, also transcribed by Muktabodha as E00011).

**Translations:**
- No complete translation exists. Partial translations of chapters on architecture (prāsādalakṣaṇa) and iconometry were produced by Libbie Mills (2011, Oxford DPhil thesis; 2019). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete diplomatic e-text transcription of NAK palm-leaf MS pra-89 (filmed as NGMPP Reel No. B 29/59; 288 folios), comprising over 110 chapters. Muktabodha entered it in two parts, completing it on Dec. 16, 2013.

**Also known as:** Bṛhadkālottara, Bṛhatkālottaratantra, Bṛhadkālottaratantra, Kālottaramahātantra, Kālottara

**Attribution:** Revealed Śaiva scripture presented as a dialogue between Īśvara (Śiva) and Kārtikeya (Skanda / Krauñcasūdana).

The Bṛhatkālottara ('Great Kālottara', also known as the Kālottaramahātantra) is the most extensive and encyclopedic redaction of the Kālottara corpus of the Śaiva Siddhānta. Set as a dialogue between Īśvara and Kārtikeya, the text provides exhaustive treatments of initiation (dīkṣā), temple architecture (prāsādalakṣaṇa), iconometry, linga installation (liṅgapratiṣṭhā), expiatory rituals (prāyaścitta), propitiatory ceremonies (śānti), and public festivals such as the damanotsava. Demonstrably later than early Kālottara recensions (such as the Sārdhatriśatikālottara) and dated by scholars to circa the tenth–eleventh century CE, it represents a crucial milestone in the development of public, temple-oriented Śaivism.

Textual scholarship (Mallinson 2025) demonstrates that this text corresponds to a shortened recension of the Dattātreyayogaśāstra that transmits vv. 34–130 and 184–192 (treating aṣṭāṅgayoga and rājayoga).

**Also known as:** Dattātreyayogaśāstra (short recension)

**Attribution:** Framed as an exposition delivered by the deity-sage Dattātreya to his disciple Sāṅkṛti. In manuscript catalogs (GOML Madras, Muktabodha) and modern scholarship, the work is treated as anonymous, with Dattātreya functioning as the legendary revealer.

The Dattātreyabodha is a Sanskrit yoga manual framed as a dialogue between the sage Dattātreya and his pupil Sāṅkṛti. Textual research by James Mallinson has shown that it represents a shortened South Indian recension of the early Haṭhayoga treatise Dattātreyayogaśāstra (ca. 13th century), focusing specifically on eightfold yoga (aṣṭāṅgayoga) and rājayoga while omitting sections on mantrayoga, layayoga, and the haṭhayoga of Kapila. The work is celebrated for its egalitarian approach, teaching that anyone—regardless of age, disease, or religious affiliation—can attain yogic success through sustained practice rather than mere sectarian insignia or textual recitation.

He venerates his elder brother Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa as guru and Vasudhendra Tīrtha (pontiff of the Rāghavendra Maṭha, 1750–1761 CE) as his vidyāguru.

The Matatrayaikyaprakāśikā ('Illumination of the Unity of the Three Systems', also titled Trimataikyaprakāśikā) is an 18th-century Vedāntic treatise by Aiyyaṇācārya, an adherent of Dvaita Vedānta and direct disciple of Vasudhendra Tīrtha (fl. 1750–1761 CE). In three chapters (paricchedas), the work undertakes an irenic harmonization of the three major Vedāntic traditions—Advaita (Śaṅkara), Viśiṣṭādvaita (Rāmānuja), and Dvaita (Madhvācārya)—arguing that the primary tenets of Advaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita ultimately accord with the Dvaita siddhānta [37-38]. The text offers rare late-medieval testimony to inter-school Vedāntic reconciliation from an explicitly Dvaita perspective.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the 142-verse recension (Bagchi's recension B), running from verse 1 to verse 142 and concluding with the colophon 'iti macchendrapādāvatārite kāmarūpisthāne yoginī prasādāllabdha(m) akulavīraṃ samāptam'.

**Also known as:** Akulavīratantram, Akulavīra

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the siddha Matsyendranātha (invoked in the text as Mīnanātha and Macchendrapāda), seminal teacher of the Yoginī Kaula and early guru of the Nātha lineage. Indological consensus views the text as an anonymous Kaula scriptural treatise preserved within the Matsyendranātha corpus rather than a historical single-author composition.

The Akulavīratantra is an early Kaula / Yoginī Kaula scripture transmitted in the corpus attributed to Matsyendranātha. It teaches an uncompromising non-dual realization of ultimate reality as the Akulavīra ('Hero of the Transcendent'), attained as innate bliss (sahajānanda) beyond all conventional dharmas. The work critiques scholastic schools (Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, Mīmāṃsā, Somasiddhānta) and formal ritualism, emphasizing that spiritual freedom arises solely from dwelling in the unconditioned, all-pervading divine essence.

The Bhogakārikā ('Verses on Worldly Experience') by Sadyojyoti is a foundational philosophical treatise of the dualist Śaiva Siddhānta tradition and one of the eight canonical primers known collectively as the Aṣṭaprakaraṇa. In 146 verses, Sadyojyoti investigates the nature of bhoga (embodied experience of pleasure and pain), explaining how the bound individual soul (paśu)—whose innate powers of consciousness and action are obscured by beginningless primordial impurity (mala)—is endowed by Śiva with bodies, faculties, and worlds evolved out of māyā to experience karmic fruit and mature its impurity. Aghoraśiva's 12th-century vṛtti elucidates Sadyojyoti's concise verses line by line, rigorously defending the realist ontology of pati (Lord), paśu (soul), and pāśa (bond) against rival arguments from Sāṅkhya, Nyāya, and Buddhist philosophy.

The text is accompanied by the vyākhyā of the 12th-century Tamil Śaiva theologian Aghoraśiva, which unpacks the polemical nuances and technical vocabulary.

The Paramokṣanirāsakārikā is an early Śaiva Siddhānta polemical and doxographical treatise by Sadyojyoti (c. late 7th to early 8th century CE), accompanied here by the comprehensive commentary (vṛtti) of Kashmirian theologian Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha II (fl. c. 950–1000 CE). Across 59 kārikās expounding a passage of the Rauravasūtra, the work systematically refutes twenty non-Śaiva and heterodox soteriological viewpoints—including Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Vedānta, Pāñcarātra, Nyāya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, Jaina, and non-Siddhānta Śaiva models—showing that liberation cannot consist in mere isolation, dissolution, cessation of consciousness, or acquisition of mundane qualities. In their place, Sadyojyoti and Rāmakaṇṭha defend the orthodox Siddhānta doctrine that liberation is the manifestation of the soul's innate, co-equal Śiva-nature (śivatvavyakti), consisting in unobstructed omniscience and omnipotence, actualized through initiation (dīkṣā).

The Tattvaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Principles') is a canonical verse primer of Śaiva Siddhānta metaphysics traditionally attributed to King Bhojadeva of Dhārā (early 11th c.). - Muktabodha header: 'Editor : caṭṭopādhyāya'; 'Publisher : dhuṇḍhirāja gaṇeśa'; 'Publication year : Pre-1900'; 'Publication city : kaśi'
- Rasikamohana Caṭṭopādhyāya's edition is the one cited in the literature (Urban 2003, 2010: Navabhārata reprint 1996; 'Explaining mantras': 'ed. RMC'); Wikipedia gives it as Nababharat, Phālguna 1285 BS
- Web search found no Kāśī/Dhuṇḍhirāja Gaṇeśa imprint

**Other editions:**

- Bṛhat Tantrasāra, ed. Upendranath Mukhopadhyaya and Satishcandra Mukhopadhyaya, Kolkata: Basumati Sahitya Mandir, 1991. — Bengali-script edition (cited in 'Explaining mantras and the efficacy of ritual').
- Bṛhattantrasāra, ed. Rāmakumāra Rāya, Vārāṇasī: Prācya Prakāśana, 1985. — Devanāgarī edition with Hindi prefatory matter (Wellcome Collection record).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Five paricchedas. The work closes with the author's final verses and the colophon 'iti mahāmahopādhyāyaśrīkṛṣṇānandavāgīśabhaṭṭācāryaviracitas tantrasāraḥ samāptaḥ' (segment 22585). A separate pariśiṣṭa follows, ending 'pariśiṣṭaṃ sampūrṇa'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Bṛhattantrasāra (Tantrasāra), paricchedas 1–5 (Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa, root text)
- Pariśiṣṭa (devatāviśeṣāṇāṃ mantrastotrādiprakaraṇa) (appendix of mantras and stotras for particular deities (Gaṅgā etc.), placed after the author's final colophon; presumably added in the printed edition)

**Also known as:** Tantrasāra

**Attribution:** Authored by Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa Bhaṭṭācārya of Navadvīpa, late 16th century CE.

A large Tantric ritual compendium (nibandha) by Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa of Navadvīpa (16th–17th c.), compiled from quotations of numerous tantras (Jñānārṇava, Nigamakalpadruma, Kriyāsāra, Viśvasāra, Nīlatantra and others). In five paricchedas it covers the qualifications of guru and disciple, initiation, puraścaraṇa, general pūjā, and the mantras, worship, kavacas and stotras of many deities, especially the Mahāvidyās (Kālī, Tārā etc.), and finally the upacāras of worship. It became the standard handbook of Bengali Śākta ritual. This e-text adds an appendix of mantras and stotras for further deities.

- Matches the text layout, chapter colophon ('iti śrīkālīdāsamahākaviviracitā cidgaganacandrikā sampūrṇā'), and the 8 concluding verses of the 1937 Calcutta edition.

**Other editions:**
- Karra Agnihotra Śāstrī (ed. & comm.), Cidgaganacandrikā with the commentary Divyacakorikā, 2 parts, Letukuru / Amalapuram: Śrī Śāradā Printing Press, 1941–1943. — First edition with the modern Sanskrit commentary Divyacakorikā.
- Raghunātha Miśra (ed. & comm.), Cidgaganacandrikā of Kālidāsa with the commentary Kramaprakāśikā, Sarasvatībhavana-Granthamālā, Vol. 115, Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit Vishvavidyalaya, 1980. — Critical edition with editor's Sanskrit commentary Kramaprakāśikā.

**Translations:**

- S. Mahalakshmi, Cidgagana Candrikā: A Tantric Study, Ph.D. dissertation, University of Madras, 2017. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Cidgaganacandrikā across all four vimarśas (totaling 312 verses), followed by 8 concluding verses and the closing blessing 'śubhaṃ kulakramaṃ kuryāt'.

**Also known as:** Kramastotrapañcikā, Cidgagana-candrikā

**Attribution:** In verses 3, 305, 306, and the chapter colophons, the author refers to himself as Kālidāsa ('servant of Kālī'), leading early editors (e.g. Swami Trivikrama Tīrtha) and traditional commentators to attribute the work to Kālidāsa. Modern scholarship (notably Navjivan Rastogi and Alexis Sanderson) has established that the work was composed by the 12th-century Krama master Śrīvatsa, who composed it as an expanded verse commentary (pañcikā) on Siddhanātha's (Erakanātha's) Kramastuti.

The Cidgaganacandrikā ('Moonlight in the Sky of Consciousness') is an influential 12th-century philosophical and liturgical poem of the Krama (Mahānaya / Kālīkrama) tradition of Kashmir Śaivism, composed by Śrīvatsa. Structured in four reflections (vimarśas) comprising 312 verses, the work functions as an elaborate poetic commentary (pañcikā) on Siddhanātha's Kramastuti. It eulogizes Goddess Kālī as supreme Parāśakti, synthesizing non-dual Śākta-Śaiva metaphysics with esoteric ritual doctrines through the exposition of cyclical emanations, the circle of the thirteen Kālīs, and the Śākta path (śāktopāya) leading to liberation.

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete Sāmānyapāda (paṭalas 1–14), which constitutes the first quarter (Volume 1) of the fourfold Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati.

**Also known as:** Tantrasārapaddhati, Tantrapaddhati, Tantrasāra, Īśānapaddhati, Siddhāntasāra

**Attribution:** Composed by Īśānaśivagurudeva (also designated Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra in colophons), an authority on ritual and temple rites in medieval Kerala, usually dated to the late 11th or 12th century CE.

The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati is an encyclopedic manual of ritual, temple consecration, and mantra-śāstra composed by the Kerala Śaiva authority Īśānaśivagurudeva (c. 11th–12th century CE). This opening division, the Sāmānyapāda (paṭalas 1–14), provides the common preliminary framework for ritual activity, including the classifications and recitation of mantras, the nature of letters (mātṛkā), the dimensions and preparation of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and diagrams (maṇḍala), morning ablutions, and the rites of the sacred fire (agnikalpa). Synthesizing Śaivasiddhānta tenets with regional Kerala tantric traditions, it serves as a key witness to medieval South Indian ritual literature.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains paṭalas 1–30 of the Kriyāpāda (the first section of the Uttarārdha / Uparibhāga), corresponding exactly to Volume III of the editio princeps. The complete four-volume work comprises four pādas: Sāmānyapāda (14 paṭalas) and Mantrapāda (38 paṭalas) in the Pūrvārdha, followed by Kriyāpāda (66 paṭalas) and Yogapāda (1 paṭala) in the Uttarārdha.

**Also known as:** Siddhāntasāra, Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati, Īśānapaddhati

**Attribution:** Consistently attributed to Īśānaśivagurudeva (or Īśānaśivagurudevamiśra) in the text colophons. The author was a prominent Śaivasiddhānta ritualist active in Kerala, commonly dated to the late 11th or 12th century CE.

The Īśānaśivagurudevapaddhati (also titled Siddhāntasāra) is an encyclopedic Śaivasiddhānta ritual compendium composed by the Kerala master Īśānaśivagurudeva around the late 11th to 12th century CE. This volume preserves the first half of the Kriyāpāda (paṭalas 1–30), covering the theological foundations of Śaivism, daily liturgy (nityapūjā), the tiered structure of Śaiva initiation (dīkṣā), and extensive treatises on temple architecture, vāstu, and iconography (vimāna, upapīṭha, adhiṣṭhāna). It remains a foundational primary source for medieval South Indian and Kerala temple ritual traditions.

**Works in this e-text:**

- Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (Abhinavagupta, commentary)

**Attribution:** The root kārikās are by Utpaladeva (fl. c. 925–975 CE). The primary commentary (vimarśinī, known as the Laghvīvimarśinī to distinguish it from the longer Vivṛtivimarśinī) is by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). The sub-commentary (ṭīkā/vyākhyā titled Bhāskarī) is by the late 18th-century Kashmiri scholar Bhāskarakaṇṭha.

The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (often termed the Laghvīvimarśinī) is Abhinavagupta's shorter commentary on Utpaladeva's foundational treatise, the Īśvarapratyabhijñākārikā, transmitted here with the eighteenth-century sub-commentary Bhāskarī by Bhāskarakaṇṭha. Structured across four adhikāras (Jñāna-, Kriyā-, Āgama-, and Tattvasaṃgraha-), the text systematically expounds the core doctrine of the Pratyabhijñā school: spiritual liberation is achieved through the recognition that the individual self is identical with the supreme conscious agent (Maheśvara/Śiva), who freely projects and absorbs the universe through his svātantrya. The commentary undertakes sustained philosophical critique against Buddhist epistemologists, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Advaita Vedānta, articulating a rigorous non-dual Śaiva philosophy of dynamic consciousness and self-awareness.

**Attribution:** The root Upaniṣads are traditional Śākta/Kaula texts affiliated with the Saubhāgyakāṇḍa of the Atharvaveda and the Ṛgveda. The commentaries and the Mahāyāgakrama / Bhāvanopaniṣatprayogavidhi were composed by the 18th-century Śrīvidyā exegete and polymath Bhāskararāya Makhin (Umānandanātha, fl. c. 1690–1785).

This compendium contains four esoteric Śākta/Kaula Upaniṣads—the Bhāvanopaniṣad, the Bahvṛcopaniṣad (here called Bahvṛcavedīyā Śrīlalitāmahātripurasundaryupaniṣad), the Devyatharvaśīrṣopaniṣad, and the Kaulopaniṣad—along with commentaries and liturgical instructions (prayogavidhi) by the 18th-century Śrīvidyā scholar Bhāskararāya. The texts formulate a nondual synthesis of Kaula ritual and Vedāntic metaphysics, equating the goddess Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī with absolute consciousness, the cosmos, the Śrīcakra, and the psychophysical body of the practitioner. Bhāskararāya's commentary internalizes esoteric Kaula worship as contemplative meditation (bhāvanā) on the identity between macrocosm and microcosm.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the 60-verse recension edited in KSTS 26, comprising 60 Kashmiri vākhs, 60 Sanskrit metrical verses, an introductory Sanskrit śloka, and a concluding dedicatory śloka and colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Lalleśvarīvākyāni (Lalleśvarī, root text)
- Arthacchāyāpadya (Bhāskarakaṇṭha, translation)

**Also known as:** Lallāvākyāni, Lallā-Vākyāni, Lallā-vākh, Sayings of Lalla, Sayings of Lal Ded

**Attribution:** The root verses are 60 Kashmiri quatrains (vākhs) attributed to the 14th-century female mystic Lallā (Lalleśvarī / Lal Dĕd). Each Kashmiri verse is paired with a metrical Sanskrit verse translation (arthacchāyāpadya) composed by Rājānaka Bhāskara, identified with the 18th-century Kashmiri Śaiva commentator Rājānaka Bhāskarakaṇṭha (commentator on the Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī).

The Lalleśvarīvākyāni ('Sayings of Lalleśvarī') comprises 60 mystical Kashmiri quatrains (vākhs) by the 14th-century poet-saint Lallā (Lal Dĕd), accompanied verse-for-verse by Sanskrit metrical translations (arthacchāyāpadya) composed by the 18th-century Kashmiri Śaiva scholar Rājānaka Bhāskarakaṇṭha. Rooted in nondual Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism, the verses convey internal yogic absorption, prāṇāyāma, mind control, critique of ritualism and external caste distinctions, and the nondual realization of the Self as Śiva. As the earliest attested literary compositions in the Kashmiri language, Lallā's verses hold foundational importance in Kashmiri literary and religious culture, while Bhāskarakaṇṭha's translation represents their earliest formal reception in classical Sanskrit scholarship.

The Mahānayaprakāśa ('Illumination of the Great Way') of Rājānaka Śitikaṇṭha is an important philosophical and ritual treatise belonging to the non-dual Śākta-Śaiva Krama tradition of medieval Kashmir. It comprises ninety-four vernacular verses (in Old Kashmiri / Apabhraṃśa / sarvabhāṣā) accompanied by the author's extensive Sanskrit prose auto-commentary (vivṛti), arranged across chapters designated as udayas. The work details the esoteric cosmology and internal esoteric liturgy of the Krama school centered on Kālī and the cycles of goddesses, presenting esoteric practices of trans-conceptual absorption (haṭhapāka, alaṃgrāsa) and internal pilgrimage where the practitioner's body serves as the sacred field (pīṭha).

Divided into nine ullāsas, it systematically presents the sequential and non-sequential cycles of divine manifestation and reabsorption, focusing on the wheels of deities (cakras), the pīṭhas, and the twelve forms of Kālī. It emphasizes the direct transmission of non-dual realization through the grace and penetrating glance of the guru (gurudṛkpāta) as superior to external ritual practices.

He was an adept of the Krama (Mahārtha) and Pratyabhijñā traditions active in South India (at Cidambaram in the Cōḻa country) circa the late 12th to 14th century.

The Mahārthamañjarī ('Bouquet of the Great Meaning') accompanied by the Parimala ('Fragrance') auto-commentary is an important synthesis of non-dual Śaiva philosophy, integrating the esoteric goddess cycles of the Krama (Kālīkrama/Mahārtha) system with Pratyabhijñā and Spanda doctrines. Composed in South India at Cidambaram by Maheśvarānanda (Gorakṣa), the work expounds supreme non-dual consciousness unfolding through sensory cognition, the thirty-six tattvas, and internal ritual. The extensive Parimala commentary quotes numerous rare and lost Krama, Pratyabhijñā, and Kula texts (including Abhinavagupta's Kramakeli), demonstrating the transmission and vitality of Kashmiri tantric traditions in medieval Tamil South India.

The Mṛgendrāgama (or Mṛgendratantra) is an authoritative scripture of dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally regarded as an upāgama of the Kāmikāgama. This e-text contains its philosophical Vidyāpāda and practical Yogapāda, which formulate core Siddhānta ontology across the categories of pati (the Lord), paśu (the bound individual), and pāśa (fetters/bonds), followed by an exposition of tantric yoga. **Attribution:** The root Netratantra is a Mantramārga Śaiva scriptural tantra presented as a dialogue between Śiva and the Goddess without a historical author. The commentary Netroddyota is composed by the 11th-century Kashmiri nondualist master Kṣemarāja, disciple of Abhinavagupta.

The Netratantra ('Tantra of the Eye'), also known as Mṛtyuñjayabhaṭṭāraka or Amṛteśatantra, is an influential scripture of the Mantramārga Śaiva tradition in 22 chapters (adhikāras), composed in Kashmir between roughly 700 and 850 CE. Centering on the worship of Amṛteśvara and Amṛtalakṣmī through the conquering of death (mṛtyuñjaya) and the eye-mantra, it expounds esoteric yoga alongside comprehensive apotropaic rites, exorcism of malignant spirits, and pacification rituals essential to early medieval royal religion. The present e-text preserves the full root scripture accompanied by the master commentary Netroddyota by the 11th-century Kashmiri theologian Kṣemarāja, which integrates these dualistic Mantramārga rituals into nondualist Trika-Pratyabhijñā philosophy.

The Parātrīśikātātparyadīpikā is an anonymous medieval Śākta-Trika metrical commentary comprising 536 anuṣṭubh verses on the Parātrīśikā (the dialogue on supreme Goddess-consciousness from the Rudrayāmala). Composed in Chidambaram (Vyāghrapurī) in South India, it represents the South Indian transmission and adaptation of non-dual Śaivism based on the Parātrīśikālaghuvṛtti ascribed to Abhinavagupta. The work provides an esoteric exposition of phonemic cosmology (mātṛkā and mālinī), the manifestation of the thirty-six tattvas, and spiritual liberation through non-dual Śiva-Śakti realization.

The digest is renowned for its vast collation and systematic synthesis of authoritative citations from tantras, purāṇas, and paddhatis.

The Mahānirvāṇatantra is an influential Śākta work structured as a discourse between Sadāśiva and the Goddess (Ādyā Śakti) on ritual and moral duty in the degraded Kali Yuga. Unusually among Tantras, it devotes extensive sections to social ethics, duties of the householder, sacramental ceremonies (saṃskāras), and civil law regarding marriage, property, and inheritance.

The Kriyāsāra ('Essence of Practice') by Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya (c. 14th–15th century CE) is a major Vīraśaiva metrical treatise harmonizing Śaiva ritual, ethical conduct, and devotional observance with the philosophical framework of the Brahmasūtras. ## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text runs from the edition's title and Bhāskararāya's introductory verses to the final colophon, i.e. all eight viśrāmas: 1–5 on the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava, ending 'viśrāmaḥ pañcamo'bhavat' (seg. 5481), and 6–8 on the Yoginīhṛdaya. Page markers of ASS 56 run from p. 2 to p. 388. Two passages are missing, and the transcribers flag them: printed pp. 25–40 (seg. 792, in viśrāma 1) and pp. 105–112 (seg. 2841, in viśrāma 2). About 24 pages of a c. 388-page volume (c. 6%) are lost, including the colophon of viśrāma 1. Other skipped page numbers (15, 138, 233) seem to be only missing markers; the text there is not flagged as missing.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (pūrvacatuḥśatī of the Vāmakeśvaratantra) (root text (viśrāmas 1–5))
- Yoginīhṛdaya (uttaracatuḥśatī) (root text (viśrāmas 6–8))
- Setubandha (Bhāskararāya, commentary on both)

**Also known as:** Vāmakeśvaratantra (with Setubandha), Vāmakeśvarīmata, Catuḥśatī, Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇavatantra, Vāmakeśvaratantrāntargatanityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (title of ASS 56)

**Attribution:** Both root texts are anonymous scriptural tantras of Śrīvidyā. The Setubandha is by Bhāskararāya (dīkṣā name Bhāsurānandanātha), son of Gambhīrarāja Dīkṣita, 18th century. The final colophon reads 'iti ... gambhīrarājabhāratīdikṣitasūnunā bhāsurānandanāthadīkṣābhidhānena bhāskararāyeṇa praṇīto nityāṣoḍaśikārṇavavyākhyānātmā setubandhaḥ saṃpūrṇaḥ' (segs. 11685–11690). Introductory verse 2 states that he comments on both 'pūrvottaracatuḥśatyau'.

The Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava (the pūrvacatuḥśatī of the Vāmakeśvaratantra) and the Yoginīhṛdaya (its uttaracatuḥśatī) are foundational scriptures of Śākta Śrīvidyā. The first sets out the outer worship of Tripurasundarī and the sixteen Nityās: mantras, the Śrīcakra, mudrās and ritual applications. The second treats the inner meaning of cakra, mantra and pūjā. This e-text gives both with the Setubandha, the extensive commentary by the 18th-century scholar Bhāskararāya, which uses Mīmāṃsā methods to treat the two parts as one tantra in eight viśrāmas.

The unique surviving manuscript testifies to the pedagogical continuation and exegetical synthesis of the non-dual Pratyabhijñā system in pre-modern Kashmir.

The Śāktapramoda ('Delight of the Śāktas') is a comprehensive late 19th-century liturgical digest (paddhati) compiled by Rājā Devanandanasiṃha Bahādur of Sheohar, Bihar, completed in 1889/1890 CE. It gathers sixteen distinct ritual manuals ('tantras'): ten dedicated to the Ten Mahāvidyās (Kālī, Tārā, Ṣoḍaśī, Bhuvaneśvarī, Chinnamastā, Tripurabhairavī, Dhūmāvatī, Bagalāmukhī, Mātaṅgī, and Kamalā), one dedicated to maiden worship (Kumārītantra), and five to the Pañcāyatana deities (Śiva, Durgā, Sūrya, Gaṇeśa, and Viṣṇu). For each deity, the manual provides iconographic meditation verses (dhyāna), mantra extraction procedures (mantroddhāra), yantra diagrams, nyāsa rites, daily worship sequences (saparyāpaddhati), kavacas, hṛdaya stotras, and litanies of names (śatanāma and sahasranāma) compiled from classical tantric scriptures.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_taaraabhaktisudhaarnavaHK`
