**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Narasiṃha Ṭhakkura. Tārābhaktisudhārṇavaḥ. Edited by Pañcānana Tarkasāṃkhyavedāntatīrtha [Bhaṭṭācārya], with a general preface by Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe). Tantrik Texts, vol. 21. Calcutta: Sanskrit Book Depot, 1940 (fascicles begun 1934).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00055), input under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (revision 0: February 9, 2009).

**Evidence:**
- The Muktabodha header (lines 1–15) explicitly names catalog no. M00055, editors Pañcānana Tarka and Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe), series Tantrik Texts vol. 21, and publisher Sanskrit Book Depot, Calcutta, 1940.
- The Sanskrit front matter (lines 19–22) reads: 'paṇḍitapravara-śrīpañcānana tarka-sāṃkhya-vedāntatīrtha-sampāditaḥ / ṭantrik ṭexts ṣeries / Calcutta 1934'.
- Embedded page break markers in the e-text (e.g. 'p. 2)' at line 46 and '165)' at line 5078) match the pagination of the 1940 Tantrik Texts edition.

**Other editions:**
- Narasiṃha Ṭhakkura. Tārābhaktisudhārṇavaḥ. Edited by Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. Tantrik Texts, vol. 21. Delhi: Bharatiya Vidya Prakashan, 1983. — Reprint of the 1940 Calcutta Tantrik Texts edition.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 11 taraṅgas ('waves'), ending at line 13370 with the colophon of the eleventh taraṅga (ekādaśastaraṅgaḥ).

**Also known as:** Tārā-bhakti-sudhārṇava

**Attribution:** Composed by Narasiṃha Ṭhakkura of Mithila (fl. late 17th century), a descendant of the Maithila scholar Govinda Ṭhakkura (author of the Kāvyapradīpa). In the opening verses (vv. 3–4), he reveres his guru Gadādhara, from whom he received instruction in diverse tantras before composing this digest.

The Tārābhaktisudhārṇava ('Ocean of the Nectar of Devotion to Tārā') is an extensive 17th-century Śākta ritual digest (nibandha) dedicated to the worship of the Mahāvidyā Tārā in her various forms (including Ugratārā, Ekajaṭā, and Nīlasarasvatī). Divided into eleven taraṅgas ('waves'), it provides comprehensive ritual guidance on guru-disciple requirements, initiation (dīkṣā), daily worship, mantra recitation (japa), yantra designs, nyāsa, puraścaraṇa, and esoteric rites such as śavasādhana, compiling canonical passages from scriptures such as the Rudrayāmala, Brahmayāmala, and Tārātantra.

**Evidence:**

**Other editions:**

- Śrīlalitāsahasranāmastotram with 'Saubhāgyabhāskara' by Bhāskararāya, edited by Batukanātha Śāstrī Khiste and Śītalā Prasāda Upādhyāya, Benares: Sarasvati Bhavan Granthamala, Vol. 79, 1944 (reprinted Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit University, 2003). — Standard scholarly edition in the Sarasvati Bhavan series.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Lalitāsahasranāma (including the introductory Pūrvapīṭhikā dialogue between Hayagrīva and Agastya, the 1000 names, and the Uttarapīṭhikā/Phalaśruti) together with Bhāskararāya's exhaustive commentary arranged in twelve kalās.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Lalitāsahasranāmastotra (root text)
- Saubhāgyabhāskara (Bhāskararāya, commentary)

**Also known as:** Lalitāsahasranāma with Saubhāgyabhāskara, Lalitāsahasranāmastotram with the commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara, Brahmāṇḍapurāṇottarabhāgīyaśrīlalitāsahasranāma with Saubhāgyabhāskara, Saubhāgyabhāskara, Lalitārahasyanāmasahasrabhāṣya

**Attribution:** The root hymn is traditionally transmitted in the Lalitopākhyāna (Uttarabhāga) of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa. The commentary Saubhāgyabhāskara was composed by Bhāskararāya Makhin (dīkṣā-name Bhāsurānandanātha), son of Gambhīrarāya Dīkṣita and Konamāmbā, and completed in 1728 CE (Vikrama Saṃvat 1785).

The Lalitāsahasranāmastotra is the foremost devotional and liturgical hymn of the Śrīvidyā tradition, situated in the Lalitopākhyāna (Uttarabhāga) of the Brahmāṇḍapurāṇa as a revelation delivered by Hayagrīva to the sage Agastya. Bhāskararāya's Saubhāgyabhāskara, completed in 1728 CE, is the definitive and encyclopedic commentary on the hymn, arranged across twelve sections termed kalās. The exegesis synthesizes Śākta Tantric theology, Śrīcakra and kuṇḍalinī metaphysics, Advaita Vedānta, and rigorous Mīmāṃsā and Vyākaraṇa hermeneutics to elucidate the esoteric multi-layered significance of each divine epithet.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_sivaagamaadimaahaatmyamHK`

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished transcript: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) Transcript No. T 1059 (111 pp.), copied from a palm-leaf manuscript belonging to G. Swaminatha Gurukkal of Tiruvāvaḍutuṟai (MS L. No. 154a).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog number M00058), data-entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (revision date February 13, 2009).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header lines 4–5 state: 'Author : jñānaprakāśa - śālivāṭipuranivāsi / Manuscript : IFP transcript 1059 copied from a ms belonging to g. swaminatha gurukkal, tiruvadudurai. MS l no. 154 a'.
- Explicit page break markers in the body text (e.g., 'p. 2)', 'p. 3)', 'p. 29)') correspond to the pagination of IFP Transcript T 1059.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the compendium according to the manuscript transcript, running from the opening polemical discussions on Āgamic prāmāṇya through section markers (e.g. śivāgamamāhātmya, śivadīkṣāmāhātmya, śivabhaktamāhātmya) to the final colophon in line 1365. Lacunae in the exemplar are represented by asterisks and dashes.

**Also known as:** Śivāgamādimāhātmya, Śivāgamādimāhātmyasaṅgraha, Śaivāgamādimāhātmyasaṃgraha

**Attribution:** Authored by the 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta theologian Jñānaprakāśa of Śālivāṭipura (Tirunelveli, Tamil Nadu; originally from Jaffna, Sri Lanka), author of the Śivajñānabodhavṛtti and Pauṣkarabhāṣya. In the closing homage (line 1366), he venerates his preceptors Devaśikhāmaṇi and Ṣaṇmukha.

The Śivāgamādimāhātmyasaṃgraha is a 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta doctrinal and apologetic compendium compiled by Jñānaprakāśa of Śālivāṭipura (Tirunelveli). Opening with a philosophical defense of the divine authorship and validity (prāmāṇya) of the Śaivāgamas against Mīmāṃsaka and smārta objections, the text establishes that both the Vedas and the Āgamas are authentic revelations produced by Paramaśiva. It systematically collates passages from the 28 Siddhānta Āgamas, the Upāgamas, the Purāṇas, and the Sūtasaṃhitā to vindicate Āgamic preeminence, the power of Śaiva initiation (śivadīkṣā), the status of devotees (bhaktas), and traditional sectarian observances such as the wearing of tripuṇḍra and rudrākṣa beads.

# Vyomavyāpistava with Laghuṭīkā

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_vyomavyaapistavaHK`

**Author:** Bhaṭṭarāmakaṇṭha, Vedajñāna

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Manuscript transcript: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) transcript T. 128 (pp. 1–70), copied from a paper manuscript of the Vyomavyāpistava preserved at the Tiruvāvaṭutuṟai Ātīṉam (Thiruvavaduthurai Adheenam).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00059), keyed by Muktabodha staff under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (revision date: February 13, 2009).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha file header segment [6]: 'Manuscript : IFP transcript T0128 which itself is copied from a paper manuscript of vyomavyaapistavam belonging to tiruvavaduthurai adheenam. tiruvavaduthurai'
- Embedded transcript page markers within the e-text (e.g. 'p. 2)', 'p. 27)') corresponding directly to IFP transcript T. 128

**Other editions:**
- Nibedita Rout, Vyomavyāpistava of Rāmakaṇṭha with the commentary (laghuṭīkā) of Vedajñāna (provisional edition based on IFP transcripts T. 112, T. 128, T. 434, and Göttingen manuscript Schrader 121, unpublished; cited in Tāntrikābhidhānakośa III, 2013). — Provisional critical edition prepared for the Tāntrikābhidhānakośa project.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Vyomavyāpistava (90 āryā verses analyzing and glossing the 81 padas of the Vyomavyāpin mantra) accompanied throughout by the complete Laghuṭīkā of Vedajñāna.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vyomavyāpistava (Bhaṭṭarāmakaṇṭha, root text)
- Laghuṭīkā (Vedajñāna, commentary)

**Also known as:** Vyomavyāpistava with Laghuṭippaṇī, Vyomavyāpistavavyākhyā

**Attribution:** The root hymn of 90 āryā verses is attributed in verse 3 of the commentary (guruṇā rāmakaṇṭhena kṛtasya...) to Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (traditionally identified with the 10th-century Kashmirian Śaiva Siddhānta master Rāmakaṇṭha II, though this attribution is not corroborated by cross-references in his undisputed philosophical works). The commentator Vedajñāna (Vedajñāna II / Nigamajñāna II / Maṟaiñāṉatēcikar) was a prominent 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta guru active at Cidambaram, who also authored an expanded, unpublished Bṛhaṭṭīkā on the same work.

The Vyomavyāpistava is a Śaiva Siddhānta hymn of 90 āryā stanzas expounding the theological and esoteric significance of the 81 distinct words (padas) that form the 368-syllable Vyomavyāpin mantra. Structured around liturgical worship on the nine-lotus mandala (navanābhamaṇḍala) documented in Āgamas such as the Mataṅga and Devīkālottara, the stanzas explain each pada as a manifestation of Paramaśiva. It is preserved here with the concise Laghuṭīkā of the 16th-century Cidambaram theologian Vedajñāna II, which provides word-by-word grammatical and ritual glosses.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Prāṇatoṣiṇī, tantraśāstrāt saṃkalayya viracitā, edited by Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācārya, Calcutta: Kalikātā Yantra (Sarasvatī Yantra), 3rd ed., 1898.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog number M00060), keyed by Muktabodha staff under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.

**Evidence:**
- The e-text title page transcription (lines 10–18) reproduces the edition's Sanskrit title page: 'prāṇatoṣiṇī śrīrāmatoṣaṇa bhaṭṭācāryeṇa tantraśāstrāt saṃkalayya viracitā | Vi, e upādhidhāriṇā paṇḍitakulapatinā śrījīvānandavidyāsāgarabhaṭṭāacaryyeṇa prakāśitā | Kalikātānagare Kalikātāyantre mudritā'.

- Muktabodha catalog header records catalog number M00060 entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski.

**Other editions:**
- Prāṇatoṣiṇī, edited and printed under the patronage of the Biswas family in Bengali script, Calcutta, 1859. — Editio princeps.
- Prāṇatoṣiṇī Tantra, edited by Ram Kumar Rai, Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1982 (reprint 1992). — Devanagari edition.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains Kāṇḍa 5 (Bhaktikāṇḍa), paricchedas 1–3 only (out of 7 paricchedas in Bhaktikāṇḍa, and out of 7 kāṇḍas in the complete Prāṇatoṣiṇī). The file opens with the summary table of contents (nirghaṇṭa) for all 7 paricchedas of Kāṇḍa 5 (lines 20–177), followed by pariccheda 1 (Gaṇeśaprakaraṇa), pariccheda 2 (Sūryaprakaraṇa), and pariccheda 3 (Śivaprakaraṇa), terminating at line 2797 with 'iti śrīprāṇatoṣiṇyāṃ pañcame bhaktikāṇḍe śivaprakaraṇakathanarūpastṛtīyaḥ paricchedaḥ'.

**Also known as:** Prāṇatoṣiṇī Tantra, Prāṇatoṣiṇītantra

**Attribution:** Compiled in 1820 CE (Śaka 1742) by the Bengali tantric scholar Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya, a great-grandson of Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa, under the patronage of the zamindar Prāṇakṛṣṇa Biśvās of Khardah.

The Prāṇatoṣiṇī is a major nineteenth-century Śākta tantric digest (nibandha) compiled in Bengal in 1820 CE by Rāmatoṣaṇa Bhaṭṭācārya under the patronage of Prāṇakṛṣṇa Biśvās. Gathering and harmonizing material from dozens of scriptural Tantras and Purāṇas, it covers theology, ritual worship, initiation, and occult practices across seven kāṇḍas. This portion contains paricchedas 1 to 3 of the fifth kāṇḍa (Bhaktikāṇḍa), detailing the devotional worship, pūjāvidhi, nyāsa, and stotras dedicated to Gaṇeśa, Sūrya, and Śiva, including extensive treatises on the classification and worship of bāṇaliṅgas and rasaliṅgas.

- Explicit printed page markers of Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara's 1898 edition are preserved in the text, e.g., 'p. 691)' at line 30, 'p. 736)' at line 1421, and 'p. 782)' at line 2816.
- The e-text concludes at line 11609 with the final colophon: 'iti śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī samāptā'.

**Other editions:**
- Prāṇatoṣiṇī, compiled by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra. Khardah / Calcutta: Prāṇakṛṣṇa Biśvās, 1820 CE (Śaka 1742). — Editio princeps.
- Prāṇatoṣiṇī, in Tantrasārādivividhatantrasaṃgraha, ed. Rasikamohana Caṭṭopādhyāya. Calcutta, 1877–1884 (Bengali script). — Nineteenth-century compendium edition.
- Prāṇatoṣiṇī, ed. with Bengali translation by Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. Calcutta: Vasumatī Sāhitya Mandir, 1928. — Standard Bengali edition with translation.
- Prāṇatoṣiṇī Tantra, ed. Ram Kumar Rai. Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1980s. — Modern Devanagari reprint.

**Translations:**
- Arthur Avalon (Sir John Woodroffe), Principles of Tantra (London: Luzac & Co., 1914–1916) and The Serpent Power (Madras: Ganesh & Co., 1919). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the concluding portion of Kāṇḍa 5 (Bhaktikāṇḍa, pariccheda 4, pp. 691–782, covering Dvārakāśilā, Viṣṇu, Devī/Mahāvidyā rituals, and Kumārīpūjā), the full Kāṇḍa 6 (Jñānakāṇḍa, lines 2816–7038, covering yogic anatomy, nāḍīs, cakras, and svarodaya), and the full Kāṇḍa 7 (Nirguṇakāṇḍa, lines 7038–11609, treating paśu, vīra, and divya bhāvas, Kaula worship, and closing recipes), ending at line 11609 with 'iti śrīprāṇatoṣiṇī samāptā'.

**Also known as:** Prāṇatoṣiṇī Tantra, Prāṇatoṣaṇī, Prāṇatoṣiṇī part 6

**Attribution:** Compiled around 1820 CE (Śaka 1742) by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra Bhaṭṭācārya, great-grandson of the noted tantric scholar Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa, under the patronage of Prāṇakṛṣṇa Biśvās (Biswas) of Khardah.

The Prāṇatoṣiṇī is an extensive Śākta tantric digest (nibandha) compiled in 1820 CE by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra under the patronage of Prāṇakṛṣṇa Biśvās. Bringing together citations from scores of Tantras, Purāṇas, and ritual compendia, it forms an encyclopedic reference work of the late traditional Bengali Śākta school. This segment contains the latter part of the Bhaktikāṇḍa (worship of sacred stones and Kumārīpūjā), the entire Jñānakāṇḍa (yogic subtle physiology, cakras, and breath divination in Svarodaya), and the entire Nirguṇakāṇḍa (the three spiritual temperaments or bhāvas, Kaula worship, and culminating verses of the entire text).

**Attribution:** An anonymous Śākta-Kaula scripture transmitted in Nepal, framed as a dialogue between Kuleśvara and Kulasundarī situated in the Karavīra cremation ground, claiming affiliation with the Śiraścheda lineage.

The Parātantra is a late medieval syncretic Śākta-Kaula scripture preserved in Nepal, framing its revelation within the Śiraścheda tradition. It systematically harmonizes the six transmissions (ṣaḍāmnāya) by assigning major Śākta lineages and deities—including Kubjikā (Western), Tripurasundarī (Southern), Guhyakālī and Siddhilakṣmī (Northern), and Vajrayoginī (Lower)—to six thrones, synthesizing them as manifestations of the singular supreme Goddess Parā. The text holds significant importance for the history of late medieval Newar esoteric liturgy and court ritual in the Kathmandu Valley.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished: IFP (Institut Français de Pondichéry) paper transcript T0351 (composite transcript of South Indian palm-leaf manuscripts, ca. 366 pp.); no printed edition of this compilation is known.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00063), entered by Muktabodha staff under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (2011).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha file header explicitly states: 'Catalog number : M00063', 'Uniform title: sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha', 'Manuscript : IFP transcript T0351', 'Description: Transcription of IFP transcript T0351.'
- Transcript page markers throughout the e-text ('p. 2)' ... 'p. 365)') and folio markers of the underlying manuscripts ('(4ā)', '(102ā)', '(110ā)'); transcript notes such as '(etadantena puṭamidaṃ samāptam ...)'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text covers IFP transcript T0351 from p. 1 to ca. p. 366 (page markers 'p. 2)' ... 'p. 365)', last marker misprinted 'p. 336)'). The Sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha itself is acephalous (begins at fol. 4a in the middle of dantadhāvana rules) and has section colophons (snāna/anuṣṭhāna/sūryapūjā, bhojanavidhi; scribal colophons naming Vedanāyaka Paṇḍita, Nāgagiri Paṇḍita and Sadāśiva Gurukkal), with transcript notes on disordered or lost bundles (e.g. around pp. 159–164). After it come the appended ritual texts listed under included_works. The e-text ends mid-list in a prose nityapūjā outline ('karaśuddhidaśa ---'), without colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha (root text (anthology of Āgama quotations on daily ritual; acephalous, begins at fol. 4a))
- Nityapūjāvidhi (attributed to the Kāmikāgama) (appended text (colophon 'iti śrīmat kāmikākhye mahātantre nityapūjā samāptā'))
- Nityakarmavidhi; grāmaśānti and pratiṣṭhā procedures; vāstu worship (appended ritual manuals)
- Śivakavaca (Brahmottarakhaṇḍa, adhyāya 34), Sūryakavaca, Vighneśvarakavaca (appended stotras)
- Snapana and prāyaścitta paṭalas from the Vātulatantra (appended extracts)
- Vināyakavratavidhipaṭala (attributed to the Aṃśumat) (appended extract)
- Nityapūjā outline (appended prose summary (breaks off))

**Also known as:** Sakalāgamasaṅgraha, Sakalāgamasāra

**Attribution:** The work is an anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta ritual compendium (saṅgraha) compiling verses from canonical Śaivāgamas. Although some modern catalog notes have tentatively associated it with the 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta teacher Nigamajñānadeśika, this attribution is not supported by the manuscript colophons or Indological scholarship.

An anonymous South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta ritual anthology that strings together quotations from Āgamas and related works (Kāmika, Cintyaviśvasādākhya, Suprabheda, Sūkṣma, Kālottara, Jñānaratnāvalī, Śivapurāṇa, Śivadharmottara, etc.) on the daily duties of the Śaiva worshipper: tooth-cleaning, bathing, sandhyā, Sūrya worship, Śiva worship (nityapūjā), the use of rudrākṣa, fire ritual, and rules of eating. The transcript T0351 appends further temple-ritual material, including a Kāmika-attributed nityapūjā, grāmaśānti and pratiṣṭhā procedures, kavaca hymns, snapana chapters of the Vātulatantra and an Aṃśumat chapter on the Vināyaka vow.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Biswanarayan Shastri (ed.), Yoginī Tantra, Delhi / Varanasi: Bhāratīya Vidyā Prakāśan, 1982.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00064, entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 2009).

**Evidence:**
- Although the Muktabodha header mistakenly claims publication by 'kṣemarāja śrī kṛṣṇa dāsa, Pre-1900, Bombay', the keyed text corresponds precisely to Biswanarayan Shastri's 1982 critical edition.
- The e-text includes Shastri's supplementary paṭalas in Part 2 (paṭalas 10–16), which are absent from all 19th- and early 20th-century editions (which terminate at Part 2, paṭala 9).
- Lines 8365–8368 reproduce Shastri's modern Hindi/Sanskrit editorial note referencing 20th-century publications: '[vārāṇaseyasārvabhaumapracārakāryālayataḥ pracāritāyāṃ paramārthasudhānāmakapatrikāyāṃ samuddhṛtāḥ ślokāḥ | guvāhāṭīnagare anuṣṭhitasya bhāratīyadarśanasammelanasya smṛtigranthe ca samudṛdhṛtāḥ || pṛṣṭham 63 ||]'.
- Square-bracketed variant readings throughout the text (e.g., '[kāmākhyāyāṃ]', '[hasanmukhīm]', '[-mahojjvalam]') match Shastri's textual notes.

**Other editions:**
- Rasikmohan Chattopadhyaya (ed.), Yoginītantra, in Vividhatantrasaṃgraha, Calcutta, 1876 / 1886 (Bengali script). — Early 19th-century printed edition; contains 19 paṭalas in Part 1 and 9 paṭalas in Part 2.
- Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara Bhaṭṭācārya (ed.), Yoginītantram, Calcutta: Sarasvati Press, 1897 (Devanagari script). — 19 paṭalas in Part 1, 9 paṭalas in Part 2.
- Kṣemarāja Śrīkṛṣṇadāsa (publ.), Yoginītantra, Bombay: Venkateshwar Steam Press, 1904 CE / Saṃvat 1960 (Devanagari script). — Bombay edition containing 19 + 9 paṭalas.
- Kanhaiyālāl Miśra (ed. & tr.), Yoginītantram, with Hindi translation, Kalyan (Bombay): Lakshmi Venkateshwar Press, 1956. — Popular edition with Hindi translation.
- Harihar Prasad Tripathi (ed. & comm.), Yoginītantram, Varanasi: Chowkhamba Krishnadas Academy, 2012. — Devanagari text with Hindi commentary.

**Translations:**
- Kanhaiyālāl Miśra (tr.), Yoginītantram, Kalyan (Bombay): Lakshmi Venkateshwar Press, 1956. (Hindi)
- Subodh Chandra Goswami (tr.), Yoginī Tantram, Gauhati: Lawyer's Book Stall, 1972. (Assamese)
- S. N. Khandelwal (ed. & tr.), Yoginītantram: Text with Hindi Translation, Varanasi: Bhāratīya Vidyā Saṃsthān, 2012. (Hindi)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete according to the expanded recension edited by Biswanarayan Shastri (1982). Contains Pūrvakhaṇḍa (19 paṭalas) and Uttarārdha / Kāmarūpādhikāra (16 paṭalas: paṭalas 1–14 complete, paṭala 15 broken at line 8353 '(atra paṭalasamāptirnāsti)', and paṭala 16 preserved as a 4-verse colophon excerpt).

**Also known as:** Yoginītantram, Yogini Tantra, Yoginītantra Kāmarūpādhikāra

**Attribution:** A major late medieval Śākta scripture composed in northeastern India (Assam / Kāmarūpa or Cooch Behar), framed as a revealed dialogue between Śiva and Girijā (Pārvatī). Scholarship dates the text to the 16th century CE (c. 1540–1600 CE) based on internal references to the Koch (Kuvacha) dynasty.

The Yoginītantra is a major late medieval Śākta tantric scripture composed in 16th-century Assam (ancient Kāmarūpa). Cast as a dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, the text is arranged in two parts: the Pūrvakhaṇḍa (19 paṭalas), which details Kaula ritual liturgy, mantra lore, dīkṣā, and worship of Kālī; and the Uttarārdha / Kāmarūpādhikāra (up to 16 paṭalas), which serves as a sacred topography and sthalapurāṇa of Kāmarūpa, detailing sacred rivers, shrines, and the worship of the goddess Kāmākhyā. It is a critical document for the religious and political history of medieval Assam, containing valuable legends and references to the Koch dynasty.

(Vol. 1 [chs. 1–11]: Purātattvaprakāśanamālā 37, Kathmandu: Nepāla Rājakīya Pustakālaya, 1966 [VS 2023]; Vol. 2 [chs. 12–32]: Purātattvaprakāśanamālā 42, Kathmandu: Rāṣṭrīyābhilekhālaya, 1968 [VS 2025]).

- Lines 8–20 of the e-text reproduce verbatim the Sanskrit front matter of volume 1: 'nepālarājakīyapustakālayasthahastalikhitaprācīnapustakānāmanyatamaḥ pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccayaḥ tasyāyamekādaśādhyāyaparyantaḥ prathamo bhāgaḥ paṇḍitabuddhisāgaraśarmaṇo 'dhyakṣatāyāṃ vedācāryadāmodaraśarmaṇā saṃpāditaḥ saṃpādakena vedāntaśāstri paṃ bābukṛṣṇaśarmaṇā ca saṃśodhitaḥ nepālarājakīyapustakālayataḥ prakāśitaḥ'.

**Other editions:**

- Gudrun Bühnemann, The Hindu Pantheon in Nepalese Line Drawings: Two Manuscripts of the Pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccaya, Varanasi: Indica Books, 2003. — Critical study reproducing the Sanskrit text of chapter 6 alongside line drawings from two 17th-century Nepalese manuscripts.

**Translations:**
- Gudrun Bühnemann, The Hindu Pantheon in Nepalese Line Drawings: Two Manuscripts of the Pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccaya, Varanasi: Indica Books, 2003. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 32 chapters (vidhis), beginning with chapter 1 (liṅgalakṣaṇa) and ending with chapter 32 (Pavitrārohaṇavidhi), covering both volumes of the printed edition.

**Also known as:** Lakṣaṇasārasamuccaya, Lakṣaṇasaṅgraha, Lakṣaṇasamuccaya, Pratiṣṭhātantra

**Attribution:** The compendium is attributed to Vairocana, as stated in the closing verse of the text (chapter 32, verse 81: 'tāvadvairocanīyā jagati ciramiyaṃ pustarūpāstu kīrtiḥ'). He is generally dated to the 11th or 12th century.

The Pratiṣṭhālakṣaṇasārasamuccaya ('Compendium of the Essence of Characteristics of Installation') is a 32-chapter Sanskrit handbook on Śaiva-dominated temple ritual, iconography, and image consecration (pratiṣṭhā), attributed to Vairocana (c. 11th–12th century). Compiled from various tantric āgamas and architectural treatises, it details temple building, iconometric proportions, ritual bathing, eye-opening ceremonies, installation of lingas and pantheon deities, and annual festivals such as pavitrārohaṇa. Transmitted chiefly in Nepal, the text is well known in art-historical literature, particularly for chapter 6, which served as a primary textual manual for Newar artists and manuscript illustrators.

Affiliating itself with the Bhagamālinīsaṃhitā of the Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava corpus, the text details transgressive and non-dual Kaula ritual practices, emphasizing liṅgapūjā, yonipūjā, and internal subtle physiology, before concluding with expositions on philosophical systems, tantric sects, and social classifications.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Spandakārikā in 4 niḥṣyandas (52/53 kārikās) together with Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa's Spandakārikāvṛtti (annotated with printed footnotes/tippaṇī) and Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha's complete Spandavivṛti concluding with its colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Spandakārikā (Vasugupta, root text)
- Spandakārikāvṛtti (Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa, commentary)
- Spandakārikāvivṛti (Rāmakaṇṭha, commentary)
- Ṭippaṇī on Spandakārikāvṛtti (sub-commentary)

**Also known as:** Spandakārikā with Spandakārikāvṛtti and Spandakārikāvivṛti, Spandakārikā with vṛtti by Kallaṭa Bhaṭṭa, tippaṇī and vivṛti by Rāmakaṇṭha, Spandavṛtti, Spandavivṛti

**Attribution:** Authorship of the root Spandakārikā is traditionally disputed: Kṣemarāja and Bhāgavatotpala attribute the verses to Vasugupta (author of the Śivasūtra), while Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, and Rāmakaṇṭha ascribe them to Vasugupta's pupil Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa (fl. c. 855–883 CE, reign of Avantivarman). The Spandakārikāvṛtti is universally attributed to Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. The Spandavivṛti was composed by Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha (Rāmakaṇṭha I / Rājānaka Rāma, 10th c. CE), disciple of Utpaladeva, not to be confused with the contemporary or slightly later Śaivasiddhānta exegete Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha (Rāmakaṇṭha II).

The Spandakārikā is a foundational philosophical and contemplative treatise of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism, expounding the doctrine of spanda—the dynamic pulsation and vibration of pure consciousness through which Śiva creates, sustains, and withdraws the universe. This composite electronic text contains the root kārikās accompanied by two early commentaries: the Spandakārikāvṛtti by Vasugupta's direct disciple Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa (late 9th c. CE), accompanied by marginal explanatory notes (tippaṇī), and the comprehensive Spandakārikāvivṛti by Utpaladeva's disciple Rājānaka Rāmakaṇṭha (10th c. CE), which interprets the Spanda system through the conceptual lens of the Pratyabhijñā school.

**E-text:** Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha Indological Research Institute under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (catalog no. M00068, 2007).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header states: 'Typed from MSs no. 1800 – 134. Formerly in the India Office collection. Now deposited in the British Library, London. This manuscript has not been edited.'
- Final colophon reads: 'iti śrīśivānandācārya viracite kulapradīpe saptamaḥ prakāśaḥ saṃpūrṇaḥ | śubhamastu | saṃvat 1788 jyeṣṭa sudī 14 bhaume śubhaṃ || ślokasaṃkhyā 1800 ||'
- This colophon corresponds exactly to India Office MS 1265 (Cat. No. 2569), which records the date Saṃvat 1788 (1731 CE). The Muktabodha designation '1800 – 134' conflates the recorded śloka count (1800) with a manuscript handlist/shelfmark index (134).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in seven prakāśas, ending with the scribal colophon dated Saṃvat 1788 (1731 CE) and recording a verse count of 1,800 ślokas.

**Attribution:** Attributed in chapter colophons to Śivānandācārya (and as Gosvāmi-Śivānanda in the colophon to prakāśa 6). In some manuscript catalogues and modern studies, he is identified with Sevānandācārya, son of the Gauḍa scholar Jagannivāsa.

The Kulapradīpa ('Lamp of the Kula') is a 17th-century or earlier Sanskrit Śākta-Kaula compendium (nibandha) in seven chapters (prakāśa) composed in verse by Śivānandācārya. Drawing heavily upon authoritative Āgamic sources such as the Kulārṇavatantra, Devīyāmala, and Pañcayāmala, it provides an exposition of the doctrines and ritual practices of the Kaula path, including the distinction between dakṣiṇa and vāma conduct, the purification and use of the five substances (pañcamakāra), dūtīyāga, and cakra worship. Manuscript evidence establishes a terminus ad quem for the work's composition of Saṃvat 1765 (1709 CE).

**Attribution:** Canonical Śākta Tantra of the Śrīvidyā (Kādi) transmission, framed traditionally as a divine revelation between Īśvara (Śiva) and Devī.

The Jñānārṇavatantra ('Ocean of Knowledge') is an authoritative scripture of the Śākta Tantric tradition and one of the principal scriptural sources for the Kādi division of Śrīvidyā. Cast in 26 paṭalas as a revelation by Īśvara to Devī, the work begins with esoteric expositions of the sacred alphabet (akṣamālā / mātṛkā), the phonematic matrix, and the threefold bindu. The remaining chapters detail the internal and ritual pūjā of Mahātripurasundarī and her attendants, yantra meditations, mantra recitation, and seasonal observances, culminating in the damanāropaṇa rite.

The Prāṇatoṣiṇī is an encyclopedic 19th-century Śākta-Tāntrika digest (nibandha) compiled in Bengal in 1820/1821 CE by Rāmatoṣaṇa Vidyālaṅkāra under the patronage of Prāṇakṛṣṇa Viśvāsa. This opening section, the Sargakāṇḍa (ten paricchedas), covers cosmogony, the manifestation of sound and language (śabdasṛṣṭi, sphoṭa, and varṇotpatti), bodily mysticism, embryology, and the classification of Tantric scriptures. The compendium is an indispensable source for Tantric textual history, preserving extensive extracts from numerous earlier tantras and digests that are otherwise rare or lost.

The Rudrayāmala is traditionally celebrated as one of the major early Śaiva-Śākta Yāmala tantras, although the ancient scripture cited by non-dual Kashmirian Śaiva authors survives only in fragmentary quotations. **Attribution:** Attributed in the colophons to Śrīmad-Ativarṇāśramācāryavarya-Śaivaparipālaka-Śivāgrayogīndra-Jñānaśivācārya (Śivāgrayogin), a 16th-century head of the Sūryanārkōvil Ādhīnam in Tamil Nadu.

The Śaivaparibhāṣā is a 16th-century Sanskrit manual of Śaiva Siddhānta philosophy composed by Śivāgrayogin, patterned after dialectical manuals such as the Vedāntaparibhāṣā. In five chapters, the work methodically details the epistemology (pramāṇa) and the three central ontological categories—the Lord (pati), the bound soul (paśu), and the fetters of bondage (pāśa)—before concluding with the path of initiation and liberation (mukti). Drawing heavily on the Saiddhāntika Āgamas (particularly the Pauṣkarāgama), it represents a major milestone in the late Sanskrit scholasticism of the school.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Also known as:** Sāmbapañcāśikāṭīkā, Sūryastotra, Paramādityastotra, Brahmādityastava, Sāmbamiśrapañcāśikā

**Attribution:** The root hymn is traditionally ascribed to Sāmba, son of Kṛṣṇa, whom Purāṇic accounts (e.g. Varāhapurāṇa, Sāmbapurāṇa) describe as worshipping the Sun god Sūrya to be cured of leprosy. Modern scholars view it as an early medieval (c. 8th-century) Kashmiri hymn blending Saura solar adoration with the esoteric yoga and metaphysics of Vāk (levels of speech). The commentary (Vivṛti or Ṭīkā) is by Rājānaka Kṣemarāja (early 11th century), disciple of Abhinavagupta, who signs his name in the closing stanza and interprets the stotra through the non-dual lens of Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism.

The Sāmbapañcāśikā is a 53-verse hymn celebrating Sūrya as Cidbhānu, the supreme luminary of pure consciousness. Traditionally attributed to Kṛṣṇa's son Sāmba, who is said to have worshipped the Sun to heal from leprosy, the hymn is an early medieval Kashmiri work that integrates solar devotion with Kundalinī yoga and the esoteric philosophy of Vāk (levels of cosmic speech). In his Vivṛti, the 11th-century polymath Rājānaka Kṣemarāja comments on the hymn from the perspective of non-dual Trika and Pratyabhijñā Śaivism, demonstrating that the solar deity is none other than the self-luminous awareness of Paraśiva.

**Also known as:** Śivārcanācandrikā

**Attribution:** An authentic liturgical manual composed by the 16th-century polymath Appayadīkṣita for his patron King Cinna Bomma (Bomma Bhūpati) of Vellore, who is explicitly mentioned in the concluding verses (v. 3809), along with praise for Jvarakaṇṭheśa (the presiding deity of the Jalakaṇṭheśvara temple in Vellore). Scholarly analysis (e.g., Elaine Fisher 2018) demonstrates that the liturgical text extensively draws on Nīlakaṇṭhaśivācārya's earlier Kriyāsāra.

The Śivārcanacandrikā ('Moonlight on the Worship of Śiva') is a comprehensive ritual manual (paddhati) composed by the 16th-century South Indian polymath Appayadīkṣita for his patron Cinna Bomma Nāyaka of Vellore. Designed to instruct initiated householders and sovereigns in personal daily Śiva worship (ātmārthapūjā), the manual synthesizes prescriptions from Śaiva Siddhānta Āgamas and Smārta-Śaiva liturgies (relying heavily on Nīlakaṇṭhaśivācārya's Kriyāsāra). It covers all primary stages of worship, including preliminary purification (pañcaśuddhi), mental preparation, installation of the deity, linga worship, naivedya, and rules concerning ritual remnants (nirmālya).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Sambandhasiddhi and its autocommentary, comprising 20 numbered verses, one unnumbered concluding stanza, and the interspersed prose vṛtti, corresponding precisely to pp. 1–15 of KSTS 34.

**Works in this e-text:**

- Sambandhasiddhivṛtti (Utpaladeva, autocommentary)

**Also known as:** Saṃbandhasiddhi, Siddhitrayī: Sambandhasiddhi

The Sambandhasiddhi ('Establishment of Relation') is one of the three foundational polemical monographs constituting Utpaladeva's Siddhitrayī (fl. c. 925–975 CE). Composed in verse with an integral prose autocommentary (vṛtti), the text defends the ontological and linguistic reality of relations (sambandha) against Buddhist nominalist critiques, particularly Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā. Integrating Bhartṛhari's grammatical philosophy with non-dual Pratyabhijñā metaphysics, Utpaladeva argues that relation as identity-in-difference cannot subsist purely among insentient entities, but necessarily depends on the synthesizing, reflective awareness (vimarśa, anusaṃdhāna) of universal consciousness (Śiva).

The Śivasaṃhitā is one of the classic Sanskrit manuals on Haṭha and Rāja Yoga, probably composed between the fourteenth and early sixteenth centuries CE in or near Varanasi. Structured as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and Pārvatī, it synthesizes Advaita Vedānta philosophy with Śākta-Śaiva subtle anatomy (nāḍīs, cakras, kuṇḍalinī), prāṇāyāma, mudrās, and meditation. It is especially noted for its inclusive soteriological stance, affirming that householders (gṛhastha) as well as renunciants can attain liberation through yoga.

Expounding 79 sūtras across three sections structured by the three means of liberation (śāmbhava-, śākta-, and āṇavopāya), Bhāskara interprets the aphorisms in close alignment with the Spanda lineage inherited through Bhaṭṭa Kallaṭa. It serves as an indispensable witness to an exegetical tradition independent of Kṣemarāja's Pratyabhijñā-oriented prose Śivasūtravimarśinī.

The Spandasaṃdoha ('Essence/Collection of Vibration') is an early exegetical work by Rājānaka Kṣemarāja (early 11th century CE) dedicated exclusively to commenting on the opening verse of the Spandakārikā ('yasyonmeṣanimeṣābhyāṃ...'). **Coverage:** complete — Complete four-pāda text of the Āgama: Kriyāpāda (lines 13–6426), Caryāpāda (lines 6427–8047), Yogapāda (lines 8048–8702), and Jñānapāda (lines 8703–9375). Despite the Muktabodha header stating '(kriyāpāda and caryāpāda)', the e-text contains all four pādas.

The Suprabhedāgama is one of the twenty-eight canonical Mūlāgamas of dualist Śaiva Siddhānta, traditionally categorized among the five Śivabhedas emanating from the Vāmadeva face of Śiva. It is one of the relatively few Āgamas preserved across all four classical divisions (pādas): Kriyāpāda (temple layout, iconography, installation of liṅgas, and daily/occasional worship rituals), Caryāpāda (initiation, duties of devotees, royal rites, and expiation), Yogapāda (subtle anatomy, prāṇāyāma, and meditation), and Jñānapāda (cosmogony, thirty-six tattvas, and the adhvans). It has long served as a prominent ritual authority for South Indian temple architecture and liturgical performance.

Āhnikas 15 through 37 form the extensive ritual, yogic, and canon-defining second half of Abhinavagupta's Tantrāloka, accompanied by Jayaratha's Viveka commentary. The text systematically expounds daily and occasional Trika worship, multiple grades and variations of initiation (dīkṣā), post-initiatory practice, construction of maṇḍalas, funerary and ancestral rites (antyeṣṭi, śrāddha), and esoteric Kaula ritual (āhnika 29). The work concludes in āhnika 37 with an evaluation of the Śaiva scriptural hierarchy, the transmission of the teaching, and Abhinavagupta's personal lineage.

The Varivasyārahasya ('Secret of Worship') is an influential 18th-century manual of Śrīvidyā theology, mantra-śāstra, and internal contemplative worship composed in 167 verses across two divisions (aṃśas) by the polymath Bhāskararāya Makhin, accompanied by his autocommentary, the Prakāśa. Synthesizing Śākta ritual theology with Advaita Vedānta, Bhāskararāya argues that the culmination of mantra worship is the non-dual realization of identity between the practitioner, the mantra, and the supreme Goddess (Lalitā Mahātripurasundarī) as pure consciousness.

The Viśvasāratantra is an extensive medieval Śākta-Śaiva scripture in eight paṭalas, structured as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva (Mahākāla) and Pārvatī. Widely cited in later Nibandha and ritual literature such as Kṛṣṇānanda Āgamavāgīśa's Tantrasāra, the work expounds cosmology, mantra- and yantra-śāstra, initiation (dīkṣā), Kuṇḍalinī yoga, and the ritual cults of various goddesses, particularly Pracaṇḍacaṇḍikā (Chinnamastā), Durgā, Guhyakālī, Tripurasundarī, and Sarasvatī. It is celebrated in Tantric literature as the source of the macrocosm-microcosm axiom 'yad ihāsti tad anyatra, yan nehāsti na tat kvacit' ('what is here is elsewhere; what is not here is nowhere').

**Also known as:** Bṛhannīlatantram, Brihan Nila Tantra, Bṛhadnīlatantra

**Attribution:** Anonymous Kaula Śākta scripture framed as a dialogue between Mahākālabhairava and Devī (Bhairavī/Śakti).

The Bṛhannīlatantra ('Great Nīla Tantra') is an important Kaula Śākta ritual work in 24 chapters (paṭalas) framed as an esoteric dialogue between Mahākālabhairava and the Goddess. Centered on the worship of the Mahāvidyās Tārā (specifically Nīlasarasvatī / Ugratārā) and Kālī, the text details mantras, yantras, dīkṣā procedures, puraścaryā, kavacas, and sahasranāmas. It also contains significant material on the Mahācīnācāra path, vīrasādhana, alchemical transmutation (rasaśāstra / dhātuvāda), and the worship of Annapūrṇā.

The Sarvollāsatantra is an important 15th-century Śākta-Kaula compendium (saṃgraha) attributed to the Bengali Tantric master Sarvānandanātha of Mehār. In 63 chapters (ullāsas), it compiles extensive citations from older tantras and āgamas on essential Kaula practices, including initiation (dīkṣā), guru veneration, the pañcatattvas, cakra-pūjā, and internal Kuṇḍalinī yoga. It is of notable historical importance for providing one of the earliest textual classifications of the ten Mahāvidyās.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete short text of 33 verses, from the guru-salutation (v. 1) to v. 33 and the colophon 'iti matsyendranāthaviracitaṃ bhaktisaṃ sampūrṇam' (the word 'bhaktisaṃ' is corrupt).

**Also known as:** Mīnanāthayogaviṣaya

**Attribution:** Ascribed to Matsyendranātha (Mīnanātha): the speaker introduces himself as 'umāśaṅkaraputro 'haṃ mīnanātho munīśvaraḥ' (v. 7) and the colophon reads 'iti matsyendranāthaviracitaṃ ...'. The ascription is traditional; the work belongs to the early Nātha/haṭha yoga literature.

The Yogaviṣaya is a short Nātha yoga text of 33 verses ascribed to Matsyendranātha (Mīnanātha), who presents it as the teaching he received from Ādinātha. After verses on the guru lineage and the qualified disciple, it describes the six cakras from ādhāra to ājñā, the nāḍīs iḍā, piṅgalā and suṣumnā, the ten vital winds, the three granthis, the haṃsa (ajapā) mantra repeated 21,600 times a day, and the liṅgas and inner nectar in the head.

- Tantrarājatantra with the Commentary Sudarśanā of Prāṇamañjarī (Chapter 1), edited by Jatindra Bimal Chaudhuri, The Contribution of Women to Sanskrit Literature, Vol. 5, Calcutta: Shree Madhab Press, 1940. — Edition of paṭala 1 with the commentary composed by Prāṇamañjarī, wife of Premānidhi Pantha.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 36 paṭalas, containing both the root kārikā verses and the running Manoramā commentary up to the closing praśasti and final colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Tantrarājatantra (root text)
- Manoramā (paṭalas 1–22) (Subhagānandanātha, commentary)
- Manoramā (paṭalas 23–36) (Prakāśānandanātha, commentary)

**Also known as:** Tantrarāja, Kādimatatantrarāja

**Attribution:** The root Tantrarājatantra is an anonymous scriptural revelation of the Kādimata division of Śrīvidyā Śāktism, framed as a dialogue between Śiva and Devī. The running commentary Manoramā was composed through paṭala 22 by Subhagānandanātha and completed for the remaining fourteen chapters (paṭalas 23–36) by his disciple Prakāśānandanātha (Prakāśānandadeśika), as explicitly recorded in the closing verses of paṭala 36 (vv. 84–86).

The Tantrarājatantra is one of the primary canonical scriptures of the Kādimata lineage within the Śākta Śrīvidyā tradition, structured in 36 chapters as an esoteric dialogue between Śiva and the Devī. It presents comprehensive instruction on the worship of Lalitā Mahā-Tripurasundarī and the fifteen Nityā goddesses, detailing mantra formulas, yantra geometry, the nyāsa rites of the Śrīcakra, and non-dual Śākta metaphysics. In this edition, the scripture is accompanied by the running Manoramā commentary, written up through chapter 22 by the Kashmirian master Subhagānandanātha and finished for chapters 23–36 by his disciple Prakāśānandanātha.

The Jayākhyasaṃhitā is one of the oldest and most authoritative canonical scriptures of the Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra tradition, celebrated as one of the three foundational 'jewels' (ratnatraya) alongside the Sātvatasaṃhitā and Pauṣkarasaṃhitā. The text was widely cited by medieval Indian philosophers and theologians, including Utpaladeva, Abhinavagupta, and Rāmānuja.

The Kāmikāgama is the first and foremost of the twenty-eight canonical Mūlāgamas of the Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. - Ram Kumar Rai (ed.), Śaktisaṅgamatantram: Kālīkhaṇḍa, Tantra Granthamala No. 9, Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1980. — Devanagari text with Hindi translation and commentary.

**Translations:**
- Ram Kumar Rai, Śaktisaṅgamatantram (with Hindi translation), 4 vols., Tantra Granthamala Nos. 9, 13, 14, 18, Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1980–1988. (Hindi)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains the complete Kālīkhaṇḍa (paṭalas 1–21), the first of the four major khaṇḍas of the Śaktisaṅgamatantra (the remaining three being Tārākhaṇḍa, Sundarīkhaṇḍa, and Chinnamastākhaṇḍa).

**Also known as:** Śaktisaṅgamatantra: Kālīkhaṇḍa, Śaktisaṃgamatantra (Kālīkhaṇḍa), Śaktisaṅgamatantra, Vol. I: Kālīkhaṇḍa

**Attribution:** Anonymous Śākta Kaula scripture, framed traditionally as a divine dialogue between Śiva and the Devī (and in subsequent chapters between Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā).

The Śaktisaṅgamatantra is a voluminous encyclopedic Śākta compendium divided into four khaṇḍas honoring Kālī, Tārā, Sundarī, and Chinnamastā, generally dated to the 16th–17th centuries CE. This first section, the Kālīkhaṇḍa (comprising 21 paṭalas), expounds the supreme theology, mantras, yantras, nyāsas, and Kaula ritual worship of Kālī. It sets forth tantric cosmology, distinguishes and systematizes the Kādi and Hādi ritual paths, and offers polemical defenses of tantric practice against non-tantric criticisms.

The Sundarīkhaṇḍa is the third section of the extensive Śākta compendium Śaktisaṅgamatantra, framed as a dialogue between Akṣobhya and Mahogratārā. **Edition used (probable):** A late-19th-century Bengali-script edition by an editor named 'Chatterjee' (Muktabodha header). This is probably one of the Calcutta tantra editions of Rasikamohana Caṭṭopādhyāya (Rasik Mohan Chatterjee), but that identification, the exact title page, the year and the publisher are not confirmed. - Muktabodha header: 'Editor : chatterjee'; 'E-text transcribed from Chatterjee's edition late 19th century in Bengali script'; 'Publisher : Unknown: late 19th century'
- Rasikamohana Caṭṭopādhyāya is the best-known late-19th-c. Calcutta editor of Bengali-script tantras (e.g. Bṛhattantrasāra, Rādhātantra, Śāktānandataraṅgiṇī, cited as 'ed. R. Chattopadhyaya, Calcutta' in the Encyclopedia of Tantra)

Gopinath Kaviraj, vols. 1–3, and Rāmaprasāda Tripāṭhī, 1970–1981). — Devanagari edition, 17 paṭalas. Its prose summary of bhūtaśuddhi at the end of paṭala 17 (p. 625) matches the end of this e-text (Ritual and Speculation in Early Tantrism, 1992, n. 1). Bibliographies cite it simply as 'In Tantrasangraha, ed. Gopinath Kaviraj, Ramaprasad Tripathi, and Vrajavallabha Dvivedi'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 17 paṭalas followed by a short closing prose summary of the bhūtaśuddhi procedure (saṃkṣepeṇa bhūtaśuddhivivaraṇam), ending at 'iti śrībhūtaśuddhitantraṃ samāptam'.

**Also known as:** Bhūtaśuddhi Tantra

**Attribution:** Revealed scriptural Śākta/Śaiva Tantra framed as an esoteric dialogue between Śrīdevī/Pārvatī and Śiva/Īśvara.

An anonymous Śākta tantra in 17 paṭalas, a dialogue between Śrīdevī and Īśvara. It treats the preliminaries of Tantric worship as a 'triad' (tattvatraya) of bhūtaśuddhi, nyāsa and prāṇāyāma, together with inner bathing and inner sandhyā, ajapā recitation, kuṇḍalinī and the six cakras, the dissolution of the 24 tattvas and inner worship. It ends with a praise of the book itself and a short prose summary of the bhūtaśuddhi procedure. Its date is uncertain; it belongs to the late, Bengal-centred layer of Śākta tantra literature.

# Mahotsavavidhi

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_mahotsavavidhikramaHK`

**Author:** Aghoraśiva

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Probably: Mahotsavavidhi(krama) Āgamaśekhara of Aghoraśiva, ed. M. Alagappa Mudaliyar, Chennai: Sivajnanabodha Press, 1910 (Grantha script), or a reprint of it. Davis transcribed this e-text from a Grantha print, emended it, and recorded the print's readings as 'k'.

**E-text:** Transcribed and corrected by Richard H. Davis; Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00131, revision 0 of 22 Sept. 2008 (https://muktabodha-digital-library.org/texts/IAST/M00131).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header (segs. 2–10): 'Editor : Richard Davis / Description: Transcribed by prof. richard davis from printed book published in south India in grantha script. bibliographical details not available. corrections by prof. Richard Davis. original readings in the printed edition noted in brackets and labeled 'k'.' So the header itself does not identify the edition.
- The k-apparatus at the start reproduces the print's title page/heading 'śivamayam mahotsavavidhikramaḥ āgamaśekharaṃ' (segs. 12–14). A recent bibliography (Cracow Indological Studies article on the Paḷḷivēṭṭa, journals.akademicka.pl/cis/article/view/1537) lists 'Mahotsavavidhikrama Āgamaśekhara. see Mahotsavavidhi of Aghoraśiva (Alagappa Mudaliyar Ed.)' and 'Mahotsavavidhi of Aghoraśiva. Ed. Alagappa Mudaliyar. Chennai: Sivajnanabodha Press, 1910.' The title match makes this edition (or a reprint) the probable source.
- Page markers 'p. 2)' ... 'p. 44)' and a few 'k: 48)'-type references show that the e-text follows a printed book's pagination. A copy of the 1910 print was not available, so the pagination could not be checked against it; hence 'probable'.

**Other editions:**
- Mahotsavavidhi of Aghoraśiva, ed. M. Alagappa Mudaliyar, Chennai: Sivajnanabodha Press, 1910 (Grantha; title 'Mahotsavavidhikrama Āgamaśekhara'). — Probable source of this e-text (see edition_used).
- Muktabodha I00004: transcription of an IFP palm-leaf manuscript of the Kriyākramadyotikā (Mahotsavavidhi with the following prāyaścittavidhi). — Independent manuscript witness; in this catalogue as SA_MB_ilx_mb_aghorazivAcArya_mahotsavavidhi_kriyAkramadyotikA_I00004.

**Translations:**
- Davis, Richard H., A Priest's Guide for the Great Festival: Aghoraśiva's Mahotsavavidhi, New York / Oxford: Oxford University Press (South Asia Research Series), 2010. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — The e-text runs from the list of festival components (vṛṣayāga, dhvajārohaṇa, bṛhattāla, aṅkurārpaṇa, yāgaśālā, astrayāga, bali, yānakrama ...) to two Kriyākramadyotikā section colophons. The first, 'vaināyakotsavādibhaktotsavavidhiḥ samāptaḥ', comes at seg. 932. The second, 'brahmattālādiṛkṣotsavāntavidhiḥ samāptaḥ', comes at seg. 1074, after the māsa-, pakṣa-, ṛkṣa- and vārotsavas. Page markers of the printed book run from 'p. 2)' to 'p. 44)'. The palm-leaf transcription of the same text (Muktabodha I00004, = SA_MB_ilx_mb_aghorazivAcArya_mahotsavavidhi_kriyAkramadyotikA_I00004) has the same two colophons and then continues with the separate prāyaścittavidhi section of the Kriyākramadyotikā. That section is not part of the Mahotsavavidhi, so this e-text gives the whole festival section. The draft's statement that the print has the text on 'pp. 1–61' followed by an Āgama anthology could not be verified and has been removed.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Mahotsavavidhi (section of the Kriyākramadyotikā) (Aghoraśiva, root text)
- Prefatory verses (maṅgala to Gaṇapati and to the guru Sadāśiva of Kāñcī) and a Kāmikāgama quotation (editorial prefix of the Grantha print, given only in the 'k' apparatus (segs. 11–29))

**Also known as:** Mahotsavavidhikrama (heading of the Grantha print; Muktabodha uniform title), Mahotsavavidhikrama Āgamaśekhara (title of the Grantha print), Festival section of the Kriyākramadyotikā

**Attribution:** The section colophons ascribe the text to Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā: 'iti parameśvarā paranāmadhyeya śrīmadaghoraśivācāryaviracitāyāṃ kriyākramadyotikāyāṃ vaināyakotsavādibhaktotsavavidhiḥ samāptaḥ' (segs. 930–932) and '... brahmattālādiṛkṣotsavāntavidhiḥ samāptaḥ' (segs. 1072–1074). The prefatory verses that the printed book has before the text (k-apparatus, segs. 11–22) are word for word the opening verses of Kacchapeśvaraśivācārya's Kriyākramadyotikāvyākhyā (cf. SA_MB_kriyakramadyotikavyakhyaHK segs. 18–30), which praise his guru Sadāśiva of Kāñcī. Davis treated them as not part of Aghoraśiva's text.

The Mahotsavavidhi is the section of Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā (12th century; Davis dates its completion to 1157 CE) on the 'great festival' (mahotsava) of Śiva temples in the Tamil Śaiva Siddhānta tradition. It prescribes the festival day by day: the preliminary rites for Vināyaka and the bull, flag-raising, the drum (bṛhattāla) rite and the sprouting of seeds, worship in the sacrificial pavilion and bali offerings, processions on vehicles and in the chariot, the final bath (tīrtha), flag-lowering and the rites for Caṇḍeśa and the devotees. It closes with shorter monthly, fortnightly, lunar-asterism and weekday festivals. Richard H. Davis translated it into English (2010).

**Attribution:** The root text contains 21 āryā verses summarizing the 36 principles of Trika Shaivism. The commentator Rājānaka Ānanda (c. 17th c.) introduces its author anonymously as 'kaścin mahāmāheśvaraḥ'. The Ṣaṭtriṃśattattvasaṃdoha ('Compendium of the Thirty-Six Principles') consists of 21 āryā verses that systematically outline the ontology of Kashmir Shaivism (Trika and Pratyabhijñā). It describes the gradual unfoldment (sṛṣṭi) of the thirty-six tattvas from ultimate consciousness (śivatattva) to gross earth (dharaṇī) as the spontaneous playful vibration (svātantrya / spanda) of Paramaśiva. The work is studied alongside the concise Sanskrit commentary (Vivaraṇa) composed by the seventeenth-century scholar Rājānaka Ānanda.

The Tantrasāra ('Essence of Tantra') is an influential prose compendium composed by the 10th–11th-century Kashmiri polymath Abhinavagupta as an accessible digest of his monumental encyclopedic treatise, the Tantrāloka. The Mālinīvijayavārttika (also known as the Mālinīślokavārttika) is a major verse commentary composed by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE) interpreting the opening sentence of the Mālinīvijayottaratantra, the foundational scriptural authority of the Trika Śaiva lineage. Arranged in two books (kāṇḍas), the text formulates a comprehensive theology of revelation (āgama), hermeneutics, and nondual metaphysics while mounting extensive polemics against Buddhist epistemologists, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, and Mīmāṃsā. Alongside the Tantrāloka and Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa, it represents one of Abhinavagupta's core scriptural syntheses.

The Uḍḍāmareśvaratantra (also styled Uḍḍāmareśvaramahātantra or Mantracintāmaṇi) is a 15-chapter applied Tantric manual dedicated primarily to pragmatic magic and ritual pharmacology (ṣaṭkarman rites such as vaśīkaraṇa, uccāṭana, stambhana, and māraṇa). The Bodhapañcadaśikā is a concise philosophical poem of fifteen stanzas (and one concluding stanza) composed by the Trika master Abhinavagupta as an accessible introduction for disciples unable to study his larger śāstric treatises. The Jñānasaṅkalinītantra ('Tantra of the Collection of Gnosis') is a concise Śākta-Śaiva tantric treatise framed as a dialogue on Mount Kailāsa between Śiva and the Devī. It subordinates external ritualism, caste prescriptions, and scholastic learning to internal non-dual knowledge (brahmajñāna) and subtle yogic contemplation. The text expounds the esoteric anatomy of the body (piṇḍa) as identical to the cosmos (brahmāṇḍa), identifying the internal channels iḍā, piṅgalā, and suṣumnā with sacred rivers (Gaṅgā, Yamunā, Sarasvatī), and explains the symbolic significance of the Praṇava (Oṃ) alongside inner mudrās such as khecarī and śāmbhavī.

**Other editions:**
- No published printed book edition exists. The text is preserved in manuscripts including Sarasvatībhavana (Saṃpūrṇānanda Sanskrit University) MS 88137, Khiste family collection, and Government Oriental Manuscripts Library, Madras (MS R. 4421 / 81 B 3 Beta). — Discussed as an unpublished Śrīvidyā ritual paddhati in modern scholarship (e.g., Madhu Khanna 1986; Gudrun Bühnemann 2000).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 9 chapters (spandas), ending on p. 275 with the colophon 'iti śrīmaccidānandanāthaviracitāyāṃ svacchandapaddhatyāṃ navamaspandaḥ || oṃ oṃ śubhaṃ bhavatu svacchandapaddhatīḥ samāptaḥ'.

**Attribution:** The opening verses (vv. 18–25) and chapter colophons attribute the work to Cidānandanātha. In the opening lineage description, Cidānandanātha traces his guruparamparā through Amṛtānandayogīndra (author of the Yoginīhṛdayadīpikā, c. early 14th c.), Brahmānanda, and Vimalānanda, placing him in the Śrīvidyā/Kaula sampradāya c. late 14th to early 15th century (fl. c. 1375–1425).

The Svacchandapaddhati by Cidānandanātha (fl. c. 1375–1425) is an extensive Kaula Śrīvidyā ritual manual organized in nine chapters (spandas). Contrary to its title, which often leads to confusion with the Trika/Bhairava cult of the Svacchandatantra, the manual is dedicated to the esoteric daily worship (nityapūjā) of Goddess Mahātripurasundarī and the Śrīcakra. It provides systematic liturgical instructions covering morning rites, bodily and elemental purification (bhūtaśuddhi), complex nyāsa procedures (including the mahāṣoḍhānyāsa), vessel preparation (pātrāsādana), and the sequential worship of the nine enclosures (āvaraṇas) of the Śrīyantra.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 35 prakāśas (chapters), concluding with the final colophon of prakāśa 35 on page 821 ('iti śrīmahāmāyāmahākālānumate merutantre śivapraṇīte kārttavīryyārjunamantrakathanaṃ nāma pañcatriṃśattamaḥ prakāśaḥ || 35 || samāptaścāyaṃ granthaḥ ||').

**Attribution:** Revealed scriptural tantra presented as a dialogue between Śiva and Śivā (śrīśivaśivāsaṃvādopanibaddha, śrīmahāmāyāmahākālānumate merutantre śivapraṇīte). The bracketed glosses, liturgical clarifications, and variant readings (ṭippanī) embedded in the text are by Paṇḍita Raghunātha Śāstrī Ojha.

The Merutantra is an encyclopedic Śaiva-Śākta tantric manual comprising 35 chapters (prakāśas), framed as a revelation given by Sadāśiva on Mount Meru to the gods after their distress under the demon Jalandhara. Functioning much like a nibandha (digest) of mantra-śāstra and ritual practice, it details initiation (dīkṣā), preliminary discipline (puraścaraṇa), nyāsa, and rituals for numerous deities, including Mahākāla, Devī, Sūrya, Viṣṇu, Gaṇeśa, and Kārtavīryārjuna. Containing notable historical anachronisms, such as predictions naming London, Christianity, and the British (chapter 35), the text in its present form dates to the early modern period (ca. 16th–18th century CE).

The Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinīvyākhyā is an anonymous South Indian sub-commentary on Abhinavagupta's Īśvarapratyabhijñāvimarśinī (the commentary on Utpaladeva's foundational Pratyabhijñākārikā). The Candrajñānāgama is the nineteenth of the canonical twenty-eight Śaiva Siddhāntāgamas and the ninth among the Rudrabhedas, transmitted in the Vīraśaiva tradition. Framed as an exposition delivered by Anantarudra to Bṛhaspati, this recension comprises the Kriyāpāda (twelve chapters) and Caryāpāda (eight chapters). The text outlines fundamental Śaiva metaphysics (Pati, Paśu, and Pāśa) and details distinctively Vīraśaiva observances, including the eight protective emblems (aṣṭāvaraṇa), the five codes of conduct (pañcācāra), daily rituals (āhnika), and death and funeral rites (śivamedha/aurdhvadehika).

The Uttarabhāga of the Makuṭāgama (also designated Makuṭottara) is a canonical Śaiva scripture preserved in the Vīraśaiva tradition, cast as an esoteric dialogue between Paraśiva and Rudra. It comprises two sections: the Kriyāpāda (five paṭalas), detailing the theology of the Śāmbhavavrata (Śirovrata), daily observance (āhnika), and the rites and implements for personal liṅga worship; and the Caryāpāda (ten paṭalas), regulating initiation, post-mortem funerary rites (śivamedha / antyeṣṭi), commemorative ceremonies, and ritual purity (āśauca). The text provides a central scriptural justification for Vīraśaiva orthopraxy and continuous liṅga-wearing.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete transcription of the manuscript on NGMCP reel H 334/6 as filmed (ms pp. 1b–71b), ending 'śubhaṃ || pūrṇam'. The first lines (segs 7–10) duplicate the closing cakrapūjā rubrics (a misplaced final leaf). The Siddhikālīstotra itself is complete but forms only a small part of the e-text.

**Works in this e-text:**

- Pañcamukhīhanumatkavaca (ascribed to the Sudarśanasaṃhitā) (kavaca (segs 754–834))
- Pratyaṅgirāstotra (ascribed to the Kubjikāmata) (stotra/mālāmantra (segs 837–1004))
- Siddhikālīstotra (ascribed to the Tridaśaḍāmara) (stotra (segs 1018–1040))
- Siddhikālīmantroddhāra (ascribed to the Tridaśaḍāmara) (mantra section (segs 1043–1077))
- Tritattvaśodhanapūjāvidhi and concluding cakrapūjā (ritual (segs 1099–1200))

**Also known as:** Tridaśaḍāmaratantre Siddhikālīstotra, Siddhikālīstotra (Tridaśaḍāmara)

**Attribution:** Anonymous Nepalese (Newar) ritual compilation; individual pieces are ascribed in their colophons to the Rudrayāmala, Sudarśanasaṃhitā, Kubjikāmata and Tridaśaḍāmara(tantra). The Mahāmāryāṣṭaka names Vararuci as its ṛṣi (traditional viniyoga), not as an author.

A Nepalese Śākta ritual manuscript with Newari rubrics, combining navagraha worship, the Mahāmāryāṣṭaka (a protective hymn to Mahāmārī/Kālī ascribed to the Rudrayāmala), a mantra-laden Śyāmā-sahasranāma, a Pañcamukhī-Hanumat-kavaca, a Pratyaṅgirā hymn ascribed to the Kubjikāmata, and the brief Siddhikālīstotra and Siddhikālī mantroddhāra ascribed to the Tridaśaḍāmara, framed by pūjā, bali and cakrapūjā procedures. It documents the Newar practice of assembling stotras and kavacas from different tantric sources into a single liturgical handbook.

In addition, the codex contains crucial liturgical and scriptural texts of the Siddhilakṣmī (Krama / Kubjikā) cult, including the Mahākaravīrayāga of the Mahākulakrama, the Siddhilakṣmīpañcaśataka accompanied by a marginal/interlinear commentary (Ṭippanaka), and a vernacular or Prakrit-influenced hymn entitled Prākṛtasiddhalakṣmīvidyā. The Mahāyāgakrama (also known as the Bhāvanopaniṣatprayoga) is an elaborate Śrīvidyā ritual manual composed by the 18th-century polymath Bhāskararāya Makhin. The Kāraṇāgama is traditionally ranked fourth among the twenty-eight canonical Siddhāntāgamas; this e-text contains the ten-chapter Kriyāpāda section of its Uttarabhāga preserved in the Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyata) tradition. The Śivadharmaśāstra is the foundational text of the early medieval Śivadharma corpus, composed approximately between the 6th and 7th centuries CE. Addressed primarily to householders and lay devotees (upāsakas) rather than ascetic initiates, it articulates a comprehensive Śaiva religious way of life, including liṅga installation and worship, temple maintenance, the merit of devotional gifts (dāna), protective chants, expiations, and a Śaiva restructuring of the stages and duties of life (varṇāśramadharma). The Śivadharmottara is an early medieval Śaiva religious treatise (c. 6th–8th century CE) forming the second foundational text of the Śivadharma corpus as a sequel to the Śivadharmaśāstra. Structured across twelve chapters as a discourse delivered by Nandikeśvara to Sanatkumāra on Mount Meru, it expounds lay and ascetic Śaiva religious practice (śivadharma), devotional liturgy, gifts (dāna), penances, and Śaiva yoga leading to liberation (mukti). It is celebrated especially for its second chapter on the gift of knowledge (vidyādāna), which contains one of premodern South Asia's most comprehensive early textual accounts of book production, manuscript copying, scribal decorum, and the ritual veneration of texts.

**Attribution:** The root paddhati is explicitly attributed to Aghoraśivācārya (12th c.) in internal colophons ('ityaghoraśivācāryaviracitāyāṃ śrīmanmṛgendrapaddhatau'). The commentary is attributed in its final colophon to Vaktraśambhu (referred to also as Naṭeśvara/Naṭeśaguru), son of Śaṅkara ('śrīnaṭeśvareṇa guruṇā vaktrādinā śambhunā śrīmacchaṅkarasūnunā viracitā ṭīkā samāptā').

The Mṛgendrapaddhati is a South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta ritual handbook attributed to Aghoraśivācārya (12th century), structured according to the ritual prescriptions of the Mṛgendrāgama's kriyāpāda. It is accompanied by the Mṛgendrapaddhatiṭīkā of Vaktraśambhu (Naṭeśaguru), which clarifies the technical procedures of the manual. The combined work sets out daily worship (nityapūjā), purificatory and expiatory rites (prāyaścitta), basic initiation (samayadīkṣā), the sacred cord festival (pavitravidhi), and icon consecration (pratiṣṭhā).

**Coverage:** partial — Transcription of IFP transcript T. 624, giving non-consecutive paṭalas in this order: Prāyaścittakāṇḍa paṭalas 40–47 (segs 8–1041, after an opening maṅgala and frame narrative); paṭala 23 (seg 1437); Naimittikakarmakāṇḍa paṭala 25 (Durgotpatti/Caṇḍībheda, seg 1555); Kāmyakāṇḍa paṭalas 29 (Navarātri) and 32 (Tulābhāra); a praśna paṭala 1 and Nityakāṇḍa paṭalas 2–3, 18–22; Kāmyakāṇḍa paṭalas numbered 45 (twice: lakṣahoma maṇḍapa; agnijanana) and 47 (colophon 'śrīvātulāgame'). The Vātulottara is a South Indian Śaiva scripture presenting itself as a supplement (uttara) to the Vātula(āgama), in the form of a Śiva–Pārvatī dialogue, with marked emphasis on Durgā/Caṇḍī worship ('durgābheda'). **DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_kaamaratnatantraHK`

**Author:** Nityanātha

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** Muktabodha header names Hemachandra Goswami Tattabhusan (ed.), Kāmaratna Tantra, Shillong: Assam Government Press, 1928. This is doubtful: the e-text opens 'atha kāmaratnam / hindīvyākhyāvibhūṣitam', i.e. it was keyed (Sanskrit only) from an edition with Hindi commentary, and follows the Nityanātha recension in 16 upadeśas, whereas Goswami's edition presents the Assamese recension with an old Assamese rendering. Most likely source type: one of the Bombay Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press (Khemrāj Śrīkṛṣṇadās) printings with Jvālāprasāda Miśra's Hindi bhāṣāṭīkā (1899 and later reprints), but this has not been checked against a copy.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog M00239), data-entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 0: Sept. 18, 2011.

**Evidence:**
- Header lines [3]-[9]: Editor Hemachandra Goswami Tattabhusan, Assam Government Press, Shilong, 1928
- Line [12]: 'hindīvyākhyāvibhūṣitam' (Hindi commentary omitted in the e-text)
- 16 colophons naming Nityanātha
- sourcelibrary.org/Wellcome record: Kāmaratnam of Nityanātha with Hindi bhāṣāṭīkā by Jvālāprasāda Miśra, Bombay, 1899 (368 pp.)

**Other editions:**
- Hemchandra Goswami Tattabhusan (ed.), Kāmaratna Tantra, with an old Assamese rendering, Shillong: Assam Government Press, 1928. — Assamese recension; named as source in the Muktabodha header.
- Kāmaratnam of Nityanātha, with Hindi bhāṣāṭīkā by Jvālāprasāda Miśra, Bombay: Khemrāj Śrīkṛṣṇadās, Śrī Veṅkaṭeśvara Press, 1899; later reprints (e.g. Bombay: Gaṅgāviṣṇu Śrīkṛṣṇadās, 1990). — Wellcome Collection copies; Hindi-commented edition of the Nityanātha recension.

**Translations:**
- Hemchandra Goswami (ed.), Kāmaratna Tantra, Shillong 1928 (old Assamese rendering). (Assamese)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 16 upadeśas (chapters 1–16), ending at segment 3729 with the colophon of the 16th upadeśa (rasādiśodhana).

**Also known as:** Kāmaratnatantra, Kāmaratna Tantra

**Attribution:** Ascribed in all sixteen upadeśa colophons to Nityanātha ("śrīnityanāthaviracite kāmaratne"). The Kāmaratna circulated in several recensions ascribed also to Śrīnātha, Nāgabhaṭṭa and others (Urban, Power of Tantra, 2010; Bendall, BM Catalogue 1893); identity with the Nityanātha of the Rasaratnākara is traditional but not established here.

A manual of practical magic and medicine in sixteen upadeśas ascribed to Nityanātha, framed as a dialogue of Īśvara and the Goddess. It covers the six magical rites (vaśīkaraṇa, ākarṣaṇa, stambhana, mohana, uccāṭana, māraṇa), aphrodisiacs (vājīkaraṇa), remedies against poison (viṣanivāraṇa), yakṣiṇī-sādhana, treasure-finding and other kautukas, and the purification of mercury and minerals (rasādiśodhana). The Kāmaratna was widely copied and printed in several recensions in North and East India.

# Varuṇapaddhati with Vilocana (dīkṣā section and beginning of pratiṣṭhā section)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_varunapaddhativyaakhyaaT1034HK`

**Author:** Varuṇaśiva, Nigamajñāna II

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition; unpublished transcription of IFP/EFEO paper transcript T. 1034 (Institut Français de Pondichéry), pp. 800–c. 898 (Muktabodha catalog no. M00240).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, data-entered by the staff under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (Revision 0: Sept. 18, 2011).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Catalog number : M00240', 'Main title: varuṇpaddhativyākhyā with commentary vilocana by nigamajñāna 2', 'Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T01034'; title lines in the text 'īFP ṭ. no. 1034)'.
- Transcript page markers 'p. 800)' to 'p. 898)' (partly mis-numbered).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Covers IFP/EFEO transcript T. 1034, pp. 800–c. 898 (page numbering in the e-text partly erratic: e.g. 888, 871, 843, 844, 812 out of sequence). Segs 9–1320: the dīkṣā section, complete with colophon (seg 1321–1322). Segs 1323–2020: the pratiṣṭhā section (definition of pratiṣṭhā, liṅga types, prāsāda parts, etc.), breaking off mid-sentence ('atha pratiṣṭhāyām mūrtimūrtīśvaratattvatattveśvaranyāsaḥ'). The rest of the pratiṣṭhā section of the commentary is missing.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Varuṇapaddhati (Varuṇaśiva, root text)
- Vilocana (Nigamajñāna II, commentary)

**Also known as:** Varuṇapaddhativyākhyā, Varuṇapaddhativyākhyāna, Vilocana

**Attribution:** The root Varuṇapaddhati (a short manual summarising the 'two seeds' of dīkṣā and pratiṣṭhā) is by the ācārya Varuṇaśiva ('ācāryo varuṇābhidhānaḥ', seg 25). The Vilocana is by Nigamajñānadeva of Vyāghrapura (Chidambaram) (colophon: 'śrīmadvyāghrapuravāsi-nigamajñānadeva-viracita-varuṇapaddhati-vyākhyāne vilocanākhyāne'), identified by Muktabodha as Nigamajñāna II (16th c.).

The Vilocana of Nigamajñānadeva of Chidambaram (Nigamajñāna II) is a commentary on Varuṇaśiva's Varuṇapaddhati, a short Śaiva Siddhānta manual on the 'seeds' (bīja) of initiation (dīkṣā) and installation (pratiṣṭhā). This e-text contains the commentary's complete section on dīkṣā (types of initiation, the six adhvans, kalās) and the opening of its section on pratiṣṭhā (definition, kinds of liṅga and temple parts), with copious quotations from Āgamas; it breaks off before the end.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Covers Upadeśas 1 to 4, but breaks off abruptly towards the end of chapter 4 (samādhi/nāda), marked explicitly at line 5263 as 'īncomplete'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Haṭhayogapradīpikā (Svātmārāma, root text)
- Jyotsnā (Brahmānanda, commentary)

**Also known as:** Haṭhapradīpikā, Haṭhapradīpikājyotsnā

**Attribution:** The root text is traditionally ascribed in colophons to Sahajānandasaṃtānacintāmaṇi Svātmārāma Yogīndra; the Sanskrit commentary Jyotsnā is by Brahmānanda.

The Haṭhayogapradīpikā is the principal medieval manual of Haṭhayoga, composed around the 15th century CE by Svātmārāma. Synthesizing Nātha lineage teachings and earlier haṭha treatises, it details āsana, purification techniques (ṣaṭkarma), prāṇāyāma (kumbhaka), and mudrā/bandha as an essential physical progression culminating in Rājayoga (samādhi and nādānusandhāna). This e-text reproduces the root text alongside Brahmānanda's prominent ṭīkā, the Jyotsnā, which explicates the physiological and philosophical terminology.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in all 18 adhyāyas of the Bhagavadgītā along with Abhinavagupta's commentary up to the closing verse and final colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Bhagavadgītā (root text)
- Gītārthasaṃgraha (Abhinavagupta, commentary)

**Also known as:** Bhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha, Gītārthasaṅgraha, Śrīmadbhagavadgītārthasaṃgraha

**Attribution:** The Gītārthasaṃgraha is solidly attributed to the Kashmirian Śaiva master Abhinavagupta (fl. late 10th to early 11th century CE), explicitly attested in introductory verses (v. 1.6: 'kṛto 'bhinavaguptena so 'yaṃ gītārthasaṃgrahaḥ'), chapter colophons, and closing verses.

The Gītārthasaṃgraha is Abhinavagupta's philosophical commentary on the Bhagavadgītā written from the perspective of non-dual Kashmir Śaivism (Pratyabhijñā). It interprets Kṛṣṇa's instruction to Arjuna as a revelation of supreme non-dual consciousness (anuttara-saṃvid), synthesizing action (karma), knowledge (jñāna), and devotion (bhakti) as integrated expressions of divine sovereignty and self-awareness (svātantrya). The work reflects the Kashmirian recension of the Bhagavadgītā, containing distinct textual variants and additional verses.

# Dīkṣāpaddhati (incomplete)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_diiksaapaddhatiHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition; transcription of manuscript no. 2379, Research Library, Jammu & Kashmir Government, Srinagar (Muktabodha catalog no. M00245, revision 0, 5 Feb. 2012). Marginal additions are given in round brackets.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (data entry by staff under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski)

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Manuscript : Manuscript no.: 2379 Research Library J. and K. Govt. Shrinigar'; 'Catalog number : M00245'
- Header note: 'This manuscript contains copious additions written in smaller characters on the margin … These noted in round brackets.'

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Day 1 (preliminary rites, kalaśa, fire), day 2 (adhivāsa, caru, the disciple's preparation, mapping of kalās and bhuvanas, the disciple's bed and dream rite; ends 'ity adhivāsaḥ') and the start of day 3 ('atha tṛtīya dine…': interpretation of dreams, then construction of the maṇḍala). It breaks off mid-word ('pūrvapatraṃ prasādyaivami', segment 4405) without a colophon. The actual nirvāṇa/putraka initiation on the main day is therefore missing.

**Attribution:** Anonymous Kashmiri compiler. The text opens with homage to the guru Kamalākarasvāmin and to Śiva identified with Parabhairava. The marginal glosses quote the Dīkṣottara and Somaśambhu, among others.

An anonymous Kashmiri manual for Śaiva (Bhairava-oriented) initiation, which Muktabodha describes as showing an intensely tantric local pantheon like Nepal's. The surviving part covers the preparatory days in detail: purification of the officiant, kalaśa installation, fire consecration, caru, and preparation of the disciple. It also maps the six paths (kalās, tattvas, bhuvanas) onto the disciple's body and gives the dream rite of the adhivāsa night. It then begins the third day (interpretation of dreams, drawing of the maṇḍala) before breaking off. Extensive marginal glosses in the manuscript are transcribed in round brackets.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** dīkṣāpaddhati

**Description:** Contains a Kashmiri initiatory rite. Here as in other liturgical works from Kashmir we learn about the deities of the Kashmiri Hindus. It is a very intensely tantric pantheon, reminiscent of what we find in Nepal.

**Notes:** Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S. G.Dyczkowski.

**Publication country:** India

# Agnikāryapaddhati (incomplete)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_agnikaaryapaddhatiHK.`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition; the e-text is an unpublished transcription of manuscript no. 781, Research Library, Jammu & Kashmir Government, Srinagar (Muktabodha catalog no. M00246, revision 0, 5 Feb. 2012).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (data entry by staff under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski)

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Manuscript : Manuscript no.: 781 Research Library J. and K. Govt. Shrinigar'
- Catalog number: M00246; Revision 0: Feb. 5, 2012
- The text carries transcriber's query marks ('*?', '?') of the kind found in Muktabodha manuscript transcriptions

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Starts at the beginning (maṅgala to Bhairavāgama, then 'atha vistare satyagnikāryapaddhatir likhyate'). It breaks off mid-verse (segment 3279) in the rules for the sacrificial animal (paśu), where it distributes the victim's parts to the deities. Muktabodha marks the end 'uncomplete', and there is no final colophon. The work's full extent is not known: the only witness is this manuscript.

**Attribution:** Anonymous manual of the Kashmiri Tantric Śaiva/Śākta ritual tradition.

An anonymous Kashmiri ritual manual (paddhati) for the fire ritual (agnikārya/homa) in a Bhairava/Kaula-oriented Śaiva setting. It begins with worship of Pustakavāgīśvarī (Sarasvatī) and Gaṇapati, kalaśa worship, purification of the subtle body, and preparation and consecration of the kuṇḍa and fire. It then gives oblation and tarpaṇa sequences for many deities, including Durgā, the Lokeśas and the planets, and ends with an incomplete section on animal sacrifice. The Muktabodha description stresses its incidental information on Kashmiri cults, e.g. the goddess Siddhalakṣmī. The e-text is long (c. 224,000 characters), even though Muktabodha calls it 'short'.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** agnikāryapaddhati

**Description:** A short liturgical manual from Kashmir on fire sacrifice. Contains very interesting incidental information on the deities worshipped in Kashmir. Some are main stream Kaula Tantra of the early period, such as Siddhalakṣmī who was the tutelary goddess of the Malla kings in Nepal.

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute
