## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Raghu Vira and Shodo Taki (eds.), Dakṣiṇāmūrti's Uddhāra-kośa: A Dictionary of the Secret Tantric Syllabic Code. Sarasvati Vihara Series, vol. 4. Lahore: International Academy of Indian Culture, 1938.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00247, supervised by Mark S. G. Dyczkowski)

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header explicitly names editors Raghu Vira and Taki Shodo, publication city Lahore, year 1938.
- Lines 15–16 read: 'ācārya-raghuvīreṇa tadantevāsinā takivaṃśodbhavena śodavena ca pariṣkṛtaḥ / Original edition first published in 1938'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in seven kalpas, concluding with the saptama kalpa colophon (segment 1708-1709).

**Also known as:** Mantroddhārakośa, Dakṣiṇāmūrtyuddhārakośa, Dakṣiṇāmūrti-Uddhārakośa

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the divine sage Dakṣiṇāmūrti; the actual historical author of this medieval tantric lexicon is anonymous.

The Uddhārakośa is a tantric lexicon (kośa) traditionally attributed to Dakṣiṇāmūrti that decodes the esoteric syllabic vocabulary used in mantroddhāra ('extraction of mantras'). Arranged in seven chapters (kalpas), it provides the key to decrypting the coded names of seed-syllables (bījas) and phonemes employed across Śaiva and Śākta ritual systems.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Begins without heading in the middle of paṭala 2 (mantroddhāra; its colophon "iti śrīkālottare mantroddhārapaṭalo dvitīyaḥ" follows), so paṭala 1 and the start of 2 are missing. Chapter colophons then run (with numbering irregularities and an apparent jump from paṭala 8 to 13) up to about paṭala 69 (vajrakavāṭalakṣaṇa / śivakūṭa sections), followed by further chapters on samaya rules; the transcript ends "(incomplete yāvanmātṛkaṃ likhitam)" at p. 371, i.e. copied as far as the exemplar went.

**Also known as:** Kālottara

**Attribution:** Anonymous Śaiva Siddhānta scripture (dialogue of Śiva and Skanda/Ṣaḍānana). This long South Indian recension refers in colophons to itself as part of a "dvādaśasahasrasaṃhitā" and "ayutatrayasaṃhitā" of the Kālottara.

A long South Indian recension of the Kālottara, a Śaiva Siddhānta scripture known in many recensions of very different length. In some seventy paṭalas this version treats mantra extraction, bathing, worship, mudrā and maṇḍala, dīkṣā and the six adhvans, yoga (nāḍīcakra, dhāraṇā, "vajrakavāṭa" meditations), vratas, prāyaścitta, gifts such as tulābhāra and hiraṇyagarbha, liṅga characteristics, installation (pratiṣṭhā), temple building and settlement planning. Its compilatory character suggests a relatively late redaction distinct from the short Sārdhatriśatikālottara commented on by Rāmakaṇṭha.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished transcript: Institut Français de Pondichéry / École française d'Extrême-Orient Transcript No. T0767 (transcribed from IFP MS RE 20294).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00249), data-entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (Revision 0: 5 Feb. 2012).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Catalog number : M00249', 'Uniform title: ṣatṣahasrakālottarāgama', 'Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T0767', 'Description: Copied from a MS belonging to the French Institute of Pondicherry, No. RE 20294'.
- Transcript page markers 'p. 2)' to 'p. 158)' and continuous verse numbering 1–2343 in the e-text.

**Other editions:**
- Bhatt, N. R. (ed.). 1979. Sārdhatriśatikālottarāgama (avec le commentaire de Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha). Publications de l'Institut Français d'Indologie 61. Pondichéry: Institut Français d'Indologie. — Edition of the short 350-verse recension (Sārdhatriśatikālottara); not the source of this e-text. No edition of the Ṣaṭsahasra recension is known.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcript T0767 pp. 2–158, verses numbered continuously 1–2343. Kālottara section (pp. 2–36, vv. 1–495): opens without title in a passage on maṇḍala and exegesis (vv. 1–2 repeated as 20–21), then chapters with Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara colophons: gaṇapatipūjā, aghorakalpa, rudraśānti, āśrama, gocara (paṭala 14), samayācāra, guruvicāra (16) and aṃśakatālakṣaṇa (17); paṭala numbering is irregular and many chapters of a 6,000-verse work are absent. From v. 496 (p. 36) the text is a compilation on worship, homa, kuṇḍas, iconography, pratiṣṭhā, festivals and Śivarātri, with source rubrics such as 'iti kāraṇe', 'iti bhīmakāraṇe pratiṣṭhātantre vināyakavratavidhipaṭalaḥ', 'sūkṣmatantre', 'dīptatantre', 'iti vijayākhya mahātantre śivarātrividhiḥ'; it ends abruptly at v. 2343 (flower/leaf substitutes in worship) with no colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Ṣaṭsahasrakālottarāgama (selected paṭalas) (root text (verses 1–495))
- Anthology of ritual extracts from Kāraṇa, Bhīmakāraṇa, Sūkṣma, Dīpta, Vijaya and other Āgamas (appended compilation (verses 496–2343, incomplete))

**Also known as:** Ṣaṭsahasrikālottara, Ṣaṭsahasrakālottara

**Attribution:** Revealed scriptural work belonging to the Siddhāntatantra / Kālottara corpus of the Śaiva tradition.

The e-text begins with selected chapters of the Ṣaṭsahasra ('6,000-verse') recension of the Kālottara, a Śaiva Siddhānta scripture known in recensions of very different length; they deal with Gaṇapati worship, an Aghora ritual (aghorakalpa), the rite of pacification (rudraśānti), the āśramas, astrological suitability (gocara), the conduct of ācāryas and initiates, the examination of the guru and the aṃśaka division. Most of the transcript, however, is a South Indian temple-ritual compilation quoting the Kāraṇa, Sūkṣma, Dīpta, Vijaya and other Āgamas on homa and kuṇḍas, images, liṅgas, installation, festivals and Śivarātri.

This South Indian transcript gives a series of ritual chapters, many labelled as belonging to its 'Pratiṣṭhātantra': personal purification, mantroddhāra, daily worship, mudrās, bathing rites (snapana), festivals and their expiations, pavitrārohaṇa, the Kṛttikā lamp festival, homa and kuṇḍas, and temple and liṅga proportions.

# Timirodghāṭatantra (paṭalas 1–12, with other texts from the same manuscript)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_timirodghataHK`

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition; unpublished transcription of National Archives Kathmandu MS 5/690, NGMPP reel A 1380/9 (Muktabodha catalog no. M00258).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, data-entered by the staff under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (Revision 0: April 6, 2012).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header lines [1]-[4]: 'Catalog number : M00258; Manuscript : NGMPP access no. 5/690 reel no: A 1380/9; Description: Copied from NGMPP manuscript access no. 5/690 reel no: A 1380/9; Data entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the direction of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski.'
- Manuscript page markers in the text ('p. 2)', 'p. 2b)', ... 'p. 45)'), lacuna marks and query marks typical of a diplomatic transcription.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Composite NGMPP manuscript. Segs 8–378 (ms pp. 1–24): an Arjuna–Kṛṣṇa (Saṃjaya-framed) dialogue unrelated to the Timirodghāṭa. Segs 379–889: the Timirodghāṭa, opening with a Kārtikeya–Maheśvara dialogue on haṃsa; chapter colophons 'iti timirodghāṭane ... paṭalaḥ' for paṭalas 2 and 4–12 (paṭala 1 apparently ends at seg 438 '... iti', the colophon of 3 is lost), the last reading 'dvādaśamaḥ paṭalaḥ samāptaḥ || 12 ||' (seg 889). Segs 890–1085: further untitled material (a yāga section ending 'ete yāgasadbhāvasamāptaḥ' at seg 1031, then a Bhairava–Devī section breaking off). Heavy lacunae ('* * *', '?'); page markers are out of sequence (e.g. p. 42 before p. 30, p. 33), showing disordered leaves. Whether 12 paṭalas are the full extent of the work cannot be verified (no other witness or edition).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Unidentified Arjuna–Kṛṣṇa dialogue on jñāna and yoga (Gītā-type text) (preceding text in the same manuscript (segs 8–378))
- Timirodghāṭatantra (Timirodghāṭana) (root text (segs 379–889, paṭalas 1–12))
- Unidentified Kaula/Śaiva fragments (incl. a yāga section ending 'ete yāgasadbhāvasamāptaḥ', attributed to Mīnanātha/Siddhanātha, and a further Bhairava–Devī section) (following texts in the same manuscript (segs 890–1085))

**Also known as:** Timirodghāṭana, Timirodghāṭa

**Attribution:** Anonymous Śaiva/Kaula scripture (Bhairava–Devī dialogue; the first section is a Kārtikeya–Maheśvara dialogue on haṃsa). A Timirodghāṭa is cited by Kṣemarāja (e.g. Śivasūtravimarśinī; cf. Alper 1989) and listed by Sanderson among Kashmirian Kaula/Trika scriptural sources; the quoted verse ('mahāghorāḥ pīṭhadevyaḥ ...') was not found in this defective transcription, so the identity of this text with the work quoted by Kṣemarāja is not verified.

A defective transcription of a Nepalese composite manuscript whose core is the Timirodghāṭa(na), an anonymous Śaiva/Kaula scripture in twelve paṭalas cast mainly as a Bhairava–Devī dialogue on haṃsa, mantra, subtle-body yoga and ritual. It is preceded by an unrelated Gītā-type Arjuna–Kṛṣṇa dialogue on jñāna and followed by further Kaula ritual and yogic fragments. A Timirodghāṭa is cited by Kṣemarāja and listed among Kaula/Trika sources, but this text's relation to the quoted work has not been established.

It is a major classical source for Śrīvaiṣṇava temple liturgy and ritual philosophy.

Folios 9–19 are lost; the e-text breaks off on p. 8b, and line 182 reads 'page 9 to 19 missing'. An anonymous Śaiva yoga text in which Śiva instructs Skanda. It covers the subtle body (the nine doors, nāḍīs such as piṅgalā and suṣumṇā, the vital winds), the 'joining to brahman' (brahmasandhāna) through the brahmadvāra, and yogic exit at death (utkrānti). It also treats the cosmogony from cicchakti, the composition of the human body, the nāda as brahman, and a purely mental worship (mānasayāga) with bathing at the inner Śivatīrtha. It closes with an internal fire worship (agnipūjā), in which the five breaths are offered into the fire in the heart.

**Edition used (determined):** Unedited manuscript: Banaras Hindu University Library MS C4257 (leaves 251a–260). This is a transcription of the manuscript, not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00268, data-entered under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 0 of 7 Apr. 2012 (https://muktabodha-digital-library.org/texts/IAST/M00268).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header (segs. 2–6): 'Uniform title: prāṇāgnihotra / Manuscript : BHU C4257 / Revision 0: April 7, 2012'.
- Leaf markers 'p. 251a)' ... 'p. 257b)', 'p. 260)' in the e-text; the e-text ends mid-word directly before the Muktabodha footer.
- ilx_skt metadata/muktabodha.csv (M00268): 'incomplete', colophon 'no'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcription of a short text within a larger manuscript, BHU C4257 (page markers 'p. 251a)' to 'p. 257b)', then 'p. 260)'; '250b' after '251a' is evidently a slip for 251b). The text runs straight on from 257b to the leaf marked 260, mid-verse ('prāṇāgnihotra yatnena kuryāccaiva vidhānataḥ | sarvapāpavinirmukto ...'), so '260' is probably a misnumbering rather than a sign of lost leaves. The e-text ends mid-word with 'sa' (seg. 161), with no closing colophon. ilx_skt metadata: 'incomplete', colophon 'no'. How much of the end is lost is unknown.

**Attribution:** An anonymous Śaiva dialogue. Ṣaṇmukha (Skanda) asks Śiva (addressed as Śūlabhṛt) for the prāṇāgnihotra on behalf of 'alpavittā narāḥ' who cannot keep the Vedic agnihotra, and Śiva answers. Its question list ('śarīre'smin katy agnayaḥ, ko yajamānaḥ, kā patnī ...') and the answer 'puruṣo yajamānaḥ, prakṛtiḥ patnī ...' belong to the same tradition of the inner, bodily fire sacrifice as the Prāṇāgnihotra Upaniṣad. However, the frame and much of the wording differ, and the e-text is not a copy of that Upaniṣad. No source for the text was identified.

A short anonymous Śaiva text in verse and prose on the 'agnihotra in the breath' (prāṇāgnihotra), taught by Śiva to Ṣaṇmukha for people who cannot afford the Vedic fire ritual. It maps the elements of the śrauta sacrifice (the fires, sacrificer, wife, priests, offerings, implements, altar and so on) onto the body, its faculties and the cosmos. It then describes the five vital breaths and their deities, and the eating of food as an inner fire offering. The surviving text breaks off in this last section.

- Candrajñāna chapters: Śivotsavavidhi (21st, colophon also names the Śrīmukhatantra), Lakṣmīpratiṣṭhāvidhi (paṭala 79, uttarabhāga), Pañcākṣarapaṭala (kriyāpāda), Ārdrāvratavidhi (22), Śivarātrivratakalpa (23), Balidānavidhi (24), Āśaucavidhi (20), Mahotsavavidhi ('candrajñānabhede devyā mate'), Jñānadarśanapaṭala (root text (selected chapters))

**Also known as:** Candrajñāna

**Attribution:** The Candrajñāna is one of the 28 Siddhānta Āgamas in the South Indian lists (Muktabodha calls it an upāgama and a pratiṣṭhātantra). The surviving South Indian material is a late scriptural corpus. The chapters here are cast as dialogues of Īśvara with Candra (Niśākara/Kalānātha) and Bṛhaspati.

A compilation of chapters from the South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta scripture Candrajñāna, preserved in an IFP transcript. It covers the esoteric meaning of the five-syllable mantra (pañcākṣara) and temple festivals (utsava, mahotsava with flag-hoisting). It also gives the installation of Lakṣmī, the Ārdrā and Śivarātri observances, bali offerings, detailed impurity rules (āśauca) by caste and occupation, and a closing doctrinal chapter on knowledge (jñānadarśana) of the tattvas and liberation as union with Śiva (sāyujya).

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unedited manuscript: National Archives Kathmandu 6/1748, microfilmed by the NGMCP as reel A 989/23 (transcription of fols. 1a–15a). This is not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, catalogue no. M00277, revision 0 of 16 Dec. 2013 (https://www.muktabodha.org, Digital Library).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header inside the e-text (segments 1–6): 'Catalog number : M00277 / Uniform title: bhāvacūḍāmaṇi / Author : vidyākaṇṭha / Manuscript : NGMCP 6/1748 reel number A 989/23 / Notes: Revision 0: December 16, 2013'
- Folio markers 'p. 1a)' ... 'p. 15a)' in the e-text
- The e-text ends mid-word, followed directly by the Muktabodha copyright footer

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcription of fols. 1a–15a of NGMCP 6/1748 (reel A 989/23), with folio markers 'p. 1a)' to 'p. 15a)'. It covers the prose opening, the guru lineages (divyaugha, siddhaugha, mānavaugha) for Kālikā, Tārā and other goddesses, and the doctrine of the three bhāvas (divya, vīra, paśu). It breaks off at the start of the exposition of paśubhāva ('paśubhāvaṃ pravakṣyāmi ... yathāvidhi paśorddāṃ'), with no final colophon. The full extent of the work is unknown.

**Also known as:** Bhāvacūḍāmaṇitantra

**Attribution:** The Muktabodha catalogue (M00277) gives the author as Vidyākaṇṭha, which conflates this text with Bhaṭṭa Vidyākaṇṭha II's Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi, a Saiddhāntika commentary on the Mayasaṃgraha that survives in a Jammu manuscript (Muktabodha M00575). Goodall, Kiraṇavṛtti vol. 1 (1998), introduction n. 10: 'There survive Nepalese manuscripts of a tantra called the Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi whose ... discussion between Devī and Bhairava in which Bhairava is asking the questions, and it is not a tantra of the Śaiva Siddhānta.' The present text is such a Nepalese manuscript. It is quoted in later Śākta digests: the verse 'bhāvas tu trividho deva divyavīrapaśukramāt' (seg. 146) is cited as Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi by Bharati (The Tantric Tradition), and the Encyclopedia of Tantra cites Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi quotations via the Śyāmārahasya and Tantrasāra.

This is a Śākta/Kaula text in the form of a dialogue in which Bhairava questions the Goddess. Its prose opening says that mantras do not succeed without the right inner disposition (bhāva). The surviving portion lists the divine, perfected and human lineages of gurus (divyaugha, siddhaugha, mānavaugha) for the cults of Kālikā, Tārā and other goddesses, then sets out the doctrine of the three dispositions of the practitioner (divya, vīra, paśu) and stresses that guru and kula are required for any entitlement to tantric practice. Verses from this Bhāvacūḍāmaṇi are quoted in later Śākta digests.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete transcription of the manuscript from folio 1a to the concluding colophon (chapters 1–15).

**Also known as:** Hāhārāva Tantra, Atharvaṇasaṃhitā (Hāhārāvatantra)

**Attribution:** Canonical Śākta-Kaula tantric scripture presenting itself as an Atharvaṇasaṃhitā (associated with the Atharvaveda tradition).

The Hāhārāvatantra is a Nepalese Śākta-Kaula tantra affiliated with the Atharvaveda tradition (Atharvaṇasaṃhitā), centering on the worship of Kaula goddesses with an emphasis on Guhyakālī and Pratyaṅgirā. The text details dhyānas, yantras, a thousand names (sahasranāma) of Guhyakālī, protective hymns (kavaca), indrajāla and other magical rites, and Kaula ritual worship using sacrificial vessels (pātras). It survives primarily in Kathmandu Valley manuscript collections.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** hāhārāvatantra

**Description:** The Hāhārāvatantra (the Tantra of the Roaring Haa, Haa) teaches the worship of Kaula goddesses, especially forms of Kālī, with a very clear preference for Guhyakālī. Guhyakaalii is one of the most popular form of Kaalii in the Kathmandu Valley, although hardly known outside it. The main Tantra of Guhyakālī is the massive Mahākālasaṃhitā which may well have been redacted in Kathmandu Valley probably after the 14th century. It is likely that the Hāhārāvatantra is also of Nepalese as its preference for Guhyakālī suggests and absence of manuscripts or references to it outside the Valley. Another indication that this so is the presence in the text of the typical Nepalese corruption mahākarmārcana for mahaakramārcana denoting the Kaula liturgy for the worship of Kaula goddesses. This Tantra calls itself an atharvanasaṃhitā and so affiliates itself to the tradition of the Atharva Veda. This is probably because of its extensive treatment of magical rites, incantations and magical potions.

# Kulānanda, with Kapālalakṣaṇa from the Picumata and fragments of Kaula ritual texts

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_kulanandadiHK`

**Author:** Matsyendranātha

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unedited manuscript: National Archives Kathmandu 1-1376/v, microfilmed by the NGMCP as reel A 40/6 (transcription of the whole manuscript, including its gaps). Not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00284, data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 0 of 17 Dec. 2003 (https://muktabodha-digital-library.org/texts/IAST/M00284).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header (segs. 1–7): 'Uniform title: kulānandādi / Manuscript : NGMCP 1-1376/ v reel number A40/6 / Description: The manuscript called Kulānandādi contains short tracts and fragments of early Kaula works. The first is called Kulānanda covers the first seven folios ... / Revision 0: December 17, 2003'.
- Folio markers '1b)' ... '8b)', then restarting at '1a)', in the e-text; the transcriber's note 'īncomplete' at the end.
- ilx_skt metadata/muktabodha.csv (M00284): 'fragments; 2 excerpts (2nd is fragmentary, lacking explicit+colophon)', with the colophons 'iti matsyendrapādāvatārikaṃ kulānandasamāptam' and 'iti kapālakṣaṇaṃ picumate'.

**Other editions:**
- Bagchi, Prabodh Chandra (ed.), Kaulajñāna-nirṇaya and Some Minor Texts of the School of Matsyendranātha, Calcutta Sanskrit Series 3, Calcutta: Metropolitan Printing & Publishing House, 1934. — Contains an edition of the Kulānanda from a Nepalese manuscript. Only the Kulānanda portion corresponds; page numbers not verified. Muktabodha has a separate Kulānanda e-text (M00513) with P. C. Bagchi as editor.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The Kulānanda is complete, with its colophon at seg. 155. The rest of the manuscript is fragmentary. Fols. 7b–8b contain only a few broken lines before and after 'iti kapālakṣaṇaṃ picumate' (seg. 163). Folio numbering then restarts at '1a)' (seg. 182) and again at '1a)' (seg. 254), so several separate bundles have been bound together. The e-text ends after 'bhairava vali ||' with the editor's note 'īncomplete' (seg. 738).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kulānanda (Matsyendranātha (traditional), root text (complete; fols. 1b–7a, segs. 8–156))
- Kapālalakṣaṇa (from the Picumata/Brahmayāmala) (scriptural fragment (segs. 158–253; damaged and lacunose))
- Anonymous Kaula ritual texts (maṇḍala/toraṇa/dhvaja rites with Vedic mantras, homa, bali to Vaṭuka, yoginīs, Kṣetrapāla, Gaṇapati and Bhairava, Kubjikā, Tārā and Śrīvidyā samayavidyās) (ritual fragments (segs. 254–738; break off incomplete))

**Also known as:** Kulānandādi (Muktabodha uniform title), Kulānandatantra

**Attribution:** The Kulānanda's colophon calls it 'revealed through Matsyendrapāda' (matsyendrapādāvatārita). The verse that follows praises the guru lineage from Ādinātha (segs. 158–159). The Kapālalakṣaṇa is ascribed by its colophon to the Picumata, i.e. the Brahmayāmala; whether it matches the transmitted Brahmayāmala was not checked. The ritual sections are anonymous.

A transcription of a Nepalese Kaula miscellany manuscript. It opens with the complete Kulānanda, a short dialogue between Bhairava and the Goddess ascribed to Matsyendranātha. The Kulānanda teaches yogic 'piercing' (vedha) of the bodily centres and the signs of possession (āveśa) and other immediate experiences (sadyapratyaya). Next comes a damaged passage on the marks of skull-bowls (kapāla), ascribed to the Picumata. The rest consists of fragmentary ritual texts: maṇḍala and gateway rites using Vedic mantras, homa, bali offerings, and samaya-vidyās of Kubjikā, Tārā and the Śrīvidyā goddesses.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulānandādi

**Description:** The manuscript called Kulānandādi contains short tracts and fragments of early Kaula works. The first is called Kulānanda covers the first seven folios. As it attributed to Matsyendranātha, it is important although short. It deals with aspects of Kaula Yoga, focused around the -piercing - (vedha) of spiritual energy through centres of the subtle body following from above and the piercing of Kuṇḍalinī upwards. The character and form of the exposition, which is in line with other Kaula tracts attributed to Matsyendranātha, supports the view that this is indeed an early Kaula work. The next 4 folios deal with the charateristics of a skull bowl (kapāla) which is said to be drawn from the Picumata (i.e. the Brahmayāmala) which is quite possible as this text does indeed deal with this topic. The rest of the manuscript contains prescriptions for Kaula ritual. The goddesses belong to the early period, including Kubjikā, Kālasaṃkarṣiṇī, Bhagamālinī and others. Notably Tripurā is absent, although Kāmeśvarī, one of her precursors is not.

**Notes:** In the manuscript anusvāra and visarga occur together.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Fols. 1a–19a of NAK 3-251 (folio markers '1b)' to '19a)'). Kulasārasaṃgraha: from the opening 'śrīdevyuvāca' to the colophons of paṭalas 24 (seg. 72), 25 (segs. 182–183) and 26 (seg. 228). Muktabodha says the manuscript 'begins with chapter 24'; chapters 1–23 and anything after 26 are absent. Kulācāranirṇaya: paṭalas 1–4 have explicit colophons (segs. 284, 320, 387, 460); a fifth chapter ends 'iti śrīkulācāranirṇaye paṭalaṃ samāptaṃ' (seg. 628). The total extent of the work is unknown. Antyeṣṭikrama: one complete chapter, ending 'iti tatvāmarśāṃtyaṣṭikramaḥ aṣṭādaśollāsaḥ saṃpūrṇaṃ' (seg. 734), then the note on Subhagānandanātha and the date 'samvat 1929 śubham'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kulasārasaṃgraha (part of the Somabhujāvalī), paṭalas 24–26 (root text, excerpt (segs. 9–228; fols. 1a–6b))
- Kulācāranirṇaya, paṭalas 1–5 (root text, excerpt (segs. 229–628; fols. 6b–16b))
- Antyeṣṭikrama, 18th ullāsa of an unidentified Śrīvidyā-related work ('tatvāmarśa-') (single chapter (segs. 629–734; fols. 16b–19a))

**Also known as:** Kulasāra (manuscript label; Muktabodha uniform title), Kaulasārasaṃgraha (Muktabodha secondary title), Somabhujāvalī (larger work named in the Kulasārasaṃgraha colophons)

**Attribution:** All three pieces are anonymous dialogues between Śiva and the Goddess. The Kulācāranirṇaya colophons call it 'śivapraṇīta'/'śivokta'. After the last chapter, a note (segs. 735–736) reports that according to Subhagānandanātha it cannot be said whether this 18th ullāsa was spoken by Īśvara or composed by ācāryas. The work it belongs to is not identified. The manuscript is dated 'samvat 1929', which is 1872 CE if read as Vikrama saṃvat; a Nepāla saṃvat reading is impossible.

A Nepalese manuscript labelled Kulasāra that actually contains chapters of three late Kaula works in the form of dialogues between Śiva and the Goddess. Chapters 24–26 of the Kulasārasaṃgraha, said to be part of the Somabhujāvalī, open with the myth of how the gods lost wine and discuss its purification and the vessels used for it. Chapters 1–5 of the Kulācāranirṇaya treat devotion to the guru and Kaula samaya conduct. A final 18th chapter (ullāsa) on Kaula funerary rites (antyeṣṭi) is followed by a note citing Subhagānandanātha. Muktabodha dates such texts after the 13th century.

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulasāra

**Description:** This manuscript is called Kulasāra, but is in fact a collection of fragment of three Kaula tracts. The first is Kaulsārasaṃgraha which, according to the colophons is a part of the Somabhujavalī. It begins with chapter 24 and extends up to to chapter 26. It is followed by the Kulaacāranirṇaya which extends from chapter 1 to 5. The third fragment is chapter eighteen of a work belonging to the śrīvidyā lineage of Subhagānandanātha. It deals with the funerary rites of a Kaula. The texts of which these are fragments in the format of a Tantra, outlining the principles of Kaula ritual and practice. They are typical Kaula work belonging to the latter period, that is, after the 13th century. Indeed such texts can be treated as an independent class of Kaula works of which the Kulārṇavatantra is one of the earliest.

The Āścaryayogamālā ('Rosary of Wondrous Recipes/Applications'), also known as Yogaratnamālā or Yogaratnāvalī, is a medieval manual of magic and occult recipes (ṣaṭkarman) attributed to Nāgārjuna. Comprising approximately 140 verses, it details preparations and spells for subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), dissension (vidveṣaṇa), immobilization (stambhana), invisibility, poison remedies, and other marvels. It is accompanied by the concise commentary (Laghuvṛtti) of the Śvetāmbara Jaina scholar Guṇākara.

**Uniform title:** āścaryayogamālā

**Author:** nāgārjuna

**Commentator:** guṇākara

**Description:** āścaryayogamālā (also called Yogaratnāvalī or Yogaratnamālā) (the Rosary of Astonishing Yogas) by Nāgārjuna with a short commentary (laghuvṛtti) by Guṇākara who is a Jaina (śvetāmbara) scholar. This Nāgārjuna is famous as the author (or the namesake of various authors) of works on magic (ṣaṭkarma). A manuscript in the Asiatic Society in Bombay dates the composition of the work as 1240 CE. It was written, the text tells us, to serve people needs and delight them. It deals with standard matters of magic beginning with control of others (vaśīkaraṇa), then the checking of an enemies army (stambhana), killing of enemies (śatrumāraṇa), attraction of women (akarṣaṇa) and ways of attaining various magical powers (siddhi) through the preparation of potions, which the text describes in detail, and mantras.

Preserved in Nepalese manuscripts, it represents an important early stratum in medieval Indian tantric alchemy.

She is the consort (Umādevī) of the five headed Bhairava, who is probably with Svacchandabhairava, who is in some of his aspects a medicine god. They are seated on mount Kailāsa. After imploring him for the knowledge that leads to liberation, the god promising to do so, teaches the preparation of herbs for healing and magic most especially he focuses on the magical preparation of alchemical mercury making this an important unpublished work on Indian alchemy.

The Gorakṣaguṭikā ('Pill/Amulet of Gorakṣa') is a late Nātha liturgical and mythological text framed as a Tantric Haragaurīsaṃvāda (dialogue between Śiva and Gaurī), claiming affiliation to the Kalpadrumavivekinī (or Kalpadrumasaṃhitā). Unlike standard Haṭha Yoga treatises, it centers on devotional ritual and Guru worship, recounting the miraculous birth and deeds of Gorakṣanātha in its opening chapter, followed by protective kavacas, mantras, and stotras (including his dvādaśanāma, aṣṭottaraśatanāma, and sahasranāma) across nine chapters (taraṅgas).

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** gorakṣaguṭikā

**Author:** gorakṣanātha

**Description:** The Goraksaguṭikā (the Magic Pill of Gorakṣa) is attributed to Gorakṣa (alias Gorakhnātha) the famous founder of Haṭha Yoga. The colophons state that it is part of the Kalpadrumavivekinii and that it is a commentary (bhyāsa) on Yoga. It is framed in the format of a Tantra as a dialogue between śiva and Gaurī. Although Gorakṣanātha was a yogi, as are his followers the Naatha Yogis today, and so should not be concerned with ritual practice, in actual fact the Nātha tradition has developed an extensive liturgy centered on the worship of its Gurus. This short tract contains a series of hymns (stotra) praising Gorakṣanātha and myths that narrate their origins.

**Evidence:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Preserved fragment of an incomplete Nepalese manuscript; opens abruptly in chapter (paṭala) 4, followed by chapters 8 to 17, where it ends abruptly.

**Attribution:** Scriptural Kaula tantra presented as divine revelation in dialogue form.

The Kulasāra is an early Kaula Śaiva scripture surviving in archaic Nepalese manuscripts and cited by non-dual Kashmiri Śaiva authors prior to the eleventh century. It expounds Kaula metaphysics—including the categories of piṇḍa, pada, rūpa, and rūpātīta, as well as Akula and Kula—combined with yogic practices for bodily internalization, mantra protection, visualization of Bhairava and yoginīs, non-dual ritual purity, and internal pilgrimage (caryā). This e-text preserves an unedited diplomatic transcript of chapters 4 (fragment) and 8–17 (incomplete).

## Muktabodha catalog metadata

**Uniform title:** kulasāra

**Description:** The manuscript is incomplete. It begins abruptly in the middle of chapter (paṭala) four and then continues from chapter eight to seventeen where it ends abruptly. The Kulasāra is quoted by non-dualist Kashmiri Shaiva authors and so preceeds the 11th century. It belongs to a genre of Kaula Tantras that are focused on the attainment of the direct experience of essential metaphysical principles and yogic powers through the practice of Yoga and insight. Through knowledge of these principles the Kaula Yogi attains liberation in this life (jñānāvabhāsena jīvanmuktye vyavasthitaḥ fl. 33b) and numerous yogic powers. The text focuses also on the worship of Bhairava and Devī and the host of Yoginīs. The first chapters are concerned with the four principles commonly mentioned in Kaula works, namely, Piṇḍa, Pada, ṛūpa and Rūpātīta. Unfortunately, here the manuscript is incomplete. Chapter nine deals with the attainment of the pervasion of transcendental śiva by the abandonment of śakti (9). The following chapter teaches the attainment of the supreme reality which is the Inexplicable free of phenomenal qualities, immobile and pervasive like the sky by merger with the space contained in the jar of the psycho-physical body (10). The next chapter deals with transcendent Akula and immanent Kula along with Kaula which is the union of the two (11). Chapter twelve describes the ascent through the centres of the body from the feet to the head. Corresponding to the spheres of the gross elements, they are the abodes of numerous types of Yoginīs the text describes and the damage they can do. The Yogi should know them and by his devotion to the deity, fire and the guru and practice of Yoga be protected from them. Those who are immoral are consummed by them. The chapter ends with a series of visualizations designed to protect the body of the Yogi (12). The next chapter continues with similar concerns for protection and the overcoming of disease and death by the use of Bhairava Mantra and visualization of his form which appears to be that of Svacchandabhairava and accompanying forms and their consorts (13). The next chapter discusses non-duality in the sense of the absence of pure and impure with regards to food and drink and the defects of those who do not follow this path. It goes on to talk about freedom from dualistic thought constructs and the purification of the mind and purification of the sacrificial substances that takes place in this way. It is applied to the sacrificial meat and then wine (14). Chapter fifteen deals with the observance (caryā) of the Kaula adept (vīra). He should travel to the inner Kaula sacred sites (pīṭha, kṣetra) in the body following the vital breath rather than the outer ones. There he plays with the Yoginīs and worships them and does so externally also with a pure mind. The manner the pilgrimage is to be performed externally is described next.The last chapter deals with the Three Jewels of Shiva, Shakti and the Self, their attainment and experience.

The Vimalāvatītantra (also termed Vimalāvatī or Vimalāvatīpaddhati) is an extensive Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual composed by Vimalaśiva, an ācārya who resided in Vārāṇasī. The work details worship procedures (pūjā), fire sacrifices (vahnikārya, homa), festive ritual observances such as pavitrarohaṇa and damanāropaṇa, subtle breath yoga, and various degrees of initiation (dīkṣā) alongside conduct codes for initiates.

**Author:** vimalaśiva

**Description:** This is a work on Siddhānta ritual written by Vimalaśiva who lived in the thirteenth century. He declares with pride that he had taken the vow of residing all his life in Benares (kāśīvāsa). The first chapter deals with the accomplishment and fruits of worship (pūjāsiddhi). Chapter two deals with the procedure for making the sacrificial; fire (vahnikārya) and three the offerings to it (homa). Four deals with the seasonal offering to the deity of a sacred thread (pavitra) and the next with the offering of garlands (dāmana). The fifth deals with the rites of initiation. The text continues to elaborate on the details concerning initiation. It includes several interesting inner purificatory practices linked with the movement of the vital breath and the movement of Kuṇḍalinī. The rules of right conduct for initiate of various kinds are ennumerated and other matters taught concerning his duties and those of Shaivites in general both as householders and renouncers. Various initiatory rites are described for different types and levels of initiands.

The Devīrahasya is a Śākta tantric digest and ritual compilation framed as part of the Rudrayāmala, composed in Kashmir. It is structured into a Pūrvārdha of 25 paṭalas dealing with initiation, mantra vitalization and unlocking, puraścaraṇa, yantras, and ritual ingredients, followed by an Uttarārdha of 35 paṭalas providing pañcāṅgas (paṭala, kavaca, paddhati, sahasranāma, and stotra) for various deities. The appended text is the Uddhārakośa of Dakṣiṇāmūrtimuni, a 7-kalpa lexicon defining and deciphering tantric mantras.

# Kriyākramadyotikāvyākhyā

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_kriyakramadyotikavyakhyaHK`

**Author:** Kacchapeśvaraśivācārya

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) transcript T. 109 (373 pp.), copied from a manuscript belonging to Śiva Śrī Svāminātha Śivācārya of Tiruvaduturai (Thanjavur Dt.). Not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00324, data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 0 of 21 Nov. 2014 (https://muktabodha-digital-library.org/texts/IAST/M00324).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header in the e-text (segs. 1–9): 'Catalog number : M00324 / ... Manuscript : IFP transcript T00109 / Description: IFP transcript T00109 copied from a manuscript belonging to Siva Sri Swaminatha Sivacharya of Tiruvaduturai Tanjavur Dt. / Revision 0: Nov. 21, 2014'.
- Page markers 'p. 1)' ... 'p. 373)' in the e-text (pagination of the transcript).
- Sanderson, The Śaiva Age (2009), cites this work as 'Kriyākramadyotikāvyākhyā of Kacchapeśvaraśiva. IFP MS Transcript 109' (bibliography) and quotes it by page and line (p. 80, ll. 4–7), i.e. the same unpublished transcript.

**Other editions:**
- No printed edition of Kacchapeśvara's commentary was found. — The root text, Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā, was printed in Grantha script with Nirmalamaṇi's Prabhā commentary, ed. Rāmaśāstrin and Ambalavāṇa Jñānasambandhaparāśaktisvāmin, Chidambaram, 1927 (per IFP catalogue records). The draft's references to editions of 1898 (Shanmukasundara Mudaliar) and Tenkasi 1974 could not be verified and have been dropped.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — The commentary is complete as transmitted: it ends with the section colophon 'iti damana pūjāvidhiḥ samāptaḥ' (seg. 4664), the commentator's closing verses and the final colophon 'iti śrīmatkacchapeśvara śivācāryaviracitā śrīmadaghoraśivācāryakṛtakriyākramadyotikāvyākhyā samāptam' (segs. 4669–4670), followed by the Muktabodha footer. Page markers run continuously from 'p. 1)' to 'p. 373)'. The commentary covers only the first part of Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā (daily rites: snāna, sandhyā, nyāsa, pūjā, agnikārya etc.; then pavitrārohaṇa and damanapūjā), not the later sections on dīkṣā, pratiṣṭhā, antyeṣṭi etc.; Nirmalamaṇi's Prabhā commentary (Muktabodha M00126) likewise ends with the damanavidhi. Whether Kacchapeśvara ever commented on the remaining sections is unknown.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kriyākramadyotikāvyākhyā (Kacchapeśvaraśivācārya, commentary)
- Kriyākramadyotikā (Aghoraśiva, root text (cited by pratīka/lemmata only, not given in full))

**Also known as:** Aghoraśivapaddhativyākhyā, Kriyākramadyotikā-vyākhyā

**Attribution:** Composed by Kacchapeśvaraśivācārya of Kāñcī. In the opening verses he names his guru Sadāśiva of Kāñcī (seg. 29). He describes himself as a worshipper (pūjaka) of Ekāmranātha ('ekamākaṃdanāmāṃghri pūjakena', seg. 4665). Sanderson cites him as Kacchapeśvaraśiva. The draft claim that he calls Aghoraśiva his teacher (from Dyczkowski's description) does not follow from the text, which names Sadāśiva as 'asmadguru'.

A Sanskrit commentary (vyākhyā) by Kacchapeśvaraśivācārya of Kāñcīpuram on the Kriyākramadyotikā, the ritual manual (paddhati) composed by Aghoraśiva in the 12th century. The Kriyākramadyotikā is the standard handbook of the Śaiva Siddhānta temple priests of Tamil Nadu. The commentary explains the root text's procedures for daily worship, the fire ritual and the seasonal pavitrārohaṇa and damanapūjā, citing many Āgamas, and ends with the damanapūjā. It survives only as the IFP transcript and has not been printed.

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

- E-text label 't1013' and page markers 'p. 1)' to 'p. 334)'; final note 'apūrṇaḥ'.

**Other editions:**
- S. Sambandhaśivācārya and T. Ganesan (eds.), Sūkṣmāgama, Volume I (chapters 1–13), Collection Indologie 114.1, Pondichéry: IFP/EFEO, 2010. — Critical edition based on eight paper manuscripts.
- Sūkṣmāgama, Volume II, Collection Indologie 114.2, Pondichéry: IFP/EFEO (ISBN 978-81-8470-190-6). — Second volume of the same critical edition (chapter range not verified; presumably chs. 14–53).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcript pp. 1–334. Chapters 1–8 have unnumbered colophons (arcanavidhi, ghṛtakambala-pūjā, niśipūjā, utsavasūcana, tīrthakālanirṇaya, dīpāvali, etc.); numbered colophons then run from paṭala 9 (paścimadvārārcana) to 59 (nāgalakṣaṇa) with some numbering slips (e.g. two chapters numbered 11, 'ṣaṭpañcatvāriṃśat' for 46). The final chapter (balipīṭhavidhi, = paṭala 60) breaks off at v. 218½, and the transcript notes 'apūrṇaḥ'. The IFP/EFEO critical edition counts 85 chapters, so roughly the last quarter of the work is missing; the chapter order of this transcript also differs from the edition (e.g. edition vol. I begins with puṇyāhavācana).

**Also known as:** Sūkṣmaśāstra, Sūkṣmatantra

**Attribution:** Revealed Śaiva Siddhānta scripture, one of the 28 Siddhāntāgamas (traditionally among the ten Śivabheda Āgamas). Colophons call it Sūkṣmaśāstra or Sūkṣmatantra; some place chapters in a 'kriyāpāda'. The surviving text is a South Indian temple-ritual (kriyā) work.

The Sūkṣmāgama is a South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta scripture counted among the 28 Siddhāntāgamas. The chapters in this transcript deal with temple ritual: daily and nightly worship, the great festival (aṅkurārpaṇa, flag-hoisting, drumming, processions, sea bath), private worship (ātmārthapūjā), installation of Gaurī, pacification rites for portents, expiation for priests and villages, pearl gathering, protection of the king, the thousand-stream bath, and finally iconometry of nāgas and bali pedestals.

The Liṅgadhāraṇacandrikā is a major Vīraśaiva apologetic and theological treatise composed by Nandikeśvara. Applying Mīmāṃsā hermeneutical principles to Vedic, Upaniṣadic, Āgamic, and Smṛti citations, the work establishes the scriptural validity, necessity, and orthodoxy of constantly bearing the personal liṅga on the body (iṣṭaliṅgadhāraṇa) and examines associated Liṅgāyat funerary practices (nikṣepa/burial). **Attribution:** The Yogavāsiṣṭha is traditionally attributed to sage Vālmīki as part of the epic cycle, but modern scholarship establishes it as a composite Advaitic philosophical reworking (c. 10th–12th century CE) derived from the earlier Kashmiri Mokṣopāya. The first book (Vairāgyaprakaraṇa, 33 sargas) of the Yogavāsiṣṭha describes the profound disillusionment and existential grief of the young prince Rāma after his pilgrimage across the country. Confronting the transience of life, wealth, youth, and the physical body, Rāma articulates his despair before king Daśaratha and the royal assembly, creating the need for sage Vasiṣṭha's extensive exposition of non-dual liberation. Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī's accompanying commentary Tātparyaprakāśa provides word-by-word glosses and an orthodox Advaita Vedānta framing.

**Attribution:** The Yogavāsiṣṭha (or Mokṣopāya) is traditionally attributed to the sage Vālmīki, though modern Indological scholarship shows it to be an anonymous composite work originating in Kashmir (c. 10th century CE) and expanding across northern and western India. The Sthitiprakaraṇa constitutes the fourth book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha (consisting of 62 sargas), elucidating the apparent preservation and sustenance (sthiti) of the manifest phenomenal cosmos from the perspective of radical non-dualism. Sage Vasiṣṭha instructs Prince Rāma through philosophical discourse and pedagogical narratives—such as the allegorical tales of Dāma, Vyāla, and Kaṭa, and the story of the ascetic Dāśūra—demonstrating that the universe possesses no independent reality and is merely an ungrounded vibration of consciousness (cittaspanda) sustained by delusion. The accompanying commentary, the Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendra Sarasvatī, elucidates the text in terms of classical Advaita Vedānta epistemology and metaphysics.

## Contents

**Attribution:** A collection of 312 Vajrayāna liturgical and visualization manuals (sādhanas) composed by various tantric masters between the 7th and 12th centuries (e.g., Saraha, Nāgārjuna, Indrabhūti, Kukkurīpāda, Advayavajra, Anupamarakṣita) as well as anonymous practitioners, compiled into standard Nepalese manuscript anthologies.

The Sādhanamālā is an extensive Sanskrit anthology of Buddhist Vajrayāna ritual and meditation texts (sādhanas) composed between the 7th and 12th centuries CE by various tantric masters (including Saraha, Nāgārjuna, Advayavajra, and Anupamarakṣita) as well as anonymous authors. Each text details the visualization, iconography, mantras, and ritual procedures for propitiating specific deities such as Mañjuśrī, Avalokiteśvara, Tārā, and Bhṛkuṭī. Volume 1 comprises sādhanas 1 through 170 and serves as a foundational source for the study of Buddhist tantric liturgy and iconography.

(reprinted as Sarasvatībhavana-granthamālā 15, Varanasi: Vārāṇaseya Saṃskṛta Viśvavidyālaya, 1965), or a reprint of it.

The earlier draft's 'Medical Hall Press, Benares, 1893' is unsupported and has been dropped.

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete for the Jñānakhaṇḍa: all 22 adhyāyas with commentary, from the maṅgala 'oṃ namaḥ kāraṇānandarūpiṇī' to the final colophons and Śrīnivāsa's nine concluding verses (Kali 4932). Checked in the source text file (sanskrit-texts/texts/SA_MB_tripuraarahasyaHK.txt and ilx_skt src M00344); no DharmaNexus segments exist for this filename. Page markers run p. 2–452.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Tripurārahasya, Jñānakhaṇḍa (Hāritāyana, root text)
- Tātparyadīpikā (Śrīnivāsa, commentary)

**Also known as:** Tripurārahasya (Jñānakhaṇḍa), Tripurārahasyajñānakhaṇḍa, Hāritāyanasaṃhitā

**Attribution:** Root text traditionally ascribed to Sumedhas Hāritāyana (colophon: 'śrīmaditihāsottame tripurārahasye dvādaśasāhasryāṃ saṃhitāyāṃ jñānakhaṇḍe'). The Tātparyadīpikā is by Śrīnivāsa(bhaṭṭa), son of Vaidyanātha (Yajvan/Dīkṣita), of Mahāpuṣkaragrāma near Hālāsya (Madurai); its closing verses date it Kali 4932 = 1831 CE.

The Jñānakhaṇḍa ('Section on Knowledge') of the Tripurārahasya, ascribed to Hāritāyana, is a Śākta Advaita work in 22 chapters (c. 2,160 verses) framed as Dattātreya's teaching to Paraśurāma, illustrated by narratives such as the Hemacūḍa story and the Aṣṭāvakra episodes; it presents liberation as recognition of the Goddess Tripurā as pure self-luminous consciousness (citi). This e-text gives the root text with the Tātparyadīpikā of Śrīnivāsa, son of Vaidyanātha, completed in 1831 CE.

The commentary Tātparyaprakāśa was composed by Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī, pupil's pupil of Sarvajñasarasvatī, interpreting the text in terms of classical Advaita Vedānta.

The Nirvāṇaprakaraṇa is the sixth and by far the longest book of the Yogavāsiṣṭha, divided into two halves (Pūrvārdha and Uttarārdha). It brings the philosophical instructions of sage Vasiṣṭha to Prince Rāma to their culmination, expounding the nature of ultimate liberation (nirvāṇa), the total dissolution of the conceptual mind and world-appearance into pure non-dual consciousness, and the state of the living-liberated sage (jīvanmukta). This volume preserves the text according to the vulgate tradition along with the Advaita commentary Tātparyaprakāśa by Ānandabodhendrasarasvatī.

The Śrīkarabhāṣya is the primary Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) bhāṣya on Bādarāyaṇa's Brahmasūtras, expounding the doctrine designated as Viśeṣādvaita or Bhedābhedātmaka-Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita. **Attribution:** The abridgement of the Yogavāsiṣṭha into approximately 6,000 verses is attributed in its colophons to the Gauḍa scholar Abhinanda (son of Jayanta Bhaṭṭa, c. 9th–10th century). The running commentary is composite: prakaraṇas 1–3 are accompanied by Ātmasukha's Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā, while prakaraṇas 4–6 are accompanied by Mummaḍi Devarāya's Saṃsārataraṇī (often treated together under the blanket title Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā in printed editions).

The Laghuyogavāsiṣṭha is an influential c. 6,000-verse abridgement by the Kashmirian scholar Abhinanda of the large philosophical work Mokṣopāya / Yogavāsiṣṭha. Framed as a dialogue between Sage Vasiṣṭha and Prince Rāma, it expounds non-dual Vedānta, the nature of the mind, and liberation-in-life (jīvanmukti) through philosophical narratives. This edition contains the standard composite commentary consisting of Ātmasukha's Vāsiṣṭhacandrikā on prakaraṇas 1–3 and Mummaḍi Devarāya's Saṃsārataraṇī on prakaraṇas 4–6.

The Pārānandasūtra (also called Pārānandamīmāṃsā) is an anonymous Śākta-Kaula ritual code written in sūtras, in two adhyāyas of seven āhnikas each, modelled on the Vedic and Mīmāṃsā sūtra style. It teaches one supreme Self, the Īśvaras and the countless souls. It describes the three paths of practice (dakṣiṇa, vāma and uttara), the qualifications of guru and disciple, initiation and order of precedence, daily and special worship, sacrificial sessions (satra) with offerings of wine and animals, expiations, and rules of conduct, and it often cites the differing opinions of named authorities.

These chapters treat dramatic structure and junctures (sandhi and sandhyaṅga), the major and minor play types (daśarūpaka), dramatic styles (vṛtti), costuming and make-up (āhāryābhinaya), character classification and acting conventions, and theatrical success (siddhi). Abhinavagupta's commentary integrates dramatic practice with non-dual Kashmir Śaiva philosophy and rasa aesthetics.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M0222), entered by Muktabodha staff under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski (2011).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header states: 'Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T0231' and 'Description: E-text created from IFP/EFEO transcript T0231'.

- Einoo & Takashima (eds.), From Material to Deity (2005) cite "Jñānaratnāvali (T.231)", i.e. the same IFP transcript, confirming that the work is used from transcripts and not from a printed edition

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Nearly complete: the transcript (IFP T0231, 643 pp.) begins with the note "prathama patraṃ na dṛśyate" (first leaf not found), so the opening (maṅgala and the first part of the snāna section) is lost; the text then runs to the closing verses and the final colophon "śrīmajjñānaratnāvalī samāptā". **Also known as:** Jñānaśivapaddhati

**Attribution:** Composed at Vārāṇasī by Jñānaśiva (Jñānaśambhu), pupil of Vyomaśambhu in the Golakī-maṭha lineage (closing verses: Golakīsthāna, Somaśambhu, Dharmaśambhu "Lakṣādhyāyī", Vyomaśambhu, "vāraṇasīvāsinā śrīmajjñānaśivena"). Sanderson (The Śaiva Age, 2009) places him as the teacher of Trilocanaśiva and a near-contemporary of Aghoraśiva (Kriyākramadyotikā completed 1157 CE).

The Jñānaratnāvalī is a comprehensive 12th-century Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual (paddhati) composed in Vārāṇasī by Jñānaśiva, a master in the Golakī-maṭha lineage. The work systematically expounds Saiddhāntika ritual praxis, including purificatory rites, daily worship (nityapūjā), the extensive sequence of initiation rituals (dīkṣā), installation (pratiṣṭhā), and seasonal ceremonies. Together with the Somaśambhupaddhati and Aghoraśiva's ritual works, it is one of the most critical textual witnesses for the reconstruction of medieval Śaiva liturgical traditions.

# Uttaraṣaṭka with Kuladīpikā, Tripurāsārasamuccaya with Saṃpradāyadīpikā (Uttaraṣaṭka incomplete at beginning)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_MB_kuladiipikaaHK`

**Author:** Tryambakabhaṭṭāraka, Bhaṭṭanāga

**Collection / category:** Muktabodha / MB (Muktabodha)

**Source:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute

**Link:** [muktabodha.org](https://www.muktabodha.org) (Digital Library, search by title)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished: Institut Français de Pondichéry / EFEO transcript T. 1046 (c. 213 pp.). Not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00230, data-entered under the direction of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, revision 0 of 18 Sept. 2011 (https://muktabodha-digital-library.org/texts/IAST/M00230).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header (segs. 1–8): 'Uniform title: kuladīpikā / Main title: Kuladīpikā uttaraṣaṭkam ṣaḍvidyāprakāśikā / Author : tryambakabhaṭṭaraka / Manuscript : IFP/EFEO transcript T01046 / Revision 0: Sept. 18, 2011'.
- Page markers 'p. 2)' ... 'p. 213)' (transcript pagination).
- ilx_skt metadata/muktabodha.csv (M00230) classifies the file as '4 excerpts' and lists the same four colophons.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Composite transcript. The Uttaraṣaṭka begins abruptly mid-verse ('koṭisamaprabham |', seg. 13), so its opening is missing (the first page marker is 'p. 2)'). It runs to the colophon 'iti śrīrudrayāmale ... uttarabhāge nityaklinnā prakaraṇe ṣaḍvidyā prakāśāyāmuttaraṣaṭkaṃ saṃpūrṇam' (seg. 332). The Kuladīpikā has the colophons 'ityuttaraṣaṭkavivaraṇe kuladīpikāyāṃ prathamaḥ paṭaḥ' to '... pañcamaḥ paṭalaḥ' and ends 'prakāśita rahasyārthā samāptā kuladīpikā' (seg. 904), so it is complete. The Tripurāsārasamuccaya has paṭalas 1–10, ending 'iti śrī bhaṭṭanāgaviracite tripurāsārasamuccaye daśamaḥ paṭalaḥ' (seg. 1613). The colophon of paṭala 3 was not found and may be missing. The Saṃpradāyadīpikā has paṭalas 1–10, ending at seg. 1791, followed by the scribal verse. After that, a short unidentified passage of Tripurā pūjā prose (pp. 212–213, segs. 1795–1800) breaks off mid-sentence. Page markers run to 'p. 213)'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Uttaraṣaṭka (Ṣaḍvidyāprakāśa, ascribed to the Rudrayāmala, Nityaklinnāprakaraṇa) (root text (6 paṭalas; segs. 9–332; beginning missing))
- Kuladīpikā (Uttaraṣaṭkavivaraṇa) (Tryambakabhaṭṭāraka (per Muktabodha), commentary on the Uttaraṣaṭka (5 paṭas/paṭalas + conclusion; segs. 333–904))
- Tripurāsārasamuccaya (Bhaṭṭanāga (Nāgabhaṭṭa), independent Śrīvidyā manual (10 paṭalas; segs. 905–1613))
- Saṃpradāyadīpikā (uncertain (Kṛṣṇānanda, pupil of Tejānandanātha, named as writer/copyist), commentary on the Tripurāsārasamuccaya (10 paṭalas; segs. 1614–1793))

**Also known as:** Kuladīpikā (uttaraṣaṭkam) ṣaḍvidyāprakāśikā (Muktabodha main title), Ṣaḍvidyāprakāśa, Uttaraṣaṭkavivaraṇa

**Attribution:** The text itself never names Tryambakabhaṭṭāraka; the attribution comes from the Muktabodha catalogue only. The Tripurāsārasamuccaya colophons read 'iti śrī bhaṭṭanāgaviracite tripurāsārasamuccaye ... paṭalaḥ'; manuscript catalogues also give the name as Nāgabhaṭṭa. The verse after the Saṃpradāyadīpikā, 'tejānandasya śiṣyena kṛṣṇānandasya sūriṇā | likhitaṃ saṃpradāyasya dīpikā cāmbikājñayā' (seg. 1793), may name Kṛṣṇānanda as the author or only as the scribe ('likhitam'). The draft's link with the legendary Tryambaka of the Kashmirian lineage is speculative and has been dropped.

The e-text transcribes a South Indian composite manuscript of Kaula and Śrīvidyā works. It contains (1) the Uttaraṣaṭka or Ṣaḍvidyāprakāśa, ascribed to the Rudrayāmala (Nityaklinnā section), on yonimudrā, the revival of defective mantras, kuṇḍalinī yoga and the six vidyās; (2) the Kuladīpikā, a commentary on it in five chapters; (3) Bhaṭṭanāga's Tripurāsārasamuccaya, a ten-chapter Śrīvidyā manual on Tripurasundarī worship, nyāsa, the cakras, yantras and homa; and (4) the Saṃpradāyadīpikā, a commentary on the Tripurāsārasamuccaya.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Contains paṭalas 1–14 of the Ādikāṇḍa (ending with prāsādadevatāsaṃsthāpanapaṭala on p. 88 of the printed edition, verse 325 of the section). The full Ādikāṇḍa contains 42 chapters, and the entire Saṃhitā encompasses four kāṇḍas (Ādikāṇḍa, Saṃkarṣaṇakāṇḍa, Liṅgakāṇḍa, Saurakāṇḍa).

**Also known as:** Hayaśīrṣasaṃhitā, The Hayasirsa Paancharatram, Mahāpañcarātra Dvādaśasāhasrika

**Attribution:** A revealed Vaiṣṇava Pāñcarātra Āgama, traditionally framed as a dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Bhṛgu reporting instructions from Brahmā derived from the equine-headed manifestation of Viṣṇu (Hayaśīrṣa/Hayagrīva). The Sanskrit commentary/notes interspersed in the text are by the editor Bhuban Mohan Sankhyatirtha.

The Hayaśīrṣapañcarātra is a major northern Pāñcarātra scripture focusing on temple architecture (vāstuśāstra), sacred geography, iconometry (mūrtilakṣaṇa), and image installation (pratiṣṭhā). This initial section (Ādikāṇḍa, paṭalas 1–14) covers the mythical descent of the text, site examination (bhūmisaṅgraha), soil purification, layout of the vāstumaṇḍala, laying of the foundation stone (iṣṭakānyāsa), and placement of primary sanctum deities.

**Other editions:**

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 90 adhyāyas, ending at 90.42 with 'iti śrīkālikāpurāṇe navatitamo'dhyāyaḥ || 90 || iti śrīkālikāpurāṇaṃ samāptam |'.

**Also known as:** Kālikāpurāṇam, Kālīpurāṇa, Satīpurāṇa

**Attribution:** Traditionally framed as spoken by Mārkaṇḍeya to Kamaṭha and other sages, stemming ultimately from Brahmā; anonymous Upapurāṇa composed in medieval Kāmarūpa (Assam).

The Kālikāpurāṇa is an influential Śākta Upapurāṇa composed in medieval Kāmarūpa (Assam), generally assigned to the 9th–11th centuries CE. It details the mythology of the Goddess in her manifestations as Kālī, Satī, Pārvatī, and Kāmākhyā, tracing the narrative of Satī's self-immolation and the dispersion of her limbs across sacred pīṭhas. The work serves as a foundational manual for Śākta ritual and worship in northeastern India, containing extensive sections on iconography, mantras, pilgrimage geography, and the famous Rudhirādhyāya on blood sacrifice.

An anonymous Nepalese ritual manual for the worship of Mahāguhyakālī, a form of Kālī. **Also known as:** Parātrīśikāvivaraṇa, Tattvaviveka

**Attribution:** The root verses of the Parātriṃśikā (or Parātrīśikā) are an anonymous canonical revelation, traditionally regarded as part of the Rudrayāmalatantra. The Vivaraṇa commentary (also entitled Tattvaviveka) was composed by Abhinavagupta (fl. c. 975–1025 CE). The embedded bracketed glosses represent the commentary/editorial annotations supplied by the editor, Mahāmahopādhyāya Paṇḍit Mukunda Rāma Śāstrī.

The Parātriṃśikāvivaraṇa (also entitled Tattvaviveka) is Abhinavagupta's exhaustive philosophical commentary on the Parātriṃśikā, a concise Śaiva scriptural revelation associated with the Rudrayāmala. Through thirty-seven root verses, Abhinavagupta elaborates non-dual Trika metaphysics, phonemic mysticism (mātṛkācakra), the nature of the ultimate reality (anuttara), and the dynamic of divine emission (visarga). Composed in Kashmir around 1000 CE, the work is considered one of the highest achievements of classical Indian tantric philosophy.

The Mokṣopāya is a philosophical work composed in Kashmir in the 10th century CE, which forms the original recension of the widely disseminated Yogavāsiṣṭha. The Ṛgveda (or Ṛgvedasaṃhitā) is the oldest preserved text of the Indo-European language family and the primary canonical scripture of the Vedic tradition, composed in the northwestern Indian subcontinent during the mid-to-late second millennium BCE. The Rājataraṅgiṇī of Jonarāja (commonly termed the Dvitīyā Rājataraṅgiṇī) is a 15th-century Sanskrit metrical chronicle of the rulers of Kashmir, composed at the court of Sulṭān Zayn al-ʿĀbidīn (r. 1420–1470 CE). The Kathāsaritsāgara ('Ocean of the Streams of Story') is an encyclopedic 11th-century Sanskrit narrative poem composed in Kashmir by Somadeva for Queen Sūryavatī. Arranged into 18 lambakas and 124 taraṅgas, it preserves a major Kashmiri verse recension of Guṇāḍhya's lost Paiśācī epic, the Bṛhatkathā. The central frame tale follows Prince Naravāhanadatta's romantic adventures and quest to attain sovereignty over the Vidyādharas, embedding numerous cycles of folk tales, fables, and romances, including the Vetālapañcaviṃśatikā.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete across all 8 adhyāyas (chapters) and their respective khaṇḍas, covering both the mūla text and Śaṅkara's bhāṣya up to the final colophon at 8.15.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Chāndogyopaniṣad (root text)
- Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya (Śaṅkara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Chāndogya-Upaniṣad, Chāndogyopaniṣat, Chāndogyopaniṣadvivaraṇa

**Attribution:** Mūla: Chāndogyopaniṣad (Sāmaveda), anonymous. Commentary: Śaṅkara's Chāndogyopaniṣadbhāṣya (final colophon: '... śrīmacchaṅkarabhagavatpādakṛtau chāndogyopaniṣadvivaraṇe aṣṭamo 'dhyāyaḥ'), generally accepted as authentic. Segment [10] contains an intrusive phrase naming Narendrapurī's ṭippaṇa. This is a keying conflation, not an included work (see edition evidence).

The Chāndogyopaniṣad is one of the earliest and most important mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads, belonging to the Kauthuma/Rāṇāyanīya recension of the Sāmaveda. In eight adhyāyas, it progresses from esoteric meditations on the chanting of the Sāman and the sacred syllable Om (udgītha) to quintessential metaphysical doctrines of early Vedānta, including the Śāṇḍilya-vidyā, the dialogue of Satyakāma Jābāla, Uddālaka Āruṇi's instruction to Śvetaketu culminating in the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' (6.8.7), and Prajāpati's teachings on the four states of the self. The accompanying commentary by Śaṅkarācārya interprets the text as an exposition of non-dual reality (advaita), demonstrating that ritual action produces transient heavenly realms, whereas direct knowledge of the non-dual Brahman-Ātman leads to absolute liberation (mokṣa).

Chapter 9 of Vasubandhu's Abhidharmakośabhāṣya, commonly titled Pudgalaviniścaya ('Examination of the Person') or Ātmavādapratiṣedha ('Refutation of the Self Theory'), is an independent prose treatise appended to the main eight-chapter auto-commentary. A canonical Sanskrit discourse belonging to the Sarvāstivāda Saṃyuktāgama, corresponding to the Pāli Soṇa Sutta (SN 22.49) and Chinese Saṃyuktāgama (T 99, no. 259). The elder Śāriputra explains to the householder's son Śroṇa that recluses and brahmins who construct conceits of superiority, equality, or inferiority based on the impermanent five skandhas do not see reality as it is. Realizing that the aggregates are neither self nor belonging to self ('naitan mama naiṣo ’ham asmi naiṣa me ātmā'), Śroṇa attains the dharma-eye (dharmacakṣu) and takes refuge as an upāsaka.

The foundational scripture of Kashmir Shaivism, the Śivasūtra, expounds non-dual Śaiva metaphysics and yogic realization across three sections corresponding to the divine (śāmbhava), cognitive (śākta), and individual (āṇava) means. **Attribution:** The root collection of Āgamic verses is by Umāpatiśivācārya (early 14th century CE), a prominent Śaiva Siddhānta theologian of Cidambaram. The commentary, titled Śataratnollekhanī (lines 28, 2879), refers to Umāpati in the third person (line 40) and aligns itself with the exegetical lineage of Sadyojyotis, Rāmakaṇṭha, Nārāyaṇakaṇṭha, and Aghoraśiva. It is either an auto-commentary written in the objective style or the work of an immediate disciple.

The Śataratnasaṃgraha is a classical Śaiva Siddhānta anthology compiled by Umāpatiśivācārya (c. 14th century), selecting approximately one hundred core verses from canonical Āgamas including the Svāyambhuva, Mataṅga, Kiraṇa, Niśvāsa, Mṛgendra, and Sarvajñānottara. The verses outline the central tenets of the tradition, specifically the threefold ontology of Pati (the Lord), Paśu (the individual soul), and Pāśa (the binding bonds), along with the efficacy of dīkṣā (initiation) and jñāna (gnosis) in achieving liberation. In this e-text, the verses are accompanied throughout by the Śataratnollekhanī, an extensive prose commentary that glosses and contextualizes each Āgamic quotation in accordance with classical dualistic Śaiva Siddhānta exegesis.

Nidāna, narrative frame and the rest of the sūtra (which occupies a little less than five folios in the manuscript) are not included.

**Also known as:** Bodha-sūtra (Dīrghāgama no. 21, Yuganipāta)

**Attribution:** Sūtra no. 21 of the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda Dīrghāgama (Yuganipāta), transmitted in the Gilgit/Afghanistan birch-bark Dīrghāgama manuscript (Gilgit-Bamiyan Type II script). Parallel to the Pali Bodhirājakumārasutta (MN 85); the Sanskrit sūtra abbreviates the Buddha's life story to a few sentences (Hartmann in Dhammadinna ed. 2014).

Section of the Bodhasūtra, sūtra no. 21 of the (Mūla-)Sarvāstivāda Dīrghāgama, preserved in the Gilgit/Afghanistan birch-bark Dīrghāgama manuscript and parallel to the Pali Bodhirājakumārasutta (MN 85). Prince Bodha asks how many factors a noble disciple needs to reach the destruction of the āsravas quickly; using the analogy of a pupil learning the prince's hereditary arts (elephant and horse riding, chariot, archery, writing and calculation), the Buddha teaches the five factors of striving (prādhānikāṅga): faith, freedom from illness, honesty, energy and insight into rise and fall. The section ends with Bodha's joyful exclamation.

The Manusmṛti (or Mānavadharmaśāstra), comprising twelve chapters and roughly 2,685 verses, is the classical benchmark treatise of Brahmanical dharma. Structured as a discourse delivered by Bhṛgu upon instruction from Manu, it systematically articulates the duties of the four varṇas and āśramas, rites of passage (saṃskāras), rules of marriage and domestic life, civil and criminal law (the eighteen vyavahārapadas), the obligations of kingship (rājadharma), ritual expiations (prāyaścitta), and the doctrines of karma and liberation.

The Sthitiprakaraṇa is the fourth book of the Mokṣopāya, an influential 10th-century Kashmirian philosophical epic that represents the original recension later reworked into the vulgate Yogavāsiṣṭha. The Viṃśatikākārikā ('Twenty Verses on Representation-Only') is a foundational Yogācāra-Vijñānavāda polemical treatise composed by Vasubandhu. The text refutes the reality of mind-independent external physical objects (bāhyārtha) through a rigorous critique of atomism (paramāṇuvāda), demonstrating that atomic partlessness and spatial extension are mutually incompatible. Śaṅkara's commentary elaborates the distinction between the ritual path (karmakāṇḍa) and knowledge of the non-dual self (jñānakāṇḍa), arguing that knowledge of Brahman alone destroys avidyā.

The Āgamaśāstra (frequently called the Gauḍapādakārikā or Māṇḍūkyakārikā) is the earliest extant systematic verse treatise of Advaita Vedānta, traditionally attributed to Gauḍapāda (c. 6th century CE). The first chapter interprets the Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad's four states of consciousness culminating in turīya, while the subsequent chapters systematically deconstruct the ontological reality of external objects, change, and plurality, drawing extensively on the dialectic and terminology of contemporary Buddhist philosophy.

**Attribution:** The root Mokṣopāya is an anonymous ca. 10th-century Kashmirian philosophical narrative in epic style. The commentary Mokṣopāyaṭīkā was composed in the late 18th century by the Kashmirian scholar Bhāskarakaṇṭha, son of Avatārakaṇṭha and grandson of Vaiḍūryakaṇṭha, as explicitly confirmed in the closing colophon.

The Mumukṣuvyavahāraprakaraṇa is the second book of the Mokṣopāya, the Kashmirian philosophical ancestor of the widely known Yogavāsiṣṭha. It outlines the preliminary qualifications and conduct of a spiritual aspirant, placing central emphasis on personal exertion (pauruṣa) over fatalism (daiva) and detailing the four gatekeepers of liberation: tranquility (śama), inquiry (vicāra), contentment (saṃtoṣa), and association with virtuous teachers (sādhasaṅga). The embedded commentary by the late 18th-century Kashmirian scholar Bhāskarakaṇṭha provides a close gloss interpreting the text through the conceptual vocabulary of Kashmir Śaivism (Pratyabhijñā).

The full text is in Valentina Stache-Rosen, Dogmatische Begriffsreihen im älteren Buddhismus II: Das Saṅgītisūtra und sein Kommentar Saṅgītiparyāya, nach Vorarbeiten von Kusum Mittal bearbeitet, Teil 1–2, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1968 (Sanskrittexte aus den Turfanfunden IX), pp. 41–206, which incorporates Waldschmidt 1955.

**E-text:** SuttaCentral; transcribed in the early 1990s at the University of Queensland by David Dargie, Michelle Styles-Williams and Barbara Nelson, prepared for SuttaCentral by Bhikkhu Sujato; transcription commissioned by Roderick S. Bucknell (https://suttacentral.net/sf253/san/waldschmidt).

- SC root-text bibliography also lists Stache-Rosen 1968: 41–206 '(This incorporates the above.)'. Waldschmidt 1955 covers only the introduction, so the doctrinal lists (Wal_1.1–10.2.4) must come from Stache-Rosen 1968; SC does not state how the two were combined.

**Translations:**
- Maurice Walshe, The Long Discourses of the Buddha, Boston: Wisdom, 1995 (DN 33, Pāli parallel). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — The whole sūtra as reconstructed: introduction (Wal_a–Wal_z: Pāpā, the new assembly hall of the Mallas, the schism of the Nirgranthas after Jñātiputra's death), groups of one to ten (Wal_1.1–Wal_10.2) and the Buddha's approval and closing (Wal_10.2.1–10.2.4). About 70 lacunae marked '…' and some missing items (e.g. 5.11–12, 8.5; 8.4 only the heading). The work is not truncated, so the title has no partial marker.

**Also known as:** Saṅgītisutta (Pāli parallel, DN 33), SF 253

**Attribution:** Canonical discourse belonging to the Sanskrit Dīrghāgama of the Sarvāstivāda tradition, delivered primarily by Śāriputra and confirmed by the Buddha.

An Āgama sūtra of the Sarvāstivāda Dīrghāgama, parallel to the Pāli Saṅgītisutta (DN 33). At Pāpā, in the new assembly hall of the Mallas, Śāriputra notes that the Jain community split after Nirgrantha Jñātiputra's death. To prevent such a split he recites the Buddha's teachings in numerical groups from one to ten, and the Buddha approves. It is the basis of the Abhidharma treatise Saṅgītiparyāya.

The Candrasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse relating the lunar eclipse myth corresponding to the Pāli Candima Sutta (SN 2.9). The Vajrabhairavatantra (also known as Vajramahābhairavatantra) is a central Anuttarayogatantra text centered on the wrathful deity Yamāntaka/Vajrabhairava, closely affiliated with the Mañjuśrī cycle. In seven kalpas, it details the construction of the wrathful maṇḍala in cremation grounds, ferocious magical and protective rites (ṣaṭkarmāṇi), visualisations of the buffalo-headed deity, and initiation protocols. First critically edited in Sanskrit by Aleksandra Wenta in 2020, it holds major historical significance for Tibetan Buddhist esoteric ritualism, particularly within the Sakya and Gelug traditions.

The accompanying commentary, the Mahāsukhaprakāśikā by Bhikṣu Jñānacandra (Dhyānacandra), provides detailed esoteric interpretations encompassing outer ritual worship (bāhyapūjā), subtle body physiology (cakra, nāḍī, bodhicitta), mantra extraction (mantroddhāra), and initiation procedures.

The DSBC page gives no editor or publication, and its source has not been identified. The existing catalog metadata names a transcription by Vijayarāja Vajrācārya (CUTS). This has not been verified.
- Manuscript: Asiatic Society (Kolkata) MS G 4732, the unique Sanskrit witness (Newman, 'Epoch of the Kālacakra'). — Not an edition. It is the basis of all the e-texts.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text (segs. 0–276, closing 'iti kālacakrāvatāraḥ samāptaḥ || kṛtiriyaṃ paṇḍitābhayākaraguptapādānām'), followed by Dānaśrīmitra's damaged calendrical appendix (segs. 277–284). The OCR has dropped the numerals in the appendix ('śakābde ......').

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kālacakrāvatāra (Abhayākaragupta, root text)
- Appendix to the Kālacakrāvatāra manuscript (calendrical notes) (Dānaśrīmitra, appendix)

**Also known as:** Śrīkālacakrāvatāra

**Attribution:** Attributed in the opening and closing colophons to paṇḍita Abhayākaragupta (fl. late 11th–early 12th c.). The short calendrical appendix after the colophon (segs. 277–284) is not by Abhayākaragupta: Newman ('Epoch of the Kālacakra') ascribes it to Dānaśrīmitra, who wrote it in the unique manuscript (Asiatic Society MS G 4732) and dates it to Śaka 1047 (c. 1124/25 CE). Cf. the e-text '[ā]likhitaṃ śrīman śrī(macchrī)mitre[ṇa]' in seg. 281.

The Kālacakrāvatāra is a short astronomical and calendrical manual (karaṇa) by Abhayākaragupta, built on the jyotiṣa of the Kālacakratantra. It gives procedures for the year and month constants, weekdays, tithis, nakṣatras, yogas and karaṇas, the true positions of the planets, and the calculation of eclipses (rāhuśuddhi). Its epoch (mleccha 463) is important for the chronology of the Kālacakra calendar. The unique manuscript also carries Dānaśrīmitra's calendrical appendix, dated Śaka 1047.

Vajrapāṇi's Laghutantraṭīkā ("Sphuṭakuliśapadānveṣikā") is a commentary on the first chapter of the Cakrasaṃvara (Laghusaṃvara) tantra by one of the three Kālacakra-oriented "Bodhisattva" commentators. It sets out the purpose of the tantra and distinguishes neyārtha and nītārtha readings, with Kālacakra-style correlations of time, breath and the zodiac. It then gives detailed ritual instructions on samaya worship, the yoginīs' movement through the body, the pīṭhas, bali offerings and the recitation programmes for the mantras of the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala.

Segments 0–1591: Sanskrit commentary from the opening verses through seven paricchedas, ending "iti … karmaprasarasādhanopadeśaḥ saptamaḥ paricchedaḥ dvitīya paṭalaḥ samāptaḥ" (i.e. covering HT I.1–I.2). Segments 1592–1781: the beginning of the commentary on the devatāpaṭala (HT I.3), breaking off after verse 79. Segments 1782–3641: the Tibetan translation (Tōh. 1180) in Tibetan script, with many OCR errors. Segments 3642–3946: the editor's notes, mantra lists and verse appendices (partly English). Dan Martin: two Sanskrit manuscripts were used, neither complete, and the parts missing in Sanskrit are summarized from the Tibetan.

**Also known as:** Ṣaṭsāhasrikā Hevajraṭīkā, Hevajrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā, Ṣaṭsāhasrikākhyā Hevajratantrapiṇḍārthaṭīkā

**Attribution:** The introductory verses name the author as "śrīmatā vajragarbheṇa … daśabhūmīśvareṇa" (seg. 11–12). Vajragarbha is one of the three "Bodhisattva" commentators of the Kālacakra milieu (with Puṇḍarīka and Vajrapāṇi); the commentary reads the Hevajratantra in light of Kālacakra doctrine. The traditional attribution to the Bodhisattva is not historical; the work is generally dated to the early 11th century.

Vajragarbha's Ṣaṭsāhasrikā ("six thousand [ślokas]") is a commentary on the Hevajratantra by one of the Kālacakra "Bodhisattva" commentators; it reads the tantra through Kālacakra doctrine (nāḍīs, vowels and consonants as zodiacal and temporal cycles, sambhoga/nirmāṇa cakras). The surviving Sanskrit covers the commentary on the first two paṭalas of part I (with sections such as the nāḍikānirṇaya and the karmaprasarasādhana) and the beginning of the devatāpaṭala; it also opens with polemical verses on false teachers.

- Jātinirākṛti (Jitāri, section 1 (complete))
- Digambaramataparīkṣā (Anekāntavādanirāsa) (Jitāri, section 2 (complete))
- Pratyabhijñā section (untitled) (Jitāri, fragment (opening half-verse only))
- Editorial footnotes of H. R. Rangaswami Iyengar (modern annotations interleaved in the e-text)

Jitāri's Vādasthānāni ('Some points of debate', 10th c.) is a collection of short polemical tracts in the Dharmakīrtian tradition. The e-text contains the first, the Jātinirākṛti, which argues that universals (jāti, sāmānya) can be described neither as different from nor identical with individuals and therefore are not real, rejecting the Nyāya definition and Kumārila's appeal to recognition; and the second, the Digambaramataparīkṣā, which refutes the Jaina doctrine of non-one-sidedness (anekāntavāda). The Dharmottaraṭippanaka is an early gloss (ṭippanaka) by the Jaina logician Mallavādin on Dharmottara's Nyāyabinduṭīkā (which comments on Dharmakīrti's Nyāyabindu). ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all 26 chapters (parīkṣā) and 3,646 kārikās of the Tattvasaṅgraha along with Kamalaśīla's complete Pañjikā commentary down to the final verse and concluding colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**

**Attribution:** Traditional and modern scholarship unanimously attribute the kārikā text to Śāntarakṣita (8th century CE) and the Pañjikā commentary to his disciple Kamalaśīla, as confirmed by the opening and concluding verses and colophons of both authors in the e-text.

The Tattvasaṅgraha ('Compendium of True Realities') is an encyclopedic 8th-century philosophical and epistemological treatise by the Buddhist master Śāntarakṣita, consisting of 3,646 metrical verses divided into 26 topical investigations (parīkṣā). From a late Madhyamaka-Yogācāra perspective informed by Dharmakīrtian pramāṇa methodology, it systematically examines and refutes rival non-Buddhist ontologies and epistemologies (including Sāṅkhya, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Jaina, and Cārvāka) as well as internal Buddhist positions on topics such as the soul (ātman), God (īśvara), substance, universals, causality, external reality, testimony, and omniscience. Kamalaśīla's companion commentary, the Tattvasaṅgrahapañjikā, meticulously elucidates Śāntarakṣita's terse verses and preserves crucial quotations and arguments from otherwise lost classical Indian philosophical works.

Prajñākaragupta interprets Dharmakīrtian logic from a sākāravāda and ultimate non-dual (advaita) standpoint, addressing foundational epistemological topics including the nature of valid cognition, perception, reflexivity (svasaṃvedana), and omniscience.

In the work, Dharmakīrti simplified the classical Indian debate theory by reducing the traditional twenty-two points of defeat (nigrahasthāna) to two fundamental categories: failure to state an essential part of the proof (asādhanāṅgavacana) and stating a non-existent defect in the opponent's argument (adoṣodbhāvana). The Avayavinirākaraṇa is a short philosophical treatise by the late Buddhist logician Paṇḍita Aśoka (c. 10th–11th century CE) dedicated to refuting the Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika doctrine of the 'whole' (avayavin) as an ontological real distinct from its parts (avayava). Operating in the tradition of Dharmakīrti, Aśoka utilizes the epistemological reason of vyāpakaviruddhopalabdhi (perception of that which is incompatible with the pervader) to demonstrate that positing a single entity that simultaneously admits contradictory properties (such as moving and unmoving, covered and uncovered, or coloured and uncoloured) violates basic principles of non-contradiction.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text across all 12 aras (spokes) of the Dvādaśāranayacakra along with the complete Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī commentary and Jambūvijaya's Ṭippaṇa.
