**Also known as:** Dvādaśāranayacakra, Nayacakra, Nayacakravālavṛtti

**Attribution:** The original root work by Mallavādin Kṣamāśramaṇa (ca. 5th–6th c. CE) does not survive in independent manuscripts; its text is reconstructed through pratīkas preserved in Siṃhasūri Gaṇin's commentary Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī (Nayacakravālavṛtti, ca. 7th c. CE). The e-text also incorporates the editorial Sanskrit Ṭippaṇa by Muni Jambūvijaya.

The Dvādaśāranayacakra ('Twelve-Spoked Wheel of Standpoints') by the Śvetāmbara Jaina dialectician Mallavādin (ca. 5th–6th c. CE) is an influential masterwork of classical Indian doxography and Jaina philosophical pluralism (anekāntavāda). Mallavādin arranges twelve non-Jaina philosophical standpoints into a self-contained dialectical wheel where each school systematically refutes the preceding one and is in turn overthrown by the next, demonstrating how partial viewpoints fall into internal contradiction unless synthesized within Jaina anekāntavāda. Because Mallavādin's original text survives only embedded as pratīkas within Siṃhasūri Gaṇin's 7th-century commentary Nyāyāgamānusāriṇī, the commentary forms an integral part of the surviving tradition.

The Padārthadharmasaṅgraha (also known as the Praśastapādabhāṣya), composed by Praśastapāda around the 6th century CE, is the defining classical exposition of the Vaiśeṣika philosophical school. Rather than commenting sequentially on Kaṇāda's Vaiśeṣikasūtra, it presents an independent systematic categorization of reality into six fundamental ontological categories (padārthas: dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya), establishing the conceptual foundation for all subsequent classical Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika philosophy.

- Hariharānanda Āraṇya, Swāmi, Yoga Philosophy of Patañjali: Containing His Yoga Aphorisms with the Commentary of Vyāsa, Calcutta: University of Calcutta, 1963 (rev. ed. 1981). (English)
- Jha, Ganganatha, The Yoga Darśana: The Sutras of Patañjali with the Bhāṣya of Vyāsa, Bombay: Tattva-Vivechaka Press, 1907. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of all four pādas of the sūtras along with the bhāṣya: Samādhipāda (YS 1.1–1.51), Sādhanapāda (YS 2.1–2.55), Vibhūtipāda (YS 3.1–3.55), and Kaivalyapāda (YS 4.1–4.34), ending at segment 1795 with the final colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Yogasūtra (Patañjali, root text)
- Vyāsabhāṣya (Vyāsa, commentary)

**Also known as:** Yogasūtra with Vyāsabhāṣya, Yogabhāṣya, Sāṅkhyapravacana Yogaśāstra

**Attribution:** While later Indian tradition distinguishes the sūtras composed by Patañjali from an independent commentary (bhāṣya) composed by Vyāsa (hence 'Vyāsabhāṣya'), philological research by Albrecht Wezler, Johannes Bronkhorst, and Philipp Maas demonstrates that the sūtras and bhāṣya form an integral textual whole (the Pātañjalayogaśāstra), composed or compiled by a single author named Patañjali (c. 350–450 CE).

The Pātañjalayogaśāstra is the foundational philosophical text of classical Yoga (Pātañjala Yoga). Organized into four chapters (Samādhipāda, Sādhanapāda, Vibhūtipāda, and Kaivalyapāda), it presents an eightfold discipline of practice (aṣṭāṅgayoga) and meditative absorption within a dualist Sāṅkhya metaphysical framework. The system directs the practitioner toward the cessation of mental operations (cittavṛttinirodha) and ultimate spiritual liberation (kaivalya), defined as the isolation of pure consciousness (puruṣa) from material nature (prakṛti).

# Yogasūtra with Rājamārtaṇḍa

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GSP34_rajamartandu`

**Author:** Patañjali, Bhoja

**Collection / category:** Treatises / GSP34 (GSP34 Philosophy Yoga (Śāstra 3))

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** No printed edition. Suryansu Ray transcribed the text from a privately held Devanāgarī palm-leaf manuscript (the manuscript of his family's guru, copied by him in the mid-1950s). He later compared it with printed materials in Delhi libraries and gave variants in brackets marked 'pa0' (pāṭhāntara). SARIT published it in TEI (Suryansu Ray 2012; SARIT edition dated 2011–2016).

**E-text:** Suryansu Ray (transcription), SARIT (TEI encoding and distribution, sarit.indology.info; file bhoja-rajamartanda.xml).

**Evidence:**
- SARIT TEI header (local copy ~/data/sanskrit/SARIT-corpus/bhoja-rajamartanda.xml), notesStmt: 'Rājamārtaṇḍa Pātañjalavṛtti of Bhoja, transcribed by Suryansu Ray from a manuscript.'
- sourceDesc: 'The material was typed by Suryamsu Ray personally from traditional old manuscript belonging to his family guru.'
- revisionDesc, Ray's letter to D. Wujastyk (26 March 2010): the guru 'carried a palm-leaf manuscript of this Bhojavṛtti in the Devanāgarī script'. Ray copied it into notebooks in the mid-1950s and typed it out over 15 years, and he 'compared the material with materials in libraries in Delhi', recording accepted variants 'in square brackets with pa0'. He also 'made a separate section in which all the yoga sūtras are given in one place', which is the appended sūtrapāṭha.
- The manuscript is not otherwise identified.
- In the SARIT XML the variant readings are <note> elements (e.g. '<note>pā0 pratyakṣāyamāṇāḥ ...</note>', '<note>(dhā0 pā0 4|67)</note>'). The DharmaNexus segments leave these notes out ('pratyakṣāyamāṇāḥ' and 'dhā0' do not occur in them), so the e-text gives only Ray's main readings.

**Other editions:**
- Rājendralāla Mitra (ed. & tr.), The Yoga Aphorisms of Patañjali with the Commentary of Bhoja Rājā, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal (Bibliotheca Indica), 1883. — Edition with English translation.
- Kāśīnātha Śāstrī Āgāśe (ed.), Pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi ... Vyāsabhāṣya ... tathā Bhojadevaviracitarājamārtaṇḍābhidhavṛttisametāni, Poona: Ānandāśrama (Ānandāśrama Sanskrit Series 47), 1904. — Includes Bhoja's vṛtti together with the Vyāsabhāṣya and Tattvavaiśāradī.

**Translations:**
- Rajendralala Mitra, The Yoga Aphorisms of Patañjali with the Commentary of Bhoja Rājā, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1883. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — All four pādas of the Yogasūtra with Bhoja's vṛtti. Each pāda ends with a colophon ('iti dhāreśvarabhojadevaviracitāyāṃ rājamārtaṇḍābhidhāyāṃ pātañjalavṛttau ...'). After that comes the transcriber's separate sūtrapāṭha (from about segment 2076 to 'iti pātañjalayogasūtrāṇi'). The English article that the transcriber appended in his original file is not in the SARIT text.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Yogasūtra (Patañjali, root text)
- Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhoja, commentary)
- Yogasūtra (sūtrapāṭha) (Patañjali, appendix)

**Also known as:** Bhojavṛtti, Rājamārtaṇḍavṛtti, Pātañjalayogasūtravṛtti

**Attribution:** The Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhojavṛtti) is traditionally attributed to the Paramāra king Bhojadeva of Dhārā (11th century CE). The root sūtras are attributed to Patañjali.

The Rājamārtaṇḍa (Bhojavṛtti) is a concise commentary on Patañjali's Yogasūtra attributed to King Bhoja of Dhārā (11th century). Its introductory verses criticise earlier commentators for being prolix and promise a clear exposition. It explains all four pādas sūtra by sūtra, and in this e-text it is followed by a separate sūtrapāṭha.

In the DharmaNexus segmentation, however, the text of the sūtras (TEI <ab type="sūtra">, 4,816 elements) has been dropped. Only their labels ('SK n', 'AS a-p-s') and Bhaṭṭoji's vṛtti survive. The Siddhāntakaumudī (also called Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakaumudī) is an early modern grammatical masterpiece composed by Bhaṭṭoji Dīkṣita in the early 17th century. It rearranges the entire rule inventory of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī according to subject-matter categories (derivational prakriyā rather than original sūtra order), appending concise explanatory prose glosses. It became the dominant textbook and standard authority on Pāṇinian grammar throughout India.

Structured largely along the nosological classification established by Mādhava's Rugviniścaya (Mādhavanidāna), the treatise systematically details medicinal recipes, dietetics, and panchakarma treatment regimens. It is a landmark text in the history of Indian medicine for its early, widespread integration of metallic and mercurial preparations (rasaśāstra) into standard medical practice.

The Siddhayoga (also known as Vṛndamādhava) by Vṛnda is a major Sanskrit medical treatise on therapeutics (cikitsā) composed around the 9th or 10th century CE. It systematically arranges medicinal recipes and therapeutic treatments according to the nosological order established by Mādhava's Rugviniścaya (Mādhavanidāna). The work served as a primary foundation and source for Cakrapāṇidatta's 11th-century Cakradatta.

The Rāvaṇavaha ('The Slaying of Rāvaṇa', also known as Setubandha) is a celebrated Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit mahākāvya in 15 āśvāsas attributed to the Vākāṭaka ruler Pravarasena II (5th century CE). Composed chiefly in the skandhaka metre, the poem recounts the Rāmāyaṇa episode spanning the construction of the causeway across the ocean to Laṅkā up to the slaying of Rāvaṇa. Highly praised by classical Sanskrit literary theorists including Daṇḍin, Bāṇabhaṭṭa, and Ānandavardhana, it stands as the preeminent masterwork of Prakrit court epic poetry.

The Nalacampū (also known as Damayantīkathā), composed by Trivikramabhaṭṭa around 915 CE, is the earliest extant representative of the campū genre (mixed prose and verse kāvya) in classical Sanskrit literature. Treating the Mahābhārata narrative of Nala and Damayantī, the text survives in seven ucchvāsas ending before Nala's downfall and separation. The Saduktikarṇāmṛta ('Nectar for the Ears of Good Sayings') is a major Sanskrit subhāṣita anthology compiled in 1205/1206 CE by Śrīdharadāsa at the court of King Lakṣmaṇasena of Bengal. It is systematically arranged into five 'streams' (pravāhas)—Deva (or Amara), Śṛṅgāra, Cāṭu, Apadeśa, and Uccāvaca—each divided into thematic quintets (vīcis), containing 2,380 verses attributed to nearly 500 poets. The anthology is an indispensable source for the history of classical Sanskrit lyric poetry, particularly the courtly and devotional literature of late early-medieval eastern India.

Ratneśvara composed the Ratnadarpaṇa on paricchedas 1–3 under the patronage of Prince Rāmasiṃhadeva. The commentary on paricchedas 4–5 was supplied by the Maithila scholar Jagaddhara.

The Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa is an encyclopedic treatise on Sanskrit poetics and dramaturgy (Alaṃkāraśāstra) attributed to King Bhoja of Dhārā (11th century). In five exhaustive paricchedas, it systematically classifies poetic flaws (doṣa), excellences (guṇa), verbal figures (śabdālaṃkāra), semantic figures (arthālaṃkāra), and aesthetic experience (rasa), highlighting Bhoja's synthesis of poetic ornament with rasa theory. This digital text transmits the complete work alongside its primary classical commentaries: Ratneśvara's Ratnadarpaṇa on chapters 1–3 and Jagaddhara's gloss on chapters 4–5.

This DSBC e-text combines two Buddhist tantric works. ## Contents

**Attribution:** Revealed tantric scripture of the Yogatantra class; traditionally considered the word of the Buddha (Vajrasattva / Tathāgatas).

The Paramādya (Śrīparamādya) is a Yogatantra scripture closely related to the Adhyardhaśatikā Prajñāpāramitā (Nayasūtra) and the Sarvatathāgatatattvasaṃgraha, centred on Vajrasattva and mahāsukha. No complete Sanskrit text has been published; the work survives in Tibetan and, in part, in Chinese. This e-text collects Sanskrit verses of the Paramādya quoted in later works such as the Sarvabuddhasamāyoga, the Trisamayarājatantraṭīkā, Abhayākaragupta's Āmnāyamañjarī and Vajrāvalī, and the Viṃśatividhi.

**DSBC catalog:** [https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/971](https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/971)

Several sections are incomplete (§§4, 6, 7, 8, 11), and §§12–17, including the Great Miracle itself, are not preserved. The e-text ends mid-sentence at §11.4, where the grove-keeper Gaṇḍaka brings a tree from Mount Gandhamādana by magic power ('… anekapakṣigaṇ(a)|||').

**Also known as:** Mahāpratihāryasūtra (DSBC heading), *(Mahā)prātihārya(sūtra) (no title preserved in the Gilgit MSS)

**Attribution:** Mūlasarvāstivāda version of the Great Miracle at Śrāvastī, preserved in two Gilgit birch-bark manuscripts in the National Archives of India (New Delhi Collection serial no. 21, five folios, and no. 56h, one folio; 7th–8th c.). These had earlier been misidentified as the Divyāvadāna Prātihāryasūtra. No title is preserved; the name is reconstructed from citations (Tarkajvālā, Śamathadeva).

The Gilgit (Mūlasarvāstivāda) version of the story of the Buddha's Great Miracle at Śrāvastī. Māra takes the form of each of the six rival teachers led by Pūraṇa and makes each believe that the others have supernatural powers. The teachers resent the honours given to the Buddha and challenge him to a contest of miracles. They go to King Bimbisāra and then follow the Buddha to Śrāvastī and King Prasenajit, and they look for allies. The text breaks off as preparations for the contest begin and the grove-keeper Gaṇḍaka brings a tree from Mount Gandhamādana by magic power; the Great Miracle itself is not preserved.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Transcription, directly or through a copy, of the palm-leaf manuscript of the Hevajraprakāśa in the collection of Hemrāj Śākya, Uku Bāhāl, Patan. It was copied by the śrāmaṇera Jitāriśrī of the Dharmadhātuvihāra for the paramopāsaka Rāṇa in Śaka 1194 = 1272 CE ('1800 years 11 months 4 days after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa'). No printed edition is named.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West), input by Anjana Shakya, proofread by Miroj Shakya, 2008 (DSBC book 960; TEI header).

**Evidence:**
- The e-text reproduces the unique post-colophon of the Hemrāj Śākya manuscript ('deyadharmo 'yaṃ … paramopāsakaśrīrāṇasya … likhitam idaṃ dharmadhātuvihārīya 'dhivāsin śrāmaṇera śrījitāriśriyeneti'), as published by M. R. Pant from B. Kölver's photocopy in Bechert (ed.), The Dating of the Historical Buddha, Part 1 (1991), pp. 358–362.
- The e-text misreads that colophon ('śata 2800', 'śakāvrā 1104' for Pant's '1800' and 'śakābdā 1194'), so it is not keyed from Pant's corrected reading; Gemini's date of 1272 CE is correct only with Pant's reading.
- The DSBC record (book 960) gives no editor, publisher or year (a bibliography listing shows only 'pp. 1–49').
- Gerloff (2017) says he 'refines earlier editions' of the Hevajraprakāśa; which earlier edition, if any, underlies the DSBC text could not be established. Status is therefore 'probable' (manuscript lineage), not 'determined'.

**Other editions:**
- Torsten Gerloff, Saroruhavajra's Hevajra-Lineage: A Close Study of the Surviving Sanskrit and Tibetan Works. PhD dissertation, Universität Hamburg, 2017 (ediss 7370). — Improved critical edition of the Hevajraprakāśa with its Tibetan translation and an English translation.

**Translations:**
- Dpal kye rdo rje'i sgrub pa'i thabs rab tu gsal ba zhes bya ba (Prakāśa-nāma-śrīhevajrasādhana), Tōh. 1238, tr. Vanaratna and Gzhon nu dpal. (Tibetan)
- Gerloff 2017 (see above). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete. The text runs through all 32 sūtras of the sādhana from pūjācakra to punar utthāna (§32), followed by the avasāna verses, the author colophon, the ye dharmā verse, and the donor's and scribe's post-colophon. The opening maṅgala is not transcribed: the e-text begins with the editorial placeholder '[namaskriyā, maṇgalācaraṇa, etc.]' and places a summary verse of the sūtras before 'namaḥ śrīherukāya'.

**Also known as:** Pañcakramānuttarahevajraprakāśa (colophon), Prakāśa nāma śrīhevajrasādhana (Tōh. 1238), Dpal kye rdo rje'i sgrub pa'i thabs rab tu gsal ba

**Attribution:** Colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ mahāmaṇḍalācāryaśrīrāhulaguptapādānām'. In the Tibetan canon the work is ascribed to Sgra gcan gsang ba (Rāhulagupta; Tōh. 1238, tr. Vanaratna and Gzhon nu dpal). In the introduction the author says he combines Jālandharipāda's Vajrapradīpā (a ṭippaṇī on Saroruha's Hevajrasādhana) with Bhadrapāda's Dveṣavajrasādhana.

A Hevajra sādhana by the mahāmaṇḍalācārya Rāhulagupta. Written for practitioners of lesser ability, it combines Jālandharipāda's Vajrapradīpā on Saroruha's Hevajrasādhana with Bhadrapāda's Dveṣavajrasādhana into one manual. The manual is organised in 32 'sūtras', from the preliminary worship and brahmavihāras through the generation of the maṇḍala, consecration, the six-limbed yoga and clear light, to mantra recitation, bali, subtle yoga, daily conduct and re-emergence. The only known Sanskrit manuscript (1272 CE) is noted for its post-colophon dated in years from the Buddha's parinirvāṇa.

## Source

**Source corpus:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC)

**DSBC catalog:** [https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/960](https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/960)

Part II: Commentarial Works (Indian and Tibetan Studies 7.2), Hamburg: Department of Indian and Tibetan Studies, Universität Hamburg, 2020. — Critical edition from the Sanskrit manuscripts, with a semi-critical edition of the Tibetan translation and an annotated translation.
- Manuscripts include one in the Tucci collection (Sferra 2008, no. 50: 'Hevajrasādhanavajrapradīpa', colophon '... vajrapradīpānāmaṭippaṇī viśuddhiḥ samāptā || kṛtir iyam paṇḍitācāryaśrīmatsuratapādānām'). — Manuscript witness, not an edition.

**Translations:**
- Tibetan translation in the Tengyur, D 1237 (Kye rdo rje'i sgrub thabs kyi mdor bshad pa dag pa rdo rje sgron ma). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary explaining thirty-two sadhana limbs (dvātriṁśatsādhanasūtra), from the opening udghātaḥ to the concluding verses and colophon at segments 361–365.

**Also known as:** Vajrapradīpā nāma ṭippaṇī, Vajrapradīpā nāma ṭippaṇiviśuddhiḥ, Hevajrasādhana-vajrapradīpa-nāma-śuddha-ṭippanī, Viśuddhikramaṭippaṇī

**Attribution:** The author calls himself Suratavajra ('kṛtvā suratavajreṇa viśuddhikramaṭippaṇīm') and says he is known as Jālandharī ('mayā jālandharīti khyātena'); the colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṁ paṇḍitācāryaśrīmatsuratapādānām'. Gerloff calls him Jālandharipāda. DSBC lists Saroruha as author, which is wrong: Saroruha wrote the root sādhana. The Tibetan translation is in the Tengyur (D 1237 per the Tucci catalogue).

The Vajrapradīpā (also known as Vajrapradīpā nāma ṭippaṇī or Viśuddhikramaṭippaṇī) is an eighth- to ninth-century Vajrayāna commentary composed by Suratavajra (also known by his mahāsiddha epithet Jālandhari/Jālandharipāda) on Saroruhapāda's (Saroruhavajra's) foundational Hevajrasādhana. Adhering to the utpattikrama (generation stage) of the Hevajra cycle, the work systematically explains thirty-two sadhana topics (dvātriṁśatsādhanasūtra), analyzing the purificatory symbolism (viśuddhi) of the mandala deities, the eight cremation grounds (śmaśāna), ritual implements, and seed syllables.

The verses systematically praise the eight-faced, sixteen-armed form of Hevajra embracing Nairātmyā (vv. 1–8), followed by individual invocations of the eight yoginīs of his maṇḍala (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śabarī, Caṇḍālī, and Ḍombī; vv. 9–16), their collective qualities (vv. 17–19), and a concluding philosophical praise of the nondual deity (v. 20).

A sādhana (practice manual) for the generation stage (utpattikrama) of Hevajra by Saroruha(vajra), widely regarded as the most influential Hevajra practice text in Sanskrit. It sets out the preliminaries (worship, the four brahmavihāras, refuge and confession), the protective circle, the visualization of the maṇḍala with Hevajra, Nairātmyā and the eight goddesses (Gaurī, Caurī, etc.), mantra recitation and post-meditative conduct. The first critical edition, Gerloff 2017, is later than the DSBC input of 2008, so the e-text cannot derive from it. - dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/951: all bibliographic fields are empty.
- Gerloff 2017 (Hamburg dissertation, ediss 7370) presents his edition of the Dveṣavajrasādhana as an editio princeps, so no printed Sanskrit edition existed in 2008.
- The e-text has editorial section headings (upodghātaḥ, sādhanam, avasānam) and uncorrected corruptions (e.g. 'sukhapahala-', 'nūrtaṃ'), which point to a transcription rather than a critical edition.

PhD dissertation, Universität Hamburg, 2017 (online 2020: ediss.sub.uni-hamburg.de/handle/ediss/7370), Part III. — Editio princeps (critical edition) of the Sanskrit, with a semi-critical edition of the Tibetan canonical translation and an annotated English translation.

**Translations:**
- Tibetan canonical translation (edited semi-critically in Gerloff 2017, Part III; the Tōhoku number was not verified here). (Tibetan)
- Torsten Gerloff 2017 (see above), annotated translation. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete sādhana from the opening homage (upodghāta) to the final colophon (lines 0–193).

**Also known as:** Dveśavajrasādhana (DSBC spelling)

**Attribution:** The author calls himself Bhadra, a descendant in the lineage of Saroruhapāda ('saroruhapādanaptṛsutaputreṇa bhadranāmnā'), writing at the request of Kodāli, and names Rāhulapāda among his gurus. The colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṃ siddhācāryaśrīmadbhadrapādānām'. Gerloff (2017) treats the work as Bhadrapāda's and places the authors of Saroruha's lineage between the late 9th and the 11th century.

A Hevajra sādhana by Bhadrapāda, a later member of the lineage of Saroruhavajra. Following the Hevajratantra and Saroruha's instructions, it teaches the meditation on Hevajra/Heruka with Nairātmyā as 'Dveṣavajra' (the hatred-vajra form). It covers the preliminaries, worship by the eight goddesses (Gaurī, Caurī, etc.), the sevenfold worship and the brahmavihāras, the generation of the maṇḍala, consecration, mantra recitation, bali and subtle yoga, and closes with the assignment of the vajrīs to the senses. The concluding verses name Rāhulapāda among the author's gurus.

**Edition used (determined):** Zhen Liu and Johannes Schneider (eds.), Buddhist Hymns: A New Collection, Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region 24, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2022, §3.1 'Jambhalastotra' (standardized text; editio princeps of the Sanskrit, from the Drepung palm-leaf ms., fol. 1b).

**Evidence:**
- Liu & Schneider state that the Sanskrit Jambhalastotra is 'published here for the first time'; apart from stanza 7 no other Sanskrit witness was known, so the DSBC text can only derive from this edition.
- E-text agrees verbatim with the standardized edition (reference-literature OCR, lines 967-1006), including the editors' emendations against the manuscript: 2a dayālur (ms. dayalur), 5a ratnavarṣaṃ (ms. ratnaṃ varṣaṃ), 6b kuto (ms. kute), 7d bhagavān (ms. bhavatā), 9b samīhita (ms. samīhi), and the colophon.
- DSBC book page lists no bibliographic data.

**Other editions:**
- Zhen Liu and Johannes Schneider (eds.), Buddhist Hymns: A New Collection, Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region 24, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2022, diplomatic transcript of the Drepung manuscript (ch. 2). — Diplomatic transcript in the same volume, alongside the standardized text used here.
- Zhen Liu, 'Das Jambhalastotra von Candragomin, ein erst kürzlich entdeckter Sanskrit-Text' (announced as forthcoming in Liu & Schneider 2022). — Planned critical edition with the Tibetan version; publication not verified.

**Translations:**
- Tibetan Tengyur translation by Muditaśrījñāna and Nyi ma grags (per Liu & Schneider 2022). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Nine āryā stanzas with opening 'oṁ namo jambhalāya' (e-text typo 'jambhālāya') and colophon; identical in extent to the edition of Liu & Schneider 2022, §3.1.

**Also known as:** Āryajambhalastotra ('Phags pa dzam bha la la bstod pa, Tibetan)

**Attribution:** Colophon: 'iti candragomiviracitaṁ jambhalastotraṁ samāptam' (Drepung ms.), agreeing with the Tengyur attribution to Candragomin. Liu & Schneider 2022 note that iconographic considerations may point to a later (tantric) Candragomin rather than the 5th-century grammarian. Stanza 7 was previously known from a citation (Bendall's Śikṣāsamuccaya note / Vilāsavajra).

The Jambhalastotra is a concise nine-verse Sanskrit hymn in Āryā metre attributed to Candragomin, praising Jambhala, the Buddhist deity of wealth and abundance. The poet approaches the compassionate deity as an afflicted, weeping devotee, contrasting inanimate wish-granting objects with Jambhala's living mercy and lamenting that poverty continues to afflict him. The hymn concludes with a dedication wishing that by the merit of this prayer, living beings may become like Jambhala in bestowing all desired gifts.

# Deśanāstava

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T01_desanastavau`

**Author:** Candragomin

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T01 (Stotra)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Zhen Liu and Johannes Schneider (eds.), Buddhist Hymns: A New Collection, Sanskrit Texts from the Tibetan Autonomous Region 24, Beijing: China Tibetology Publishing House / Vienna: Austrian Academy of Sciences Press, 2022 [2023], § 3.3 Deśanāstava, pp. 53 ff. (standardized text), based on a single manuscript from Tibet published in facsimile in the PRC.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC, book 946); input and proofreading credited to Miroj Shakya (TEI header dated 2008); TEI header by the Intellexus project.

**Evidence:**
- Collation of the DSBC e-text with the standardized text of Liu & Schneider (open-access PDF, doi:10.1553/978OEAW89183): the 52 verses agree word for word, including the editors' emendations of manuscript errors listed in their apparatus (e.g. nirdahan for ms. nirdahana, sarva for sava, saṃvṛtiṃ for samvṛti, prekṣya for prekṣa, vidravann for vidruvann, vīkṣya for vīkṣa, anudbhavo for anubhavo). Remaining differences are few (visīdati/viṣīdati, śātrur/śatrur, nirvartate/nivartate, kleśanakramākara-/kleśanakramakara-) and look like typing slips.
- Liu & Schneider state that their volume presents the Sanskrit Deśanāstava 'for the first time', and the DSBC book page names no editor, publisher or year. The agreement with the editors' emendations suggests the DSBC text was keyed from their edition (or from a pre-publication version of it), but this conflicts with the 2008 date in the DSBC TEI header (probably a generic project date). Hence 'probable', not 'determined'.

**Other editions:**
- Mark Joseph Tatz, 'Candragomin and the Bodhisattva Vow', PhD dissertation, Vancouver: University of British Columbia, 1978, pp. 469–544. — Critical edition of the Tibetan version (bShags pa'i bstod pa) with the commentary of Buddhaśānti; English translation pp. 84–175.
- Michael Hahn, 'A Difficult Beginning: Comments on an English Translation of Candragomin's Deśanāstava', in: Ram Karan Sharma (ed.), Researches in Indian and Buddhist Philosophy: Essays in Honour of Professor Alex Wayman, Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1993. — Review of Tatz's translation, with philological discussion (based on the Tibetan).

**Translations:**
- Mark Tatz, Difficult Beginnings: Three Works on the Bodhisattva Path by Candragomin, Boston: Shambhala, 1985, pp. 39–110 (from the Tibetan, with Buddhaśānti's commentary). (English)
- Michael Hahn and Astrid Lohöfer, Der Mahāyāna-Buddhismus in den Augen des Dichters Candragomin: Candragomins Schauspiel Freude für die Menschen, sein Brief an die Schüler und sein Hymnus in Form eines Sündenbekenntnisses, Indologica Marpurgensia 8, München: P. Kirchheim, 2016, pp. 134–140, 215–218 (from the Tibetan). (German)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: 52 verses in rathoddhatā with 'namo buddhāya', the colophon 'deśanāstavaḥ samāptaḥ' and 'kṛtir iyaṃ candragomipādānām iti'. (The Tibetan version has 51 stanzas; Sanskrit v. 52 has no Tibetan counterpart, per Liu & Schneider 2022.)

**Also known as:** bShags pa'i bstod pa

**Attribution:** Colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ candragomipādānām'. Hahn (1993; also in his paper on Carpaṭi's Avalokiteśvarastotra) counts the Deśanāstava, with the Lokānandanāṭaka and Śiṣyalekha, among the works safely attributable to Candragomin the poet and grammarian.

The Deśanāstava ('Hymn in the form of a confession') is a 52-verse Mahāyāna hymn in rathoddhatā metre ascribed in its colophon to Candragomin, which combines praise of the Buddha with confession: the speaker describes how each remedy he tries (the four brahmavihāras, generosity, patience, insight into emptiness) is undone by a further defilement. Hahn and later scholars regard it as a genuine work of Candragomin, the author of the Lokānandanāṭaka and Śiṣyalekha. It was long known only from the Tibetan Tengyur translation with Buddhaśānti's commentary; the Sanskrit text was published from a manuscript from Tibet by Liu and Schneider (2022).

## Source

**Source corpus:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC)

**DSBC catalog:** [https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/946](https://www.dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/946)

- Shastri 1990 (Sarnath, 'Pandita series 1'): edition and translation of the hymn from a Nepalese Sanskrit manuscript, as cited by Liu & Schneider 2022 (§3.2 and bibliography); full bibliographic details not verified. — Earlier Sanskrit edition based on a Nepalese manuscript.

Tschannerl, Swisttal-Odendorf: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 2000. — Study of the hymn and its title (cited by Roesler); whether it contains a full Sanskrit edition was not verified.

**Also known as:** Devatāvimarśastuti (title proposed by M. Hahn 2000), Lha las phul du byung bar bstod pa (Tibetan)

**Attribution:** Colophon: 'kṛtir iyam ācāryabhaṭṭavarāhasvāminaḥ' (= Drepung palm-leaf ms., Old Bengali script, c. 13th/14th c.). The Tibetan Tengyur translation (with Prajñāvarman's commentary) attributes the hymn to Śaṃkarasvāmin/Śaṃkarapati (bDe byed bdag po); Schneider 2014 uses that attribution, Liu & Schneider 2022 treat Varāhasvāmin and Śaṃkarasvāmin as names of the same author.

A hymn of 21 stanzas in several metres arguing for the Buddha's superiority over the Brahmanical gods (Viṣṇu, Śiva, Skanda, Brahmā, Indra, Pārvatī, Vināyaka): the gods' weapons, passions and violent deeds are contrasted with the Buddha's peacefulness, compassion and freedom from faults. The poet addresses the reader rather than the Buddha, so the text is as much an apology for conversion to Buddhism as a hymn. It was translated into Tibetan together with Prajñāvarman's commentary, which became a source for Tibetan knowledge of Indian epic narratives.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in 25 stanzas (the recension of Drepung ms. D1, which has two stanzas unattested elsewhere and lacks one known from other versions; other editions have 24), with title and author colophon. Bracketed numbers give the stanza numbers of an earlier edition.

**Also known as:** Suprabhātastotra, Suprabhātastavastotra

**Attribution:** Colophon ascribes it to King Śrīharṣa ('kṛtir iyaṁ rājñaḥ śrīharṣasya'). The other Sanskrit version (Pandey 1994, no. 89) has 'śrīharṣadevabhūpativiracitam'. Liu & Schneider (2022) treat the ascription to Harṣa of Kanauj as possible but not certain.

The Suprabhātastava ('Praise of the Auspicious Dawn') is a Buddhist hymn, mostly in mālinī, in which the poet contrasts the ever-awake Buddha with Hindu gods and sages (Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, Agni, Balarāma, Gaṇeśa, Kumāra, the ṛṣis), all shown as asleep in passion, under the refrain 'daśabala tava nityaṃ suprabhātaṃ prabhātam'. The colophon ascribes it to King Śrīharṣa. This e-text has the 25 stanzas of a Drepung manuscript, a longer recension than the usual 24.

The Mūlamadhyamakakārikā ('Root Verses on the Middle Way') is the foundational treatise of the Madhyamaka philosophical school, composed by Nāgārjuna (ca. 2nd–3rd century CE). Across 27 chapters, it rigorously examines and deconstructs core metaphysical categories and conceptual frameworks—including causation, motion, sense faculties, the skandhas, the self, time, suffering, defilements, the four noble truths, and nirvāṇa. Nāgārjuna demonstrates that all phenomena are empty (śūnya) of intrinsic nature (svabhāva) precisely because they are dependently originated (pratītyasamutpanna), establishing emptiness as the middle way between the ontological extremes of substantialism and nihilism.

**Other editions:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete. Prose with 81 numbered verses, ending '[318] ādikarmāvatāraḥ samāptaḥ', followed by closing verses, the grantha count (śata 5) and the author colophon.

**Attribution:** Ascribed to Paṇḍita Sthavira Mañjukīrti in the incipit ([0]) and the colophon ([324]: 'kṛtir iyaṃ paṇḍitasthaviramañjukīrtipādānām'). Mañjukīrti was a scholar active in Magadha. His date is uncertain, but the work comes from before ca. 1200 (the manuscript is thought to have been copied in Magadha in the 11th–12th century). A Tibetan title note on the Göttingen manuscript reads 'Slob dpon 'Jam dpal grags pas mdzad pa'i Las dang po pa'i bya ba'.

The Ādikarmāvatāra is a Mahāyāna Buddhist ritual and daily practice manual intended for novice practitioners (ādikarmika), preserved in the Nepalese Sanskrit manuscript tradition. It delineates fundamental daily observances including taking refuge in the Three Jewels, moral confession (pāpadeśanā), generating bodhicitta, receiving the upāsaka precepts, cleaning and arranging the shrine, offering maṇḍalas and flowers, reciting dhāraṇīs, and honouring the spiritual teacher (guru). The work consists of instructional prose interspersed with 81 mnemonic verses and sūtra citations.

**Evidence:**
- The TEI header gives only the input personnel and proofreader, with no source.
- dsbcproject.org/canon-text/book/923 shows '-' for every bibliographic field.
- Bracketed editorial corrections in the text (e.g. 'sva(su)rekhojjvalā', 'maṇḍa[la]ka', 'pūrva[vi]dehe') suggest an edited printing or a careful transcription of a manuscript, but no printed edition could be found.
- Checked: reference literature (only Dan Martin's Tibskrit and La Vallée Poussin, Bouddhisme: études et matériaux, the latter on the Buddhādipūjana section of the Ādikarmapradīpa, which is a different text), INBUDS (no hits) and a web search.

**Coverage:** partial — Opening verse 1: 'buddhaṃ praṇamya lokeśaṃ vāgīśaṃ tāriṇīm api / teṣāṃ pūjākramaṃ brūmo yathāmnāyaṃ samāsataḥ'. The e-text gives the daily preliminaries, the maṇḍalaka of the Pañcatathāgatas and their consorts, the pūjā and mantras (verses 1–35), 'buddhamaṇḍalaṃ samāptam', and the arghya/pādya offerings with the iconography of the eight Bodhisattvas. It then begins 'atha śrīmatkhasarpaṇabhaṭṭārakapūjā…' and breaks off mid-sentence ('pūrve pūrvavidehe vairocanam | dakṣiṇe'). The sections on Lokeśa/Khasarpaṇa (most of it), Vāgīśa (Mañjuśrī) and Tārā are missing.

**Attribution:** Anonymous in the e-text. Dan Martin's Tibskrit (citing Bandurski 1994, pp. 86–87) records a Sanskrit manuscript 'Buddhādipūjāvidhi' (Tib. added title Sangs rgyas la sogs pa mchod pa'i cho ga) in the Sāṅkṛtyāyana photographs at Göttingen, next to Mañjuśrīkīrti's Ādikarmāvatāra and its supplement. The opening 'iha khalu kathitakramāt … labdhopāsakasaṃvareṇa' presupposes an earlier text on refuge and lay vows, which fits such a series. Identification with that manuscript and attribution to Mañjuśrīkīrti remain unverified.

An anonymous Sanskrit manual (pūjākrama) for the daily worship of the Buddha and of the deities named in the opening verse: Lokeśa, Vāgīśa (Mañjuśrī) and Tāriṇī. The surviving part covers the morning observances and bath mantras, the preparation and consecration of the maṇḍalaka, and the visualisation of the Pañcatathāgatas with their consorts on Sumeru and the four continents, with mantras, offerings and praise. It then gives the arghya and pādya offerings with the iconography of the eight great Bodhisattvas, and breaks off at the beginning of the worship of Khasarpaṇa Avalokiteśvara.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), book 921; input and proofreading Miroj Shakya (Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West); TEI via ERC Intellexus.

**Evidence:**
- The e-text reproduces the line division of Steinkellner's critical text, including hyphenated line breaks: e.g. 'kutas tannimitto vyapadeśaḥ| yathānyagataiḥ karmādibhir anyasam-/bandhī na bhavaty asambandhāt', 'sva-/bhāvabhedo 'yaṁ … sasthi-/raikasvabhāvānāṁ', 'krau-/ddha-anvitasya pustakam' (edition p. 35 vs. e-text seg. 261–272).
- Verse markers [v.1]–[v.25] and the lacuna in v.2 ('sva . . . . sa svarūpaśleṣaḥ') are identical to the edition; the edition's emendations (e.g. 'sambandhaparīkṣāvṛttiḥ samāptā', reconstructed 'śāntiḥ') are adopted, so it is the critical text, not the diplomatic one.
- The DSBC TEI header names only personnel (Miroj Shakya) and no edition; the edition was checked in the open-access PDF (austriaca.at).

**Other editions:**
- Erich Frauwallner, 'Dharmakīrtis Saṃbandhaparīkṣā. Text und Übersetzung', WZKM 41 (1934), pp. 261–300 (= Kleine Schriften, 1982, pp. 490–529). — 22 kārikās reconstructed from Jaina citations and Tibetan translations, with the Tibetan Vṛtti (Narthang).
- Muni Jambūvijaya, 'Jain dārśanika sāhitya ane Sambandhaparīkṣā', in Śrīmad Vijaya-Rājendrasūri-smāraka-grantha, Bhavnagar 1957, pp. 774–789. — Kārikās with Tibetan translation and Jaina citations.
- Swami Dwarikadas Shastri (ed.), Vādanyāyaprakaraṇa … and Sambandhaparīkṣā with the Commentary of Prabhācandra, Bauddha Bharati Series 8, Varanasi 1972, pp. 139–149. — 22 kārikās with Prabhācandra's commentary from the Prameyakamalamārtaṇḍa.
- Hideomi Yaita, Bukkyō chishikiron no genten kenkyū (Three Sanskrit Texts from the Buddhist Pramāṇa-Tradition), Narita 2005, pp. 69*–72*. — First and last three kārikās identified in the Tarkarahasya (earlier Yaita 1986, 1990).

**Translations:**
- Erich Frauwallner, WZKM 41 (1934) (see above). (German)
- V. N. Jha, The Philosophy of Relations, Bibliotheca Indo-Buddhica 66, Delhi: Sri Satguru, 1990 (kārikās with Prabhācandra's commentary, text copied from Shastri 1972). (English)
- Shimizu Yō, 'Dharmakīrti Sambandhaparīkṣā no wayaku kaisetsu', Bukkyōgaku kenkyū 37 (1981) (SP 1–22). (Japanese)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete Vṛtti with all 25 kārikās (verse markers [v.1]–[v.25]), ending with the colophon 'sambandhaparīkṣāvṛttiḥ samāptā | kṛtir ācāryadevendrabuddheḥ | krauddha-anvitasya pustakam'. Lacunae of the manuscript remain as dots (e.g. seg. 16 'sva ……… sa svarūpaśleṣaḥ', as in the edition).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Sambandhaparīkṣā (Dharmakīrti, root text)
- Sambandhaparīkṣāvṛtti (Devendrabuddhi, commentary)

**Also known as:** Sambandhaparīkṣāvṛtti, 'Brel pa brtag pa'i 'grel pa

**Attribution:** Root kārikās (25) by Dharmakīrti. The Vṛtti was transmitted in Tibetan (Toh 4215) as Dharmakīrti's autocommentary, but the Drepung Sanskrit manuscript names Devendrabuddhi; Steinkellner 2022 (Introduction, 'On the Sambandhaparīkṣāvṛtti's authorship') accepts Devendrabuddhi. In his apparatus the closing 'sambandhaparīkṣāvṛttiḥ samāptā' is an emendation and 'śāntiḥ', 'sarvabhāvasvabhāvāḥ' are reconstructed from the Tibetan.

Dharmakīrti's Sambandhaparīkṣā ('Examination of relation') argues in 25 verses that relations such as dependence, conjunction, inherence and causality are not real entities but conceptual constructions superimposed on mutually distinct, momentary things. This e-text gives the prose Vṛtti on the verses, which the only Sanskrit manuscript (from Drepung) ascribes to Dharmakīrti's pupil Devendrabuddhi, together with the full set of kārikās, as critically edited by Ernst Steinkellner in 2022.

**Other editions:**
- Bhagwan Dash, Tibetan Medicine, with special reference to Yoga Śataka, Dharamsala: Library of Tibetan Works and Archives, 1976. — Tibetan version with Sanskrit text and English translation; according to Filliozat its Sanskrit is based on a Sinhalese printed edition, not on manuscripts.

**Translations:**
- Filliozat 1979 (French translation). (French)
- Dash 1976 (English translation). (English)

Filliozat discusses the attribution and the variant ascription to Vararuci in some manuscripts. Whether this medical author is the same as the Madhyamaka philosopher is uncertain.

The Yogaśataka is a short Āyurvedic compendium of about a hundred medical formulas (109 stanzas in this text), arranged by disease, beginning with fevers (jvaracikitsā), and attributed to Nāgārjuna. It circulated widely and was translated into Tibetan and Tocharian (Kuchean), which shows its early importance in Buddhist medicine.

# Catuṣpariṣatsūtra (fragment: §§ 0.1–0.11)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T16_bhavanayogau`

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T16 (Vividha)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** The manuscript-line text, with restorations in parentheses, of the Central Asian (Turfan) fragments as printed in Ernst Waldschmidt, Das Catuṣpariṣatsūtra … Teil I, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1952 (Abh. DAW, Kl. für Sprachen, Literatur und Kunst), § 0.1–0.11.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), book 913 (content 3041), input and proofread by Miroj Shakya, Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West.

**Evidence:**
- The section numbering 1–11 and the wording match Waldschmidt's § 0.1–0.11 (SuttaCentral sf259 'Wal_0.x') and DSBC's own Catuṣpariṣatsūtra (book 38) §§ 1–11.
- The e-text keeps short manuscript lines with hyphenated word breaks and bracketed restorations, '(ekaṁ samayaṁ bodhisattvo / bhagavān) (u)rubilvā(yāṁ'. This is the diplomatic presentation of the Turfan fragments found in Waldschmidt's edition. It is not a running critical text.
- The DSBC book page 913 leaves the bibliographic fields blank, so the identification with Waldschmidt's print is inferred and not stated by the DSBC.

**Other editions:**
- Ernst Waldschmidt, Das Catuṣpariṣatsūtra, Teil I–III, Berlin: Akademie-Verlag, 1952, 1957, 1962. — Standard edition of the whole sūtra (also SuttaCentral sf259, DharmaNexus SA_K14_sf259_sc, DSBC book 38 / SA_K14_n285u).
- Raniero Gnoli, The Gilgit Manuscript of the Saṅghabhedavastu, Part I, Rome: IsMEO, 1977 (SOR 49.1). — Parallel Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya version of the same passage.

**Translations:**
- Ria Kloppenborg, The Sūtra on the Foundation of the Buddhist Order (Catuṣpariṣatsūtra), Leiden: Brill, 1973.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Only §§ 0.1–0.11 of Waldschmidt's text: the Bodhisattva at Uruvilvā in the first watch (ṛddhiviṣaya, pūrvanivāsānusmṛti) and the start of the middle watch (divyaśrotra). It breaks off before the divine eye, the knowledge of others' minds and the destruction of the āsravas, i.e. before the enlightenment and the rest of the sūtra (Vorgänge 1–28). The layout keeps the manuscript lines with restorations in parentheses. The manuscript reads 'āniñjyaprāpto' where the edited text has 'sātatyakārī nipako'.

**Also known as:** Bhāvanāyoga (DSBC title), Bhāvanāyogam

**Attribution:** Anonymous canonical sūtra of the (Mūla)sarvāstivāda tradition. The same passage appears in the Saṅghabhedavastu of the Mūlasarvāstivāda Vinaya (Gnoli 1977, Part I).

The opening of the Catuṣpariṣatsūtra, in a fragmentary manuscript-line text with restorations. The Bodhisattva sits under the bodhi tree on the bank of the Nairañjanā at Uruvilvā, devoted to the cultivation of the factors of awakening. In the first watch of the night he experiences the supernormal powers (ṛddhiviṣaya) and recollects his former lives, and in the middle watch he attains the divine ear. The text breaks off there.

Buddhodaya is a modern Sanskrit kāvya in ten cantos by Śāntibhikṣu Śāstrī, completed in Buddha era 2514 (ca. 1970/71) while he taught at Vidyālaṅkāra University in Sri Lanka. It celebrates the life of Śākyamuni, from the Bodhisattva's vow before Dīpaṃkara and his birth at Lumbinī to his awakening and teaching. Classical metres alternate with song-like (geya) stanzas that have refrains.

- ilx_skt TEI header (dsbc/prajñāhṛdayavyākhyā_book_904.xml) names no printed source.

R. C. Negi's Atīśaviracitā Ekādaśagranthāḥ (Bibliotheca Indo-Tibetica 24, Sarnath: CIHTS 1992; Tibetan text with Sanskrit restoration) was found, but its catalogue description ('treatises on Tantric Buddhism') gives no evidence that it contains this Heart Sūtra commentary.

**Other editions:**
- Tibetan translation in the Tengyur (Shes rab snying po'i rnam par bshad pa), by Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna and Nag tsho Tshul khrims rgyal ba; Derge/Peking numbers as given in the draft (Toh 3821 / P 5222) not re-verified. — Only pre-modern witness; no Sanskrit manuscript is known.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the commentary, ending with the author's final verses and the translators' colophon.

**Also known as:** Prajñāpāramitāhṛdayavyākhyā, Shes rab snying po'i rnam par bshad pa

**Attribution:** Attributed to Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna (982–1054 CE); the work survives in Tibetan in the Tengyur (Shes rab snying po'i rnam par bshad pa), translated by Atīśa himself with Nag tsho Tshul khrims rgyal ba (rendered 'bhikṣu Śīlajina'). The Sanskrit e-text is a modern restoration from the Tibetan, not an original Sanskrit transmission. Tengyur numbers given in the draft (Toh 3821, P 5222) were not re-verified in this review.

A short commentary on the Heart Sūtra (Prajñāpāramitāhṛdaya) attributed to Atīśa Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna, composed in Tibet at the request of a monk Sādhuprajña (per the closing verses). It frames the sūtra with Dignāga's account of the sūtra introduction (citing Prajñāpāramitāpiṇḍārtha 3–4) and Vimalamitra's eightfold exegesis, and reads the sūtra as teaching the five paths, the eight profound points and, for those of sharp faculties, the mantra. The Sanskrit text here is a modern restoration from the Tibetan translation.

It integrates Madhyamaka philosophy into the Mahāyāna path structure of the ten bodhisattva stages (daśabhūmi) and perfections (pāramitā). The Mahāvastu (or Mahāvastvavadāna) is an extensive canonical biography of the Buddha preserved in Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit, representing the Vinayapiṭaka tradition of the Lokottaravāda branch of the Mahāsāṅghika school. It frames the life of Śākyamuni Buddha within a cosmic perspective of past buddhas and numerous rebirth stories (jātakas and avadānas), reflecting early Lokottaravāda docetism. Volume 2 details the Bodhisattva's final rebirth from his descent from the Tuṣita heaven, conception, birth, princely life, and great renunciation through the attainment of awakening, interspersed with major narratives including the Śyāmajātaka and Kuśajātaka.

The Chappaṇṇayagāhāo is an anthology of 164 Prakrit didactic and gnomic stanzas (subhāṣita) composed in the gāhā (āryā) metre. Commencing with salutations to Jina Mahāvīra, the work imparts practical ethics, reflections on fate and karma, righteous conduct, the qualities of true friends and noble people (sujana), and worldly wisdom. It forms an integral part of the classical Jain tradition of sententious gnomic literature.

The Pāiyalacchīnāmamālā ('Garland of Names of the Prakrit Fortune') is a Prakrit synonym lexicon (koṣa) composed in 279 Āryā/Gāhā stanzas by the Jain poet Dhanapāla. Modern scholarship treats the collection as an evolving anthology of Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit muktaka stanzas compiled and augmented over several centuries (roughly 3rd to 8th centuries CE).

The Sattasaī (Gāhāsattasaī, Sanskrit: Gāthāsaptaśatī) is an anthology of lyric stanzas (muktaka) in the āryā (gāhā) metre in Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit, traditionally attributed to the Sātavāhana ruler Hāla. The poems evoke vignettes of pastoral and domestic life in the Deccan, focusing primarily on the nuances of erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra), courtship, jealousy, and the distress of separation. It holds a pivotal place in Indian poetic tradition and was frequently cited by classical Sanskrit rhetoricians as the exemplar of dhvani (poetic suggestion).

Contains verses 1–3 and the Sanskrit auto-commentary, breaking off mid-sentence in the introduction to verse 4 ('idānīṁ nānādēśaprasiddhabhāṣāsvativyāptiparihārārthaṁ dēśīlakṣaṇ'). - Deśīnāmamālāvṛtti (Hemacandra, commentary)

The Deśīnāmamālā (also known as Rayanāvalī or Ratnāvalī) is Hemacandra's celebrated lexicographical treatise recording Prakrit deśī vocabulary—words current in regional Prakrit usage that are neither tatsama nor regular tadbhava derivatives from Sanskrit. The Prakrit verses are accompanied by Hemacandra's Sanskrit auto-commentary (vṛtti), which defines and contextualizes each term. This e-text is an incomplete transcription fragment containing only the opening mangala and introductory verses 1–3.

The Gāhārayaṇakosa (Sanskrit: Gāthāratnakośa) is a Prakrit poetic anthology compiled by the Śvetāmbara Jain monk Jineśvarasūri in VS 1251 (1194 CE). The Rāvaṇavaho (commonly known as Setubandha) is a premier Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit mahākāvya in fifteen āśvāsas, composed primarily in the skandhaka metre. Attributed to the Vākāṭaka ruler Pravarasena II (5th century CE), it retells the events of the Rāmāyaṇa from Rāma's seasonal lamentation and the alliance with Sugrīva through the engineering of the ocean bridge (setu) to the final defeat of Rāvaṇa. **Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the legendary authority on metrics Piṅgala (or Piṅgalanāga / Phaṇirāja), but compiled by an anonymous anthologist in the early 14th century CE.

The Prākṛtapaiṅgalam is an influential 14th-century manual of Prakrit and Apabhraṃśa metrics traditionally attributed to Piṅgala. Composed mainly in Avahaṭṭa (late Apabhraṃśa), it provides definitions and rules for both moraic (mātrā) and syllabic (varṇa) meters, illustrated by verses celebrating regional rulers such as Hammīra of Ranthambore as well as devotional and secular lyric poetry. It represents a vital linguistic and poetic link in the transition from Middle Indo-Aryan to early New Indo-Aryan vernacular literatures.

**Also known as:** Prākṛtalakṣaṇa, Prākṛtaprakāśavṛtti, Manoramāvṛtti

**Attribution:** The root aphorisms are traditionally ascribed to Vararuci. Modern philological consensus treats chapters 1–9 (Mahārāṣṭrī) as the nuclear text, with chapters 10–12 as subsequent additions. The introductory verse (VaraBhā.2) explicitly identifies the commentator as Bhāmaha ('vararuciracitaprākṛtalakṣaṇasūtrāṇi lakṣyamārgeṇa / buddhvā cakāra vṛttiṃ saṃkṣiptāṃ bhāmahaḥ spaṣṭām').

The Prākṛtaprakāśa of Vararuci is the earliest extant and historically foundational Sanskrit treatise on Prakrit grammar. Consisting of twelve chapters, it derives Prakrit phonology and morphology from Sanskrit, taking Mahārāṣṭrī as the normative base dialect (chapters 1–9) followed by specific rules for Paiśācī, Māgadhī, and Śaurasenī (chapters 10–12). The accompanying Manoramā commentary by Bhāmaha (ca. 7th century) offers concise glosses and illustrative citations.

**Attribution:** The Prākṛtaprakāśa is traditionally attributed to Vararuci. The text here provides the sūtrapāṭha followed by colophons referencing Vasantarāja's Prākṛtasañjīvanī commentary, though the commentary prose itself is omitted.

The Prākṛtaprakāśa, attributed to Vararuci, is the earliest extant treatise on Prakrit grammar. Composed in Sanskrit sūtras, it systematically outlines the phonological and morphological transformations from Sanskrit to Prakrit, treating Mahārāṣṭrī Prakrit as the baseline language. This e-text preserves the sūtrapāṭha across eight paricchedas according to the recension associated with Vasantarāja's commentary Prākṛtasañjīvanī.

Vora), 2 vols. (Part I: uddesas 1–46, 1962; Part II: uddesas 47–118, 1968), Prakrit Text Society Series Nos. 6 & 12, Varanasi / Ahmedabad: Prakrit Text Society.

**E-text:** Prakrit Digital Text Project (PDTP), compiled & edited by Andrew Ollett (file: txt/Vimala/PaumaCa.txt / tei/Vimala/PaumaCa.xml).

**Evidence:**
- PDTP TEI header and repository metadata explicitly credit the Prakrit Text Society revised edition by Muni Punyavijayaji.
- Page numbers in the e-text ('[p. 1]', '[p. 2]', etc.) and editorial Sanskrit section rubrics ('[suttavihāṇaṁ]', '[maṅgalam —]', '[abhidhēyam —]', '[dēhāvayavasāphalyam —]') directly match the PTS edition.

**Other editions:**
- Hermann Jacobi (ed.), Paumacariyaṁ: The Oldest Jaina Rāmāyaṇa in Prakrit, Bhavnagar: Jaina Dharma Prasāraka Sabhā, 1914. — First critical edition of the text.
- K. R. Chandra, A Critical Study of Paumacariyaṁ, Vaishali: Research Institute of Prakrit, Jainology & Ahimsa, 1970. — Monograph with exhaustive study and text analysis.

**Translations:**
- Shantilal M. Vora (trans.), Hindi translation accompanying Muni Shri Punyavijayaji's edition of Paümacariyaṁ, 2 vols., Varanasi/Ahmedabad: Prakrit Text Society, 1962, 1968. (Hindi)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text across all 118 uddesas (cantos), concluding with the 119 verses of uddesa 118 (Padmanirvāṇagamana).

**Also known as:** Paümacariyaṃ, Paumacariya, Paumacariyam, Padmacarita, Rāhavacariya

**Attribution:** The concluding colophon of the text (uddesa 118, vv. 117–118) explicitly attributes authorship to Vimalasūri (sūrivimala), disciple of Vijayācārya and grand-disciple of Rāhusūri of the Nāilakula lineage. The text contains an internal date of 530 years after Mahāvīra's nirvāṇa (c. 4 CE), though modern scholars generally date the composition to between the 3rd and 5th centuries CE.

The Paümacariya (Padmacarita) of Vimalasūri is the earliest surviving Jaina retelling of the Rāma story (Rāmāyaṇa), composed in Jaina Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit verse across 118 uddesas. The work explicitly rationalizes and corrects Vālmīki's epic in light of Jaina doctrine, presenting Rāvaṇa and the Rākṣasas as civilized Vidyādhara aerial beings rather than blood-drinking demons, and Sugrīva and the Vānaras as a dynasty bearing the monkey emblem rather than beasts. Emphasizing karma, ahiṃsā, and monastic renunciation, it culminates in Rāma's attainment of omniscience (kevalajñāna) and ultimate liberation (nirvāṇa), serving as the foundational prototype for subsequent Jaina Rāmakathā literature in Sanskrit, Prakrit, and Apabhraṃśa.

# Gaüḍavaha

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GK23_gaudavahamu`

**Author:** Vākpatirāja

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** N. G. Suru (ed.), Gaüḍavahaṁ by Kavirāja Vākpatirāja, Prakrit Text Society Series No. 18, Ahmedabad: Prakrit Text Society, 1975 (reprint 2020).

**E-text:** Prakrit Digital Text Project (PDTP), compiled and edited by Andrew Ollett (tei/Vākpatirāja/GaüḍVa.xml).

- PDTP repository metadata and TEI header specify the source edition as N. G. Suru, Gaüḍavahaṁ, Prakrit Text Society.
- Page markers embedded in the e-text [p. 1] to [p. 178] match the pagination of Suru's edition.

**Other editions:**
- Shankar Pandurang Pandit (ed.), The Gaüḍavaho: A Historical Poem in Prâkṛit by Vâkpati, Bombay Sanskrit Series No. XXXIV, Bombay: Government Central Book Depôt, 1887. — First printed edition with Haripāla's commentary.
- Narayan Bapuji Utgikar (ed.), The Gaüḍavaho: A Historical Poem in Prâkṛit by Vâkpati, 2nd edition, Poona: Bhandarkar Oriental Research Institute, 1927. — Revised second edition of Pandit's work with new introduction and notes.

**Translations:**
- N. G. Suru, Gaüḍavaho by Vākpatirāja, Prakrit Text Society Series No. 18, Ahmedabad: Prakrit Text Society, 1975. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete as extant; contains all 1209 verses (gāthās) of the introductory section (gāthāpīṭha), which is all that survives of the poem in the manuscript tradition.

**Also known as:** Gauḍavaha, Gauḍavadha, Gaüḍavaho, Gaüḍavahaṁ

**Attribution:** Vākpatirāja explicitly names himself in the text and colophon (kaïrāa-lañchaṇassa vappaïrāassa gauḍavahē gāhāvīḍhaṁ samattaṁ).

The Gaüḍavaha ('The Slaying of the Gauda [King]') is an 8th-century Maharashtri Prakrit mahākāvya composed in āryā meter by Vākpatirāja, court poet of King Yaśovarman of Kanauj (c. 725–753 CE). Although planned to celebrate Yaśovarman's digvijaya and victory over the Gauda monarch, the extant text preserves only the introductory portion (gāthāpīṭha, 1209 verses), concluding before the actual battle. The text contains elaborate invocations of Viṣṇu and Vindhyavāsinī (Durgā), reflections on the nature and sweetness of Prakrit poetry, descriptions of seasons and village life, and eulogies of King Yaśovarman.

**Also known as:** Ācārāṅgasūtra, Āyāro, Ācārasūtra, Ayaramga Sutta, Aṅgasutta 1

**Attribution:** Traditionally regarded as the direct preaching of the Jina Mahāvīra, memorized and transmitted by his chief disciple, the Gaṇadhara Sudharman.

The Āyāraṅgasutta (Sanskrit: Ācārāṅgasūtra) is the first of the eleven surviving Aṅgas of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. Composed in an archaic stratum of Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, its first Śrutaskandha forms one of the earliest surviving witnesses to Jaina ascetic practice, laying down fundamental tenets of ahiṃsā (non-violence) toward all six classes of living beings, rigorous wandering discipline, and monastic detachment. Its ninth chapter, the Upadhānaśruta, preserves an ancient poetic account of the austerities, hardships, and enlightenment of Mahāvīra.

The Sūyagaḍaṅga (Sanskrit: Sūtrakṛtāṅga) is the second of the twelve Aṅgas of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. Composed in Ardhamāgadhī Prakrit, it comprises two books: the first in metrical verse and the second primarily in prose. It is historically significant for its doxographical refutations of rival religious and philosophical schools (including early Buddhist doctrines, materialists, and fatalist Niyativādins) and its detailed instructions on Jaina ascetic discipline, non-violence (ahiṃsā), and liberation from karma.

The Nandīsūtra is one of the two Cūlikāsūtras ('appendices' or introductory compendia) of the Śvetāmbara Jaina canon. Composed in Jaina Māhārāṣṭrī Prakrit, it opens with an important sthavirāvalī (lineage of Jain teachers) and proceeds to an epistemological discussion of the five varieties of knowledge (jñāna), focusing especially on scriptural cognition (śrutajñāna). It is an essential historical source for the taxonomy, classification, and transmission of the Jaina canonical corpus.

It describes how the five Tathāgatas (Vairocana, Akṣobhya, Ratnasambhava, Amitābha, Amoghasiddhi) arise from the Buddha at the great dissolution. The Sumukhadhāraṇī ('Dhāraṇī of the Auspicious Entrance', Toh 614/915) is a Buddhist protective text in which the Buddha and Vajrapāṇi, followed by protective rākṣasīs, devīs, and bodhisattvas, pronounce dhāraṇī-formulas to safeguard practitioners. Once widely studied across Central Asia and East Asia, it survives in Sanskrit manuscript fragments from Central Asia as well as Tibetan, Chinese, and Khotanese translations. This e-text provides a standardized composite transcription of five published Sanskrit fragments.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T01_Vasudhārā_Buddhastotra`

**Author:** Vasudhārā

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished manuscript transcription, based on Cambridge University Library MS Or.143.

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- Header line 2: 'Source: Cambridge University Library Or.143'
- Header line 3: 'Tibetan: 1114'
- Notes describe scribal context filling horror vacui in a later hand in CUL MS Or.143.

**Translations:**
- Degé Tengyur, bsTod tshogs, Toh 1114: Sangs rgyas kyi bstod pa (attributed to slob dpon ma nor rgyun ma). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Preserves approximately two and a half stanzas of an eight-stanza praise of the Buddha.

**Also known as:** Sangs rgyas kyi bstod pa

**Attribution:** Identified with Toh 1114 (Sangs rgyas kyi bstod pa), where the author is given as Nor rgyun ma (*Vasudhārā). Sanskrit title reconstructed.

A Sanskrit fragment preserving approximately two and a half stanzas of an eight-verse hymn in praise of the Buddha (*Buddhastotra), matching Toh 1114 in the Tibetan Tengyur where it is attributed to the female author Vasudhārā (Nor rgyun ma). The stanzas praise the Buddha's bodily self-sacrifice (duṣkarakārin) and mastery over passions and Māra.

# Saptajinastava

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T01_anon_Saptajinastava`

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Alexander von Staël-Holstein, K'ien-ch'ui-fan-tsan (Gaṇḍīstotragāthā) sokhranivshijsia v kitajskoj transkriptsii sanskritskij gimn Açvaghoshi; Ts'i-fuh-tsan-pai-k'ie-t'o (Saptajinastava) i Fuh-shwoh-wan-shu-shi-li-yih-poh-pah-ming-fan-tsan (Āryamañjuśrīnāmāṣṭaka), izdal i pri pomoshchi tibetskago perevoda ob"jasnil. Bibliotheca Buddhica 15. St. Petersburg: Imprimerie de l'Académie Impériale des Sciences, 1913, pp. 82–84.

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- Explicitly stated in e-text header line 2: 'Source: Staël-Holstein 1913, pp. 82–84 (reconstructed from a Chinese transcription)'.

**Other editions:**
- Alexander von Staël-Holstein, 'On a Peking, a St. Petersburg, and a Kyoto Reconstruction of a Sanskrit Stanza (Saptajinastava) Transcribed with Chinese Characters under the Northern Sung Dynasty', in: Studies Presented to Ts'ai Yüan-p'ei on His Sixty-Fifth Birthday, Part 1, Peiping: Academia Sinica, 1933, pp. 419–424. — Discussion and re-examination of stanza reconstructions.
- Leo Both, Das Saptabuddhastotra: ein Lehrgedicht des Mahāyāna-Buddhismus. Indica et Tibetica 26. Marburg: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 1995. — Critical edition and analysis of the closely related Saptabuddhastotra textual tradition.

**Translations:**
- Alexander von Staël-Holstein, Bibliotheca Buddhica 15, St. Petersburg, 1913, pp. 82–84. (Russian)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of 9 verses praising the Seven Buddhas of the past and Maitreya, ending with 'saptajinastavaḥ samāptaḥ'.

**Also known as:** Saptabuddhastotra, Saptajinastotra, Qifo zanbei jiatuo (七佛讚唄伽陀), Sangs rgyas rabs bdun gyi bstod pa

**Attribution:** Anonymous Buddhist hymn; preserved in Tibetan translation in the Tanjur (Toh 1165, D 1170) and transcribed phonetically into Chinese characters during the Northern Song dynasty (Taishō 1682).

The Saptajinastava is a concise Buddhist devotional hymn consisting of nine verses extolling the Seven Buddhas of antiquity (Vipaśyin, Śikhin, Viśvabhuj, Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, Kāśyapa, and Śākyamuni) and the future Buddha Maitreya, followed by a merit dedication verse. The Sanskrit original was restored by Alexander von Staël-Holstein from the Chinese phonetic transcription dating to the Northern Song (Taishō 1682) alongside the Tibetan translation preserved in the Tanjur (Toh 1165).

The Vanaratnastotra (also known as the Vanaratnastotrasaptaka) is a seven-verse hymn composed in praise of the tantric master Vanaratna (1384–1468), traditionally regarded as the last great Indian Buddhist paṇḍita to visit Tibet. Composed during Vanaratna's lifetime by his Magadhan lay disciple Āditya, it was translated into Tibetan by 'Gos Lo tsā ba Gzhon nu dpal (Tōh. 1177 / D 1177). The e-text contains the complete edited Sanskrit text alternating with the canonical Tibetan translation.

Tschannerl (eds.), Vividharatnakaraṇḍaka: Festgabe für Adelheid Mette, Swisttal-Odendorf: Indica et Tibetica Verlag, 2000, pp. 313–326. — Editio princeps of the Sanskrit text based on a Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the stotra in 21 verses with concluding colophon.

**Also known as:** Devatāvimarśastuti

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarasvāmin (reputed to be the brother of Udbhaṭasiddhasvāmin, author of the companion Viśeṣastava). The manuscript preserved in Tibet collated by Liu & Schneider (2023) records the variant author name Varāhasvāmin.

The Devātiśayastotra (also titled Devatāvimarśastuti in Sanskrit manuscripts) is a 21-verse Buddhist apologetic hymn attributed to Śaṅkarasvāmin. It contrasts the supreme peacefulness, freedom from passion, and universal benevolence of the Buddha with the warlike, passionate, and wrathful character of Brahmanical deities such as Viṣṇu, Śiva, Brahmā, Skanda, and Umā. Prajñāvarman's commentary (ca. 800 CE) made the hymn famous in Tibet, where it served as a foundational source for knowledge of Indian mythology and legendary history.

**Attribution:** Aparārka (Aparāditya I) was a Śilāhāra monarch of Northern Konkan (fl. c. 1115–1140 CE). His work is formally titled Yājñavalkīyadharmaśāstranibandha or Aparārka.

The Ācārādhyāya (first book) of the Yājñavalkyasmṛti together with the extensive commentary and digest (nibandha) Aparārka by the Śilāhāra ruler Aparāditya I (12th century). This section treats religious conduct and personal status (ācāra), encompassing sacraments (saṃskāra), studenthood, marriage, food regulations, śrāddha ceremonies, worship of Vināyaka and the planets (grahaśānti), and statecraft (rājadharma). Aparārka's work is renowned in Dharmaśāstra literature as an encyclopedic nibandha that preserves numerous quotations from lost smṛti texts and Purāṇas.

Devaṇabhaṭṭa synthesizes numerous smṛti and purāṇic citations using Mīmāṃsā principles of legal hermeneutics.

**Also known as:** Smṛticandrikāyāṃ Śrāddhakāṇḍaḥ, Devaṇṇabhaṭṭa's Smṛticandrikā: Śrāddhakāṇḍa

**Attribution:** Colophon explicitly attributes authorship to Yājñika Devaṇabhaṭṭopādhyāya Somayājin, son of Keśavādityabhaṭṭopādhyāya (line 4853).

The Śrāddhakāṇḍa forms the fourth section of the Smṛticandrikā, a major late 12th- or early 13th-century nibandha composed by Devaṇabhaṭṭa in southern India. It constitutes an exhaustive digest on ancestral offerings (śrāddha), assembling and analyzing authoritative Vedic, smṛti, and purāṇic testimonia on ritual classifications (such as nitya, naimittika, kāmya, and sapiṇḍīkaraṇa), qualifications of performers and guests, lunar and seasonal timings, and rites performed at sacred pilgrimage places (tīrthaśrāddha).

Its Vyavahārakāṇḍa treats civil and criminal jurisprudence in two parts: judicial court organization, plaint, reply, and proof (vyavahāramātṛkā, including documents, witnesses, and divine ordeals); and substantive adjudication over the eighteen classical titles of dispute (vyavahārapada, such as non-payment of debt, partition/inheritance, boundary disputes, and assault). Haradatta's Ujjvalā is the classical commentary, elucidating grammatical points, resolving interpretive ambiguities, and citing Vedic and smṛti parallels.

- Opening verses mentioning King Mahādeva and Hemādri, and concluding colophon (iti śrīmadrājādhirājaśrīmahādevīyasamastakaraṇādhīśvara-sakalavidyāviśāradaśrīhemādriviracite caturvargacitāmaṇau pariśeṣakhaṇḍe kālanirṇayaḥ samāptaḥ) correspond precisely to this BI volume.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Kālanirṇaya subdivision of the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa, covering pp. 1–925 of the Bibliotheca Indica edition.

**Also known as:** Kālanirṇaya, Kālanirṇayaprakaraṇa

**Attribution:** Composed by Hemādri (fl. late 13th century), chief minister (karaṇādhipa / sarvaśrīkaraṇaprabhu) under the Seuna/Yādava monarchs Mahādeva and Rāmacandra of Devagiri.

The Kālanirṇaya constitutes the second part of the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa (the supplementary section) of Hemādri's 13th-century encyclopedic Dharmaśāstra digest, the Caturvargacintāmaṇi. It details the auspicious and inauspicious astronomical timings (tithi, vāra, nakṣatra, saṅkrānti, malamāsa, and ṛtu) for performing religious duties, vows, and ancestral rites (śrāddha), reconciling conflicting Smṛti passages using Mīmāṃsā hermeneutics.

The Caturvargacintāmaṇi is an encyclopaedic 13th-century Dharmaśāstra digest composed by Hemādri, minister of the Seuna (Yādava) kingdom. The Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa ('supplementary section') contains extensive treatises on ancestral rites (Śrāddhakalpa), expiation (Prāyaścittakhaṇḍa), and auspicious time reckoning (Kālanirṇaya). This first volume of the Śrāddhakalpa systematically details the scriptural eulogy of śrāddha, ritual eligibility, appropriate temporal intervals and lunar days, suitable sacred localities, and the qualifications and disqualifications of Brāhmaṇas invited to the ancestor feast.

The Śrāddhakalpa of the Pariśeṣakhaṇḍa is the encyclopaedic section on ancestral offerings in Hemādri's 13th-century ritual digest, the Caturvargacintāmaṇi. This second half focuses on the practical performance of the śrāddha ritual, detailing purificatory baths (snāna), libations (tarpaṇa), brāhmaṇa invitations, preliminary preparations, homa offerings into the sacred fire, the presentation of funeral cakes (piṇḍadāna), and conclusion of the rites. Hemādri collates extensive textual authorities from the Vedas, Gṛhyasūtras, Smṛtis, and Purāṇas with exhaustive analytical commentary.

It constitutes an encyclopaedic compendium of religious observances, vows, and fasts (vratas), collecting thousands of prescriptive citations from Purāṇic and Smṛti literature systematically classified by calendar day (tithi), planetary weekday (vāra), asterism (nakṣatra), and season. This first part opens with a detailed concordance of Purāṇic citations and covers general vrata principles along with tithi-based observances up to the dvādaśī-vratas.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Ludo Rocher (ed. and trans.), Jīmūtavāhana's Dāyabhāga: The Hindu Law of Inheritance in Bengal. New York: Oxford University Press, 2002. The Sanskrit text is transcribed with Rocher's chapter/paragraph numbering and source identifications.

**E-text:** Roman transcription by the Resource Library for Dharmaśāstra Studies, South Asia Institute, University of Texas at Austin (Sanskrit OER; Olivelle, Davis, Lubin): https://sites.utexas.edu/sanskrit/resources/dharmasastra/dayabhaga/. The transcription is unproofread.

- The e-text has the structure of Rocher's edition: 15 chapters ('CHAPTER 1' ... 'CHAPTER FIFTEEN'), paragraph numbers in angle brackets on the Colebrooke model (<1.1>, <4.2.17>, <11.1.25>), source identifications in square brackets with abbreviations of smṛti authors ([N 13.1], [M 9.103], [B 26.2ab], [Y 2.126], [Va 17.71], [H 4.10]), and an editorial footnote ('[1] Not found in the edition of Viśvarūpa').

**Other editions:**
- Dāyabhāga of Jīmūtavāhana with the commentaries of Śrīkṛṣṇa Tarkālaṅkāra, Śrīnātha Ācāryacūḍāmaṇi, Acyuta Cakravartin, Maheśvara, Raghunandana and others, Calcutta, 1863–66 (Bharatchandra Śiromaṇi). — The standard Calcutta edition with several commentaries. The exact imprint was not verified here.
- Dāyabhāga, ed. Jīvānanda Vidyāsāgara, Calcutta, 1893. — A later Calcutta edition. The imprint was not verified here.

**Translations:**
- Colebrooke, H. T., Two Treatises on the Hindu Law of Inheritance: Dāyabhāga and Mitākṣarā, Calcutta: Hindoostanee Press, 1810. (English)
- Rocher, Ludo, Jīmūtavāhana's Dāyabhāga: The Hindu Law of Inheritance in Bengal, Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2002. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 15 chapters, concluding with verses 15.1–15.2 and the final colophon.

**Also known as:** Dharmaratna (section 3: Dāyabhāga)

**Attribution:** Attributed in the concluding colophon to Pāribhadrīya Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrī Jīmūtavāhana as part of his Dharmaratna.

The Dāyabhāga ('Partition of Heritage') of Jīmūtavāhana (ca. 11th–12th century CE) is the foundational digest of the Bengal (Gauḍīya) school of traditional Hindu law, forming the third treatise of his larger compendium Dharmaratna (alongside Kālaviveka and Vyavahāramātṛkā). In direct contrast to the Mitākṣarā of Vijñāneśvara, it formulates the doctrine that sons acquire rights in ancestral property not by birth but upon the death of the father (or other prior owner), and develops distinctive rules regarding widows' rights and strīdhana. Recognized as the preeminent legal authority for Bengal and Assam in Anglo-Hindu law, it is one of the most celebrated treatises on inheritance in Sanskrit jurisprudence.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Śūdradharmatattvaprakāśa alias Śūdrakamalākara by Kamalākaraśarman, edited with Marathi translation, Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgara Press, 1895 (reprints 1910, 1928), collated with an undated pothi-form print (siglum 'P').

**E-text:** Roman transcription by the Resource Library for Dharmaśāstra Studies, South Asia Institute, University of Texas at Austin (Sanskrit OER; Olivelle, Davis, Lubin): https://sites.utexas.edu/sanskrit/resources/dharmasastra/sudradharmatattvaprakasa/. The transcription is unproofread.

**Evidence:**
- The UT Austin page lists as edition 'Śūdradharmatattvaprakāśa alias Śūdrakamalākara by Kamalākaraśarman. Edited with Marathi translation. Nirnaya Sagar Press, Bombay, 1895; reprint 1910, 1928'. Its 'Scanned Original' is a different print: 'Edited in Pothi form. No date or place of publication' (Google Books).
- The e-text's apparatus records 97 variants from a witness 'P' (most likely the pothi-form print) and one note citing 'Nirnaya' ([4237] 'Nirnaya: -pratāpa'). The base text is therefore one of these two prints, collated against the other. Most likely the base is the Nirṇaya Sāgara edition, with 'P' marking pothi variants, but the single 'Nirnaya' note leaves this uncertain.
- Printed page numbers survive in the e-text ([1] ... [291], e.g. '[3] mukhabāhūrupajjātās ...'), but which print they belong to has not been checked.

**Translations:**
- Marathi translation printed with the Nirṇaya Sāgara edition, Bombay 1895 (reprints 1910, 1928). (Marathi)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete. The text runs from the Adhikārasiddhiprakaraṇa through saṃskāras, daily rites, śrāddha, āśauca, women and mixed castes to the final section on śūdra-like mixed castes and their occupations. It ends with the author's verse and the colophon 'samāptaś cāyaṃ nibandhaḥ' ([4149]). This is followed by 98 transcriber's variant notes ([4150]–[4247]), keyed to footnote numbers in the text.

**Also known as:** Śūdradharmatattvaprakāśa, Śūdrakamalākara

**Attribution:** Kamalākarabhaṭṭa was a Mīmāṃsaka and Dharmaśāstra author of the Bhaṭṭa family of Benares, active in the early 17th century (his Nirṇayasindhu is dated 1612). The opening verse names his father Rāmakṛṣṇa ('kamalākaraśarmaṇā rāmakṛṣṇatanūjena śūdradharmo nirūpyate'), and the closing verse and colophon give his full lineage.

The Śūdradharmatattva (Śūdrakamalākara) is an early-17th-century Dharmaśāstra digest by Kamalākarabhaṭṭa of Benares on the religious duties and entitlements of śūdras. It begins with a Mīmāṃsā discussion of the śūdra's eligibility (adhikāra) for Vedic and smārta rites. It then treats the saṃskāras, mantradīkṣā and worship, daily rites, śrāddha and āśauca. It ends with long sections on mixed castes (saṃkarajāti) and their occupations. It became one of the most cited authorities on śūdra status in early modern western India.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: 20 sargas (prathamaḥ ... viṃśaḥ sargaḥ), from 1.1 'yasya prabhāvād bhuvanaṃ ...' to 20.64 'tasmād gajādhikabalo nṛpatiḥ sadā syāt'. Each sarga has a prakaraṇa heading (e.g. 'indriyajayaprakaraṇam'), and there are no colophons. One text-critical footnote is included ([1] at 14.50, 'Editions read: khanidvīpavanādīnāṃ').

**Also known as:** Kāmandakīyanītisāra, Kāmandakīya

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Kāmandaki (or Kāmandaka), follower of Viṣṇugupta Kauṭilya, whom he praises in verses 1.4–6.

The Nītisāra of Kāmandaki is a verse digest of political science in 20 sargas. It opens by praising Viṣṇugupta (Kauṭilya) and restates the teaching of the Arthaśāstra in verse. Topics include the king's self-control (indriyajaya), the seven constituents of the state (saptāṅga), ministers and counsel, the maṇḍala of states and the six measures of foreign policy, espionage, and military marches, formations and warfare, ending with the value of elephants. It is usually dated to the second half of the first millennium CE.

The Mānavadharmaśāstra (Manusmṛti) is the most influential Sanskrit treatise on dharma, covering creation, the sources of dharma, life-cycle rites, the duties of the student and householder, food and impurity, the duties of women, kingship and judicial procedure, inheritance, mixed classes, penances and karma and liberation. Kullūka Bhaṭṭa's Manvarthamuktāvalī is a concise commentary drawing on the earlier commentators Medhātithi and Govindarāja, and became the most widely used commentary in the printed tradition and in early colonial translations.

It gathers, organizes, and explains canonical Vedic, smṛti, and purāṇic texts concerning the student āśrama. Topics covered include the sacraments (saṃskāras) from conception to Vedic initiation (upanayana), student disciplines and study, and the concluding formal bath (snāna/samāvartana).

The Nāradasmṛti (c. 4th–5th century CE) is a seminal classical Sanskrit legal treatise that marks an important stage in the evolution of Indian jurisprudence. Unlike earlier smṛtis such as the Manusmṛti and Yājñavalkyasmṛti, it focuses almost exclusively on procedural and substantive civil and criminal law (vyavahāra), omitting ritual duties (ācāra) and expiation (prāyaścitta). The treatise opens with an extensive treatment of judicial court procedure and evidence (mātṛkā) before examining the eighteen traditional titles of law (vyavahārapada) and trial by ordeal (divya).

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to King Madanasiṃhadeva (son of Śaktisiṃha, fl. c. 1425–1450 CE), though composed by the pandits of his court.

The Vyavahāravivekoddyota (or Vyavahāroddyota) is the substantive law and judicial procedure section of the Madanaratnapradīpa, a large Dharmaśāstra digest compiled under King Madanasiṃhadeva in the 15th century. It covers court procedure (vyavahāramātṛkā), forms of evidence (witnesses, documents, possession, and ordeals), and the traditional eighteen titles of law (vyavahārapada). The work is especially prized by historians of Hindu law for its extensive citations of otherwise lost passages from classical smṛti jurists like Bṛhaspati and Kātyāyana.

The Vyavahārakāṇḍa of the Parāśaramādhavīya constitutes Mādhava's influential 14th-century CE treatise on substantive Hindu law and jurisprudence, written in the Vijayanagara Empire. Because the root Parāśarasmṛti omits litigation, Mādhava constructed an independent, exhaustive digest citing authorities such as Manu, Yājñavalkya, Nārada, Bṛhaspati, and Kātyāyana. This volume covers the substantive titles of dispute (vyavahārapada) beginning with deposits (nikṣepa) through partnership, sale without ownership, non-delivery of gifts, breach of contract of service, boundary disputes, abuse, assault, theft, violence, adultery, inheritance and partition (dāyabhāga), and miscellaneous matters.

Maskarin's commentary (Maskaribhāṣya), composed by Maskarin son of Vāmana, is a comprehensive exposition providing detailed exegesis of the sūtras, integrating Vedic citations, Mīmāṃsā hermeneutics, and smṛti parallels on the duties of the four varṇas, life stages (āśramas), domestic rituals, legal proceedings, and penances.
