The Āpastambadharmasūtra is one of the earliest preserved normative treatises on Dharma, traditionally forming Praśnas 28 and 29 of the Āpastamba Kalpasūtra of the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda (dated approximately to the 4th–3rd century BCE). Arranged in two books (praśnas), it addresses social duty according to class (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama), Vedic initiation (upanayana), student discipline (brahmacarya), household obligations, dietary rules, penances (prāyaścitta), civil and criminal law, and royal duties. It is notably distinguished by the Adhyātmapaṭala (1.8.22–23), an early Vedāntic philosophical disquisition on the universal self and liberation.

The Baudhāyanadharmasūtra is an ancient prose legal manual (dharmasūtra) belonging to the Baudhāyana carana of the Taittirīya recension of the Black Yajurveda. Arranged in four books (praśnas), it outlines sources of dharma, regional customs, student life, marriage, inheritance, penances (prāyaścitta), dietary rules, and ascetic codes. Modern scholarship dates the foundational core (praśnas 1–2) to roughly the 3rd–2nd century BCE, with praśnas 3–4 reflecting later accretions.

**Also known as:** Vasiṣṭhadharmasūtra, Vāsiṣṭhadharmaśāstra, Vāsiṣṭha Smṛti

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the Vedic ṛṣi Vasiṣṭha and historically associated with the Ṛgvedic tradition, though composed as an ancient aphoristic legal treatise.

The Vāsiṣṭhadharmasūtra is one of the four surviving major prose-verse Dharmasūtras of ancient India, traditionally associated with the Ṛgveda. Across thirty adhyāyas, it treats the foundational topics of dharmaśāstra: the geographic boundaries of Āryāvarta, the valid sources of dharma, duties of the four varṇas and āśramas, marriage forms, adoption and inheritance, rules of purity and diet, the duties of the king, legal procedure, and extensive penances (prāyaścittas). It is generally dated to the late Vedic or post-Vedic period (c. 3rd–1st century BCE).

The Yājñavalkyadharmaśāstra (commonly known as the Yājñavalkyasmṛti) is one of the foundational metrical treatises of classical Hindu jurisprudence, composed around the 4th to 5th centuries CE. Systematically structured into three divisions—Ācāra (proper conduct and sacraments), Vyavahāra (legal procedure, civil and criminal law, and property rights), and Prāyaścitta (expiatory penance and ritual purification)—it presents a more concise and procedurally sophisticated framework than the Mānava Dharmaśāstra. Its vyavahāra section served as the basis for Vijñāneśvara's 11th-century Mitākṣarā, which became the primary legal authority on succession and coparcenary throughout most of pre-colonial and British India.

The work critically evaluates earlier commentators, particularly Vijñāneśvara and Mādhavācārya.

It primarily outlines the daily duties (āhnika) and codes of conduct for the four life stages (āśrama), placing special emphasis on the virtues and responsibilities of the householder (gṛhastha). The Vyavahāracintāmaṇi is a seminal late 15th-century Dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) on judicial procedure (vyavahāra) composed by the Maithila scholar Vācaspati Miśra under King Harinārāyaṇa of Mithilā. Organizing judicial proceedings according to the classical fourfold division of litigation (catuṣpāt: complaint, plea/answer, evidentiary proof including witnesses, documents, and ordeals, and judgment), it offers an authoritative synthesis of smṛti jurisprudence specifically intended for court practice.

**Attribution:** A primary Vedic prose Upaniṣad belonging to the Śukla Yajurveda tradition (forming the concluding section of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa; this text presents the Kāṇva recension).

The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad is commonly considered the oldest and longest of the classical Upaniṣads (c. 8th–7th century BCE), forming the final portion of the Śukla Yajurveda's Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa. Organized into six chapters across three traditional sections (Madhukāṇḍa, Yājñavalkyakāṇḍa or Munikāṇḍa, and Khilakāṇḍa), it centres on the philosophical debates and dialogues of the sage Yājñavalkya at the court of King Janaka of Videha, along with his exchanges with his wife Maitreyī and the interlocutor Gārgī Vācaknavī. It provides foundational expositions of the non-dual reality of ātman and brahman, the apophatic formulation neti neti, the earliest clear articulations of karma and rebirth, and famous dicta such as 'ahaṃ brahmāsmi'.

The Taittirīya Upaniṣad is one of the earliest and most influential mukhya (principal) Upaniṣads, forming chapters 7, 8, and 9 of the Taittirīya Āraṇyaka of the Black Yajurveda. The rubric calls it a ḍima-type nṛtyanāṭaka in which vīra, raudra, bhayānaka and karuṇa predominate, written to be staged at the great gate of the Nālandā University ruins.

Nālandādahana ('The Burning of Nālandā') is a modern Sanskrit dance-drama of the ḍima type by V. Subramaniam. It is composed as Carnatic-style songs (pallavi, anupallavi, caraṇam) in various rāgas, mostly in ādi tāla. Students sing the praise of Nālandā, the abbot and senior monks discuss how to resist the coming Turkish army, and the destruction of the monastery follows. It ends with the librarian nun proclaiming that the fame and the truths of the Buddha's teaching taught at Nālandā cannot be destroyed.

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Nānāsiddhopadeśaḥ, edition published in 1994 (cited thus, 'Siddhas', Brill's Encyclopedia of Buddhism, vol. 2). It was presumably issued by the Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit, CIHTS Sarnath, in Dhīḥ; the volume (probably 17 or 18) was not verified. It is based on the manuscript Kathmandu, National Archives, tṛtīya 366-3, fols. 9b3–11a6.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West), 2008, DSBC book 79 (category sahajayāna); retrieved via the ilx_skt TEI corpus (dsbc/nānāsiddhopadeśa_book_79.xml).

**Evidence:**
- Szántó ('Siddhas', Brill's Encyclopedia of Buddhism): 'A similar, but much shorter, compilation has been published as the Nānāsiddhopadeśaḥ (1994). Here we count 14 siddhas'. The DSBC title Nānāsiddhopadeśaḥ and the 14 siddhas of the e-text match.
- Davidson, Indian Esoteric Buddhism (2002), ch. 7 n. 24, locates the text in NAK tṛtīya 366-3, fols. 9b3–11a6, and mentions a modern copy in the Asiatic Society.
- The e-text has editorial brackets typical of a printed edition: corrections in round brackets '(rṇo)', '(ko'pi)', '(pa)'; supplements in square brackets '[prajñā]'; '(?)'.
- The DSBC page (book 79) leaves editor, publisher and year blank. Because the venue and volume of the 1994 publication could not be confirmed (the web-search budget was exhausted; no INBUDS hit), the status remains 'probable'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete short text: the 14 siddhas' instructions, the uddeśasamuccaya, and the closing 'iti nānāsiddhopadeśaḥ'. In the source manuscript it is a section of a multi-text codex (Davidson: NAK tṛtīya 366-3, the so-called Yogāvatārādisaṃgraha, fols. 9b3–11a6).

**Attribution:** An anonymous compilation of short instructions ascribed to 14 siddhas: Padmāṅkura, Prajñārakṣita, Nelīpāda, Ravigupta, Kṛṣṇācārya, Sarahapāda, Mahīdhara, Bhūripāda, Vīṇāpāda, Virūpācārya, Nāgabuddhi, Diṅnāga, Mātali and Matsyendra. Davidson counts 13. It closes with an explanatory 'uddeśasamuccaya' (spelled 'uddeśamamuccayaḥ' in the e-text). There is no Tibetan translation.

A short anonymous Sanskrit anthology of yogic instructions (upadeśa) ascribed to fourteen siddhas, among them Saraha, Kṛṣṇācārya, Virūpa, Vīṇāpāda, Diṅnāga and Matsyendra. The instructions deal with caṇḍālī, the 'swing' (dolā) of the breath, the drop (bindu) and seed-syllables in the cakras, and the kākatuṇḍī breathing technique, and are followed by an explanatory summary (uddeśasamuccaya). It is preserved only in a Nepalese manuscript and has no Tibetan translation.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** V. Subramaniam, Buddhism, Dance and Drama: Five 'Dima' Dance Dramas Stressing Vira, Raudra and Karuna = Ḍimapañcakam. New Delhi: Ashish Publishing House, 1985. 104 pp. (OCLC 14149467). Play no. 5: 'Nṛtyaprasutiḥ'.

**E-text:** Digital Sanskrit Buddhist Canon (DSBC), book 273 (content 1143), Nagarjuna Institute of Exact Methods / University of the West. Input personnel are not named.

**Evidence:**
- The UPenn catalogue record for Ḍimapañcakam (1985) lists the contents: Nalagiridamanam; Kuṇḍalakeśapribhātam; Nāladādahanam; Salāmāvināśam; Nṛtyaprasutiḥ.
- DSBC books 272 (Nālandādahana) and 273 (Nṛtyaprasūti) are adjacent in the DSBC nāṭaka section, and both are ascribed to Subrahmaṇya. The 1985 collection is described as containing three wholly Buddhist plays and two with only Buddhist prayers. This matches the Buddhist nāndī of this otherwise Śaiva play.
- The DSBC book page leaves all bibliographic fields empty. No page markers are in the e-text, so the dependence on the 1985 print is inferred and not proven.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Nāndī and two scenes (prathamaṃ dṛśyam, dvitīyaṃ dṛśyam), ending with the closing song to Śiva and Pārvatī. There is no final colophon, but the play's structure is complete.

**Attribution:** Modern Sanskrit dance-drama (nṛtyanāṭaka) of the ḍima type by V. (Venkateswarier) Subramaniam (b. 1920), a political scientist at Carleton University, Ottawa, and a composer of Sanskrit dance-dramas. The e-text's rubric gives the name as Śrīsubrahmaṇyadīkṣita (garbled 'śrīsuvrahmaṇyadīkṣivena'). The play is no. 5 in his Ḍimapañcakam (New Delhi 1985).

Nṛtyaprasūti ('The Birth of Dance') is a modern Sanskrit dance-drama of the ḍima type by V. Subramaniam, written as songs set to Carnatic rāgas (Gauḷa, Haṃsadhvani, Darbār, Nāṭakuriñji, Pantuvarāḷi, Nītimati, etc.) with pallavi/anupallavi/caraṇam divisions. The nāndī praises the Buddha as conqueror of Māra, tamer of the elephant and turner of the dharmacakra under the tree. The two scenes then show the gods oppressed by the Tripura demons and appealing to Śiva, the destruction of Tripura (narrated by Nārada at Pārvatī's request), and the gods celebrating Śiva's tāṇḍava and Pārvatī's lāsya at Kailāsa as the origin of dance.

Because the Sanskrit names no author, the author field is left empty. The three entries of this text should be handled consistently.

A short Sanskrit verse manual of oneiromancy, which presents itself as composed by Bṛhaspati and opens with 'namo buddhāya'. It states when a dream bears fruit according to the watch of the night in which it is seen. It then lists auspicious and inauspicious dream images, such as mounting elephants and palaces, eating human flesh, drinking blood, wine or milk, embracing women dressed in red or white, and things on fire. The only Sanskrit witness is a manuscript in the Tibet Autonomous Region, and the Tibetan translation is attributed to Vibhūticandra.

The Ḍākārṇava (Ḍākārṇavamahāyoginītantrarāja) is a late Cakrasaṃvara-cycle Yoginītantra in 51 chapters, partly written in Apabhraṃśa. This e-text gives only a Sanskrit rendering of its 28 Apabhraṃśa verse sections, which encode bīja-mantras by phonetic descriptions and sing of sahaja and mahāsukha. These verses were first published by Haraprasad Shastri (1916) and studied by N. N. Chaudhuri (1935).

The Paramārthasāra ('Essence of Ultimate Truth'), traditionally attributed to Ādiśeṣa, is a concise philosophical poem of 85 āryā stanzas setting forth an early form of non-dualist Vedānta with strong Vaiṣṇava and Sāṅkhya-Yoga affinities. Identifying the ultimate reality (Brahman) with Viṣṇu, it elucidates the relationship between prakṛti and puruṣa, the nature of cosmic illusion (māyā/avidyā), and final release through knowledge. **Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Āpastambaśulbasūtra along with all three running commentaries, concluding at line 6183: 'iti sundararājīyaṃ saṃpūrṇaṃ samāptaḥ savyākhya āpastambīyaśulbapraśnaḥ'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Āpastambaśulbasūtra (Āpastamba, root text)
- Kapardibhāṣya (Kapardisvāmin, commentary)
- Karavindīyā (Karavinda, commentary)
- Śulbapradīpa (Sundararāja, commentary)

**Attribution:** The Āpastambaśulbasūtra is the 30th praśna of the Āpastamba Kalpasūtra (Taittirīya, Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda). Kapardin/Kapardisvāmin's commentary is the oldest (he is cited by Rāmānuja); Karavinda ('karavindādhipa', Karavindīyā) and Sundararāja (Śulbapradīpa) depend on it.

The Āpastambaśulbasūtra constitutes the 30th Praśna of the Āpastamba-Kalpasūtra within the Taittirīya tradition of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. It contains classical Vedic geometry and measurement techniques for the layout and construction of sacrificial altars (vedis and citis), including methods for squaring the circle, transformation of areas, and the geometric property of the diagonal. This digital edition includes the root sūtras along with three South Indian commentaries: Kapardisvāmin's Kapardibhāṣya, Karavinda's Karavindīyā, and Sundararāja's Śulbapradīpa.

The Bower Manuscript is a famous birch-bark codex discovered in 1890 near Kucha along the Silk Road, datable to ca. the 4th to 6th centuries CE. It contains seven distinct Sanskrit texts, notably the Navanītaka (a foundational early Ayurvedic compendium of medical recipes, decoctions, and rasāyanas), two dice divination treatises (Pāśakakevalī), and portions of the Buddhist dhāraṇī scripture Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī. It constitutes one of the earliest extant physical manuscripts from the Indian medical and Buddhist traditions.

It relates that when the moon deity is seized during an eclipse by the asura king Rāhu, the deity takes refuge in the Buddha. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in three parihāsas (parihāsas 1–3), concluding at verse 3.113 and the author's final signature colophon.

**Attribution:** Explicitly attributed to Kṣemendra under his well-known epithet Vyāsadāsa in the colophon (KNarm_3.113ff.: kṛtir vyāsadāsāparanāmnaḥ kṣemendrasyeti śivam).

The Narmamālā ('Garland of Mirth' or 'Garland of Satires') is a satirical poem in three chapters (parihāsas) composed in 11th-century Kashmir during the reign of King Ananta. It presents a caustic caricature and expose of corrupt scribe-officials (Kāyasthas and diviras), detailing their greed, oppression of the public, administrative malpractice, religious charlatanism, and domestic vices. Together with the Deśopadeśa, it is a key satirical source for socio-political life in medieval Kashmir.

The Sudhanakinnaryavadāna constitutes the 64th chapter (pallava) of Kṣemendra's 11th-century kāvya work, the Bodhisattvāvadānakalpalatā. The Advayasiddhi ('Attainment of Non-Duality') is a concise Tantric treatise in 36 verses attributed to the female mahāsiddhā Lakṣmīṅkarā. It represents an early Sahajayāna orientation, teaching that enlightenment is directly attainable within the innate body without external asceticism, rituals, or conventional caste distinctions, while emphasizing guru devotion and the omnipresence of Vajrasattva. The work is counted as one of the eight foundational Siddhi texts (Aṣṭasiddhi) of Indian Vajrayāna.

The Mahāmāyūrīvidyārājñī ('Great Peacock Queen of Spells') is one of the earliest and most celebrated Buddhist rakṣā (protective) and dhāraṇī scriptures, subsequently included as one of the Five Protective Deities (Pañcarakṣā). Framed around the story of the novice monk Svāti being bitten by a poisonous snake while gathering wood for the bathhouse, the Buddha imparts the Mahāmāyūrī spell to Ānanda for protection against snakebites, poisons, malevolent spirits, and disasters. The scripture is also renowned for preserving an extensive geographical list of local tutelary yakṣas across the Indian subcontinent and adjacent regions.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete across all five adhyāyas (ending with the closing Vedic Śatarudrīya/Īśāna formula at 5.47: śivaḥ). The e-text is an analytical version prepared by Reinhold Grünendahl, presenting each sūtra first in saṃhitāpāṭha form and then repeated in hyphenated padapāṭha analysis.

**Also known as:** Pāśupatasūtrāṇi, Pañcārthasūtra

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to Lakulīśa (Nakulīśa, c. 2nd century CE), regarded as an avatāra of Śiva and the systematizer/human founder of the Pāśupata movement.

The Pāśupatasūtra is the foundational textual authority of the Pāśupata order, the earliest attested sectarian Śaiva tradition. In five chapters, the work details the five primary ontological and practical principles (pañcārtha): cause (kāraṇa, Śiva/Paśupati), effect (kārya, the bound soul and created world), yoga (contemplative union with Rudra), vidhi (ascetic practices, including smearing ashes, ritual laughter and dance, simulated madness, and inducing public contempt), and duḥkhānta (the final cessation of suffering and attainment of divine powers/fellowship with Śiva).

The Rākṣasakāvya is a brief 20-verse poem in the vasantatilakā meter describing the arrival of the monsoon season. Notable for its dense wordplay, alliteration (yamaka), and obscure periphrastic expressions, the poem depicts a youthful traveler admiring rain clouds, peacocks, and flowering trees before returning home in a bullock cart with his wife. It is accompanied by the Sajjanānandadāyinī commentary, traditionally attributed to Ravideva and expanded by Kṛṣṇadhara Vyāḍi.

The Tattvasaṃgraha of Śāntarakṣita (8th century) is a verse compendium of c. 3,646 kārikās in 26 chapters that examines and refutes the doctrines of rival schools (Sāṅkhya, Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Mīmāṃsā, Jaina, Lokāyata and Buddhist Pudgalavāda, among others) on God, primordial matter, the self, universals, word and meaning, the means of knowledge, and the authority of the Veda, ending with a long defence of the Buddha's omniscience. This e-text is not the running verse text but a word-by-word grammatical analysis of every verse by Timothy C. Cahill and Elliot Stern, in which the words of each verse are listed with morphological tags.

The Vajrāvalī (or Vajrāvalīnāmamaṇḍalopāyikā) by Abhayākaragupta (fl. late 11th–early 12th century, Vikramaśīla) is a comprehensive ritual compendium of late Indian tantric Buddhism. Structured around approximately fifty sequential rites (vidhi), it details the selection and purification of the ritual ground, maṇḍala construction and coloration, installation and consecration of images and monastic dwellings (pratiṣṭhā), the full progression of tantric initiations (abhiṣeka), post-initiatory observances (vrata), fire rituals (homa), and maṇḍala dissolution. Providing the liturgical framework for the maṇḍalas described iconographically in Abhayākaragupta's Niṣpannayogāvalī, the work became a foundational ritual authority in Nepalese and Tibetan Buddhist traditions.

The Sārasvataprakriyā (or Sārasvatavyākaraṇa) by Anubhūtisvarūpācārya (c. 13th–14th century CE) is the standard introductory and procedural treatise of the non-Pāṇinian Sārasvata school of Sanskrit grammar. The Ācāryakriyāsamuccaya (commonly known as the Kriyāsamuccaya), composed by the late Indian tantric master Jagaddarpaṇa (Darpaṇācārya, c. 11th–12th century), is a comprehensive ritual manual synthesizing Vajrayāna liturgical practices across various tantric classes. This excerpt preserves the initiation section (abhiṣekapaṭala), treating essential preliminary purifications, the gurumaṇḍala rite, taking the vows (poṣadha), disciple admittance (śiṣyapraveśavidhi), and empowerment rites including the mālābhiṣeka. **E-text:** Input by Yiming Shen. Harunaga Isaacson supplied two pages that had been left untyped and made numerous corrections, including the edition's three pages of corrigenda. Distributed through the Hamburg Sanskrit Etext Repository and converted to TEI by the ERC Intellexus project (ilx_skt, corpus/hamburg/daṇḍin_avantisundarīkathā.xml).

- ilx_skt TEI legacy header: 'Avantisundarīkathā of Daṇḍin. Text after edition by Pillai, Trivandrum 1954, Trivandrum Sanskrit Series 172. The edition is based on one lacunose and corrupt MS. …'
- The sourceDesc says 'Based on edition: Pillai, Trivandrum. 1954. Trivandrum Sanskrit Series 172.'
- The draft also named K. Sāmbaśiva Śāstrī as editor. Nothing supports this: the TEI header and the bibliography (e.g. the Wikipedia Daṇḍin article) name only Suranad Kunjan Pillai.

**Other editions:**
- Avantisundarīkathā and Avantisundarīkathāsāra, Dakṣiṇabhāratī Series 3, Madras, 1924 (editor given as S. K. Rāmanātha Śāstrī; M. Ramakrishna Kavi is also credited with editing the prose fragment). — Editio princeps of the short first prose fragment (about 25 printed pages) and of the verse summary.
- Avantisundarīkathāsāra, ed. G. Harihara Sastri, Madras: Kuppuswami Sastri Research Institute, 1957. — An anonymous verse summary of the whole work, which helps reconstruct the lost portions. It is a separate work.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Covers everything the 1954 edition contains: the introductory verses 1–27 (with gaps), the autobiographical prose frame, and the main narrative about the families of Rājahaṃsa and Mānasāra. This corresponds roughly to the Pūrvapīṭhikā part of the Daśakumāracarita story. Lacunae, marked '......', are frequent throughout. The text breaks off in mid-sentence in an embedded episode involving Mahāśvetā and Kādambarī, before the scribal colophon. The later portion of the work is lost; its contents are partly known from the verse summary Avantisundarīkathāsāra.

**Also known as:** Avantisundarī

**Attribution:** The opening rubric ('ācāryadaṇḍiviracitā avantisundarī') and the final colophon ('ityācāryadaṇḍinā kṛtā avantisundarī samāptā') ascribe the work to Daṇḍin, the author of the Kāvyādarśa, who is usually placed around the late 7th / early 8th century at the Pallava court of Kāñcī. Most scholars accept this ascription. The verse introduction praises earlier poets and gives an autobiographical account of the author's ancestry (Bhāravi/Dāmodara).

The Avantisundarīkathā is a long ornate prose romance (kathā) ascribed to Daṇḍin. It opens with verses praising earlier poets (Vālmīki, Vyāsa, Subandhu, Śūdraka, Bhāsa, Sarvasena, Kālidāsa, Bāṇa, Mayūra and others), followed by an autobiographical account of the author's family and its connection with the Pallava court of Kāñcī. The main narrative tells, at much greater length, the story found in the Pūrvapīṭhikā of the Daśakumāracarita. The surviving text is lacunose and breaks off incomplete.

In 155 chapters, it narrates the cosmic deeds and avataras of Gaṇeśa across the four yugas: Mahotkaṭa in the Kṛtayuga, Mayūreśvara in the Tretāyuga, Gajānana in the Dvāparayuga, and Dhūmraketu in the Kaliyuga. The Prè Rup inscription (K. 806) is a Sanskrit mahākāvya-style praśasti of 298 stanzas engraved on a four-sided stele at the temple-mountain of Prè Rup in Angkor, Cambodia, dated Śaka 883 (961 CE). The Rājataraṅgiṇī ('River of Kings'), composed by the Kashmiri poet Kalhaṇa between 1148 and 1150 CE, is the foremost work of historical narrative (itihāsa) in classical Sanskrit literature. Structured in eight books ('waves', taraṅgas) encompassing nearly 8,000 ślokas, it chronicles the dynastic history of Kashmir from mythological beginnings to the reign of Kalhaṇa's contemporary monarch Jayasiṃha. Written in the style of mahākāvya, the work explicitly takes śāntarasa (the aesthetic sentiment of peace and detachment) as its predominant mood while demonstrating critical use of earlier regional chronicles, inscriptions, and coins.

The Meghadūta ('Cloud Messenger') is a celebrated Sanskrit lyric poem (khaṇḍakāvya / sandeśakāvya) in Mandākrāntā meter composed by Kālidāsa (c. 4th–5th century CE). It recounts the longing of an exiled Yakṣa who implores a passing monsoon cloud to carry a message of reassurance to his pining wife in the celestial city of Alakā. This digital edition presents the poem accompanied by four major Sanskrit commentaries: Vallabhadeva's Pañcikā, Dakṣiṇāvartanātha's Pradīpa, Mallinātha's Sañjīvinī, and Sumativijaya's Sugamānvayā Vṛtti (covering the Pūrvamegha).

**Coverage:** complete — Covers all ten tattvas announced in v. 2 (rakṣācakra, cakra, jāpa, two sekas [guhyābhiṣeka, prajñājñānābhiṣeka], haṭha, bali, two pratyaṅgirās [bhāvya, lekhya], puṭodghāta) up to the concluding verse and colophon, but with lacunae from the incomplete single manuscript: a folio is missing at the beginning of the rakṣācakra section (segment 11 'FOLIO MISSING') and another near the end of the puṭodghāta section (segment 621 '[folio missing]'). The ilx/Hamburg header marks the file as '(not final)'.

**Also known as:** The Compendium of the Ten Fundamentals

**Attribution:** Colophon: 'kṛtir iyaṃ daśatattvasaṃgrahaḥ paṇḍitakṣitiga⟨rbha⟩syeti' (supplement by the editor). Kṣitigarbha (paṇḍita) of the Jñānapāda school of Guhyasamāja exegesis; to be distinguished from other bearers of the name (e.g. the Tibetan-period ācārya Sa'i snying po). No Tibetan translation of this work is known (Hamburg project page).

The Daśatattvasaṃgraha is a manual of the Jñānapāda school of Guhyasamāja exegesis setting out ten ritual 'fundamentals' (tattva) of the tantric master: the protective circle, the maṇḍala visualisation centred on Vajrasattva/Samantabhadra, mantra recitation, the secret and wisdom-knowledge consecrations, forceful practice (haṭha), bali offerings, two kinds of counter-magic (pratyaṅgirā) and the 'opening of the casket' (puṭodghāta). It combines verse with prose explanation and quotes tantras and Jñānapāda works such as Dīpaṃkarabhadra's Guhyasamājamaṇḍalavidhi. It survives in a single incomplete manuscript.

The prose Sanskrit commentary (Vivaraṇa) is by Bandhuṣeṇa, as stated in the opening invocation ('padmāvatyā hi kalpapravaravivaraṇaṃ vakṣyate banduṣeṇaiḥ').

The Bhairavapadmāvatīkalpa is an influential 11th-century Digambara Jaina tantric manual dedicated to the goddess Padmāvatī, the yakṣiṇī and attendant deity (śāsanadevatā) of the 23rd Tīrthaṅkara Pārśvanātha. Composed across ten chapters (adhikāras), it expounds mantra lore, diagrammatic amulets (yantra), sakalīkaraṇa, nyāsa, the classical six esoteric magical operations (ṣaṭkarmāṇi, including stambhana, vaśīkaraṇa, and ākarṣaṇa), omenology (nimitta), and toxicology/anti-venom remedies (gāruḍatantra). The accompanying Sanskrit commentary (Vivaraṇa) by Bandhuṣeṇa provides word-by-word glosses and detailed ritual guidelines.

**Attribution:** A scriptural Pāñcarātra Āgama saṃhitā traditionally revealed by Bhagavān / Kapila to Padma and transmitted through Saṃvarta and Kaṇva; canonical and anonymous.

The Pādmasaṃhitā is one of the most influential Saṃhitās of the Pāñcarātra Vaiṣṇava tradition and one of the few that preserve the full four-part structure (catuṣpāda): Jñānapāda (cosmology and theology, framed as Kaṇva's report of Saṃvarta's teaching), Yogapāda, Kriyāpāda (temple building, iconography and installation), and Caryāpāda (daily and festival worship, mantroddhāra, expiations, domestic worship). It remains an authoritative ritual manual in South Indian Śrīvaiṣṇava temples. Its theology has been studied by S. Schwarz Linder (Vienna 2014).

A 15-canto Sanskrit mahākāvya composed in the 13th century CE by Someśvaradeva, court priest to the Caulukya/Vāghelā rulers of Gujarat. Elaborating on the foundational framing story of the Devīmāhātmya from the Mārkaṇḍeyapurāṇa, the epic narrates the life of King Suratha: his loss of sovereignty, forest retreat, devotion and rigorous penance to the Goddess, her destruction of the demon army, and Suratha's restoration to power. **Edition used (probable):** The Sūktimuktāvalī of Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa, ed. Embar Krishnamacharya, Gaekwad's Oriental Series 82, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1938.

**E-text:** Input by Harunaga Isaacson (Hamburg Sanskrit Etext Repository). Converted to basic TEI by the ERC Intellexus project (ilx_skt, corpus/hamburg/sūktimuktāvalī.xml).

**Evidence:**
- The TEI header names only the inputter (Harunaga Isaacson). Its <bibl> is empty and there is no legacy note on the source edition.
- GOS 82 (1938) is the only printed edition (the editio princeps, based on five manuscripts) recorded in library catalogues and on Wikipedia, and several scans exist on archive.org (e.g. in.ernet.dli.2015.283789). An e-text of the full anthology with numbered paddhatis is therefore almost certainly keyed from it.
- The paddhati numbers in the e-text ('(115)', '(116)') suggest a printed source with numbered sections. A direct check against the GOS scan failed because the archive.org downloads were unavailable from this environment, so the status stays 'probable'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** unclear — The e-text runs from the maṅgala and genealogical praśasti through the thematic paddhatis, with headings numbered up to 'dānapaddhatiḥ (116)', followed by the mitra, guṇa, kṣamā, dayā and vairāgya paddhatis. It ends inside an unnumbered section of Śiva-stuti verses (vv. 1–20, last attribution 'kayorapyetau'), with no section colophon and no closing matter. The edition is described as covering 133 topics, so the e-text may stop roughly ten sections short of the end. This could not be checked against the printed volume, so coverage is left as unclear (probably partial).

**Attribution:** The anthology was compiled in the name of Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa, elephant commander (ārohaka) and minister of the Yādava king Kṛṣṇa of Devagiri, in the mid-13th century (c. 1257/58). Krishnamacharya's introduction to the edition suggests that the scholar Bhānu did the actual compiling for his patron. The anthologised verses are by many poets, and the attributions follow each verse or group of verses (e.g. 'utpaladevasyaitau', 'kayorapyetau').

The Sūktimuktāvalī is a large thematically arranged subhāṣita anthology compiled in the mid-13th century under Bhagadatta Jalhaṇa, a minister and commander of the Yādava king Kṛṣṇa of Devagiri. After a genealogical praśasti of the compiler's family, it collects verses by many named poets in more than a hundred paddhatis. The topics range from poets and poetry, good and bad men and animals and nature, through love and the seasons, to fate, generosity, forbearance, renunciation and praise of Śiva. It is an important source for verses and poet attributions that are otherwise lost, including the series of verses on poets ascribed to Rājaśekhara.

The Sūktiratnakośa is a subhāṣita anthology of 659 verses compiled by Lakṣmaṇa Dīkṣita, whose family is described in the closing praśasti. It opens with verses in praise of the Jina (Ṛṣabha, Mahāvīra), Śiva and Viṣṇu, and on poets (Vālmīki, Kālidāsa). These are followed by thematic sections of gnomic, erotic and descriptive verses, many of which are also found in other anthologies and in poets such as Bhartṛhari. It survives in manuscripts from western Indian Jaina libraries.

Spanning 25 chapters, it systematically sets forth temple rituals, daily worship (nityapūjā), the fivefold division of time (pañcakāla), temple layout, iconography, image consecration (pratiṣṭhā), initiation (dīkṣā), and expiation (prāyaścitta). It is historically significant in the South Indian Śrīvaiṣṇava tradition, notably informing ritual practice at Melkote (Yadugiri).

The Kātantra (also known as Kalāpa or Kaumāra), attributed to Śarvavarman, is the foundational work of the earliest post-Pāṇinian Sanskrit grammatical school. Designed as an accessible alternative to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī without employing the complex Śivasūtra pratyāhāra apparatus, it systematically treats phonology and sandhi, nominal morphology and compounds, verbal conjugation, and primary derivatives across four books. Durgasiṃha's Kātantravṛtti is the canonical commentary elucidating the sūtras, which established the school's doctrinal authority and ensured its widespread transmission throughout Kashmir, eastern India, Central Asia, and Tibet.

It expounds preparatory purifications, generation of the deity and maṇḍala, internal cakras, mantra recitations, and bali offerings. Composed by the late Indian master Śākyarakṣita (ca. 11th–12th c.), it represents a major witness to the esoteric goddess practices of late Indian Vajrayāna.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Diplomatic transcription of a damaged multi-text bundle (IFP RE 30504, 133 images, 4–5 blank folios), with many lacunae marked (....). The Ātmārpaṇastava is complete (vv. 1–50). The Śivatattvaviveka breaks off before its last verses (c. vv. 58/59–60 missing). The Śivajñānabodhopanyāsa runs from sūtra 1 to its colophon. The Śrīcakranirmāṇavidhi ends with a colophon. A final unidentified prose fragment breaks off mid-sentence. ilx_skt metadata classifies the file as 'fragments' (4 texts in the same file).

**Works in this e-text:**

- Śikhariṇīmālā with Śivatattvaviveka (Appayya Dīkṣita, verses with autocommentary (segs. 208–2956). The introduction announces 60 verses ('padyaiḥ ṣaṣṭyā'), but the text breaks off after the commentary's introduction to verse 58/59, without colophon.)
- Śivajñānabodhopanyāsa (Nigamajñānadeśika, exposition of the twelve sūtras of the Śivajñānabodha (segs. 2957–3232, from '||prathamasūtram||' to the colophon 'iti bālabodhanāya saundaranāthaprītaye vyāghrapuravāsinā nigamajñānadeśikena viracitaśivajñānabodhopanyāsaḥ samāptaḥ'))
- Śrīcakranirmāṇavidhi (short anonymous text (segs. 3233–3265; the opening verses are badly garbled). Colophon '[evaṃ śrīcakranirmāṇavidhiḥ]')
- Unidentified prose fragment (segs. 3265–3298. Śaiva exegesis of 'hrīś ca te lakṣmīś ca patnyau' and of the kinds of mukti, in the style of the Śivatattvaviveka (possibly misplaced leaves of it). Breaks off.)

**Also known as:** Ātmārpaṇastuti / Unmattapañcāśat (= Ātmārpaṇastava), Śikhariṇīmālā with Śivatattvaviveka (= Śivatattvaviveka)

**Attribution:** Appayya Dīkṣita (16th c.) is the author of the Ātmārpaṇastuti and of the Śikhariṇīmālā with its autocommentary Śivatattvaviveka. Nigamajñānadeśika of Vyāghrapura is named in the colophon of the Śivajñānabodhopanyāsa. The Muktabodha metadata lists him as 'Nigamajñānadeśika (i.e. Nigamajñānadeva)'; which of the homonymous Nigamajñānas is meant was not determined. The Śrīcakranirmāṇavidhi and the final fragment are anonymous.

A transcription of a damaged South Indian palm-leaf bundle containing several Śaiva works. It opens with Appayya Dīkṣita's devotional hymn Ātmārpaṇastava (Ātmārpaṇastuti, 50 verses). Next comes his Śikhariṇīmālā with his own commentary Śivatattvaviveka, a polemical defence of Śiva's supremacy through Vedic, Purāṇic and Brahmasūtra exegesis, which breaks off near its end. Nigamajñānadeśika's Śivajñānabodhopanyāsa, an exposition of the twelve sūtras of the Śivajñānabodha, follows, and then a short Śrīcakranirmāṇavidhi and an unidentified prose fragment.

The Ṣaḍāmnāyapūjāvidhi is an anonymous Śākta ritual manual (paddhati) detailing daily worship rituals focused on Mahātripurasundarī structured by the six regional traditions (ṣaḍāmnāya) of Kaulism and Śrīvidyā. The Agastyasaṃhitā is a foundational Vaiṣṇava ritual handbook framed as a dialogue between the sage Agastya and his disciple Sutīkṣṇa, incorporating teachings revealed by Śiva to Pārvatī. Dating between the 10th and 12th centuries CE, it is among the earliest extant saṃhitās documenting the institutionalized sectarian worship of Rāma.

This text contains two major ritual sections from Aghoraśiva's 12th-century Śaivasiddhānta paddhati, the Kriyākramadyotikā: the Mahotsavavidhi and the Prāyaścittavidhi. **Attribution:** Root text by Trilocanaśivācārya (12th c., Tamil Nadu), who is named in the commentator's introduction as resident of the Āmardaka maṭha. Commentary by Anantaśambhu (Anantaśivācārya), probably 14th c. The manuscript also contains, on fols. 7b–9b, unrelated ritual extracts, including a Kṣauravidhi ascribed to Aghoraśivācārya.

The Siddhāntasārāvalī of Trilocanaśivācārya (12th c.) is a verse compendium of Śaiva Siddhānta doctrine and ritual, arranged in the four pādas: jñāna, kriyā, yoga and caryā. Anantaśambhu's commentary explains it with extensive quotations from the Siddhāntāgamas and ritual manuals. Its topics include the categories pati, paśu and pāśa, the tattvas, daily and occasional worship, initiation (dīkṣā), yoga, and festivals and pratiṣṭhā (installation). This e-text transcribes a single incomplete and partly disordered IFP palm-leaf manuscript.

This corresponds to the KKD rule 'ācāryasādhakaputrāṇām antyeṣṭir adhvaśuddhiyutā kartavyā, samayinas tadvarjitā', quoted in Nirmalamaṇi's Prabhā (Muktabodha M00126, p. 83). A South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta funerary manual for initiates, transcribed from a single palm-leaf bundle. Its main part is the funeral 'with purification of the paths' (adhvaśuddhiyutāntyeṣṭi) for ācāryas, sādhakas and putrakas. It includes the post-mortem initiation (mṛtakadīkṣā) with the purification of the four kalās and their tattvas, bhuvanas, varṇas, padas and mantras, followed by cremation, and its colophon assigns it to Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā. Further rites follow, each with its own colophon: Rudrabali, the setting up of the stone (pāṣāṇa), Sapiṇḍīkaraṇa, and a short rite for a samayin.

Excerpts from the temple-festival (mahotsava) portion of the Kriyākramadyotikā of Aghoraśiva (12th c.), the most authoritative South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta paddhati, transcribed from a palm-leaf bundle. The excerpts cover the bṛhattāla rite (with its drum rhythms and invocations of the guardians of the directions), the navasandhi, monthly, full-moon and asterism festivals, a pacificatory fire rite (śāntihoma) and a long section on expiation (prāyaścitta) for ritual faults and pollution. It ends with an incomplete instruction on the fivefold seat worship (pañcāsana) and Āgama citations on Śivarātri.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text begins mid-sentence ('yena saptavāramati dīptāstrābhimantritena …') inside the daily rite (nityakarman; Sūryapūjā colophon at seg. 173, nityakarmavidhi colophon at seg. 621–622), so the opening leaves are lost. It then contains, each with a colophon: mudrālakṣaṇa, prāyaścittavidhi, samayadīkṣāvidhi, (nirvāṇa)dīkṣāvidhi, sādhakābhiṣekavidhi, ācāryābhiṣekavidhi, ṣaḍvidhādhvanirṇaya, pavitrakavidhi, and the pratiṣṭhā section (pāda-, liṅga-, dvāra-, hṛt- and dhvajapratiṣṭhā) down to the jīrṇoddhāravidhi. That colophon (seg. 2454) is followed by a fragmentary scribal date ('samvat … jyeṣṭha kṛṣṇa'). Segments 2455–2492 hold further, badly damaged material (renovation rite, lists of kalās and kṣetrapālas) that breaks off. The ilx_skt metadata classifies the file as 'incomplete' with the work colophon 'in middle'.

**Also known as:** Siddhāntapaddhati (variant in colophons, segs. 1136, 1239)

**Attribution:** The section colophons ascribe the work to Mahārājādhirāja (Parameśvara) Bhojadeva, i.e. Bhoja of Dhārā (11th c.). Muktabodha records the author as 'bhojadeva ascribed to'. Sanderson (The Śaiva Age, 2009, main text near n. 39–40 and n. 611) cites the Siddhāntasārapaddhati of Mahārājādhirāja Bhojadeva of Dhārā (by folio of a manuscript, f. 41v) as the earliest source for the Sūryapūjā as a preliminary of Śiva worship and as a source used by the Somaśambhupaddhati.

An early Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual (paddhati) ascribed in its colophons to King Bhojadeva of Dhārā (11th c.). It is preserved here in an old Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript that has lost its opening leaves. It covers the daily rite (with the Sūrya worship that precedes Śiva worship), mudrās, expiation, the samaya- and nirvāṇa-initiations, the consecration of sādhaka and ācārya, the sixfold path (ṣaḍadhvan), the pavitraka festival, the installation of temple, liṅga, door, 'heart' and flagstaff, and the renovation of damaged images (jīrṇoddhāra). Sanderson has shown that the later Somaśambhupaddhati depends on it.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished diplomatic transcript of Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP) palm-leaf manuscript RE 30720.

**E-text:** Transcribed by Sambandhan Anandavardhana and Arul Nandi under the supervision of Dr. Deviprasad Mishra for the Muktabodha Indological Research Institute in collaboration with the IFP (Pondicherry, 2023), Muktabodha catalog no. I00017.

**Evidence:**
- Opening editorial note indicates manuscript shelfmark '(re-30720.p1)' and folio size '17x2 inches'.
- End of manuscript note states 'end of the manuscript re - 30720.' at line 2012.
- TEI header confirms transcription from IFP MS 30720 by IFP staff supervised by Dr. Deviprasad Mishra.

**Other editions:**
- Various Baudhāyana ritual manuals (such as Baudhāyanagṛhyaprayoga or Baudhāyanāparaprayoga) have been printed in South India (e.g., Mysore Government Oriental Library series; Vavilla Press, Madras), but Pañcākṣaranātha's Karmaprakāśikā is unpublished in print. — Unpublished manuscript text.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete transcription of palm-leaf manuscript IFP RE 30720 (folios 1a–88b). It comprises the Nityakarmapariccheda of the Karmaprakāśikā (fols. 1a–54b) followed by the Bodhāyanamantrapraśna in ten āśvāsas (fols. 55a–88b).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Karmaprakāśikā (Nityakarmapariccheda) (Pañcākṣaranātha, ritual manual)
- Bodhāyanamantrapraśna (mantra collection)

**Also known as:** Karmaprakāśikā, Bodhāyanāhnika, Pañcākṣaranāthaviracitanityakarmapariccheda, Bodhāyanamantrapraśna

**Attribution:** The first section (fols. 1a–54b) is composed by Pañcākṣaranātha (Pañcākṣaraguru), a Śaiva-Smārta teacher descending from Jñānaśivācārya (Kāśyapa gotra). The second section (fols. 55a–88b) is an anonymous liturgical compilation of Vedic mantras for Baudhāyana rituals.

A South Indian ritual manual (prayoga) following the Baudhāyana tradition of the Black Yajurveda (Kṛṣṇayajurveda), reflecting an integration of Smārta domestic rites and Śaiva ritual practices. The text consists of two major sections: the Karmaprakāśikā (Nityakarmapariccheda) by Pañcākṣaranātha, describing daily duties (āhnika, snāna, sandhyāvandana, mahānyāsa, Śiva-pūjā, bhojanavidhi, and gṛhasthadharma), and the Bodhāyanamantrapraśna, an arrangement of Vedic mantras divided into ten āśvāsas for domestic sacraments.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete short tract in approximately 42 verses ending with the colophon 'iti maheśvareṇaviracitaṃ candrāvalokanam sampūrṇaṃ'.

**Also known as:** Candrāvalokanam

**Attribution:** Cast as an esoteric dialogue between Maheśvara and Matsyendranātha; colophon attributes it to Maheśvara ('iti maheśvareṇaviracitaṃ candrāvalokanam').

The Candrāvalokana is a short Haṭhayogic tract framed as a dialogue between Maheśvara (Śiva) and Matsyendranātha. It is best known in yoga historiography as a key early source for the definition of śāmbhavīmudrā and the absorption (laya) of mind and breath, famously cited in chapter 4 of the Haṭhapradīpikā. It interprets esoteric yogic gazes through lunar allegories (amāvāsyā, pratipad, and paurṇamāsī).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcription of a manuscript in very bad condition (IFP RE 32608). It runs from folio 1a to folio 36a, with folio 20 missing and many lacunae. The transcriber lists 24 section headings: mantravāsa (f. 1a), nityārcana (f. 2a), trikālapūjā, dārumaya, pīṭhalakṣaṇa, pūjākāla, saurapūjā, indrapūjā, arcanāphala, āsanavidhi and pañcaśuddhi, bhūtaśuddhi, mantraśuddhi (f. 24a), siṃhāsana, vāmabrahmamantra, sadāśiva, āvāhana, naivedya and snapana, abhiṣekakrama, and phalodakavidhi (f. 36a). The text breaks off within the phalodakavidhi ('gojalair abhiṣekaṃ tu …', '(End of RE32608.)'). ilx_skt metadata classifies it as 'incomplete'.

**Also known as:** Candrajñānāgama, Candrajñāna – Nityārcanavidhi – Mantravāsa (Muktabodha title)

**Attribution:** Scriptural (āgamic) text. The colophon 'iti candrajñāne' (seg. 50) ascribes the material to the Candrajñāna, one of the 28 Siddhāntāgamas. The relation of this manuscript text to other transmitted forms of the Candrajñānāgama was not checked.

Verse sections of the Śaiva Siddhānta scripture Candrajñāna(āgama) on the 'dwelling of mantras' (mantravāsa) and on the daily worship of Śiva (nityārcana), transcribed from a badly damaged South Indian palm-leaf manuscript. The surviving text covers the times of worship, images of wood, pedestals, the worship of Sūrya and Indra, the fruits of worship, the seats and the five purifications (bhūta-, mantra-śuddhi etc.), the lion-throne, the Sadāśiva form, invocation, food offering and bathing, and the bathing of the liṅga with various substances.

The Caturvedārthatātparyasaṃgraha (commonly known as the Śrutisūktimālā) is a 150-verse Śaiva philosophical and polemical work composed by Haradatta. Through an exegesis of Vedic passages, mantras, and Upaniṣadic texts, Haradatta demonstrates that Lord Śiva is the supreme Brahman and the ultimate purism (tātparya) of the four Vedas, defending Śaiva theism against rival school interpretations.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā ending at segment 531 with a full colophon, followed by an editorial/manuscript appendix quoting verses 67–70 of upadeśa 13 from Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya's Kriyāsāra (segments 532–541).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā (Cannabasaveśvara, root text)

**Also known as:** Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā of Sudhāpurastha Cannabasaveśvara

**Attribution:** Authored by Cannabasaveśvara (Cannabasavārya Deśika) residing in Sudhāpura. As stated in verses 2–5, he traces his teaching lineage through Toṇṭada Siddhamaheśvara, Murughā Śāntavīra Yati, and Gurusiddha Deśika. The TEI header specifies 'attributed to' to distinguish him from the 12th-century Liṅgāyata leader Cannabasava.

The Vīraśaivotkarṣapradīpikā ('Illumination of the Excellence of Vīraśaivism') is a doctrinal polemical and theological treatise composed in mixed prose and verse by Sudhāpurastha Cannabasaveśvarasvāmin, affiliated with the Toṇṭada and Murughā Vīraśaiva lineages. Written in response to doctrinal questions raised by a scholar named Murughāya, it defends the Vedic status and spiritual supremacy of Vīraśaiva philosophy and practice, drawing upon Upaniṣadic, Purāṇic, and Śaivāgama authorities to elucidate key tenets such as the ṣaṭsthala, aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra, and atyāśrama. The e-text concludes with a brief excerpt from the thirteenth chapter of Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya's Kriyāsāra concerning qualifications for Śaiva consecration.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Diplomatic transcription of MS 4919, Raghunath Temple Library, Jammu (J&K), unpublished manuscript transcription.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (transcribed by Muktabodha staff under supervision of Anirban Dash, April 2024)

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha TEI header explicitly records: 'Manuscript : Ragunath Temple, Jammu, JandK manuscript 4919. Notes: Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Anirban Dash. Revision 0: Apr. 6, 2024 Diplomatic transcription'.

**Other editions:**
- Hans-Georg Türstig (ed.), Yantracintāmaṇiḥ of Dāmodara: Critically Edited with an Introduction, Stuttgart: Franz Steiner Verlag, 1988 (Beiträge zur Südasienforschung, Bd. 121). — Critical edition based on multiple manuscripts.
- Ram Kumar Rai (ed. & comm.), Yantracintāmaṇi of Dāmodara, Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1984. — Printed edition with Hindi translation.

**Translations:**
- Ram Kumar Rai, Yantracintāmaṇi of Dāmodara: Translated into Hindi with Commentary, Varanasi: Prachya Prakashan, 1984. (Hindi)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete transcription of manuscript 4919, preserving the introductory pīṭhikā and the eight thematic sections (adhikāras) treating the ṣaṭkarmas, śānti, rakṣā, and bandhamokṣa, ending with the concluding colophon: iti śrīdāmodareṇa śivājñākareṇa paṇḍitarājena viracito yantracintāmaṇiḥ samāptaḥ.

**Also known as:** Kalpacintāmaṇi

**Attribution:** Dāmodara introduces his lineage in the opening stanzas (vv. 1–6: Mahādeva -> Devadatta -> Gaṅgādhara -> Dāmodara) and states that Śiva inspired him in a dream to compile this yantra treatise based on various Śaiva, Saura, and Śākta texts.

The Yantracintāmaṇi is a widely cited medieval Sanskrit tantric treatise on yantras composed by Dāmodara, son of Gaṅgādhara. Structured as a dialogue between Umā and Maheśvara upon Mount Kailāsa, the work provides detailed instructions for constructing, inscribing, and ritually activating yantras across eight principal sections corresponding to the ṣaṭkarman (vaśya, ākarṣaṇa, stambhana, vidveṣaṇa, māraṇa, uccāṭana) as well as rites for pacification (śānti), protection (rakṣā), and liberation from physical confinement (bandhamokṣa).

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished transcription of MS 4886, Raghunatha Temple Library, Jammu (copied by Vaṃśīdhara). No printed edition is known.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute: data-entered by Muktabodha staff under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, catalog no. M00521, revision 0, 12 Sept. 2021, https://muktabodha-digital-library.org/texts/IAST/M00521. TEI conversion: ERC Intellexus project (ilx_skt corpus/muktabodha/dAzarathIyatantram_M00521.xml).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Catalog number : M00521 / Manuscript : MS 4886 Ragunatha Temple Library, Jammu / Description: An unusual vaiṣṇava tantra as it is focused on the worship of rāma. / Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: Sept. 12, 2021.'
- Scribal colophon (segs. 22421–22434) naming the copyist Vaṃśīdhara

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Beginning missing: the e-text opens at adhyāya 1, v. 15 ('…rīśīlavṛttaphalaṃ śrutaṃ || 15 ||'). Otherwise the text runs through the pūrvabhāga (chapter colophons up to 'ekonaṣaṣṭitamo 'dhyāyaḥ', seg. 13044) and the uttarabhāga (adhyāyas 1–45). It ends with the final chapter colophon '… uttarabhāge saubhāgyavidhodaye rājavidyāmāhātmye śāstrarahasyakathanaṃ nāma paṃcacatvāriṃśo 'dhyāyaḥ' (seg. 22420), a phalaśruti and the scribe's colophon. Some chapter colophons are missing or garbled in the transcription, so internal losses cannot be excluded. ilx_skt metadata classifies it as 'incomplete' with the colophon 'almost at end'.

**Also known as:** Anuttarabrahmatattvarahasya (colophon frame title), Vedārthasaṃgraha / Vedasārārthasaṃgraha (colophon subtitle)

**Attribution:** Anonymous Vaiṣṇava (Rāma-centred) tantra in which Ṛṣyaśṛṅga is the narrator. The closing verse says the pūrvabhāga was taught by Nārāyaṇa and the uttarabhāga by Śaṅkara to Girijā. The final verses (segs. 22421–22434) are a scribal colophon of Vaṃśīdhara of the Bhāradvāja gotra, a devotee of Rāma and of the Śrīcakra (Rājarājeśvarī), with a śaka date in word numerals.

A long Vaiṣṇava tantra that teaches the worship of Rāma, son of Daśaratha, as the supreme brahman. It is framed as Ṛṣyaśṛṅga's teaching to Śatānanda and other sages and styles itself a 'compendium of the meaning of the Veda' (Vedārthasaṃgraha). The first part (59 chapters) treats cosmology, dharma, mantra, initiation, puraścaraṇa and worship. The second part (45 chapters), with the sections Saubhāgyavidyodaya and Rājavidyāmāhātmya, adds strongly Śākta material, including Śrīcakra worship and the Rājarājeśvarī and Lakṣmīnārāyaṇa vidyās. The e-text is a transcription of a single Jammu manuscript.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Pondicherry: Institut Français de Pondichéry (IFP), palm-leaf manuscript bundle RE 32578 (diplomatic transcription prepared by IFP scholars under the supervision of Dr. Deviprasad Mishra, funded by the Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, 2023).

**E-text:** Institut Français de Pondichéry / Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog I00061)

**Evidence:**
- The TEI header notes: 'Manuscript: IFP manuscript bundle RE32578', prepared under Dr. Deviprasad Mishra.
- Opening lines of transcription record: 're-32578 dīkṣāvidhiḥ (maṇipravālam) ... total number of folios/pictures = 55, folio dimensions 365x30mm'.
- Scribal colophon in seg. 562 names copyist Aruṇācalaguru, son of Agastīśvaragurukkaḷ of Śālaveḍu.

**Other editions:**
- Kriyākramadyotikā of Aghoraśivācārya, with the Prabhā commentary of Nirmalamaṇi, edited by K. Shanmugasundara Mudaliar, Chidambaram, 1927 (Grantha script). — Standard print edition of the Sanskrit root text with Nirmalamaṇi's commentary.
- Kriyākramadyotikā (Aghoraśivācāryapaddhati), South Indian Archaka Association, Madras, 1974 (Grantha script). — Liturgical edition widely used by temple priests in Tamil Nadu.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Covers the initiation section of the Kriyākramadyotikā, comprising the pavilion preparations, Adhivāsanavidhi, Samayadīkṣāvidhi (concluding at seg. 239), and Nirvāṇadīkṣāvidhi (concluding at seg. 562), transcribed from 55 folios of IFP MS RE 32578.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kriyākramadyotikā (Dīkṣāvidhi) (Aghoraśiva, root text)
- Dīkṣāvidhimaṇipravāḷavyākhyā (commentary)

**Also known as:** Dīkṣāvidhi-maṇipravālam, Aghoraśivapaddhati (Dīkṣāvidhi), Kriyākramadyotikā (Nirvāṇadīkṣāvidhi)

**Attribution:** Aghoraśivācārya (12th century CE) composed the Sanskrit Kriyākramadyotikā. The bilingual Maṇipravāḷam commentary and ritual exposition in Tamil and Sanskrit is an anonymous South Indian liturgical transmission.

The Dīkṣāvidhi forms the initiation section of the Kriyākramadyotikā (also known as Aghoraśivapaddhati) by the 12th-century Śaiva Siddhānta preceptor Aghoraśivācārya. This text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of palm-leaf manuscript RE 32578 from the Institut Français de Pondichéry, presenting Sanskrit root formulas and procedures embedded in an extensive Maṇipravāḷam (Tamil-Sanskrit) ritual commentary. It details the preliminary rites (adhivāsana), foundational entrance initiation (samayadīkṣā), and final liberating initiation (nirvāṇadīkṣā).

**Coverage:** complete — Complete diplomatic transcription of the single manuscript NGMCP Reel A 39/12 (pra. 736), beginning with initial verses to Lakulin and concluding with the antyeṣṭividhi colophon.

**Works in this e-text:**

- Gārgyapādopadiṣṭaprāyaścittavidhi (root text)
- Antyeṣṭividhi (root text)

**Also known as:** Saṃskāravidhi, Pāśupatadīkṣāvidhi

**Attribution:** A Pāśupata ritual compendium opening with salutation to Lakulin (v. 1: tasmai lakuline namaḥ) and preserving a chapter on expiations attributed to Gārgyapāda (line 379: iti gārgyapādopadiṣṭaprāyaścittaḥ...).

An unpublished Pāśupata ritual handbook transcribed from a unique Nepalese manuscript (NGMCP Reel A 39/12). The text opens with an invocation of Lakulin and details the rituals of initiation and purification (saṃskāravidhi), rules regarding the ascetic's vessel (pātravidhi), prāyaścitta expiations attributed to the Pāśupata teacher Gārgyapāda, and funerary burial practices for ascetics (antyeṣṭividhi).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Transcription of an incomplete manuscript: the folio sequence starts at fol. 2a (fol. 1 lost; the e-text opens mid-sentence 'cene devitvaṃ ...') and ends at fol. 24a, breaking off in an untitled Tripurasundarī hymn after the Mahātripurasundarīstotra. The Dīpayāgavidhi proper (lines 1–189) lacks only its opening; it is followed by a Gurustava, a short caru/dīpa rite, paśuyāga, homa and ārātika rubrics and hymns.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Dīpayāgavidhi (root text (ritual manual; colophon at line 189: iti śrīkulaśāsane ūrddhvāmnāyamate dīpajāgavidhiḥ samāptaḥ))
- Gurustava (from the Tantrarāja) (appended hymn (colophon line 302))
- Kulasamayārasvalpacarudīpayāpratyārambhavidhi (appended ritual section (colophon line 324))
- Paśuyāgavidhi, homa and ārātikavidhi (appended ritual rubrics (lines 325–377))
- Mahātripurasundarīstotra (Jagatānanda, appended hymn (colophon line 408))
- Tripurasundarī hymn (untitled) (appended hymn, breaks off (lines 409–414))

**Also known as:** Dīpajāgavidhi

**Attribution:** The paddhati is an anonymous ritual compilation from Nepal. An included hymn towards the end (lines 404–408) is attributed in its colophon to Jagatānanda.

A Nepalese Śākta ritual manual (paddhati) of the Kulaśāsana / Ūrdhvāmnāya, i.e. Śrīvidyā (Tripurasundarī) tradition with Kubjikā elements, for the worship of the goddess through lamp offerings (dīpayāga): kumbha-, dīpa- and balipūjā with mantras, mudrās, short stotra verses and Newari ritual rubrics. The manuscript appends a Gurustava ascribed to the Tantrarāja, a short caru/dīpa rite, paśuyāga, homa and ārātika rubrics, and a Mahātripurasundarīstotra ascribed to Jagatānanda.

The Dakṣiṇāmūrtisaṃhitā is a Śākta Tantric scripture of the Śrīvidyā tradition framed as a dialogue between Īśvara and Devī. Across 33 paṭalas, it expounds the ritual worship, mantras, yantras, and mudrās of Tripurasundarī and various manifestations of Lakṣmī. It details both daily ritual practices (nityapūjā) and periodic or seasonal observances (naimittikapūjā), concluding with the damanakāropaṇa rite.

The Dattātreyatantra is a practical tantric handbook devoted to occult rituals and the sixfold magic acts (ṣaṭkarman). Structured as an inquiry by Dattātreya answered by Śiva on Mount Kailāsa, it details incantations, herbal preparations, and yantras for pacification, subjugation (vaśīkaraṇa), eradication (uccāṭana), and lethal destruction (māraṇa), concluding with formulas for warding off wild beasts, serpents, and poisons.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** A printed booklet published in Mumbai (Bombay) in 1927, according to the Muktabodha record. Title page, publisher and editor are not recorded, and no library record of this print was found.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute: data-entered by Muktabodha staff under the supervision of Mark S. G. Dyczkowski, catalog no. M00507, revision 0, 14 Aug. 2021, https://muktabodha-digital-library.org/texts/IAST/M00507. TEI conversion: ERC Intellexus project (ilx_skt corpus/muktabodha/devIpUjA_M00507.xml).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha header: 'Catalog number : M00507 / Uniform title: devīpūjā / Description: The text contains durgapūjā - mahārājñīstava - bhadararūpabhavānīvākyamañjarī and sarasvatīstuti / … Revision 0: August 14 2021 / Publication year : 1927 / Publication city : Mumbai'
- The e-text opens with 'paropakārāya prākāśyaṃ nītā |', a printer's or publisher's formula indicating a printed source
- Status stays 'probable' because only place and year are known: the specific print (publisher, editor, title) could not be identified. A web search found no catalogue record.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Each of the four parts ends with its own colophon ('iti durgāpūjā sampūrṇā', 'iti … mahārājñīstavaḥ sampūrṇaḥ', 'iti … vākyamañjarī sampūrṇā', 'iti sarasvatīstutiḥ'). The first line, 'paropakārāya prākāśyaṃ nītā', is the end of a title-page or publication formula of the printed source.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Devīpūjā (Durgāpūjā) (Kashmiri Śākta liturgy (segs. 1–295))
- Mahārājñīstava (Kṛṣṇakavi, Sanskrit hymn to Mahārājñī (Khīr Bhavānī) (segs. 296–471))
- Vākyamañjarī (sayings of Rūpa Bhavānī / Alakṣyeśvarī), opening with a Nirvāṇadaśaka (Rūpa Bhavānī, collection of mystical sayings, largely in Kashmiri (segs. 472–731))
- Sarasvatīstuti (hymn of 10 āryā verses (segs. 733–754))

**Also known as:** Durgāpūjā (incipit and colophon of the first part)

**Attribution:** Kashmiri Śākta compilation. The Mahārājñīstava is ascribed to 'Paṇḍita Kṛṣṇakavi' (or Kṛṣṇaka). The third part is ascribed to Rūpa Bhavānī, called Alakṣyeśvarī (Kashmiri Alakhīśvarī), the Kashmiri woman mystic of the 17th–18th c. whose vākhs are in Kashmiri. The Durgāpūjā liturgy and the Sarasvatīstuti are anonymous.

A Kashmiri Śākta devotional booklet. It opens with a liturgy for the worship of the Goddess (Durgāpūjā) that invokes the Kashmiri goddesses Śārikā, Mahārājñī, Jvālāmukhī and others, with seat purification, nyāsa, invocation and offerings. A Sanskrit hymn to Mahārājñī (Khīr Bhavānī) by Paṇḍita Kṛṣṇa(kavi) follows. Then comes a collection of mystical sayings (vākyamañjarī) of the Kashmiri saint Rūpa Bhavānī (Alakṣyeśvarī), largely in Kashmiri and opening with a 'Nirvāṇadaśaka'. A ten-verse Sarasvatīstuti closes the booklet.

Hanumat: 6–9; Sūrya: 10; Śiva: 11, colophons at lines 159–1594), followed by a closing section on testing mantras (siddha/sādhya/susiddha/ari, akathaha-cakra citing Lakṣmīkulārṇava) and the consecration of rosaries (mālāpratiṣṭhā), which breaks off mid-sentence ('…mūlamantreṇa hutvā'). The final line is a scribal note '(maṃtracaṃdrikā sūcisameta patre 85 śloka 2700)', i.e. the manuscript's own extent statement; the text body stops before the end of the work.

**Attribution:** The introductory verses (vv. 10–14) and recurring chapter colophons identify the author as Janārdana (Janārdanabhaṭṭa), son of Jagannivāsa and grandson of Śrīnivāsa (the author of Śivārcanacandrikā).

A mantraśāstra compendium by Janārdanabhaṭṭa (Janārdana Gosvāmin), son of Jagannivāsa and grandson of Śrīnivāsa, author of the Śivārcanacandrikā; it presents, with ṛṣi, chandas, ṣaḍaṅganyāsa, dhyāna and japa rules, the mantras that Śrīnivāsa had only listed in that work. It covers in eleven prakāśas the mantras of Gaṇapati, the Goddess, Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa (including Hanumat), Sūrya and Śiva, and closes with the testing of mantras (siddhādiśodhana) and the consecration of rosaries.

**Attribution:** Referred to in the internal colophons as Śrīmatparamaśivayogirāṭparivrājakācārya Śrī-Toṃṭadārya, but specified as Maritoṃṭadārya in the edition's title page and in modern scholarly literature (e.g. Potter EIP).

The Kaivalyasāra is a foundational Sanskrit Vīraśaiva theological and philosophical treatise composed by Maritoṃṭadārya (ca. 16th century CE). Structured around the system of 101 progressive spiritual stations (ekottaraśatasthala) divided across six major prakaraṇas, the treatise correlates Upaniṣadic śruti passages with Śaivāgamic doctrines to articulate the Śivādvaita philosophy. It systematically expounds the metaphysical non-dual union (aṅgaliṅgasāmarasya) between the individual practitioner (aṅga) and transcendent-immanent Śiva (liṅga).

The Mṛtitattvānusmaraṇa is an eschatological and ritual text framed as a dialogue between Śrībhairava and Bhairavī, traditionally transmitted as a section of the Kashmiri Śaiva Bhṛṅgīśasaṃhitā. It provides a detailed account of the post-mortem journey of the soul, the geography and punishments of Yamaloka, the accounting of deeds by Citragupta, and the specific duties of relatives during dying, cremation (śāvasnāna, antyeṣṭi), the ten-day period (daśāha), and the performance of dīpaśrāddha to dispel the darkness of the pretamārga.

**Edition used (probable):** A printed edition of the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā (Vādakāṇḍa) published in Varanasi in 1936 (editor and publisher not recorded in the Muktabodha header and not traced).

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (catalog no. M00611; data entry supervised by Anirban Dash; rev. 0 Aug. 22, 2021, rev. 1 Mar. 27, 2022).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha TEI header: 'Publication year : 1936 / Publication city : Varanasi / Publication country : India'. Muktabodha uses these fields for the printed source of keyed texts.

**Coverage:** partial — Complete Vādakāṇḍa: introductory verses 1–5 and prose, through the 24th prakaraṇa (vīraśaivamatotkarṣatanniṣṭhaśivabhaktotkarṣanirūpaṇa) and the final colophon 'vādakāṇḍaḥ samāptaḥ'. The Kriyākāṇḍa of the same work is not contained.

**Attribution:** Colophons: composed by Maritoṇṭadārya, who received his knowledge through the grace of Toṇṭada Siddheśvara, as instruction (upadeśa) for Basava (Basavappa Nāyaka) of the Keladi dynasty (keladisadāśivarāyanāyakavaṃśa…basavavasudhāsaṅkrandana). The Vādakāṇḍa of the Vīraśaivānandacandrikā by Maritoṇṭadārya, written as instruction for Basava(ppa) Nāyaka of Keladi as a sequel to the work's Kriyākāṇḍa. In 24 prakaraṇas it sets out the Vīraśaiva siddhānta (ṣaṭsthala, liṅgāṅgasāmarasya, liṅgadhāraṇa, Śiva's supremacy) and refutes rival systems: Cārvāka, the four Buddhist schools, Jainas, Pāśupata divisions, Pāñcarātra (Mādhva and Rāmānuja), Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Mīmāṃsā and Advaita vivartavāda.

The Nityārcanapaṭala (also termed Vāsanārcanavidhi) from the Vātulatantra (Sahasrasaṃhitā recension) is an āgamic manual of daily Śaiva worship according to Śaivasiddhānta ritual doctrine. It details the classification of liṅgas (śailaja, ratnaja, lohaja, dāruja, mṛṇmaya, kṣaṇika), the distinction between ātmārtha (private) and parārtha (public) worship, the ritual roles of Ādiśaiva priests, preliminary purifications (pañcaśuddhi), āsanas, prāṇāyāma, and the full sequence of Śiva-pūjā.

The Śrītattvacintāmaṇi is a comprehensive 16th-century Śākta Tantric digest composed in Bengal by Pūrṇānanda Paramahaṃsa Giri. This portion comprises prakāśas 6 to 10: it includes the conclusion of the well-known Ṣaṭcakranirūpaṇa (from verse 21 onward, dealing with the internal subtle centres, Kuṇḍalinī, and yoga) and continues through ritual and liturgical topics including kuṇḍa (sacrificial pit) construction, homa rituals, and mantroddhāra. Both root kārikās and the detailed modern Sanskrit commentary of Bhuvanamohana Sāṅkhyatīrtha are included.

This is a Newar ritual manual (paddhati) of the Kubjikā cult (Paścimāmnāya, the 'Western Transmission'), mixing Sanskrit mantras with Newari ritual instructions. The Prabhuliṅgalīlā is a Sanskrit Vīraśaiva hagiographical text presented as part of the Bhaviṣyatpurāṇa, narrating the life, deeds, and teachings of the 12th-century saint Allama Prabhu. Closely related to Cāmarasa's 15th-century Kannada epic Prabhuliṅgalīle, it depicts Allama Prabhu's conquest of Māyā and his spiritual dialogues with prominent Vīraśaiva figures such as Gorakṣanātha, Muktāyakkā, and Basava, elucidating Vīraśaiva philosophical principles including the Ṣaṭsthala system.

Written at the behest of Mahārāja Jayavantsiṃha of Maruvāṭa for the instruction of beginners (bālabodha), it synthesizes the viewpoints of Brahmādvaita, Śivādvaita, and Mahādvaita, articulating Pratyabhijñā and Spanda philosophy in accessible terms.

A compendium of Śābara (vernacular folk-tantric) incantations, protective mantras, and healing rituals attributed to Rāmasiṃha. The text interweaves early modern vernacular North Indian formulas invoking deities (Śiva, Pārvatī, Hanumān), Nātha siddhas (Gorakhnāth), and Muslim pīrs (Sulaimān) to treat physical ailments, fevers, and encounters with wild animals.

The Śrīkṛṣṇālaṃkāra (or Kṛṣṇālaṅkāra) is a commentary by Acyutakṛṣṇānandatīrtha on Appaya Dīkṣita's Siddhāntaleśasaṃgraha, the classic Advaita Vedānta doxography compiling diverse views within the post-Śaṅkara tradition. A large commentary by Viśveśvara, son of Lakṣmīdhara, on the Tārāsahasranāma (the thousand names of Tārā, beginning "kailāsaśikharāsīnam"). In its colophons it is called Girijābhidhārthacintāmaṇi and it is divided into twelve mayūkhas. Each name is explained grammatically and etymologically, with citations from lexica, Purāṇas, tantras and śāstra works. The e-text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of a Jammu manuscript dated saṃvat 1942 (1885/86 CE).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the ritual manual as preserved in Jammu MS 1309 (colophon at line 522), followed by a scribal addition of the Saṃkaṣṭanāśanagaṇeśastotra from the Nāradapurāṇa (lines 536–547).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vāñchākalpalatā (Buddhirāja, root text)
- Saṃkaṣṭanāśanagaṇeśastotra (appendix)

**Also known as:** Vāñchāmanorvidhi, Vāñchākalpalatāprayoga

**Attribution:** Authored by Buddhirāja as stated in verse 1. The work incorporates mantras and rites associated with the Atharvaveda, Kaumārīsaṃhitā, and Prayogapārijāta.

The Vāñchākalpalatā is a Śākta-Gāṇapatya ritual manual compiled by Buddhirāja. It outlines the upasthāna, nyāsa, and recitation procedures for the Vāñchākalpalatā-Gaṇapati mantra (a syncretic Śrīvidyā-Gaṇapati rite), drawing on Atharvavedic mantras, the Kaumārīsaṃhitā, and the Prayogapārijāta. The transcript concludes with the short Saṃkaṣṭanāśanagaṇeśastotra appended from the Nāradapurāṇa.

The Vātulāgama (or Vātulaśuddhāgama) is traditionally enumerated as the twenty-eighth and concluding mūlāgama of the Śaiva Siddhānta canon. This e-text is an unpublished diplomatic transcription of IFP palm-leaf manuscript RE 26381, preserving sections on temple ritual, primarily the Nityārcanavidhipaṭala, liṅga worship, festival rites (utsava), and expiatory rites (prāyaścitta). It concludes with a Tamil scribal colophon recording its completion by Ṣaṇmukha Gurukkal.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished diplomatic transcription of MS 4865, Raghunath Temple Library, Jammu.

**E-text:** Data-entered by staff of Muktabodha Indological Research Institute under the supervision of Anirban Dash (Apr. 6, 2024, catalog no. M00656).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha TEI header: 'Manuscript : Ragunath Temple, Jammu, JandK manuscript 4865'
- Muktabodha TEI header: 'Notes: Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Anirban Dash. Revision 0: Apr. 6, 2024 Diplomatic transcription'
- Muktabodha TEI header: 'Catalog number : M00656'

**Other editions:**
- Muṇḍamālātantram, ed. Pañcānana Śāstrī, Calcutta: Navabhārata Publishers (year not verified). — Edition of the Muṇḍamālātantra cited by H. Urban, The Power of Tantra (2010). Not collated with this manuscript, and which recension it prints was not checked.
- Muṇḍamālātantra, in Tantrasaṅgraha, ed. Gopinath Kaviraj, Ramaprasad Tripathi and Vrajavallabha Dvivedi, 5 vols., Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit University (volume not verified). — Cited in the reference literature. Not collated.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Jammu, Raghunath Temple MS 4865. The Vīracūḍāmaṇi has paṭala colophons 1–11. The 11th ("iti °cūḍāmaṇau kāmyanitya° ekādaśaḥ paṭalaḥ") has no explicit samāpti, so whether the work is complete cannot be established. The Muṇḍamālātantra follows with paṭala 1 (mahāvidyās), paṭala 2 (akṣamālā), paṭala 3 (pīṭhas, abbreviated colophon "i° mu° tṛ° pa°") and the beginning of paṭala 4 (balidāna). It breaks off mid-sentence ("surādānena deveśi mahā..."). ilx_skt: "Completeness: incomplete".

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vīracūḍāmaṇi (root text (paṭalas 1–11))
- Muṇḍamālātantra (second text in the same manuscript (paṭalas 1–3, 4 incomplete))

**Also known as:** Vīracūḍāmaṇitantra, Muṇḍamālā (Muktabodha title)

**Attribution:** Both are anonymous Śākta tantras in Śiva–Devī dialogue. The Vīracūḍāmaṇi deals with the krama of Mahānīla(sarasvatī)/Tārā/Ekajaṭā in vīrācāra. Its 11th paṭala colophon is preceded by a stray colophon "iti muṇḍa° dvitīyaḥ paṭalaḥ" after a passage on the japamālā, which suggests the two texts are mixed in the manuscript.

A manuscript with two Śākta tantras. The Vīracūḍāmaṇi (11 paṭalas) gives the vīrācāra worship of Mahānīlasarasvatī/Tārā: morning rites, haṃsa-sādhana, offering japa to the deities of the cakras, dīkṣā, pūjā, mantroddhāra, homa and kāmya rites. It is followed by the first three and a half paṭalas of a Muṇḍamālātantra, on the mahāvidyās, the akṣamālā, the four great pīṭhas and balidāna, which breaks off.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Transcription of a 21-folio manuscript of the Vīratantra from the Kashi Jangamwadi Matha, Varanasi (shelfmark not given). Data-entered by Muktabodha staff under Anirban Dash from sources supplied by Elaine Fisher (Revision 0: Aug. 22, 2021; Revision 1: Mar. 27, 2022). No printed edition.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute (staff under the supervision of Dr. Anirban Dash)

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha TEI header: "Manuscript : Manuscript from Kashi Jangamwadi Matha"
- Muktabodha announcement on the INDOLOGY list, 5 Sept. 2021 (list.indology.info attachment 20210905/ac2e3a7e): "Vīratantra manuscript from Kashi Jangamwadi Matha (21 folios)", among 14 Vīraśaiva e-texts from sources provided by Elaine Fisher
- Reference literature and web searches found no printed edition

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text begins with the maṅgala and frame verses and the thesis on the supremacy of the Vīraśaiva, supported by quotations from Śāṅkarasaṃhitā, Pārameśvara, Kūrma and Sūtasaṃhitā. It continues through arguments on aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra and ṣaṭsthala, and on iṣṭaliṅga versus sthiraliṅga worship. It breaks off mid-sentence ("tathā ca jaṅgamatattvasya sarvābhya..."). The manuscript has 21 folios (Muktabodha 2021 announcement). ilx_skt: "Completeness: incomplete".

**Attribution:** The frame verses (vv. 3–7) praise Toṭada Siddheśvara and Murigā Śāntavīra Yati, and present the guru Vīracannabasava(ārya) ("vīracaṃna basavāya edhate", v. 5) answering the paṇḍita Muragaya. The author is therefore Vīracannabasava or a pupil recording his teaching. The attribution rests only on these verses.

A late Vīraśaiva theological and polemical treatise composed in mixed verse and prose by Vīracannabasava of Sudhāpurī, writing within the lineage of the 15th–16th century saint Tōṭada Siddhēśvara and Murigā Śāntavīra. The work expounds classical Vīraśaiva doctrine, focusing on the eight protective shields (aṣṭāvaraṇa), five conducts (pañcācāra), six stages (ṣaṭsthala), and the superiority of personal liṅga worship (iṣṭaliṅga) over temple idols (sthiraliṅga). It supports its positions by citing extensive passages from Purāṇic and Tantric/Āgamic texts such as the Śāṅkarasaṃhitā, Pārameśvara, Kūrmapurāṇa, and Sūtasaṃhitā.

Tracing the author's lineage back to the renowned Ārādhyadīkṣā master Mallikārjuna Paṇḍitārādhya, the work synthesizes Vīraśaiva theology, ritual codes, liṅga worship, initiation, and devotional duties with extensive citations from Vedic, Upaniṣadic, Purāṇic, and Śaivāgama literature.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Paṭalas 1–12 complete with colophons (1 bhaktisthala, 2 māheśvarasthala, 3 prasādasthala, 4 prāṇaliṅgadala, 5 śaraṇasthala, 6 śivaliṅgaikya/ṣaḍdala, 7 niṣkala prāṇaliṅga, 8 vīrāgamarahasya, 9 niṣkalaprāṇaliṅganirṇaya, 10 jñānaliṅgavidhi, 11 [title damaged], 12 darśaviśeṣamahimāvidhi); the 13th, on sacred ash, breaks off without colophon (seg. 1039–1183), followed by the transcriber's note '[asamāpto'yaṃ granthaḥ asaṃpūrṇaśca]' (seg. 1184). The full extent of the work is unknown.

**Also known as:** Vīrāgama, Vīraśaivāgama of the Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā (colophon: 'iti śrīvīraśaivāgame sahasrakoṭisaṃhitāyām')

The chapter colophons place it in a 'Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā' (e.g. seg. 190–191: 'iti vīraśaivāgame sahasrakoṭisaṃhitāyāṃ prāṇaliṅgasaṃbandhānāṃ bhaktistalaṃ nāma prathamaḥ paṭalaḥ'). N. N. Bhattacharyya (History of the Tantric Religion) cites a 'Vīrāgama' for a fourfold classification of Śaivas; whether that is the same text was not verified.

An anonymous Vīraśaiva scripture cast as a dialogue between Devī and Śiva, whose colophons assign it to a 'Sahasrakoṭisaṃhitā'. It opens with a classification of Śaiva and other sectarian traditions and declares Vīraśaivism superior to them. Its chapters set out the stages (sthala) of Vīraśaiva devotion and the doctrine and worship of the prāṇaliṅga and its six petals (ṣaḍdala). The surviving part of the last chapter deals with the preparation and wearing of sacred ash (bhasma).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Incomplete; covers gaṇendravibhava, initiation, sandhyā, and morning homa up to śivāgni meditation, ending with '|| [asaṃpūrṇo'yaṃ gnanthaḥ] ||'.

**Also known as:** Siddhāntottarakaumudī

**Attribution:** The author Vīrabhadrārādhya identifies himself in vv. 14–17 as the son of Candraśekhara and Annapūrṇā, of the Bhāradvāja gotra and the lineage of Udbhavārādhya.

The Vīraśaivasiddhāntottarakaumudī is a Vīraśaiva theological and ritual manual (paddhati) composed by Vīrabhadrārādhya. Drawing on Śaiva scriptures and āgamic traditions, it details the descent and role of the Gaṇendras, the path of bhakti, initiation (ṣaḍadhvadīkṣā), the bearing of the liṅga (liṅgadhāraṇa), and daily ritual observances (dinakarma) including sandhyopāsanā, bhasmasnāna, and agnikārya.

The Virūpākṣapañcāśikā is a concise South Indian non-dual Śaiva treatise in 53 verses attributed to Virūpākṣanātha, deeply rooted in Pratyabhijñā and Trika philosophy. Arranged in four sections (skandhas), the work expounds that the objective universe constitutes the body of supreme consciousness (viśvaśarīratva), the ultimate unity of consciousness and manifest reality (prakāśaikātmya), reflexive awareness (pratyavamarśa), and mystical attainments (vibhūti/siddhi). This e-text features the root verses embedded within the authoritative Vivṛti commentary composed by Vidyācakravartin in the 14th century.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished: diplomatic transcription of Raghunath Temple Library, Jammu (J&K), MS 1480k. Not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00645, data-entered by Muktabodha staff under the supervision of Anirban Dash (rev. 0: 6 Apr 2024, 'Diplomatic transcription'); TEI conversion by Intellexus (ilx_skt).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha TEI header: 'Manuscript : Ragunath Temple, Jammu, JandK manuscript 1480k', 'Data-entered by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Anirban Dash. Revision 0: Apr. 6, 2024 Diplomatic transcription'.
- The e-text reproduces scriptio continua with manuscript line breaks and orthography (v for b, anusvāra for nasals), as expected in a diplomatic transcription

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text runs from the maṅgala verses through all 25 paṭalas of the Śāradātilaka. Paṭala colophons in verse are preserved, e.g. 3rd (seg. 3156), 4th (seg. 4055) and 6th (seg. 4978). The commentary on the Śāradātilaka's final verses explains the 25 paṭalas as matching the 25 tattvas (seg. 13535–13540). It then breaks off mid-word in Premanidhi's own concluding verses (seg. 13563 'prodūṣaṇā thaṃ spṛ'). Muktabodha marks it 'incomplete'. Some of the 25 paṭala colophons are absent or garbled in the transcription. Only a few closing verses are probably missing.

**Also known as:** Śāradātilakaṭīkā (Śabdārthacintāmaṇi)

**Attribution:** The colophon verses give the author's family: 'yasyodyotamatī satī guṇavatī mātā pitomāpatir nāma premanidhīti panthakulabhūḥ kūrmācalo janmabhūḥ ... vārāṇasīvāsabhūḥ' (seg. 11468–11470). This makes him Premanidhi of the Pantha family, son of Umāpati, born in Kūrmācala (Kumaon) and resident in Vārāṇasī. He names himself again in seg. 7 ('premanidher dvijāt') and seg. 13561, and he worships Kārtavīryārjuna. He is the 18th-century tantric author whose wife Prāṇamañjarī commented on the Tantrarāja (N. N. Bhattacharyya, History of the Tantric Religion; Bharati, The Tantric Tradition).

The Śabdārthacintāmaṇi is a large commentary by Premanidhi Pantha (18th c.) on Lakṣmaṇadeśika's Śāradātilaka, a major compendium of mantraśāstra in 25 paṭalas. It explains the verses at length with grammatical analysis, Nyāya-Mīmāṃsā argument and many citations from tantras. It also gives detailed procedures for ritual, maṇḍalas and fire-pits (kuṇḍa), yantras, nyāsa and the mantras of many deities.
