**Also known as:** Śaktiyāgapūjāvidhi (seg. 21: 'atha śaktiyāgapūjāvidhir ucyate'), Śaktimaṇḍapapūjā

**Attribution:** An anonymous South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta ritual compilation preserved in manuscript form.

An anonymous South Indian ritual manual of the late Śaiva Siddhānta for worship of the Goddess in the sacrificial pavilion (śaktimaṇṭapa / śaktiyāga). It prescribes the preparation of the pavilion and vessels (vardhanī), the worship of the four doorways and their toraṇas (caturdvārapūjā), the altar (vedikārcana) and the āvaraṇa deities, and the invocation of Gaurī. Appended are several nyāsa procedures: Dūtikānyāsa, Devīśrīkaṇṭhanyāsa, Devīṣaḍadhvanyāsa, kalānyāsa and Śrīkaṇṭhamātṛkānyāsa.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** A printed edition published at Hooli (Pūvvallī, Belgaum/Belagavi district, Karnataka), presumably by or for the Pūvvallī Pañcavarṇa Mahāmaṭha. Publisher and year not determined. It may be the same as the edition 'published in Belgaon in 1928' cited by Gaurinath Sastri, since Hooli is in Belgaum district.

**E-text:** Muktabodha Indological Research Institute, catalogue no. M00606, data-entered by Muktabodha staff under the supervision of Anirban Dash (rev. 0: 22 Aug 2021; rev. 1: 27 Mar 2022); TEI conversion by Intellexus (ilx_skt).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha/ilx_skt TEI header: 'Publication city : Hooli; Publication country : India' (Muktabodha gives a publication place only for e-texts keyed from printed books)
- The e-text reproduces the apparatus of a printed edition: the note on verse 3 '(śloko'yam adhiko mudritaḥ)' ('this verse is printed as an addition'), variant notes ('vṛṣaketave' iti pāṭhāntaram) and bracketed source references for Upaniṣad and Brahmasūtra quotations ('(śvetāśvataropaniṣadi 4-14)', '(brahmasūtraṃ 1-1-1)')
- Gaurinath Sastri, introduction to Vyomavatī, part 1 (Varanasi: Sampurnanand Sanskrit Vishvavidyalaya), p. iii: 'Śivādvaita-darpaṇa (published in Belgaon in 1928), a work belonging to the Vīraśaiva school', with the lineage table that names Śivāditya. The e-text has the same lineage (seg. 18–19). (https://jainqq.org/explore/020943/7)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in four paricchedas. Chapter colophons include 'iti jīvatattvavivekaḥ' (seg. 753), 'iti śivādvaitavivekaḥ | iti tṛtīyaḥ' (seg. 1067) and 'iti mahāvākyārthavivekaḥ || iti caturthaparicchedaḥ' (seg. 1318–1319). The work ends with a closing verse and the full colophon '... śrīśivādvaitadarpaṇaḥ sampūrṇaḥ' (seg. 1329). Seg. 0 ('atha dvitīyaparicchedasthaviṣayāḥ') looks like a stray line from the table of contents of the printed book.

**Attribution:** Author: Śivānubhava Śivācārya, disciple of Cidghana Śivācārya, head of the Pūvvallī (Hooli) Pañcavarṇa Mahāmaṭha (final colophon, seg. 1322–1329; verse 16 'tatkarāmbhojajātena śivānubhavayoginā'). The opening verses give a lineage: Siddhacaitanya → Śivāditya, 'vaiśeṣikācārya' → Viśveśvara Śivācārya → Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, author of the Brahmasūtra-bhāṣya → Cidghana. Gaurinath Sastri cites this guru list from the Śivādvaitadarpaṇa printed in 1928 to identify Śivāditya, author of the Saptapadārthī (Vyomavatī, part 1, introduction).

The Śivādvaitadarpaṇa is a Vīraśaiva treatise in four paricchedas by Śivānubhava Śivācārya of the Pūvvallī (Hooli) maṭha. It defends the Śivādvaita or Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita reading of the Brahmasūtras in the line of Nīlakaṇṭha (Śrīkaṇṭha) Śivācārya's bhāṣya. Its chapters discuss the meaning of 'atha' in Brahmasūtra 1.1.1 and the Ānandamaya section, the nature of the soul (jīvatattvaviveka), Śivādvaita doctrine including dīkṣā and liṅgadhāraṇa (śivādvaitaviveka), and the meaning of the Upaniṣadic great sentences (mahāvākyārthaviveka). Its opening guru list has been used as evidence for the identity of Śivāditya, author of the Saptapadārthī.

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished: transcription of Institut Français de Pondichéry palm-leaf manuscript RE 15527. Not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Institut Français de Pondichéry: Sambandhan Anandavardhana and Arul Nandi, under the supervision of Deviprasad Mishra, for the IFP–Muktabodha project; Muktabodha catalogue no. I00001 (© 2023); TEI conversion by Intellexus (ilx_skt).

**Evidence:**
- TEI header specifies: 'Manuscript : IFP manuscript 15527', 'prepared by the staff of the IFP, Sambandhan Anandavardhana (Research Associate) and Arul Nandi (Research Assistant) under the supervision of Dr. Deviprasad Mishra (Project Co-ordinator)', funded by Muktabodha Indological Research Institute.
- Explicit manuscript pagination and folio references in the e-text matching MS RE 15527: opening line '[0] (re15527.)', '[12] (1a, 1st line)', and closing line '[12235] || (end of re 15527) ||'.

**Other editions:**
- Śivāgrayogīndrajñānaśivācāryasvāmibhiḥ viracitā Kriyādīpikā. Madras 1929 (in Grantha script). — Cited as 'KD' in the bibliography of the Tāntrikābhidhānakośa (Austrian Academy of Sciences), entry 'Kriyādīpikā, Jñānaśivācārya [= Śivāgrayogīndra]'. Relation to the IFP manuscript not checked.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The Kriyādīpikā runs to the end of paṭala 6 (antyeṣṭividhi, seg. 6666). Colophons for paṭalas 2 and 4 are not marked in the e-text. Another IFP manuscript of the Kriyādīpikā is described in the IFP catalogue as having 8 paṭalas, so this e-text probably lacks the last part of the work, though the material after seg. 6666 has not been checked against it. The codex continues with a heterogeneous anthology and has a lacuna: '(148 to 157 missing.)' at seg. 7739. The transcription ends with '(end of re 15527)' (seg. 12235).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Kriyādīpikā, paṭalas 1–6 (Śivāgrayogin, main text (seg. 10–6666; colophons of paṭalas 1, 3, 5, 6 preserved))
- Khananavidhi and other saṃnyāsin rites; Dīkṣābhedakramagranthasaṃgraha (appended ritual material (seg. 6667–7280); possibly further Kriyādīpikā material, not confirmed)
- Varuṇapaddhati (extract) (Varuṇaśiva, included work (to seg. 7711))
- Kriyākramadyotikā (antyeṣṭi, pratiṣṭhādhivāsa, pratiṣṭhāvidhi sections) (Aghoraśiva, included work (seg. 7753, 8623–8624, 9616–9617))
- Jñānapūjāvidhipaṭala of the Vātulatantra, and other dīkṣā texts (included extracts (seg. 9887–10555))
- Rudrākṣavidhi (from the Sakalāgamasāra) (included extract (seg. 11448))
- Śāradātilaka paṭala 13 (Subrahmaṇya), Subrahmaṇyakavaca, Subrahmaṇyastotra, Subrahmaṇyanāmāṣṭottaraśataka, mātṛkānyāsa and further Āgama quotations (appended stotra and mantra material (seg. 11817–12234))

**Also known as:** Kriyādīpikā and minor works (Muktabodha main title)

**Attribution:** Kriyādīpikā colophons: 'iti (śrīmad)ativarṇāśramācāryavaryaśaivaparipālakaśivāgrayogiviracitāyāṃ kriyādīpikāyām ...' (seg. 524–526, 3058–3059, 5913–5914, 6665–6666). Śivāgrayogin (Śivāgrayogīndra Jñānaśivācārya, 16th c.) also wrote the Śaivaparibhāṣā. The remaining texts in the codex are by other authors (Varuṇaśiva, Aghoraśiva) or are Āgamic extracts.

The Kriyādīpikā of Śivāgrayogin (16th c.) is a Śaiva Siddhānta ritual manual for Śaivas of the fourth varṇa (sat-śūdras). The transcribed part covers daily conduct and saṃdhyā, pavitrāropaṇa and the cāturmāsya vow, initiation, the consecration of the ācārya (ācāryābhiṣeka) and funerary rites (antyeṣṭi). The manuscript transcribed here (IFP RE 15527) adds an anthology of other ritual texts. It includes extracts from Varuṇaśiva's Varuṇapaddhati and Aghoraśiva's Kriyākramadyotikā on pratiṣṭhā and antyeṣṭi, and Āgamic sections on jñānadīkṣā and rudrākṣa. **Coverage:** partial — The table of contents on p. 4b–5a (seg. 16–19, in Tamil and Sanskrit) lists sections up to leaf 101ff. (subrahmaṇyapūjā, agnikārya, nayanonmīlana ...) and 136–140 (vighneśvara-, subrahmaṇya- and devīnityapūjā). The e-text contains the Śiva pratiṣṭhā material: śāntihoma, saṃprokṣaṇa, adhivāsana, prāṇapratiṣṭhā, pratiṣṭhāvidhi, ṣaḍadhvārcana, mṛtsaṃgrahaṇa, vāstupūjā, rakṣābandhana and aṣṭabandhana. It breaks off mid-sentence at the opening of the Subrahmaṇyamaṇṭapapūjā (p. 51b–52a, f. 76a, seg. 928–934). The Subrahmaṇya and Gaṇapati sections of the 109-folio bundle RE30970 are therefore not transcribed.

- Saṃprokṣaṇavidhipaṭala (extract (colophon: 'ity aṃśumāntantre saṃprokṣaṇavidhipaṭalaḥ', seg. 207))

- Subrahmaṇyamaṇṭapapūjā (section, incomplete (seg. 928–934))

**Also known as:** Śivagaṇapatisubrahmaṇyapratiṣṭhā, Śiva-Gaṇapati-Subrahmaṇyapratiṣṭhā

**Attribution:** An anonymous South Indian compilation of pratiṣṭhā rites for Śiva, Subrahmaṇya and Gaṇapati. It combines rubrics with extracts named in colophons from the Kāraṇa (Pratiṣṭhātantra), Aṃśumat, Śivālayanirmāṇadīpikā and Sakalaniṣkalasaṃvāda, and quotations from the Dīpta, Uttarakāmika, Siddhāntasārāvalī and others. Rubrics and the table of contents are partly in Tamil.

An anonymous late Śaiva Siddhānta ritual compilation for installing (pratiṣṭhā) images of Śiva, Subrahmaṇya and Gaṇapati, preserved in an IFP palm-leaf bundle. The transcribed part covers the Śiva rites: pacificatory fire offering (śāntihoma), reconsecration (saṃprokṣaṇa), preliminary rites (adhivāsana), the infusion of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), worship of the six paths (ṣaḍadhvārcana), collecting earth and sowing sprouts, vāstupūjā, the protective thread (rakṣābandhana) and the aṣṭabandhana fixing. Extracts are drawn from Āgamas and paddhatis such as the Kāraṇa, Aṃśumat and Śivālayanirmāṇadīpikā.

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished: transcription of Institut Français de Pondichéry palm-leaf manuscript RE 30494. Not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Institut Français de Pondichéry: Sambandhan Anandavardhana and Arul Nandi, under the supervision of Deviprasad Mishra, for the IFP–Muktabodha project; Muktabodha catalogue no. I00010 (rev. 0: 14 May 2023; rev. 1: 19 Nov 2023); TEI conversion by Intellexus (ilx_skt).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The Śivajñānasiddhisvapakṣadṛṣṭāntasaṅgraha is complete, with colophons for sūtras 2–12 (seg. 1427 ... 2831) and a final colophon at seg. 2832; the colophon at seg. 741 (sūtra 1) is damaged. The Saptalakṣaṇa section has five treatises with closing colophons (seg. 3050, 3166, 3341, 3385, 3520). The last text, a list of aniṅgya words, breaks off amid leaf damage at the end of the bundle (P83a, seg. 3560, 'End of RE 30494'). Leaf damage is marked throughout.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Śivajñānasiddhisvapakṣadṛṣṭāntasaṅgraha (Vedajñāna (Vedajñāna II / Nigamajñānadeśika), anthology of scriptural quotations arranged by the 12 sūtras of the Śivajñānabodha (seg. 0–2832))
- Samānasandhivyākhyāna (Padadarpaṇa) (Mallayārya, Saptalakṣaṇa treatise (seg. 2833–3050))
- Vilaṅghyavyākhyāna (Saptalakṣaṇa treatise (to seg. 3166))
- Hrasvasaṃgraha / Avarṇi (Saptalakṣaṇa treatise (to seg. 3341))
- Avarṇyāvarṇayorvyākhyāna (Saptalakṣaṇa treatise (to seg. 3385))
- Aniṅgyaparibhāṣā with commentary (Saptalakṣaṇa treatise (seg. 3386–3520; the commentary refers to 'śrīvatsāṅka', seg. 3519))
- Untitled list of aniṅgya words (Saptalakṣaṇa material, incomplete (seg. 3521–3560))

**Also known as:** Śivajñānasiddhi (colophon, seg. 2832), Padadarpaṇa (Mallayārya's Samānasandhivyākhyāna, seg. 2838)

**Attribution:** Goodall, Bhaṭṭa Rāmakaṇṭha's Commentary on the Kiraṇatantra, vol. 1 (Pondicherry 1998), introduction: Nigamajñānadeśika's 'unpublished Śivajñānasiddhisvapakṣadṛṣṭāntasaṅgraha, a collection of quotations from scripture chosen to substantiate and illustrate the second half of the Śivajñānabodha'. The same work identifies the author as Vedajñāna II, alias Nigamajñāna (16th c.). Goodall's Parākhyatantra (2004) lists the anthology among the unedited South Indian works that quote the Parākhya. Mallayārya names himself in the opening verse of the Samānasandhivyākhyāna: 'samānasandher vyākhyānaṃ ... kriyate mallāyāryeṇa padadarpaṇasaṃjñakam' (seg. 2837–2838).

A transcription of a composite palm-leaf codex, IFP RE 30494. The first and larger part is Vedajñāna II's Śivajñānasiddhisvapakṣadṛṣṭāntasaṅgraha, an unpublished 16th-century Śaiva Siddhānta anthology. It collects quotations from Āgamas and related texts (Svāyambhuva, Ajita, Pauṣkara, Cintyaviśva, Mataṅga, Siddhatantra, Suprabheda, etc.) under the twelve sūtras of the Śivajñānabodha. The second part contains Saptalakṣaṇa treatises on the phonetics of the Taittirīya pada and saṃhitā texts, treating vowel sandhi, avagraha, short vowels and unanalysable words (aniṅgya). Among them is Mallayārya's Samānasandhivyākhyāna (Padadarpaṇa).

- Śivasūtravṛtti (commentary)

**Also known as:** Shiva Sutra Vritti, Śivasūtravṛtti

**Attribution:** The root Śivasūtras are traditionally held to have been revealed by Śiva to the Kashmiri master Vasugupta (c. early 9th century CE). The accompanying Śivasūtravṛtti is an anonymous concise gloss; while sometimes traditionally ascribed to Vasugupta, modern scholarship regards it as an anonymous digest closely related to Kṣemarāja's Śivasūtravimarśinī.

The Śivasūtra is the foundational scriptural text of non-dual Kashmir Shaivism (Trika/Pratyabhijñā), traditionally revealed to Vasugupta on Mount Mahādeva. It expounds the nature of ultimate consciousness and liberation through three sequential stages: Śāmbhavopāya, Śāktopāya, and Āṇavopāya. The Śivasūtravṛtti is a concise anonymous commentary explicating each sūtra with glosses and scriptural citations from texts such as the Mālinīvijayottaratantra and Ucchuṣmabhairava.

**Edition used (probable):** A printed edition of the Śivasiddhāntacandrikā published at Hooli (Pūvallī, Belagavi district, Karnataka) in 1920, presumably by the Hooli (Pūvallī) Bṛhanmaṭha; the publisher and the editor/commentator were not determined. Only the verses were keyed.

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha/ilx_skt TEI header: 'Publication year : 1920; Publication city : Hooli; Publication country : India; Description: Verses only without commentary'. A publication year and place show that the source was a printed book, and 'without commentary' implies the print included a commentary that was not keyed.
- Editorial square brackets for colophons and section headings and numbered verses are consistent with keying from a print.
- Web searches for a library record of the 1920 Hooli print found none, so title page, publisher and editor remain unconfirmed.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Upodghātapariccheda (29 vv., colophon seg. 69–71) and four paricchedas (colophons of the 1st–3rd at seg. 187–191, 333–334, 487–489). The 4th ends with v. 80 and '[samāptā]' (seg. 656). Muktabodha notes 'Verses only without commentary', so any commentary in the printed source was not keyed.

**Attribution:** Siddhanañjeśa Śivācārya, holder of the Pūvallī (Hooli) bhāṣyasiṃhāsana of the Pañcavarṇasūtra lineage of Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya. The work recasts a dialogue (saṃvāda) between King Satyendra Cola and the guru Cidghana (vv. 8–9). The final, bracketed verse 80 says the Candrikā was taught for Cannavīrā Mahādevī and Cikkanañjeśvara ('cannavīrāmahādevyai cikkanaṃjeśvarāya ca / śivajñānaikasiddhyarthaṃ proktā siddhāṃtacaṃdrikā'). This explains Muktabodha's mistaken author entry.

The Śivasiddhāntacandrikā is a Vīraśaiva (Śivādvaita) verse treatise by Siddhanañjeśa Śivācārya of the Pūvallī (Hooli) maṭha. It has an introductory chapter and four paricchedas. It is framed as a dialogue in which the guru Cidghana, disciple of Nīlakaṇṭha Śivācārya, instructs King Satyendra Cola after initiating him. The teaching covers Śivādvaita doctrine with the Vīraśaiva aṣṭāvaraṇa, pañcācāra, ṣaṭsthala, liṅgadhāraṇa and liṅgāṅgaikya, and ends with the liberation in life (jīvanmukti) of the king.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished: transcription of Institut Français de Pondichéry palm-leaf manuscript RE 27544 (200 folios/pictures). Not a printed edition.

**E-text:** Institut Français de Pondichéry: Sambandhan Anandavardhana and Arul Nandi, under the supervision of Deviprasad Mishra, for the IFP–Muktabodha project; Muktabodha catalogue no. I00021 (© 2023); TEI conversion by Intellexus (ilx_skt).

**Evidence:**
- Muktabodha/ilx_skt TEI header: 'Catalog number : I00021 / Uniform title: śivotsavavidhi / Manuscript : IFP manuscript 27544 / ... There are 200 folios in this bundle'
- Picture and line markers in the e-text from '(P. 5b,1st line)' (seg. 0) to '(P200a., 1st line)' (seg. 5828)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The transcription runs from picture P5b to P200a of the 200-picture bundle; 'P' numbers are photograph numbers, and the folio numbering restarts within sections. It starts with a section heading on P5b, so the first pictures probably contain only covers or blank leaves; this was not verified. It ends mid-sentence on P200a (seg. 5838) in the rites after the utsavavidhi that ends at seg. 5733, without a colophon. The material on the following leaves is therefore lost or not photographed. Individual Āgama chapters are mostly complete with paṭala colophons. Muktabodha marks completeness as 'uncertain'.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Dhanurmāsapūjāvidhi, Kṛttikādīpanirṇayavidhi, Dīpāvalisnāna, Navarātryutsavavidhi (short ritual tracts with Āgama quotations (seg. 1–253))
- Skandaṣaṣṭhīvratotsava from the Kāmika utsavapaddhati (extract (colophon seg. 254))
- Ekākṣaranighaṇṭu (lexical tract (from seg. 257))
- Rakṣoghnahomavidhi (ritual tract (seg. 425–468))
- Mudrālakṣaṇa, Ṣoḍaśopacāra (ritual tracts (seg. 546ff., 860ff.))
- Dravyāhutihomavidhipaṭala from the Sakalāgamasārasaṅgraha (extract (seg. 984–1083))
- Navarātrividhi; Cintya (Pratiṣṭhātantra): mahānavamī/śamīpūjā and the śivotsava chapters (utsavaprakaraṇa, aṅkurārpaṇa, dhvajārohaṇa ... maunabali) (Āgama extracts (seg. 1085–2327; colophon 'kālīśvaraguruṇā likhite cintye śivotsavavidhi samāptaḥ'))
- Cintya: utsava-prāyaścitta chapters (Āgama extracts (seg. 2328–2883))
- Sūkṣmāgama utsavavidhipaṭala (Āgama extract (to seg. 4108))
- Makuṭāgama utsavavidhipaṭala (Āgama extract (to seg. 4629))
- Kāraṇa (Pratiṣṭhātantra): āḍipūra utsavavidhi (Āgama extract (to seg. 5156))
- Navarātrividhi from the Sakalāgamasaṅgraha (Aghoraśiva (as attributed in the colophon), extract (colophon seg. 5313: 'iti sakalāgamasaṅgrahe aghoraśivācāryaviracitāyāṃ navarātrividhiḥ samāptaḥ'))
- Utsavavidhi (ends seg. 5733) and the kṛṣṇagandhalepana/Naṭeśa rites (ritual prose, incomplete (seg. 5314–5838))

**Also known as:** Cintye śivotsavavidhi (seg. 2327)

**Attribution:** Anonymous compilation. The colophon at seg. 2327 names one Kālīśvaraguru as the writer or copyist of the Cintya śivotsava section ('kālīśvaraguruṇā likhite'). A note at seg. 1083 records the dravyāhuti section as written in the owner's own hand ('(அப்பா/அய்யா) svahastalikhitam'). One colophon attributes a Sakalāgamasaṅgraha to Aghoraśivācārya; that attribution is reported, not verified.

A composite South Indian Śaiva Siddhānta manuscript on temple festivals (utsava) and seasonal observances. It contains short tracts on the Dhanurmāsa worship, the Kṛttikā lamp festival, Dīpāvali and Navarātri, as well as rakṣoghnahoma, mudrās, the sixteen upacāras and dravyāhuti homa. Its core is a series of festival chapters from the Cintya (Pratiṣṭhātantra), covering sprouting, flag-hoisting, drum-beating, bali processions, vehicle and chariot processions, tīrtha and cūrṇotsava, with the corresponding expiations (prāyaścitta). It also has utsava chapters of the Sūkṣma, Makuṭa and Kāraṇa Āgamas.

It also gives procedures for rekindling the domestic fire (agnisandhāna), aupāsana, the student's aupāsana and pañcagavya. It ends with a cosmographic saṅkalpa formula and fragmentary Tamil–Maṇipravāḷa notes.

**Coverage:** complete — All 43 adhyāyas are present, with chapter-end colophons for every chapter. The text begins '[śrīvyāsoktabasavapurāṇaṃ prārabhyate] [prathamo'dhyāyaḥ] agastyapraśnaḥ' and ends with the colophon of the 43rd adhyāya and '[śrībasaveśvarapurāṇaṃ saṃpūrṇaṃ]'. Some colophons are irregular in the e-text: the 29th is headed '[ekonaviṃśo'dhyāyaḥ]' but its colophon reads 'ekontriṃśo'dhyāyaḥ', and the 26th lacks an end colophon.

**Also known as:** Basaveśvarapurāṇa, Śrīvyāsoktabasavapurāṇa, Basavapurāṇa (Sanskrit)

**Attribution:** The ascription to Bādarāyaṇa/Vyāsa is pseudepigraphic. Colophons present the work as a 'svarūpagrantha' and 'paramarahasya' in the form of a dialogue between Skanda (Kumāra) and Agastya. It is a Sanskrit Vīraśaiva work and should not be confused with the Telugu Basavapurāṇamu of Pālkuriki Somanātha (13th c.) or the Kannada Basavapurāṇa of Bhīma Kavi (1369). No date for the Sanskrit work was established from the sources consulted.

The Sanskrit Basavapurāṇa (Basaveśvarapurāṇa) is a Vīraśaiva (Liṅgāyat) purāṇa in 43 adhyāyas, framed as a dialogue in which Skanda answers Agastya's questions. It narrates the birth of Basava (Basaveśvara) as a partial incarnation of Nandin, his marriage, his service at the court of Bijjala and his miracles. It also tells the legends of many Śaiva and Vīraśaiva devotees (e.g. Kannappa, Dīpada Kaliya, Moligemāra, Śivanāgadeva) and argues for Vīraśaiva doctrine and practice against Vedic ritualism and rival sects. It closes with a scene in which Viśvakarman weighs the work against Vyāsa's other compositions and finds it the best of all purāṇas.

Advaitānubhūti is a short Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa in 84 anuṣṭubh verses expounding non-dualism. Employing classic Vedāntic analogies (the single moon appearing double to defective vision, space enclosed within diverse pots, water turning to hail, and mirages), it teaches that the pure conscious Self is immutable, ever-free, and distinct from the three bodies (sthūla, sūkṣma, kāraṇa) and the three states of experience (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti).

Through the recurring question and refrain 'tataḥ kiṃ ... yena svātmā naiva sākṣātkṛto 'bhūt' ('what then of it, if one has not directly realized one's own Self?'), the text systematically dismisses secular learning, wealth, physical pleasures, social honors, austerities, yogic powers, and celestial realms as worthless in the absence of direct Self-realization (ātmasākṣātkāra).

- Bhedojjīvanavyākhyāna (Kāśikā) (Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya, commentary (ṭippaṇī))
- Bhedojjīvanavyākhyā (Śarkarā Śrīnivāsa, commentary (ṭippaṇī))

**Also known as:** Bhedojjīvanam, Bhedojjīvanabhāvapradīpa (Bhagavantarāya's commentary, also called Bhedojjīvanapañcikā), Bhedacintāratna (Ānandatīrtha), Bhedacandrikā (Vāsudevācārya), Bhedasañjīvanī / Bhedasañjīvinī (Śrīnātha), Kāśikā (Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya's commentary, as it is commonly called)

**Attribution:** The root text is by Vyāsatīrtha (Vyāsarāja, c. 1460–1539); the root colophon reads 'brahmaṇyatīrthapūjyapādaśiṣyeṇa vyāsayatinā kṛtaṃ bhedojjīvanaṃ samāptam'. The commentators as identified in the e-text: (1) Bhagavantarāya, 'bhagavannāmnā', a pupil of Bhāskarī Veṅkaṭavarāhācārya (seg. 4 and 8661). (2) Ānandatīrtha, son of Mudgalārya, of Janārdanapura (seg. 66 and 8706–8710); he is not Madhva. (3) Vāsudevācārya, son of Kumbhārī Nārāyaṇācārya (seg. 91 and 8725). (4) Śrīnātha, called Hulagī Śrīnāthācārya in the heading, of Vyāghrapurī and son of Vāsudevārya (seg. 156 and 8740–8744). (5) Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya, called Kāśī Tirumalācārya in the colophon (seg. 173 and 8748). (6) Śarkarā Śrīnivāsācārya (seg. 192 and 8788–8792). None of the commentators is dated here. The Gemini draft took the whole commentary layer for Śarkarā Śrīnivāsa's alone; that was wrong.

The Bhedojjīvana ('Reviving Difference') is a short polemical treatise by the Dvaita scholar Vyāsatīrtha (c. 1460–1539). It defends the reality of the five kinds of difference (pañcabheda), especially between God and souls and between souls, with perception, inference and scripture, against Advaita. In this e-text each passage of the root text is followed by six later Mādhva commentaries and glosses, by Bhagavantarāya, Ānandatīrtha (son of Mudgalārya), Kumbhārī Vāsudevācārya, Hulagī Śrīnātha, Kāśī Timmaṇṇācārya and Śarkarā Śrīnivāsa. Much of this commentary is navya-nyāya analysis of the inferences used.

Best candidate (unverified): Daśopaniṣadbhāṣyakāraviracitā Śrībhāṣyavyākhyāśrutaprakāśikāvyākhyā Bhāvaprakāśikā, ed. Uttamur T. Viraraghavacharya, Tirupati: Tirumala-Tirupati Devasthanams, 1958. It is a standalone edition of the Bhāvaprakāśikā, as the e-text is, and its title matches the colophon wording; I could not compare it with the e-text.

**E-text:** Sanskrit Wikisource (page भावप्रकाशिका and four adhyāya sub-pages, created by user 'Shubha' on 14 June 2024 with an empty source/notes header); TEI-encoded in the ilx_skt corpus (corpus/wikisource/darśanāni/bhāvaprakāśikā.xml).

**Evidence:**
- Wikisource API: first revision of भावप्रकाशिका by Shubha, 2024-06-14; the {{header}} has empty author/year/notes fields, and the page gives no source. The same user uploaded other Viśiṣṭādvaita texts (Sūtrārtharatnāvalī, Stotraratna, etc.) the same week, also without sources.
- The garbles (e.g. 'brāhṛ' for brahma, 'hmad' for hṛd, 'sāmathrya', 'sūtraṣṭadṛlvā' for sūtrasaṅkhyā) are systematic legacy-font-to-Unicode conversion errors, not Grantha OCR errors. The Gemini draft's inference of the Kumbakonam 1906–08 Grantha edition is therefore unfounded.
- Editorial query brackets such as '(śravaṇe ?)', '(naḥ ?)' and '(ka)' point to a printed critical edition with editorial interventions.
- Potter, EIP Bibliography 23.1.59 lists the Kumbakonam 1906–08 Grantha edition with the Śrībhāṣya and Śrutaprakāśikā. The e-text does not contain those base texts, which makes that edition a less likely source than a standalone one.
- PhilArchive 'similar works' record (via web search) for the Tirupati 1958 TTD edition, ed. Uttamur T. Viraraghavacharya.

**Other editions:**
- Śrībhāṣya with Sudarśana's Śrutaprakāśikā and Raṅgarāmānuja's Bhāvaprakāśikā, ed. V. N. Krishnamacharya, Kumbakonam, 1906–1908 (Grantha script). — Potter, EIP Bibliography 23.1.59.
- Daśopaniṣadbhāṣyakāraviracitā Śrībhāṣyavyākhyāśrutaprakāśikāvyākhyā Bhāvaprakāśikā, ed. Uttamur T. Viraraghavacharya, Tirupati: Tirumala-Tirupati Devasthanams, 1958. — Known from a PhilArchive catalogue listing only; details not verified.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: the e-text has four adhyāyas (Wikisource sub-pages prathamo- to caturtho 'dhyāyaḥ) and ends with the colophon of adhyāya 4, pāda 4 (jagadvyāpāravarjādhikaraṇa), 'samāptaś cādhyāyaḥ', and the totals 'adhikaraṇasaṅkhyā 156, sūtrasaṅkhyā 544'.

**Also known as:** Śrutaprakāśikāvyākhyā Bhāvaprakāśikā, Śrībhāṣyavyākhyāśrutaprakāśikāvyākhyā Bhāvaprakāśikā

**Attribution:** Author: Raṅgarāmānuja Muni, called Daśopaniṣadbhāṣyakāra in the colophon, a Viśiṣṭādvaita commentator who postdates Vedāntadeśika. The work comments on Sudarśanasūri's Śrutaprakāśikā, itself a commentary on Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya. The e-text contains only the Bhāvaprakāśikā, with pratīkas from the Śrībhāṣya and Śrutaprakāśikā, not the full texts of those works.

The Bhāvaprakāśikā by Raṅgarāmānuja Muni is a Viśiṣṭādvaita sub-commentary on Sudarśanasūri's Śrutaprakāśikā, the principal commentary on Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtra. It explains the Śrutaprakāśikā pratīka by pratīka through all four adhyāyas, often raising and answering objections and citing other authors such as Vedāntadeśika (Nyāyasiddhāñjana) and Vācaspati.

The Bhāṭṭarahasya (also called Bhāṭṭatantrarahasya) is a 17th-century treatise by Khaṇḍadeva on the semantics of verbal cognition (śābdabodha) according to the Bhāṭṭa Mīmāṃsā school. Formulated in the precise terminology of Navya-Nyāya, it examines the definitions of dharma and adharma, the semantic import of injunctive endings (vidhi) and productive agency (bhāvanā), verbal roots (dhātu), verbal suffixes (ākhyāta), and case terminations (vibhakti). ## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Bṛhatstotraratnākaraḥ, prathamaḥ bhāgaḥ (vol. 1), ed. Rāmasvāmī Śāstrī, Madras: Vāvilla Press (Vāvilla mudraṇālaya), 1953. The hymn is on PDF scan pp. 336–338, i.e. printed pp. 328–330 by the Index pagelist offset (9=1).

**E-text:** Sanskrit Wikisource: proofread transcription from the scan, page created by user Soorya Hebbar on 2021-08-31 (revid 320134) during the 'पाठशुद्धिस्पर्धा आगस्ट् 2021' contest. Compiled, IAST-transliterated and TEI-encoded by the Intellexus project (ilx_skt).

**Evidence:**
- Wikisource page wikitext (first revision 320134): {{header | author = शङ्कराचार्यः | year = १९५३}} <pages index="बृहत्स्तोत्ररत्नाकरः (प्रथमः भागः).pdf" from="336" to="338" />, categories बृहत्स्तोत्ररत्नाकरः and शिवस्तोत्राणि.
- Wikisource Index page for बृहत्स्तोत्ररत्नाकरः (प्रथमः भागः).pdf: editor रामस्वामी शास्त्री, publisher वाविल्ला मुद्रणालयः, Madras, 1953, pagelist 9=1. This was verified for the sibling entries SA_GK19_ilx_ws_suvarnamalastutih_brhatstotraratnakarantargata and ..._mrtyunjayamanasikapujastotram_....
- The Gemini draft's 'Nirṇaya Sāgara, ed. Nārāyaṇa Rāma Ācārya' is not the source.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: 10 verses, all ending in the refrain 'tasmin me hṛdayaṃ sukhena ramatāṃ sāmbe parabrahmaṇi', which is abbreviated 'tasmin me ...' from verse 3 on, followed by the colophon. Some verses are corrupt as printed, e.g. vv. 2 and 10.

**Also known as:** Daśaślokīstutiḥ (Bṛhatstotraratnākarāntargatā) (Wikisource page title), Sāmbadaśaślokīstuti

**Attribution:** The colophon attributes it to Śaṅkarācārya ('iti śrīmacchaṅkarācāryaviracitā daśaślokīstutiḥ'), as do the Bṛhatstotraratnākara and the Wikisource header. Like most stotras ascribed to Śaṅkara, the attribution is traditional and unverified. Not to be confused with the Advaita Daśaślokī (also ascribed to Śaṅkara) and its commentary Siddhāntabindu.

The Daśaślokīstuti is a ten-verse devotional hymn (stotra) dedicated to Śiva accompanied by Ambā (Sāmba), traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Verse 1 invokes Sāmba across all eight grammatical cases (vibhakti-stuti), while the subsequent verses praise his cosmic supremacy and purāṇic exploits—such as the burning of Tripura, the drinking of the Hālāhala poison, and his superiority over Brahmā and Viṣṇu—each concluding with the refrain 'tasmin me hṛdayaṃ sukhena ramatāṃ sāmbe parabrahmaṇi'.

The Dvaitadyumaṇipariśiṣṭa is a Dvaita Vedānta polemical treatise functioning as a supplement (pariśiṣṭa) to the Dvaitadyumaṇi. It critiques Advaita Vedānta epistemology and ontology, focusing on the reality of difference (bheda) between jīva and Brahman even in liberation (mukti), the analysis of the supreme human end (parameṣṭa / puruṣārtha), and theories of error and non-existence (such as anirvacanīyakhyāti, asatkhyāti, and shell-silver illusion).

**Coverage:** complete — Contains all 12 stotras of the Dvādaśastotra (segments 1–289) followed by the Kandukastuti (segments 290–295) and the editor's concluding dedication (segments 298–303).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Dvādaśastotra (Madhva, root text)
- Kandukastuti (Madhva, appendix)

**Also known as:** Dvādaśastotram, Dvādaśastotrāṇi

**Attribution:** The texts are traditionally attributed to Madhvācārya under his ascetic ordination name Śrīmad-Ānandatīrtha Bhagavatpāda.

The Dvādaśastotra is a collection of twelve devotional hymns composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha, 13th c.), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. Addressed to Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, the hymns combine personal devotion and iconographic meditation with Dvaita theological doctrines, emphasizing the absolute sovereignty and independence of Viṣṇu. Appended to the text is the Kandukastuti, a short praise poem describing Kṛṣṇa playing with a ball.

The Dṛgdṛśyaviveka (also known as Vākyasudhā) is a concise 46-verse Advaita Vedānta introductory treatise (prakaraṇagrantha) analyzing the fundamental distinction between the unchanging subject/seer (dṛś, sākṣin) and the changing objective realm/seen (dṛśya). It outlines the two powers of māyā (vikṣepa and āvaraṇa), the threefold definition of the individual soul (jīva: pāramārthika, vyāvahārika, and prātibhāsika), and describes six kinds of samādhi (savikalpa and nirvikalpa, internal and external) as practical means for realizing non-dual Brahman.

A short Advaita Vedānta text in five verses traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya, describing the illusory power of māyā. Each verse ends with the refrain celebrating māyā as expert in producing the impossible ('aghaṭitaghaṭanāpaṭīyasī māyā'), illustrating how the undifferentiated, non-dual consciousness is made to appear divided into jīva, īśvara, social hierarchy, and cosmic forms.

The Mīmāṃsāparibhāṣā of Kṛṣṇayajvan (ca. 17th century) is a widely read elementary manual (prakaraṇa) of the Bhāṭṭa school of Pūrvamīmāṃsā. Composed in clear introductory prose for students (bālānām), it systematizes the essential categories of ritual hermeneutics, including the definition of dharma, the classification of Vedic injunctions (vidhi, arthavāda, mantra, nāmadheya, niṣedha), the six means of subsidiary application (viniyogapramāṇas), and the six principles governing ritual sequence (krama). Along with the Mīmāṃsānyāyaprakāśa of Āpadeva and the Arthasaṃgraha of Laugākṣi Bhāskara, it serves as a standard textbook for classical Indian ritual and exegetical theory.

The text provides a systematic philosophical defense of Advaita Vedānta soteriology, arguing that liberation (mokṣa) is achieved solely through knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self and rejecting the necessity of ritual action (karma) or the combination of knowledge and action (jñānakarmasamuccaya). The Kārikāvalī (also known as Bhāṣāpariccheda) together with its auto-commentary, the Nyāyasiddhāntamuktāvalī, is a standard 17th-century manual of the syncretic Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika system composed by Viśvanātha Pañcānana Bhaṭṭācārya. Due to its precision and accessible pedagogical organization, it became one of the standard foundational textbooks of Navya-Nyāya philosophy across traditional pandit schools.

The Pañcadaśī ('Fifteen Chapters') is an influential 14th-century manual of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Vidyāraṇya (and in part to Bhāratītīrtha). It is divided into three pentads corresponding to the tripartite nature of Brahman: Viveka-pañcaka (discrimination of existence, sat), Dīpa-pañcaka (illumination of consciousness, cit), and Ānanda-pañcaka (nature of bliss, ānanda). The treatise systematically analyzes definitions, scopes, and fallacies, defending Dvaita realism against Advaita and other rivals.

The Pramāṇapaddhati is an influential primer of Dvaita epistemology and logic composed by Jayatīrtha (14th century CE). Systematizing the epistemological doctrine set forth in Madhvācārya's Pramāṇalakṣaṇa, the treatise is divided into three sections corresponding to the three valid means of knowledge accepted in Dvaita: perception (pratyakṣa), inference (anumāna), and verbal testimony (āgama). It provides clear definitions of pramāṇa, discusses truth and error, expounds syllogistic reasoning and fallacies (hetvābhāsas), and defends the authoritativeness and intrinsic validity (svataḥprāmāṇya) of Vedic scripture.

Structured largely as an instructional dialogue between guru and disciple, it systematically treats the four qualifications for study (anubandhacatuṣṭaya), discrimination of real and unreal (nityānityavastuviveka), renunciation, the nature of avidyā and superimposition (adhyāropa/apavāda), the interpretation of the Upaniṣadic mahāvākyas, and the attainment of jīvanmukti.

The Smṛtimuktāvalī of Kṛṣṇācārya, a pupil of Rāghavendra Tīrtha, is a dharmaśāstra digest (nibandha) written for the Mādhva (Dvaita) community. It argues that Mādhva practice rests on smṛti, that ritual duties are to be done without desire for results as worship of Hari, and that smṛti and purāṇa are authoritative. It then sets out calendrical rules (seasons, months, intercalary and 'empty' months, Cāturmāsya, fortnights). The e-text breaks off in the section on the time for the single daily meal (ekabhukta).

It guides the qualified spiritual seeker through the discernment of the five sheaths (pañcakośaviveka) to reveal the true Self (ātman) beyond body and mind, explains the mahāvākya 'tat tvam asi' via direct and implied meanings (vācyārtha and lakṣyārtha), and depicts the experiential state of kaivalya achieved upon liberation.

The header 'śrīmadānandatīrthabhagavatpādapraṇītasarvamūsagranthāḥ' suggests an origin in a modern Sarvamūlagrantha digital compilation (e.g., following Bannanje Govindacharya's or Dvaita Matha editions).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete in four adhyāyas (adhyāya 1 ends at v. 154, line 154; adhyāya 2 ends at v. 50, line 204; adhyāya 3 ends at v. 325, line 529; adhyāya 4 ends at v. 70, line 680). The terminal colophon after chapter 4 is omitted in the Wikisource transcription.

**Also known as:** Tantrasāra

**Attribution:** Authored by Ānandatīrtha (Madhva, c. 1238–1317), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta; listed among the 37 works forming his canonical Sarvamūlagrantha collection.

The Tantrasārasaṅgraha is a practical liturgical and ritual treatise in four chapters by the Dvaita Vedānta teacher Madhva (13th century). Drawing upon Pāñcarātra and tantric ritual traditions, it outlines mantroddhāra (with particular focus on the Praṇava, Nārāyaṇāṣṭākṣara, and Dvādaśākṣara mantras), the construction of altars and sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa-maṇḍala), temple building, image installation (pratiṣṭhā), and daily icon worship grounded in Vedic hymns.

The Taptacakrāṅkanavidhvaṃsana is an Advaita polemical treatise composed by Garuḍācalayajvan of the Veṅkaṭagiri court. It rejects the Pāñcarātra and Śrīvaiṣṇava practice of bodily branding with hot iron emblems of Viṣṇu's disc and conch (taptacakrāṅkana), demonstrating through Mīmāṃsā exegetical rules and Dharmaśāstra citations that Vedic passages like 'pavitraṃ te vitatam' pertain to Śrauta rituals (such as the droṇakalaśa filter in Somayāga) rather than corporal branding.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the prakaraṇa in 13 topical divisions, beginning with the maṅgala verse (vāsudevendrayogīndraṃ natvā...) and concluding with the standard colophon (iti tattvabodhaprakaraṇaṃ samāptam).

**Also known as:** Tattvabodhaprakaraṇa

**Attribution:** Universally attributed in the Advaita tradition to Śaṅkara, though modern critical scholarship regards it as a later didactic manual by a follower of the tradition (the opening verse pays homage to Vāsudevendrayogīndra).

The Tattvabodha is a concise introductory catechism (prakaraṇa) of Advaita Vedānta traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. Written primarily in simple didactic prose, it defines fundamental concepts and technical terms, including the fourfold preliminary qualifications (sādhanacatuṣṭaya), the three bodies (śarīratraya), the five sheaths (pañcakośa), the three states of experience (avasthātraya), and the manifestation of the twenty-four cosmic principles. It culminates in an exposition of the non-difference between the individual soul and the supreme reality (jīveśvaraikya) and describes the nature and state of the liberated being (jīvanmukta).

The Tattvasāra is a metrical compendium in 104 verses by Vātsya Varadaguru (Nadādūr Ammāḷ, 13th century) that systematically encapsulates the tenets of Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtras according to Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta. It outlines the pramāṇas (epistemology), prameyas (ontology), the nature of Brahman as the antaryāmin and material/instrumental cause, the individual self (jīva), and liberation. This e-text includes the commentary Ratnasāriṇī composed by Vādhūla Vīrarāghavadāsa.

**Attribution:** The root sūtras are traditionally attributed to Patañjali. The Tattvavaiśāradī is a sub-commentary on the Vyāsabhāṣya composed by Vācaspatimiśra (ca. 10th century CE).

The Tattvavaiśāradī (also known as Pātañjalabhāṣyavyākhyā) is the fundamental classical sub-commentary on the Pātañjalayogaśāstrabhāṣya (Vyāsabhāṣya), composed by the tenth-century polymath Vācaspatimiśra. This text presents the four pādas of the Yogasūtra together with Vācaspati's extensive explanation of the Bhāṣya, clarifying technical Yoga psychology and metaphysics while defending the dualist system against Buddhist and other philosophical interlocutors. It remains one of the primary authorities in the classical Yoga tradition.

The Tattvaṭīkā is an extensive sub-commentary by Veṅkaṭanātha (Vedāntadeśika, c. 1269–1370) on Rāmānuja's Śrībhāṣya on the Brahmasūtra. Conceived as a line-by-line philosophical defense of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta incorporating rigorous Mīmāṃsā and Nyāya hermeneutics, only the section on the first adhikaraṇa (Jijñāsādhikaraṇa, Brahmasūtra 1.1.1) survives. This digital text represents an incomplete transcription from Sanskrit Wikisource covering the introductory debates concerning the sūtra's opening word 'atha'.

The Tithinirṇaya is a short astronomical and calendrical treatise of 29 verses composed by Madhva (Ānandatīrtha) as part of his Sarvamūlagrantha corpus. It sets forth mathematical procedures, sine tables (jyāvākya), and correctional calculations (saṃskāra) for establishing the exact duration of lunar days (tithi). The text is intended to settle the proper timing for ritual fasts (upoṣaṇa), particularly Ekādaśī and Dvādaśī, in accordance with Dvaita tradition.

The Vaiśeṣikasūtra attributed to Kaṇāda is the foundational text of the Vaiśeṣika school, establishing its realist ontological ontology around six ontological categories (padārthas): dravya, guṇa, karma, sāmānya, viśeṣa, and samavāya (with non-existence, abhāva, treated subsequently). The Viṣṇutattvavinirṇaya is the longest and doctrinally central treatise among the ten philosophical monographs (Daśaprakaraṇa) of Madhva (13th c. CE), the founder of Dvaita Vedānta. In three chapters (paricchedas), it establishes the intrinsic validity of knowledge (svataḥprāmāṇya), the authorlessness (apauruṣeyatva) and primary authority of the Vedas, and the ontological reality of difference (bheda) against Advaita non-dualism and the doctrine of māyā. The second and third chapters demonstrate that the supreme deity Viṣṇu (Nārāyaṇa) is entirely free from imperfections (nirdoṣa) and possessed of infinite auspicious attributes (aśeṣasadguṇapūrṇa).

The text runs from the maṅgala verses ('śrīveṅkaṭeśaṃ kariśailanāthaṃ ...') to the final colophon of the 10th avatāra. It includes Sanskrit topical subheadings (e.g. 'tattvaikyasya pratijñā', 'padārthasamuddeśaḥ'), which probably come from the printed source and are not part of the author's text.

**Also known as:** Śārīrakaparibhāṣā, Yatipatimatadīpikā

**Attribution:** The author calls himself Śrīnivāsadāsa of the Vādhūla family, first disciple of Mahācārya (Doḍḍayācārya). He is also called Śrīnivāsācārya or Vādhūla Śrīnivāsa, and Otto's German translation names him 'Nivāsa'. He is a 17th-century Viśiṣṭādvaitin and should not be confused with the Nimbārkan Śrīnivāsa.

The Yatīndramatadīpikā ('Lamp on the doctrine of the king of ascetics', i.e. Rāmānuja), also called the Śārīrakaparibhāṣā, is a short introductory manual of Viśiṣṭādvaita Vedānta by Śrīnivāsadāsa, a disciple of Mahācārya (17th c.). Its ten chapters (avatāras) first treat the three means of knowledge (perception, inference, verbal testimony) and then the categories of the knowable: prakṛti, time, the eternal realm (nityavibhūti), attributive knowledge (dharmabhūtajñāna, with the means of liberation), the individual self, God, and the non-substances (adravya). It is widely used as a primer of Rāmānuja's system.

The Yogatārāvalī is a short Sanskrit treatise in 29 verses bridging Haṭhayoga physical practices with Rājayoga meditation. It describes the practice of the three bandhas (mūla, uḍḍīyana, jālandhara), kevalakumbhaka, and absorption in inner sound (nādānusandhāna) as the means to dissolve mental fluctuations into amanaska (the transcendent mindless state) and yoganidrā. While traditionally ascribed to Ādi Śaṅkara, it is characteristic of the late medieval syncretism between Haṭhayogic methods and non-dual Advaita metaphysics.

The Śarīravāda is a short Viśiṣṭādvaita polemical treatise (vāda) by Anantārya of Yādavādri (Melkote) on the defining property (pravṛttinimitta) of the word 'body' (śarīra). It argues that 'bodyhood' is not a jāti and examines the Śrībhāṣya definition: a substance that a conscious being can wholly control and support for its own purposes, and that is entirely subsidiary (śeṣa) to it. It does so with reference to the Śrutaprakāśikā and the Nyāyasiddhāñjana, in Navya-Nyāya style. It also discusses related questions such as the inner self's entering (anupraveśa) and the soul's departure and movement.

The Śataślokī is an Advaita Vedānta verse compendium composed in sragdharā metre and traditionally attributed to Śaṅkarācārya. Across 101 verses, it systematically expounds key Advaitic teachings, including the role of the guru, the illusion of the empirical world, self-realization through discrimination between ātman and anātman, the interpretation of Upaniṣadic Mahāvākyas, and the nature of jīvanmukti. While firmly integrated into the Advaita curriculum, modern philology regards the work as an unauthentic composition of the later Śaṅkara tradition.

**Coverage:** partial — Partial. The e-text begins mid-way through the Jyotiradhikaraṇa (BS 1.1.24–27), which ends at seg. 135; all earlier parts of BS 1.1 are missing. It continues with BS 2.1: Smṛti- (seg. 314), Vilakṣaṇa- (561), Śiṣṭāparigraha- (601), Bhoktrāpatti- (700) and Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa (940), followed by the author's closing verses and 'samāpto 'yaṃ śāṃkarapādabhūṣaṇābhidho granthaḥ'. The Wikisource page has only six adhikaraṇa sub-pages, starting with the Jyotiradhikaraṇa.

**Also known as:** Śāṃkarapādabhūṣaṇa (colophon), Śaṃkarapādabhūṣaṇa

**Attribution:** By Raghunātha Śāstrī Parvate (c. 1821–1869, according to P. K. Gode), also known as Raghunāthasūri. The closing verses (segs. 930–939) say that the work was completed and lithographed ('aṅkitaś ca śilākṣaraiḥ') under the patronage of the Pant Sacivs of Bhor (residence on the Nīrā river; 'Nānāsāheb'), with the support of their chief judge (prāḍvivāka) Viṣṇu Bhiḍe, son of Gopāla. The Dvaita reply Candrikābhūṣaṇa was written against it (Potter).

The Śaṅkarapādabhūṣaṇa is a 19th-century Advaita polemical work by Raghunātha Śāstrī Parvate. It defends Śaṅkara's interpretation of selected Brahmasūtra adhikaraṇas (from the first pādas of adhyāyas 1 and 2) against the Mādhva criticism of Vyāsatīrtha's Tātparyacandrikā and the 'Ānandatīrthīya' interpretations. This e-text contains the end of the Jyotiradhikaraṇa and the BS 2.1 adhikaraṇas from Smṛti- to Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa.

Designed as a more direct and concise companion to his monumental Śrutaprakāśikā, it elucidates the core philosophical arguments, scriptural citations, and doctrinal distinctions across all four adhyāyas.

- The Wikisource page (raw wikitext checked) has footnotes citing Dāmodaralāla Gosvāmī's remarks and Guṇaratna's readings, which points to an edition based on Gosvāmī's Chowkhamba text.

- Luigi Suali (ed.), Ṣaḍ-darśana-samuccaya ... with Guṇaratna's commentary Tarkarahasyadīpikā, Bibliotheca Indica, Calcutta: Asiatic Society, 1905–1914. — Edition with Guṇaratna's commentary.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya (Haribhadrasūri, root text)
- Laghuvṛtti (Maṇibhadra, commentary)

**Also known as:** Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccayaḥ maṇibhadrakṛtalaghuvṛttisaṃvalitaḥ

**Attribution:** Root kārikās by the Jaina author Haribhadrasūri (c. 8th c.). The Laghuvṛtti is ascribed to Maṇibhadra in this text and in the Chowkhamba edition of Dāmodaralāla Gosvāmī; library catalogues note that the Laghuvṛtti is 'sometimes attributed to Maṇibhadra', and the Bhāratīya Jñānapīṭha edition prints a Laghuvṛtti under the name of Somatilakasūri, so the attribution of the vṛtti is not settled.

The Ṣaḍdarśanasamuccaya ('Compendium of the Six Philosophical Systems') of the Jain polymath Haribhadrasūri (c. 8th century CE) is an early and influential doxography summarizing six major Indian philosophical traditions: Bauddha, Naiyāyika, Sāṃkhya, Jaina, Vaiśeṣika, and Jaiminīya (Mīmāṃsā), followed by a brief examination of the materialist Cārvāka/Lokāyata school. Composed in 87 concise anuṣṭubh stanzas, it is celebrated for its irenic and objective presentation of rival schools. This e-text incorporates the root kārikās alongside the concise commentary (Laghuvṛtti) by Maṇibhadra.

The Amarakoṣa (formally Nāmaliṅgānuśāsana) of Amarasiṃha (c. 6th century CE) is the foundational synonymic and homonymic verse lexicon of Classical Sanskrit. Structured into three kāṇḍas (svarga-, bhūmi-, and sāmānya-kāṇḍa), it arranges nouns conceptually by taxonomy, cosmology, society, and grammatical categories. The Amaraviveka of Maheśvara is an influential commentary elucidating word origins, alternative grammatical readings, and referencing classical lexicographical and grammatical sources.

The Samarāṅgaṇasūtradhāra is an encyclopedic 11th-century Sanskrit treatise on classical Indian architecture (vāstuśāstra), urban planning, civil engineering, painting (citraśāstra), and iconography, composed by King Bhoja of Dhārā (r. c. 1010–1055 CE). Comprising 83 chapters, the work covers town and palace planning, residential layout, temple typologies (including detailed treatments of Nāgara and Bhūmija styles), mechanical apparatuses and automata (yantras, ch. 31), painting methods, and dance-based sculptural postures and hand gestures.

The Saṅgītaratnākara ('Ocean of Music'), authored in the early 13th century by Śārṅgadeva at the court of King Siṅghaṇa II of Devagiri, is the foundational medieval treatise on Indian music and performing arts. Arranged into seven chapters (saptādhyāyī), it provides an exhaustive analysis of notes and intervals (svara), melodic modes (rāga), miscellaneous musicological concepts (prakīrṇa), song and meter forms (prabandha), rhythm and metrics (tāla), musical instruments (vādya), and dance (nartana). The treatise forms an essential transition between ancient dramatic musical theory (gāndharva/mārga) and the regional performance traditions (deśī) that developed into modern Hindustani and Carnatic classical music.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Breaks off at verse 110 in the first adhyāya (gītaprakaraṇa), in the middle of the treatment of the jātis. The printed edition continues with verse 111 ff. and further chapters.

**Attribution:** The printed edition attributes the work to Ghanaśyāmadāsa; in his self-introduction (as given in the edition) the author also calls himself Narahari Dāsa. He is identified with the 18th-century Bengali Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava author Narahari Cakravartin (Ghanaśyāmadāsa).

The Saṅgītasārasaṃgraha is an 18th-century musicological compendium compiled by the Gauḍīya Vaiṣṇava scholar Narahari Cakravartin (Ghanaśyāmadāsa). The treatise systematically synthesizes classical and medieval authorities on Indian musicology (saṅgītaśāstra), citing works such as the Saṅgītadāmodara, Saṅgītapārijāta, Saṅgītaśiromaṇi, and Harināyaka. This partial e-text contains the first 110 verses of the opening chapter on vocal music (gīta), discussing the divine origin and merit of music, sound (nāda), notes (svara), microtones (śruti), and parent scales (jāti).

The Bhaviṣyapurāṇa is one of the eighteen Mahāpurāṇas, in the vulgate divided into Brāhma-, Madhyama-, Pratisarga- and Uttaraparvan. The Brāhmaparvan is known for its material on sun worship and the Maga (Bhojaka) priests. The Pratisargaparvan contains genealogies and 'prophecies' that run up to the Mughal and British periods and are evidently very late additions. The Uttaraparvan (also transmitted separately as Bhaviṣyottarapurāṇa) is largely a compendium of vratas, dānas and festivals, told as a dialogue between Kṛṣṇa and Yudhiṣṭhira.

The early Skandapurāṇa (composed c. 6th–8th century CE in northern India) is an independent Śaiva purāṇa distinct from the late composite 7-khaṇḍa compilation of the same name. Framed as a dialogue between Sanatkumāra and Vyāsa, it narrates the birth and martial deeds of Skanda/Kārttikeya, major myths of Śiva and Devī (including the slayings of Mahiṣāsura, Andhaka, and Tāraka), early Śaiva cosmography, sacred geography (notably Vārāṇasī), and Pāśupata-oriented rituals and theology.

It is uniquely significant in the Dharmaśāstra tradition for formulating lenient and detailed purificatory penances (śuddhi and prāyaścitta) allowing persons of all four varṇas, including women, who were abducted, forcibly converted, or otherwise compromised by foreigners (mlecchas) to be reintegrated into society.

It provides rare extant specimens of several dramatic types seldom preserved elsewhere in classical Sanskrit literature.

The Abhiṣekanāṭaka ('The Consecration Play') is a six-act Sanskrit drama dramatizing events from the Kiṣkindhā-, Sundara-, and Yuddha-kāṇḍas of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa. Shama Sastry, 1921, Sanskrit Series 58); Part III (ed. R. Shama Sastry, 1923, Sanskrit Series 62); Part IV (ed. D. Srinivasachar, 1929, Sanskrit Series 72). — Complete editio princeps. The other parts are separate catalog entries (alankaramaniharah1–4).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Part 4 of 4 (saras 105–126). Opens with the rasavad-alaṅkāras (105–111) and continues through the śabdālaṅkāras and citrabandhas (to 126). It then has the concluding section, ending 'samāpto 'yaṃ prabandhaḥ', and the appended collection of definition verses, ending 'samāptā alaṃkāramaṇihāralakṣaṇaślokāḥ'. This is the end of the whole work.

**Also known as:** Alaṃkāramaṇihāra

**Attribution:** Root text, example verses (in praise of Śrīnivāsa/Veṅkaṭeśa) and prose commentary are all by Śrī Kṛṣṇabrahmatantra Parakāla Svāmin, pontiff of the Brahmatantra Parakāla Maṭha, Mysore (late 19th–early 20th c.). His exact position in the line of pontiffs is not given in the sources checked.

The Alaṅkāramaṇihāra is a large treatise on Sanskrit poetic figures (alaṅkāraśāstra) by Kṛṣṇabrahmatantra Parakālasvāmin, pontiff of the Brahmatantra Parakāla Maṭha in Mysore (late 19th–early 20th c.). It is arranged in 'saras' (one per figure), each with a definition, the author's own illustrative verses in praise of Śrīnivāsa/Veṅkaṭeśa, and his prose auto-commentary. The commentary discusses earlier authorities such as Appayya Dīkṣita and Jagannātha's Rasagaṅgādhara. This fourth and final part covers the rasavat group (rasavat, preyas, ūrjasvin, samāhita, bhāvodaya etc.), the śabdālaṅkāras and citrabandhas (saras 105–126), the concluding section and an appended collection of the definition verses (lakṣaṇaślokāḥ).

The Alaṅkārasaṅgraha is a 14th-century treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) and dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra) composed in 11 paricchedas by Amṛtānandayogin under the patronage of King Manma. It integrates poetic theory with theatrical rules, discussing auspicious syllabic patterns (varṇagaṇa), word and meaning (śabdārtha), aesthetic sentiment (rasa), heroes and heroines (netṛbheda), figures of speech (alaṅkāra), poetic faults and virtues (doṣa and guṇa), dramatic junctures and plots (sandhyaṅga), major dramatic genres (rūpaka), theatrical embellishments (nāṭyālaṅkāra), and court panegyric compositions (cāṭuprabandha).

The Annapūrṇāstotra is a devotional hymn dedicated to Goddess Annapūrṇā as the presiding deity of nourishment and benevolence in Vārāṇasī (Kāśī). The Ardhanārīnaṭeśvarastotra (or Ardhanārīnaṭeśvarāṣṭaka) is an eight-verse hymn dedicated to the androgynous composite form of Śiva and Pārvatī (Ardhanārīśvara). In each stanza, the poet pairs and contrasts the feminine half (Pārvatī) and the masculine half (Śiva) in appearance, ornaments, and cosmic roles (such as creation through lāsya and cosmic dissolution through tāṇḍava), closing each verse with the dual refrain 'namaḥ śivāyai ca namaḥ śivāya'. Traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya, the poem concludes with a phalaśruti verse promising auspiciousness and longevity.

The Aucityavicāracarcā is an 11th-century treatise on poetic theory by the Kashmiri polymath Kṣemendra. Formulating the Aucitya doctrine of alaṅkāraśāstra, Kṣemendra establishes appropriateness or propriety (aucitya) as the vital essence (jīvita) of poetic art, arguing that poetic ornaments (alaṅkāra) and qualities (guṇa) fail without it. The treatise defines and analyzes twenty-seven distinct loci of propriety (including word, case, verbal syntax, gender, meter, time, place, and rasa), examining each through classical quotations illustrative of poetic excellence or flaw.

The Bhāvaprakāśa of Bhāvamiśra (16th century CE) is one of the three authoritative treatises constituting the Laghutrayī ('Lesser Triad') of classical Indian medicine. Structured into three parts (Pūrvakhaṇḍa, Madhyakhaṇḍa, and Uttarakhaṇḍa), it provides an encyclopedic synthesis of Āyurvedic theory, nosology, dravyaguṇa (materia medica), therapeutics, and rejuvenation (rasāyana). **Attribution:** Traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkarācārya (Śaṅkara). Like many minor prakaraṇa and stotra texts attributed to him, modern scholarship regards the attribution as unverified / apocryphal.

The Brahmajñānāvalīmālā is a short Advaita Vedānta prakaraṇa of 21 verses traditionally attributed to Śaṅkara. It summarizes non-dual metaphysics and the nature of the self through rhythmic, meditative declarations of identity with unattached, non-dual consciousness (Brahman). Verse 20 contains the celebrated summary maxim of Advaita: 'brahma satyaṃ jaganmithyā jīvo brahmaiva nāparaḥ'.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete drama in five acts (aṅkas 1–5), including prologue (sthāpanā), Prakrit passages with inline Sanskrit chāyā, and the concluding bharatavākya (ending: 'pañcamo'ṅkaḥ | avasitaṃ bālacaritam |').

**Also known as:** Bālacaritam

**Attribution:** Conventionally ascribed to the classical dramatist Bhāsa following T. Gaṇapati Śāstrī's discovery of the thirteen Kerala manuscript plays (Bhāsanāṭakacakra); the attribution remains debated in modern scholarship.

The Bālacarita ('The Deeds of the Boy') is a five-act Sanskrit drama dramatizing the early life of Kṛṣṇa. The narrative follows his birth in Mathurā, his transfer to Gokula, the subduing of the serpent Kāliya, the slaying of various demons (such as Dhenuka, Ariṣṭa, and Keśin), and his eventual overthrow of King Kaṃsa in the wrestling arena. A distinctive dramaturgical feature of the play is the stage personification of Viṣṇu's divine weapons and an appearance by the goddess Kātyāyanī.

The Bālamukundāṣṭaka is a short Vaiṣṇava devotional hymn in eight verses addressed to baby Kṛṣṇa (Bālamukunda). The verses celebrate iconic episodes and forms of Kṛṣṇa's early childhood, opening with the famous depiction of the infant lying upon a banyan leaf (vaṭapatraśāyī) sucking his lotus-foot, followed by scenes of butter-stealing, the subduing of the serpent Kāliya, and the breaking of the Yamalārjuna trees.

Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgara Press, 1903 (several reprints, e.g. rev. ed. by Nārāyaṇa Rāma Ācārya 'Kāvyatīrtha', 1950). — Standard NSP edition with commentary.
- Bhāratacampūḥ of Śrīmad-Anantabhaṭṭa, with 'Candrikā' Hindi commentary by Srīkānta Paṇḍeya. Varanasi: Chaukhambha Orientalia, 1984. — Popular Indian edition with Hindi commentary.

The Campūbhārata (or Bhāratacampū) of Anantabhaṭṭa is a classic Sanskrit campūkāvya (mixed verse and prose) that narrates the events of the Mahābhārata in twelve stabakas. Renowned for its elaborate śleṣa, yamaka, and classical ornate style, it has long served as a prominent standard work in classical Sanskrit literature curricula. This e-text is an abandoned digital fragment containing only the opening section of the first stabaka.

**Coverage:** partial — Incomplete. Āraṇyakāṇḍa, Kiṣkindhākāṇḍa, the rest of Sundarakāṇḍa, and the Yuddhakāṇḍa are omitted.

**Also known as:** Bhojacampū, Rāmāyaṇacampū

**Attribution:** The first five kāṇḍas of the Campūrāmāyaṇa (Bāla-, Ayodhyā-, Āraṇya-, Kiṣkindhā-, and Sundarakāṇḍa) are traditionally attributed to the Paramāra king Bhoja of Dhārā (11th century CE). The work was left incomplete and was supplemented with the sixth kāṇḍa (Yuddhakāṇḍa) by Lakṣmaṇa Bhaṭṭa (Lakṣmaṇa Sūri).

The Campūrāmāyaṇa (also known as Bhojacampū) is a celebrated Sanskrit mahācampū combining prose and verse to retell the Rāmāyaṇa narrative. Attributed to King Bhoja of Dhārā (11th century CE), it is regarded as a classic of the campū genre, renowned for its rhythmic prose and stylistic elegance. This online transcription is incomplete, containing only Bālakāṇḍa, Ayodhyākāṇḍa, and an unfinished Sundarakāṇḍa.

The Citramīmāṃsā is an influential treatise on Sanskrit alaṅkāraśāstra (rhetoric/poetics) by Appayya Dīkṣita (late 16th century). Intended as an exhaustive study of figures of sense (arthālaṅkāra), the work breaks off unfinished during the treatment of atiśayokti (hyperbole). Its critical definitions and illustrative verses became a central reference point in late classical poetics, prompting Paṇḍitarāja Jagannātha's polemical critique, the Citramīmāṃsākhaṇḍana.

Cārudatta (also known as Daridracārudatta) is a classical Sanskrit-Prakrit play in four acts attributed to Bhāsa. It relates the romance between Cārudatta, an impoverished and noble merchant of Ujjayinī, and the wealthy courtesan Vasantasenā, intertwined with scenes involving the thief Sajjalaka (Śarvilaka) and the thief's burglary of Cārudatta's house. The surviving text breaks off at the end of the fourth act without a formal conclusion or bharatavākya, paralleling the first four acts of Śūdraka's ten-act Mṛcchakaṭikā.

**Also known as:** Dattastava

**Attribution:** Composed by Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī (Tembē Svāmī, 1854–1914), a prominent 19th/20th-century ascetic and teacher in the Datta Sampradāya.

The Dattastavastotra (also known simply as Dattastava) is a nine-verse Sanskrit hymn in praise of Dattātreya composed by the Datta Sampradāya master Vāsudevānanda Sarasvatī (Tembē Svāmī, 1854–1914). Verses 1–8 invoke Dattātreya with the refrain 'dattātreyaṃ namāmi taṃ' for protection against malignant spirits (bhūtas, pretas, piśācas), physical afflictions, epidemic diseases, and poison, concluding with a phalaśruti promising divine favor.

The Dhūrtasamāgama ('The Gathering of Rogues') is a satirical farce (prahasana) composed in the early 14th century by the Maithili court poet and scholar Jyotirīśvara Kaviśekhara. Written under the Karṇāṭa ruler Narasiṃhadeva of Mithila, the play mocks the moral hypocrisy and greed of religious ascetics and legal figures. Its plot depicts a wandering ascetic (Viśvanagara) and his disciple (Durācāra) quarreling over the favors of a courtesan (Anaṅgasenā), who then submit their dispute to a corrupt and lascivious Brahmin arbitrator (Asajjātimiśra).

The Siṃhāsanadvātriṃśikā ('Thirty-Two Tales of the Throne'), also known as Vikramacarita or Dvātriṃśatputtalikā, is an acclaimed Sanskrit frame-story cycle celebrating the generosity, courage, and moral rectitude of the legendary King Vikramāditya. Whenever King Bhoja of Dhārā attempts to ascend the unearthed magical throne of Vikrama, each of the thirty-two statuettes (puttalikā) restraining him narrates an episode from Vikramāditya's life, challenging Bhoja to match such magnanimity. This e-text provides the complete Northern vulgate recension, including the opening Bhartṛhari legends, all thirty-two tales, and the liberation of the statues from their curse.

The Hammīramahākāvya is a 15th-century historical Sanskrit epic (mahākāvya) composed by the Jain monk Nayacandrasūri. The work combines classical court-poetic conventions with historical and regional bardic narratives.

The Kātyāyanyaṣṭaka is a nine-verse Sanskrit stotra dedicated to the goddess Kātyāyanī, specifically associated with the temple tradition at Aversa/Chatrapuri in coastal Karnataka. The text praises her attributes as the slayer of Mahiṣāsura, invokes her attendant deities and kulagotra lineages, and concludes with a phalaśruti verse attributed to or mentioning Kumṭhācārya.

A Vaishnava devotional hymn (stotra) enumerating one thousand names of Kṛṣṇa. The Madhyamavyāyoga ('The Middle One') is a one-act Sanskrit drama belonging to the vyāyoga genre, traditionally attributed to Bhāsa. Drawing on characters from the Mahābhārata, the play depicts Ghaṭotkaca demanding the sacrifice of the middle son of a wandering Brahmin family as food for his mother Hiḍimbā. Bhīma, the middle Pāṇḍava, intervenes by offering himself as the substitute victim, leading to a trial of strength and the joyful reunion of Bhīma with his demon-born son and wife.

This e-text preserves an anonymous metrical Sanskrit translation composed on the banks of the Tapti river.

- Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra (Śaṅkara, root text)
- Mānasollāsa (Sureśvara, commentary)

**Also known as:** Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotravārttika, Dakṣiṇāmūrtivārttika, Mānasollāsavārttika, Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotrabhāvārthavārtika

Modern scholars (including Paul Hacker and Karl H. Potter) note doctrinal differences between the Mānasollāsa and Sureśvara's undisputed vārttikas, suggesting the Mānasollāsa may be by a later namesake or follower of the Advaita school.

The Mānasollāsa is an influential metrical exposition (vārttika) in ten chapters (ullāsas) expounding Śaṅkara's celebrated ten-verse hymn, the Dakṣiṇāmūrtistotra. Traditionally ascribed to Sureśvara, the text systematically develops the hymn's pithy Advaita Vedānta doctrines, treating themes such as the illusory nature of phenomenal diversity (māyā/vivarta), the mirror-like reflection of the world in pure consciousness, the critiques of rival philosophical views (including Buddhist Śūnyavāda and Nyāya-Vaiśeṣika), and the ultimate identity of the individual soul (jīva) with Parameśvara (Śiva-Dakṣiṇāmūrti).

The Mṛtyuñjayamānasikapūjāstotra is a 46-verse devotional hymn attributed to Śaṅkara providing an elaborate mental worship (mānasapūjā) directed to Śiva as Mṛtyuñjaya. The Naiṣadhīyacarita (or Naiṣadha) by the philosopher-poet Śrīharṣa (12th century CE) is one of the five celebrated mahākāvyas ('great court epics') of classical Sanskrit literature. Across 22 cantos, it narrates the story of King Nala and Princess Damayantī up to their wedding and honeymoon, elaborating on the Nalopākhyāna from the Mahābhārata. Famed for its intricate linguistic craftsmanship, double entendres (śleṣa), and profound philosophical references, the work is traditionally regarded as the ultimate test of scholarship ('naiṣadhaṃ vidvad-auṣadham').

**Coverage:** complete — 8 adhyāyas, ending with the colophon of adhyāya 8 (rājavyāpārakathana, 100 vv.) and 'nītiprakāśikā samāptā'; mūla only, no commentary.

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the epic sage Vaiśampāyana (a pupil of Vyāsa), who recites political and military doctrine to King Janamejaya at Takṣaśilā. Modern scholarship considers the work a late medieval or early modern compilation on Dhanurveda and Nītiśāstra.

The Nītiprakāśikā is a Sanskrit treatise on statecraft (nītiśāstra) and the science of warfare (dhanurveda), framed as a dialogue between the sage Vaiśampāyana and King Janamejaya. It provides detailed classifications and descriptions of traditional weapons (mukta, amukta, muktāmukta, yantramukta), battle formations (vyūha), military tactics, and the ethical and administrative duties of kings (rājavyāpāra).

The Padminīpariṇaya is a ten-act Sanskrit drama (styled a prakaraṇa in its opening) by Elattūr Sundararāja Bhaṭṭācārya, a nineteenth-century South Indian Vaiṣṇava poet. Under the story of prince Bhāskara (the sun) winning princess Padminī (the lotus), with a sub-plot of Kumudākara and Kaumudī and the guidance of the yogin Śāradānanda, it allegorically retells the Rāmāyaṇa (Bhāskara = Rāma, Padminī = Sītā/Lakṣmī, Jīmūta = Rāvaṇa), as Varadarāja's prefatory Kathāsaṅgraha explains.

Structured around nine core philosophical propositions (prameyas) derived from the Mādhva tradition—including the supreme reality of Viṣṇu/Kṛṣṇa, the ontological reality of the created world, the real distinction between souls and God, and the three means of valid knowledge (pratyakṣa, anumāna, and śabda)—the work validates Gauḍīya theology through extensive śruti, smṛti, and Purāṇic citations.

The Pratimānāṭaka ('The Statue Play') is a seven-act drama attributed to Bhāsa, dramatizing the Rāmāyaṇa story from the aborted consecration of Rāma to his return to Ayodhyā. The central dramatic invention occurs in Act 3 in the ancestral gallery (pratimāgṛha), where Bharata deduces King Daśaratha's death upon seeing his portrait statue installed alongside those of deceased ancestors. The play portrays Kaikeyī's demands in a sympathetic light, explaining them through an inescapable ancestral curse rather than malice.

**Attribution:** Composed in Sanskrit and embedded in the Uttarakāṇḍa of Gosvāmī Tulasīdāsa's Rāmacaritamānasa, recited by a brāhmaṇa devotee to propitiate Rudra on behalf of his disciple (later Kākabhusuṇḍi).

The Rudrāṣṭaka is an eight-stanza Sanskrit hymn (plus a concluding phalaśruti verse) in praise of Śiva, composed by Tulasīdāsa in the Uttarakāṇḍa of his Rāmacaritamānasa. It is placed in the mouth of a brāhmaṇa praying to pacify Śiva's wrath against his disrespectful student. The stotra extols Śiva both as the nirguṇa, transcendental reality beyond name and form, and as the compassionate, iconic saguṇa deity.

The Kuvalayānanda of Appayya Dīkṣita (16th c.) is a standard handbook of arthālaṃkāras whose definition-and-example kārikās are largely taken from Jayadeva's Candrāloka. This e-text gives the kārikās for the figures from Upamā to Udātta (vv. 1–104) without Appayya's prose vṛtti, each explained in T. K. Rāmacandra Ayyar's modern Sanskrit commentary Samanvayā, which glosses words, analyses compounds and shows how each definition fits its example (lakṣaṇasamanvaya), with further illustrative verses.

The text was transcribed and proofread from a scan of the 1953 Vavilla edition (Index 'बृहत्स्तोत्ररत्नाकरः (प्रथमः भागः).pdf'), and the page was created on 2021-08-31 by user Soorya Hebbar (revid 320150) during the 'पाठशुद्धिस्पर्धा आगस्ट् 2021' proofreading contest. ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — An alphabetical hymn with an opening verse ('atha kathamapi …') and one verse for each letter from a to kṣa, about 50 in all, with the refrain 'sāmba sadāśiva …'. It ends with the colophon 'suvarṇamālāstutiḥ sampūrṇā'. The e-text's verse numbering is erratic: many numbers are missing, and the second-last verse is numbered 41.

**Also known as:** Suvarṇamālāstotra, Varṇamālāstotra, Śivasuvarṇamālāstuti

The Suvarṇamālāstuti is an alphabetical devotional hymn (mātṛkā- or akṣaramālāstuti) addressed to Śiva as Sāmba Sadāśiva, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. Comprising 50 verses, each stanza begins with a sequential letter of the Sanskrit varṇamālā (from the vowel 'a' to 'kṣa') and incorporates the refrain 'sāmba sadāśiva śambho śaṅkara śaraṇaṃ me tava caraṇayugam'. The text blends Vedāntic philosophical references (such as śruti citations and upādhi terminology) with Śaiva devotional praise.

The Tulajāṣṭaka is a short Śākta devotional stotra addressed to the goddess Tulajā Bhavānī, the prominent Kuladevatā of Maharashtra worshipped at Tuljapur. Composed of eight descriptive verses each ending with the refrain 'vande 'ham ādyāṃ tulajābhavānīm', it extols the divine mother's beauty, adorned attire, weapons, and cosmic worship by Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva, followed by a two-verse phalaśruti.

Celebrated as the paramount dramatic expression of the pathetic sentiment (karuṇarasa), especially in the third act ('Chāyā'), the play reimagines the tragic conclusion of the Vālmīki Rāmāyaṇa into a poignant dramatic reconciliation.

The Veṅkaṭeśastotra is an 11-verse Śrīvaiṣṇava hymn to Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala. It is the second of the four parts of the daily morning recitation at Tirupati, after the Suprabhāta, and tradition ascribes it to Prativādibhayaṅkara Aṇṇa. The verses ask the lord of Veṅkaṭa (Vṛṣaśaila) for protection and forgiveness, and declare exclusive devotion to him in his Kṛṣṇa and Rāma forms (vv. 4–8).

The Vyaktiviveka is an 11th-century treatise on Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) by Rājānaka Mahimabhaṭṭa of Kashmir. It was written to refute the theory of suggestion (dhvani/vyañjanā) formulated by Ānandavardhana, arguing that all implied aesthetic meanings are fully explainable by logical inference (anumāna). This first chapter (vimarśa 1) mounts an epistemological critique of Ānandavardhana's definition and main divisions of dhvani.

The Āmnāyastotra is a 22-verse metrical manual of the Advaita monastic tradition outlining the four cardinal monastic seats (maṭhas) attributed to Śaṅkara: Dvārakā (west), Govardhana/Purī (east), Badarikāśrama (north), and Śṛṅgerī (south). For each maṭha, it systematically details the associated Veda, Mahāvākya, founding disciple (Padmapāda, Hastāmalaka, Toṭaka, Sureśvara), presiding deity, Śakti, tīrtha, sampradāya, and Daśanāmī ascetic titles.

The fifth sarga of the Janmakāṇḍa of the Ānandarāmāyaṇa recounts the recitation and efficacy of the Rāmarakṣā hymn. Framed as a dialogue between Rāmadāsa and Viṣṇudāsa, it narrates how Śiva revealed this protective kavaca to Pārvatī to empower Skanda to defeat Tārakāsura, and how Vālmīki later employed it to protect Sītā's son Kuśa from baleful planetary spirits. - Bṛhatstotraratnākara, ed. Nārāyaṇa Rāma Ācārya, Bombay: Nirnaya Sagar Press, 1952. — Standard devotional compendium containing the vulgate text.

**Translations:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete stotra as extracted from Mahābhārata Anuśāsanaparvan 17 (vulgate numbering), comprising an invocatory dhyāna verse, 182 numbered ślokas (introductory narrative, 1,000 names, and phalaśruti), and closing colophon.

**Also known as:** Śivasahasranāma, Taṇḍikṛtaśivasahasranāmastotra, Mahābhārata, Anuśāsanaparvan, adhyāya 17

**Attribution:** Within the Mahābhārata frame, Kṛṣṇa narrates to Yudhiṣṭhira the stotra as taught by Upamanyu, who received it from the sage Taṇḍi. The larger epic is traditionally ascribed to Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana Vyāsa.

The Śivasahasranāmastotra ('Hymn of the Thousand Names of Śiva') is a major Śaiva devotional hymn extracted from the Anuśāsanaparvan of the Mahābhārata (adhyāya 17). Narrated by Upamanyu to Kṛṣṇa, who in turn recounts it to Yudhiṣṭhira, the hymn contains the one thousand epithets of Śiva originally revealed to the sage Taṇḍi. It synthesizes Vedic, cosmogonic, and philosophical aspects of Śiva and forms one of the standard liturgical sahasranāmas of the Hindu tradition.

The Śivānandalaharī ('Wave of the bliss of Śiva') is a hymn of 100 verses to Śiva in various metres, traditionally ascribed to Śaṅkara. It joins Advaita themes to fervent bhakti, using extended images for the devotee's mind: an elephant to be bound with the chain of devotion, a monkey, a bride. It also uses images of devotion itself, such as the hunter Kaṇṇappa's offering. The closing verses offer the poem to Śiva as a bride and assert his supremacy over Brahmā and Viṣṇu.

The Candraśekharāṣṭaka is a popular Śaiva devotional hymn (stotra) comprising eight stanzas in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita metre addressed to Śiva as Candraśekhara ('he who wears the crescent moon as crest-jewel'). Traditionally attributed to the young sage Mārkaṇḍeya seeking refuge against Yama, each verse invokes Śiva's mythological deeds and iconographical forms, culminating in the refrain asserting fearlessness before death.

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_GK19_ilx_ws_srikrsnavilasam`

**Author:** Sukumāra

**Collection / category:** Poetry / GK19

**Source:** Sanskrit Wikisource

**Link:** [https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%B6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%95%E0%A5%83%E0%A4%B7%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A3%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%B2%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AE%E0%A5%8D](https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/%E0%A4%B6%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%B0%E0%A5%80%E0%A4%95%E0%A5%83%E0%A4%B7%E0%A5%8D%E0%A4%A3%E0%A4%B5%E0%A4%BF%E0%A4%B2%E0%A4%BE%E0%A4%B8%E0%A4%AE%E0%A5%8D)

**Retrieved via:** ilx_skt meta-repository of Sanskrit etexts (Intellexus project), [https://github.com/con-jo-ry/ilx_skt](https://github.com/con-jo-ry/ilx_skt), file `corpus/wikisource/sāhitya/śrīkṛṣṇavilāsam.xml` (commit `222bcc4`)

**License (source text):** Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike 4.0 International (CC BY-SA 4.0) — https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/

**License (ilx_skt TEI markup & metadata):** Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0), https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** not determined

**E-text:** Sanskrit Wikisource contributors (https://sa.wikisource.org/wiki/श्रीकृष्णविलासम्, plain transcription, no scan or print source given); transliterated to IAST and encoded in TEI by the ERC Intellexus project (ilx_skt, commit 222bcc4).

**Evidence:**
- The Wikisource wikitext has no scan, Index page, year or source note; it gives only the author and the poem divided into four sargas (checked via the sa.wikisource API).
- The same text, with the same verse numbering style (1-01 …), the same extent (4 sargas, ending at 4-86) and the same colophon, is on sanskritdocuments.org (doc_vishhnu/shrIkRiShNavilAsakAvyam.html), 'Encoded and proofread by PSA Easwaran', transliteration credited to N. S. Panicker (Malayalam transliteration blog), updated 2 Aug 2012. That page names no print source either. The Wikisource text very probably derives from it.
- The four-sarga extent matches T. K. Ramachandra Aiyar's popular Palghat edition (first four cantos with the Vilāsinī), but no reading-level comparison was possible, so this is not claimed as the source.

**Other editions:**
- Kṛṣṇavilāsa of Sukumāra, ed. K. Jayammal, Madras: Higginbothams, 1982 (originally a PhD thesis, University of Madras, 1979). — The only edition of the complete text in 12 sargas (according to the INDOLOGY list, Oct. 2013).
- Kṛṣṇavilāsa with the Vilāsinī commentary of Rāmapāṇivāda, ed. T. K. Ramachandra Aiyar, Palghat: R. S. Vadhyar & Sons ('Sanskrit study made easy' series), 3rd ed. — Popular school edition of the first four cantos.
- Kṛṣṇavilāsa, Kerala Granthamālā series, Palghat, 1906–1908. — Incomplete edition (8 sargas), cited without a precise title on the INDOLOGY list.

**Translations:**
- K. P. A. Menon, Nine Gems of Sanskrit Literature, vol. 1, Delhi: Nag Publishers, 1996 (text with English translation and notes). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Sargas 1–4 only. Sarga 4 ends at v. 4.86 with the colophon 'iti sukumārakṛtau kṛṣṇavilāsakāvye caturthaḥ sargaḥ'. The complete poem has 12 sargas (K. Jayammal's 1982 edition, the only one of the complete text). Sargas 1–4 are the portion in common school use; the popular Palghat edition with the Vilāsinī commentary also has only the first four cantos.

**Also known as:** Śrīkṛṣṇavilāsa, Śrīkṛṣṇavilāsakāvya

**Attribution:** Ascribed to the Kerala poet Sukumāra (Sukumārakavi) in the heading and the colophons. His date is uncertain and is not given here.

The Kṛṣṇavilāsa is a Sanskrit mahākāvya by the Kerala poet Sukumāra on the life of Kṛṣṇa, written in a lucid Vaidarbhī style and long used as a textbook kāvya in Kerala. This e-text contains sargas 1–4. They begin with the description of Mount Meru and the gods' appeal to Viṣṇu over the burden of the Earth, and go on to Kṛṣṇa's birth and his childhood in Gokula, ending with Kṛṣṇa and Balarāma tending the herds in Vraja.
