The Kṛṣṇāṣṭaka is a devotional octet addressed to Kṛṣṇa, in which each stanza concludes with the refrain 'namāmi rādhikādhipam' ('I bow to the lord of Rādhikā'). It celebrates Kṛṣṇa's divine deeds from his childhood in Vraja to the Mahābhārata war, closing with a ninth verse promising liberation from rebirth.

- Ānandarāmāyaṇa, edited by Rāmateja Śāstrī Pāṇḍeya, Vārāṇasī: Paṇḍita Pustakālaya, 1958 (reprinted Chaukhambha Sanskrit Sansthan). — Standard edition containing the Manoharakāṇḍa, sarga 13.

The Rāmagītā is an Advaita Vedānta philosophical dialogue forming the fifth chapter of the Uttarakāṇḍa of the Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa. In response to questions posed by Lakṣmaṇa, Rāma teaches that release from saṃsāra is attained not by ritual works (karma) or a combination of knowledge and action (jñānakarmasamuccaya), but solely through direct knowledge (jñāna) of the non-dual Self (ātman). The work systematically synthesizes classical Upaniṣadic Advaita epistemology with devotion to Rāma.

The Rāmahṛdaya ('Heart of Rāma') is a nine-verse Advaita teaching from the first sarga of the Bālakāṇḍa of the Adhyātmarāmāyaṇa, which circulates on its own as a stotra. A short Vaiṣṇava devotional song (gīta/stotra) consisting of 18 verses in praise of Rāma, Sītā, and Lakṣmaṇa. The first 16 verses comprise rhyming stanzas celebrating their virtues, deeds, and divine attributes, each concluding with the refrain 'rahasi naumi tau sītārāmalakṣmaṇau'. The final two verses consist of rhythmic nāmasaṅkīrtana repetitions of the divine names of Rāma, Sītā, Kṛṣṇa, and Rādhā.

The Śrīveṅkaṭeśaprapatti is a 16-verse Śrīvaiṣṇava stotra of ritual self-surrender (śaraṇāgati/prapatti) addressed to Lord Veṅkaṭeśvara of Tirumala. It constitutes the second section of the traditional four-part liturgical dawn service (Suprabhāta, Stotra, Prapatti, and Maṅgalaśāsana) recited daily at the Tirumala temple. The opening verse invokes Śrī (Lakṣmī) as the divine mediator (puruṣakāra), followed by fourteen verses praising the Lord's lotus feet, and a closing declaration of service (kaiṅkarya).

The Śṛṅgāraprakāśa is an encyclopedic masterwork of Sanskrit poetics (alaṅkāraśāstra) and dramaturgy (nāṭyaśāstra) in 36 chapters (prakāśas) composed by King Bhoja of Dhārā (11th century). The Ūrubhaṅga ('The Shattering of the Thighs') is a one-act Sanskrit drama (often classified as an utsṛṣṭikāṅka) attributed to Bhāsa, based on the final mace duel between Duryodhana and Bhīma in the Mahābhārata. Formatted as an instructional dialogue between Prajāpati and Guha (Kārttikeya), it describes the proper materials, construction, stringing, and ritual consecration of a japa rosary (akṣamālā). The Atharvaśikhopaniṣad is a minor Śaiva text associated with the Atharvaveda, listed among the fourteen Śaiva Upaniṣads in the Muktikā canon. Framed as a discourse delivered by the sage Atharvan to Pippalāda, Aṅgiras, and Sanatkumāra, it expounds meditation upon the sacred syllable Om (Praṇava). The text identifies the constituent mātrās of Om with Vedic fires, deities, worlds, and states of consciousness, establishing the fourth transcendental quarter (turīya) as Śiva (Īśāna, Śaṃbhu), who is the ultimate reality and sole cause to be meditated upon.

Consisting of thirteen verses and a concluding prose formula, it praises the supreme non-dual principle (identified with the single syllable Oṃ / Brahman) as both the transcendent origin and the immanent cosmic creator manifesting as Rudra, Viṣṇu, Hiraṇyagarbha, and all living forms. The Sarvasāropaniṣad is a short Sāmānya-Vedānta Upaniṣad structured as a catechistic glossary of Advaita metaphysics. In twenty-one prose passages and concluding verses, it poses and answers questions defining fundamental concepts: bondage (bandha), liberation (mokṣa), avidyā, vidyā, the four states of consciousness (jāgrat, svapna, suṣupti, turīya), the five sheaths (pañcakośa), the soul and witness consciousness (kartṛ, jīva, kṣetrajña, sākṣin, kūṭastha, antaryāmin), concluding with the identification of the innermost self (pratyagātman) with unconditioned Brahman.

The Skandopaniṣad is a minor Upanishad associated with the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda (No. 51 in the Muktikā canon). Opening with a speaker's declaration to Mahādeva of his identity with Acyuta and Śiva (attributed to Skanda), the text teaches radical non-difference between the individual soul (jīva) and Śiva, as well as the ultimate identity of Śiva and Viṣṇu ('śivāya viṣṇurūpāya śivarūpāya viṣṇave'). It synthesizes Śaiva and Vaiṣṇava devotional motifs into Advaita Vedānta, concluding with the Vedic refrain 'tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam'.

It details cosmogony from primal darkness (tamas) through the cosmic egg and the cosmic Puruṣa, followed by dissolution (pralaya) of elements back into the supreme deity Nārāyaṇa. The Vajrasūcyupaniṣad ('Diamond Needle Upaniṣad') is a short prose treatise traditionally linked to the Sāmaveda that critically examines the defining criteria of a Brāhmaṇa. Through sequential refutations, it denies that brāhmaṇahood consists in the individual self (jīva), the physical body (deha), caste or lineage by birth (jāti), scriptural learning (jñāna), ritual action (karma), or religious merit (dhārmika). It concludes that a true Brāhmaṇa is defined exclusively by direct experiential realization of the non-dual, attribute-free Brahman (sat-cit-ānanda) coupled with self-mastery and absence of egotism.

This e-text comes from Brahmaśaṅkara Miśra's revised edition of the Bhaiṣajyaratnāvalī, a widely used Āyurvedic formulary ascribed to Govindadāsa. It contains Brahmaśaṅkara's Pariśiṣṭa (treatments for pitta and kapha disorders and a collection of formulae he had tried himself, anubhūtayoga), his concluding verses on the revision, and chapters 90–106 of the main text. These chapters cover 'special diseases' such as ojomeha, lasīkāmeha, dhvajabhaṅga, kidney and kloman disorders, phiraṅga (syphilis), mercury poisoning, brain disorders, sunstroke and gynaecological complaints, and end with the reviving of the apparently dying (apamumūrṣu).

The Bhāṣikasūtra (or Bhāṣikapariśiṣṭasūtra), traditionally attributed to Kātyāyana, is a short phonetic treatise (pariśiṣṭa) of the Śukla Yajurveda setting forth the rules of accentuation (bhāṣikasvara) in Brāhmaṇa prose, particularly the Śatapathabrāhmaṇa. It formulates the two-accent system (udātta and anudātta) of the Brāhmaṇa in contrast to the tripartite mantra accentuation, describes verbal accent shift, and correlates recitation tones with musical pitches.

The Chāndogyabrāhmaṇa (widely known as the Mantrabrāhmaṇa) is a Vedic ritual text of the Kauthuma śākhā of the Sāmaveda comprising two prapāṭhakas of eight khaṇḍas each. **Also known as:** Dhanurveda, Śivaproktadhanurveda, Sadāśivaproktadhanurveda

**Attribution:** The treatise frames its instruction on archery and warfare as divine revelation from Sadāśiva (Śiva).

The Sadāśivadhanurveda is a classical Sanskrit treatise on the martial arts and archery traditionally framed as revealed by Sadāśiva (Śiva). It covers social eligibility and ritual initiation into weaponry, astrological timing for training, protective aṅganyāsa formulas, weapon dimensions and classifications, bowmanship techniques, target practice (vedha), omenology on the battlefield, and army deployment (vyūha).

The Hārītasaṃhitā is a Sanskrit Āyurvedic treatise presented as an instructional dialogue between the sage Ātreya and his pupil Hārīta. Divided into six divisions (sthānas)—including Prathama- (Prakīrṇa- / Sūtra-), Dvitīya- (Doṣadhātu-), Tṛtīya- (Cikitsā-), Kalpa-, and Śārīrasthāna, followed by a pariśiṣṭa—it treats nosology, clinical therapy, pharmacology, and dietetics. In four adhyāyas it gives esoteric interpretations of the sāman chant (especially the gāyatra-sāman and the udgītha), the syllable om, prāṇa and the correspondences between ritual, cosmos and person. - P. V. Tewari (ed. & trans.), Kāśyapa-Saṃhitā or Vṛddhajīvakīya Tantra, Varanasi: Chaukhambha Visvabharati, 1996. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text keeps the gaps of the single Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript. It contains parts of the Sūtrasthāna (ending 'sūtrasthānasyaitāvān eva bhāga upalabdhaḥ'), Vimānasthāna (likewise), Śārīra-, Indriya-, Cikitsā- (fragmentary), Siddhi- (chapters 1–7) and Kalpasthāna (ending 'samāptaṃ ca kalpasthānam samāptā ceyaṃ saṃhitā'). The Nidānasthāna is missing. The Khilasthāna breaks off in the chapter on regions ('dakṣiṇāṃ diśam āśritya deśā vi---') with the editorial note 'khilasthānasyaitāvān eva bhāga upalabdhaḥ ... etāvaty evopalabdhabhāge viśrāmyati'. The text itself gives its full extent as 120 chapters plus the Khila.

**Also known as:** Vṛddhajīvakīyatantra

**Attribution:** Presented as the teaching of Mārīca Kaśyapa to Vṛddhajīvaka (hence Vṛddhajīvakīyatantra) and 'restored' by Vātsya (colophons: 'vṛddhajīvakīye kaumārabhṛtye vātsyapratisaṃskṛte').

The Kāśyapasaṃhitā (Vṛddhajīvakīyatantra) is an early Āyurvedic compendium centred on kaumārabhṛtya (care of children, together with pregnancy and the postnatal period). It is framed as Kaśyapa's teaching to Vṛddhajīvaka and was redacted by Vātsya. It covers infant feeding and electuaries (lehana), dentition, children's diseases, demonic seizers (grahas) including the Revatīkalpa, and treatments for mothers and wet-nurses. It survives only in one incomplete Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript, first published by Hemarāja Śarmā in 1938.

Combining metrical yajus mantras with archaic brāhmaṇa-style ritual and mythological expositions, it provides the liturgical foundation for Vedic ceremonies such as the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnyādheya, Agnicayana, and Aśvamedha.

The Mādhavanidāna (originally titled Rogaviniścaya) is a foundational 7th–8th-century Ayurvedic treatise devoted to pathology and clinical diagnosis (nidāna). Composed by Mādhavakara, the text systematizes the five diagnostic factors (pañcanidāna: nidāna, pūrvarūpa, rūpa, upaśaya, and saṃprāpti) across sixty-nine disease classifications, forming the earliest and central work of Ayurveda's 'minor triad' (laghutrayī).

**Attribution:** The pulse-examination manual is traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. The opening verses (segments 2–3) were composed by Śaṅkara (styled 'Brahmānvita-Śaṅkara'), who wrote the Hindi commentary 'Vaidyapriyā' at the request of publisher Jayakṛṣṇadāsa.

The Nāḍīparīkṣā ('Examination of the Pulse') is an Āyurvedic manual of pulse diagnosis traditionally attributed to Maharṣi Kaṇāda. It describes the palpation of the radial pulse (jīvanāḍī) at the wrist with three fingers, interpreting rhythm, speed, and volume via metaphorical animal gaits (leech, serpent, frog, crow, swan) corresponding to vāta, pitta, kapha, and their combinations. It further details diagnostic pulse variations across various morbid states and fatal prognostic signs (ariṣṭalakṣaṇa).

The Taittirīyabrāhmaṇa is the principal Brāhmaṇa prose text of the Taittirīya recension of the Kṛṣṇa (Black) Yajurveda. Structured into three kāṇḍas, it expounds the theological rationale, liturgical formulas, and rituals of major śrauta rites including the Agnyādhāna, Gavāmayana, Vājapeya, Soma sacrifices, Nakṣatreṣṭis, Sautrāmaṇī, Aśvamedha, and Agnicayana. The third kāṇḍa also preserves significant theological and cosmological narratives, notably an archaic version of the Naciketas story (3.11.8).

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (not determined):** Not determined; a Wikisource compilation from several unnamed sources.

**E-text:** Sanskrit Wikisource contributors; compiled, transliterated to IAST and TEI-encoded by the Intellexus project (ilx_skt)

**Evidence:**
- Wikisource page and ilx_skt TEI header name no source.
- The Suśruta/Ḍalhaṇa part has the colophon form of the Jādavjī Trikamjī Ācārya edition (Nirṇaya Sāgara), but this is common to all reprints and was not verified against page or line markers.
- The opening section carries modern reference abbreviations ('hṛ sū 5 84', 'hṛ śā 3 55', 'saṅgrahe u a 50'), so it was probably taken from a modern edition or textbook compilation.

**Other editions:**
- Suśrutasaṃhitā with Ḍalhaṇa's Nibandhasaṅgraha and Gayadāsa's Nyāyacandrikā, ed. Jādavjī Trikamjī Ācārya, Bombay: Nirṇaya Sāgara Press, 1938 (and reprints). — Standard edition of Suśruta Utt. 65 with Ḍalhaṇa.
- W. K. Lele, The Doctrine of the Tantrayuktis, Varanasi: Chaukhamba Surabharati Prakashan, 1981. — Study that collates the tantrayukti lists (not an edition of this e-text).

## Contents

**Coverage:** excerpt — Lines (of 454 text lines): 1–140 opening exposition of tantraguṇas/tantradoṣas; 141–~210 Indu on AS Utt. 50; ~211–246 Caraka Si. 12.41–48 with commentary; 247–364 Suśruta Utt. 65 with Ḍalhaṇa, complete with colophons; 365–~412 Indu's section repeated; ~413–454 a further exposition of the tantrayuktis that partly duplicates the opening section. Each is an excerpt of a larger work; nothing in the e-text is a complete independent work except Suśruta Utt. 65 with Ḍalhaṇa.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Exposition of tantraguṇas: 36 tantrayuktis, 7 kalpanās, arthāśrayas, 17 tācchīlyas, 15 tantradoṣas (lines 1–140), with examples from the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and a citation of the Saṅgraha (Uttara 50) (commentary passage (source not identified; apparently from a commentary on the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, possibly Aruṇadatta's Sarvāṅgasundarī))
- Śaśilekhā on Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha, Uttarasthāna 50 (tantrayukti section), headed 'indu tantrayuktiḥ' (Indu, commentary (with root verses))
- Carakasaṃhitā, Siddhisthāna 12.41–48 (tantrayukti verses) with Āyurvedadīpikā (Caraka (Dṛḍhabala), Cakrapāṇidatta, root text with commentary (attribution inferred from content: verse numbers 42–48, mention of Bhaṭṭāra Haricandra))
- Suśrutasaṃhitā, Uttaratantra 65 (Tantrayuktyadhyāya) with Nibandhasaṅgraha (Suśruta, Ḍalhaṇa, root text with commentary (colophons present))
- Indu's tantrayukti section again (duplicate) and a further, partly repeated exposition of the tantrayuktis with Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya/Caraka examples (duplicate / unidentified commentary passages)

**Also known as:** Tantrayuktayaḥ, Tantrayuktyadhyāya

**Attribution:** Composite Wikisource page. Identified parts: Indu's Śaśilekhā on Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha Uttara 50 (explicit heading 'indu tantrayuktiḥ'); Suśruta Uttara 65 with Ḍalhaṇa (explicit colophons 'iti suśrutasaṃhitāyām uttaratantre tantrabhūṣaṇādhyāyeṣu tantrayuktir nāma' / 'iti śrīḍalhaṇaviracitāyāṃ nibandhasaṅgrahākhyāyāṃ ... pañcaṣaṣṭitamo'dhyāyaḥ'); a commentary on Caraka Siddhi 12.41–48 that is in content Cakrapāṇi's Āyurvedadīpikā (inferred, not verified against the printed text). The long opening exposition and the closing passage are not identified.

An anthology of Sanskrit passages on tantrayukti, the set of 32 or 36 devices used to compose and interpret technical treatises, as discussed in the Āyurvedic classics. It contains an exposition of tantraguṇas, kalpanās, tācchīlyas and tantradoṣas illustrated from the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya, Indu's commentary on the tantrayukti section of the Aṣṭāṅgasaṅgraha, the tantrayukti verses of Caraka's Siddhisthāna with commentary, and the Tantrayukti chapter of the Suśrutasaṃhitā (Uttaratantra 65) with Ḍalhaṇa's Nibandhasaṅgraha. Some passages are duplicated.

The teacher lineages trace back from historical teachers through ancient ṛṣis to divine figures and ultimately to Brahman Svayambhū.

The Āyurvedaprakāśa of Upādhyāya Mādhava (c. 17th c.) is a rasaśāstra treatise on preparing and using mercury, minerals, metals, gems and poisons in medicine. **Attribution:** The Dhātupāṭha is an essential ancillary text (upadeśa) of the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition. Although the root list in its earliest form goes back to Pāṇini (ca. 4th century BCE), the meaning glosses (arthanirdeśa) were traditionally considered an addition by Bhīmasena or subsequent grammarians.

The Dhātupāṭha is the canonical verbal inventory of the Pāṇinian grammatical tradition (Vyākaraṇa), serving as the foundational auxiliary text to the Aṣṭādhyāyī. It arranges approximately two thousand verbal roots into ten conjugation classes (gaṇas), starting from bhvādi and ending with curādi. Each entry provides the root's base form with diacritical markers (anubandhas) denoting accent, voice (parasmaipada, ātmanepada, or ubhayapada), and morphophonological traits, alongside traditional semantic glosses.

The Aṣṭādhyāyī of Pāṇini (c. 4th century BCE) is the foundational masterpiece of Sanskrit linguistics and the primary Vedāṅga text for grammar (Vyākaraṇa), formulating nearly 4,000 highly condensed aphoristic rules across eight chapters. The Baudhāyanagṛhyasūtra is a principal domestic ritual manual of the Baudhāyana school of the Black Yajurveda (Kṛṣṇayajurveda, Taittirīya śākhā). Structured in four praśnas, it covers the seven standard pākayajña archetypes and life-cycle rites (saṃskāras) from marriage (vivāha) through pregnancy, birth, childhood ceremonies, Vedic initiation (upanayana), study vows, ancestral offerings, house construction, and domestic prāyaścittas. It constitutes the gṛhya component of the comprehensive Baudhāyana Kalpasūtra.

It prescribes, largely from the Adhvaryu's standpoint, the solemn rites from the Darśapūrṇamāsa, Agnyādheya, Agnihotra, Paśubandha and Cāturmāsya through the Agniṣṭoma, Agnicayana, Vājapeya, Rājasūya, Aśvamedha and sattras. Distinctive are its discursive Dvaidha sections recording differing opinions of Baudhāyana, Śālīki, Aupamanyava and other teachers, followed by Karmānta and Prāyaścitta sections.

The Bhāradvājagṛhyasūtra is a Vedic manual of domestic ritual affiliated with the Bhāradvāja school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Arranged in three praśnas, the work systematically describes lifecycle rites (saṃskāras) such as upanayana (vedic initiation), vivāha (marriage), and simantonnayana/childbirth ceremonies, followed by domestic oblations (pākayajñas), ancestral offerings, and prāyaścitta expiations.

The Bhāṣāvṛtti is a concise 12th-century commentary on Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī by the Buddhist grammarian Puruṣottamadeva of Bengal. It systematically treats only the sūtras applicable to classical Sanskrit (bhāṣā), deliberately omitting rules restricted to Vedic usage (chāndasa) and Vedic accentuation (svara). - The chapter division into 8 adhyāyas and verse numbering corresponds to the recension popularized by Arthur A. Macdonell (1904), but Sanskrit Wikisource gives no printed edition citation or critical apparatus.

**Other editions:**
- Macdonell, Arthur Anthony (ed.), The Bṛhad-devatā Attributed to Śaunaka: A Summary of the Deities and Myths of the Ṛgveda, Part 1: Sanskrit Text and Introduction, Harvard Oriental Series, vol. 5, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1904 (repr. Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1965, 1994). — Standard critical edition with introduction and textual notes.
- Rajendralala Mitra (ed.), The Bṛhad-devatā; or, An Index to the Gods of the Rigveda, by Śaunaka, Bibliotheca Indica, work no. 127, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1889–1892. — Editio princeps.
- Tokunaga, Muneo (ed.), The Bṛhaddevatā: Text of the Śaunaka Śākhā, Kyoto: Rinsen Book Co., 1997. — Revised critical edition based on manuscripts of the Śaunaka recension.

**Translations:**
- Macdonell, Arthur Anthony, The Bṛhad-devatā Attributed to Śaunaka: A Summary of the Deities and Myths of the Ṛgveda, Part 2: Translation and Notes, Harvard Oriental Series, vol. 6, Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1904. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text in 8 adhyāyas, extending from Adhyāya 1, verse 1 to Adhyāya 8, verse 140 (concluding with the traditional final verse 'sa brahyāmṛtamatyantaṃ... viśati jyotiruttamam || 140||').

**Also known as:** Śaunakīya Bṛhaddevatā

**Attribution:** The Bṛhaddevatā is traditionally ascribed to the ancient teacher Śaunaka, though modern scholarship (Macdonell, Tokunaga) views it as a product of the Śaunaka school, likely composed around the 4th century BCE or slightly later.

The Bṛhaddevatā ('Great [Index of] Deities') is an extensive metrical treatise in eight adhyāyas belonging to the Vedāṅga and Anukramaṇī literature of the Ṛgveda, traditionally attributed to Śaunaka. Composed predominantly in anuṣṭubh verses, it systematically catalogs the deities presiding over every hymn, verse, hemistich, and quarter-verse of the Ṛgveda Saṃhitā in sequential order. In addition to ritual classification and etymological remarks reflecting Nirukta traditions, the work is especially renowned for preserving early narrative legends (ākhyānas) explaining the mythical contexts of the hymns.

- Siddhāntaśiromaṇiḥ svopajñavāsanābhāṣyasaṃvalito Nṛsiṃhadaivajñakṛtavārttikopetaśca, ed. Muralīdhara Caturveda, Pustakālaya-durlabhagrantha-prakāśana-yojanā series, Varanasi. — Includes the Vāsanābhāṣya with Nṛsiṃha's Vāsanāvārttika. Known only from a library-catalogue snippet, with no year checked.

**Translations:**
- Lancelot Wilkinson (trans.), revised by Bāpū Deva Śāstrin, The Siddhānta Śiromaṇi: Golādhyāya. Bibliotheca Indica, Calcutta, 1861. (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — This is Part 1 of the Ānandāśrama Golādhyāya ('Siddhāntaśiromaṇeḥ prathamo bhāgaḥ' in the Wikisource title). It runs from the beginning (Golapraśaṃsā / Praśnādhyāya, Bhuvanakośa, Madhyagativāsanā, Jyotpatti, etc.) to the end of the Golabandhādhikāra, numbered chapter 27 in the edition's continuous numbering. The remaining adhikāras, such as Tripraśnavāsanā, Grahaṇavāsanā, Yantrādhyāya and Ṛtuvarṇana, are missing. The text is uncorrected OCR with many errors and includes page headers (e.g. '144 gaulādhyāyai').

**Works in this e-text:**
- Golādhyāya (Siddhāntaśiromaṇi) (Bhāskara, root text)
- Vāsanābhāṣya (Bhāskara, auto-commentary)
- Marīci (Munīśvara, commentary)
- Sanskrit introduction by the editor (upodghāta) (Balavanta Śarmā Āpaṭe, appendix)

**Also known as:** Siddhāntaśiromaṇi, Golādhyāya, Golādhyāya with Marīciṭīkā

**Attribution:** Bhāskara II (Bhāskarācārya, b. 1114 CE) completed the Siddhāntaśiromaṇi in Śaka 1072 (1150 CE). The Golādhyāya is its last division, and Bhāskara wrote his own Vāsanābhāṣya on it. Munīśvara, also called Viśvarūpa, was the son of Raṅganātha and was born in Śaka 1525 (1603 CE). According to the editor's introduction, he finished the two halves of the Marīci in Śaka 1557 and 1560. The opening segments [0]–[16] are the edition's Sanskrit introduction, signed by Balavanta Śarmā Āpaṭe, son of Dattātreya, and dated Mārgaśīrṣa Śaka 1865 (1943) at Puṇyapattana (Pune).

The Golādhyāya is the last division of Bhāskara II's Siddhāntaśiromaṇi (1150 CE). It covers spherical astronomy and cosmology: the shape and support of the earth, the bhuvanakośa, the rationale (vāsanā) of mean and true planetary motion, sines, and the construction of the armillary sphere. This e-text gives the first half of the Golādhyāya with Bhāskara's own Vāsanābhāṣya and the long 17th-century Marīci commentary by Munīśvara, which quotes earlier authorities at length. The text is preceded by the editor's Sanskrit introduction.

The Jaṭāmaṇivyākhyāna (or Jaṭāmaṇitātparya) is an ancillary Vedic phonetic-recitational treatise (vikṛti-lakṣaṇa) explaining the rules and sandhi adjustments required for reciting the Taittirīya Saṃhitā in the jaṭāpāṭha ('braided') modification. Referring to the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya and related grammatical rules, it treats standard two-word combinations as well as complex three-word sequences (trikrama), illustrating the permutations (anuloma and viloma) through sacrificial mantra citations.

**Attribution:** A Kalpasūtra manual belonging to the Khādira / Drāhyāyaṇa śākhā of the Sāmaveda; essentially an abridged recension based on the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra.

The Khādiragṛhyasūtra (also known as the Drāhyāyaṇagṛhyasūtra) is an aphoristic Kalpasūtra manual of domestic ritual belonging to the Sāmaveda, closely related to the Gobhilagṛhyasūtra of which it represents an abridged and systematized recension. Structured across four paṭalas, it prescribes domestic sacrifices (pākayajña), life-cycle ceremonies (saṃskāras) such as marriage, pregnancy rites, tonsure (caula), and Vedic initiation (upanayana), as well as seasonal, ancestral (aṣṭakā, śrāddha), and hospitality rituals (argha).

The Laghubhūṣaṇakānti (or Kānti) is a detailed Sanskrit commentary by Gopāladeva on Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa's Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra, an influential 17th-century work on the philosophy and semantics of Pāṇinian vyākaraṇa. Reflecting the late traditional Varanasi school of Bālambhaṭṭa Pāyaguṇḍa, it elucidates root semantics (dhātvartha), case and nominal meanings (subartha, kāraka), compounding (samāsa), and the ontological theory of speech (sphoṭa), systematically defending grammarian semantics against Mīmāṃsā and Navya-Nyāya critiques.

The Laghumādhyandinīyaśikṣā is a short metrical phonetic treatise (śikṣā) of 28 verses outlining the characteristic pronunciation and recitation conventions of the Mādhyandina recension of the Śukla Yajurveda. It sets out rules for phonetic substitutions, including the realization of uncombined word-initial y- as j-, intervocalic ṣ- as kh-, light versus heavy v-, phonetic coloring of the visarga, and accompanying hand and finger gestures (mocana) used during recitational chanting.

The Lakṣmīkāntaśikṣā (Varṇakramacatuḥślokī) is a very short Taittirīya śikṣā. In four verses it states the rules of varṇakrama (gemination of consonants, abhinidhāna, insertion of yamas and other transition sounds, nasal treatment), drawing on the Taittirīya Prātiśākhya. On Wikisource, and so in this e-text, it is followed by a second, anonymous text under the same heading: a verse list of Taittirīya words sorted alphabetically by accent type (antodātta and ādyudātta).

- Wikisource page (fetched): no source note, scan or editor. Only links to related pages निघण्टुशास्त्रम् and निरुक्तशास्त्रम्.
- Not derived from the GRETIL Nirukta (sa_yAska-nirukta.xml, based on Sarup, input by M. Tokunaga). That file uses a different, dotted word-split format and has no Nighaṇṭu or Pariśiṣṭa.
- The pariśiṣṭa paragraph numbering (e.g. '13.48', '14 34') and the bracketed word counts in the Nighaṇṭu match the layout of Sarup's and similar Indian editions, but no specific edition could be confirmed.

**Other editions:**
- Rudolf von Roth (ed.), Jâska's Nirukta sammt den Nighaṇṭavas, Göttingen: Dieterichsche Buchhandlung, 1852. — First critical Western edition of the Nighaṇṭu and Nirukta.
- Satyavrata Sāmaśramī (ed.), The Nirukta, with Commentaries, 4 vols., Bibliotheca Indica 89, Calcutta: Asiatic Society of Bengal, 1882–1891. — Edition featuring the commentaries of Devarājayajvan on the Nighaṇṭu and Durgācārya on the Nirukta.
- Lakshman Sarup (ed.), The Nighaṇṭu and the Nirukta, the Oldest Indian Treatise on Etymology, Philology, and Semantics: Critically Edited from Original Manuscripts, Lahore: University of the Panjab, 1927 (reprint Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1967). — Standard critical edition of both texts.
- H. M. Bhadkamkar & R. G. Bhadkamkar (eds.), The Nirukta of Yāska with the Commentary of Durga, 2 vols., Bombay Sanskrit and Prakrit Series 73 & 85, Bombay: Government Central Press, 1918, 1942. — Critical edition with Durgācārya's Ṛjvartha commentary.

**Translations:**
- Lakshman Sarup, The Nighaṇṭu and the Nirukta: English Translation and Notes, London: Oxford University Press, 1921 (reprint Delhi: Motilal Banarsidass, 1967). (English)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Nighaṇṭu 1–5 (segments up to 'devapatnyaḥ … | 6 |'), Nirukta 1–12 (pūrvaṣaṭka 1–6 'iti naigamaṃ kāṇḍaṃ pūrvārdhañca samāptam'; uttaraṣaṭka 7–12 'iti daivataṃ kāṇḍamuttarārdhaṃ ca samāptam'), and the Pariśiṣṭa (13–14).

**Works in this e-text:**
- Nighaṇṭu (root text (5 adhyāyas, with bracketed counts of the words in each list))
- Nirukta (Yāska, commentary (adhyāyas 1–12, introduced 'śrīyāskamuniviracitaṃ niruktaṃ prārabhyate'))
- Nirukta-pariśiṣṭa (appendix (two adhyāyas, numbered 13–14, ending 'iti pariśiṣṭam'; traditionally transmitted with the Nirukta but generally regarded as later))

**Also known as:** Nirukta, Nighaṇṭunirukta, Yāskanirukta

**Attribution:** The Nighaṇṭu is an anonymous Vedic wordlist representing early Vedic lexicographical traditions. The Nirukta is Yāska's foundational commentary and treatise on Vedic etymology and semantics (c. 5th–4th century BCE).

The Nighaṇṭu is the oldest surviving Vedic word-list. It has three parts: synonym lists (naighaṇṭuka-kāṇḍa, adhyāyas 1–3), difficult and homonymous words (naigama, 4) and names of deities (daivata, 5). Yāska's Nirukta is the Vedāṅga treatise on etymology and Vedic exegesis and is built as a commentary on the Nighaṇṭu. It sets out the four word classes (nāman, ākhyāta, upasarga, nipāta), defends the derivation of nouns from verbal roots, and explains the Vedic words and deities with citations of the mantras. The e-text adds the later Pariśiṣṭa (adhyāyas 13–14).

It records the anuvākas and vākyas of the Taittirīyasaṃhitā in a kaṭapayādi-type syllable notation.

A short Vedic lakṣaṇa (śikṣā) tract from the Taittirīya tradition. It explains the Nāradabaiṭ, a mnemonic syllable code ascribed to Nārada that encodes the counts of anuvākas and vākyas in the Taittirīyasaṃhitā. Seven paribhāṣā verses set out the rules (which vowels count, how conjunct consonants count in kaṭapayādi fashion, and the bindu-marked syllables ma, da, ga, ta, sa standing for tens). The author's prose commentary, Bhāvaprakāśikā, follows, and then the code strings for all seven kāṇḍas.

It classifies clusters into analogical categories such as ayaḥpiṇḍa (compact like an iron ball), dārupiṇḍa (moderately bound like wood), and tūlapiṇḍa (loosely bound like cotton), depending on whether stops, semivowels, sibilants, or nasals are conjoined. In three brief prose sections, it formulates the core rules governing Vedic accentuation (udātta, anudātta, svarita, and the bhāṣika tone of the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa) as well as Mādhyandina-specific pronunciation practices, including the realization of semivowels (such as y as j), retroflex sibilants (ṣ as kh), and anusvāra.

The included Śeṣavāsanā is the author's own supplementary exposition clarifying subtle mathematical demonstrations and geometrical rationales.

The Sāmavedasaptalakṣaṇa ('Saptalakṣaṇa') is a metrical collection of seven lakṣaṇa treatises auxiliary to the Sāmaveda padapāṭha, cataloguing words subject to particular sandhi phenomena: visarga elision (Śamāna, with notes on visarga retention and the nasal raṅga), e/ai-final words (Viliṅghya), n-final words before n- (Napara), t-final words (Tapara), shortened vowels (Hrasvasaṃgrahaṇa), word-initial a-vowels (Avarṇi) and words without avagraha (Anavagrahalakṣaṇa). Each rule is illustrated by mnemonic lists of Sāmaveda word forms with counts of the sūtras covered.

In 24 adhyāyas, it provides detailed rules on phonetic inventory, euphonic combination (sandhi), accentuation (svara), moric quantity, and pronunciation necessary to transition between the continuous saṃhitāpāṭha and the uncombined padapāṭha. It cites numerous early phoneticians, including Ātreya, Pauṣkarasādi, Plākṣi, and Vālmīki.

The Vaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇasāra is an influential 17th-century treatise on semantic theory and linguistic philosophy in the Pāṇinian school by Kauṇḍabhaṭṭa. It serves as an abridgement of his larger Bṛhadvaiyākaraṇabhūṣaṇa, commenting on the 74 kārikās of the Vaiyākaraṇasiddhāntakārikā composed by his uncle Bhaṭṭojīdīkṣita. The work systematically articulates and defends the grammarians' semantic doctrines regarding the meaning of verbal roots (dhātvartha), suffixes (tiṅartha, kṛdartha), nominal cases (subartha), compounds (samāsa), and sphoṭa against the opposing positions of the Nyāya and Mīmāṃsā traditions.

Madhusūdana Maskarin's Aṣṭavikṛtivivṛti is cited from the vikṛti works collected there (INDOLOGY list, April 2011). It is not verified whether the Vyāliśikṣā is included.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Vyāliśikṣā vv. 1–8 with its colophon, then Madhusūdana's treatise vv. 1–54 with its colophon. Both works appear complete.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vyāliśikṣā (Vyāḍi, root text (8 verses on ghanapāṭha))
- Aṣṭavikṛtivivṛti (Madhusūdana, independent treatise appended (54 verses on the eight vikṛtis))

**Attribution:** The Vyāliśikṣā's attribution to Vyāḍi (Vyāli) is traditional and based on the title only; the text says it was taught with the approval of Brahman and Sahasravadana. The second work is by Madhusūdana, a maskarin (renunciant), disciple of Nṛhari and son of Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana ('guruśrīkṛṣṇadvaipāyanatanubhavo maskarī', v. 1). He writes 'with Vyāḍi's approval'. The vikṛti literature knows him as Madhusūdana Maskarin, with dated manuscripts from c. AD 1790 onwards.

The e-text combines two short metrical manuals on the modified recitation of the Veda (vikṛtipāṭha). The Vyāliśikṣā (8 verses) sets out the number of sandhis and padas and the procedure for ghana recitation. Madhusūdana Maskarin's Aṣṭavikṛtivivṛti (54 verses) defines and discusses the eight vikṛtis (jaṭā, mālā, daṇḍa, rekhā, ratha, dhvaja, śikhā, ghana) for the Ṛgveda, including detailed rules on how pragṛhya vowels and sandhi are treated in reverse sequences (vyutkrama).

The Vākyapadīya (c. 5th century CE) by Bhartṛhari is the foundational treatise of the philosophy of grammar (Vyākaraṇadarśana) and classical Indian semantic theory. Comprising three books—Brahmakāṇḍa (on Śabdabrahman and the metaphysics of language), Vākyakāṇḍa (on sentence-meaning wholism and the sphoṭa doctrine), and Padakāṇḍa or Prakīrṇaka (fourteen specialized treatises exploring universals, particulars, relations, time, action, and case-roles)—it articulates a non-dualist linguistic philosophy that shaped subsequent debates across Buddhist, Mīmāṃsā, and Nyāya traditions. This e-text contains the complete kārikās across all three books together with their principal classical Sanskrit commentaries.

The Saptalakṣaṇa is a set of seven mnemonic treatises for the Taittirīya Saṃhitā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. They list the words that need special treatment when the padapāṭha is converted into saṃhitā, and the reverse. The parts cover the elision of visarjanīya after ā (śamāna), words that resist the usual sandhi (vilaṅghya), words followed by n- or t- (napara, tapara), groups of words with a- and ā- (avarṇi, āvarṇi), and words that are not divided by avagraha in the padapāṭha (aniṅgya). Recitation students use it as a reference aid.

This points to a Sūribhaṭṭa of Homakanyāpura as author or source, but the attribution is not confirmed in the literature consulted. Freund's references list a separate prose commentary, the Yohibhāṣya, which survives in several South Indian manuscripts. It is not part of this e-text. Freund's Śikṣā index lists the commentary as 'Yohi Bhāṣya of Sūribhaṭṭa', i.e. he takes Sūribhaṭṭa as author of the bhāṣya; verse 1 of the mūla ('vakṣye ... yad dhomakanyāpurasūribhaṭṭaḥ') can be read as following Sūribhaṭṭa's teaching. The authorship of the 23 mūla verses remains unconfirmed.

This is a short Vedalakṣaṇa/śikṣā manual in 23 verses (anuṣṭubh, after a maṅgala verse in upajāti) on the accentuation of finite verbs (kriyāsvara) in the Taittirīya (Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda) texts. It lists the verbs and contexts in which the verb keeps its udātta, especially after relative and causal words such as yaḥ, yat, yadi, yathā and hi (hence the name 'yo-hi-prāpti'). It also names the exceptions. In its final verse the text says it was composed to show these accents to learners (bālānām).

The Yājuṣajyotiṣa is the Yajurvedic recension of the Vedāṅgajyotiṣa, the earliest extant Indian astronomical text, traditionally attributed to the sage Lagadha. Designed to determine the correct seasons and calendar dates for Vedic sacrifices, it describes a five-year luni-solar yuga cycle, the computation of solstices, tithis, parvans, and the positions of the sun and moon relative to the twenty-seven nakṣatras.

The Āgniveśyagṛhyasūtra is a domestic ritual manual belonging to the Agniveśya school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, closely affiliated with the Vādhūla ritual tradition. The Āpastambaśrautasūtra is a primary Vedic ritual manual belonging to the Taittirīya school of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda, prescribing the procedures for solemn (śrauta) sacrifices. This e-text reproduces the opening portion of A. Chinnaswami Sastri's GOS edition, comprising his introductory study (Āpastambakalpasūtraparicaya) along with Praśnas 1–5 accompanied by Dhūrtasvāmin's Bhāṣya and Rāmāgnicit's Vṛtti. The transcription is incomplete, terminating in Praśna 5 (Agnyādheya).

The Āpiśalaśikṣā is an ancient Sanskrit phonetic treatise (śikṣā) traditionally attributed to the pre-Pāṇinian grammarian Āpiśali. Composed predominantly in brief prose sūtras framed by introductory and concluding anuṣṭubh verses, it provides a rigorous physiological analysis of Sanskrit sound production across sthāna (articulatory place), karaṇa (active articulator), antaḥprayatna (internal effort), bāhyaprayatna (external effort), articulatory pressure (sthānapīḍa), and phonation/accentuation processes (prakrama). It is regarded as one of the earliest and most systematically organized phonetic manuals in the Vedāṅga tradition.

**Attribution:** Maśaka Gārgya is the traditional sūtrakāra of this Sāmavedic kalpa text. The commentary was composed by Varadarāja, son of Vāmana (Vāmānārya).

The Ārṣeyakalpa (Maśakakalpasūtra), attributed to Maśaka Gārgya, is the Śrautasūtra of the Kauthuma-Rāṇāyanīya Sāmaveda that lists, rite by rite, the sāmans (identified by their ṛṣi-names and pratīkas) to be chanted in the stotras of the Soma sacrifices: ekāhas, ahīnas and sattras. The Ātharvaṇajyotiṣa is a short astrological text of the Atharvaveda tradition, framed as Brahmā's instruction to Kāśyapa. It is not a recension of the calendrical Vedāṅgajyotiṣa of the Ṛg- and Yajurveda. It deals with electional astrology: which activities suit each of the fifteen muhūrtas, the eleven karaṇas, the tithis and their five classes, the seven weekdays, and the nine groups of nakṣatras counted from one's birth star.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete root text, comprising the opening anukramaṇikā kārikās (vv. 1–18) and all 14 adhyāyas (vv. 1–293), ending at segment 705 with 'ity ātreyaśikṣāmūlaṃ saṃpūrṇam'.

**Also known as:** Ātreyaśikṣākārikā, Ātreyī Śikṣā

**Attribution:** Traditionally attributed to the sage Ātreya and affiliated with the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda.

The Ātreyaśikṣā is a metrical Vedāṅga treatise on phonetics and recitation practice affiliated with the Taittirīya śākhā of the Kṛṣṇa Yajurveda. Beginning with an 18-verse anukramaṇikā and paribhāṣā, the text spans 14 chapters covering vowel length, places and efforts of articulation (sthāna, prayatna), accents (udātta, anudātta, svarita, kampa), and the phonetic mechanics of the Vedic recitation modifications (vikṛtipāṭha such as pada, krama, and jaṭā).

The Śaunakaśikṣā is a Vedāṅga phonetic treatise (śikṣā) in 67 verses associated with the tradition of Śaunaka, focusing on orthoepic rules for the recitation of the Ṛgveda. A large commentary by Viśveśvara Sūri (Pārvatīya, 18th century), pupil of Lakṣmīdhara, on the sūtras of Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī, covering adhyāyas 1–3. In the opening adhyāya it discusses the Mahābhāṣya and the later Pāṇinian literature in detail, using the technical language of Navya-Nyāya. Later sections become much briefer, often giving only a short gloss and examples for each sūtra.

The Śābdikābharaṇa (also designated in colophons as Dhātupratyayapañcikā) is a Pāṇinian grammatical work on verbal morphology composed by Hariyogin (Prollanācārya). The treatise begins with an epistemological and philosophical preface (bhūmikā) evaluating the eternity (nityatva) versus non-eternity (anityatva) of phonemes (varṇa) and recognitive cognition (pratyabhijñā), before providing a systematic grammatical commentary on the roots of the ten verbal classes (daśagaṇa), the kaṇḍvādayaḥ, and sautradhātus according to Pāṇini's Aṣṭādhyāyī.

The Paramapuruṣasaṃhitā is a Vaiṣṇava Āgama text belonging to the Pāñcarātra corpus, presented as an exposition given by Nārada to sages on the banks of the Bhāgīrathī. In ten adhyāyas (comprising roughly one thousand verses), the text addresses the duties, qualifications, and classifications of temple priests (arcaka) and temple servants (paricāraka), the ritual worship of Viṣṇu, and the significance of the Ekādaśī vrata.

**Attribution:** Traditional attribution to Advayavajra (Maitrīgupta, c. 11th century) confirmed by the colophon.

The Kudṛṣṭinirghātādivākyaṭippinikā is an extremely brief prose gloss (ṭippinikā) by Advayavajra (11th century) explaining key Mahāyāna doctrinal terminology associated with his Kudṛṣṭinirghāta. The Śokavinodana ('Dispelling Grief') is a short Buddhist homiletic work of 40 verses in anuṣṭubh meter attributed to Aśvaghoṣa. Designed to console someone suffering from the loss of a loved one, it meditates on the universality of impermanence (anityatā), the inevitability of death across all realms of existence, and the deceptive nature of saṃsāric relations across lifetimes, concluding with an exhortation to turn toward liberation (mokṣa). Long known only through Tibetan translations (Toh 4177, 4505), its Sanskrit text was recently recovered from citations preserved in the Tridaṇḍamālā and manuscript witnesses.

The Ṣaḍgatikārikā is a concise versified Buddhist handbook of 105 stanzas describing the six realms of cyclic existence (ṣaḍgati): hell beings, animals, hungry ghosts, humans, demigods, and gods. It outlines the specific karmic causes leading to rebirth in each realm and concludes with verses urging the practice of morality (śīla), meditation (dhyāna), and correct understanding to attain liberation. Colophonically ascribed to Aśvaghoṣa, the stanzas are an anthology excerpted from the Saddharmasmṛtyupasthānasūtra.

The Śākyasiṃhastotra is a short Buddhist devotional stotra of 23 verses preserved within a Nepalese Jātakamālā manuscript tradition. Attributed in the narrative frame to the Earth goddess Kṣmādevī (Pṛthivī), it praises the Buddha Śākyasiṃha by surveying his past bodhisattva lives and exemplary deeds (including the births as Viśvantara, Maitrībala, and the hare) before concluding with a protective phalaśruti.

Stanza 1 begins from CUL Or. 722.4 (a single-folio fragment that breaks off in st. 1) and is completed from CUL Add. 1697.7. Each Sanskrit stanza is followed by the Derge Tibetan translation with Derge folio markers ({242a5} ... {243b6}), and the Tibetan colophon and the translators' syllable count are included at the end.

**Works in this e-text:**
- Vajraḍākastotradaṇḍaka (Śrīcakrasaṃvaradaṇḍakastuti), Sanskrit (Dharmakīrti (traditional attribution), root text)

**Also known as:** Śrīcakrasaṃvaradaṇḍakastuti (Sanskrit colophon), Śrīvajraḍākasya stotradaṇḍaka, Dpal rdo rje mkha' 'gro'i bstod pa rgyun chags (Tôh. 1442), Bde mchog gi bstod pa rgyun chags

**Attribution:** The Tibetan Tanjur colophon attributes the hymn to Dharmakīrti, 'crown jewel of the logicians'. Tibetan canonical lists also record 'bde mchog gi bstod pa rgyun chags chos kyi grags pas mdzad' (Eimer & Germano, Many Canons of Tibetan Buddhism). Ascribing a Cakrasaṃvara hymn to the 7th-century epistemologist is generally regarded as doubtful or pseudepigraphic, and the work may be by a later homonymous Dharmakīrti. Van der Kuijp (cited in Dan Martin) notes that it is written in a complicated daṇḍaka metre with more than 26 syllables per quarter. The Tibetan translation is by Maṇikaśrījñāna and Chag lo tsā ba Chos rje dpal (Dharmasvāmin).

This is an ornate hymn in four long daṇḍaka stanzas to Vajraḍāka/Heruka Cakrasaṃvara. Stanza 1 describes the deity's iconography: blue-black, four-faced and twelve-armed, trampling Bhairava and Kālarātri, embracing Vajravārāhī. Stanza 2 praises him with his retinue of the four ḍākinīs (Ḍākinī, Lāmā, Khaṇḍarohā, Rūpiṇī) and the goddesses of the intermediate directions. Stanza 3 praises him as the nondual embodiment of the three bodies of a buddha. Stanza 4 evokes the eight charnel grounds and dedicates the merit of the praise to the awakening of beings.

A short anonymous Sanskrit hagiographical narrative recounting the legendary life of the celebrated 8th-century Madhyamaka master Śāntideva. It relates his birth as prince to King Mañjuvarman, his renunciation following his mother's warning, spiritual attainment under the siddha Mañjuvajra, service as a royal bodyguard (under the name Acalasena) armed with a wooden sword, and admission to the Nālandā monastery under the name Śāntideva (nicknamed Bhusuku). ## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete work in 85 verses plus introductory and concluding mantras and rubrics, ending with the author colophon and a scribal dating colophon (NS 589 / 1469 CE).

**Also known as:** Mṛtasugatiniyojanāntyeṣṭividhāna, Antyeṣṭividhāna, Shi ba bde 'gror 'god pa, Shi ba bde 'gror 'dzud pa

**Attribution:** Attributed in the colophon to Paṇḍita Śrī Śūnyasamādhivajra (often vocalized as Śūnyatāsamādhivajra in the Tibetan Tengyur traditions).

The Mṛtasugatiniyojana is an 85-verse esoteric Buddhist funerary ritual manual (antyeṣṭividhāna) attributed to Śūnyasamādhivajra. The first section (vv. 1–34) details a method of post-mortem revival and transference (mṛtasaṃjīvanī) based on Guhyasamājatantra chapter 14, in which the officiant reinstalls the deceased's consciousness into the body to bestow initiation and direct it through the cranial aperture toward liberation or a pure land. The second section (vv. 34–85) details cremation and post-cremation cleansing rituals based on the Sarvadurgatipariśodhanatantra to safeguard the deceased from rebirth in bad states.

It provides instructions on purification using consecrated water, self-protection (ātmarakṣā) via the Mahāpratisarā mantra, drawing and consecration of the circular maṇḍala (accompanied by six pāramitā verses), invocation (āvāhana) of Mañjughoṣa, and offerings to him and his four retinue deities (Jālinīprabha, Candraprabhā, Keśinī, and Upakeśinī). The manuscript includes a Tibetan translation colophon involving the 15th-century master Vanaratna, followed by an incomplete appended Sanskrit stotra.

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (probable):** Unpublished e-text, probably transcribed from a manuscript that is not identified. It is not a direct keying of the only printed edition, Pandey 1998.

**Evidence:**

**Other editions:**
- Janardan Shastri Pandey (ed.), Yoginīsañcāratantram with Nibandha of Tathāgatarakṣita and Upadeśānusāriṇīvyākhyā of Alakakalaśa, Rare Buddhist Texts Series 21, Sarnath: Central Institute of Higher Tibetan Studies, 1998. — Editio princeps and only published edition. The commentaries are printed with the root text (Alakakalaśa's introduction is on p. 4).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Introductory synopsis of the 17 chapters, chapter 1 complete (segs. 0–195), then chapter 2 (bodhipākṣikadharmas: smṛtyupasthānas, ṛddhipādas, indriyas, balas, bodhyaṅgas, aṣṭāṅgamārga) up to the start of the samyakprahāṇas. It breaks off at seg. 340 ('[29] svarūpaṃ punaḥ |'). Chapters 3–17 are missing.

**Also known as:** Upadeśānusāriṇīvyākhyā, Yoginīsañcāratantraṭīkā Upadeśānusāriṇī

**Attribution:** Colophon (seg. 195): 'iti śrīpaṇḍitācāryaalakakalaśaviracitāyāṃ yoginīsaṃcāratantraṭīkāyām upadeśānusāriṇyabhidhānāyāṃ prathamapaṭale vistaravyākhyā'. Alakakalaśa (Tib. Lcang lo can gyi bum pa) was a teacher and co-translator of Steng pa lo tsā ba, so 12th c. (perhaps born late 11th).

Alakakalaśa's Upadeśānusāriṇī is a commentary on the Yoginīsaṃcāratantra, an explanatory tantra of the Cakrasaṃvara cycle. It opens with a synopsis of the tantra's seventeen chapters and an exegesis of the opening verse in terms of piṇḍārtha and padārtha. It then explains the purification of the skandhas, āyatanas and dhātus (ch. 1) and the thirty-seven bodhipākṣika factors and their mapping onto the maṇḍala deities (ch. 2), citing Yogācāra verse sources. The e-text has chapter 1 and part of chapter 2.

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- Header explicitly references 'Tokyo University Library New 450 Old 296', Petech 1984:44, and Matsunami's catalogue entry 454.
- Scribal colophon verbatim transcribes Tokyo MS New 450 mentioning the reign of King Baladeva at Śrīmānadevamahāvihāra.

**Translations:**
- Tibetan translation: Cakrasamvarodaya-nāma-maṇḍalavidhi (Dpal 'khor lo bde mchog 'byung ba zhes bya ba'i dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga), Toh 1538 (Derge Tanjur, rgyud, za, 117v2–150r5); Peking Tanjur (Ōtani 2249). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete ritual manual in 790 verses plus interspersed prose and ritual mantras, ending with the author colophon and dated historical scribal colophon.

**Also known as:** Samvarodayā nāma maṇḍalopāyikā, Cakrasamvarodaya-nāma-maṇḍalavidhi, Dpal 'khor lo bde mchog 'byung ba zhes bya ba'i dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga, Svarodayāmaṇḍalopāyikā

In the Tibetan canonical transmissions (Toh 1538 / Ōtani 2249), the author name is rendered variously as Dbus pa blo ldan (*Madhyadeśikamati) or Dbu ba / Bhu ba blo ldan pa (*Bhuvamati / *Ariṣṭadhīmat).

The Samvarodayānāmamaṇḍalopāyikā is an extensive Vajrayāna maṇḍala ritual manual (maṇḍalavidhi) associated with the Saṃvarodayatantra in the Cakrasaṃvara tradition. Composed by Bhūvācārya at the monastic complex of Ratnagiri in Odisha, it provides comprehensive ritual procedures for maṇḍala layout, consecration (pratiṣṭhā), oblations (homa, bali), visualization, and initiation. The text is preserved in a mid-11th-century Newari palm-leaf manuscript copied at the Śrīmānadevamahāvihāra in the Kathmandu Valley during the reign of King Baladeva.

- Foliation marker at segment [105]: '(f. 160r5–7)'

**Translations:**
- dPal kye rdo rje zhes bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs (Śrīhevajranāmasādhana), translated into Tibetan by Dīpaṅkaracandra and Lha btsan po Muni Rāja (Degé Tengyur D 1227, rgyud, zha, 31b2–34a6; Peking Q 2356). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete sādhana preserved across 106 segments, providing the Sanskrit text from MS HSS 14 (ff. 155v5–160r7) intercalated line-by-line with the Tibetan translation from Degé Tengyur D 1227 (ff. 31b–34a).

**Also known as:** Hevajrasādhana, Śrīherukasādhana, Śrīhevajranāmasādhana, dPal kye rdo rje zhes bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs

The Tibetan colophon identifies the author as Slob dpon Byang chub snying po (Bodhigarbha).

The Herukasādhana (also known as Hevajrasādhana) is a tantric liturgical manual belonging to the Hevajra cycle, composed by Ācārya Bodhigarbha (Garbhapāda). The text instructs the practitioner on the generation stage of Heruka/Hevajra, opening with the veneration of the lineage, the selection of practice grounds (cremation grounds, isolated trees), preliminary meditations on the four brahmavihāras and emptiness, and the generation of the protection circle. It proceeds to the detailed visualization of eight-faced, sixteen-armed Heruka and the retinue of eight goddesses (Gaurī, Caurī, Vetālī, Ghasmarī, Pukkasī, Śavarī, Caṇḍālī, and Dombī), concluding with deity yoga, mantra recitation, and the yogic realization that all activities and perceptions are inseparable from Heruka.

## Contents

The Ātmasādhanāvatāra is a major doctrinal treatise by Buddhajñānapāda (c. late 8th–early 9th century CE), founder of the Jñānapāda school of the Guhyasamājatantra. Integrating Madhyamaka epistemological analysis and Yogācāra philosophy with Anuttarayogatantra ritual principles, the text argues that saṃsāra is merely conceptual fabrication (vikalpa), refutes external reality, and defends the soteriological validity of self-worship (ātmasādhana/ātmapūjā) through identity with the maṇḍala deities.

The Prajñāpradīpāvalī (or Prajñāpāramitopadeśaśāstrābhisamayālaṃkāravivṛti) is an Indian commentary on the Abhisamayālaṃkāra attributed to Buddhaśrījñāna (Buddhaśrījñānapāda, ca. late 8th to early 9th century). The surviving Sanskrit manuscript, photographed by Rāhula Sāṅkṛtyāyana in Lhasa in 1935, covers only the eighth chapter (Dharmakāyābhisamaya) and the summary verses, dealing extensively with the four-body (caturkāya) doctrine and the enlightened activities (kāritra) following Haribhadra. Notably, the Sanskrit text diverges from the canonical Tibetan translation (Toh 3800) and displays significant textual agreement with Abhayākaragupta's Munimatālaṃkāra.

A small manuscript (CUL Or. 155) of Cakrasaṃvara texts by the lay devotee (paramopāsaka) Chātrakumāradatta, in the tradition of Luyīpāda's sādhana. It contains a list of the names of the heroes and heroines (vīra/vīreśvarī) of the Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala; a pūjā manual, damaged by the loss of fol. 2; and an annotated outline of the stages of the sādhana, from the preliminary pūjā and brahmavihāras through the purification of skandhas, protective circle, emptiness, generation of the maṇḍala, consecration, nectar, nyāsa, mantra recitation and bali. The author names his guru 'residing in Kanyārāma' (Rāḍhā, Bengal) and the mahāmaṇḍalācārya Sauṣṭhavapāda; Szántó dates the toponym's attestation to c. 1100–1150 CE.

## Contents

**Coverage:** fragment — Preserves approximately two folios from the end of the text, ending abruptly in the dedication verse ('śrīsamājāt samuddhṛ<tya> kṛtvā yāgavidhiṃ mama / kuśalaṃ yat samu[end]').

A fragmentary Tantric Buddhist ritual procedure (yāgavidhi) elaborating healing and apotropaic practices based on Guhyasamājatantra 13.72ff. It includes rituals for dispelling epidemic disease and protecting settlements via the Sarvarogāpanayanavajrasambhava and Buddhasamayameghavyūha samādhis, as well as a concluding śāntika homa, gaṇapūjā, and amṛta visualization for patients. The text is preserved uniquely in an incomplete two-folio Nepalese manuscript.

# Mitapadāpañjikā (on Catuṣpīṭhatantra 1.1–3.4; with lacunae)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T02_Durjayacandra_Mitapadā-pañjikā`

**Author:** Durjayacandra

**Tibetan:** Ø

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Formatted diplomatic edition (unpublished; LaTeX/ledmac) of the codex unicus Kathmandu, National Archives, MS 3-336 = NGMPP B 23/14, palm-leaf, copied by the bhikṣu Suvarṇabhadra of Southern Patan in NS 261 (1 April 1141 CE) under Narendradeva. The Tucci paper apograph (Sferra/Saccone images) is a copy of it and adds no text.

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- E-text header '\chapter{Formatted Diplomatic Edition}' with folio markers (\sorszam{[1\recto]}…) and an apparatus of scribal corrections (MS ac/pc).
- Catalog raw_metadata: 'Edition / witness: codex unicus NAK 3-336 = NGMPP B 23/14 (the Tucci ms. is an apograph)'.
- Szántó, Selected Chapters from the Catuṣpīṭhatantra (DPhil, Oxford 2012), vol. 1, §3.2.4, describes the same manuscript, its lacunae and the colophon given in the e-text.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Commentary on Catuṣpīṭhatantra 1.1 to 3.4 (Ātmapīṭha, Parapīṭha, Yogapīṭha), closing with 'iti mahāmaṇḍalācāryadurjayacandrakṛtāyāṃ mitapadāyāṃ pañjikāyāṃ yogapīṭhaḥ samāpta[ḥ]' and the scribal colophon of NS 261 (1141 CE). According to Szántó (2012, §3.2.4), the codex unicus NAK 3-336 (60 surviving leaves) has lost ff. 2–3 (the e-text's '[lacuna]' after 1.1.1) and an unknown number of leaves after f. 61, which breaks off in the comment on 3.4.34. The last leaf resumes at 3.4.69, and the commentary then stops with 'alam bahunā', although 3.4 has 151 units. Durjayacandra apparently never commented on the fourth pīṭha, which he knew as the *Jñānapīṭha; there is no Tibetan translation.

**Also known as:** Mitapadā, Catuṣpīṭhatantramitapadāpañjikā, Catuṣpīṭhapañjikā Mitapadā

**Attribution:** Colophons consistently attribute the work to Mahāmaṇḍalācārya Durjayacandra (e.g., 'iti mahāmaṇḍalācāryadurjayacandrakṛtāyāṃ mitapadāyāṃ pañjikāyāṃ...').

Durjayacandra's Mitapadā ('of measured words') is a pañjikā on difficult words and passages (sandehapada) of the Catuṣpīṭhatantra. It explains the yogic physiology of breath and channels, the maṇḍalas of Yogāmbara and Jñānaḍākinī, mantra, nyāsa and the sexual rites of the Yogapīṭha. The author, a mahāmaṇḍalācārya and probably a Bengali, was active in the late 10th century; he also wrote commentaries on the Hevajra and other tantras. The Mitapadā survives only in a Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript of 1141 CE, and Szántó suggests that it was left unfinished and circulated little.

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the sādhana, spanning from initial namaskāra through the colophon and concluding benedictory verses.

**Also known as:** Ṣaḍaṅgasādhananāma, Yan lag drug pa zhes bya ba'i sgrub thabs

Structured around the six limbs of meditation set forth in the fourth chapter of the Ḍākinīvajrapañjaratantra, the text covers both generation-stage visualizations (mandala, Hevajra, and Nairātmyā) and completion-stage contemplation. It played an influential role in early Tibetan translations and the Sakya Lamdré (Lam 'bras) exegetical tradition.

It provides word-by-word glosses and doctrinal expositions on the tantra's verses, clarifying mandala structures, cremation ground symbolism, internal and external sacred geography (pīṭhas), and esoteric ritual practices. In the closing verses, the author notes that he was a monk originally from Sri Lanka who composed the text at the Agrabodhi vihāra.

- Lacunae are marked '[...]' inside otherwise metrical verses, e.g. [314], [379], [386]. This suggests the verses were assembled from surviving Sanskrit testimonia, such as citations in Samantabhadra's Sāramañjarī commentary and the Tibet Museum birch-bark fragments, rather than retranslated from Tibetan. This inference is not stated in the file.

**Other editions:**
- Tibetan translation: Śrīsamantabhadranāmasādhana (dPal kun tu bzang po zhes bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs), Derge Tengyur Toh. 1855. — Canonical Tibetan translation of the complete work.
- Margherita Serena Saccone and Péter-Dániel Szántó, Tantra and Pramāṇa: A Study of the Sāramañjarī, Naples: UniorPress, 2023. — Critical edition of Samantabhadra's Sanskrit commentary (Sāramañjarī) on the Samantabhadrasādhana, an important source for the root verses.
- Kazuo Kano and Péter-Dániel Szántó, 'New pages from the Tibet Museum birch-bark manuscript (1): Fragments related to Jñānapāda', 2020. — Edits Sanskrit fragments related to the Samantabhadrasādhana and a commentary on it (vv. 17–18, 23–24).

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — All 164 verses of the sādhana are present, from the opening maṅgala (v. 1) to the closing dedication (vv. 163–164), with the mantras inserted ([76] etc.). Several verses keep lacunae marked '[...]' (e.g. vv. 74, 88), so this is a reconstruction with gaps, not a fully transmitted text.

**Also known as:** Caturaṅgasādhana-Samantabhadrī, Caturaṅgasādhana, Śrīsamantabhadrasādhana, Samantabhadranāmasādhana

**Attribution:** Attributed to Jñānapāda (Buddhajñānapāda / Buddhaśrījñāna, late 8th to early 9th century CE), founder of the Jñānapāda tradition (Ye shes zhabs lugs) of Guhyasamāja practice.

The Samantabhadrasādhana, also known as Caturaṅgasādhana Samantabhadrī, is the basic generation-stage (utpattikrama) sādhana of Jñānapāda's Guhyasamāja tradition (ca. late 8th to early 9th c.). In āryā verses it sets out the preliminaries (purification, confession, refuge, bodhicitta, meditation on emptiness), the visualisation of the dharmodayā, the palace and the Mañjuvajra maṇḍala with its deities, and the concluding dedication. This file is a modern Sanskrit reconstruction of the 164 verses, with some lacunae.

**Edition used (determined):** Working text of the Katipayākṣarā, transcribed from Kaiser Library (Kathmandu) MS 229 (NGMPP C 26/2; palm-leaf, copied at Vikramaśīla) and collated with the editio princeps in Dhīḥ 37 (2004), pp. 149–170. Unpublished in this form.

- Isaacson (Hamburg handout, isaacson_ho.pdf): 'Kaiser Library MS 229 (= NGMPP C 26/2); edited in Dhīḥ 37 (2004), pp. 149-170'. He quotes the passage at [533] as 'f. 5v, ed. p. 160'.

**Other editions:**
- Rare Buddhist Texts Research Unit (ed.), 'Herukābhyudayapañjikā Katipayākṣarā' [title as printed not verified], Dhīḥ: Journal of Rare Buddhist Texts 37 (Sarnath: CIHTS, 2004), pp. 149–170. — Editio princeps from Kaiser Library MS 229. Sanderson's bibliography (OCR) shows 'Dhīh 27', which conflicts with the Dharmamitra header and Isaacson's 'Dhīḥ 37 (2004)'; 37 is adopted.

**Translations:**

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The e-text covers the commentary on chapters 1–28 and stops after the first gloss on 29.1 ([536]–[537]), with no colophon. The manuscript (Kaiser Library 229) is complete in 10 folios, with the final colophon on fol. 10v (Sferra 2008). The e-text's last folio marker is [5v] at [502], and Isaacson cites the ch. 28 passage at [533] as 'f. 5v, ed. p. 160' of the Dhīḥ edition (pp. 149–170). The Katipayākṣarā ('of few syllables') is a brief pañjikā by Kumāracandra on the Herukābhyudayatantra, a Cakrasaṃvara-cycle scripture. Its only Sanskrit manuscript is a Vikramaśīla palm-leaf now in the Kaiser Library, Kathmandu. It glosses selected words chapter by chapter, including the yuga/ānanda scheme of ch. 1, the mantroddhāra of ch. 2, and in ch. 28 a ranking of tantra classes ('paripācanaṃ yogatantreṇa, mocanaṃ yogottareṇa') with criticism of kriyātantra practitioners. This e-text reaches the beginning of ch. 29.

The Dohākoṣa of the Buddhist Mahāsiddha Kāṇhapāda (c. 9th–10th century) is a short cycle of 32 rhymed Apabhraṃśa verses (dohā) teaching the Sahajayāna path of non-dual realization and innate bliss (sahaja). It criticizes external scholastic and Vedic rituals while elucidating esoteric internal yogic physiology (including the channels lalanā, rasanā, and avadhūtī). The accompanying Sanskrit commentary, the Mekhalāṭīkā (attributed to Amṛtavajra), provides word-for-word grammatical and doctrinal interpretations supported by citations from Buddhist tantras such as the Hevajratantra and the Caturdevīparipṛcchā.

It outlines the preliminary purification of ordinary conceit, the generation of the protective enclosure, the internal mapping of bodily aggregates and sensory faculties to the thirty-two mandala deities, and the dissolution back into the clear light (prabhāsvara).

The Mahāmāyāsādhana is a short tantric visualization ritual (sādhana) dedicated to the four-faced, four-armed wrathful deity Mahāmāyā and his retinue of four yoginīs (Vajraḍākinī, Ratnaḍākinī, Padmaḍākinī, and Viśvaḍākinī), preserved as sādhana no. 239 in the Sādhanamālā. Composed by the 11th-century scholar Ratnākaraśānti, the work details preliminary purifications, deity generation prompted by Apabhraṃśa vajragīti songs, bindu meditation, mantra recitation, and daily post-meditation conduct.

The Svapnādhyāya is a short versified treatise on dream interpretation (oneiromancy) preserved in an incomplete Sanskrit manuscript in Tibet. Attributed pseudepigraphically in verse 1 to Bṛhaspati, it details the expected timing of dream fruition according to the watch of the night, followed by an enumeration of auspicious and inauspicious signs. The text was carried to Tibet and translated into Tibetan by the late 12th/early 13th-century pandita Vibhūticandra.

The Nāmamantrārthāvalokinī ('Beholding the Meaning of the Name-Mantras') by Vilāsavajra (fl. late 8th century) is one of the earliest and most influential Indian commentaries on the Mañjuśrīnāmasaṃgīti. Structured in fourteen chapters (adhikāras), it interprets the text's verses and epithets in terms of the five gnoses (pañcajñāna), the five Buddha families, and Yoga/Māyājāla tantric frameworks. It is also of exceptional historical value for preserving numerous citations of early Buddhist tantric scriptures (including the Mahāvairocanābhisaṃbodhi, Guhyendutilaka, and proto-Cakrasamvara sources).

- Tibetan translation: Toh 1924 / D 1924, dPal gshin rje'i gshed kyi rgyud kyi dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga (translators: Dīpaṅkaraśrījñāna and Rgya brtson 'grus seng ge). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete ritual text spanning 23 topical sections from bhūmiparigraha through the higher initiations and concluding verses (segments 0–587).

**Also known as:** Yamārimaṇḍalopāyikā, Śrīyamamārimaṇḍalavidhi, Kṛṣṇayamārimaṇḍalavidhi

**Attribution:** Attributed to Ācārya Śrīdhara in the colophon (segment 586). Corresponds to Tibetan Tanjur Toh 1924 / D 1924 (dPal gshin rje'i gshed kyi rgyud kyi dkyil 'khor gyi cho ga).

The Yamāritantramaṇḍalopāyikā is a Buddhist tantric ritual manual (maṇḍalavidhi) by Ācārya Śrīdhara detailing the ritual performance of the Kṛṣṇayamāri maṇḍala. It guides the master through site selection (bhūmiparigraha), earth pacification, drawing the colored powder mandala (rajaḥpāta), jar consecrations, fire offerings (homa), entrance into the mandala, and the full sequence of empowerments (abhiṣeka) through the prajñājñānābhiṣeka.

**Attribution:** The editio princeps and the concluding colophon (line 585) attribute the text to Mahācārya Śubhākaragupta. However, Alexis Sanderson (2009: 174, n. 423) notes that this attribution in the sole edition is erroneous against manuscript evidence, pointing instead to Śākyarakṣita as the author.

The Abhisamayamañjarī is an extensive Anuttarayogatantra ritual manual (sādhana) dedicated to the visualization and realization of Vajrayoginī / Vajravārāhī within the Cakrasaṃvara cycle. It outlines purification procedures, mantra recitations, bali offerings, the generation of the maṇḍala with accompanying retinue deities, and internal yogic meditations. Produced in late North Indian Buddhist circles (ca. 11th–12th century), it represents an important source for the development of late medieval Vajrayoginī practice.

Byang chub rtse mo and Skyob pa dpal bzang po). No printed edition of the Sanskrit text is known.

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Sanskrit only for the opening of the work: segments 2–82 (benediction, preliminaries, worship, refuge/bodhicitta, up to the abhiṣeka of the self-generated deity), transcribed from the Nor codex (Göttingen Xc 14/39) with folio markers [84r], [85v]. The manuscript text breaks off there; segments 83–357 (ca. 89% of the e-text) are the Tibetan translation from the Derge Tanjur (Tōh. 1277, vol. ta), from ca. fol. 109b7 to the colophon at 130a6, with Derge folio-line numbers embedded. The full Tibetan text runs fols. 105a6–130a6, so the Sanskrit covers roughly the first sixth of the work.

**Also known as:** Śrīhevajrābhisamayatilaka, Dpal kye rdo rje'i mngon par rtogs pa'i thig le

**Attribution:** Attributed in the Tibetan tradition (Tôhoku 1277) to Mahāsthavira Śākyarakṣita (Tib. Shākya srung ba; historically sometimes reconstructed as *Śākyapāla or *Buddharakṣita).

The Hevajrābhisamayatilaka is an extensive sādhana/abhisamaya manual of the Hevajra cycle by Śākyarakṣita, focused on Hevajra in the form Trailokyākṣepavīra. The Sanskrit part of the e-text covers the opening: preliminary protection, outer/secret/reality worship with Gaurī and the other yoginīs, the sevenfold supreme worship, refuge, bodhicitta and the brahmavihāras, and the consecration of the visualised deity. The remainder, transmitted only in Tibetan, treats armouring, offerings and bali rites, rosaries and mantra recitation, and the samayas.

A Tantric Buddhist ritual meditation manual (sādhana) dedicated to the Heruka Cakrasaṃvara maṇḍala, composed by a direct disciple of Ratnākaraśānti (most likely Śūnyasamādhivajra / Divākaracandra). The text exhibits substantial textual parallels with the Bhramahara and the Bhugmalokeśvarasādhana, and utilizes the Jñānodayatantra for its completion stage.

The Pañcasthānasūtra is a canonical Buddhist discourse prescribing five facts that householders and monastics alike should frequently contemplate (abhīkṣṇaṃ pratyavekṣitavyam): vulnerability to disease (vyādhidharmatā), aging (jarādharmatā), death (maraṇadharmatā), separation from loved ones (viprayoga), and ownership of one's own actions (karmasvakatā). Contemplation of these realities dismantles pride in health, youth, and life, and motivates cultivation of the Noble Eightfold Path to eliminate the fetters (saṃyojana).

- Matsuda 2020 (IBK 69.1) identifies twelve stanzas on the Tathāgata's ten titles in the 37th tridaṇḍa (Dhvajāgrasūtra) quoted in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa — the e-text consists of exactly twelve such stanzas.

## Contents

**Coverage:** excerpt — Twelve stanzas (bhagavat, two on tathāgata, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha, vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, sugata, lokavid, anuttara, naradamyasārathi, śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, buddha) forming section 37.3 as edited by Matsuda; the introductory verses and the Dhvajāgrasūtra of tridaṇḍa 37 are not included. A few akṣaras illegible (x).

**Also known as:** Sūtrālaṃkāra stanzas on the ten epithets (Matsuda's attribution)

**Attribution:** The Tridaṇḍamālā (single palm-leaf manuscript formerly at sPos khang monastery, Tibet, c. 11th c., known from Tucci's photographs) is ascribed in its colophon to Aśvaghoṣa. It is a Sarvāstivāda liturgical compilation of forty 'tridaṇḍas', each consisting of introductory verses (x.1), an Āgama sūtra (x.2) and concluding verses (x.3). Johnston (1939) doubted that this Aśvaghoṣa is the poet; K. Matsuda has shown that many of its verses come from Aśvaghoṣa's Buddhacarita and (he argues) his lost Sūtrālaṃkāra. Author kept as Aśvaghoṣa for all Tridaṇḍamālā entries (colophon attribution). Matsuda (2020) shows that these twelve stanzas on the ten epithets are quoted unchanged in Kumārajīva's *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa (Da zhidu lun) and, one of them, in Subhūticandra's Kavikāmadhenu, and attributes them to Aśvaghoṣa's lost Sūtrālaṃkāra (not Kumāralāta's Kalpanāmaṇḍitikā, T 201).

Twelve stanzas from the concluding section of the thirty-seventh tridaṇḍa of the Tridaṇḍamālā giving etymological explanations of the ten standard epithets of the Buddha (bhagavat, tathāgata, arhat, samyaksaṃbuddha, vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, sugata, lokavid, anuttara puruṣadamyasārathi, śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, buddha). The same stanzas are quoted in Kumārajīva's Chinese *Mahāprajñāpāramitopadeśa, and Matsuda attributes them to Aśvaghoṣa's lost Sūtrālaṃkāra.

The Chandoratnākara is an 11th-century Buddhist treatise on Sanskrit metrics (chandaḥśāstra) by the Vikramaśīla polymath Ratnākaraśānti, accompanied by his own prose autocommentary (Svopajñavṛtti). Spanning six chapters, it systematically describes mātrā- and akṣara-based meters, claiming eight structural improvements over earlier treatises by Piṅgala and Jayadeva. Preserved in rare Nepalese and Bihar manuscripts as well as in Tibetan translation (Tengyur, D 4459), it is one of the very few surviving Buddhist works on classical Sanskrit prosody.

The Amanasikārādhāra ('Justification of Non-Mental Engagement') is a short doctrinal treatise by Advayavajra (Maitrīpa, 11th century) vindicating the term and practice of amanasikāra ('absence of conceptual mental engagement') against critics. Defending the formation grammatically against the charge of being ungrammatical (apaśabda) through Pāṇini 6.3.14 (aluksamāsa) and semantic analysis of negation (prasajyapratiṣedha vs paryudāsa), Advayavajra demonstrates that the term does not entail nihilism (ucchedavāda). Drawing citations from canonical Mahāyāna sūtras/dhāraṇīs (Avikalpapraveśadhāraṇī, Sarvabuddhaviṣayāvatārajñānālokālaṃkāra) and tantras (Hevajratantra, Nāmasaṅgīti), he establishes that amanasikāra culminates in the non-dual realization of inseparable emptiness and compassion (śūnyatākaruṇābhinna-yuganaddha).

The Yogāmbarasādhanopāyikā is an 11th-century Vajrayāna ritual manual composed by Amitavajra in Bengal, belonging to the Catuṣpīṭhatantra cycle and focusing on the worship of the deity Yogāmbara. It details the practitioner's preparatory rites, hand gestures (mudrā), body purification, seed syllables (bīja), visualization sequences, and maṇḍala offering according to Catuṣpīṭha conventions. The primary palm-leaf manuscript transcribed here preserves a historical colophon dating the copy to regnal year 13 of the Pāla monarch Vigrahapāla III.

Composed by the Vikramaśīla master Durjayacandra (c. 11th century), the ritual outlines the generation-stage visualization, protective perimeter, iconography, mantra recitation, and the correlation of the seven mandala deities with the seven factors of awakening (sambodhyaṅga) as well as the six bone ornaments with the six perfections (pāramitā).

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- Manuscript folio numbers in the text ([3], [6], [9], [10], 'fol. 11 ends with', '16 starts with'); Sanskrit lines marked ':'; Tibetan in Wylie with Derge folio markers (@225B … @237B).

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — Sanskrit (c. 35,000 characters): introduction (lacunae marked [...]), sādhana, mantroddhāra, japa, bali, tilaka, udvartana and añjana (each with its colophon), and the beginning of the caryā section, where the testimony of MS A (B 31/8; 'almost complete' per Szántó) ends ('[ends]'). Szántó thinks little is lacking. Then follows a one-folio fragment (fol. 16) on mahāmudrā that may belong to a different work. The Tibetan translation (Derge Tanjur, rgyud, za 225r6–237r1/b) is given in parallel and to the end, including the colophon ('dpal rdo rje rnal 'byor ma'i 'grel pa tses bcu'i mchod pa'i rtog pa') and an appended Tibetan bali-mantra and hṛdaya section by Klu'i sbyin pa. All of this Tibetan portion is Tibetan-only.

**Also known as:** Yogānusāriṇī nāma vajrayoginīṭīkā, Rnal 'byor gyi rjes su 'brang ba zhes bya ba rdo rje rnal 'byor ma'i 'grel ba, Dpal rdo rje rnal 'byor ma'i 'grel pa tses bcu'i mchod pa'i rtog pa

In the Sanskrit manuscripts the title and author are lost. The e-text's header maps 'Dārikapāda –> *Kuṭali, disciple of Saraha': the author says he wrote a Svādhiṣṭhānavyākhyā on his master's Svādhiṣṭhāna, and that commentary probably survives in China under the name *Kuṭali. A line quoted from the master matches Tōh. 2275, ascribed to Saraha. The catalog keeps the traditional attribution; *Kuṭali is the likelier author of the Sanskrit text.

A Sanskrit commentary-cum-manual on the sādhana of Vajrayoginī/Vajravārāhī. It opens with an ornate introduction that mentions King Indrabhūti's Ḍākinīrahasya and the author's master's Svādhiṣṭhāna, and then treats the sādhana, extraction of the mantra, recitation, bali, tilaka, unguent (udvartana), collyrium (añjana) and finally caryā. The Sanskrit survives in incomplete Nepalese manuscripts and is given here in parallel with the Tibetan translation of Tōh. 1565 (ascribed to Dārikapāda), followed by a stray Sanskrit fragment on mahāmudrā.

Composed in 14th-century Nepal by Jagadānandajīvabhadra based on the Ātmapīṭha section of the Catuṣpīṭha literature, it became the foundation for surviving Newar Buddhist liturgical traditions of Yogāmbara and corresponds closely to the ritual portion of the Nepalese Yogāmbaramahātantra.

**Also known as:** Catuṣpīṭhāloka, Gūḍhagranthivibodhanī, Gdan bzhi pa'i dka' 'grel

The Catuṣpīṭhapañjikā (also titled Catuṣpīṭhāloka or Gūḍhagranthivibodhanī) by Kalyāṇavarman is the oldest known Sanskrit commentary on the Catuṣpīṭhatantra, an early esoteric Buddhist yoginītantra. Kalyāṇavarman comments on the first three sections (pīṭhas)—Ātmapīṭha, Parapīṭha, and Yogapīṭha—elucidating complex esoteric terminology, subtle physiology (nāḍīs and prāṇas), ritual procedures, and maṇḍala practices. The Sanskrit original survives in a single dated palm-leaf codex from Nepal copied in 1012 CE (NS 132).

# Daśatattvasaṃgraha (excerpts: rakṣācakra, cakra and seka sections)

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished partial transcription from the manuscript IASWR MBB-II-208 (Institute for Advanced Studies of World Religions microfiche), which lacks folio 2. No printed edition is known.

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- E-text header [0]–[2]: 'Kṣitigarbha's Daśatattvasaṃgraha apud Jnānapāda / [in the retinue of Vanaratna, died at mChims phu] / IASWR MBB-II-208 (missing folia: 2 )'.
- Folio markers [1r], [1v], [3r], [6v], [7v], '[on 22r]', [23v], '[on 28r]', '[ends on 41r]' show a selective transcription of the manuscript.
- Editorial brackets and conjectures ('[rbha]', '<dma>', '(?)') indicate a working transcription, not a printed edition.

## Contents

**Coverage:** excerpt — The manuscript runs to fol. 41r, and folio 2 is missing in the manuscript itself (header [2]; lacuna at [13]). The transcription covers fols. 1v–ca. 9 (introductory verses, rakṣācakra, maṇḍala/cakra visualisation up to [177]). It then jumps ('[on 22r]', [178]) to the seka section (guhyābhiṣeka, prajñājñānābhiṣeka, vidyāvrata, [179]–[255]) and stops at '[on 28r]' ([256]). Only the final colophon of fol. 41r follows ([257]–[260]). Of the ten tattvas listed in v. 2, the rest of the cakra section, japa, haṭha, bali, the two pratyaṅgirās and the saṃpuṭodghāṭa are not transcribed, except for the closing line 'iti saṃpuṭodghāṭavidhiḥ'.

**Attribution:** The colophon reads 'kṛtir iyaṃ daśatattvasaṃgrahaḥ paṇḍitakṣitiga[rbha]sya' ([260]). The Dharmamitra header ([1]) adds that Kṣitigarbha was in the retinue of Vanaratna (1384–1468) and died at mChims phu. The work follows the Jñānapāda tradition of the Guhyasamāja ('jñānapādakrameṇa', [5]).

The Daśatattvasaṃgraha of the paṇḍita Kṣitigarbha (15th c., in the circle of Vanaratna) is a manual in the Jñānapāda tradition of the Guhyasamāja. It sets out ten ritual 'principles' (tattva): protective circle, maṇḍala (cakra), recitation, the two higher consecrations, haṭha, bali, the two pratyaṅgirā rites and the opening of the box (puṭodghāṭa). The e-text gives the opening verses, the rakṣācakra and much of the maṇḍala visualisation of Mañjuvajra/Samantabhadra, and the guhya and prajñājñāna consecrations with the vidyāvrata. The remainder is untranscribed apart from the final colophon.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete commentary on the 164 verses of Buddhajñānapāda's Caturaṅgasādhana (fol. 1a to fol. 45b3), concluding with the author's closing verse, colophon, and scribal Pratītyasamutpāda verse.

**Also known as:** Caturaṅgasādhanaṭīkā Sāramañjarī, Caturaṅgasādhanavyākhyā Sāramañjarī

**Attribution:** Samantabhadra was a prominent master in the Jñānapāda (Jñānapādamata) tradition of the Guhyasamāja tantra, flourishing around the late 8th to 10th century CE. He is distinct from the Digambara Jain philosopher of the same name and the Mahāyāna bodhisattva.

The Sāramañjarī is an extensive Sanskrit commentary by the master Samantabhadra on Buddhajñānapāda's Caturaṅgasādhana (also known as the Samantabhadrasādhana), a fundamental manual of the Guhyasamāja creation stage (utpattikrama). It provides detailed exegesis of the four limbs of yoga (caturaṅga) according to the Jñānapādamata tradition, elucidating visualization, deity generation, mantra recitation, and the philosophical defense of tantric deity yoga.

## Edition and provenance

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished transcription of the two folia in NAK 3-359 vi. bauddhadarśana (NGMPP A 38/8), read from b/w photographs of the microfilm. The text is described and discussed, Selected Chapters from the Catuṣpīṭhatantra, DPhil thesis, University of Oxford, 2012, vol. 1, §3.4.1 'The Catuṣpīṭhasādhanasaṃkṣepa (anonymous)'.
