**Evidence:**
- Header segs. 0–21: 'NGMPP A 38/8 = the notorious NAK 3/359 … 9 folia as follows …', which lists the SRS, balihomayāga and CaPīNibandha folia.
- Szántó 2012 §3.4.1: 'Source: Fragment of two folia out of nine in NAK 3-359 … I have read this ms. from b/w photographs of the microfilm'. He quotes the same colophons as segs. 98–101.

**Other editions:**
- Péter-Dániel Szántó, Selected Chapters from the Catuṣpīṭhatantra, DPhil thesis, University of Oxford, 2012, vol. 1, §3.4.1. — Description, partial quotation and discussion of the fragment and its colophon. It is not a full edition.

**Coverage:** fragment — Two folia, out of nine in the bundle NAK 3-359 (NGMPP A 38/8). The text begins acephalous with the samayamudrās of the last two goddesses (reworking Catuṣpīṭha 2.3.76–77) and runs to the end of the work: bali, homa into fire, homa into water, rules for śāntika/pauṣṭika/vaśya/abhicāra, then the colophons. The earlier sādhana is lost. Segs. 0–21 are Dharmamitra's description of the bundle, not text.

**Also known as:** Catuṣpīṭhabalihomayāga, Balihomayāgavidhi

**Attribution:** Anonymous satellite text of the Catuṣpīṭhatantra. Its closing colophon reads 'saṃkṣepato balihomayāgavidhayaḥ śrīcatuṣpīṭhatantrāmnāyena likhitā iti || catuṣpīṭhasādhanaṃ saṃ<kṣe> + + + samāpteti'. The scribal colophon names Śākyabhikṣu Kumāracandra at the Dharmacakramahāvihāra founded by Guṇakāmadeva (Taran Bahal, Kathmandu) under King Bhāskaradeva in [Nepal] Saṃvat 165 = 1045 CE. The text shows no awareness of Yogāmbara.

A two-folio fragment of an anonymous ritual manual of the Catuṣpīṭhatantra cycle, probably a sādhana followed by an appendix on bali, homa and worship. The surviving part covers the last goddesses' mudrās, the vajra-and-bell songs in Apabhraṃśa and the hymn from Catuṣpīṭha 2.3, the bali with meat and fish, a fire-homa with the Jñānaḍākinī maṇḍala, a water-homa, and the adaptation of the rites to the four karmans. Its scribal colophon dates the manuscript to 1045 CE, written by Kumāracandra, who also copied ms. H of the Sampuṭa.

He notes that on fol. 265 it 'prefixes the song (which is copied here in a rather garbled manner) with the note: tatrāyaṃ praveśamantraḥ', which matches segs. 33–38. On fol. 266 'has this gesture … in conjunction with the mantras HA, HO, HRĪ' corresponds to segs. 54–55 (haṃkāreṇa … hokāreṇa … hrīḥkāreṇa), just after the 266r marker. At 269 he cites a rule against eating to satiety.
- The text differs from the Hamburg/Intellexus e-text of the Gaṇacakravidhi attributed to Ratnākaraśānti.

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete: from the maṅgala ('oṃ namaḥ śrīnairātmikāyai') to the final colophon 'balicakravidhiḥ samāptaḥ' (seg. 200). The work occupies about fols. 265–269 of the codex.

An anonymous manual for the gaṇacakra feast and bali offering in the Hevajra tradition. It covers the proper times and places, the qualities of the presiding master, the participants and the karmavajrin, the seating rows, the entrance song in Apabhraṃśa, and the purification of the sacramental substances with HA, HO and HRĪḤ. It ends with verses on enjoying the sacraments as purified passions and on the bliss of the yoginīcakra. Szántó cites it as a parallel for Catuṣpīṭha gaṇacakra procedure.

**Attribution:** Attributed in the scribal colophon to Āryadevapāda. In Buddhist studies, this author is distinguished from the early Madhyamaka philosopher and identified as Tantric Āryadeva (ca. 9th–10th century), author of the Caryāmelāpakapradīpa.

The Pratipattisāraśataka ('Essence of Practice in One Hundred Verses') is a late Vajrayāna treatise attributed to Tantric Āryadeva. The text integrates Madhyamaka emptiness dialectic with anuttarayogatantra internal yoga, dealing with the non-duality of prajñā and upāya, the esoteric function of the avadhūtī channel, the four cakras, innate great bliss (mahāsukha), and the ultimate interpretation of the pāramitās. In Sanskrit it survives in a unique fragmentary Nepalese palm-leaf manuscript containing only the second half.

# Yogāmbarīsādhanaratnamālā (incomplete; with fragments of other works)

**DharmaNexus ID:** `SA_T02_anon_Yogāmbarīsādhanaratnamālā`

**Collection / category:** Buddhist_Non-Scriptures / T02

**Source:** OCR / Dharmamitra

## Edition and provenance

_LLM-generated summary, please double-check before citing._

**Edition used (determined):** Unpublished transcription of Tokyo University Library MS Matsunami 312 (old no. 230), a composite palm-leaf codex catalogued as 'Yogāmbarīsādhanaratnamālā'. The manuscript is described and partly, Selected Chapters from the Catuṣpīṭhatantra, DPhil thesis, University of Oxford, 2012, vol. 1, §3.4.15 'The Ratnamālā (anonymous) with fragments'.

**E-text:** Dharmamitra (OCR)

**Evidence:**
- Header segs. 1–2: 'Matsunami 312 (old no. 230) [I.] / this is actually a composite codex'.
- Szántó 2012 §3.4.15: 'The sole source for this text is an incomplete Sanskrit ms. in the composite codex catalogued under the title Yogāmbarīsādhanaratnamālā'. His folio list (fol. 2 starts '-malam ākalayya', fol. 8 'pratyālīḍhāsana', fol. 12 '-cūṣiṇīṣu', fol. 15 'vajrāñjalim', fol. 19 '-nna san') matches the e-text's folio markers at segs. 18, 228, 712, 768 and 857.
- He quotes the closing verses as in segs. 882–892 (e-text 'yatnataḥ' = his ms. reading; he conjectures 'yena').

## Contents

**Coverage:** partial — The Ratnamālā occupies segs. 3–266 (fols. 1–6 and 8; seg. 226 is an empty fol. 7 slot), segs. 663–766 (fols. 11–12) and segs. 768–893 (fols. 15–19, ending with the closing verses, which break off at 'yogāmbarīsā'). Fols. 7, 9–10 and 13–14 are lost. Segs. 268–557 (another series of folia 6, 7, 9, 10, 13, 14 on the Yogāmbara maṇḍala), 558–662 (a series of folia 8–13) and 895–948 (fols. 2–3, ending '[end of 3]') are fragments of other works from the composite codex. The '=====' separator lines are segments too.

**Also known as:** Ratnamālā

**Attribution:** Anonymous. In the opening verses the author honours Nāgārjuna and, following Szántó's emendation of the manuscript's 'āryavarma+' to Āryadeva, Āryadeva. In the closing verses he names his guru Kalyāṇavarman ('VarmāntaKalyāṇapadābhidhānam'), 'ornament of Nepal' and author of a Catuṣpīṭhasamādhiratna, which this work elaborates. Szántó suggests that this Kalyāṇavarman is probably the Catuṣpīṭha commentator (Pañjikā).

The Yogāmbarīsādhanaratnamālā ('Ratnamālā') is an anonymous Catuṣpīṭha-cycle manual for the worship of Yogāmbarī, written by a disciple of the Nepalese master Kalyāṇavarman. It is very rich in ritual detail. The surviving folia cover the purification of hand and tongue, arghya and pūjā with mudrās and mantras, the ādiyoga and later yogas, the twelve special places of practice (cremation ground, mountain, cave, etc.), the four balis (for deities, nāgas, yakṣas and bhūtas), the gaṇacakra, rosary and japa rules, the ucchiṣṭabali, and the dismissal and closing rites. It survives only in the Tokyo manuscript, which has no Tibetan translation.

It details mantric phonology, ritual bījas, esoteric application of mantras (mantraprayoga), mandala rites, and specialized internal yogas such as the prajñāvajrāvatāraṇayoga.

**Evidence:**
- Header explicitly states: 'Amṛtaprabhāsādhanopāyikā of Ḍombīheruka / = Matsunaga 307 IV. / = Sādhanamālā 228. / = readings reported by editor'.
- Inline manuscript folio markers: [ 20r], [ 21r], [ 21v].
- Inline printed page markers from Bhattacharyya (1928): p. 443., p. 444., p. 445., p. 446.

**Other editions:**
- Benoytosh Bhattacharyya (ed.), Sādhanamālā, Vol. II, Baroda: Oriental Institute, 1928 (Gaekwad's Oriental Series, No. 41), no. 228, pp. 443–447. — First critical/printed edition based on Cambridge and Asiatic Society manuscripts.

**Translations:**
- Tibetan canonical translation: bDud rtsi'i 'od ces bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs, translated by Prajñāśrīgupta and Chos kyi brtson 'grus (Toh 1313 / D 1313; Otani 2399 / P 2399). (Tibetan)

## Contents

**Coverage:** complete — Complete text of the sādhanopāyikā in 149 lines/units, concluding with the colophon '|| amṛtaprabhā nāma sādhanopāyikā samāptā ||'.

**Also known as:** Amṛtaprabhā nāma sādhanopāyikā, Amṛtaprabhā, Nairātmyāsādhana (Sādhanamālā 228)

**Attribution:** Explicitly attributed in verse 1 (ḍombīherukapādair devīcakrasya bhāvanā kathitā) and in the final verses (vv. 144–147) mentioning the author riding a tiger and ornamented with serpents. Corresponds to Tengyur Toh 1313 / D 1313 (bDud rtsi'i 'od ces bya ba'i sgrub pa'i thabs).

The Amṛtaprabhāsādhanopāyikā is an Indian Vajrayāna ritual text detailing the visualization and realization of the fifteen-deity maṇḍala of Nairātmyā, based on the Hevajratantra. Attributed to the mahāsiddha Ḍombīheruka, it guides the practitioner through the protective circle, bījamantras of the yoginīs, generation stage (utpattikrama), and completion stage (utpannakrama).
